## A029: Hybrid fixation vs bilateral VBT in AIS: striking the balance between durability and motion

Altug Yucekul

1

, Feyzi Kilic

2

, Fedde Weenink

3

, Gokhan Ergene

4

, Sahin Senay

5

, Elif Gizem Carus

2

, Tais Zulemyan

2

, Caglar Yilgor

6

, Ahmet Alanay

1

1
Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, istanbul, Turkey,

2
Comprehensive Spine Center, Acibadem Maslak Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey,

3
Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam Faculty of Medicine, Amsterdam, The Netherlands,

4
Department of Operating Room Services, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University Vocational School of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey,

5
Department of Cardiovascular Surgery, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey,

6

Koc University Hospital Spine Center, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Hybrid fixation-thoracic posterior instrumentation and fusion combined with lumbar vertebral body tethering (VBT)-and bilateral VBT (thoracic and lumbar) are increasingly used motion-preserving strategies for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Hybrid constructs offer durable correction in the thoracic spine while aiming to preserve lumbar mobility, whereas bilateral VBT provides flexibility across both regions but may carry higher tether-related complication risks. To date, no direct comparison between these two approaches has been reported. This study presents the first matched, follow-up-equalized analysis comparing hybrid fixation and bilateral VBT, evaluating radiographic, patient-reported, pulmonary, complication, and implant-survival outcomes. Materials and Methods: Prospectively collected data were retrospectively analyzed. A 1:1 matched cohort (15 pairs) was created using preoperative thoracolumbar/lumbar Cobb (± 5°) and Sanders stage (± 1), incorporating CVM (± 2). For each pair, analyses were capped at the shorter follow-up (pairwise cap: median 25.3 months, IQR 23.8-28.1). Upper thoracic (UT), main thoracic (MT), and thoracolumbar/lumbar (TLL) Cobb angles were compared at preoperative, first-erect, and latest follow-up ≤ cap. SRS-22 domain changes (pre to latest ≤ cap) and pulmonary function (percent-predicted FVC, FEV1) were compared as Hybrid change - Bilateral change (ΔΔ). Complications were assessed with McNemar’s test; implant survival (time to first tether break) was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier with log-rank. Results: Fifty AIS patients (25 Hybrid, 25 Bilateral) were included. Mean age was 13.3 ± 1.3 years (Hybrid) and 12.9 ± 2.0 years (Bilateral). Lenke types in the Hybrid group were Type 1 (6), Type 2 (3), Type 4 (4), and Type 5 (2) with lumbar modifiers B (35.7%) and C (64.3%). The Bilateral group included Type 1 (5), Type 2 (4), Type 3 (3), and Type 6 (3) with lumbar modifiers B (13.3%) and C (86.7%). Preoperative UT, MT, and TLL Cobb angles were 36.8° ± 10.5°, 62.1° ± 17.5°, and 50.4° ± 8.5° (Hybrid) vs 29.9° ± 9.6°, 59.7° ± 10.2°, and 49.9° ± 8.6° (Bilateral). Group comparability (Hybrid - Bilateral) was UT +7.2° (p = 0.152), MT +2.2° (p = 0.678), and TLL +1.1° (p = 0.080). At first-erect, differences favored Hybrid: UT -12.5° (p = 0.0017), MT -20.0° (p < 0.001), and TLL -5.5° (p = 0.049). At latest ≤ cap, differences persisted: UT -10.1° (p = 0.020), MT -17.1° (p < 0.001), and TLL -9.7° (p = 0.014). SRS-22 ΔΔ were: Function -0.47 (p = 0.014), Pain -0.17 (p = 0.539), Self-image +0.39 (p = 0.298), and Mental Health -0.51 (p = 0.113). Pulmonary function changes were not significant between groups: ΔΔ FVC -4.0 (p = 0.561), ΔΔ FEV1 -1.5 (p = 0.802). Complications were fewer in Hybrid (tether breaks 2) vs Bilateral (9) (p = 0.023). Kaplan-Meier survival free of tether break was higher in Hybrid: 12 months 1.00 vs 0.857; 24 months 0.825 vs 0.455 (log-rank p = 0.015). Conclusion: In this first matched, follow-up-equalized comparison of motion-preserving strategies in AIS, Hybrid fixation achieved lower UT/MT/TLL Cobb angles both immediately and at mid-term, and demonstrated higher implant survival with fewer tether failures. Bilateral VBT showed greater improvement in SRS-Function, while other SRS domains and pulmonary outcomes were comparable. These findings suggest Hybrid fixation may offer greater durability, whereas Bilateral VBT may confer functional advantages. Larger, longer-term studies are needed to validate these results.

## A030: Comparison of magec rods and APC technique in the management of early onset scoliosis

Uzair Rashid

1

1

Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan

Background: Early Onset Scoliosis (EOS) provides special challenges because continuous spinal deformity correction and preservation of growth must be in balance. The two least invasive approaches that are currently applied to EOS are magnetically controlled growing rods (Magec) and the Active Apex Correction (APC) technique. This study compares their efficacy, safety, and clinical outcomes. Materials and Methods: 60 pediatric patients (4-10 years old) with EOS, treated in 2021-2024, were put under analysis. Magec rod implantation was done on 30 patients, and the APC technique was also done on 30 patients. Measures of outcomes were curve correction (Cobb angle), complication rates, frequency of reoperation, and quality of life (QoL). Preoperative radiographic measurements were recorded at 6, 12, and 24 months. T-tests and Chi-squares were used to do a statistical analysis. Conclusion: Magec rods and the APC technique are effective in the management of EOS with comparable results in terms of deformity correction and growth preservation. Magec rods minimize reoperational rates but have more risks of implant complications, whereas APC demonstrates superior results in QoL. Decisions on treatment must be customized based on the nature of the curves and on patient/family preferences. The Magec rod is expensive, while APC is an economic technique. We need long-term data and results to determine which technique is more effective.

## A031: Preoperative pelvic incidence-thoracic kyphosis mismatch predicts correction of pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch in Scheuermann’s kyphosis

Kylie Callan

1

, Joshua Klatt

1

, Joshua Speirs

1

, Laura Bellaire

1

, Joel Turtle

1

1

University of Utah Hospital, Salt Lake City, United States

Introduction: Scheuermann’s kyphosis is the most common structural kyphosis in adolescents. Treatment ranges from observation to surgical intervention, with recommendations largely based on curve magnitude, and surgery typically indicated for kyphosis greater than 75 degrees. This approach does not account for overall spinal and pelvic geometry. The objective of this study was to determine whether pelvic incidence-thoracic kyphosis (PI-TK) mismatch is a better predictor of surgical outcomes than thoracic kyphosis alone, with the hypothesis that PI-TK mismatch more accurately reflects functional alignment. Material and Methods: Patients with Scheuermann’s kyphosis who underwent surgery were identified using CPT and ICD codes. Preoperative, one-month postoperative, and six-month postoperative radiographs were reviewed when available. Measurements included maximum kyphosis, maximum lordosis, T1-T12 kyphosis, pelvic incidence, and sagittal balance. Demographic information was collected from chart review. Correlations between preoperative PI-TK mismatch and preoperative PI-lumbar lordosis (LL) mismatch were assessed. Paired t-tests compared preoperative and postoperative PI-LL mismatch. Additional analyses examined the relationship of preoperative PI-TK mismatch and preoperative maximum kyphosis with PI-LL correction. Results: Fifty-three patients had complete radiographs at six months postoperatively and were included in the analysis. Twenty-four (45.3%) were female. The mean age at surgery was 15.9 ± 1.7 years. The mean BMI was 24.6 ± 7.1. Preoperative PI-TK and PI-LL mismatch demonstrated a strong correlation (r = 0.67, p < 0.00001). PI-LL mismatch significantly improved from preoperative (-36.4°) to postoperative (-16.4°) at six months (p < 0.0001). Preoperative PI-TK mismatch correlated modestly with PI-LL correction (r = -0.28, p = 0.04), while preoperative maximum kyphosis was not significantly associated with PI-LL correction (r = 0.23, p = 0.11). Conclusion: This study demonstrates that PI-TK mismatch is more closely related to postoperative sagittal alignment correction than maximum kyphosis, supporting the hypothesis that mismatch is a more clinically relevant marker of pathology than curve magnitude alone. The strong association between PI-TK and PI-LL mismatch further suggests that PI-TK may serve as a surrogate marker of disability, similar to the established role of PI-LL in the adult spine. By highlighting the limitations of using kyphotic angle alone, these findings underscore the importance of incorporating spinopelvic parameters into surgical decision-making for Scheuermann’s kyphosis. PI-TK mismatch may improve patient selection, enhance preoperative counseling, and provide a more accurate framework for predicting outcomes. Future prospective studies including patient-reported measures are warranted to validate PI-TK mismatch as a marker of functional disability and surgical indication in this population.

## A032: Acute abdominal compartment syndrome following scoliosis surgery in a patient with Rett syndrome

Mesut Kılıç

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Private Kolmed Hospital, Amasya, Turkey

Introduction: Rett syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder often associated with scoliosis. Surgical correction carries high complication risks.This paper aims to present a case of acute abdominal compartment syndrome (AACS) as a rare, life-threatening complication of scoliosis surgery in Rett syndrome. Material and Methods: A 17-year-old female with Rett syndrome underwent T3-iliac posterior instrumentation and pelvic fixation. Intraoperatively, AACS developed, requiring urgent decompressive laparotomy. Results: After spinal correction, the patient developed hypotension and bradycardia, requiring inotropic support. Conclusion: Scoliosis surgery in Rett syndrome has high complication rates. To our knowledge, this is the first report of AACS in such a patient. If untreated, mortality approaches 100%.

## A033: The predictive value of proximal femur maturity index (PFMI)-based nomogram for distal adding-on following posterior hemivertebra resection and fusion

Youwei Ai

1

, Yongdi Wang

1

, Hong Ding

1

, Ce Zhu

1

, Zhuojie Xiao

1

, Limin Liu

1

1

West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China

Introduction: Distal adding-on is a common complication in patients with congenital scoliosis due to hemivertebra (HV) after posterior hemivertebra resection and fusion, associated with skeletal maturity status. However, the Sanders staging (SS) and the distal radius and ulna (DRU) classification require a hand-wrist radiograph, and the accuracy of the Risser sign in patients with scoliosis is a matter of concern. Recently, a novel proximal femur maturity index (PFMI) has been proposed as a reliable tool to determine skeletal growth. Material and Methods: Patients with congenital scoliosis due to HV who underwent posterior hemivertebra resection and fusion at our department between 2012 and 2021 were selected, and their demographic data and radiographic assessments were collected. We carried out a ROC curve analysis to assess the efficacy of the PFMI in independently predicting distal adding-on. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) method was performed to select the risk factors and then establish a nomogram to predict the rate of distal adding-on. The concordance index (C-index), the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the calibration curve were used to evaluate the performance of the nomogram. Results: 108 patients met the inclusion criteria. 22 patients (20.3%) developed distal adding-on. The AUC of the PFMI is 0.756 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.658-0.853) and the optimal threshold is 2.5 (sensitivity: 72.7%, specificity: 74.4%). After LASSO regression analysis, seven potential risk factors were selected, including BMI, Risser sign, location of HV, preoperative Cobb angle, preoperative TK, preoperative SVA, and the PFMI. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of the nomogram was 0.919, the C-index was 0.919, and the calibration curve of the nomogram demonstrated good results in predicting adding-on. Conclusion: A patient with a PFMI grade of 2 or less has a high risk of developing distal adding-on after posterior hemivertebra resection and fusion. This PFMI-based nomogram provides a valuable tool for assessing the incidence of distal adding-on.

## A034: Hip reduction surgery versus scoliosis correction in non-ambulant neuromuscular patients. Which surgery as a first step?

Mostafa Meshneb

1

, Mohammed Patel

1

, Nasir Quraishi

1

1

Queens Medical Centre Nottingham University Hospitals, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: Children and young adults with neuromuscular disorders have a high incidence of both spine and hip deformities, the severity of which is associated with severity of the neurological compromise. There are not widely accepted clinical or radiological guidelines to facilitate decision making on which of these conditions should be primarily addressed. The aim of this study was to evaluate the outcome of either primary scoliosis or hip surgery in children and young adults with neuromuscular disorders and its effect on progression of the other deformity, as well as the need for of a second operation. Material and Methods: A retrospective study was conducted on all children and young adults with neuromuscular related synchronous hip subluxation / dislocation and scoliosis undergoing hip or scoliosis surgeries in our institution between 2012 and 2021, with a minimum follow up of 24 months. Demographic and operative data were collected; hip migration percentage (MP), Cobb angle of the main curve and degree of pelvic obliquity were measured pre- and post-operatively at final follow up. The need for correction of the “other” remaining pathology after the primary operation was analyzed. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 23 with p < 0.05 for significance. Results: 40 neuromuscular patients (25cerebral palsy, 11syndromic, 2SMS and 2DMD) with synchronous hip displacement and scoliosis were included. Twenty patients with an average age of 10.2 years (6-17) had hip correction surgery performed primarily (hip first), with a mean follow up of 54.9 (14-96) months compared to a second group consisting of 20 patients of average age 12.4 years (10-24) who had scoliosis correction first), with a mean follow-up of 40 (13-60) months. In the “hip first” group, pelvic obliquity, hip MI and Cobb angle were 16.8°, 70%, and 49°, respectively. At final follow up, the mean pelvic obliquity and Cobb angles significantly progressed post-operatively to 27.2° (p = 0.003) and 82.2° (p = 0.0016) respectively. 18 patients (90%) required scoliosis correction after the hip surgery. In the “scoliosis first” group, the mean pelvic obliquity, hip MP and Cobb angle were 21.2°, 49 % and 65.5°, respectively. At final follow-up, both pelvic obliquity and the Cobb angle significantly improved to 8.44° (p = 0.003) and 23.4° (p = 0.0013) respectively. In 11/20 (55%) patients, the hip MP had significantly increased following the spinal surgery to 65% (p = 0.0017), but only 5/20 (25%) patients underwent hip surgery after scoliosis correction. Conclusion: In neuromuscular patients presenting with synchronous hip displacement and scoliosis deformity, corrective scoliosis surgery is associated with significant correction of pelvic obliquity and lower rates of secondary hip surgery. On the other hand, hip surgery does not reduce the risk of pelvic obliquity and scoliosis deformity progression.

## A035: Impact of preoperative halo gravity traction on posterior spinal fusion outcomes in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta: the first comparative analysis

Paolo Brigato

1

, Salim Al Rawahi

2

, Yousef Aljamaan

3

, Oded Rabau

4

, Kai Sheng

2

, Neil Saran

2

, Jean Ouellet

2

1
University Hospital Campus Bio-Medico of Rome, Rome, Italy,

2
McGill University, Montreal, Canada,

3
Imam Abdulrahman bin Faisal University, Dammam, Saudi Arabia,

4

Yitzhak Shamir Medical Center, Tel Aviv, Israel

Introduction: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) is a rare connective tissue disorder frequently complicated by severe scoliosis, which is resistant to bracing due to bone fragility and ligamentous laxity. Posterior spinal fusion (PSF) with pedicle screws has been shown to achieve up to 60% of coronal curve correction. Preoperative halo-gravity traction (HGT) may further improve deformity, respiratory function, and nutritional status, though it carries inherent risks. This study assesses whether HGT provides meaningful perioperative and radiographic benefits over PSF alone in this rare and vulnerable patient population. Methods: The study included 36 pediatric OI patients with spinal deformity, treated between January 2002 and Decembre 2020, with a minimum 2-year follow-up. The primary outcome was the coronal correction rate (CR) of scoliosis curves. Secondary outcomes included major postoperative complications (classified according to the Modified Clavien-Dindo-Sink Classification (MCDS), operative time, blood loss, length of hospital stay (LOS) and coronal plane loss of correction at the last FUP. Statistical analysis was performed using Mann-Whitney U test, and Chi-Squared tests, with significance set at 0.05. An a priori power analysis (80% power, medium effect size 0.3, α = 0.05) indicated that a minimum of 10 patients per parameter was required to detect the intended effect. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all comparisons. Results: The patients were divided into a HGT+PSF group (N = 19) and a PSF-only group (N=17), which were comparable preoperatively regarding sex, age, OI type, curve characteristics, and bone mineral density. Postoperative CR for major and minor curves was 60.2 ± 20.6% and 66.5 ± 19.6% in the HGT+PSF group, and 55.1 ± 19.8% and 37.7 ± 16.7% in the PSF group (p = 0.337 and p = 0.003). At last follow-up, CR was 51.1 ± 14.2% and 38.8 ± 25.9% for HGT+PSF, and 44.9 ± 21.6% and 25.2 ± 13.3% for PSF (p = 0.298 and p = 0.238). Mean blood loss was 1235.2 ± 736.8 mL versus 1368.3 ± 976.1 mL (p = 0.972), and total surgical time was 443.1 ± 92.7 min versus 410.1 ± 81.1 min (p = 0.490) for the HGT+PSF and PSF groups, respectively. Mean LOS was 12.6 ± 6 days versus 9.5 ± 2.9 days (p = 0.186). Perioperative complications occurred in 11 patients (57.9%) in the HGT+PSF group and 5 patients (29.4%) in the PSF group (p = 0.367), with major complications (MCDS Grade ≥ III) more frequent in HGT+PSF (4 patients, 36%) than PSF (1 patient, 20%). Conclusions: Preoperative HGT provided modest additional coronal correction but did not reduce perioperative complications, blood loss, operative time, or LOS compared to PSF alone. While it may offer radiographic benefits, its routine use should be carefully considered against potential risks and resource demands in pediatric OI patients. Future prospective, multicenter studies are warranted to better define the role of HGT in this population and optimize surgical planning and outcomes.

Fedde Weenink

1

, Bing Wui Ng

2

, Feyzi Kilic

, Bayron Valenzuela C

5

, Elif Gizem Carus

, Tais Zulemyan

, Nuri Demirci

, Caglar Yilgor

7

, Altug Yucekul

8

, Ahmet Alanay

Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam Faculty of Medicine, Amsterdam, The Netherlands,

Spine Unit, Hospital Pakar Kanak-kanak UKM, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia,

Comprehensive Spine Center, Acibadem Maslak Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey,

Department of Neurosurgery, Hospitla Clínico Universidsd de Chile, Santiago, Chile,

5
Department of Neurological Surgery, University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan, Nigeria,

7
Koc University Hospital Spine Center, Istanbul, Turkey,

8

Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: The ideal timing of hemivertebra resection remains debated, as earlier intervention may optimize correction but surgery under the age of three poses unique anatomical and technical challenges. This study aimed to evaluate the safety profile, radiological outcomes, and specific technical aspects of posterior hemivertebra resection in this distinct patient population. Materials and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on patients who underwent hemivertebra resection before the age of three. Inclusion criteria were the presence of congenital spinal deformities caused by single or multi-level hemivertebrae and a minimum follow-up of 2 years. Patients with additional segmentation failures or prior spinal surgery were excluded. Patients who underwent a 2-rod construct were compared with those who underwent 3- or 4-multirod constructs. All resections were carried out using modern surgical techniques, including multimodal neuromonitoring, intraoperative CT navigation, microsurgical dissection with meticulous hemostasis, and multirod/hook-assisted stabilization strategies. Conclusion: Posterior hemivertebra resection in children under 3 years of age is a neurologically safe and highly effective method for deformity correction when performed with modern surgical techniques and by experienced teams. Early intervention offers permanent results with an acceptable complication profile and should be considered a definitive treatment strategy in this patient group. Furthermore, the application of multi-rod constructs and hook-assisted compression may provide superior stability, protecting patients from the burden of postoperative casting.

## A038: GLP1 receptor agonists in patients with spinal cord injury: a propensity-matched analysis of clinical and functional outcomes

Hanna von Riegen

1

, Alireza Mirahmadi

1

, Mario Keko

1

, Jason Pittman

1

, Sapan Gandhi

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School in Boston, MA, Boston, United States

Introduction: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is associated with high morbidity and complex rehabilitation trajectories. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RAs) have demonstrated neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties in preclinical models, but their real-world safety and impact in SCI populations remain unclear. The objective of this study is to evaluate and compare the functional and clinical outcomes associated with GLP1-RA use in individuals with SCI, using real-world data from a multi-institutional database. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the 2017-2024 data from TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Routinely documented clinical data from electronic health records of participating institutions were available for up to one year after the index surgery and extracted through the TriNetX platform for analysis. Primary outcomes included functional status (mobility, spasticity, bladder/bowel dysfunction), opioid use, fatigue, readmission, ICU stay, mortality and complications (UTI, sepsis, DVT, pressure ulcers). While ICU admissions were lower in the GLP group, the difference was not significant (28.7% vs. 36.2%, p = 0.065). There were no significant increases in complications such as infection, wound issues, or mortality. Functional outcomes (mobility, neurogenic dysfunction, sensitivity) remained comparable across groups. Conclusion: In this propensity-matched analysis, GLP1-RA use in SCI patients was associated with reduced opioid use, less fatigue, and fewer readmissions without increasing the risk of complications or mortality. These findings support potential benefits of GLP1-RA use in SCI populations and suggest further investigation of potential mechanisms of benefit.

## A039: Impact of a transitional care clinic on 30-day readmissions after elective spine fusion surgery: a retrospective cohort analysis

Denyse Pitak

1

, Puya Alikhani

2

, Mohsen Rostami

2

, Diego Soto Rubio

2

, Dana Saleh

2

, Luba Ayzenshtat

1

1
Tampa General Hospital, Neuroscience Service Line, Tampa, United States,

2

University of South Florida Department of Neurosurgery, Brain and Spine, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Hospital readmissions following elective spine fusion surgery remain a persistent challenge, impacting patient recovery, healthcare resource utilization, and institutional quality metrics. While predictors of readmission have been widely studied, few evidence-based strategies have demonstrated success in reducing these events in spine surgery. Transitional Care Clinics (TCCs), designed to bridge the critical gap between hospital discharge and outpatient follow-up, have shown benefits in other surgical populations but remain unexplored in the spine population. The role of TCC programs in optimizing post-discharge outcomes across all spinal fusion types are not well understood. This study evaluated the impact of a structured, multidisciplinary TCC program on 30-day readmissions following elective spine fusions surgery at a large academic medical center. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort analysis of adult patients (≥18 years) undergoing elective cervical, thoracic, or lumbar spine fusion between May 2024 and May 2025. Exclusion criteria were trauma, infection, malignancy, and emergent cases. The intervention group participated in a structured TCC program implemented from November 2024 to May 2025. Key program elements included a follow-up visit (in-person or telehealth) within 7 days of discharge, comprehensive wound evaluation, medication review, adjustment of pain management, physical therapy coordination, and escalation of care if required. The pre-intervention group (May-October 2024) received standard discharge instructions only. The primary outcome was 30-day hospital readmission. Secondary outcomes included emergency department (ED) visits and skilled nursing facility (SNF) use. Fischer’s exact test was used to examine the association between TCC participation and readmission. Results: There was a total of 345 patients who underwent an elective cervical, thoracic, or lumbar spinal fusion between May 2024 and May 2025. The pre-intervention cohort had 202 patients, while the post-intervention cohort had 143 patients. Pre-intervention cohort patients had a readmission rate of 21.3%, while post-intervention cohort patients had a rate of 5.6%. Fisher's exact test revealed a significant association between TCC intervention and readmission, showing that patients with TCC intervention had a 78% decrease in odds of readmission compared to those without TCC intervention (odds ratio [OR] = 0.22, 95% CI (0.08, 0.49), p = 0.00039). Conclusion: A structured TCC program significantly reduced 30-day readmissions after elective spine fusion, demonstrating its potential as a high-impact intervention in spine surgery. By providing timely follow-up, addressing complications early, and coordinating ongoing care, TCCs enhanced recovery and improved patient outcomes. The findings suggest that transitional care can be an essential component of modern spine surgery programs and may serve as a model adaptable to diverse health systems. Implementing this approach has the potential to improve quality outcomes, advance value-based care, and reduce the burden of preventable readmissions. Future prospective studies in broader settings are needed to validate these findings, evaluate cost effectiveness, and ensure that this care model can be applied across institutions and healthcare systems worldwide.

Nikos Karavidas

Mean in-brace correction (IBC) was 36.8% for thoracic and 34.8% for lumbar curves. In double curves progression rate was 33.3% and in single curves 16.7% (p = 0.004). Higher IBC and good compliance with the treatment protocol led to less progression rate. 9 patients (11.5%) underwent spinal fusion. Conclusion: Conservative treatment achieved a success rate of 70.5% in a group of scoliotic curves above 40ο with a high risk of progression at the peak of growth. A significant improvement was detected for trunk rotation (ATR), body symmetry measured by TRACE scale and quality of life measured by SRS-22 questionnaire. Non-operative treatment by bracing and PSSE can effectively treat severe scoliosis and reduce the need for surgery. The results were significantly better in single than double curves and in subjects with good compliance and IBC.

## A042: Conservative management of the adult spinal deformity patient: a biopsychosocial pain self-management intervention versus care-as-usual - A comparative treatment-based cohort study with one-year follow-up

Evelien Hoevenaars

1

, Michiel Beekhuizen

1

, Ahmet Alanay

2

, Yann Philippe Charles

3

, Frank Kleinstueck

4

, Ibrahim Obeid

5

, John O'Dowd

6

, Ferran Pellisé

7

, Javier Pizones

8

, Maarten Spruit

1

, Marinus De Kleuver

9

, Miranda van Hooff

1 9

1
Sint Maartenskliniek, Nijmegen, The Netherlands,

2
Acibadem University Maslak Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey,

3
Hôpitaux universitaires de Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France,

4
Schulthess Klinik, Zurich, Switzerland,

5
Pellegrin Bordeaux University Hospital, Bordeaux, France,

6
Hampshire Hospitals NHS Trust, Basingstoke, United Kingdom,

7
Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron, Barcelona, Spain,

8
La Paz University Hospital, Madrid, Spain,

9

Radboudumc, Nijmegen, The Netherlands

Introduction: The prevalence and societal burden of disease of adult spinal deformity (ASD) is increasing. Currently, no evidence based non-operative treatment exists for ASD patients with chronic low back pain (CLBP) and negative impact on quality of life (QoL). The aim of this study was to compare a biopsychosocial intervention to care-as-usual in symptomatic, conservatively managed ASD patients. Material and Methods: A comparative cohort study of a biopsychosocial intervention cohort (n=95) and a care-as-usual cohort (n=192) was conducted. Inclusion criteria of both cohorts were age ≥ 18, no surgical indication, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)>20, coronal Cobb angle ≥ 20, idiopathic (AdIS) or degenerative (de novo) scoliosis (DDS), baseline and one year follow-up (1yFU) ODI data. The biopsychosocial intervention was a 100-hour interdisciplinary group program, based on cognitive behavioural principles and consisted of acceptance and commitment therapy, physical exercise and pain education. The care-as-usual consisted of pain medication, brace, physical therapy, osteopathy/chiropractic and/or injections or no treatment. Primary outcome was functional status (ODIv2.1a). Secondary outcomes were pain intensity (NPRS 0-10), QoL (SF36) and pain medication use. Clinical relevance was a minimal important clinical change (MCIC; improvement in ODI ≥ 10 points) and a patient acceptable symptom state (PASS; ODI ≤ 22). Results: Demographics of the biopsychosocial intervention cohort: median age 57 (IQR 14) years, 87% female, median Cobb angle 28° (IQR 13) and 42% AdIS - 58% DDS. At 1yFU the patients in the intervention cohort showed significantly greater improvement in ODI compared to the care-as-usual cohort (z = -4.26, p = <.001). Clinical relevance: 49% of the patients in the intervention cohort reached MCIC and 34% reached a PASS, compared to 22% and 18% respectively in the care-as-usual cohort. All secondary outcomes followed a similar pattern of greater improvement in the intervention cohort. In the intervention cohort the number of patients not using pain medication increased from 20 patients at baseline to 49 patients at 1yFU, and the number of patients using opiates halved. Conclusion: This study shows clinically relevant and significantly larger improvement in function, pain, and quality of life in the biopsychosocial intervention cohort, compared to the care-as-usual cohort at 1yFU in symptomatic, conservatively managed ASD patients. In addition, it shows a decrease in pain medication use in the intervention cohort. This non-operative, biopsychosocial intervention for symptomatic ASD patients seems a promising treatment option that could help diminish the increasing burden of ASD for patients and healthcare costs.

## A043: Multidisciplinary tumor board evaluations reduce complications in nonoperative patients with spinal tumors

Thomas Buquet

1

, Fidaa Al-Shakfa

2

, Danielle Boulé

2

, Véronique Freire

1,2

, Giuseppina Laura Masucci

1,2

, Zhi Wang

1,2

, Jesse Shen

1,2

1
Université de Montréal, Montréal, Canada,

2

Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal, Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Patients with spinal tumors (ST) often present complex cases that require multidisciplinary management. Tumor boards (TB) facilitate patient-centered clinical decision-making, but few centers offer TB and, to our knowledge, no prior studies have evaluated their clinical effectiveness compared to decisions made by a single clinician. This study aims to assess whether clinical outcomes for patients with ST are improved when decisions are made through a TB rather than by an individual physician. Material and Methods: This is a single-center retrospective study including all patients with primary or metastatic ST who were managed non-surgically and evaluated by a TB composed of at least a musculoskeletal radiologist, a radiation oncologist, and a spine surgeon compared to a group of patients with no presentation to a TB, both during the period between January 2019 and June 2023. Demographic data, tumor type, choice of treatment and complications were documented. Results: Non-surgical treatment decisions and complications rates were compared between 122 patients presented to a TB and 106 patients not presented to a TB during the same period. Patients discussed at a TB had less stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) (39.3% vs 64.2%, p < 0.001) and less palliative radiotherapy (17.2% vs 31.1%, p < 0.05) but underwent vertebroplasty more frequently (13.1% vs 0.9%, p < 0.001). Conservative approaches such as observation (13.9% vs 0.9%, p < 0.001) or no intervention recommended (13.9% vs 2.8%, p < 0.05) were more frequently chosen in the TB group. Overall, patients in the TB group were less likely to receive any intervention (72.1% vs. 96.2%, p < 0.001). At more than 90 days, complication rates were significantly lower in the TB group (2.5% vs. 12.3%, p < 0.05), with radiation-induced fractures being the most common complication. These fractures occurred less frequently in the TB group (1.6% vs. 11.3%, p < 0.05). When comparing only patients who did receive an intervention, TB discussion was still associated with fewer complications (3.4% vs 12.7%, p < 0.05). Conclusion: Multidisciplinary tumor board discussion significantly influenced non-surgical treatment decisions in patients with ST, favoring more conservative approaches and reducing overall intervention rates. TB presentation was also associated with significantly fewer 90-day complications. These findings support the integration of TB discussions in the clinical management of patients with ST to optimize their treatments. This work supports further multicenter prospective studies evaluating the effectiveness of TB evaluations.

## A044: Prescription pattern of rigid cervical collar use after cervical fusion: a national multicenter survey of spine surgeons in Mexico

Cinthya Alejandra Varas-Aguilar

1

, Alexis Manuel Mazariegos-Perez

1

, Hector Ismael De Haro-Segura

1

, Daniel Torres-Fragoso

2

, Alfredo Javier Moheno-Gallardo

1

1
Highly Specialized Medical Unit of Traumatology, Orthopedics, and Rehabilitation “Dr. Victorio De La Fuente Narváez”, Mexico City, Mexico,

2

Hospital Angeles Lindavista, Mexico City, Mexico

Introduction: The use of rigid cervical collars in the postoperative management of cervical fusion has been debated for decades. Originally described by Smith and Robinson in 1958, collars were initially reserved for multilevel procedures. Over time, their use expanded based on the belief that limiting cervical motion enhances spinal stability, reduces pain, and provides patients with a sense of safety. However, no consensus currently exists on specific indications or the optimal duration of postoperative collar use. Material and Methods: A nationwide survey was designed and administered to spine surgeons in Mexico, including both orthopedic surgeons and neurosurgeons. The Delphi methodology was employed through the SurveyMonkey platform, with open-ended and multiple-choice questions. The questionnaire was developed by two spine surgeons, two orthopedic residents, and one spine fellow. Participation was anonymous, and results were analyzed using IBM SPSS 26.0. Descriptive statistics were applied, including measures of central tendency and dispersion for quantitative variables, and absolute frequencies and percentages for qualitative variables. Results: A total of 109 spine surgeons responded to the survey. The majority were male (93.6%). More than half (57.8%) worked in both public and private sectors, and 29.4% had 10-20 years of professional experience. Regarding surgical volume, 33% reported performing 16-30 cervical fusions per year. Rigid cervical collars were prescribed by 72.5% of surgeons, used in an average of 68% of their postoperative patients. Pathology type was considered by 63.3% of respondents, with longer immobilization prescribed for traumatic compared to degenerative cases (6.54 vs. 5.94 weeks, p = 0.964). Osteosynthesis material influenced decisions in 55% of cases, with self-locking interbody cage associated with longer immobilization (mean 5.15 weeks). Patient comorbidities were taken into account by 59.6% of surgeons, particularly osteoporosis, which was associated with the longest immobilization times (mean 7.57 weeks). Similarly, 55% of respondents considered the number of fused levels, prescribing longer collar use when more than three levels were involved (mean 7.58 weeks). The primary reason cited for prescribing a rigid cervical collar was patient comfort and improved perception of safety, reported by 65.1% of surgeons. Correlation analysis showed no significant association between years of professional experience and collar use (Spearman’s Rho = -0.121, p = 0.209). Comparisons between practice settings revealed no significant differences, although surgeons working exclusively in private practice demonstrated a greater tendency to prescribe collars (32.4% vs. 18.4%, p = 0.39). Conclusion: This national survey demonstrates that rigid cervical collar use after cervical fusion remains a frequent practice among spine surgeons in Mexico, despite the absence of standardized prescription guidelines. The most influential factors in decision-making were pathology type (traumatic vs. degenerative), osteosynthesis material, number of levels fused, and the presence of comorbidities, particularly osteoporosis. Professional experience and practice setting did not significantly influence prescription patterns. Importantly, patient comfort and perceived safety remain key reasons for prescribing collars, highlighting the subjective elements involved in postoperative care. These findings underscore the need to develop evidence-based clinical guidelines and establish national consensus to unify practice standards regarding postoperative immobilization in cervical fusion patients.

## A045: ERAS - An opportunity for spinal surgery - Findings from a systematic review

Caroline Büchel

1

, Caroline Treanor

2

, Benjamin Davies

3

, David Anderson

4

, Michael Fehlings

5

, Carl Zipser

1

1
Balgrist University Hospital, Zurich, Switzerland,

2
The school of Physiotherapy, Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, 123 St Stephens Greens, Dublin, Dublin, Ireland,

3
Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom, Cambridge, United Kingdom,

4
School of Health Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia., Sydney, Australia,

5

Division of Neurosurgery and Spinal Program, University of Toronto and Krembil Brain Institute, University Health Network, Toronto, ON, Canada., Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) is a multimodal perioperative care pathway providing evidence-based recommendations to improve functional outcomes after surgery. ERAS pathways have been implemented in various surgical disciplines, including spine surgery. A consensus statement for lumbar spinal fusion has been published by the ERAS® society in 2021, yet recommendations for cervical spine surgery spinal fusion are lacking. Since guideline development depends on precise information on the ERAS landscape, we conducted a systematic review to identify areas of spinal surgery where ERAS was investigated, as well as the applied interventions and outcomes of these studies. Knowledge about the spinal surgery sub-specialities using ERAS will help to inform the development of future ERAS guidelines in spine surgery. Material and Methods: We conducted a systematic review (PROSPERO no. CRD42025638293) evaluating primary research articles which were available in English. Study inclusion was based upon screening of title and abstract, with no limits set regarding publication date. A SWiM analysis of the efficacy of ERAS in comparison to traditional care was done for studies with a control group. Additionally, a meta-analysis for RCTs evaluating ERAS in the field of lumbar spine surgery was performed. Results: Eighty-one studies were included, of which a majority were cohort studies (n = 62/81, 76.5%), followed by RCTs (n = 7/81, 8.6%). Most articles addressed the use of ERAS in the field of degenerative spine pathologies (n = 35/81, 43.2%), followed by deformity (n = 29/81, 35.8%). The median number of interventions implemented was twelve. Interventions most commonly used were patient education (n = 60/81, 74.1%), recommendations on urinary catheter usage (n = 51/81, 63%), postoperative analgesia and early mobilisation (both n = 61/81, 75.3%) and early oral intake (n = 49/81, 60.5%). The most frequently assessed outcome measures were length of stay (LOS) (n = 65/81, 92.9%) and complication rates (n = 40 /81, 49.4%). A comparison of LOS between ERAS and traditional care (TDC-) patients demonstrated a shorter LOS for the ERAS group in 56 studies (93.3%, n = 60). Similarly, meta-analysis showed a statistically non-significant tendency for ERAS shortening LOS for 1 day in lumbar spine patients [95%CI -2.77, 0.71; p = 0.25]. Decreased complication rates, with a median complication rate of 8.8% for ERAS patients vs. a median of 15.6% for TDC patients, were noted. Total hospital costs were reduced in 15 articles (93.8%, n = 16), with a median total cost reduction of 1161.95$. Conclusion: Most evidence exists for the use of multimodal interventions in degenerative spine and deformity surgery, focusing on reducing LOS and complication rates, and optimizing pain management. ERAS interventions appear to effectively improve functional outcomes and reduce costs. There is need for further investigation of personalised ERAS recommendations based upon a patient diagnosis. Furthermore, despite being frequently studied, optimising pain management is a challenge, partially owed to unspecific pain assessments.

## A046: Proteome changes of structural compromised annulus fibrosus collected from degenerative disc patients

Taylor Bader

1

, Mohammed Salaam

1

, David Hart

1

, Holly Sparks

1

, Paul Salo

1

, Antoine Dufour

1

, Ganesh Swamy

1

1

University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada

Introduction: Intervertebral discs (IVDs) are comprised of a central gelatinous nucleus pulposus (NP) that is sheathed in layers of fibrocartilaginous annulus fibrosus (AF) and endplates that together act as the principal connection between vertebrae. The IVD is primary composed of core matrisome proteins, including collagens and proteoglycans. Due to limited perfusion and sparse cellularity, IVDs lose their structural integrity through progressive breakdown as individuals age. Disc degeneration (DD) is an escalation of this breakdown through proteolytic extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling that potentially leads to chronic pain, spinal deformities, and highly invasive surgery. Despite its prevalence, mechanisms of DD remain poorly defined, especially within the AF. The aim of this study is to apply a multifaceted approach combining mechanics, structure, and proteome analysis of human AF explants to provide a robust characterization of degenerative changes. We compared age-matched controls to DD individuals who had structurally compromised AF tissue measured by reductions in shear modulus (SM) and histological degeneration grading. We hypothesize that accompanying these changes are changes in the core matrisome of the AF. Material and Methods: AF tissues were obtained from minimally degenerative (nonDD) donors through the Southern Alberta Tissue Donation Program with lumbar radiographs to ensure normal morphology. DD AF tissue was obtained from patients undergoing spinal surgery at Foothills Medical Center (Ethics ID: REB 18-1308) with standing X-rays to confirm no cofounding deformity diagnosis and T2-weighted MRI images to grade degeneration using a modified Pfirrmann grade. From a larger cohort of biomechanically assessed tissues, an age-matched cohort was generated using a propensity matching algorithm (matchit) in R. The cohort included anterior AF tissue from 5 nonDD (37 ± 8; 2 females, 3 males) and 5 DD (37 ± 7; 3 females, 2 males) individuals. Each AF tissue was divided into three adjacent 5mm3 sections, two for biomechanical assessment and histological processing, and one frozen for proteome analysis. Mechanical shear testing of anterior 5mm3 AF tissue cubes was performed in circumferential (left-right) and radial (anterior-posterior) shear loading. Four strain intervals of 2.5% with 20-minutes of relaxation were applied, totaling 10% strain. Shear modulus (SM) was calculated using a line of best fit between each of the most relaxed points. These same cubes were then embedded and sectioned for hemoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and histology scoring. Degeneration was scored followed ORS Spine standardized histological scoring, using only the AF section. AF cellularity, lesions, and extracellular matrix were scored between 0-3, with higher scores noting increased degenerative changes. Two-sample two-tailed t-tests were used to compare differences in SM and histology degradation scores between groups and sexes. Proteomic analysis used quantitative detergent solubility profiling (QDSP). Soluble proteins were separated using five total buffers, each increasing in concentrations of detergents. Buffers 0 & 1, non-ionic detergents that gently isolate soluble proteins, were combined to form fraction 1 (soluble proteins). Buffers 2 & 3 included ionic detergents to denature proteins and were combined to form fraction 2 (partially soluble proteins). Lastly, the remaining pellet was isolated as fraction 3 (insoluble proteins). Fractions 1, 2, and 3 of each AF tissue included a bioinformatics pipeline of LC/MS-MS, data-independent analysis (DIA), DIA neural network (DIA-NN) spectra matching, STRING-db pathway analysis, and MSstats statistics (adjusted p < 0.05, log2 fold-change > 2). Normalized intensities of nonDD and DD compared changes in proteins and protein solubility between fractions. Results: SM was significantly reduced in the DD individuals (radial SM: 7 ± 4; circumferential SM: 32 ± 21 kPa) when compared to age-matched nonDD individuals (radial SM: 59 ± 35; circumferential SM: 195 ± 65) (p < 0.05). Radial SM was significantly increased in nonDD females compared to nonDD males (p < 0.05). Histological degradation scores were significantly increased in DD individuals (4 ± 1) when compared to nonDD individuals (2 ± 1) (p < 0.05). 1083 proteins were identified across all the samples. Notable elevated collagens in soluble (fraction 1) nonDD AF tissue included a 2-fold increase in COL1A1, COL1A2, and 2.5-fold increase in COL4A2 when compared to DD AF tissue. Insoluble matrisome proteins (fraction 3) upregulated in nonDD individuals included COL5A1 (3-fold), COL5A2 (2-fold). Additional changes were seen in proteoglycans, glycoproteins, and ECM regulators.

Conclusion: Collection of IVD tissues from patients undergoing surgery for these painful conditions provides the opportunity to explore mechanical, biological, and structural properties of ex vivo human IVD. Although not accounting for the potential inflection point (when the degeneration and pain initially develop) in DD, understanding the cross-sectional differences of age-matched individuals provides a unique understanding into potential pathological remodeling.

## A047: Does the fetus intervertebral disc acquire microbiome during the development? A metagenome analysis

S. Rajasekaran

1

, Chitraa Tangavel

2

, Divya Arunachalam

2

, Nandakumar M

2

, Gnanaprakash Gurusamy

1

1
Ganga Hospital and Medical Centre, Coimbatore, India, 
2
Ganga Orthopaedic Research and Education Foundation, Coimbatore, India
Introduction: The microbiome of the fetal Intervertebral disc (IVD) is unexplored till date and this study is attempted to document their microbiome. The IVD in healthy adults is avascular; the route of microbial entry inside the disc needs to be addressed. The objective of this study is to understand whether the microbial inoculation happens during the development of the fetus and the type of microbial species it acquires from the mother. Also to understand whether the fetuses acquire similar microbiomes. The outcome of this study is to identify and list the microbial population acquired and explore the bacterial diversity in the IVD components: Nucleus pulposus (NP); Annulus fibrosus (AF); Endplate (EP). This study would answer when the IVD acquires its microbiome. Material and Methods: Nine fetal IVD encompassing NP (n = 8), AF (n = 9), and EP (n = 9) components. 16S rRNA sequencing was used to study the bacterial diversity in the nine fetal IVDs. The tissue sample from IVD components NP (n = 8), AF (n = 9), and EP (n = 9) were used for microbial DNA extraction. Universal bacterial primers were used for V3-V4 region amplification and were sequenced in three batches. The sequenced reads were analysed using QIIME-2 pipeline. ConQuR tool was used to mitigate the batch effect. The alpha and beta diversity were analysed for the inter and intra species diversity among the IVD components. Results: A total of 33 bacterial genus were identified with sample positivity above 25%. In AF, EP and NP 14, 20 and 12 bacterial genus were found respectively. Among them ten bacterial genus Aeromonas, Albidovulum, Arthrobacter, Bacillus, Corynebacterium, Propionibacterium, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus were the common among all the fetal IVD-NP, AF and EP components. Conclusion: The human IVD is not sterile, it acquires the microbiome during the developmental stage as evidenced in this study. The bacterial genus observed among the AF, EP and NP correlates with the previous studies reported in normal adult IVD components. The species richness is more in AF compared to NP and EP. The fetus during the developmental stage is vascular with rich blood supply and would be the route for this microbial inoculation during the IVD development. This study is the first to document the presence of bacterial microbiome in the IVD components.

## A048: A semi-synthetic oxysterol (Oxy133) as a novel alternative to rhBMP-2 for bone regeneration

Marc Abdou

1

, Matthew Gallo

1

, Nicole Hang

1

, Mirbahador Athari

1

, Hua Shen

1

, Fergui Hernandez

1

, Farhad Parhami

2

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, Kiran Alluri

1

1
Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States,

2

MAX BioPharma, Inc., Santa Monica, United States

Introduction: Large bone defects remain a major challenge in orthopaedic surgery, especially when biological capacity for healing is limited. Recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) is widely used but requires supraphysiologic dosing and carries high costs and adverse effects, including heterotopic ossification. Oxysterols are cholesterol-derived signaling molecules with osteoinductive potential. Oxy133, a semi-synthetic oxysterol, has demonstrated strong preclinical performance in spinal fusion models. This study compared Oxy133 to rhBMP-2 in a rat femoral critical-sized defect model. Material and Methods: Twelve-week-old male Lewis rats underwent creation of a 6-mm mid-diaphyseal femoral defect stabilized with plate and cerclage fixation. Animals were randomized to one of three groups: Oxy133 (40 mg/200 µL, n = 14), rhBMP-2 (10 µg/200 µL, n = 14), or DMSO control (n = 5). A collagen sponge scaffold was loaded with the assigned substrate. Healing was evaluated radiographically at 4, 8, and 12 weeks. Microcomputed tomography (µCT) quantified bone volume fraction (BVF). Histology confirmed cortical and trabecular bridging. Biomechanical torsion testing assessed stiffness, torque, and energy to failure. Results: By 8 weeks, 100% of Oxy133-treated defects achieved complete radiographic union versus 86% in the rhBMP-2 group; no control animals healed. At 12 weeks, all but one rhBMP-2 specimen had healed. Radiographic scores averaged 4.7 ± 0.4 (Oxy133) vs. 4.6 ± 0.8 (rhBMP-2). µCT confirmed similar BVF (6.04 ± 2.03% vs. 5.82 ± 1.41%, p = 0.28). Histology showed robust cortical bridging and trabecular bone in both Oxy133 and rhBMP-2 groups, with no bone formation in controls. Biomechanical testing revealed comparable mechanical integrity; rhBMP-2-treated femurs demonstrated greater torsional stiffness (p = 0.04), while other parameters were equivalent. One case of heterotopic ossification occurred in the rhBMP-2 group; none were observed with Oxy133. Conclusion: Oxy133 achieved bone regeneration comparable to rhBMP-2 while promoting earlier union and avoiding complications. Its distinct mechanism of action and lack of adverse events suggest potential safety advantages over rhBMP-2. These findings support Oxy133 as a promising, scalable, and cost-effective alternative for bone regeneration, warranting further evaluation in large-animal models and translational studies.

WHRI.6310E showed a positive correlation in diseased samples there by providing clue leading to dysbiosis. The study evidenced to strengthen our hypothesis that IVDD caused by infection due to the P.aeruginosa abundance. As it facilitates co-bacterial species to polymicrobial infection which may influence the disease progression by modulating the host immunity and the IVD microbiome. Further richness of Psedomonas phages in disease group substantially prove P.aeruginosa presence in IVD and its possible role in IVDD.

## A050: Cranial and caudal shifts: a genetic perspective on transitional vertebrae and a unified enumeration algorithm

Kadir Abul

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Başakşehir Çam and Sakura City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Transitional vertebrae exemplify the interface between developmental genetics and clinical anatomy. Variations such as cervical ribs, hypoplastic T12 ribs, and sacralized L5 are not random anomalies but predictable outcomes of homeotic transformations driven by Hox gene expression boundaries. Understanding these cranial and caudal shifts offers a basic science framework for redefining spinal enumeration and addressing the persistent challenge of wrong-level surgery. Materials and Methods: We conducted a conceptual review synthesizing developmental biology, anthropological evidence, and radiological studies of transitional vertebrae. Emphasis was placed on the principle of Hox gene colinearity, which organizes vertebral identity along the cranio-caudal axis. We analyzed reported correlations between rib morphology, thoracolumbar transitional vertebrae (TLTV), lumbosacral transitional vertebrae (LSTV), and their cranial counterparts such as C7 transverse apophysiomegaly and cervical ribs. These observations were used to propose a unified spinal enumeration algorithm. Results: A reproducible pattern emerged across all three transitional zones. Caudal shifts, such as elongated T12 ribs forming accessory ribs at L1, frequently co-occurred with distinct S1-S2 disc spaces. Conversely, cranial shifts, such as hypoplastic or absent T12 ribs, correlated with sacralization of L5, including Castellvi-type variants. These lumbosacral changes were often mirrored in the cervical spine, where hypertrophic C7 transverse processes or cervical ribs were present. Together, these findings confirm that transitional vertebrae represent systematic, genetically patterned transformations rather than isolated anomalies. Conclusion: Cranial and caudal shifts can be understood through developmental genetics and consistently identified on imaging. We propose a unified spinal enumeration algorithm that defines the 20th vertebra as L1 and the 25th as S1, independent of rib morphology. Whole-spine imaging remains the gold standard for accurate numbering, yet awareness of these genetic and morphological patterns allows surgeons to anticipate anomalies even on limited radiographs. Integrating these insights into clinical practice may reduce wrong-level surgery and harmonize vertebral nomenclature.

## A051: Serum deprivation induces autophagic flux and apoptosis in human nucleus pulposus cells: implications for intervertebral disc degeneration and potential therapeutic strategy

Jong-Beom Park

1

, Young-Yul Kim

1

1

The Catholic University of Korea College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Nutritional deprivation is a critical pathological factor in intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), given the avascular nature of the disc and its dependence on diffusion through the endplate for nutrient supply. This study investigated the effects of serum deprivation on autophagic flux and apoptosis in human nucleus pulposus (NP) cells, with implications for regenerative strategies in IVDD. Material and Methods: Hima NP cells were isolated from degenerated human lumbar disc tissues which surgically obtained from surgeries of lumbar disc herniations. NP cells were cultured under varying fetal bovine serum (FBS) concentrations (10%, 1%, and 0%) to simulate progressive nutrient deprivation. Morphological changes, cell viability, DNA content, and metabolic activity were evaluated. Western blotting quantified LC3, P62, HMGB1, and cleaved caspase-3. Apoptotic cell populations were measured by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Immunofluorescence staining for LC3, P62, and cleaved caspase-3 assessed autophagic and apoptotic localization. RT-qPCR was performed to analyze expression levels of autophagy-related genes (LC3, P62) and apoptosis-related genes (Caspase-3). Results: Serum deprivation induced marked reductions in NP cell viability, altered morphology, and decreased metabolic activity in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with maximal effects at 48 hours in 0% FBS. Lower serum concentrations triggered increased autophagic activity, evidenced by LC3-II accumulation and P62 degradation, as well as enhanced expression of LC3 mRNA. Chloroquine treatment confirmed increased autophagic flux by preventing lysosomal degradation of LC3-II. HMGB1 translocated from nucleus to cytoplasm under nutrient stress, further supporting autophagy activation. Concurrently, caspase-dependent apoptosis was observed, with elevated cleaved caspase-3 protein and increased Caspase-3 mRNA levels. FACS analysis revealed significant increases in apoptotic cell populations under 0% FBS conditions. Immunofluorescence confirmed co-localization of LC3 and cleaved caspase-3, indicating simultaneous autophagy and apoptosis under nutrient deprivation. Conclusion: Serum deprivation robustly induces autophagic flux and caspase-dependent apoptosis in human NP cells, highlighting the critical role of nutritional supply in disc cell survival. The interplay between autophagy and apoptosis under nutrient stress may represent a key mechanism in IVDD progression. Clinically, these findings underscore the potential of therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring nutrient microenvironments or modulating autophagy-apoptosis balance-such as enhancing endplate permeability, supplying metabolic substrates, or pharmacologically regulating autophagy-to preserve NP cell viability and promote intervertebral disc regeneration.

Rafael Barreto Silva

Independent Researcher, São Paulo, Brazil

However, one of the main difficulties with this analysis is that the retroperitoneal structures move to a more anterior position, between the dorsal position (CT or MRI position) and the prone position (surgical position). The aim of this study is analyze the position of the retroperitoneal structures and their movement using CT scans in prone and dorsal decubitus, as well as to verify the theoretical risk of retroperitoneal injury at each of the following entry points. Methods: The inclusion criteria was as follows, Patients over the age of 18, who have consented to take part in the study by filling in the free consent form, and who have no medical contraindications to undergoing CT scans. And the exclusion criteria was patients with any pathology that makes it impossible to take the measurements proposed in the study. Patients who, for whatever reason, have a low-quality image exams. Data was compiled in a spreadsheet and analyzed using R software. Categorical variables were described as count and percentage. Population-averaged effects were estimated while accounting for within-patient correlation and sparse cells by fitting a penalized GEE for small-sample with bias-adjusted standard Effects were summarized as estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts (via emmeans) on the probability scale, with the GL versus RL contrast estimated within each level × decubitus. Also, there was a significant interaction between spine level and decubitus (F(3,27) = 6.6, p = 0.002). As for the pairwise estimated marginal means comparison regarding the risk of peritoneal violation in ventral decubitus. At L1-L2, the risk with the GL was 4% (95% CI 0.7-20%) versus 61% (46-73%) with the red line (p < 0.0001). At L2-L3, the GL yielded 0.6% (0.4-9%) compared with 36% (21-53%) for the RL (p < 0.0001). The same pattern held at lower levels: 0.6% vs 14% at L3-L4 and 7 % vs 45% at L4-L5. Conclusion: Across all lumbar levels and in both positions, the GL reference line was associated with substantially lower risk of peritoneal violation than RL. Interactions involving the access point were not significant, indicating a stable GL benefit across levels and positions.

Raphael Schmid

, Elias Schulze

, Igor Červenka

, Salim Darwiche

, Karina Klein

, Andrea Barbero

Introduction: Painful intervertebral disc disease (IDD) is a prevalent condition associated with catabolic degenerative changes in the intervertebral disc (IVD). ## A054: Molecular expression of leptin, leptin receptor variant-2, and FGF23 in hypertrophic bone from lumbar spinal stenosis patients: a novel bone-based qPCR profiling study

Ozan Aydogdu

1

, Resat Unal

2

, Derya Hazer Rosberg

3

1

Muğla Eğitim ve Araştırma Hastanesi, Mugla, Turkey

2

Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Molecular Cell Biology Division, Faculty of Science, Mugla Sitki Kocman University, Mugla, Turkey

3

Lund University Skåne, University Hospital, Lund, Sweden

Introduction: Obesity is an established risk factor for lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS). While prior studies have evaluated molecular mechanisms in ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, bone-derived molecular data in LSS remain lacking. This study investigated bone expression of Leptin (LEP), Leptin Receptor Variant-2 (LEPR-V2), and fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23) in patients undergoing surgery for LSS. To our knowledge, this is the first bone-based molecular profiling of these markers in LSS surgical specimens. ## A055: Too much of a curve? Rethinking spinal alignment strategies for high pelvic incidence patients

Devender Singh

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, John Stokes

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: Sagittal alignment is essential for spinal stability, particularly in patients with high pelvic incidence (PI > 60°). Achieving ideal sagittal balance in these patients remains challenging due to the complex interaction between pelvic morphology and spinal curvature. Existing alignment strategies may fail to provide optimal balance, leading to postural compensation and increased mechanical stress on the spine. This study assesses the effectiveness of three alignment strategies in high PI patients, evaluating compliance with key sagittal alignment parameters. We hypothesize that higher PI patients will experience greater difficulty in achieving optimal sagittal alignment due to increased pelvic morphology demands. Among the three alignment strategies (PI-LL = 10, PI-LL = 0, PI-LL = -10), certain strategies will fail more frequently, particularly in aligning C2PL and T1 slope. Material and Methods: A cohort of 20 patients with PI > 60° underwent computational modeling of three sagittal balance strategies: PI-LL = 10° (less_curve), PI-LL = 0° (ideal_curve), and PI-LL = -10° (more_curve). Each strategy was tested using three alignment goals: C2PL = 0 mm, T1PA = 10°, and T1PA = 15°. Plans were analyzed based on three criteria: T1 slope between 15°-35°, T1 pelvic angle (T1PA < 20°), and C2PL between +9 mm and -33 mm. Results: The results revealed significant variability in compliance rates across strategies. The highest compliance was observed in the C2PL = 0 mm strategy, reaching 35%, whereas the lowest compliance occurred in the T1PA = 10° strategy, with only 0%. The most frequently failed parameter was T1 Slope 15°-35, which showed failure rates exceeding 100% in some cases. Patients with high PI exhibited significant difficulty in maintaining T1 slope within the ideal range, suggesting that standard alignment strategies may not fully compensate for the increased lumbar lordosis demands of these individuals. Failure to align sagittal parameters correctly could lead to increased thoracolumbar stress, heightening the risk of postoperative instability and adjacent segment disease. Conclusion: These findings suggest that conventional spinal alignment strategies may not fully accommodate the postural needs of high PI patients. The inability to achieve consistent sagittal alignment underscores the need for refined planning techniques that incorporate global spinal balance adjustments, particularly in the thoracolumbar region. Future studies should explore dynamic models that integrate thoracic and pelvic compensatory mechanisms for improved surgical outcomes.

## A056: The impact of post-operative sagittal alignment on the development of proximal junctional kyphosis following adult spinal deformity surgery: a retrospective cohort analysis

Puya Alikhani

1

, jade vanderpool

1

, Dana Saleh

1

, Ahmad Alkadri

1

, Diego Soto Rubio

1

, Mohsen Rostami

1

1

University of South Florida, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Proximal Junctional Kyphosis (PJK) is a common and debilitating complication following long-segment fusion for adult spinal deformity (ASD). While numerous risk factors exist, the role of achieving optimal post-operative sagittal alignment remains a critical area of investigation. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 87 patients who underwent thoracolumbar fusion for ASD. Patients were divided into two cohorts: the PJK Cohort (cases, n = 38), who developed radiographically confirmed PJK, and the Control Cohort (n = 49), who underwent surgery without developing PJK. Pre- and post-operative radiographic parameters-Pelvic Incidence (PI), Lumbar Lordosis (LL), Pelvic Tilt (PT), Sagittal Vertical Axis (SVA), and PI-LL mismatch-were measured. The delta (Δ) for each parameter (post-operative minus pre-operative value) was calculated to quantify the magnitude of surgical correction. Independent samples t-tests were used to compare the mean changes between cohorts. Results: The Control Cohort demonstrated a significantly greater magnitude of improvement in key sagittal alignment parameters compared to the PJK Cohort. The mean improvement in lumbar lordosis (ΔLL: -23.5° vs. -16.2°, p = 0.037) and the mean reduction in pelvic tilt (ΔPT: -7.5° vs. -3.9°, p = 0.042) were both statistically greater in the Control Cohort. A strong trend towards a greater reduction in PI-LL mismatch was also observed in the Control Cohort (ΔPI-LL: -21.1° vs. -14.6°, p = 0.069). No significant difference was found in the change in SVA between groups (p = 0.204). A pattern of residual post-operative malalignment, particularly a PI-LL mismatch > 10°, was frequently observed in the PJK Cohort. Conclusion: Successful restoration of sagittal balance is paramount in preventing PJK. This study demonstrates that patients who developed PJK received a less robust correction of their sagittal deformity, leaving significant residual malalignment. The statistically significant differences in LL and PT correction, and the strong trend in PI-LL mismatch, indicate that inadequate correction shifts excessive biomechanical stress to the proximal junction, leading to mechanical failure. These findings underscore that achieving optimal sagittal alignment is a critical, modifiable surgical objective for mitigating the risk of PJK.

## A057: Four milligrams per level: defining the BMP threshold to prevent rod fracture and proximal junctional kyphosis in adult spinal deformity surgery

Nuri Demirci

1

, Yasemin Yavuz

2

, Munish Gupta

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Washington University in St. Louis, Saint Louis, United States

2

Department of Biostatistics, Faculty of Medicine, Ankara University, Ankara, Turkey

Introduction: Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) is widely used to enhance fusion in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery, but its optimal dosing strategy remains undefined. The ideal dose per level that decreases the risk of mechanical complications has not been established. Methods: A prospective cohort of 207 ASD patients who underwent thoracic-to-pelvis fusion with ≥ 7 levels and ≥ 2 years of follow-up was analyzed. BMP dose per level was calculated and categorized as < 3, 3-3.99 (< 4), and ≥ 4 mg/level. Outcomes were rod fracture (RF) and proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK), assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox models stratified by osteoporosis. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied using a propensity score including age, sex, BMI, osteoporosis status, number of fused levels, PSO, rod material, rod size, accessory/satellite rods, and surgical approach to balance baseline characteristics between high- and low-dose BMP groups. Results: Mean age was 62.1 ± 11.1 years, BMI 29.7 ± 5.7, and 77.8% were female; 20.8% underwent PSO and 6.3% VCR. Over a mean 46-month follow-up, 20 patients (9.7%) developed RF and 32 (15.5%) developed PJK. The mean BMP dose per fused level was 3.2 ± 1.0 mg, with a median of 3.0 (IQR 2.7-3.6, range 0.8-6.0). In Cox regression, higher BMP dose per level was significantly associated with a lower hazard of PJK (HR 0.39 per mg/level, 95% CI 0.23-0.66, p < 0.001) and showed a nonsignificant protective trend for RF (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.40-1.43, p = 0.15). Conclusion: At 36 months, rod fracture risk decreased from ∼13% with < 3 mg/level to 0% with ≥ 4 mg/level, while proximal junctional kyphosis risk decreased from ∼14% with < 4 mg/level to ∼2-3% with ≥ 4 mg/level. These findings suggest that the ideal BMP dose should be at least 4 mg per level fused meaningfully improves construct durability and lowers late mechanical complications.

## A058: Effect of fusion construct length on standing balance in adults with spinal deformity

Bethany Wilson

1

, Sara McMahan

1

, Kyle Robinson

1

, Isador Lieberman

2

1
Texas Back Institute, Plano, TX, United States, 
2
Texas Back Institute, Frisco, TX, United States
Introduction: Adult Spinal Deformity (ASD) often requires surgical intervention involving fusion with constructs of varying lengths. While spinal alignment is commonly discussed among physicians dealing with spinal deformity, standing balance is often overlooked in these discussions. At P3, SC ROSc, ROSs, SEA and SVc were similar to control levels, while LC measures remained impaired. By P12, most SC improvements persisted, remaining comparable to controls, while LC showed no changes. All p < 0.05. Conclusion: Patients with shorter constructs achieved postoperative standing balance comparable to healthy controls, with improvements sustained at one year postoperatively. Juan Sardi

, Justin Smith

1

, Brett Rocos

, Lawrence Lenke

3

, Ferran Pellisé

4

, Yong Qiu

, Randolph Gray

, Saumyajit Basu

9

, Go Yoshida

10

, Amer Aziz

11

, Stephen Lewis

12

1
Department of Neurosurgery University of Virginia, Charlottesville, United States,

2
Departments of Neurosurgery and Orthopedic Surgery, Duke University, Durham, NC, United States,

3
Columbia University Department of Orthopedic Surgery, New York, NY, United States,

4
Hospital Universitari de la Vall d’Hebron, Barcelona, Spain,

5
Spine Surgery, Drum Tower Hospital of Nanjing University Medical School, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China,

6
Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey,

7
Queen's Medical Centre Campus, Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, Nottingham, United Kingdom,

8
The Children`s Hospital Westmead, St. Leonards, Australia,

9
Kothari Medical Centre, Kolkata,, India,

10
Hamamatsu University School of Medicine, Hamamatsu, Japan,

11
Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan,

12

Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, ON, Canada

Introduction: Spinal deformity surgery has advanced significantly over the past two decades, allowing for more ambitious correction of complex pathologies. Despite these advances, procedures remain associated with substantial risk, particularly new-onset postoperative motor deficits (NOPMD), which have profound consequences for patient function, quality of life, and healthcare costs. Reported incidences vary widely, reflecting heterogeneous patient populations, inconsistent outcome measures, and reliance on retrospective data. This analysis aimed to determine the overall incidence of NOPMD and to identify clinical, radiographic, and intraoperative factors associated with their occurrence. We also sought to distinguish cord- from root-level injury patterns and assess the diagnostic accuracy of neuromonitoring. Material and Methods: This was a post-hoc analysis of the SDIM registry, which prospectively enrolled patients aged 10-80 years undergoing spinal deformity correction at 20 international centers. Eligible patients had major scoliosis (Cobb ≥ 80°), high-grade spondylolisthesis, or required posterior column or three-column osteotomies. Patients were stratified by surgical level into cord-level (T12 and above) and non-cord-level (L1 and below) groups. Neuromonitoring included MEP, SSEP, and EMG across standardized muscle groups. NOPMD was defined as ≥ 1-point decrease in ASIA-LEMS immediately after surgery. Alerts were based on ≥ 50% reductions in MEP/SSEP amplitude or sustained EMG activity. Baseline demographic, radiographic, and surgical data were compared between groups, and logistic regression identified independent predictors of NOPMD. Results: A total of 542 patients met inclusion criteria, with 195 undergoing non-cord-level and 347 cord-level procedures. The overall incidence of NOPMD was 10.1% (n = 55), significantly higher in the non-cord-level cohort (15.9%) compared with the cord-level group (6.9%). Deficits most commonly involved proximal lower extremity muscles, particularly hip flexors and knee extensors. At last follow-up, 58.2% of affected patients demonstrated complete recovery, with comparable rates between cord- and non-cord-level groups. IONM alerts were observed in 10.8% of non-cord-level and 16.1% of cord-level cases. Alerts were significantly more frequent in patients who developed NOPMD (29% vs. 7.3% in non-cord-level; 50% vs. 13.6% in cord-level; both p < 0.01). However, sensitivity of IONM for detecting root-level deficits remained poor, ranging from 5.9% to 30.8%, while specificity exceeded 93% across all muscle groups. On multivariate analysis, only age (OR 1.02, 95% CI 1.00-1.04, p = 0.019) and greater number of monitored muscle groups (OR 1.22, 95% CI 1.08-1.37, p = 0.002) independently predicted NOPMD. Conclusion: In this multicenter, prospectively collected cohort, the incidence of NOPMD was 10.1%, with deficits occurring more than twice as frequently in non-cord-level compared with cord-level spine surgeries. These deficits were predominantly consistent with nerve root rather than spinal cord injuries, most often affecting proximal muscle groups. Despite the use of standardized intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM), sensitivity for detecting root-level injuries remained poor, underscoring a critical limitation of current practice. Multivariate analysis identified older age and greater surgical complexity as independent predictors. These findings highlight the urgent need for improved neuromonitoring strategies and emphasize meticulous surgical technique and vigilance.

Fatemeh Alavi
