However, it exhibits significant variability in normal population, does not account for variability in segmental lumbar lordosis and it is unclear whether this alignment target results in lower spinal forces at the junctions. With compression force at the junction felt to be a leading factor in proximal junctional failure, this study aims to investigate the forces at the thoracolumbar junction in asymptomatic individuals that have alignments with and without ideal PI-LL mismatch. Material and Methods: We used radiographic data of an international cross-sectional study on 319 healthy volunteers over 18 years of age from four continents, without evidence of spinal disease or spine surgery. Institutional review board approval was obtained by participating centers. Radiographic parameters including PI and L1-S1 lordosis (LL) were measured based on EOS images. Individualized musculoskeletal (MSK) models based on sex, weight, height, and spine curvature were built and spinal forces were calculated using MSK analysis. Individuals were divided into two groups based on PI-LL values: Matched (PI-LL<10°) and mismatched (PI-LL>10°). In order to exclude the effect of PI on spinal force, individuals were also clustered in two groups based on PI values: PI<55° and PI>55°; and ideal mismatch was studied within subgroups. Spinal compressive and shear forces at thoracolumbar levels (T12/L1 and L1/L2) were compared between different subgroups. Results: 119 individuals (37.3%) were mismatched with a mean PI-LL of 16 4.4°. The PI value of the group with mismatch was 49.9 10.3° vs. 53.7 10.1° in the matched group (p=0.001). Shear forces at L1 and L2 levels were significantly lower in individuals with matched PI-LL(p<0.001), however, compressive forces were not different between the groups (p=0.08, p=0.5). For 121 individuals (37.9%) with PI>55, no significant difference in both shear and compression was found between alignments with and without matched PI-LL values (p=0.36, p=0.78). For the 198 individuals with PI<55° and matched PI-LL, significantly lower shear force at the upper lumbar region was noted compared to the mismatched group (p<0.001), however, compression was not different between the groups. Conclusion: While targeting ideal PI-LL match for individuals with low PI (PI<55°) can be effective in decreasing shear force at the upper lumbar region, it did not result in lower spinal compression forces in all range of normal population. This finding demonstrated the limitation of the ideal PI-LL value as a sagittal alignment target. Further investigation is needed to identify more reliable alignment targets that better reflect the spinal forces at the junctional levels.

Akinbo Olaolu

, Frank Kleinstuck

, Altug Yucekul

Department of Neurological Surgery, University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan, Nigeria,

Introduction: Short-segment (≤4 levels) fusion is frequently used for adult spinal deformity (ASD) to restore alignment and function while limiting morbidity. Mechanical complications are well recognized after long-segment fusion; however, their incidence, predictors, and impact in short-segment constructs remain poorly characterized, and the spectrum of these complications, their radiographic/clinical predictors, and their relationship to health-related quality of life (HRQoL) are insufficiently defined. We aimed to describe outcomes after short-segment fusion, compare patients with and without complications, evaluate HRQoL change and MCID attainment, and identify independent radiographic and clinical risk factors for complications. Materials and Methods: We retrospectively queried a multicenter ASD database for consecutive adults undergoing posterior instrumented fusion of ≤ 4 levels. Patients with at least 2-year follow-up were included. Complications were 26.3% Implant-related problems, 23.7% adjacent segment disease, 18.4% fractures (pedicle /sacrum), 15.8% junctional kyphosis (PJK/DJK), 7.9% pseudarthrosis and 7,9 others, respectively. In univariate radiographic comparisons, early postoperative (6W) residual-deformity measures, between non-complicated vs complicated groups were RPV (-9.45 ± 6.91, -4.99 ± 5.35; p = 0.002), PT apical translation to C7 (1.54 ± 2.45, 6.52 ± 5.87; p = 0.013), GAP score (6.52 ± 4.02, 4.03 ± 3.55; p = 0.003), and Major Cobb (28.20 ± 15.49, 21.84 ± 13.36; p = 0.032). Baseline GAP and Roussouly category distributions did not differ between groups. From baseline to Last, both groups statistically improved across HRQoL instruments. Between-group testing COMI Back change (non-complicated: Δ = 3.42 ± 2.46, p < 0.001 and complicated: Δ = 5.07 ± 1.64, p < 0.001) ( p = 0.046) and SF-36 PCS (Δ = 3.73 ± 11.82, p = 0.465 and Δ = 13.38 ± 9.71; p = 0.002, respectively) (p = 0.029) were significant, while differences in ODI and SRS-22 changes were not significant. MCID attainment for ODI, SF-36 PCS, and SRS-22 was observed in both groups. The radiographic multivariable model retained two 6W predictors-RPV (OR = 1.11 per unit; 95%CI 1.03-1.20; p = 0.004) and proximal thoracic apical translation to C7 (OR = 1.34 per unit; 95%CI 1.06-1.71; p = 0.016)-with acceptable discrimination (AUC = 0.73, Brier = 0.17). A clinical model identified prior spine surgery and current tobacco use as independent risk factors (AUC = 0.67; Brier = 0.17). Conclusion: In ≤ 4-level ASD fusions, approximately one quarter of patients experienced a complication, yet clinically meaningful improvements in pain, disability, and disease-specific HRQoL were achieved in both groups. Even in this deformity cohort not primarily addressed with extensive corrective surgery, patients achieved substantial, complication-independent improvements in HRQoL. Prior spine surgery and active smoking emerged as the strongest clinical risk factors for complications. Future comparative studies should clarify selection drivers and outcomes in similarly deformed patients treated with short-segment versus long-segment fusion.

## A062: The effect of preoperative rehabilitation on adult spinal deformity patient outcomes, patient recovery kinetics, and cost effectiveness

Peter Passias

1

, Kyriakos Chatzis

1

, Mohammad Daher

1

, Francesca Totis

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Anthony Baumann

2

, Tobi Onafowokan

1

, Max Fisher

1

, Ethan Cottrill

1

1
Duke University, Durham, United States, 
2
Cleveland Clinic, Ohio, United States
Introduction: Adult spinal deformity (ASD) is a debilitating disorder of the lumbar and thoracic spine that significantly impacts patient quality of life. Surgical correction is a proven treatment option that provides functional restoration and pain relief. Preoperative rehabilitation programs have recently been implemented to prepare patients for surgery and to promote patient health. The purpose of this study was to identify the effect of preoperative rehabilitation on surgical ASD patient outcomes. Material and methods: This is a retrospective analysis of a consecutive series of 899 ASD Patients. ASD patients with baseline (BL) and two-year (2Y) follow-up were included if they had preoperative rehabilitation data. Patients were divided into 2 groups: those who had preoperative rehabilitation (Prehab+) and those who did not (Prehab-). Prehab consisted of physical and mental components. Patients were excluded if they presented with any of the following at BL: severe neurological deficit ( < 3/5), minimal ambulation, or current depression/anxiety. Normalized HRQL scores at BL and follow-up intervals (6W, 1Y, 2Y) were generated. Normalized HRQLs were plotted and area under the curve was calculated, generating one number describing overall recovery (Integrated Health State [IHS]). Cost was calculated using the PearlDiver database. Cost per Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) at 2Y were calculated. Means comparison tests and Multivariable regression analysis assessed patient reported outcomes and cost adjusting for baseline and surgical characteristics. Results: The study included 464 patients, with 186 in the preoperative rehabilitation group (Prehab+) and 278 in the non-rehabilitation group (Prehab-). Prehab+ patients were older (65.5 ± 11.8 vs. 57.2 ± 14.9 years; p < 0.001), had a higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) (2.2 ± 1.7 vs. 1.5 ± 1.6; p < 0.001), and a higher BMI (28.4 ± 6.0 vs. 26.2 ± 5.0; p < 0.001). They also exhibited higher rates of comorbidities such as hypertension, arthritis, and diabetes compared to the Prehab- group. Despite these differences, Prehab+ patients achieved significantly better outcomes. Prehab+ patients had shorter lengths of stay (LOS) (7.0 ± 4.3 vs. 7.8 ± 4.1 days; p = 0.045) and lower estimated blood loss (1177.0 ± 1325.3 ml vs. 1532.8 ± 1410.7 ml; p = 0.006). Transfusion rates were also lower in the Prehab+ group (54% vs. 67%; p = 0.003). Early discharge was more common in the Prehab+ group, with significantly more patients discharged within three days (13.0% vs. 3.2%; p < 0.001). SICU admission rates were lower in Prehab+ patients (51.6% vs. 65.4%; p = 0.003). Prehab+ patients had a lower rate of overall complications (69.9% vs. 78.4%; p = 0.038) and medical complications (16.7% vs. 24.8%; p = 0.036). The reoperation rate was significantly reduced in the Prehab+ group (18.3% vs. 33.5%; p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis confirmed that Prehab+ patients had a lower risk of complications (OR: 0.6; 95% CI: 0.42-0.87; p = 0.035) and reoperation (OR: 0.38; 95% CI: 0.24-0.61; p < 0.001). Prehab+ patients also demonstrated superior health-related quality of life (HRQL) outcomes at two years, including higher rates of achieving the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) in SF-36 PCS at 6 weeks (42.9% vs. 15.1%; p = 0.003) and SRS-22r total score at one year (OR: 3.11; 95% CI: 1.16-8.4; p = 0.024). Cost-effectiveness analysis revealed that Prehab+ patients had a lower cost per QALY at two years ($14,463 vs. $45,515; p < 0.05). Conclusion: Preoperative rehabilitation appears to be significantly associated with a shorter length of stay, better reported clinical outcomes, greater utility gained, costs by procedure and cost effectiveness at two-year follow-up following adult spinal deformity surgery

## A063: Posterior vertebral column resection with preservation of posterior ligamentous complex for severe angular spinal kyphotic deformity: a comparative study

Lijin Zhou

1

, Honghao Yang

1

, Yong Hai

1

1

Beijing Chao-Yang Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Angular spinal kyphotic deformity could result in significant cardiopulmonary dysfunction, poor self-image, and neurological deficits. Posterior vertebral column resection (PVCR) is a highly effective technique for correcting spinal malignment. However, the limitations such as instability from radical removal of posterior elements associated with a high rate of neurological complications. The purpose of this study was to compare the effectiveness and safety of modified PVCR and traditional PVCR in the treatment of patients with angular spinal kyphotic deformity. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted. Patients who underwent PVCR for angular spinal kyphotic deformity with a minimum of 24 months follow-up from March 2018 to November 2022 were included. These patients had a focal kyphosis (FK) with deformity angular ratio greater than 20. Patients were divided into the modified PVCR group and the traditional PVCR group based on the procedures. The modified PVCR, which preserved the posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) throughout the process, was performed for patients who were admitted to the hospital after October 2020. Demographic information, radiological parameters, surgical information, health-related quality of life, and complications were collected and compared between the groups. Results: A total of 62 patients with angular spinal kyphotic deformity were recruited in this study. The mean age at surgery was 42.29 ± 12.42 years. Among the patients, 31 were in the modified PVCR group and 31 were in the traditional PVCR group. The FK was corrected from 125.54° ± 15.83° to 48.19° ± 16.07° in the modified PVCR group and 119.77° ± 17.10° to 57.20° ± 15.43° in the traditional PVCR group. The correction rate of FK in the modified PVCR group was significantly greater than the traditional PVCR group (62.26% ± 10.24% vs. 51.46% ± 15.49%, p = 0.002). There were no significant differences in the operation time, estimated blood loss, and health-related quality of life between the two groups. However, the incidence of neurological complications was 16.1% in the modified PVCR group, significantly lower than the 38.7% observed in the traditional PVCR group (p = 0.046). Conclusion: By preserving the PLC throughout the osteotomy, the modified PVCR outperformed the traditional technique in terms of both neurological complications and deformity correction.

## A064: Management of painful spinal metastases: a systematic review of GRADE-based evidence across pain types

W. Christopher Newman

1

, Konstantina Matsoukas

1

, Marie-Laure Vial

2

, Ori Barzilai

1

, Ilya Laufer

3

, on behalf of AO Spine Knowledge Forum Tumor

1
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, United States,

2
AO Foundation, AO Network Clinical Research, Davos, Switzerland,

3

NYU Langone Health, Department of Neurosurgery, New York, United States

Background: Spinal metastases affect up to 40% of patients with cancer and are a major cause of morbidity, primarily due to pain. The AO Spine Knowledge Forum Tumor recently formalized six pain types in spinal metastatic disease: mechanical-axial, mechanical-radicular, inflammatory-axial, inflammatory-radicular, neuropathic-central, and neuropathic-peripheral pain. Clear classification of these types allows a more rigorous alignment of interventions with pain mechanisms. We conducted a systematic review to assess the quality of evidence supporting different therapeutic strategies for each pain type using the GRADE framework. Methods: Following the Preferred Reporting Items of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) methodology, we conducted a systematic review of PubMed (NLM) database on March 17, 2025 for English-language studies published in the last five years (2020-2025) reporting pain outcomes for patients with spinal metastases treated with radiation therapy (RT), surgery, vertebral augmentation, ablation techniques, interventional injections, neuroablative procedures, and pharmacologic interventions. Studies were screened for explicit pain endpoints. Evidence quality was appraised using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system, categorizing interventions as high, moderate, low, or very low quality of evidence. Results: A total of 148 articles were included. High-quality evidence supports RT and opioids for inflammatory-axial pain, with strong and consistent pain reduction across randomized trials and meta-analyses. Mechanical-axial pain demonstrates high-quality evidence for kyphoplasty and vertebroplasty, and moderate-quality evidence for surgical stabilization. Inflammatory-radicular pain has moderate-quality evidence for both RT and surgical decompression, while mechanical-radicular pain is supported by moderate-quality evidence for surgical intervention. For vertebral body ablation (radiofrequency or cryoablation), evidence for inflammatory-axial pain is moderate but limited by a lack of randomized data. Intrathecal drug delivery demonstrates moderate-quality evidence for neuropathic-central and neuropathic-peripheral pain, particularly in refractory cases. Neuroablative approaches such as spinal cord stimulation, cordotomy, and dorsal root entry zone lesioning are supported by low-quality evidence, largely from retrospective series. Evidence for epidural steroid injections and neurolytic blocks remains low, with small heterogeneous studies and short follow-up periods. Conclusion: Inconsistent and vague definitions of pain types limit the overall quality of pain outcomes across various studies. Despite this, high-quality evidence exists for RT, opioids, and vertebral augmentation techniques, while other modalities remain supported by moderate or low-quality evidence. Adoption of standardized pain type definitions in future trials will improve the ability to refine and personalize evidence-based care.

## A065: A novel rat caudal spine metastasis resection model for therapeutic implant screening

Nitai Klein

1,2

, Ateeque Siddique

1

, Michael H

1,3

, Lisbet Haglund

1,2

, Derek Rosenzweig

1

1

Division of Orthopedics - McGill University Health Center, Shriner's Hospital for Children - Canada, Montreal, Montreal, Canada

2

Shriner's Hospital for Children - Canada, Montreal, Canada

3

University of Conneticut Health Center, Farmignton, United States

Introduction: The spine is the most frequent site of osseous metastases. Surgical resection often leaves critical-sized bone defects and residual tumor cells that drive recurrence. Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement is commonly used for reconstruction due to its strength and accessibility, but it lacks therapeutic function. We developed a doxorubicin (DOX)-loaded PMMA composite using mesoporous silica nanoparticles to enable sustained local drug release. While effective in vitro against breast and prostate cancer models, its performance in a relevant in vivo spinal setting has not been established. The aim of the study was to develop an in vivo spinal metastasis resection model and evaluate the efficacy of DOX-PMMA in reducing tumor recurrence. Material and Methods: Luciferase-tagged MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells were encapsulated in alginate-gelatin hydrogel and implanted into caudal vertebrae of immunodeficient rats. Six weeks later, tumors were resected and reconstructed with either control PMMA or DOX-PMMA. Tumor progression was monitored by bioluminescence and CT imaging. At 10 weeks, blood tests, micro-CT, histology, and immunohistochemistry (Caspase-3, Ki-67) were performed. Results: Tumors remained viable and stable until resection. Control animals demonstrated elevated lactate dehydrogenase and creatine kinase, consistent with disease progression. Micro-CT and histologic analyses are ongoing. Conclusion: This novel rat caudal vertebra model provides a reproducible platform for testing spinal biomaterials. Local delivery of DOX via PMMA cement reduced tumor recurrence without systemic chemotherapy. This strategy holds promise for improving local disease control and quality of life in patients with spinal metastases.

Introduction: No single indicator captures the essence of a desirable surgical outcome for primary malignant bone tumors of the spine. Composite outcome measures have been used to comprehensively define the success of achieving an optimal surgical outcome in general surgical oncology but not spinal surgery. To achieve consensus in defining a composite surgical outcome measure for use in spinal primary malignant bone tumor research. ## A067: Influence of high BMI on prognosis in patients undergoing surgery for spinal metastases

Maxwell Sahhar

1

, Ahmed Sulieman

2

, Malcolm Hamilton-Hall III

2

, Yesha Parekh

2

, Myung-Jin Cha

2

, Andrew Kim

2

, Goutham Yalla

2

, Daniel Lubelski

3

, Sang Hun Lee

2

1
Brown University Warren Alpert Medical School, Providence, United States,

2
Johns Hopkins University Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Baltimore, United States,

3

Johns Hopkins University Department of Neurological Surgery, Baltimore, United States

Introduction: Body mass index (BMI) is a widely used clinical metric with complex implications in surgical oncology. In line with population-wide increases to BMI, more patients undergoing surgery for spinal metastasis have a high BMI. While obesity is traditionally considered a risk factor in spine surgery, the impact of high BMI on patients undergoing decompression and instrumented fusion (DIF) for spinal metastases remains undefined. Material and Methods: The American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) database was queried from 2016 to 2022 for patients who underwent DIF with ICD-10 codes for metastatic spinal disease. Generalized additive models (GAM) were used to assess the relationship between BMI and 30-day postoperative mortality and major complications, adjusting for demographic, clinical, and procedural covariates. BMI was modeled as a smooth term to account for non-linear associations. Results: A total of 2,256 patients were included in the study. The mean age was 62.8 years, and the mean BMI was 27.4 kg/m2. The overall 30-day mortality rate was 6.7%, with patients undergoing thoracic and cervical DF having higher mortality than patients undergoing lumbar DF (p = 0.003). BMI was a significant non-linear predictor of mortality (EDF = 3.253, p = 0.0011) and major complications (EDF = 1.000, p = 0.0464). Mortality risk increased substantially below a BMI of 22.5 kg/m2, with a 4.45 times higher risk and 2.26 times higher risk for patients at a BMI >18.5 and 18.5-22.5, respectively (p <0.001 and p = 0.002). No significant increase in risk was seen in patients of higher BMIs, even in patients exceeding a BMI of 40 kg/m2. Functional dependence and pulmonary comorbidities were independently associated with mortality. Major complications occurred more frequently in patients with low BMI and functional impairment but these trends were not modified by spinal region in adjusted analyses. Conclusion: High BMI, even when exceeding standardized obesity cutoffs, is not a predictor of mortality and major complications following decompression and instrumented fusion for spine metastasis. Low BMI of less than 22.5 is a significant non-linear predictor of mortality and major complications. These findings suggest that BMI can serve as a practical proxy for physiological reserve in preoperative risk stratification for spine metastasis surgery.

## A068: Augmented reality-assisted resection of intradural extramedullary spinal tumor: a single-center experience

Giacomo Cammarata

1

, Francesco Certo

1

, Angelo Basile

1

, Sara Pappalardo

1

, Erica Grasso

1

, Giuseppe Sotera

1

, Giuseppe Barbagallo

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Universitary Hospital G. Rodolico-San Marco“, Catania, Italy

Introduction: The integration of augmented reality (AR) into neurosurgical practice has recently gained momentum, with the goal of enhancing intraoperative visualization and surgical precision. In spinal surgery, AR-assisted techniques offer the potential to improve the accuracy of tumor localization and resection while minimizing the need for repeated fluoroscopy or extensive bony exposure. Intradural extramedullary (IDEM) spinal tumors, which are often benign but may be infiltrative or malignant, represent an ideal setting to evaluate AR accuracy due to the need for precise localization before dural opening. This study presents a single-center experience with AR-assisted resection of IDEM spinal tumors, focusing on accuracy, histological variability, and the correlation between morphometric parameters and AR performance. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 30 patients (mean age 56.4 years, range 12-77) who underwent AR-assisted IDEM tumor resection between January 2024 and August 2025. Demographic and clinical data, tumor characteristics, surgical approach, and histopathological findings were collected. The primary endpoint was intraoperative AR shift (mm), defined as the distance between AR-predicted and true tumor localization. Secondary analyses investigated correlations between AR shift and tumor morphometrics (antero-posterior [AP], cranio-caudal [CC] diameters, tumor volume), histological subtype, and spinal region. Statistical evaluation was performed using Pearson’s correlation and analysis of variance. Results: The mean AR shift was 2.3 ± 1.0 mm, consistently within an acceptable intraoperative margin. Correlation analyses showed that larger tumors were associated with greater AR shift, particularly for cranio-caudal diameter (r = 0.64, p < 0.01), while volume (r = 0.47, p = 0.04) and AP diameter (r = 0.29, n.s.) had weaker associations. These findings confirm that elongation along the cranio-caudal axis is the most relevant predictor of reduced AR accuracy. Histology significantly influenced performance. Meningiomas and schwannomas showed the lowest shift (1.2-2.3 mm), reflecting their circumscribed nature, while more infiltrative or malignant lesions demonstrated higher values: plasmocytoma (3.0 mm), lymphomas (3.2 mm), paraganglioma (2.9 mm), and germ cell tumor (3.8 mm). Between-group comparison showed a significant difference in AR shift between circumscribed and infiltrative histologies (p = 0.03). Regional analysis revealed comparable accuracy across levels: thoracic 2.45 mm, cervical 2.35 mm, and lumbar 2.03 mm, without significant differences (p = 0.42). Variability was slightly higher in the thoracic spine, possibly due to respiratory and anatomical factors. Conclusion: AR-assisted spinal tumor resection proved highly accurate, with mean shifts consistently below 3 mm. Accuracy was greatest for circumscribed lesions and decreased modestly with larger or infiltrative tumors. Statistical analyses highlighted a strong correlation with cranio-caudal extension and significant differences across histological categories, supporting AR reliability in well-defined tumors. These results align with emerging literature reporting sub-3 mm accuracy in AR-guided spine procedures, confirming reproducibility in oncological contexts. Beyond precision, AR reduced reliance on intraoperative fluoroscopy and improved surgical orientation, particularly in challenging thoracic cases. Our findings support the feasibility and safety of AR integration in spinal oncology, suggesting it may complement navigation and intraoperative imaging. Larger, prospective studies are warranted to validate long-term outcomes and explore its role in complex, multi-level, or recurrent tumors.

## A069: Development of the Spinal Metastasis Staging (SMS) System: an international multidisciplinary expert panel and survey study

Harmen Kuijten

1

, Roxanne Gal

1

, Nicolien Kasperts

1

, Joanne van der Velden

1

, Jorrit-Jan Verlaan

1

1

University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands

Introduction: If left untreated, spinal metastases typically progress from an asymptomatic stage to advanced stages with debilitating pain, spinal instability, and neurological deficits. Timely recognition is critical, yet diagnostic and referral delays remain common as many patients first present to non-spine specialists. While several guidelines exist for managing spinal metastases, these are designed mainly for spine surgeons and radiation oncologists, treating patients who are already diagnosed with spinal metastases. This leaves a gap for simple classification and referral tools aimed at non-spine clinicians. To address this problem, we developed a preliminary Spinal Metastasis Staging (SMS) system and a corresponding referral tool. Material and Methods: The SMS system defines four stages reflecting the natural progression of spinal metastases: SMS I, asymptomatic; SMS II, inflammatory (non-mechanical) pain; SMS III, mechanical pain and/or instability; and SMS IV, neurological deficits and/or cord compression. Based on these stages, we developed a referral tool in the form of a decision tree, designed to guide clinicians on referral priorities and urgency. This referral tool can be presented in different formats (e.g., interactive online versions), but for evaluation purposes it was distributed as a concise, color-coded, two-sided pocket map. The preliminary SMS system and pocket map were revised through two regional and one international expert panel rounds. The refined pocket map was then evaluated in an international online survey distributed via professional societies and networks including AO Spine. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative feedback underwent thematic analysis for incorporation into a next version. Results: Expert panels endorsed the SMS system and suggested refinements, including clearer definitions of pain types, flowchart simplification, and radiologist involvement for consistent SINS and Bilsky reporting. In the subsequent international survey, with 120 respondents, 89% considered the pocket map easy to understand, 82% reported no missing or unclear steps or decision points, and 97% judged its format suitable. Among the 33 non-spine specialists (28% of respondents), 91% indicated the pocket map would support more timely or appropriate referrals, and 61% reported they would use the tool frequently or always, 33% occasionally, and only 6% never, mainly because they already rely on personal experience or collegial discussion. Conclusion: The SMS system and corresponding referral tool, evaluated in the form of a pocket map, were positively received in both expert panels and an international survey, with feedback supporting further refinement. The findings highlight the tool’s strong potential to facilitate earlier recognition and referral of patients with spinal metastases. The feedback is currently being incorporated into the next version for dissemination among non-spine clinicians. Further work will comprise clinical validation, using the SMS system as a classification framework to examine whether the proposed stages represent clinically distinct patient groups and how they relate to outcomes such as quality of life, survival, and healthcare costs.

Priyanshu Saha

## A072: Correlation between Adamkiewicz artery level and tumor localization in metastatic spine disease: implications for preoperative embolization

Wei-Lin Pan

1

, Yen-Heng Lin

1

, Yu Cheng Huang

1

, Fon-Yih Tsuang

1

1

National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: The Adamkiewicz artery (AKA), also known as the great anterior radiculomedullary artery, is the largest radiculomedullary artery of the spinal cord. Typically arising between T8 and L2, it provides the dominant contribution to the anterior spinal artery (ASA) and perfuses the lower two-thirds of the spinal cord. For major spinal surgeries such as total en bloc spondylectomy, preoperative transarterial embolization (TAE) of radiculomedullary arteries is recommended to reduce blood loss, operative time, and improve visualization. However, when the AKA connects to the ASA, embolization carries a high risk of spinal cord infarction and is often spared, potentially compromising surgical hemostasis. We reviewed metastatic spine tumor cases undergoing preoperative TAE, focusing on patients in whom the AKA was spared, to examine whether a correlation exists between tumor level and AKA level. Material and Methods: Patients with metastatic thoracic or lumbar spinal tumors who underwent preoperative TAE between 2022 and 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Cases with skipped or diffuse patterns were excluded. Tumor levels were numerically encoded (C7 = 0, T1 = 1 … L5 = 17); in multilevel involvement, the mean of the highest and lowest levels was assigned. Angiographic records were reviewed to identify the AKA; in patients with two AKAs (n = 4), the artery closest to the tumor was used. Spearman’s rank correlation was employed to assess the relationship between tumor and AKA levels, and a Binomial test evaluated whether tumors occurred within ±1 vertebral level of the AKA more frequently than expected by chance. Results: Forty-eight patients with identified AKAs were included. Spearman’s correlation showed a strong positive association between tumor level and AKA level (ρ = 0.884, p < 0.001). Binomial analysis revealed that 54% of tumors were located within ±1 vertebral level of the AKA, significantly higher than the expected random probability of 18% (p < 0.001). Conclusion: In patients with metastatic spinal tumors undergoing TAE, tumor levels were strongly correlated with the level of the AKA, and tumors were significantly more likely to occur near the artery than expected by chance. These findings suggest that ASA supply through the AKA may influence the localization of spinal metastases. Recognition of this association may improve embolization planning and surgical strategy, balancing hemostatic control with spinal cord safety.

## A073: The correlation between changes in radiological cervical parameters and facial asymmetry

Joana Hankollari

1

, Nikollaq Leka

2

1

Albanian University Tirana, Tirana, Albania

2

University of Medicine Tirana, Tirana, Albania

Introduction: In my daily practice as a rheumatologist, one of the most frequent complaints I deal with is related to the cervical spine. When posture changes of the cervical spine occur, it is often obvious that facial asymmetry exists. The aim of this study is to identify changes in the cervical spine that correlate with facial (a)symmetry. Identifying a potential correlation would be of great clinical significance, as doctors who treat cervical spine pathologies would be more cautious about problems related to facial asymmetry. Material and Methods: 32 patients aged 18-64 years were included in this prospective study who had complaints about their cervical spine. Cervical radiographs were used to assess parameters such as C2-C7 Lordosis (CL), T1 Slope (T1S), Thoracic Inlet Angle (TIA), Neck Tilt (NT), C2-C7 Sagittal Vertical Axis (C2-C7 SVA), cervical and cranial tilting for each patient. The assessment of facial asymmetry was done through inspection and P-A cephalometry. Results: Changes in cervical radiographic parameters occurred in 53.13 % of patients. The parameters that were most altered were: C2-C7 Lordosis (CL), T1 Slope (T1S), C2-C7 Sagittal Vertical Axis (C2-C7 SVA), cervical and cranial tilting. Facial asymmetry was found in 64.71% of patients who experienced changes in these parameters, whereas only 20% of cases without cervical radiological parameters had facial asymmetry. Conclusion: Facial asymmetry is more prevalent in patients with changes in cervical radiological parameters than in those without cervical radiological parameters changes.

## A074: Cervical pedicle inlet screws: clinical results of a novel trajectory for navigated screw placement in the sub-axial cervical spine

Christopher Martin

1

, Bishop Anyiwe

1

, Regan Carlson

1

, Kari Odland

1

1

University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States

Introduction: Lateral mass screws are widely used in the sub-axial cervical spine, but have poor pullout strength and result in a screw tulip that is medial. This medial position makes passing a rod to a nearby pedicle screw more difficult, which has particular relevance in long constructs crossing the cervico-thoracic junction. Sub-axial pedicle screws have been described, but carry a risk of neuro-vascular injury. Furthermore, many sub-axial pedicles are simply too small to safely pass a screw. The cervical pedicle inlet (CPI) trajectory involves a lateral starting point similar to a true pedicle screw which allows for easier rod passage ( ), but the tip of the screw stops in the dense bone at the pedicle inlet ( ), thus limiting neurovascular risk. Our group recently published a cadaveric biomechanical study showing that CPI screws have a higher pullout strength than lateral mass screws. However, limited clinical data exist. This study aims to report the early clinical experience with this new screw trajectory, with an emphasis on screw related complications and clinical outcomes. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 227 CPI screws from 128 consecutive cases from a single surgeon at a single center. All patients were ≥ 18 years and underwent posterior cervical fusion with navigated CPI screw placement in the sub-axial cervical spine between 2020 and 2025. All screws were placed with intra-operative O-Arm navigation. CT scans were available on all patients and were used to classify breaches with a modified Gertzbein-Robbins scale. Results: 146 of 227 screws (64%) were grade 0 (completely within bone). 72 screws (32%) had a grade 1 (< 1 mm) cortical breach. 9 screws (4%) had a grade 2 breach (> 1 mm). All of these were recognized on the intra-operative check spin with the O-arm and 4 were repositioned while the other 5 were removed. There were no neurovascular injuries or mechanical failures, and no patient had radicular pains or required a return to the OR as a result of screw related complications. There was no patient where a CPI could not be placed. Conclusion: Use of image-guidance allows for safe placement along the CPI trajectory, with no recorded screw related complications. For patients with cervical pedicles that are too small to accept a true pedicle screw, the CPI trajectory is a reasonable alternative. The lateral starting point of the CPI trajectory facilitates rod passage to other pedicle screws in the construct, and may have particular applications in minimally invasive approaches that utilize a paramedian incision.

Marco Ajello

## A077: K-line tilt as a predictor of postoperative kyphotic deformity after laminectomy for cervical myelopathy and its correlation with clinical outcomes

Laksh Agrawal

1

, Mihir Bapat

1

, Bharat Patel

1

, Amandeep Gujral

1

, Ashutosh Tripathi

1

, Rushikesh Jadhav

1

, Akshaj Sharma

1

1

Nanavati Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mumbai, India

Introduction: Laminectomy is widely performed for multilevel degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) and K-line-positive (K-line (+)) ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL). However, postoperative kyphotic deformity develops in up to one-fifth of patients and is associated with inferior neurological recovery, often necessitating additional stabilization. The risk is particularly high in patients with preoperative straight alignment. While K-line tilt-a radiographic measure of the angle between the K-line and a vertical reference-has been validated as a predictor of deformity after laminoplasty and anterior procedures, its role in laminectomy remains undefined. This study aimed to determine whether preoperative K-line tilt predicts postoperative kyphosis following laminectomy, establish an optimal cutoff value, and evaluate its relationship with clinical outcomes. Neurological function was assessed with the Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, and recovery rate was calculated. A tilt angle >21° confers a high risk of postoperative deformity and suboptimal recovery. In such cases, laminectomy alone may be insufficient, and supplemental stabilization with anterior or posterior fusion should be considered to prevent deformity and optimize outcomes.

## A078: Surgical safety strategies for cervical kyphosis in ankylosing spondylitis based on modified C7 PSO

Canhua Ye

1

, Huiren Tao

1

1

The University of Hong Kong - Shenzhen Hospital, Shenzhen, China

Introduction: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton, with a global prevalence of 0.1%-1.4% and higher incidence in males (3.4:1). Cervical kyphosis is a severe late complication, causing restricted vision, dysphagia, and poor quality of life. While cervical osteotomy is effective, its complexity raises risks. Results: The modified PSO procedure was performed at the C7 level for all 4 patients. The upper instrumented vertebrae (UIV) were primarily C3 or C4, while the lower instrumented vertebrae (LIV) were mainly T3 or T4. There were no complications such as loosening, infection, or sensory/motor deficits. Conclusion: With effective perioperative management, modified C7 PSO surgery is a safe and effective treatment for cervical kyphosis in ankylosing spondylitis patients. It significantly corrects the cervical deformity and improves the horizontal gaze function, providing a safe and effective treatment option for these patients, with important clinical implications.

## A079: Chiari I malformation and scoliosis: does posterior-fossa decompression influence the curve progression? A systematic review of the literature and meta-analysis

Davide Palombi

1

, Sergio De Salvatore

2

, Paolo Brigato

2

, Leonardo Oggiano

3

, Gianpiero Tamburrini

1

, Luca Massimi

1

, Timothée De Saint-Denis

4

1

Department of Pediatric Neurosurgery, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore di Roma, Rome, Italy

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Campus Bio Medico di Roma, Rome, Italy

3

Department of Orthopaedics, Ospedale Pediatrico Bambino Gesù di Roma, Rome, Italy

4

Service de Orthopedie et Chirurgie Reparatrice de l'Enfant, Hopital Armand Trousseau, Paris, France

Introduction: Chiari I malformation (CIM) is frequently associated with scoliosis, and syringomyelia (SyM). Posterior fossa decompression (PFD) is often performed before spinal fusion, but its impact on scoliosis progression remains debated. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess scoliosis outcomes after PFD in pediatric patients and to identify predictive factors of curve behavior. Material and Methods: A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, Medline, Scopus, and Web of Science up to January 2025, following PRISMA guidelines. Eleven retrospective studies comprising 380 pediatric patients with CIM and scoliosis treated with PFD were included. Primary outcome was scoliosis stabilization or improvement after PFD. Results: The mean age at surgery was 10.6 ± 1.8 years, and the mean preoperative major curve angle was 34.0° ± 7.4°. Syringomyelia was present in the majority of cases, with postoperative improvement documented in 81.6% of patients. The pooled success rate (improved or stable scoliosis) after PFD was 57% (95% CI: 49-65%), while curve progression occurred in 45% (95% CI: 37-54%). Subgroup analysis of patients undergoing PFD with duroplasty showed a similar success rate (54%, 95% CI: 45-63%). Meta-regression demonstrated that older age at surgery (OR per +1 year = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.10-1.39, p < 0.001) and larger preoperative Cobb angle (OR per +5° = 0.79, 95% CI: 0.65-0.96, p = 0.012) were associated with higher risk of curve progression. In the duroplasty subgroup, only age remained significant. Conclusion: PFD leads to stabilization or improvement of scoliosis in more than half of pediatric patients with CIM, but a substantial proportion still experience progression, often requiring spinal fusion. Younger age and smaller preoperative Cobb angles are associated with better outcomes. Early identification of risk factors and a multidisciplinary approach are essential to optimize surgical planning.

## A080: The hemodynamic and complication impact of anterior column release in adult spinal deformity

Diego Soto Rubio

1

, Schahin Salmanian

1

, Ahmad Alkadri

2

, Eric Cohen

2

, Daven Mejica

1

, John Lingam

3

, Shrinit Babel

1

, Dana Saleh

1

, Mohsen Rostami

1

, Puya Alikhani

1

1
Department of Neurosurgery, Brain and Spine, University of South Florida, Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States,

2
USF Health Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States,

3

University of South Florida, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Complex adult spinal deformity (ASD) correction often requires extensive resection of posterior or middle column elements, which can result in substantial intraoperative blood loss. Traditional open surgical techniques are frequently performed in a single stage, increasing the risk of significant blood loss during one operative event. Anterior column release (ACR), performed via a retroperitoneal approach, has been proposed to mitigate these risks; however, ACR often requires staged procedures, which could potentially offset this advantage. This study aimed to evaluate whether ACR reduces estimated blood loss (EBL), transfusion requirements, and perioperative medical complications compared with open osteotomy-based approaches. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 146 patients who underwent ASD correction between 2016 and 2022 with ≥ 1 year of follow-up. Demographic and surgical data were collected, including the number of instrumented levels, type of osteotomy, staging, total EBL, and transfusion requirements. Total EBL was calculated as the cumulative blood loss from all operative stages. The number of packed red blood cell (PRBC) units transfused intraoperatively and postoperatively was also recorded. Results: Thirty-two patients underwent ACR and were compared with 114 patients treated using open approaches, including pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO), intradiscal osteotomies, and Smith-Peterson osteotomies (SPO). Baseline characteristics, including age, BMI, and preoperative Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), were similar between groups. ACR patients had significantly shorter instrumented constructs compared with non-ACR cases (6.97 ± 2.41 vs. 9.04 ± 2.86 levels, p < 0.001). Percutaneous screw placement was more common in ACR cases (31.3%). ACR demonstrated substantially lower EBL compared to open approaches (634 ± 446 mL vs. 954 ± 778 mL, p = 0.001) and reduced transfusion requirements (1.34 ± 1.78 vs. 2.23 ± 2.35 PRBC units, p = 0.030). The rates of perioperative medical complications-including pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, pneumothorax, and sepsis-were low and did not differ significantly between groups (all p > 0.17). Conclusion: ACR demonstrated a significant hemodynamic advantage, with lower blood loss and decreased transfusion requirements compared to open osteotomy-based techniques. However, this reduction in EBL and transfusions did not translate into differences in overall medical complication rates. These findings suggest that the choice between ACR and open approaches should be primarily guided by the desired surgical goals and alignment correction, rather than expectations of improved perioperative recovery.

## A082: Perioperative risk stratification in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: the importance of metabolic syndrome vs obesity

Lane McCoy

1

, Travis Kotzur

1

, Brian Neuman

1,2

1

Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, St. Louis, United States

2

Barnes Jewish Hospital, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: While obesity is frequently used as a surrogate for perioperative risk in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) surgery, body mass index (BMI) alone does not reflect the underlying metabolic derangements that may contribute to adverse outcomes. Metabolic syndrome (MetS) may offer improved stratification of surgical risk. This study investigates the association between MetS and perioperative outcomes in ACDF surgery and evaluates its predictive utility relative to obesity alone. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed on patients from TriNetX databases. MetS was defined by the presence of at least three of the following: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, high central adiposity, or low high-density lipoprotein. Obesity was defined as a BMI >30 kg/m2. Patients were stratified into four cohorts: Metabolically healthy (MetH), MetS, Obese MetH, and Obese with another MetS component (without full MetS diagnosis). Primary outcomes included postoperative infection, mechanical complication, postoperative spinal implant infection (PSII), pseudoarthrosis, revision, deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism, sepsis, wound disruption, and readmission. Propensity score matching was used to control for baseline demographics and Charlson Comorbidity Index. Comparative analyses were conducted between MetS and each of the other cohorts, as well as between obesity alone and MetH. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Results: A total of 92,724 patients, aged 40-90 years, who underwent primary ACDF were matched and included among all cohorts. MetS patients had significantly increased risk in all outcomes compared to MetH patients, where greatest increases were observed in wound disruption (RR 2.45; CI 1.96-3.06; p < 0.001), postoperative infection (RR 2.41; CI 2.02-2.87; p < 0.001), and PSII (RR 1.96; CI 1.63-2.37; p < 0.001). MetS patients also had significantly increased risk in all outcomes compared to Obese MetH patients, with exception to pseudoarthrosis. The most significant increases were observed in readmission (RR 2.06; CI 1.91-2.21; p < 0.001), wound disruption (RR 1.92; CI 1.43-2.58, p < 0.001), and PSII (RR 1.89; CI 1.43-2.49; p < 0.001). Obese MetH patients were shown to have no significant increased risk for mechanical complication, PSII, or revision when compared to MetH patients. Likewise, MetS patients who were not obese were shown to have similar increased risks compared to MetH in many outcomes, specifically wound disruption (RR 2.07; CI 1.19-3.59; p = 0.008), postoperative infection (RR 2.11; CI 1.29-3.44; p = 0.002), mechanical complication (RR 1.61; CI 1.09-2.38; p = 0.015), and PSII (RR 3.26; CI 1.97-5.41; p < 0.001). Conclusion: MetS emerged as a more robust and comprehensive predictor of perioperative complications than obesity alone. Across nearly all measured outcomes, MetS was associated with substantially higher risks compared to both metabolically healthy patients and obese patients without metabolic derangements. Notably, these elevated risks persisted even among non-obese individuals with MetS, underscoring that adverse metabolic health drives much of the observed perioperative morbidity. In contrast, obesity without accompanying metabolic dysfunction did not significantly increase the risk for certain complications. These findings highlight the need to adopt a more nuanced approach that incorporates metabolic health status into preoperative counseling and optimization protocols to improve surgical outcomes.

## A083: Systematic review of surgical and complications outcomes after multilevel ALIFs

Igor Barreira

1

, Rafael Moriguchi

1

, Rodrigo Amaral

1

, Luiz Pimenta

1

, Fernando Marcelino

1

, Amabile Galeti

1

, Leandro Resende

1

, Igor Arthur Costa

1

, Gabriel Pokorny

1

, Jullyene Pokorny

1

, Bianca Soares

1

1

Instituto de Patologia da Coluna, São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Multilevel (≥ 2-level) ALIF, might carry higher complication burden than single-level ALIF, owing to greater anatomical complexity, and challenges that are usually avoided in single-level (L5-S1) approaches. As indications for multilevel ALIF expand to spinopelvic realignment, robust safety data are needed; existing studies are small and use inconsistent complication definitions. This systematic review and meta-analysis therefore seeks to quantify surgical and postoperative risks, guiding multidisciplinary planning and optimizing patient outcomes. Material and Methods: A rapid systematic review was performed (PRISMA-2020) in MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL from inception to 08 August 2025. We included English-language cohort or comparative studies that reported ≥ 2-level anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) and provided extractable data on peri-operative complications and/or at least one of the following continuous outcomes: operative time, estimated blood loss (EBL), and length of stay (LOS). Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts, assessed full texts, and extracted events, means, standard deviations, and sample sizes; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. (PROSPERO: CRD420251119413). Complication proportions were pooled with a logistic-normal random-effects generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) using the Paule-Mandel REML estimator and a 0.5-cell continuity correction. Continuous outcomes were meta-analysed with DerSimonian-Laird random effects on raw means. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified with τ2, and 95 % prediction intervals (PI) were calculated with a t-distribution (df = k - 2) to estimate the range for a future comparable study. Leave-one-out analyses explored single-study influence. Results: Twelve multilevel-ALIF cohorts were quantitatively analysed. Complications were reported in six studies (n = 30 948). A logistic-normal random-effects model yielded a pooled complication rate of 17 %, with a 95 % PI from 0.4 % to 92 %, indicating extreme between-study heterogeneity (τ2 = 1.77). Across nine multilevel-ALIF cohorts (total = 24 797 patients, 108 vascular events), the pooled risk of vascular injury was 2 %, with minimal residual heterogeneity, and with a narrow 95 % prediction interval (1.9 %-3.0 %). Five studies contributed operative metrics. Mean surgical time pooled to 144 min (95 % PI 13 - 275 min; τ2 = 1 400), and mean blood loss to 208 mL (95 % PI ≈ 0 - 504 mL; τ2 = 7 126). Length-of-stay (LOS), available in the same five cohorts, averaged 5.3 days; its 95 % PI ranged from 1.4 days (overnight discharge) to 9.2 days, with heterogeneity largely driven by a single Korean series (τ2 = 1.20). Leave-one-out analyses confirmed robustness of pooled complication and LOS estimates except when the highest-risk or longest-stay study was omitted, which reduced the pooled complication rate to 7 % and LOS to 4.4 days, respectively. Conclusion: Overall, contemporary multilevel ALIF demonstrates wide performance ranges across institutions: most centres report operative times under 2 h, blood loss under 250 mL, and hospitalisation under 1 week, but marked outliers can inflate pooled estimates and prediction bands. Evidence on ≥ 2-level ALIF remains sparse and highly inconsistent. Across 12 cohorts, the average complication rate (17 %) and wide 95% prediction interval (0.4 - 92%), compared to a very small vascular complication rate (2%), prediction interval (1.9% to 3%), suggests that different concepts of complications evaluation might generate a significant heterogeneity across studies possibly inflating the rate of overall complications, when compared to a more standardized criteria such as vascular injury.

## A084: A study on the pattern of vertebral marrow edema during normal healing process after lateral lumbar interbody fusion and its relationship with early postoperative lumbar symptoms

Xiaopeng Li

1,2,3

, Feng Li

3

, Qiang Yang

1,2,3

1

Capital Medical University Affiliated Beijing Friendship Hospital,Beijing, China,

2

Tianjin Hospital, Tianjin, China,

3

Weifang People’s Hospital, Weifang, China

Introduction: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) demonstrates significant clinical efficacy for lumbar degenerative diseases. Postoperative vertebral bone marrow edema, manifesting as distinct patterns on lumbar MRI, was observed in patients with low back pain and, notably, also in asymptomatic individuals. To investigate vertebral bone marrow edema patterns during normal LLIF healing and their association with early postoperative lumbar symptoms to guide clinical rehabilitation and complication prevention. Material and Methods: A single-center retrospective study with a minimum follow-up of 6 months. We conducted a single-centre, retrospective analysis of consecutive patients who underwent trans-psoas LLIF for degenerative lumbar disorders between September 2019 and January 2023. Baseline demographics, peri-operative details, and imaging data were extracted from the institutional database. Post-operative Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) back pain and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores were obtained by structured telephone interviews at 3 days, 3 months, and 6 months. Associations between clinical outcomes, bone mineral density (DXA) and body-mass index (BMI) were examined with SPSS software. Results: Post-operative vertebral bone-marrow oedema was classified on day-3 MRI as absent edema type, cage-surrounding type, or diffuse type. The incidence of BME was higher after three-level than single- or double-level fusions (70.6 % vs 44.9 % and 35.3 %, respectively; P < 0.05), with cage-surrounding oedema predominating in the latter groups (≈29 % each). VAS back pain scores did not differ between BME patterns at any time-point (P = 0.136, r < 0.2). On post-operative day 3, patients without oedema had lower ODI scores than those with cage-surrounding or diffuse oedema (P = 0.001), yielding a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.466, P < 0.01); this association disappeared at 3 and 6 months (P > 0.05, r < 0.2). Higher bone mineral density and BMI were observed in the no-oedema group (both P < 0.05). Weak correlations linked BME with increasing age (r = 0.393, P < 0.01) and with lower BMD (r = –0.301) and BMI (r = –0.287). Conclusions: This study is the first to delineate the vertebral bone marrow edema patterns that accompany normal healing after LLIF and to examine their relationship with early post-operative symptoms. All observed edema was contiguous with the cage. No significant association emerged between BME pattern and pain perception, whereas early lumbar function was modestly influenced by the presence of edema; this influence waned over time. Advanced age, lower bone mineral density and lower BMI were weakly but significantly associated with BME development. These findings facilitate discrimination of physiologic edema from pathologic events, refine outcome assessment and inform tailored post-operative rehabilitation after LLIF.

## A085: Preoperative prediction of ICU need following high-risk cervical spine fusion

Saleh Mostafa

1

, Omar Saleh

2

, Abduljabbar Alhammoud

1

1

University of Arizona, Tucson, United States

2

Eastern Virginia Medical School, Norfolk, United States

Introduction: Non-elective cervical spine fusion is associated with substantial risk of post-operative patient complications, including respiratory failure, hemodynamic instability, and the need for intensive care unit (ICU) admission or prolonged hospitalization. Novel patient risk assessment tools may improve perioperative planning and decrease the likelihood of acute complications following non-elective cervical spine fusion. We evaluated machine learning modeling techniques to risk stratify patients for prolonged hospital stay or ICU admission based exclusively on pre-operative factors. Materials and Methods: Adults (≥ 18) undergoing cervical fusion were identified in a large, real-world cohort (MIMIC-IV, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center) using ICD-9/10-PCS and CPT procedure codes, yielding 2,229 cervical spinal fusion procedures. The primary outcome was a composite of major postoperative complications requiring ICU-level care, defined as either an unplanned ICU transfer within 48 hours or the need for specific life-sustaining therapies including invasive mechanical ventilation, continuous vasoactive infusions, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, continuous renal replacement therapy, or massive transfusion [≥ 4 units PRBCs/24h]. A gradient boosted tree (GBT) was trained to predict ICU admission using only patient preoperative data. All predictors were restricted to factors available at admission or during surgical planning, including planned surgical approach, patient comorbidities, admission type, labs, vitals, and demographics. Model performance was evaluated using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) curve, accuracy, recall, and precision. Results: The GBT model generalized and discriminated exceptionally well regarding the need for ICU admission, achieving an AUROC of 0.879 and an overall accuracy of 0.83. The most significant factors associated with ICU admission included the indication for surgery such as tumor, infection, trauma, or degenerative causes, patient BMI, Charlson Comorbidity Index, approach (eg. anterior versus posterior), and patient pre-operative hemoglobin. Conclusion: Machine learning models, using only readily available preoperative data, demonstrate significant potential in accurately risk-stratifying patients for ICU-level care prior to non-elective cervical spine fusion. This predictive tool offers a critical advancement in perioperative planning. Proactive identification of high-risk patients can optimize resource allocation, enhance patient safety, and ultimately improve clinical outcomes.

, Sanyam Kulshrestha

1

, Janet Conway

1

1

2

Albany Medical College, Albany, United States

Introduction: Sacral and ischial pressure wounds are a devastating complication of prolonged immobility. Surgical intervention has been shown to play a critical role in the management of advanced stage III or IV ulcers, however there is limited research evaluating the efficacy of different surgical techniques and perioperative protocols. Although some articles have evaluated patient specific outcomes using general survey tools, no research to date has evaluated long term quality of life standards using a validated, pressure-ulcer specific patient reported outcome measure tool. This study aims to address this gap in knowledge by assessing outcomes following surgical intervention and strict perioperative protocol adherence in patients with high grade pressure ulcers. Functional independence, measured by the Barthel Index, showed a mean score of 71.19 ± 8.28, reflecting moderate levels of independence. Conclusion: Surgical management of advanced pressure ulcers is a necessary yet complicated procedure that confers a great impact on functional outcomes and quality of life post-procedure. This novel study elucidated promising long-term outcomes in a cohort of patients undergoing this procedure along with a strict perioperative treatment protocol. Additionally, this study provides preliminary insight into the social and functional outcomes challenging this patient population and should be used to more specifically address the needs of this community.

, Benjamin Martens

, Martin Stienen

1,2

, Felix Stengel

1,2

1
Interdisciplinary Spine Center, Cantonal Hospital of St. Gallen & Medical School of St. Gallen, H-OCH Health Ostschweiz, St. Gallen, Switzerland, St. Gallen, Switzerland,

2
Department of Neurosurgery, Cantonal Hospital of St. Gallen & Medical School of St. Gallen, H-OCH Health Ostschweiz, St. Gallen, Switzerland, St. Gallen, Switzerland,

4

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Cantonal Hospital of St. Gallen & Medical School of St. Gallen, H-OCH Health Ostschweiz, St. Gallen, Switzerland, St. Gallen, Switzerland

Introduction: Cage subsidence (CS) remains a significant complication following transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF), with potential impact on fusion success and clinical outcomes. While various risk factors have been identified, the type of interbody cage in development of CS requires further clarification. This study aimed to evaluate independent risk factors for CS at 3 months after TLIF, with particular focus on expandable versus static cage design. Material and Methods: We conducted a single-institution retrospective analysis of 530 patients who received 648 cages during single- or multi-level TLIF procedures between November 2018 and May 2025. Surgical technique factors, particularly cage positioning and sizing, also contribute to CS risk. These findings suggest that static cages may offer superior mechanical stability in the early postoperative period, challenging the presumed advantages of expandable cage technology. Careful consideration of cage selection and optimal surgical technique is essential for minimizing subsidence risk in TLIF procedures.

## A088: Does preoperative nutritional status influence complications following scoliosis surgery in patients with GMFCS IV-V cerebral palsy?

Nevzat Gönder

, Musa Bilgin

, Çağrı Karabulut

3

, Beytullah Unat

, Emre Kırkgöz

No significant difference was found between the groups in terms of WBC (p = 0.596), preoperative hgb (p = 0.17), postoperative hgb (p = 0.447), plt (p = 0.771), amount of bleeding (p = 0.793), Cobb angle (p = 0.104) and sex (p = 0.964), respectively. Per the Clavien-Dindo-Sink Complication Classification System, 3 patients experienced grade 1 complications, 5 patients had grade 2, 10 patients presented with grade 3, 6 patients encountered grade 4a, 2 patients faced grade 4b, and 1 patient suffered grade 5 issues. PNI in Group A (31.19 ± 4.24) was significantly lower than in Group B (43.1± 2.44) (p < 0.001). Furthermore, patients in Group A (13.37 ± 12.92) had to stay in the hospital longer than those in Group B (5.63 ± 1.7) (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Preoperative nutritional status, quantified by the PNI, emerged as the significant predictor of complications in GMFCS IV-V cerebral palsy patients undergoing scoliosis surgery. Lower PNI was strongly associated with higher complication rates and prolonged hospitalization. These findings highlight the critical role of nutritional optimization in improving outcomes for this vulnerable population.

## ID: AGS26/3479

## A089: Does crossing the cervicothoracic junction in multilevel posterior cervical arthrodesis impact reoperation rates for adjacent segment disease? A retrospective analysis from the University of Michigan Hospital

Jawad Saad

1

, Peyton Goethe

2

, Noojan Kazemi

2

1
Central Michigan University, Saginaw, United States, 
2
University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, United States
Introduction: Degenerative cervical spine disease as a cause of pain and disability, often requiring posterior cervical decompression and fusion, particularly for multilevel disease in aging patients. Determining the lower instrumented vertebra, which is the lowest point of the fusion, poses both anatomical and biomechanical challenges. This particularly occurs at the cervicothoracic junction (CTJ), where the flexible cervical spine transitions into the rigid thoracic spine. Ending fusion at C7 may place increased stress on the C7-T1 disc, potentially accelerating adjacent segment disease (ASD), while extending fusion into the thoracic spine may reduce this risk but limit postoperative mobility. Current literature presents conflicting data regarding whether crossing the CTJ reduces the need for reoperation due to ASD and other complications. Compare the rates of reoperation due to degeneration and complications such as pain, wound issues, and hardware failure between patients undergoing multilevel posterior cervical fusion terminating at C7 versus those extending across the cervicothoracic junction fusing at T1-T4. Material and Methods: This study is a retrospective cohort analysis using data from the University of Michigan Hospital Department of Neurosurgery. This included 393 adult patients who underwent elective multilevel posterior cervical fusion for degenerative cervical spine disease. Patients were divided into two cohorts: those whose fusions ended at or before C7 (C1-C7, n = 132) and those with constructs extending into the thoracic spine (T1-T4, n = 261). Reoperations were categorized as either for fusion extension due to degeneration or other complications like pain, hardware failure, or wound issues. Postoperative complications were also analyzed, and statistical significance was assessed using Fisher’s Exact Test (p < 0.05). Results: Among 393 patients, reoperation rates were lower in the CTJ cohort compared with those terminating at C7 (7.3% vs. 9.8%). Neurologic complications were frequent overall, with weakness affecting roughly one-quarter of patients in both groups, while radicular symptoms were higher in the CTJ group (21.8% vs. 18.9%). Wound-related complications, including surgical site infection and wound dehiscence, were also more common with CTJ extension. Additionally, dysphagia and the need for postoperative feeding tube placement occurred more often in the CTJ group, highlighting the increased morbidity associated with extending constructs across the cervicothoracic junction. Conclusion: Crossing the CTJ did not significantly reduce reoperations or surgical site complications. While pain was more frequent in the T1-T4 group, our findings differ from prior literature suggesting a protective effect of thoracic extension. Further investigation is warranted to clarify the clinical value of crossing the CTJ.

## A090: High psychosocial impact of complications and maladaptive coping strategies among spine surgeons

Rishi Kanna

1

, S. Rajasekaran

1

1

Ganga hospital, Coimbatore, India

Introduction: Surgical complications are an inevitable part of spine practice, yet their psychosocial and professional impact on surgeons remains underexplored. This study surveyed practising spine surgeons to assess the burden of complications, coping mechanisms, and burnout. Material and Methods: An anonymous invited survey was completed by 50 practicing spine surgeons. The data collected included demographics, complication frequency, psychosocial impact, coping strategies, financial considerations, and burnout domains. Descriptive analysis was performed. Results: Respondents were predominantly male (100%) orthopedic surgeons (96%) with fellowship training (86%). Most practiced in tier-1 cities (54%) under private institutions (74%). The majority had 5-20 years of experience and performed 100-400 spine surgeries annually. Nearly all surgeons (96%) admitted being psychologically affected, reporting guilt (42%), depression (38%), and anxiety (36%). Multiple psychological domains were affected in 86% of respondents, particularly sleep (80%) and general well-being (78%). Emotional response was stronger when complications involved children (56%) or known patients (56%). Coping strategies included support from colleagues (74%), mentors (52%), and family (54%), alongside personal habits such as music (34%), sports (34%), and alcohol use (34%). Financial concessions were made by two-thirds of surgeons through fee or institutional cost reduction. Burnout was prevalent, with moderate-to-severe exhaustion in 44%, depersonalization in 40%, and poor professional accomplishment in 48%. While 74% perceived spine surgery as having a higher risk of complications compared to other specialties, only 12% contemplated career changes. Institutional support was rated “good” by 56%, “mild” by 34%, and absent by 10%. Conclusion: Complications in spine surgery exert profound psychosocial and professional consequences on surgeons, with high prevalence of burnout and maladaptive coping. Structured institutional support and targeted interventions are urgently needed.

, Harvinder Singh Chhabra

, Eugen Cezar Popescu

, Jin Tee

, Cumhur Oner

12

, Alex Vaccaro

13

, Gregory Schroeder

13

, Richard Bransford

1
University of Utah, Salt Lake City, United States,

2
The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada,

3
Paracelsus Private Medical University Nuremberg, Nuremberg, Germany,

4
Assiut University, Asyut, Egypt,

5
Ganga Hospital, Coimbatore, India,

6
Hospital Costa del Sol, Malaga, Spain,

7
University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland,

8
State University of Campinas, Sao Paulo, Brazil,

9
Sri Balaji Action Medical Institute, New Delhi, India,

10
Emergency Hospital, Iasi, Romania,

11
The Alfred Hospital, Melbourne, Australia,

12
University Medical Centers, Utrecht, Netherlands,

13
Thomas Jefferson University Hospital, Philadelphia, United States,

14

University of Washington, Seattle, United States

Introduction: The role of bracing in the non-operative management of thoracolumbar burst fractures remains controversial. The objective of this study is to compare the clinical outcomes of patients treated with or without a stabilizing brace for neurologically intact thoracolumbar burst fractures. Material and Methods: This post-hoc subanalysis of a prospective, multicenter study examined patients with type A3 or A4 thoracolumbar burst fractures without neurologic deficit who were treated nonoperatively with either a stabilizing brace or no brace. ## A092: A novel surgical approach to thoracolumbar fractures: our experience

Andrea Cattalani

1

, Dora Riva

2

, Matteo Vitali

1

, Stefano Marasco

3

, Andrea Barbanera

1

1

Neurosurgery Unit, Department of Surgery, SS. Antonio e Biagio e Cesare Arrigo Hospital, Alessandria, Italy

2

Neurosurgery Unit, Department of Clinical-Surgical, Diagnostic and Pediatric Sciences, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy

3

SSD di Neurochirurgia, Ospedale Umberto Parini di Aosta, Aosta, Italy

Introduction: The global burden of spinal fractures on health, and consequently on quality of life, has experienced an upward trend in recent years. The majority of these fractures (70%) occurs at the thoraco-lumbar junction. Notwithstanding the effort to standardize surgical indications concerning fractures, the discourse surrounding the optimal treatment options continues to be a topic of ongoing debate. The objective of this study was to present our personal experience concerning thoraco-lumbar fractures through the implementation of various techniques, including a novel approach. This approach involves the positioning of pedicle screws one level above and one level below the fractured vertebra, complemented by a stenting device and short pedicle screws at the fracture site. Each procedure was evaluated based on its efficacy in correcting deformities and sustaining said corrections. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included post-traumatic thoracolumbar fractures treated between January 2020 and March 2025 at a single institution (AOU S.S. Antonio e Biagio e Cesare Arrigo, Alessandria, Italy). A total of 31 patients were included in our analysis. Inclusion criteria were the following: (1) type A (subtype A2, A3, and A4) and type B fractures according to the AOSpine Thoracolumbar Spine Injury Classification System; (2) age > 18; (3) last follow-up at least 6 months after surgery. Our cohort of patients was divided into three groups based on the type of surgical procedure they underwent: group A (short-segment fixation plus stenting AND short pedicle screws at the fracture site), group B (short-segment fixation plus stenting OR short pedicle screws at the fracture site), and group C (long-segment fixation). CT scans and/or AP and lateral radiographs were performed pre-operatively, post-operatively, at 3 months, and at last follow-up. For each radiological image, Cobb’s kyphosis angle was taken into consideration. The degree of kyphosis correction was subsequently calculated by comparing the pre- and immediately post-operative Cobb’s angles. The following radiological controls (at 3 months and at last follow-up) were compared in order to assess the potential loss of correction.Quantitative data were reported as median and interquartile range (IQR) or mean and standard deviation (SD). Categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages. Associations between patients baseline characteristics and type of surgery were assessed through two-tailed Kruskall-Wallis test or two-tailed Exact Fisher’s test. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: In Group A, considered as the reference one, Cobb’s angle significantly decreased in the post-operative follow-up compared to baseline (β = -8.71, p < 0.001). Said correction was then significantly maintained in all the following controls (at 3-months and at last follow-up). Group C exhibited a statistically significant increase in Cobb’s angle over time compared to Group A at all time points. Changes in Cobb’s angle over time in Group B were similar to those observed in Group A. Conclusion: Short-segment fixation combined with stenting and the placement of short pedicle screws at the fractured vertebra seems to be a valid and effective technique to reduce post-traumatic kyphosis angle in thoraco-lumbar fractures and to maintain such correction over time.

## A093: The AO Spine TL Classification System in acute thoracolumbar fractures: choice of treatment and implementation in clinical setting

Vahid Buyukayten

1

, Milan Ridderikhof

1

, Jos Twisk

1

, Olivier Groot

2

, Job Doornberg

3,4

, Frank Bloemers

1

1
Amsterdam UMC, Amsterdam, The Netherlands,

2
UMC Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands,

3
UMC Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands,

4

Flinders University, Adelaide, Australia

Introduction: The AO Spine TL Classification System does not provide explicit treatment advice for all thoracolumbar fractures. Further evaluation of its clinical applicability and consideration of incorporating additional relevant parameters associated with poor outcome is especially warranted. Therefore, this study investigated the association between this classification system and fracture level in deciding to treat patients with acute traumatic thoracolumbar fractures surgically or conservatively. The secondary aim was to evaluate the implementation of the classification system in clinical practice. Material and Methods: All adult (≥ 18 years) patients who presented in the Emergency Department of a level-one trauma centre, with one or more acute thoracolumbar (T1-L5) fractures were retrospectively included between 01/10/2016 and 30/06/2021. Exclusion criteria were: (1) pre-existing thoracolumbar fractures, (2) >20% missing data, (3) patients who suffered non-survivable injuries, and (4) pathological fractures. The primary outcome was definitive fracture management dichotomized into conservative or surgical treatment. Potential effect modifiers included: age, sex, comorbidities, trauma mechanism, Glasgow Coma Scale, Injury Severity Score, number of fractures and neurological injuries. The potential effect modifiers were adjusted for potential confounding. For the analyses binary logistic regression was used. The secondary outcome was adherence to the AO Spine TL Classification System in treatment decisions, calculated as the proportion of cases treated (conservatively or surgically) in line with its recommendations. Adherence was classified as poor (< 30%), intermediate (30-80%), or excellent (> 80%). Results: In total, 553 patients were included of which 387 (70%) patients received conservative treatment, and 166 (30%) patients underwent surgery. Of all fractures, 376 (68%) were type A0-A3, 46 (8.3%) type A4, 34 (6.2%) type B1, 81 (15%) type B2, and 16 (2.9%) type C. Patients with type A4 fractures were treated surgically more often than patients with type A0, A1, A2, or A3 fractures (OR = 31.85; 95% CI = 13.21-76.80; p ≤ 0.01). Fracture level was not associated with choice of treatment (OR = 0.93; 95% CI = 0.61-1.42; p = 0.75). For both associations, none of the investigated eight parameters were effect modifiers (all p > 0.10). Adherence of physicians to the morphology components of the classification system was 95% as to types A0-A3, 86% as to B2-B3, and 100% as to C. As to A4 and B1, adherence could be determined, as the choice of treatment is left to the discretion of the physician. Adherence to the neurological and modifier components of the classification system could not be determined, due to a lack of documentations by physicians. Conclusion: As expected, patients with type A4 fractures are treated surgically more often than patients with A0, A1, A2, or A3 fractures. The analyses of patient and vertebral fracture characteristics showed no effect modifiers. The implementation of the AO Spine TL Classification System regarding the morphological components appears to be excellent. However, the implementation of the overall algorithm of the classification system remains suboptimal.

## A094: Removal versus retention of posterior spinal implants in patients with healed thoracolumbar junction fractures: analysis of clinical and radiographic outcomes

Raboudi Hamza

1

, Jlidi Mohamed

1

, mouldi lamouchi

1

, Karim Mallek

1

, Ismail Karray

1

, Jihed Bechikh

1

, Sami Mbarki
