, Hedi Atig

1

, Walid Bouaicha

1

, Selim Daas

1

1

Orthopedics and Traumatology Department, Hospital of Mohamed Taher Maamouri, Nabeul, Tunisia

Introduction: Implant removal following successful bone union is a common practice in orthopedic surgeries, including spinal procedures. General indications for spinal implant removal include infection, nonunion, symptomatic misplacement, implant breakage or loosening, local irritation, or growth disturbance. However, there is controversy regarding the benefits and indications for routine spinal implant removal in asymptomatic patients with successful unions. The objective of our study is to evaluate the impact of implant removal on functional and radiological outcomes. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of 120 patients operated on for thoracolumbar junction fractures between January 2010 and January 2020. Patients were divided into two groups: Group A including 38 patients who underwent implant removal, and Group B including 82 patients without implant removal. Functional and clinical outcomes were evaluated by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and Dallas Pain Questionnaire. Radiological outcomes were evaluated by measuring regional kyphosis, vertebral kyphosis, traumatic regional angulation, and Beck index at postoperative and the last follow-up. The evaluation of the results was done by calculating the loss of correction of radiological parameters between the postoperative radiographs and the last follow-up radiographs as well as at final follow-up. Results: The mean age was 34.84 years in Group A and 50.40 years in Group B. Group A included 17 women and 21 men, whereas Group B included 29 women and 53 men. Regarding the radiological outcomes, we didn’t noted a significant difference between the two groups in terms of the loss of reduction of vertebral kyphosis, regional kyphosis, traumatic regional angulation, and Beck index did not differ significantly between the two groups. Furthermore, UCLA grading at the last follow-up showed no statistically significant differences between the two groups (p = 0.31). Conclusion: Our findings suggest that implant removal does not significantly affect either functional outcomes or radiological outcomes after thoracolumbar junction fractures. Further studies are required to identify specific subgroups of patients who may benefit from implant removal.

## A096: Patient Reported Outcomes following Operative and Non-Operative Management of A3 vs A4 Thoracolumbar Burst Fractures

Barry Kweh1, Charlotte Dandurand

, Alex Vaccaro

, Klaus Schnake

, Mohammad El-Sharkawi
5
, Richard Bransford

, Harvinder Singh Chhabra

, Ulrich Spiegl

, Dimitri Hauri
9
, Cumhur Oner
10
, Gregory Schroeder3, Jin Tee1,11,12

1National Trauma Research Institute, Melbourne, Australia, 2Combined Neurosurgical and Orthopedic Spine Program, Vancouver General Hospital, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, 3Rothman Institute, Philadelphia, United States, 4Center for Spinal and Scoliosis Surgery, Malteser Waldkrankenhaus St. Marien Erlangen, Germany, Erlangen, Germany, 5Department of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, Assiut University, Egypt, Egypt, 6Department of Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine, Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington, Seattle, United States, 7Department of Orthopaedics and Spine Surgery, Ganga Hospital, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India, 8Clinics of Trauma Surgery, Orthopaedics, and Reconstructive Surgery, München Klinik Harlaching, Sanatoriumplatz 2, 81545, Munich, Germany, 9AO Foundation, Stettbachstrasse 6, 8600, Dübendorf, Switzerland, 10University Medical Centers,, Utrecht, Netherlands, 11Alfred Hospital, Melbourne, Australia, 12Monash University, Melbourne, Australia

Introduction: The quality of life that patients experience after sustaining thoracolumbar burst fractures is often overlooked in preference of radiographic features or neurological function. The objective of this study was to evaluate functional and quality of life outcomes following operative and non-operative management of thoracolumbar burst fractures. Material and Methods: A prospective multi-centre observational study of neurologically intact patients who sustained traumatic thoracolumbar burst fractures managed surgically or non-surgically was performed. Outcome measures included the EQ-5D index, EQ-5D visual analogue scale (VAS), pain numerical rating scale (NRS), the pioneering AO Spine Patient Reported Outcome Spine Trauma (PROST) tool and patient satisfaction. Follow-up time points included at discharge, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year and 2 years. The Wilcoxon rank sum test was used to evaluate differences between A3 and A4 fracture morphologies for continuous variables whilst the Cochran-Armitage trend test was utilized to evaluate differences in the ordinal outcome anxiety and depression. Mixed models for repeated measures (MMRM) were used for continuous outcomes using unstructured covariance. A generalized estimating equations (GEE) model was employed for the ordinal outcomes of anxiety and depression.. The models were adjusted for key variables including sex, age, BMI, smoking status. TLICS score and treatment modalities. Results: 198 patients were identified. The EQ-5D index determined there was no statistically significant difference for A3 and A4 fractures at 2 year follow-up for operative (p=0.48) and non-operative management (p=0.51). A similar finding was noted with the EQ-5D VAS measure for surgical (p=0.33) and non-surgical treatment (p=0.21). Adjusted mixed effects model for the EQ-5D index and EQ-5D VAS confirmed patients with operatively and non-operatively managed A3 (p<0.001) and A4 fractures (p<0.001) improved at every follow-up checkpoint up to 2 years. A GEE model demonstrated there was a higher proportion of patients who were less anxious or depressed among operatively managed patients with A4 fractures compared to A3 fractures at 2 year follow-up (OR 7.7, 95% CI 1.5 − 40.5, p=0.02) but this was not true for those non-operatively treated (OR 0.8, 95% CI 0.1 − 4.4, p=0.78). MMRM for pain NRS and AO Spine PROST suggested there was a significant improvement in outcome compared to discharge for both surgically and non-surgically treated patients (p<0.01) but no significant difference between the surgical subgroups. Patient satisfaction was similar between A3 and A4 fractures for non-operatively (p=0.62) and operatively treated patients (p=0.50) at final follow-up). Conclusion: Contemporary management of thoracolumbar burst fractures in neurologically intact patients has evolved to the extent that there is improvement in function, pain and disability for both A3 and A4 fractures regardless of whether surgical or non-surgical management is pursued. We demonstrated that the cohort of patients who sustain the more severe A4 morphology experienced improved mental health outcomes upon final 2 year follow-up if operatively managed. Ultimately patient satisfaction was similar on long-term follow-up. These findings suggest that larger randomized studies using the AO Spine Thoracolumbar Injury Classification System are still required to adequately comprehend the biopsychosocial effect of these fractures.

## A097: Against all odds: six-year outcomes of thoracolumbar burst fracture surgery in a district hospital of Bangladesh

Mahamudul Hasan

1,2

Bangladesh Spine and orthopaedic Hospital, Dhaka, Bangladesh

2

Satkhira Medical College Hospital, Satkhira, Bangladesh

Introduction: Thoracolumbar burst fractures represent one of the most frequent and challenging spine injuries. This study evaluates surgical outcomes over six years from a single surgeon operating in a district hospital in Bangladesh, highlighting the factors that influence recovery despite infrastructural constraints. ODI scores at baseline and 3 months were compared between patients who returned to work and those who did not by 3 months. Baseline and 1-year ODI scores were compared between patients who returned to work and those who did not by 1 year. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were plotted with median event times and a 95% CI calculated separately for patients with non-operative and operative management. Kaplan-Meier curves were compared using a log-rank test. A multivariable Cox regression model was fitted to compare the hazard ratio (HR) of RTW between treatment groups. Results: 198 eligible and enrolled patients without major protocol deviations were recruited from fourteen sites across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. 122 patients (61.6%) were treated surgically, and 76 (38.4%) were treated nonsurgically. Patients who had not returned to work by 3 months were more frequently smokers (19.2% vs 8.2%, p = 0.04) and experienced more frequently a low-energy trauma (25.6% vs 12.9%, p = 0.04) and had a higher ODI at 3 months (mean (SD) 21.2 (14.6) versus 11.1 (11.0), p < 0.01) than RTW patients. Patients who had not returned to work by one year were significantly more frequently of Asian ethnicity (22.7% vs 15.0%) or of other origin (9.1% vs 0.8%), were more often smokers (31.8% vs 10.2%, p = 0.01), had a shorter time from injury to treatment decision (mean (SD) 1.4 (1.5) vs 2.4 (2.2), p = 0.02) and had higher ODI values at baseline (mean (SD) 70.3 (16.4) vs 55.4 (19.7) vs p < 0.01) and at 1 year (mean (SD) 16.0 (14.4) vs 6.4 (8.4) vs p < 0.01). No significant differences were found in primary injury type or other patient and injury characteristics, and treatment modality. Median time to RTW did not significantly differ between surgical and nonsurgical groups (84.0 days [95% CI: 67.0-96.0] vs. 120.0 days [95% CI: 71.0- 136.0], p = 0.236). Multivariable Cox regression showed no significant difference between the surgical and the non-operative treatment groups (HR: 1.23, 95%-CI: 0.79, 1.92). Conclusion: When considering RTW by 3 months and 1 year, smoking and higher ODI at the respective timepoints correlated with no return to work. Otherwise, all patient demographics and injury characteristics did not correlate with RTW. There was no statistically significant difference in time to RTW between surgical and nonsurgical treatment of TL burst fractures in neurologically intact patients within one year.

## A100: Sterile wound healing or deep infection? Serum protein signatures identify mechanistic pathways after spinal surgery: a prospective matched-cohort study

Siegmund Lang

1

, Pia Fehrenbach

2,3

, Daniel Haschtmann

4

, Tamas Fekete

4

, Maja Gocević

4

, Puk Kwant

2

, Esther de Jong

3

, T. Fintan Moriarty

2

, Sibylle Grad

2

, Markus Loibl

4

1

University Hospital Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany,

2

AO Research Institute Davos, Davos, Switzerland,

3

Amsterdam UMC, Amsterdam Institute for Infection and Immunity, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdem, Netherlands,

4

Schulthess Clinic Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

Background: Surgical site infection (SSI) after spinal fusion remains a severe complication with high morbidity. Conventional markers such as CRP or leukocyte count often lack specificity to distinguish SSI from sterile post-operative inflammation. Little is known about the mechanistic pathways that drive SSI in contrast to normal healing. This study therefore aimed to identify plasma protein signatures that not only differentiate SSI from uncomplicated recovery but also provide insights into the underlying immunopathology using targeted proteomics. Materials and Methods: Between October 2020 and May 2024, 43 spine-surgery patients were prospectively enrolled, 22 with SSI and 21 without SSI. After exclusion for matching and technical criteria, 17 infected patients (I) and 20 non-infected controls (NI) were analyzed. Controls were matched to infected patients for age, sex, and surgical invasiveness. Plasma samples were collected pre-operatively and 6 weeks post-operatively in non-infected patients, and at SSI diagnosis in infected patients. Ninety-two proteins were quantified using the OLINK inflammation panel (NPX log2 scale). Group comparisons were performed using Wilcoxon rank-based tests. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and all patients gave written informed consent. Results: The mean age was 63.4 ± 15.7 years in infected patients and 63.0 ± 10.3 years in controls (p = 0.91), with 47.1% vs. 45.0% females (p = 0.87). The surgical spectrum ranged from single-level decompressions to multilevel fusions without differences in operated levels. Median time to SSI diagnosis was 18.8 days, and Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequent isolate (n = 10). In NI patients, post-operative changes reflected a controlled sterile response: Compared to pre-operative levels, EN-RAGE (p = 0.0012) and IL-33 (p = 0.0433) increased, reflecting the systemic response to the surgical intervention, while 4E-BP1 (p = 0.0335), SIRT2 (p = 0.0216), STAMBP (p = 0.0195), and Flt3L (p = 0.0084) decreased, suggesting attenuation of translational and metabolic stress. Comparing NI and I patients postoperatively displayed a pronounced inflammatory signature in I patients with higher levels of IL-17A, IL-6, IL-8, CXCL1, CCL3, and MCP-3, driving neutrophil recruitment. Angiogenic mediators VEGFA, HGF, and TGF-α were elevated compared to NI patients, indicating infection-associated tissue remodeling. Importantly, an elevated osteolytic protein cluster was evident in I patients: OSM, MMP-1, and TNFSF14 were upregulated, consistent with infection-driven matrix degradation, while TRANCE (RANKL)was paradoxically reduced (all markers p < 0.001). Conclusion: Proteomic profiling distinguished sterile wound healing from SSI. While uncomplicated healing was marked by transient alarmin release with resolution of stress pathways, SSI was characterized by an IL-17/chemokine surge, angiogenic activation, and induction of osteolytic mediators, supporting the development of biomarker panels for early and specific SSI detection.

## A101: Immune profiling identifies specific cell alterations in postoperative spinal infections: a prospective matched-control study

Siegmund Lang

1

, Pia Fehrenbach

2,3

, Daniel Haschtmann

4

, Tamas Fekete

4

, Maja Gocević

4

, Puk Kwant

2

, Esther de Jong

3

, T. Fintan Moriarty

2

, Sibylle Grad

2

, Markus Loibl

4

1
University Hospital Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany,

2
AO Research Institute Davos, Davos, Switzerland,

3
Amsterdam UMC, Amsterdam Institute for Infection and Immunity, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdem, The Netherlands,

4

Schulthess Clinic Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

Introduction: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are serious complications following spine surgery. They are associated with increased patient morbidity, longer hospitalization, and the need for complex revision procedures. The aim was to identify immune cell alterations associated with SSIs and to understand how these differ from those in patients without SSIs. Materials and Methods: A total of 43 patients undergoing lumbar spine surgery were prospectively enrolled. After quality control and matching, 17 patients who developed SSIs (group I) and 20 matched non-infected patients (group NI) were included for immune profiling. Matching parameters included age, sex, BMI, and surgical invasiveness. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from blood samples drawn postoperatively and analyzed using high-dimensional mass cytometry (43 markers). Cell types and activation/exhaustion markers were identified using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction, PhenoGraph clustering, and statistical comparisons. Results: The mean age of patients was 63.4 ± 15.7 years in group I and 63.0 ± 10.3 years in group NI. The gender distribution was similar (47% vs. 45% female). SSIs occurred after a median of 18.8 days and were predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (n = 10), coagulase-negative staphylococci (n = 2), and Escherichia coli (n = 2). Surgical procedures included both minor (e.g., decompression) and major interventions (e.g., multilevel fusions), equally distributed between groups. Mass cytometry identified 46 immune metaclusters, of which 30 differed significantly between infected and non-infected patients. Six clusters were upregulated in the infection group and 24 downregulated. Innate immune cells such as NK cells (p = 0.0043), monocytes (p = 0.0357), myeloid DCs (p = 0.0011), plasmacytoid DCs (p = 0.0458), and CD1+ DCs (p = 0.0057) were reduced in infected patients. Furthermore, γδ T cells (p = 0.0070) and double-positive T cells (p = 0.0152) were also decreased. In contrast, B cells (p = 0.0305) and Th17 cells (p = 0.0152) were elevated in infected patients. While total CD4+ and CD8+ T cell counts did not differ significantly, activation markers showed differences on CD4+ T cells- CD69+ CD4+ T cell (p = 0.0023) and HLA-DR+ CD4+ T cell (p = 0.0032)) were increased in infected patients. Moreover, PD-1+ CD4+ T cell (p = 0.0141) were increased in infected patients. HLA-DR+ CD8+ T cells (p = 0.0424) and OX-40+ CD8+ T cells (p = 0.0470) were reduced in infected patients. Discussion: This study suggests that patients developing SSIs following spinal surgery exhibit a distinct immune cell signature. Infected patients showed a suppressed innate immune profile. These findings support the relevance of high-dimensional immune profiling for better understanding the host response to SSI. Further research is warranted to validate immune-based markers for clinical risk stratification and early diagnosis.

## A102: In vivo segmental vertebral kinematics in patients with degenerative lumbar scoliosis

Fei Xu

1

, Weishi Li

1

1

Orthopaedic Department, Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: This study aimed to find a standard of the vertebra kinematics during functional weight-bearing activities in degenerative lumbar scoliosis (DLS) patients. Material and Methods: Fifty-four patients were involved into this study with forty-two in DLS group and twelve in the control group. The three-dimensional (3D) vertebral models from L1 to S1 of each participant were reconstructed by computed tomography (CT). Dual-orthogonal fluoroscopic imaging, along with FluoMotion and Rhinoceros software, was used to record segmental vertebral kinematics during functional weight-bearing activities. The AP and CC translations at L5-S1 were higher than those at L1-2, L2-3, and L3-4. During left-right torsion of the trunk, the AP translation at L5-S1 was higher as compared to other levels. Conclusion: The greatest coupled translation was observed at L5-S1 in patients with DLS. Coupled AP and ML translations at L5-S1 were higher than those in healthy participants. These data improved the understanding of DLS motion characteristics.

## A103: Free calcium and the extracellular calcium-sensing receptor regulate intervertebral disc degeneration and calcification

Michael Grant

1

, Laura Epure

1

, John Antoniou

1

, Fackson Mwale

1

1

McGill University, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Degenerative disc disease (DDD) is a common cause of lower back pain. Calcification of the intervertebral disc (IVD) has been correlated with DDD, and is especially prevalent in scoliotic discs. The appearance of calcium deposits has been shown to increase with age, and its occurrence has been associated with several other disorders such as hyperparathyroidism, chondrocalcinosis, and arthritis. Trauma, vertebral fusion and infection have also been shown to increase the incidence of IVD calcification. Our data indicate that Ca2+ and expression of the extracellular calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) are significantly increased in mild to severely degenerative human IVDs. In this study, we evaluated the effects of Ca2+ and CaSR on the degeneration and calcification of IVDs. Material and Methods: IVD tissue and cells were isolated from donor tissue. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed to determine expression of CaSR. Free calcium levels were measured and compared between Thompson graded discs. Western blotting and RT-qPCR were performed on cultured human NP and AF cells to demonstrate expression of CaSR, matrix proteins aggrecan and collagen, and catabolic enzymes following incubation in either increasing concentrations of Ca2+ [1.0-5.0 mM], CaSR allosteric agonist (cincalcet, 1 uM), or IL-1b [5 ng/mL] for 7 days. Ex vivo bovine IVD organ cultures were prepared using PrimeGrowth Disc Isolation System (Wisent Bioproducts). IVDs were cultured in 1.0, 2.5 mM Ca2+ or with cinacalcet for 21 days. Histology and Western blotting were performed to measure changes matrix composition. Structural stiffness of disc tissues due to calcification was determined using the MACH-1 mechanical testing system (Biomomentum, Laval, Quebec). Results: Human disc tissue demonstrated significant increases in free calcium from early (G2) to severe (G4) degeneration (p < 0.001; n = 6-15 discs per grade). Treatment with either Ca2+ the CaSR agonist or Il-1b significantly decreased matrix protein synthesis (aggrecan and Col II; p < 0.001; n = 4). However, only IL-1b upregulated catabolic enzyme expression (p < 0.0001; n = 4). Similar effects were observed in whole organ cultures, as Ca2+ and cinacalcet decreased proteoglycan and collagen content. Ca2+-treated IVDs demonstrated with calcium deposits in NP and AF tissues yet both Ca2+ and CaSR agonist increased alkaline phosphate expression (p < 0.01; n = 4). Biomechanical studies on Ca2+-treated IVDs demonstrated significant increases in stiffness of NP and AF tissues (p < 0.001 and p < 0.05, respectively; n = 3). Interestingly, IL-1b dose-dependently increased CaSR expression in IVD cells and in IVD organ cultures. Conclusion: Our results suggest that changes in the local concentrations of calcium and activation of CaSR occur in disc degeneration and effect matrix protein synthesis, calcification and IVD biomechanics. Inflammation may be a driving force for CaSR expression in disc cells enhancing Ca2+-induced degeneration. The effects of Ca2+ on IVD degeneration should be considered when investigating repair strategies of the disc.

## A104: Molecular characterization and classification of chordoma dictate individualized therapeutic strategies

Tong Meng

1

1

Shanghai General Hospital, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Chordoma, a rare and heterogeneous mesenchymal malignancy, presents with distinct clinical and biological behaviors. To guide individualized therapeutic strategy, we described the comprehensive clinical features of chordoma along with its underlying biological characteristics. Additionally, the accurate molecular classification and specific therapeutic options were also determined. Material and Methods: We enrolled a large cohort of chordoma including 102 patients and described their clinical, imaging and histopathological features. Conclusion: Our work sheds light on clinical-proteomic characteristics of chordoma that deepens our understanding of this rare disease and provides candidate precision treatment strategies for chordoma according to molecular classification, underscoring their potential for clinical application.

## A105: Dual mechanisms of susceptibility: distinct immune and inflammatory landscapes of type 1 and type 2 diabetes in murine spinal implant-associated infection and the potential for metabolic intervention

Thomas Olson

1

, Trevor LLoyd

1

, Rene Chun

1

, Autreen Golzar

1

, Joshua Wiener

1

, Chris Hamad

1

, John Adams

1

, Nicholas Bernthal

1

, William Sheppard

1

1

UCLA, Los Angeles, United States

Background: Diabetes mellitus is a well-recognized risk factor for infection and wound complications following spinal and orthopedic surgery. However, clinical studies often group type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) together, overlooking their distinct pathophysiology. This study directly compared infection burden, wound healing, and immune response between T1DM and T2DM in a murine spinal implant-associated infection model. Methods: T1DM was induced by streptozotocin injection and T2DM by high-fat, high-sucrose diet in C57BL/6J mice. Stainless steel spinal implants were placed, with select groups inoculated with bioluminescent Staphylococcus aureus (Xen36). Infectious burden was quantified longitudinally by noninvasive bioluminescent imaging and post-mortem colony forming units. Wound integrity was assessed by Kaplan-Meier survival of dehiscence. Systemic immunity was profiled by complete blood counts and multiplex cytokine analysis. Rescue was evaluated in both cohorts using semaglutide to evaluate the impact of metabolic modulation. Results: Both T1DM and T2DM mice exhibited significantly greater infectious burden compared with controls. T2DM mice demonstrated the highest and most sustained bacterial load, with bioluminescence peaking early and remaining elevated. T1DM mice showed a delayed but pronounced infectious peak, suggesting differential bacterial persistence. Wound complications were most severe in T1DM, with rapid and frequent dehiscence occurring within the first postoperative week. T2DM animals exhibited intermediate rates and timing of wound breakdown. Control wounds in both cohorts demonstrated zero cases of dehiscence. Cytokine profiling revealed distinct inflammatory landscapes. T2DM mice had elevated baseline cytokine levels, including C-reactive protein, G-CSF, GM-CSF, and IL-6, but mounted only minimal increases after infection, consistent with a state of chronic inflammation and blunted acute responsiveness. In contrast, T1DM mice displayed lower baseline cytokines yet demonstrated more robust infection-induced increases, indicating an acutely reactive but less durable immune profile. Complete blood counts supported these differences: both T1DM and T2DM groups had lower total white blood cells, lymphocytes, and red blood cell counts compared with controls, though neutrophil increases after infection were proportionally greater in diabetics. Semaglutide treatment in T1DM and T2DM mice improved glucose tolerance and decreased both peak and cumulative infectious burden. Wound dehiscence was delayed and less frequent compared with untreated T2DM, supporting the potential for metabolic intervention to enhance host defense. Conclusions: T1DM and T2DM impair defense against spinal implant infection through distinct mechanisms. T2DM is characterized by obesity, chronic systemic inflammation, and an attenuated acute immune response, while T1DM exhibits lower baseline immune tone but rapid, fragile responses accompanied by severe wound failure. Both groups demonstrated impaired hematopoiesis and reduced adaptive cell counts, contributing to heightened infection susceptibility. Metabolic modulation with semaglutide mitigated infectious and wound complications, underscoring the potential for tailored perioperative strategies in both diabetic subtypes.

## A106: The impact of histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition on neurobehavioural outcomes in preclinical models of traumatic and non-traumatic spinal cord injury: a systematic review

Natalia Jogodzinska

1

, Caleb Cole

1

, Jamie Brannigan

1

, Renuka Chintapalli

1

, Benjamin Davies

1

, Mark Kotter

1

, Oliver Mowforth

1

1

Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Introduction: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a traumatic injury resulting in significant life-changing disability. Elucidating the molecular processes associated with SCI may help to design novel therapeutics targeted at improving patient outcomes. Current pharmacological candidates include histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, which have been studied in the context of cancer, neurodegenerative and rheumatological disease. The anti-inflammatory properties of HDAC inhibitors have been postulated to be of value in SCI. The objective of this review was to synthesise the impact of HDAC inhibitors on neurobehavioural outcomes in preclinical studies of traumatic and non-traumatic SCI and to evaluate the suitability of HDAC inhibitors for clinical trials in patients with SCI. Materials and Methods: The review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023477882) and conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE and Embase were searched. Studies of animal models of traumatic or non-traumatic spinal cord injury evaluating the effect of HDAC inhibitors on neurobehavioural outcomes were eligible for inclusion. The SYRCLE checklist was used to assess for risk of bias. Screening, data-extraction and risk of bias assessments were completed in duplicate. Results: Of 10,549 studies identified by database searching, 42 studies met inclusion criteria. Animals used were rats (n = 28), mice (n = 13) and rabbits (n = 1). SCI models included spinal cord contusion (n = 24), epidural compression (n = 2), compression with a vascular clip (n = 6), hemisection (n = 5), ischaemia/reperfusion injury (n = 4) and dorsolateral funiculus crush (n = 1). Valproate was the most frequently used HDAC inhibitor (n = 20). Three studies used Sirt1 inhibitor EX527 administered simultaneously with an activator molecule: melatonin (n = 1), oxymatrine (n = 1) and MLN4924 (n = 1). Pain and anxiety were evaluated in one study, in which significant improvement was demonstrated. Locomotor function was assessed in 98% (41/42) of studies; The direction of effect demonstrated improvement in locomotor outcome in 73% (30/41) of studies, deterioration in 5% (2/41) of studies and no effect or conflicting findings in 22% (9/41) of studies. Conclusion: HDAC inhibitors are associated with functional motor recovery and improved anxiety and pain scores in preclinical models of SCI. However, the results should be interpreted with caution as risk of bias of included studies was unclear. These results support investigation of HDAC inhibitors as targets for translational research and clinical trials in patients with spinal cord injury.

## A107: Reprogramming the immune microenvironment with an antimicrobial peptide-loaded nano-hydroxyapatite/collagen hydrogel for enhanced bone regeneration in osteomyelitis

Jinzheng Liang

1

, Liang Wang

1

, Wensheng Zhang

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, The third Affiliated Hospital, Southern Medical University, Academy of Orthopaedics, Guangdong Province, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Bone and Joint Degeneration Diseases, Guangzhou, China

Introduction: Osteomyelitis is a refractory bone infection characterized by progressive bone destruction, sequestrum formation, and high recurrence rates. Current treatments are often limited by bacterial biofilm formation, antibiotic resistance, and insufficient bone regeneration. This study aimed to develop a collagen-based hydrogel co-loaded with an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) and nano-hydroxyapatite (nHA) (Col-AMP/nHA) to achieve integrated antibacterial, immunomodulatory, and osteogenic effects, and to investigate its underlying mechanisms. Material and Methods: The pro-inflammatory effects of Staphylococcus aureus and its component peptidoglycan (PGN) on primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and rat tibiae were first evaluated. A cationic hydrogel system was constructed by conjugating a positively charged AMP into a collagen hydrogel and incorporating nHA, enabling the capture of anionic pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g., PGN) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g., free DNA). The antibacterial and anti-biofilm efficacy of the hydrogel against S. aureus was assessed. Using RAW264.7 cells, HEK-Blue™ hTLR2 cells, and primary BMDMs, the regulatory effects of the hydrogel on macrophage polarization and osteoclast differentiation under PGN stimulation were investigated via ELISA, immunofluorescence, and single-cell RNA sequencing. Its osteoinductive capacity was evaluated in a co-culture system with rat bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). Finally, a rat tibial osteomyelitis model infected with S. aureus was established, and the hydrogel was implanted after debridement. Therapeutic outcomes were comprehensively assessed through histological, radiological, and molecular analyses. Results: PGN derived from S. aureus significantly induced M1 macrophage polarization and pro-inflammatory responses. The Col-AMP/nHA hydrogel exhibited broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and potent anti-biofilm effects. It effectively neutralized PGN, inhibited TLR2/NF-κB pathway activation, reversed M1 polarization in RAW264.7 cells, and suppressed excessive osteoclast differentiation. Single-cell transcriptomics further confirmed that the hydrogel cleared PGN and blocked NF-κB signaling. Moreover, it markedly enhanced the expression of osteogenesis-related genes and mineralized nodule formation in BMSCs. In vivo, treatment with Col-AMP/nHA effectively cleared the infection, attenuated local inflammation, and significantly promoted new bone formation in the defect areas. Conclusion: This study successfully developed a multifunctional collagen-based hydrogel system that integrates the antibacterial and immunomodulatory functions of AMP with the osteogenic properties of collagen and nHA, enabling multi-target regulation of the osteomyelitic microenvironment. By clearing PAMPs/DAMPs to mitigate excessive inflammation and promoting osteogenic differentiation to accelerate bone regeneration, this strategy presents a transformative potential for the clinical treatment of drug-resistant osteomyelitis.

## A108: A clinico-molecular classification scheme for ossification of ligamentum flavum: based on 1034 cases

Longjie Wang

1

, Shuo Tian

1

, Jialiang Lin

1

, Chuiguo Sun

1

, Weishi Li

1

1

Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Thoracic ossification of the ligamentum flavum (TOLF) is characterized by ectopic bone formation within the ligamentum flavum and often leads to severe myelopathy. Its etiology remains unclear, hindering targeted management. This study aimed to establish a novel classification system integrating clinical, radiological, and molecular characteristics to elucidate its underlying pathogenesis. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of 1,034 surgically treated TOLF patients at our institution from January 2010 to December 2023. This framework provides valuable insights into the diverse pathogenesis of TOLF and could inform future research and personalized treatment strategies.

## A109: Comparative analysis of MRI-based VBQ Score and CT-based HU with DEXA-Based T-Score in assessing BMD in degenerative spine

Ajoy P Shetty

1

, Karthik Ramachandran

1

, Arul kumaran N

1

, S. Rajasekaran

1

1

Ganga Medical Centre and Hospital, Coimbatore, India

Introduction: In spine surgery, accurate assessment of bone mineral density (BMD) is critical for surgical planning and postoperative outcomes. Although DEXA remains the standard method for assessing osteoporosis, its accuracy is reduced in degenerative spinal conditions due to artefactual interference. This study examines the diagnostic performance of CT-derived Hounsfield Units (HU) and MRI-based Vertebral Bone Quality (VBQ) scores by comparing them with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) T-scores in patients with degenerative spine. The operative notes were reviewed to identify cases in which intraoperative ultrasound was used and whether any change to the operative course was undertaken based on the ultrasound findings. Descriptive statistics and Chi-squared tests were employed. Results: 525 patients who underwent surgery for acute spine trauma were identified between January 2020 and December 2024. Based on the operative report, intraoperative ultrasound was documented in 143 patients (113 cervical injuries, 15 thoracic injuries, and 15 lumbar injuries). Laminectomies were performed in all these cases (136 for symptomatic spinal cord or conus level compression, 4 for acute cauda equina syndrome, and 3 cases with nerve root compression present). Ultrasound confirmed decompression of the neural elements along the length of decompression in 120 (83.9%) cases. Intraoperative ultrasound findings altered treatment in 23 (16.1%) cases: The laminectomy was extended proximally or distally in 16 (11.2%) of cases. Expansile duraplasty was undertaken in 4 (2.8%) patients. A transpedicular decompression was performed based on ultrasound in one patient with a burst fracture and the neck was repositioned to generate more lordosis to address ventral compression in one cervical case. There was no noted difference in the proportion ultrasound guided intervention based on underlying spine region or the presence of bony injury (p = 0.784, 0.243 respectively). Conclusion: Intraoperative ultrasound is a useful intraoperative modality particularly in confirming decompression or providing actionable information regarding the adequacy of posterior based decompression. Given its low cost and relative ease of use, surgeons may find this modality helpful in intraoperative assessment of posterior based decompressions, particularly in spine trauma.

## A111: Comparative analysis of DXA, vBMD, CT-HU, and VBQ score as independent risk factors and correlates of cage subsidence following LLIF

Hanming Bian

1

, Qiang Yang

1,2

, Chao Chen

1

, Dong Zhao

1

, Gang Liu

1

1

Capital Medical University Affiliated Beijing Friendship Hospital, Tianjin Hospital, Tianjin, China

Introduction: While it is established that cage subsidence following LLIF is significantly associated with vertebral bone mineral density, there remains a lack of predictive models based on preoperative CT data to accurately forecast individualized subsidence risk. Therefore, this study aims to investigate whether four bone mineral density (BMD) measurement methods-DXA T-score, vertebral BMD (vBMD), CT Hounsfield unit (HU) value, and Vertebral Bone Quality (VBQ) score-can serve as independent risk factors for cage subsidence after Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion (LLIF), and to compare their correlations with the extent of cage subsidence. Material and Methods: A retrospective case analysis was conducted to explore the relationship between the four BMD measurement methods and cage subsidence after LLIF. Patients who underwent single-level LLIF for lumbar degenerative diseases between January 2019 and December 2023 were included. DXA T-scores were obtained from medical records, while lumbar CT-HU values, vBMD, and VBQ scores were measured based on preoperative CT and MRI scans. Cage subsidence was assessed using X-rays at 12 months postoperatively, and the cage subsidence distance (CSD) was measured. Logistic regression analysis was used to identify risk factors for cage subsidence. Pearson correlation analysis was employed to examine the correlation between identified risk factors and CSD, and Williams' test was used to compare the statistical differences in correlation coefficients. Results: According to the inclusion/exclusion criteria, 94 patients who underwent single-level LLIF were included. Among them, 61 were female (64.9%), with a mean age of 63.2 ± 8.1 years. Based on the presence of cage subsidence at 12 months postoperatively, patients were divided into two groups: the subsidence group (34 cases, mean CSD 3.22 ± 0.61 mm) and the non-subsidence group (60 cases, mean CSD 1.07 ± 0.73 mm). There were no significant differences in demographic data or preoperative disc height (DH), lumbar lordosis (LL), or segmental lordosis (SL) between the two groups (p > 0.05). The subsidence group had significantly lower DXA T-scores (-1.87 ± 0.43 vs. -0.66 ± 0.31, p < 0.05), CT HU values (88.37 ± 22.85 vs. 168.44 ± 20.71, p < 0.05), and vBMD values (74.48 ± 10.75 vs. 127.61 ± 13.12, p < 0.05), and a significantly higher VBQ score (4.61 ± 1.08 vs. 3.77 ± 0.96, p < 0.05) compared to the non-subsidence group. Logistic regression analysis identified CT HU value (OR = 0.902, p = 0.003), vBMD (OR = 0.961, p < 0.001), and VBQ score (OR = 1.328, p = 0.037) as independent risk factors for cage subsidence after LLIF. Pearson correlation analysis showed that CT HU value (r = -0.579, p < 0.001) and vBMD (r = -0.703, p < 0.001) were negatively correlated with CSD, while VBQ score was not significantly correlated with CSD (r = 0.293, p = 0.086). Williams' test indicated that the correlation coefficient between vBMD and CSD was significantly greater than that between CT-HU and CSD (p = 0.039). Conclusion: vBMD, CT HU value, and VBQ score can serve as independent risk factors for cage subsidence, but vBMD demonstrates a stronger correlation with the extent of subsidence. Therefore, vBMD is selected as the preferred B parameter for predicting cage subsidence and will be used as the BMD evaluation parameter in subsequent methods for calculating vertebral mechanical properties based on BMD.

Arvind G Kulkarni

1

1

Mumbai Spine Scoliosis & Disc Replacement Center, Bombay Hospital, Breach Candy Hospital, Mumbai, India

Introduction: Body Roundness Index (BRI) is a novel anthropometric measure reflecting central obesity and visceral adiposity, which may influence surgical outcomes. ## A113: How low can we go? Can we further reduce radiation exposure during scoliosis radiographic examination?

Rachelle Imbeault

1

, Marjolaine Roy-Beaudry

1

, Sylvain Deschenes

1

, Justin Dufresne

1

, Stefan Parent

1

1

CHU Sainte-Justine, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: From diagnosis, pediatric patients with idiopathic scoliosis require frequent radiological evaluations. Due to their longer life expectancy and greater radiosensitivity, technologies must minimize radiation dose while optimizing image quality. This study aims to compare two biplane radiography systems, one using photon counting and dose modulation, the other using energy integration and fixed dose throughout acquisition. Material and Methods: Fifty patients were recruited between June 2023 and July 2024. All patients had a diagnosis of idiopathic scoliosis, with an average Cobb angle of 29.7° ± 15.0° and a mean age of 13.7 years. Each patient underwent two successive biplanar examinations (PA and lateral views), one using the dose modulating system and the other using a fixed dose system. Furthermore, analysis of specific anatomical structures showed that visibility is improved for more than 84% of the anatomical landmarks being scored (p-value ≤ 0.05). Conclusion: Results indicate that dose modulation can reduce patient exposure to radiation by 48%, while improving global image quality. Alexandry Carvalho

, Jerônimo Milano

, Facundo Van Isseldyk

, Matias Pereira Duarte

9

, Martin Gagliardi

10

, Jefferson Soares Leal

11

1

Clínica Ortomed, Teresina - Piauí, Brazil,

2

Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG), Columna Institute, Belo Horizonte, Brazil,

3

Clínica de Cuyo, Mendoza, Argentina,

4

Santa Casa de São Paulo, Medical School and Hospitals, São Paulo, Brazil,

Neurological Institute of Curitiba, Curitiba, Brazil,

10

Northern Ontario School of Medicine University, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada,

11

Federal University of Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) at the L5-S1 level is a widely accepted technique for addressing degenerative, deformity, and instability conditions of the lumbosacral junction. Its advantages include direct disc space access, restoration of disc height, and favorable sagittal alignment correction. However, in a subset of the population where the confluence of the common iliac veins is located more distally, mobilization of the left iliac vein may be technically demanding. Spinopelvic parameters, particularly pelvic incidence (PI), are key determinants of sagittal spinal alignment and pelvic morphology. PI, a fixed morphological parameter in adults, influences the orientation of the sacrum and, consequently, the spatial relationship between the sacral plateau and surrounding vascular structures, potentially altering the position of the iliac vessels relative to the L5-S1 disc. Adult patients (> 18 years of age) who underwent standing whole-spine radiographs and lumbosacral magnetic resonance imaging were included. Patients with prior lumbosacral/abdominal surgery, spinal trauma, tumor, or infection were excluded. Demographic data such as age, sex and ethnicity were assessed. In addition, the main parameters measured were pelvic incidence and vein-free vascular window, defined as the ratio of the interiliac distance (between the right and left iliac veins) to the total L5-S1 disc space, expressed as a percentage. The patients were divided into 3 groups: group 1: PI < 45°, group 2: PI 45°-60° and group 3: PI > 60°. Results: Seventy-nine patients were included so far, being 60,7% female, with a mean age of 57 years/old. The main indications for imaging examinations in the patients included in the study were: low back pain (48.1%), sciatica (15.1%) and low back pain associated with radicular pain (12.6%). Among the main associated diseases were: degenerative disc disease (39.7%), spondylolisthesis (14.2%), degenerative scoliosis (10.2%), lumbar stenosis (8.9%). In relation to the parameters evaluated, the mean PI was 53.8° +- 12.4° (51.1° in men and 55.5° in women). The most frequent group according to PI was group 2, corresponding to 41.7% (n33), followed by group 3 31,6% (n25) and group 1 26,5% (n21). The mean value of the vein-free vascular window according to each group was: 54.74% (group 1), 55.92% (group 2) and 64.65% (group 3), however the relationship between high/low PI and the vascular window was not statistically significant (p = 0.247). Conclusion: Preliminary results suggest that patients with a high pelvic incidence (> 60°) tend to have a larger average vein-free vascular window. However, further study with a larger cohort and a more even distribution among the three groups is needed to validate these observations and elucidate the possible association between pelvic incidence and vascular anatomy.

Junyu Li

, Gengyu Han

, Hanwen Zhang

, Zhuo Ran Sun

, Yongqiang Wang

1

, Miao Yu

, Weishi Li

, Lin Zeng

, Yan Zeng

3

MF FI was significantly higher in the complication-presence group (p = .045). Conclusion: Multifidus degeneration is significantly associated with QoL, sagittal parameters and mechanical complications in OVCF patients with kyphosis deformity. ## A116: Preoperative paraspinal muscle quality is an independent predictor of prolonged hospitalization after surgical intervention for lumbar spine trauma

Nathan McLaughlin

1

, Zachary Lowe

1

, Advika Srinivas

1

, Amir Fanaei

1

, Mauricio Avila

1

1

Saint Louis University, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Paraspinal muscle atrophy is a known predictor of poor outcomes in degenerative spine disease, but its prognostic role in acute spinal trauma is not well characterized. We hypothesized that poor preoperative paraspinal muscle quality, characterized by high fatty infiltration, is associated with worse short-term outcomes in patients undergoing surgery for acute traumatic lumbar spine injuries. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on adult patients who underwent surgical intervention for acute lumbar trauma in a regional level 1 trauma. Preoperative T1-weighted MRI was used to measure paraspinal cross-sectional area (CSA) of erector spinae (ES) and multifidus (MF) at L3-L4 and L4-L5 levels. Fatty infiltration (FI) of paraspinal muscles was graded on a 0-5 scale and analyzed across four groups (Goutallier classification, 0 being normal muscle) (0, 1, 2, and 3+). Primary outcomes were total hospital length of stay (LOS) and 90-day complications. Associations were assessed using Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U, and Chi-square tests. Multivariable linear regression was used to determine if FI was an independent predictor of log-transformed LOS after controlling for patient age. Results: A total of 83 eligible patients were included. A significant association was found between FI grade and hospital LOS (Kruskal-Wallis, p = 0.005). Median LOS was similar for patients with FI grades 0, 1, and 2 (7.2, 7.0, and 7.0 days, respectively), but more than doubled for patients with grade 3+ FI (17.4 days). In multivariable regression, FI remained independently associated with longer LOS after adjusting for age (β = 0.186, p = 0.047), corresponding to an approximate 20% increase in LOS per grade increase. In contrast, muscle CSA was not significantly associated with LOS (p > 0.05). Neither FI grade nor CSA was significantly associated with 90-day complication rates or a post-operative loss of independent ambulation (p > 0.05). Conclusion: Preoperative paraspinal muscle quality, as measured by fatty infiltration, is a significant predictor of prolonged hospitalization following surgery for acute lumbar spinal trauma. This association remains independent of patient age. Muscle quality appears more prognostic for short-term recovery than overall muscle size, offering a valuable MRI-based metric for preoperative risk stratification and resource allocation after surgery.

## A117: Evaluating the prognostic role of computed tomography hounsfield units in anticipating spinal outcomes post-instrumentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Chinedu Egu

1

, Elie Najjar

1

, Spyridon Komaitis

1

, Edidiong Essiet

1

, Samuel Akintunde

1

, Vusumuzi Sibanda

1

, Khalid Salem

1

, Opinder Sahota

1

, Nasir Quraishi

1

1

Centre for Spinal Studies and Surgery, Queens Medical Centre, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: The use of Hounsfield unit (HU) measurements derived from preoperative computed tomography (CT) scans has emerged as a promising surrogate for assessing bone mineral density (BMD). This systematic review aims to elucidate the role of HU in predicting spinal outcomes in patients undergoing spinal instrumentation. Material and Methods: A comprehensive systematic review of the English-language literature was performed across multiple databases, focusing specifically on adult patients who underwent spinal instrumentation. Adhering to PRISMA guidelines, studies published between 2017 and 2024 that investigated the correlation between HU measurements and spinal outcomes were included. Data extraction and subsequent meta-analysis were conducted utilizing a random effects model. The methodologi cal quality of the included studies was appraised using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and statistical analyses were executed with R software. Results: A total of thirty-five retrospective studies met the inclusion criteria, encompassing a cohort of 3,927 patients. The reported rates of complications included cage subsidence at 35.5%, pedicle screw loosening at 27.9%, proximal junctional failure at 28.6%, and pseudoarthrosis at 66.7%. Notably, lower HU values were significantly associated with an increased incidence of complications across all studies. The delineated HU cutoff thresholds for predicting specific complications were as follows: 198 HU for lumbar interbody fusion cage subsidence; 116 HU and 126 HU for pedicle screw loosening in lumbar and thoracic spine fusions, respectively; 151 HU for proximal junctional failure in thoracolumbar spinal fusion; and 240-260 HU for pseudoarthrosis following anterior odontoid screw fixation. HU measurements were typically calculated as the mean HU of the vertebrae in the operational segments: cervical (C2-C7), thoracic (T1-T12), lumbar (L1-L4), or sacral (S1). Conclusion: This meta-analysis substantiates a significant correlation between reduced HU values and spinal complications following instrumentation. Specifically, thresholds of below 130 HU for thoracic and lumbar pedicle screw loosening, below 200 HU for lumbar cage subsidence, approximately 150 HU for proximal junctional failure in the thoracolumbar region, and below 260 HU for pseudoarthrosis subsequent to anterior odontoid screw fixation were identified. The mean vertebral HU of the surgical segments serves as a reliable metric for this assessment.

## A118: Sustainability in lumbar decompression surgery - Small tweeks leading to greater wins

Tahir Khaleeq

1

, Siddhant Kapoor

2

, Shahnawaz Haleem

2

1
Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 
2
Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, Birmingham, United Kingdom
Background: Healthcare contributes ∼5% of global CO2 emissions, with operating theatres among the most energy- and waste-intensive hospital areas. Spinal surgery is particularly resource-heavy, due to high implant use, complex technology, long procedures, reliance on single-use items, and transport of heavy trays from central sterile services. A recent study estimated that a single lumbar microdiscectomy generates ∼478 kg CO2e. This evaluation sought to quantify inefficiencies in routine spinal surgery and identify opportunities to reduce cost, waste, and environmental impact. Aim: To assess the utilisation of instruments and single-use items in lumbar decompression surgery, and to quantify associated financial and carbon costs. Methods: A prospective service evaluation was undertaken at a tertiary spinal centre, analysing 20 consecutive lumbar decompressions. For each case, the standard spinal tray list was cross-referenced with instruments actually used, as recorded by the scrub team. Instruments consistently unused across all cases were identified. Data were also collected on single-use consumables, implants, and waste. Procurement and sterile services provided sterilisation costs, and carbon emissions were estimated using published values (66-77 g CO2e per instrument per cycle). Findings were corroborated against theatre logs and operative notes. Results: Of 46 instruments in the Spinal Extras tray, approximately 40% were never used across any of the 20 procedures. These could be safely removed from the tray, reclassifying it from Category G (41-50 items; £59.30 per cycle) to Category F (31-40 items; £48.83 per cycle). This reduction equates to a saving of £20.47 per case. Based on 553 lumbar decompressions performed in 2024-25, annual savings would be at least £10,789, with potential for greater reductions if all consistently unused instruments were removed. From an environmental perspective, removing 6-10 unused instruments would reduce 770-1400 g CO2e per case, equivalent to 823 kg CO2e annually. Additional unquantified waste was noted from routinely opened but unused single-use drapes and consumables, further increasing the environmental burden. Conclusion: This study highlights the hidden financial and carbon cost of unnecessary instruments and consumables in spinal surgery. Tray rationalisation alone could save >£10,700 and >400 kg CO2e annually at a single centre, with greater benefits possible if consistently unused instruments are removed. In addition, substantial waste was observed from single-use items, underlining the need for broader strategies targeting consumables, implants, and sterilisation processes. Tray optimisation represents an achievable “quick win” that complements wider sustainability initiatives and supports alignment with NHS Net Zero targets.

## A119: Improved outcomes using a novel low-modulus 3D-printed porous titanium alloy cage (Osteo Match) versus PEEK cage in osteoporotic patients undergoing lumbar interbody fusion: an early-stage follow-up with CT scans

Weishi Li

1

1

Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: The cage subsidence and failure of fusion occur frequently, due to diminished bone density and compromised mechanical strength of osteoporotic spine. The elastic modulus of current cage structure remains higher than the vertebral bone modulus in osteoporotic patients. The modulus mismatch between the cage and host bone predisposes to localized stress concentration. We firstly investigated the clinical use of a novel low-modulus 3D-printed porous Ti-alloy cage named Osteo Match, which has elastic modulus of < 1GPa matching the bony elastic modulus of osteoporotic patients. Cage subsidence of over 2mm in depth and the fusion status were assessed at 6 months follow-up with CT scans. VAS, ODI, and JOA were recorded for analyzing clinical outcomes. Results: A total of 103 patients were followed-up at 6 months after the surgery. All of the postoperative clinical scores were significantly improved compared with the preoperative scores (p < 0.001). No revision surgery was required and no fatigue cracking of Osteo Match cage was observed. The ratio of female was higher in patients using PEEK cages, but other baseline factors including BMD measured in T-score and CT-HU were comparable between the two types of patients. There were 139 fusion segments in total, including 42 segments in the Ti-alloy group, and 97 segments in the PEEK-group. At 6 months follow-up, the cage subsidence rate was significantly lower in Ti-alloy group than in PEEK group (21.4% vs. 63.9%, p < 0.001). The use of Osteo Match Ti-alloy cage (OR 0.321; 95%CI 0.126-0.817, p = 0.017) was the independent protective factor of occurrence of cage subsidence. The Ti-alloy group achieved higher fusion rate than the PEEK-group (64.3% vs. 44.3%, p = 0.031). Conclusion: Compared with PEEK cages, the novel low-modulus 3D-printed porous Ti-alloy cage has advantages in reducing subsidence risk and promoting interbody fusion in osteoporotic patients. Multicenter study with longer follow-up duration is needed for further investigation.

## A121: Outcomes of health metrics after lumbar decompression and fusion

Jahan Aslami

1

, Praveer Vyas

, Daniel Altman

1
Drexel University College of Medicine, Pittsburgh, United States, 
2
Allegheny Health Network, Pittsburgh, United States

While functional outcomes following lumbar fusion are well-documented, its impact on physical health metrics remains underexplored. The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) provides concise and standardized population-level assessments of physical, mental, and social health. We hypothesized that increased function following lumbar fusion would lead to long-term improvements in health metrics. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent lumbar decompression and fusion at a single institution, excluding those with chronic debilitating conditions (e.g., COPD). Patient demographics and physical health metrics-including BMI, heart rate, blood pressure, A1C, lipid profiles, and PROMIS scores-were collected at one year preoperatively and at 1, 2, and 3 years postoperatively. Paired t-tests were used to compare postoperative values to preoperative baselines, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction applied for multiple comparisons. p < 0.05 denotes significance. Results: A total of 1,336 patients were included over six years. Triglycerides decreased from 149.3 ± 103.8 mg/dL preoperatively to 125.3 ± 55.9 mg/dL at 3 years postoperatively (mean reduction 24.0 mg/dL, p = 0.0016). Total cholesterol decreased from 175.5 ± 37.6 mg/dL to 165.4 ± 42.7 mg/dL at 3 years (mean reduction 10.1 mg/dL, p = 0.0017). A1C declined from 6.61 ± 1.19% to 6.45 ± 0.82% at 3 years (mean reduction 0.16%, p = 0.31), and LDL dropped from 98.6 ± 31.3 mg/dL to 93.5 ± 37.4 mg/dL (mean reduction 5.1 mg/dL, p = 0.20), though the change were not statistically significant. Diastolic blood pressure showed significant improvement, decreasing from 80.0 ± 8.7 mmHg to 77.5 ± 8.7 mmHg at 3 years (mean reduction 2.5 mmHg, p < 0.001). Systolic blood pressure decreased from 133.2 ± 13.9 mmHg to 131.6 ± 15.1 mmHg (mean reduction 1.6 mmHg, p = 0.056), narrowly missing statistical significance. No significant differences were observed in BMI (31.8 ± 5.9 to 31.8 ± 6.2, p = 0.64), HDL (49.8 ± 14.5 to 49.8 ± 16.3, p = 0.98), or heart rate (74.6 ± 13.1 to 72.8 ± 12.1, p = 0.56). At one year, all PROMIS domains showed significant improvement. Anxiety decreased from 51.3 ± 8.9 to 47.1 ± 8.7 (p = 0.009), depression from 50.6 ± 8.0 to 46.0 ± 8.7 (p < 0.001), fatigue from 58.2 ± 8.3 to 53.0 ± 8.4 (p = 0.014), pain interference from 67.8 ± 5.0 to 59.1 ± 9.3 (p < 0.001), and sleep disturbance from 57.8 ± 8.1 to 54.2 ± 8.9 (p = 0.008). Physical function increased from 34.0 ± 4.9 to 39.9 ± 8.9 (p < 0.001), social participation from 38.6 ± 6.1 to 46.5 ± 9.8 (p < 0.001), and upper extremity function from 38.2 ± 6.0 to 45.6 ± 9.1 (p = 0.002). PROMIS data at two and three years were insufficient for further longitudinal analysis. Conclusion: Our findings suggest that lumbar decompression and fusion may contribute to improved physical health metrics. All metrics except for BMI and HDL decreased from baseline. These results suggest improved patients’ physical health. This may be due to increased mobility post-fusion, as well as more regular outpatient follow-up. All PROMIS scores improved significantly at one year, aligning with existing literature. Further, the mean difference in PROMIS scores exceeded the minimal clinically-important differences reported in the literature (usually 2-5). These findings underscore the procedure’s value across multiple domains, including reductions in anxiety, depression, fatigue, and sleep disturbance, as well as improvements in physical function and social participation. Limitations include the inability to control for medications, which may have influenced blood pressure, A1C and lipid values.

## A122: Sex specific analysis of the prognostic factors associated with reaching minimally clinically important difference one-year post surgery across common degenerative lumbar conditions: a CSORN study

Aazad Abbas

1

, Karlo Pedro

2

, Chris Bailey

3

, Philippe Phan

4

, Jennifer Urquhart

3

, Raja Rampersaud

1,5

, CSORN Investigators

1

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

2

Division of Neurosurgery, Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, Canada

3

Combined Orthopaedic and Neurosurgical Spine Program, London Health Sciences Centre, London, Canada

4

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, The Ottawa Hospital, Ottawa, Canada

5

Schroeder Arthritis Institute, Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Up to one-third of patients experience limited benefit following surgical intervention for common degenerative lumbar conditions. There is significant variability in reported prognostic factors with studies being limited by the number of variables and/or sample size as well as a specific diagnosis. Furthermore, although there is growing recognition that outcomes vary by sex, there has been relatively limited work taking a sex-specific approach to investigating predictors of outcome in this clinical population. As such, the objective of this study is to determine unique prognostic factors associated with patient reported pain related disability outcome one-year following spine surgery in males and females. Material and Methods: Data from the Canadian Spine Outcomes and Research Network (CSORN) database (2015-2023) was analyzed for patients with common degenerative lumbar diagnoses. Multivariate logistic regression models were created to predict minimally clinically important difference (MCID) achievement based on 30% improvement in the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at one-year follow-up. Sex stratified analysis was conducted to analysis differences between men and women. Patient diagnosis and a comprehensive list of patient factors (n = 110 variables) were used as inputs. Stepwise selection minimized the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), with significance set at p < 0.05. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for each variable. Results: The study included 6,214 patients, with diagnoses of lumbar spinal stenosis-LSS (2,175), degenerative disc-DD (456), disc herniation-LDH (1,279), degenerative spondylolisthesis-DLS (1,591), isthmic spondylolisthesis-IS (361), and degenerative scoliosis-DS (352). The average (SD) age was 60.1 (13.4) with men and women evenly distributed (3,142 (50.6%) and 3,072 (49.4%), respectively). A summary of factors across both cohorts is found in Table 1. Key common predictive factors across both male and female cohorts were age, baseline ODI score, comorbidities, DLS, IS, smoking, unemployed/other work status, those on worker’s compensation, and daily narcotics use. Factors that were only significant in the male cohort were postgraduate education, employed but not working, legal consultation obtained, medication for back pain, medication duration use > 1 year, intermittent narcotics use, and expected improvement in sporting activities. Factors that were only significant in the female cohort were BMI, baseline back and leg pain, and over the counter medication use.When combining both cohorts and adjusting for sex, the factors that were significant but not in each cohort separately with ORs (95% CI) were living with a partner 1.23 (1.06, 1.43) and less than high school education 0.8 (0.66, 0.97). Conclusion: This study outlines prognostic factors related to achieving MCID for pain related disability across common degenerative lumbar conditions one-year following surgery. A number of factors uniquely influenced outcomes for males and females, suggesting that simply adjusting for sex effects in regression analyses may not be sufficient to identify sex differences. This has implications for the interpretation and use of current prognostic evidence; and future development of predictive algorithms for ODI outcome following spine surgery. It also has implications for patient education and decision-making, and suggests that interventions to optimize outcomes may require a sex-specific approach.

## A123: Impact of preoperative glucagon-like peptide analog therapy on 90-day and 1-year complications following laminectomy in overweight adults: a large multicenter propensity-matched study

Muaz Wahid

1

, Zuhair Zaidi

1

, Asim Mohamed

1

, Salah Aoun

1

1

UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, United States

Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide (GLP) analogs are widely prescribed for obesity and diabetes, yet perioperative effects in spine surgery are incompletely defined. This study represents one of the first large-scale, decompression-only analyses linking preoperative GLP exposure to postoperative outcomes after laminectomy/laminotomy among overweight adults, with effects assessed at 90 days and 1 year. Material and Methods: Adults with overweight or obesity undergoing cervical, thoracic, or lumbar laminectomy/laminotomy were identified in the TriNetX US Collaborative Network (72 health systems; 2010-2024). Prior fusion or bariatric surgery was excluded. Exposure was ≥ 6 months of GLP prescriptions; comparators were non-users. Outcomes (sepsis, acute kidney injury [AKI], deep-vein thrombosis [DVT], myocardial infarction [MI], pneumonia, post-laminectomy syndrome, wound dehiscence, surgical site infection, stroke, and death) were assessed from postoperative day 1 through day 365. Propensity score matching across 33 covariates yielded balanced cohorts (n = 5,680 each). Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. Results: After matching, 11,360 patients were analyzed (median follow-up, 365 days per group). At 90 days, GLP exposure was associated with lower odds of sepsis (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.25-0.56), DVT (0.26, 0.16-0.43), post-laminectomy syndrome (0.45, 0.32-0.62), wound dehiscence (0.38, 0.27-0.51), surgical site infection (0.37, 0.28-0.50), and death (0.30, 0.17-0.54; all p < 0.001); associations for AKI, MI, pneumonia, and stroke were not significant. At 1 year, benefits persisted for sepsis (0.52, 0.40-0.68), DVT (0.41, 0.29-0.57), post-laminectomy syndrome (0.45, 0.37-0.55), wound dehiscence (0.47, 0.36-0.62), surgical site infection (0.43, 0.33-0.56), and death (0.48, 0.35-0.65). AKI showed borderline reduction (0.80, 0.65-1.00; p = 0.046); MI, pneumonia, and stroke remained non-significant. Absolute effects at 1 year underscore clinical impact: mortality was 1.04% in GLP users vs 2.15% in non-users (absolute risk reduction [ARR] 1.11%; approximate NNT ≈ 90); sepsis was 1.7% vs 3.3% (ARR 1.6%; NNT ≈ 63). At 90 days, representative event rates likewise favored GLP exposure (e.g., DVT ∼0.5% vs 1.8%; surgical site infection ∼1.3% vs 3.4%), aligning with 60-70% relative reductions. These patterns concentrate in infection, wound-healing, and thromboembolic domains, with neutral signals for macrovascular ischemia (MI, stroke) and pneumonia, suggesting pathway specificity rather than a global reduction in all postoperative risks. Conclusion: Preoperative GLP exposure was associated with consistent, domain-specific risk reductions-approximately 40-70% lower odds and meaningful absolute benefits-in sepsis, surgical-site morbidity, thromboembolism, and mortality after laminectomy, with effects sustained through 1 year. To our knowledge, no prior decompression-only spine cohort has demonstrated such consistent, domain-specific perioperative benefits of GLP therapy. The combination of large effect sizes, persistence across time horizons, and selective pathway signal (infection/wound/thromboembolism, not MI/stroke) provides actionable insight: GLP therapy functions as a potentially modifiable perioperative risk factor rather than solely a metabolic treatment. These findings support evaluating GLP continuation/optimization within perioperative pathways for overweight patients undergoing decompression, with prospective studies needed to test causality, timing, and class-specific effects.

## A124: The differential impact of tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, and cannabis on postoperative complications after lumbar decompression

Abdel Diab

1

, Reme Arhewoh

1

, Omar Diab

2

, Rakesh Patel

1

, Ilyas Aleem

1

, Joshua Piche

1

1
University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, United States, 
2
University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, United States
Introduction: Tobacco smoking is widely recognized for its negative impact on surgical outcomes. However, the differential effects of non-tobacco nicotine products and marijuana use on postoperative outcomes remain poorly characterized. With increasing adoption of e-cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, and legalized marijuana, understanding their implications in lumbar decompression surgery is crucial for perioperative risk stratification. This study examines the distinct associations of tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine dependence (NTND), and marijuana use to better inform perioperative risk stratification. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted using the TriNetX database, encompassing 104 healthcare organizations. Propensity score matching was employed to balance cohorts for age, gender, BMI, and key comorbidities including diabetes, hypertension, and CKD. Primary outcomes included 90-day complications, readmissions, and reoperations. Secondary outcomes encompassed sepsis, surgical site infection, myocardial infarction, acute renal failure, and mortality. Long-term outcomes were assessed at 2 years. Statistical analyses included risk differences, odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis for reoperation rates. Results: The study analyzed three cohorts: tobacco users (N = 3,012), cannabis users (N = 1,367), NTND users (N = 1,019), and respectively matched controls. After matching, baseline characteristics were well-balanced across groups. Tobacco use was significantly associated with increased risks of surgical site infection (2.4% vs 1.7%, p < 0.001; OR 1.42), sepsis (1.0% vs 0.6%, p = 0.001; OR 1.58), myocardial infarction (0.7% vs 0.4%, p = 0.001; OR 1.76), acute renal failure (1.7% vs 1.2%, p < 0.001; OR 1.44), 90-day readmissions (7.8% vs 5.6%, p < 0.001; OR 1.44), and mortality (0.4% vs 0.2%, p = 0.037; OR 1.60). However, tobacco users exhibited lower reoperation rates at two years (3.6% vs 4.3%, p = 0.004; OR 0.83), an observation requiring cautious interpretation due to potential survivorship bias and variations in follow-up patterns. Cannabis use was linked to higher 90-day readmission rates (8.4% vs 5.4%, p = 0.002; OR 1.61) but did not significantly impact other complications. NTND showed no increased risk across any measured outcomes. Conclusion: Tobacco use remains a critical modifiable risk factor for short-term complications and mortality following lumbar decompression surgery. Cannabis use was primarily associated with elevated 90-day readmission rates, underscoring the need for targeted perioperative monitoring. In contrast, NTND demonstrated no measurable impact on postoperative outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of tailored preoperative counseling for tobacco and marijuana users to mitigate risks and improve surgical outcomes. The observed association between tobacco use and reduced reoperation rates warrants further investigation, as it may reflect underlying data artifacts or survivorship biases. Future research should explore the long-term effects of NTND and cannabis use, particularly as their societal adoption continues to grow, to enhance perioperative risk assessment and patient care strategies.

## A125: 3D morphometric evaluation of surgical strategies for lumbar sagittal alignment restoration

Mete Özer

1,2

, Ersin Taşkın

1

, Tamer Atan

1

, Bedri Karaismailoğlu

2,3,4

, Mehmet Ali Talmac

1

, Önder Aydıngöz

3

1

Başakşehir Çam And Sakura City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Istanbul University - Cerrahpaşa, Institute of Graduate Studies, Istanbul, Turkey

3

Istanbul University - Cerrahpaşa, Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey

4

Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, CAST (Cerrahpasa Research, Simulation and Design Laboratory), Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: This study compared the sagittal correction achieved by different surgical techniques for lumbar sagittal balance using three-dimensional model-based morphometric analysis. Material and Methods: Six lumbar CT datasets were reconstructed into three-dimensional models with Mimics and 3-Matic software. Four surgical scenarios were simulated at standardized levels: (1) single-level Smith-Petersen osteotomy (SPO) at L4-5, (2) single-level anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) at L4-5, (3) two-level Ponte osteotomy (L3-4 and L4-5), and (4) two-level oblique/lateral lumbar interbody fusion (OLIF/LLIF) with posterior pedicle screw fixation (L3-4 and L4-5). MATLAB-based morphometric analysis was performed to measure global and segmental lordosis, pelvic parameters, foraminal height, and disc height. Results: All techniques provided measurable improvements in sagittal alignment. Single-level ALIF and SPO achieved comparable angular correction, with ALIF yielding greater disc and foraminal height restoration. Two-level Ponte and OLIF/LLIF approaches resulted in cumulative angular gains, with Ponte showing more effective posterior column shortening and OLIF/LLIF demonstrating significant disc and foraminal height restoration. Conclusion: Different surgical techniques for lumbar sagittal balance provide distinct morphometric advantages. While single-level ALIF offers the strongest segmental correction with substantial height restoration, SPO provides posterior-based angular gain. Two-level Ponte osteotomy and OLIF/LLIF achieve comparable cumulative lordotic correction through different mechanisms-posterior column resection versus anterior column distraction. These findings highlight the importance of 3D model-based evaluation in guiding the selection of surgical strategy tailored to patient-specific deformity patterns.

Despite these promising clinical benefits, lateral-decubitus ALIF remains relatively novel, with a paucity of published series and limited follow-up. Conclusion: Single position ALIF with navigated posterior screws has good outcome and patient satisfaction. ## A128: Surgical outcomes of posterior-only surgery for thoracolumbar spinal tuberculosis: a five-year case series of 83 patients from a high-burden region

Phuc Diep

1

, Hanh Nguyen

1

, Truc Vu

1

, Tuan Ha

1

1

Hospital for Traumatology and Orthopaedics, Ho Chi Minh city, Viet Nam

Introduction: Thoracolumbar spinal tuberculosis (TLSTB) is a common form of musculoskeletal tuberculosis and remains a significant health burden in developing countries. Although anterior approaches have long been the standard, posterior-only surgery has emerged as a promising alternative, offering advantages in deformity correction, reduced invasiveness, and shorter hospitalization. However, robust evidence on its long-term outcomes and complication profile remains limited. This study provides context-specific evidence by evaluating clinical and radiological outcomes, as well as perioperative complications, of posterior-only surgery in TLSTB. Radiological parameters were kyphotic Cobb angle, fusion by Bridwell criteria, and hardware failure. All variables were measured preoperatively, postoperatively, and at final follow-up. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of poor outcomes. Conclusion: Posterior-only surgery provides significant improvements in pain, neurological function, and deformity correction in TLSTB, supporting its role as a valuable alternative to conventional approaches. Nonetheless, limitations such as hardware failure, nonunion, and residual risks highlight the need for careful patient selection and long-term follow-up.
