## A129: Reassessing neurological risk in spinal tuberculosis: the dominant role of mechanical instability over others

S. Rajasekaran

1

, Harikrishna R.R

2

, Sri Vijay Anand KS

2

, Ajoy P Shetty

2

, Rishi Kanna

2

1

Ganga Hospital and Medical Centre, Coimbatore, India

2

Ganga Medical Centre and Hospital, Coimbatore, India

Background: Spinal tuberculosis (TB) remains a major cause of morbidity worldwide, with neurological deficits occurring in approximately 10-30% of cases. While traditional predictors such as canal encroachment, kyphosis, and cord signal changes have received attention, the independent role of mechanical instability in neurologic impairment is unclear. This study reassesses the contribution of instability, as quantified by the Tuberculosis Spine Instability Score (TSIS), and compares its predictive value to established radiological factors in thoracic spinal TB. Methods: A retrospective review was conducted at a single tertiary center, including 122 patients diagnosed with thoracic spinal TB. Clinical, and radiological data were collected, with neurological status classified using the Frankel grading system and spinal stability using TSIS by Prof.S.Rajasekaran. Statistical analysis included univariate and multivariate logistic regression to determine independent risk factors for neurological deficit, with additional analysis of the interaction between instability with epidural compression and Canal encroachment area (CEA). Results: Univariate analysis showed that age, CEA, cord signal changes, epidural compression, and instability were significantly associated with neurological deficit. On Multivariate analysis, although CEA demonstrated a notable association, definite instability, as defined by TSIS, carried higher odds for neurological deficit (adjusted odds ratio = 8, p = 0.001) compared to it, while cord signal change and epidural compression losing statistical significance. The predicted probability of neurological deficit ranged from 1% (stable spine with no epidural compression) to 63% (unstable spine with epidural compression), confirming instability as the most prominent risk factor across subgroup. In stable spine, elevated CEA correlated with neurological deficit, but in unstable spines, the difference in CEA was less prominent, underscoring the predominant impact of instability over canal encroachment. Conclusion: Mechanical instability, as defined by TSIS, is the most robust and independent predictor of neurological deficit in thoracic spinal TB, superseding conventional radiological measures. Incorporating TSIS into routine evaluation enables early identification and prioritization of high-risk patients for surgical stabilization, thereby providing a practical, evidence-based shift from compression-based to instability-guided management and helping to prevent irreversible neurologic injury.

## A130: Fluoroscopic guidance gives more useful results than CT guidance in transpedicular spine biopsy

Rishi Kanna

1

, Sai Keerthan

1

, Ajoy P Shetty

1

1

Ganga Hospital, Coimbatore, India

Introduction: Even though spinal biopsy is an important investigatory tool to diagnose spinal lesions (infections or tumors), the optimal image guidance to perform a biopsy is still unclear. While both Computerized tomography (CT) and Fluoroscopy are commonly used, the selection of one over the other is largely subjective based on availability of resources, clinician’s preference, and cost of care. Material and Methods: Case records of consecutive patients with spinal lesions (n = 206), inconclusively diagnosed as infection/primary tumor/metastasis in MRI and whom underwent a percutaneous biopsy were studied. The biopsy was performed through either CT (CTB, n = 101) guidance in the radiology suite or fluoroscopy (FLB, n = 105) guidance in the operating room. All CTB were done under local anesthesia with Jamshidi needle. FLB was performed under LA (n = 60) or GA (n = 45), with both Jamshidi needle and thin tissue forceps. The tissue was subjected to pyogenic culture, GenXpert test, histopathological examination and tubercular culture. The results were grouped into three categories: Highly Useful, Useful and Not useful. Results: FLB had a significantly higher number of useful results than CTB. In FLB, 58 (55.2%) were highly useful, 31 (29.5%) were useful, and 16 (15.2%) were not useful, while in CTB, 51 (50.5%) were highly useful, 6 (5.9%) were useful and 44 (43.6%) were not useful. FLB identified 89/105 disease-positive cases (sensitivity - 84.8%), while CTB identified 57/101 disease-positive cases, yielding a sensitivity of 56.4% (p = 0.0001, 4.29 higher odds and 1.5 times higher chances of predicting the disease). A high number of “not useful” results in CT guided biopsy were noted in the lumbar region (50.8%) and in patients with suspected infection (49.1%). Conclusion: Fluoroscopy guided biopsies performed in operating suite with combination of Jamshidi needle and tissue forceps are better than CT guided biopsies in planning further treatment, especially in patients with spinal infections.

## A131: Surgical site infection from posterior cervical fusion: a 10 year institutional experience

Ben Carnovale

1

, Samuel Wakelin

1

, Nicole Don

1

, Ayesha Waheed

1

, Hansen Deng

1,2

, Kojo Hamilton

1,2,3

, Nitin Agarwal

1,2,3

1

Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA, United States

2

Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, PA, United States

3

Neurological Surgery, Veterans Affairs Pittsburgh Healthcare System, Pittsburgh, PA, United States

Introduction: Surgical Site Infection (SSI) is a significant concern postoperatively to spine surgeries, contributing to extended hospital stays, increased healthcare costs, morbidity, and mortality. In many cases, SSI requires re-opening of the surgical wound and a wash-out, as well as pharmaceutical treatment. Furthermore, the presence and severity of these infections may vary based upon surgery type and location, with posterior cervical fusion contributing unique risk factors for susceptibility to and spread of infection. The regimen surrounding these SSIs typically is well defined, involving empirical antibiotics preceding characterization of pathogens that inform a full treatment course. However, further investigation of these infections may better inform empirical regimens for patients presenting with potential SSI following posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF). In this study, we aimed to characterize SSI following PCDF at a single, quaternary care institution and characterize the species and resistance profiles of the isolated organisms. Materials and Methods: We performed a retrospective review of posterior cervical fusions at a single institution over the past ten years. The electronic medical record was used to extract demographic, clinical, surgical, and outcome variables including age, sex, comorbidities, surgical indication, operative details, and presence of an infection. For each SSI, the time to wash-out, pathogenic organism, antibiotic type and duration, and resistance matrices (where performed) were recorded. Associations between SSI incidence and demographic, clinical, and surgical factors including body mass index (BMI), age, diabetes status, smoking status, surgical indication (degenerative, deformity, trauma, revision), and number of levels fused were assessed with univariate statistics and multiple logistic regression. Additionally, Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens were separated for a separate subanalysis. Results: Records for 590 posterior cervical fusions were recorded, with 47 noted infections (8.0%). The average time to wash-out was 31.4 days. BMI was positively associated with risk of infection in both univariate (p = 0.018, Odds Ratio 1.0464) and multiple logistic regression (p = 0.0272, Odds Ratio 1.0457). Coagulase negative Staphylococcus (20), Staphylococcus aureus (16), and Propionibacterium species (9) were the most common organisms detected. Seventeen SSIs included multiple pathogens. Patients with SSI had an average antibiotic course of 30.7 days. Sensitivity matrices were recorded for 35 of the positive cultures, with 20 (57%) exhibiting resistance to at least one antibiotic. The most commonly-resisted drugs were Oxacillin (11) and Erythromycin (6). Operative time was positively associated with odds of gram-negative bacterial infection (p = 0.038, Odds Ratio: 1.005). Conclusion: Surgical site infection following posterior cervical fusion remains a clinically significant complication, with an incidence of 8% in this cohort. Elevated BMI was identified as an independent risk factor, underscoring the importance of patient optimization prior to surgery. Additionally, increased operative time was associated with increased risk of gram-negative infection, potentially indicating a more severe infectious phenotype in longer operations. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus and Staphylococcus aureus were the most isolated organisms, with over half of cultures demonstrating resistance to at least one antibiotic, most frequently oxacillin and erythromycin. These findings highlight the need for heightened awareness of resistant pathogens in tailoring empirical antibiotic regimens in patients with surgical site infection.

## A132: Prevalence of spinal tuberculosis among extrapulmonary TB including MDR spinal TB: a systematic review

Julian Scherer

1,2,3

, Cornelia Gnägi

4

, Harvinder Singh Chhabra

5

, S. Rajasekaran

6

1

University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa

2

University Hospital of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

3

Center for Musculoskeletal Surgery, Charite - University Medicine, Berlin, Germany

4

Tygerberg Hospital, Cape Town, South Africa

5

Sri Balaji Action Medical Institute, Delhi, India

6

Ganga Hospital, Coimbatore, India

Introduction: Spinal Tuberculosis (STB) is thought to represent most cases amongst Musculoskeletal TB (MSKTB) and can result in spinal instability, neurological fallout, severe pain and general TB symptoms. The WHO tuberculosis report does not report MSKTB cases and therefore also does not allow to estimate STB cases. When digging into international literature, data on prevalence and incidence of STB are derived from small case series, which leads to the question whether the epidemiological numbers on Extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) as well as MSKTB including STB are reliable. Similarly, the numbers on drug-resistant STB are questionable. The aim of this systematic review was to assess published cohorts examining different forms of tuberculosis to unravel a more precise prevalence of STB and MDR-STB. Material and Methods: We conducted a systematic review of the literature according to the PRISMA checklist and algorithm, aiming to assess all articles reporting on EPTB and STB. We performed an initial search of Web of ScienceTM for eligible investigations. The search terms were: (“extrapulmonary tuberculosis”) AND (“spinal tuberculosis”) (All Fields). We limited the search to cohort studies, randomized controlled trials and large case series, while systematic reviews, meta-analyses, small case series and case reports were excluded. We included papers published in English until November 2024. Results: The initial search revealed 180 publications of which 16 were included into the final synthesis. Five papers (Group A) were focusing on EPTB, Pulmonary TB (PTB) and STB comprising a total of 12,017 patients. The majority of patients had PTB (80.6%), and 19.4% had EPTB. Only 292 patients had STB which reflects 2.4% amongst all assessed patients and 12.5% amongst all EPTB patients. Three studies out of Group A were focusing specifically on STB and MSTK and revealed that less than a quarter (17.7%) of all EPTB cases were MSKTB and STB was the most frequent entity amongst MSKTB cases (67.5%). Eleven studies focused on EPTB and STB cases (Group B). However, most of the EPTB cases in these publications were MSKTB cases which may skew the results. Synthesis of these papers revealed a total of 7,736 patients of which 65.7% were STB cases. Nine studies specifically analyzed STB amongst MSKTB cases with a frequency of 67.5%. Taking all publications together which strictly analyzed STB and MSKTB cases (n=12; from Group A and B), the majority (67.3%) of all MSTKB cases accounted for STB. Only three amongst all assessed studies in this review analyzed drug resistance and showed that 11.83% (range 8.5% to 14.5%) of all STB cases were MDR-STB cases. Conclusion: Our results indicate that the incidence of spinal TB amongst EPTB as well as the incidence of MDR-STB in general might be underestimated. However, these data should be handled with caution since the assessed studies did not strictly aim to determine incidence or prevalence rates. Further, the assessed studies were mainly of retrospective nature and the study sites were not equally internationally distributed. Thus, prospective international registries should be implemented to further investigate the true incidence of STB and MDR-STB.

## A133: Intraoperative 0.05% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) irrigation reduces surgical site infections in thoracolumbar spine trauma

Dallas Kramer

1

, Pauline Hoffman

1,2

, Caitlin Barrett

1,2

, Praveer Vyas

1

, Seung Jeong

1

, Daniel Altman

1,2

, Alex Yu

1,2

1

Allegheny Health Network, Pittsburgh, United States,

2

Drexel University College of Medicine, Pittsburgh, United States

Introduction: Surgery for traumatic thoracolumbar injuries carries nearly twice the risk of surgical site infection (SSI) compared to elective fusion for lumbar degenerative disc disease. Efforts to mitigate infection risks include dilute antibiotic and/or antiseptic (povidone-iodine) irrigation and vancomycin powder. Despite being available as a topical antiseptic in spine surgery for over 50 years, to date there is no literature on the use of intraoperative chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) irrigation. Material and Methods: Retrospective review of patients undergoing surgery for traumatic thoracolumbar injuries between 2017-2023. Rates of SSI were compared among cases using diluted antibiotic irrigation with or without the addition of 0.05% CHG irrigation (450mL/bottle). Clinical and surgical data were collected from the electronic health records, including: age, sex, BMI, obesity, diabetes mellitus, tobacco use, spine region, number of intervertebral levels, surgery time, estimated blood loss, and subfascial vancomycin powder. Statistical analysis was performed using student’s t-test and chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests (p < 0.05). Potential confounding variables for SSI were evaluated using bivariate analysis and multiple logistic regression. Results: 210 patients (82 control, 128 CHG) met inclusion criteria. There were no significant differences in patient demographics or surgical data besides greater utilization of vancomycin powder in the CHG group (43.0% vs. 20.7%, p < 0.005). There was a trend towards significantly fewer SSI with CHG irrigation (4.7% vs. 12.2%, p = 0.083). After controlling for potentially confounding variables including vancomycin powder, there was a significantly reduced risk of SSI with CHG irrigation (aOR 0.26 [95% CI; 0.06-0.83]; p = 0.028). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one SSI was 11 patients. Conclusion: This is the first investigation of intraoperative 0.05% CHG irrigation during spine surgery, showing a significant reduction in the incidence of SSI in the setting of thoracolumbar spine trauma.

## A134: Oral iron supplementation after lumbar decompression and fusion is associated with increased infection risk

Melissa Romoff

1

, Michael Kim

1

, Emily Tse

1

, Courtney Spitzer

1

, Andy Ton

1

, Vivian Chen

1

, Ryan Le

1

, Abhinav Sharma

1

, Justin Chan

1

, Emily Mills

1

, Hao-Hua Wu

1

, Don Park

1

, Yu-po Lee

1

, Nitin Bhatia

1

, Sohaib Hashmi

1

1

Univeristy of California, Irvine, Orange, United States

Introduction: Oral iron is commonly used to treat anemia, particularly in surgical patients who may be at risk of perioperative blood loss. While iron is known to positively drive red blood cell production, recent evidence suggests elevated free serum iron may promote bacterial overgrowth and impair immunity. In orthopedic and spinal procedures, postoperative infections are a major cause of surgical dissatisfaction, as they can lead to hardware failure and increased morbidity. However, the impact of postoperative iron supplementation on infection risk following lumbar spine surgery remains unexplored. Given the rising prevalence of spine surgeries and routine oral iron administration, greater insight into its effects on postoperative infection rate is critical. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the TriNetX United States Collaborative Network, a database including over 117 million patients. Patients who underwent lumbar spine fusion and decompression surgery between 2015 and 2024 were identified using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes. Two cohorts were assembled: patients who received oral iron supplementation within 60 days of surgery and those who did not receive iron of any supplementation before or after surgery. Propensity score matching was performed to minimize confounders between groups based on key variables, age, sex, comorbidities, preoperative anemia, and postoperative blood transfusion status. Statistical analyses included the calculation of odds ratios (ORs) to evaluate relative risk, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis to measure infection-free survival probability, and hazard ratios (HRs) between groups. The primary outcome was the incidence of spinal fixation device-related infections within one year postoperatively. Results: A total of 48,528 patients met the study criteria (24,264 in each cohort). The incidence of spinal fixation device-related infections was significantly higher in the iron-supplemented cohort (0.874%) compared to the non-iron cohort (0.495%), with a statistically significant difference (p < 0.0001). Patients receiving oral iron had a 76.4% higher odds of developing infections compared to the non-iron cohort (OR: 1.764, 95% CI: [1.415-2.215], p < 0.0001) Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed a significantly increased hazard in the iron cohort, with 76.5% higher risk of developing an infection within one year postoperatively (HR: 1.765, 95% CI [1.412-2.206], p < 0.0001). Conclusion: Postoperative oral iron supplementation is associated with a significantly increased risk of spinal fixation device-related infections following lumbar fusion and decompression surgery. The increased infection rate may be attributed to iron’s role in fostering bacterial growth and modulating immune response; however, future prospective studies are needed to further elucidate the underlying mechanisms and identify strategies to improve patient outcomes. These findings underscore the need to critically evaluate routine iron supplementation practices in surgical patients.

## A135: Age- and localization-dependent pathogen distribution and mortality in pyogenic spondylodiscitis: insights from 10,801 nationwide cases

Siegmund Lang

1

, Volker Alt

1

, Nicolas H. von der Höh

2

1
University Hospital Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany, 
2
University Hospital Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany
Introduction: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis is a rare but life-threatening spinal infection with rising incidence, particularly among elderly patients. Although Staphylococcus aureus is traditionally considered the leading pathogen, clinical experience suggests that Gram-negative bacilli and Enterococci become more relevant with age, potentially impacting empiric therapy. Large-scale, population-based confirmation of these shifts has been lacking. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of 10,801 patients with pyogenic spondylodiscitis from German nationwide hospital discharge data (InEK, 2024). Patients were stratified by age (< 65, 65-79, ≥ 80 years) and by infection site (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, multisegmental). Pathogen groups and resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, MRGN) were identified from ICD-10 codes. Outcomes included in-hospital mortality. Statistical analyses comprised χ2 tests and logistic regression with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: Lumbar infections were most common (50.7%), followed by thoracic (25.3%), multisegmental (12.5%), and cervical (11.5%). In-hospital mortality increased stepwise with age (2.6% < 65 y; 5.1% 65-79 y; 10.9% ≥ 80 y) and differed by localization, being lowest in lumbar infections (6.2%) and highest in multisegmental disease (12.9%). Pathogen distribution showed clear age-related shifts. Staphylococci overall declined significantly with age (35.7%, 28.5%, 21.3%; p < 0.001). Within this group, Staphylococcus aureus accounted for the majority of isolates but decreased more steeply (24.8%, 18.1%, 12.9%), whereas coagulase-negative and other staphylococci remained relatively stable (10.9%, 10.4%, 8.4%). In contrast, Enterobacterales (17.3%, 21.4%, 21.4%) and Enterococci (3.9%, 8.7%, 11.8%) increased with advancing age (both p < 0.001). Pseudomonas spp. were more frequent in elderly patients (up to 4.6 %), while anaerobes decreased (4.8% to 2.0 %). Resistant organisms were rare overall (1.5-3.2%) but rose with age (p < 0.001). By localization, S. aureus and other staphylococci predominated in cervical and thoracic disease (34.5% and 30.7%), while Enterobacterales and Enterococci were most common in lumbar and multisegmental infections (up to 23.5% and 13.4%, respectively; p < 0.001). Mortality analyses within age strata revealed distinct patterns. In patients < 65 years, Enterococci (7.4%, OR 3.27, 95% CI 1.53-7.00) and resistant organisms (12.2%, OR 5.55, 95% CI 2.11-14.59) carried the highest risk, while Staphylococcal infections were not associated with increased mortality. Among those aged 65-79 years, mortality was significantly elevated for Staphylococci (8.4%, OR 2.34, 95 % CI 1.79-3.07), Enterobacterales (7.7%, OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.34-2.39), Enterococci (8.7%, OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.29-2.78), Pseudomonas spp. (10.3%, OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.40-3.60), and resistant organisms (11.6%, OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.46-4.44). In patients ≥ 80 years, S. aureus and other staphylococci (15.5%, OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.36-2.17) and Enterobacterales (13.6%, OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.10-1.77) remained significantly associated with mortality, while other groups did not. Conclusion: This nationwide study demonstrates that both pathogen distribution and mortality in pyogenic spondylodiscitis are strongly dependent on age and localization. With increasing age, Gram-negative bacilli and Enterococci gain importance while S. aureus declines. Mortality increases stepwise with age and is linked to Enterobacterales, Enterococci, and resistant organisms in younger and middle-aged adults, and to staphylococci in the elderly. These findings support the need for age- and localization-adapted empiric treatment strategies to improve early coverage in pyogenic spondylodiscitis.

## A136: Surgical management of traumatic C2-C3 subluxation with bilateral carotid artery dissection

Vinicius Ricieri Ferraz

1

, Marcelo Ochoa Coelho de Souza Furlan

2

, Heber Martim

3

, Cesar Massami Yukita

3

1

Dr. José de Carvalho Florence Hospital, The Regional Hospital of São José dos Campos - Dr. Rubens Savastano, São José dos Campos, São Paulo, Brazil

2

Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, Curitiba, Brazil

3

Department of Neurosurgery, The Regional Hospital of São José dos Campos - Dr. Rubens Savastano, São José dos Campos, São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Traumatic cervical spine injuries associated with vascular lesions are infrequent but present significant surgical challenges. An infrequent condition involves C2-C3 subluxation combined with bilateral carotid artery dissection, necessitating rapid diagnosis and a multidisciplinary treatment approach. This article outlines the surgical and endovascular techniques employed to manage such complex cases, highlighting critical technical aspects that facilitated effective stabilization and vascular preservation. Material and Methods: A 48-year-old male patient experienced a high-energy motorcycle collision resulting in severe cervical trauma. Imaging studies identified traumatic subluxation of the C2-C3 vertebral levels, bilateral dissection of the internal carotid arteries, and complete occlusion of the left vertebral artery. Due to the elevated risk of secondary ischemic injury, a multidisciplinary approach was implemented. Surgical stabilization was carried out via a posterior approach utilizing lateral mass and pedicle screw fixation extending from C1 to C4. During the procedure, meticulous care was taken to preserve vascular integrity and minimize cervical manipulation, thereby reducing the likelihood of further arterial compromise. Following spinal stabilization, the patient underwent an adjunctive endovascular intervention. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed bilateral carotid dissections, and subsequent stent placement coupled with antithrombotic therapy was performed to re-establish vascular flow and mitigate the risk of thromboembolic events. Results: The posterior fixation provided immediate spinal stabilization and restored cervical alignment without intraoperative complications. Postoperative imaging confirmed proper hardware placement and effective decompression. The endovascular procedure successfully re-established carotid lumen patency, and subsequent perfusion studies indicated improved cerebral blood flow. The patient’s neurological condition remained stable throughout hospitalization, with gradual motor recovery during rehabilitation. At 12-month follow-up, spinal fusion was solidly achieved, vascular patency was maintained, and no ischemic events occurred. Conclusion: The coexistence of traumatic cervical instability and bilateral carotid dissection necessitates a meticulously coordinated therapeutic approach. Posterior cervical fixation offers dependable stabilization with minimal disturbance to injured vessels, whereas endovascular therapy stands as a safe and efficacious modality for restoring carotid flow. This case underscores the significance of integrating advanced spinal instrumentation with endovascular techniques to enhance patient outcomes in cases involving concurrent spinal and vascular trauma. Early multidisciplinary intervention is paramount to avert catastrophic neurological sequelae and to secure long-term functional recovery.

## A138: Anterior spinal artery visualization on CT angiography as a prognostic marker in acute cervical spinal cord injury

Baptiste Boukebous

1

, Amal Abayed

2

, Pierre Antoine Allain

2

, Myriam Lamamri

2

, Mohamed Zoghlami

2

, Bilal El Hachache

2

, Marc-Antoine Rousseau

1

1

APHP, Université Paris Cité, Paris, France

2

APHP, Paris, France

Introduction: There are very few data regarding the involvement of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) in acute cervical spinal cord injuries (SCI), including decompensation of cervical spondylotic myelopathy, traumatic fractures or dislocations, or spinal cord injury without radiological abnormalities (SCIWORA). Some authors have reported the consistent visualization of this artery on CT angiography in severe spinal cord trauma, whereas others have noted that it is poorly visualized. We hypothesize that, when visible, the presence of the ASA in the cervical region on CT angiography represents an indicator of initial severity and a predictor of poor neurological recovery. Materials and Methods: A total of 37 patients admitted to the intensive care unit for acute cervical trauma were analyzed (mean age 40 years, mean follow-up 145 days): 16 SCIWORA, 5 cases of cervical spondylotic myelopathy decompensation, 7 fracture-dislocations treated surgically, and 9 minor fractures treated with a cervical collar (e.g., transverse process). None of these patients had associated traumatic brain injury or thoracolumbar spinal cord injury. The ASA was assessed on CT angiography performed as part of the initial trauma evaluation. Two independent readings were performed, one of them blinded to the neurological status. Initial and last follow-up neurological status were assessed using the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale. The Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) was collected to assess overall trauma severity. Results: At admission, the ASIA distribution was: 12/37 A, 6/37 B, 2/37 C, 6/37 D, and 11/37 E. The ASA was detected in 13/37 patients (35%) by both readers, with inter-observer agreement in 35/37 cases. No significant difference in SAPS was observed between patients with or without a visible ASA. Considering the ASIA score as a progressive numerical scale (A = 1, E = 5) and accounting for each patient’s potential for recovery (e.g., an ASIA E patient has no recovery potential, whereas an ASIA A patient may gain up to 4 points), patients without a visible ASA had a recovery potential of +72% relative to their baseline, compared with +33% for patients with a visible ASA, corresponding to an average 40% reduction in neurological recovery potential for patients with a visible ASA (CI95%[-69%, -10%], p = 0.01). For example, among the 5 patients initially graded ASIA A without a visible ASA, all improved to at least ASIA D; among the 7 patients initially ASIA A with a visible ASA, only 2 improved to at least D. All SCIWORA patients without a visible ASA reached at least ASIA D at the last follow-up, regardless of their initial neurological status. Conclusion: Whether due to arterial spasm, increased blood flow, occlusion, or raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure, the reasons why the ASA became visible in patients with poorer prognosis SCI remain unclear. However, this observation paves the way for further investigations. The visibility of the ASA could already be considered an early prognostic factor for neurological recovery.

## A139: Mortality risk in type ii dens fractures: the role of pneumonia and neurocognitive disorders after anterior screw fixation in a German level 1 trauma center

Kenny Hagar

1

, Zaccaria Richard

1

, Jan Wulf

1

, Wolfgang Böcker

1

, Carl Neuerburg

1

, Suero Eduardo

1

1

LMU München, MUM - Muskuloskelettale Universitätsmedizin München, Trauma and Orthopedic Surgery, Munich, Germany

Introduction: Due to demographic changes and the globally progressing aging of the population, the number of osteoporotic vertebral fractures is steadily increasing. Dens fractures account for approximately 15-20% of all cervical spine fractures. Depending on associated comorbidities, this type of fracture may carry an increased risk of mortality following surgical treatment using ventral screw osteosynthesis. The aim of this study is to evaluate the clinical outcomes of anterior screw fixation in patients with type II dens fractures and to identify the influence of various comorbidities on mortality in this patient population. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included 82 patients with a mean age of 75.7 years who were treated between January 2011 and December 2019 at two hospital locations and by two specialized departments. All patients underwent anterior screw fixation for type II dens fractures according to the Anderson and D”Alonzo classification. The study aimed to assess the influence of demographic and clinical factors on mortality in this context. We first conducted a Cox regression analysis to evaluate potential risk factors. Next, we identified predictors of overall mortality using logistic regression models, with postoperative death as the dependent variable. Results: The occurrence of postoperative delirium significantly increased both 30-day and overall mortality (p < 0.05). Similarly, patients who developed postoperative pneumonia had significantly higher mortality rates (p < 0.05). Other comorbidities, however, did not show a significant impact on mortality (p > 0.05). Additionally, pre-existing dementia correlates with a higher postoperative mortality rate. The risk of death increases substantially when these factors occur in combination. Therefore, effective prevention and management of delirium and pneumonia are critical in the postoperative care of these patients. Although dysphagia was not associated with increased mortality, early involvement of speech-language therapy following surgery may be beneficial. Surgical complications themselves did not influence mortality. The optimal management of type II dens fractures remains a subject of ongoing scientific discussion.

## A140: The role of Hounsfield Units in predicting cage subsidence after lateral lumbar interbody fusion: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Chen Zhang

1

, Zachary Chu

2

, Jonathan Boey

3

, Reuben Soh

3

1

Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia

2

Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore, National University Health System, Singapore, Singapore

3

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined cohort studies investigating the relationship between vertebral Hounsfield unit (HU) measurements on preoperative computed tomography (CT) scans and postoperative cage subsidence (CS) in patients undergoing lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF). Future studies should explore the cut-off value of 120 HU to validate its predictive capability.

Introduction: Coincident traumatic atlantoaxial fractures are common among older patients. These fractures pose challenges for management and outcomes data for patients with fractures are limited. The current study provides an institutional experience for clinical management. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 68 cases at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital (San Francisco, California) with traumatic atlantoaxial fractures between 2003 and 2024. Univariate analyses were performed to identify factors associated with inpatient mortality, operative versus non-operative treatment, and fracture union. Multivariable logistic regression, using best subset logistic regression with a maximum of two predictors due to the number of patients, as well as multivariable logistic regression using expert selected variables, was used to identify factors associated with mortality and operative treatment. Univariate odds ratios from logistic regression were used to analyze fracture patterns. Results: Coincident traumatic atlantoaxial fractures predominantly happen in elderly individuals (74.2 years, range 23.0-100.0), and 48.5% of patients had neurological deficits. Univariate analyses demonstrated patients who expired during admission had high rates of neurologic deficits (82.4% vs. 37.3%, p = 0.001). These fractures have high rates of bony non-union in conservatively managed cases (44.4% of 9 patients with follow-up), while no non-union was observed amongst surgical cases. A smaller proportion of females underwent surgery (23.5% of surgical cases, vs 54.9% of managed nonoperatively cases, p = 0.025). Of 51 patients who survived hospitalization, 4 (7.8%) died within 1 year, and 9 (17.6%) in total (longest follow-up 126 months). On univariate logistic regression analysis, lateral structures were often injured together (occipital condyle with C1/C2 transverse foramen (odds ratio 8.33, p < 0.05), C1/C2 transverse foramen with the C2 lateral mass (odds ratio 5, p < 0.05), and C1 Landells Type III fractures with the C2 lateral mass (odds ratio 3.75, p < 0.05). On multivariable analysis, the presence of neurological deficits was associated with inpatient mortality (p = 0.004), while there were no significant associations between operative treatment and predictor variables. Conclusion: Traumatic atlantoaxial fractures occurred in a predominantly elderly and have a high rate of bony non-union with non-operative management, though fibrous nonunion can occur. Patients with this fracture pattern have high inpatient and post-discharge mortality rates. Surgery was not statistically associated with either expiration during admission or long-term survival. For management, these fractures require individualized decision making, and we propose that in select patients, surgery can help maximize the chances of bony union.

## A142: A rare case of delayed intra cranial hypotension with unilateral multiple cranial nerve palsies from cerebro spinal fluid leak in a whiplash injury

Debasish Hajra

1

, Ankita Hajra

2

, Akshima Ghosh

3

, Radu Beltechi

4

1

University Hospital of Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust, Coventry, United Kingdom

2

University College London, London, United Kingdom

3

University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom

4

University Hospital of Coventry and Warwickshire NHS trust, Coventry, United Kingdom

Introduction: Intracranial hypotension resulting from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak in the neuraxis is divided into either primary or spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) and secondary, like in trauma or iatrogenic cases. We present a rare secondary intracranial hypotension, with multiple unilateral cranial nerve palsies and to our knowledge not reported so far in literature. Material and Methods: We present a 33-year-old male who was diagnosed with a whiplash injury after a road traffic accident. He had persistent headaches and developed unilateral VI, VII and VIII cranial nerve palsies. This is rare and literature search has shown that there is either single unilateral cranial nerve palsy with dural leak or multiple unilateral cranial nerve palsies in epidural analgesia without a dural leak. MRI and lumbar puncture with opening pressure of 5.8 cms of water, strongly suggested intra-cranial hypotension. CT myelogram confirmed overflow of dye at C1-C2 level. Nearly 30-70% of SIH, improves with epidural blood patches but definitive cure in type 1, type 2 and type 3 (classification by Schievink WI et all), mostly requires surgical closure. Results: Our patient opted for surgery. He had a posterior hemilaminectomy of C1 and C2 and repair of leak. He recovered well and was discharged. Conclusion: Delayed CSF leak and the resultant intracranial hypotension has always been an entity which has been the cause of persistent headache and is commonly misdiagnosed, resulting in significant delay in the initiation of managements and the risks associated with treatment for disorders that mimic intracranial hypotension. The postural headache, which is the clinical hallmark of intracranial hypotension, is most likely due to the direct result of reduced CSF volume with loss of buoyancy resulting in caudal displacement of the brain, causing traction and irritation on pain-sensitive structures. over the time this becomes less prominent as the untreated CSF leak becomes chronic. This case highlights cervical whiplash in RTAs as an important and under-considered cause of traumatic dural tear and CSF leakage with a delayed presentation. Associated multiple unilateral cranial nerve palsies make our case unique, and reports of such presentation have not been seen in literature so far. Increasing the awareness of this type of headaches and associated cranial nerve palsies whenever they are present is required to decrease the high rate of misdiagnosis.

## A143: Micro-structural MRI is a biomarker which predicts baseline heterogeneity & outcomes after acute cervical spinal cord injury-insights from the RISCIS imaging sub-study

Mohammed Ali Alvi

1

, Mouad Elganga

2

, Karlo Pedro

1

, Raman Abbaspour

2

, Michael Fehlings

1

1
University Health Network, University of Toronto, Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, Canada,

2

University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Early prognostic biomarkers are essential to optimize management strategies and improve the design of clinical trials in spinal cord injury (SCI). The RISCIS Trial (Safety and Efficacy of Riluzole in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study), found that patients treated with riluzole demonstrated improvements in functional recovery in patients with an acute cervical SCI (ASIA A-C). In the current analysis, we analyzed a subset of patients enrolled in the RISCIS trial with acute (within 72 hrs after SCI) MRIs to assess the association of SCI lesion morphometrics with baseline and follow up neurological and functional outcomes. Materials and Methods: A total of 24 patients (12 Riluzole and 12 Placebo) were analyzed. For each patient, T2W sequence MRIs (obtained within 72-hrs of injury) were processed using the SpinalCordToolbox (SCT) v7.1 sct_deepseg lesion_sci_t2 command. Quantitative metrics including ventral, dorsal and total tissue bridge width and lesion volume were extracted. We examined the association between lesion morphometrics and baseline motor and functional scores as well as the change in motor and functional scores. We also assessed interactions effect between treatment (Riluzole) and imaging biometrics. Results: The mean age of the cohort was 52.5 years and 71% (n = 17) were males. The distribution of ASIA grade at baseline was: ASIA A 25% (n = 6), ASIA B 16.7% (n = 4), ASIA C 54.2% (n = 13), and ASIA D 4.2% (n = 1), and was also found to be comparable between the two groups (p = 0.433). At baseline, we observed strong correlations for ventral tissue bridge width (VTBW) and total tissue bridge width (TTBW) with total motor score (R2 = 0.303, p = 0.016; and R2 = 0.288, p = 0.020), and with upper motor score (R2 = 0.333, p = 0.010; and R2 = 0.266, p = 0.030) after adjusting for age and ASIA grade. At follow-up, we observed a strong correlation between TTBW and spinal cord independence measure (SCIM). The interaction between treatment type (Riluzole or Placebo) and TTBW (p = 0.042) or VTBW (p = 0.049) was found to be significant for total motor score change. The extent of preserved tissue bridge was predictive of recovery in motor score at follow-up for patients receiving Riluzole. We also analyzed a global outcome score, a Global rank-sum score calculated by summing pooled ranks across ANCOVA-adjusted endpoints: Total motor score, SF-36 physical component, and SCIM. We found strong correlation between TTBW and the global outcome (B = 6.794, p = 0.044) as well as VTBW (B = 9.98, p = 0.046) and the global outcome. Conclusion: Our results indicate that quantitative MRI metrics obtained from a semi-automated AI-facilitated pipeline may help prognosticate outcomes after acute cervical SCI and may thus be used for potential risk stratification, as well as for targeted personalized interventions.

## A144: MRI signal intensity and extension as predictors of clinical outcomes in cervical spinal cord injuries

Enrico Giordan

1

, Andrea Valenti

1

, Luca Chinellato

1

, Giuseppe Canova

1

1

Aulss 2 Marca Trevigiana, Treviso, Italy

Introduction: Traumatic cervical spinal cord injury (cSCI) is a complex condition with unpredictable neurological outcomes. While magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for initial assessment, its ability to predict functional recovery is unclear. This study explores whether the volumetric extent and signal intensity of cSCI on preoperative MRI correlate with neurological and functional outcomes after early surgical decompression and rehabilitation. Material and Methods: This retrospective study involved 45 adult patients with acute cervical spinal cord injury (cSCI) who underwent urgent spinal decompression within 12 hours of injury. Preoperative cervical MRI T2-weighted sequences assessed signal intensity and cSCI volume (3D volumetric analysis, %VSCI) and peak hyperintensity (SCIir). Functional and neurological outcomes were measured preoperatively, postoperatively, and after rehabilitation using the ASIA Impairment Scale, modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score, and Barthel Index (BI). Multiple regression analyses, adjusted for age and sex, examined the relationships between imaging parameters and outcomes. Results: Regression analysis revealed that increased %VSCI was independently associated with lower preoperative mJOA scores (p = 0.014) and lower post-rehabilitation mJOA scores (p = 0.001). No significant associations were found between %VSCI and ASIA score variation (p = 0.234), nor between SCIir and pre- or postoperative ASIA or mJOA scores (p > 0.5 in all cases). The mean mJOA score improved from 8.9 ± 3.2 to 12.6 ± 5.1 (p < 0.001), and 40.9% of patients reached ASIA E at final follow-up. Conclusion: This retrospective study demonstrates that neither the volumetric extent nor the signal intensity of cSCI on preoperative MRI-T2weighted images is a reliable predictor of postoperative neurological recovery. Although associations were found with baseline disability scores, no significant correlations with clinical improvement emerged after decompression and rehabilitation. These findings suggest that MRI characteristics alone cannot capture the complexity of SCI prognosis. In conclusion, while MRI remains a cornerstone in the diagnostic workup of cSCI, it should not be solely relied upon to guide prognostication.

## A145: The effectiveness and safety of staged halo-pelvic traction combined with posterior spinal fusion in the treatment of severe rigid spine deformity: a prospective cohort study

Lijin Zhou

1

, Honghao Yang

1

, Yong Hai

1

1

Beijing Chao-Yang Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Severe rigid spinal deformities present significant challenges in correction surgery due to complexity and associated comorbidities. To mitigate the surgical risks, preoperative halo-pelvic traction (HPT) have been employed. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of staged HPT combined with posterior spinal fusion (PSF) in the treatment of severe rigid spine deformity. Material and Methods: This is a prospective cohort study. From 2020 to 2022, 61 consecutive patients (mean age 26.2 years) with severe rigid spine deformity who underwent staged HPT combined with PSF with a minimum 24-month follow-up were recruited. Radiographic parameters, clinical information, pulmonary functions tests, and perioperative complications were recorded. Results: The mean preoperative coronal Cobb angle was 114.2° ± 38°, and the mean MK was 105.8° ± 34.7°. Following the HPT (mean duration 19.2 weeks), the mean coronal Cobb angle were corrected to 55.3° post-traction (50.6%) and 47.4° after PSF (58.3%); the mean MK angle were corrected to 52.6° post-traction (49.5%) and 38.1° after PSF (63.4%). The overall complication rate during HPT was 16.4%, while surgery-related complications were 18.0%, with no permanent neurological deficits observed. Conclusion: Staged HPT combine with PSF is effective and safe for patients with severe rigid spine deformities. HPT could mitigate the severity of spine deformity, minimize the need for invasive three-column osteotomies, and reduce the risk of complications for correction surgery.

## A146: Underestimated subtype in coronal type C degenerative scoliosis: absence of lumbar fractional curve increase postoperative coronal imbalance risk

Yong Qiu

1

, Zezhang Zhu

1

, Zhen Liu

1

, Ming Wang

1

, Xiaodong Qin

1

, Saihu Mao

1

, Benlong Shi

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, The Affiliated Hospital of Medical School, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China, Nanjing, China

Introduction: To investigate the influence of distal lumbar fractional curve (FC) on postoperative coronal imbalance (CIB) in patients with coronal type C degenerative scoliosis (DS) undergoing sequential correction techniques. Material and Methods: Patients with coronal type C DS undergoing sequential correction were included. Based on the presence of FC (L3-L5 Cobb angle > 10° with the convex side opposite to the major curve), patients were divided into FC and Non-FC groups. At final follow-up, patients were further categorized into CIB+ (coronal balance distance > 3 cm) and CIB- groups. Demographics, radiographic parameters, surgical data, patient-reported outcomes, and complications were compared using chi-square and Student t-tests. The cutoff values for L4 and L5 tilt were determined based on maximal chi-square values. Results: A total of 43 patients (61.5 ± 7.4 years) were enrolled, with 21 in the FC group and 22 in the Non-FC group. Compared to the FC group, the Non-FC group had a significantly higher incidence of postoperative CIB (54.5% vs 14.3%, p < 0.001), which persisted at the final follow-up (36.4% vs 9.5%, p < 0.001). The Non-FC group exhibited greater L5 tilt both postoperatively and at final follow-up. The correction rates for L4 tilt, and L5 tilt were significantly higher in the CIB- group (p < 0.05). Additionally, patients in the CIB- group demonstrated significantly lower L4 tilt, L5 tilt, and apical vertebral translation at final follow-up compared to the CIB+ group. The optimal correction targets were defined as L4 tilt ≤ 13° and L5 tilt ≤ 7°. Conclusion: This study identified two subtypes of coronal type C DS based on distal lumbar FC. Non-FC patients had a higher risk of postoperative CIB. Achieving L4 tilt ≤ 13° and L5 tilt ≤ 7° in Non-FC patients may reduce the incidence of CIB. For FC patients, conventional sequential correction techniques can achieve satisfactory coronal balance.

## A147: Optimizing spinal realignment: a comparative analysis of correction and complications of osteotomy techniques in adult spinal deformity

Diego Soto Rubio

1

, Cesar Carballo

1

, Kiana Yeganeh

2

, Schahin Salmanian

1

, Bryan Clampitt

, Mohsen Rostami

, Jay I. Kumar

1

, Puya Alikhani

Department of Neurosurgery, Brain and Spine, University of South Florida, Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States

2

Ponce Health Sciences University School of Medicine, Ponce, Puerto Rico, USA, Ponce, United States

3

USF Health Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States

4

Department of Neurological Surgery, Pauline Braathen Neurological Center, Cleveland Clinic Florida, Weston, FL, USA, Weston, United States

Introduction: Osteotomies are fundamental for correcting adult spinal deformity (ASD). We compared the effectiveness of anterior column realignment (ACR), pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO), intradiscal osteotomy (IDO), and Ponte osteotomies in achieving spinopelvic correction, their clinical outcomes, and complications. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 146 patients who underwent posterior fusions for ASD correction between 2016 and 2022, considering only patients with ≥ 1 year of follow-up. Patients were grouped according to the osteotomies with the most significant impact on sagittal alignment change. IDO, PSO, ACR or Ponte. Spinopelvic parameters, including pelvic tilt (PT), pelvic incidence (PI), sacral slope (SS), lumbar lordosis (LL), PI-LL mismatch, and sagittal vertical axis (SVA), and their changes from preoperative to postoperative images were compared. Surgical and clinical variables were collected, including mechanical complications (proximal junctional kyphosis [PJK], and failure [PJF], different types of hardware failure [HF]), estimated blood loss [EBL], packed red blood cell [PRBC] transfusions, and length of stay [LOS]. Clinical status was measured with the Oswestry disability index [ODI]. Revision-free survival time was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves, with patients followed from index surgery until revision or last follow-up, and differences between osteotomy types were assessed. Results: A total of 146 patients underwent ASD correction with IDO (n = 23), PSO (n = 21), ACR (n = 32), or Ponte (n = 70) osteotomies. Groups were comparable in age, BMI, preoperative disability, and most spinopelvic parameters. PJK occurred most frequently in ACR (31.3%) and Ponte (21.7%), while IDO had the lowest rate (8.7%). Hardware complications were common but similar across groups, with screw pullout more frequent in ACR. Kaplan-Meier analysis of revision-free survival up to 50 months showed no significant differences among groups (p = 0.478), with the earliest reoperations occurring in Ponte, followed by ACR and PSO. Conclusion: PSO achieved the greatest sagittal correction, while IDO and ACR provided intermediate correction. IDO demonstrated the highest revision-free survival, with the earliest reoperations occurring in Ponte, followed by ACR and PSO. These findings highlight the importance of osteotomy selection in optimizing long-term durability and maintaining alignment.

## A148: Is crossing the thoracolumbar junction necessary? Reevaluating upper instrumented vertebra selection to minimize proximal junctional complications

Atahan Durbas

1

, Francis Lovecchio

1

, Tejas Subramanian

1

, Renaud Lafage

2

, Christopher Ames

3

, Shay Bess

4

, Robert Eastlack

5

, Munish Gupta

6

, Richard Hostin

7

, Khaled Kebaish

8

, Eric Klineberg

9

, Gregory Mundis

10

, David Okonkwo

11

, Frank Schwab

2

, Christopher Shaffrey

12

, Justin Smith

13

, Virginie Lafage

2

, Han Jo Kim

1

, Andrea Pezzi

1

1

Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

2

Lenox Hill Hospital, New York, United States

3

University of San Francisco, San Francisco, United States

4

Denver International Spine Center, Denver, United States

5

10

San Diego Spine, La Jolla, United States

11

University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, United States

12

Duke University, Durham, United States

13

University of Virginia Health System, Charlottesville, United States

Introduction: The choice of upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery remains controversial, particularly regarding whether constructs should extend above the thoracolumbar junction (TLJ). Proponents of crossing and reaching above the TLJ suggest that this reduces proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and associated mechanical complications, though supportive evidence is limited. Furthermore, traditional PJK definitions may not clearly distinguish between physiological adaptation and true pathological changes at the TLJ. This study aimed to evaluate whether extending fusion across the TLJ reduces proximal junctional pathology compared with stopping below it. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of ASD patients undergoing instrumented fusion from either T11/T12 (above the TLJ, ATLJ) or L1/L2 (below the TLJ, BTLJ) to the sacrum or pelvis, with a follow-up period of at least 2 years. Exclusion criteria included prior fusions with UIV above L3 or using prophylactic tethers in their index surgery. Primary outcomes were proximal junctional complications: PJK (proximal junctional angle [PJA] ≥ 10°/ΔPJA ≥ 10°), proximal junctional failure (PJF; PJA ≥ 28°/ΔPJA ≥ 22° or proximal extension of fusion), and abnormal PJA (≥ 2 SD from normative UIV-specific means). Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed based on demographics, baseline alignment, and L1 pelvic angle correction. Results: A total of 131 patients (88 females, 43 males; 84 ATLJ, 47 BTLJ) with a mean age of 65.3 ( ± 9.7) years, BMI of 28.8 ( ± 5.0) kg/m2, and mean PI of 57.8° ( ± 11.4) were included, with an average follow-up of 2.3 years. In the ATLJ group (n = 84), UIVs were T11 in 86% and T12 in 14%. In the BTLJ group (n = 47), UIVs were L1 in 46% and L2 in 54%. The rate of PJK was higher in the ATLJ group compared to BTLJ (67% vs. 32%, p < 0.001), while the rates of PJF (20% vs. 15%, p = 0.4) and abnormal PJA (45% vs. 51%, p = 0.5) did not differ. After PSM, each group consisted of 34 patients, with a well-balanced distribution (ATLJ: T11/T12, 88%/12%; BTLJ: L1/L2, 56%/44%). Postoperative alignment parameters were largely comparable, although BTLJ patients demonstrated slightly greater PI-LL mismatch (2° vs. 8°, p = 0.001) and less kyphotic T10-L2 segment (13° vs. 6°, p = 0.04). ATLJ patients continued to have higher PJK rates (68% vs. 32%, p = 0.004), whereas PJF (21% vs. 12%, p = 0.3) and abnormal PJA (31% vs. 47%, p = 0.6) remained similar. Stratified analysis by specific UIV confirmed no differences in PJF (p = 0.55) or abnormal PJA (p = 0.34) between groups. Conclusion: Crossing the TLJ does not reduce proximal junctional complications in ASD surgery. Fusing to the pelvis with a UIV of L1 or L2 is an acceptable strategy in ASD surgery, as the actual rates of proximal junctional pathology are similar to those observed when constructs cross the TLJ. The higher rate of PJK observed in ATLJ patients may reflect limitations of current PJK definitions in differentiating between pathological and mechanical changes at the TLJ, rather than indicating a true clinical disadvantage.

## A149: How imaging speaks: the role of supine versus standing radiology in adult degenerative deformity surgery

Buse Sarigul

1

, Sedat Dalbayrak

2

, Mesut Yilmaz

2

1

Umraniye Research and Training Hospital, Department of Neurosurgery, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Medicana Atasehir Hospital, Department of Neurosurgery, Norospinal Akademi, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: With an aging population, the incidence of degenerative spinal deformities is increasing. Surgical treatment in these patients remains challenging due to high complication and revision rates, advanced age, and comorbidities. Accurate radiological evaluation, in correlation with clinical findings, is crucial for determining surgical levels, the necessity of osteotomy, and the type of osteotomy to be performed. This study aimed to investigate the impact of standing versus supine imaging on surgical planning in degenerative deformity. Material and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on 86 consecutive patients who were diagnosed with degenerative spinal deformity. Preoperative imaging included standing full-spine scoliosis radiographs (AP/lateral), dynamic radiographs, MRI, and CT with AP/lateral scanograms. All images were analyzed using RadiAnt DICOM Viewer. Parameters measured included spinopelvic parameters (PI, PT, SS), coronal Cobb angle, lumbar lordosis (LL), thoracic kyphosis (TK), sagittal vertical axis (SVA) and PI-LL mismatch. Vertebral rotation was graded by Nash-Moe. Measurements obtained from standing radiographs were compared with those from supine MRI/CT. Their effect on fusion length and osteotomy type (segmental vs. major) was assessed. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of major osteotomy requirement. Results: 86 patients were included in the study. 82 were female and 4 were male. The mean age was 68.71 ± 7.47 years. The mean coronal Cobb angle was 32.57 ± 9.83° on standing radiographs and 20.41 ± 8.72° on supine imaging (p < 0.001). Lumbar lordosis measured 23.34 ± 11.62° in standing versus 32.21 ± 10.87° in supine position (p < 0.001). PI-LL mismatch improved significantly from 16.83 ± 10.24° standing to 9.37 ± 8.61° supine (p < 0.001). SVA reduced from 58.23 ± 34.71 mm to 34.46 ± 29.13 mm (p = 0.004). Vertebral rotation regressed ≥ 1 grade in 28 patients (32.56%). Thoracic kyphosis did not differ significantly. Conclusion: Combined assessment of standing and supine imaging provides a more accurate understanding of the true deformity load and its clinical correlation in degenerative spinal deformity surgery. This approach enables more precise surgical planning, avoids unnecessary long fusions and major osteotomies, and may help reduce complication and revision rates.

## A150: Evaluating clinically meaningful outcomes in adult spinal deformity surgery: MCID analysis of functional and social improvements

Devender Singh

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

, John Stokes

1

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: Adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery aims to alleviate pain and improve physical function and quality of life. Given the complexity of the surgical intervention, it is essential to determine whether postoperative changes are clinically meaningful. The Minimum Clinically Important Difference (MCID) helps to assess the smallest change in a patient's outcome that is perceived as beneficial. We aim to calculate and evaluate the clinical significance of MCID in PROMIS Physical Function, Pain Interference, and Social Role outcomes among adult deformity patients undergoing spinal correction surgery. Measurements were taken preoperatively and at the 1-year postoperative mark. Our hypothesize was that a significant proportion of patients undergoing adult deformity surgery will achieve meaningful improvements in physical function and social role, but fewer will achieve clinically important improvements in pain interference. Material and Methods: We conducted an analysis of 84 adult deformity patients who underwent spinal correction surgery via the traditional posterior open approach. Patient-reported outcomes were collected preoperatively and at 1 year postoperatively, including PROMIS Physical Function (PF), Pain Interference (PI), Social Role (SR), and Scoliosis Research Society (SRS) scores. MCID was calculated using the 0.5 Standard Deviation (SD) method, which is a widely accepted distribution-based method. Results: The mean age of the cohort was 56.2 years, with an equal distribution of male and female patients. The MCID values for each outcome were: 3.21 for PF, 3.32 for PI, and 3.92 for SR. A total of 68.2% of patients achieved the MCID for PF, while only 6.8% for PI. Similarly, 68.2% of patients reached the MCID for SR, suggesting that improvements in physical function and social interaction were more pronounced than improvements in pain. Older patients (≥ 60 yrs.) were more likely to achieve clinically meaningful improvements in PF, with 75% of patients in this age group achieving MCID compared to 60% in patients younger than 60. This may be explained by the fact that older patients with advanced deformity or functional limitations might experience a more noticeable improvement in mobility following surgery, whereas younger patients may already have a higher baseline level of function and experience less perceived benefit from the intervention. Postoperative improvements in SR were strongly correlated with improvements in PF (r = 0.65, p < 0.05), indicating that improved mobility was linked to greater social participation. However, there was no significant correlation between changes in PI and PF, suggesting that pain management remains a challenge in this patient population. Conclusion: The majority of patients undergoing adult spinal deformity surgery experienced clinically meaningful improvements in PF and SR, with over two-thirds of patients achieving MCID for these outcomes. PI, however, showed limited improvement, as only 6.8% of patients achieved MCID. This suggests that while the surgery successfully restores mobility and improves social participation, postoperative pain management requires further attention. The results of this study align with existing literature that reports greater improvements in function and quality of life compared to pain outcomes in this patient population.

## A151: Radiographic predictors of functional and pain outcomes in Scheuermann’s kyphosis: a ROC-based minimal clinically important difference (MCID) analysis

Devender Singh

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, John Stokes

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: Scheuermann's Kyphosis (SK) is a structural spinal deformity that often necessitates surgical correction to improve sagittal balance and alleviate pain and functional impairments. The primary goal of such interventions is to achieve meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes such as pain relief and functional ability. Radiographic parameters, including Pelvic Incidence-Lumbar Lordosis (PI-LL) mismatch, Thoracic Kyphosis (TK), Lumbar Lordosis (LL), and T1 Pelvic Angle (TPA), are critical in guiding surgical planning and evaluating the success of corrective surgery. However, the relationship between changes in these parameters and patient-reported outcomes remains variable, warranting further investigation into their clinical relevance. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical significance of key radiographic parameters in SK correction by calculating the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve method. The analysis sought to determine the radiographic thresholds that best predict patient-reported improvements in function and pain, based on Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores at 2 years postoperative follow up. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis of 40 patients who underwent surgical correction for SK was conducted. Key radiographic parameters, including PI-LL mismatch, TK, LL, and TPA, were analyzed at the final follow-up. The MCID was calculated using the ROC curve method, with thresholds defined by the patient-reported outcomes of functional improvement (ODI) and pain relief (VAS). The Area Under the Curve (AUC) was used to assess the predictive power of each radiographic parameter. Comparisons were made with established literature standards to evaluate whether the cohort required more stringent corrections to achieve clinically meaningful outcomes. Results: The cohort consisted of 52.2% male with a mean age of 19.7 years, a mean BMI of 24.8, and Sanders Score of 7.23. The analysis revealed that PI-LL mismatch and TK were the strongest predictors of patient-reported improvements. For PI-LL mismatch, the ROC-based MCID threshold was 6.0°, more stringent than the commonly accepted threshold of ≤10° in the literature. The final PI-LL mismatch values ranged from -7.0° to 8.0° in the cohort. The AUC for PI-LL mismatch was 0.68 for ODI, indicating that it was a fair predictor of functional improvement. In contrast, its AUC for VAS was 0.54, suggesting it had poor predictive value for pain relief. TK demonstrated a significant association with pain relief, with an ROC-based MCID threshold of 0.40° and an AUC of 0.69 for VAS, making it a fair predictor of pain improvement. However, its predictive value for functional improvement was limited, as evidenced by an AUC of 0.51 for ODI. LL had ROC thresholds of 47.0° for ODI and 48.0° for VAS, with AUC values of 0.54 and 0.60, respectively, indicating poor predictive ability for both functional and pain improvements. Similarly, TPA showed limited predictive power, with ROC thresholds of -3.0° for ODI and 9.0° for VAS, and corresponding AUC values of 0.61 and 0.54. These results suggest that while LL and TPA are important for overall sagittal balance, their direct impact on patient-reported outcomes in this cohort was minimal. Conclusion: The ROC-based MCID analysis identified PI-LL mismatch and TK as the most clinically significant predictors of improvement in patients undergoing surgical correction for SK. Stricter corrections in PI-LL mismatch and TK were associated with better patient-reported outcomes, particularly in terms of functional improvement and pain relief, respectively. In contrast, LL and TPA, while essential for sagittal alignment, were poor predictors of meaningful clinical improvements. These findings suggest that surgical planning for SK should prioritize achieving tighter corrections in PI-LL mismatch and TK to maximize patient outcomes. Surgeons should focus on these parameters during preoperative planning and intraoperative correction to enhance patient outcomes, as LL and TPA showed limited predictive value for clinical improvement in this cohort.

## A152: Impact of pre-operative staged skull-femoral traction followed by spinal osteotomy and posterior instrumented fusion in severe rigid spine deformity: two-year prospective outcomes

Sharif Jonayed

1

1

National Institute of Traumatology & Orthopaedic Rehabilitation (NITOR), Dhaka, Bangladesh

Introduction: Severe rigid spinal deformities (Cobb angle > 90°, flexibility < 25%) remain among the most challenging conditions in spine surgery, with high risks of neurological injury, cardiopulmonary compromise, and suboptimal correction. Pre-operative staged skull-femoral traction (SFT) may facilitate gradual deformity mobilization and pulmonary optimization, potentially reducing the morbidity of subsequent spinal osteotomy and posterior instrumented spinal fusion (PSF). This study evaluates the radiographic, pulmonary, and functional outcomes of this staged approach at three-year follow-up. Material and Methods: Seventeen consecutive patients (11 females, 6 males; mean age 22.4 ± 6.1 years) with severe rigid scoliosis or kyphoscoliosis underwent staged SFT (mean duration 19.1 ± 4.6 days; mean traction weight 36.2% ± 6.1% body weight) followed by spinal osteotomy and PSF between 2021-2023. Minimum follow-up was 24 months (mean 26.8 ± 2.4). Outcomes included coronal and sagittal correction, pulmonary function (FVC % predicted), complications, and SRS-22 functional scores. Results: The mean pre-traction coronal Cobb angle of 116.9° ± 13.4° improved to 73.5° ± 11.2° after traction and further to 50.7° ± 9.6° post-fusion, representing an overall correction of 57%. Sagittal kyphosis decreased from 95.1° ± 15.1° to 55.6° ± 10.2° postoperatively (42% correction). Pulmonary function improved significantly, with mean FVC increasing from 57.6% ± 6.8% predicted preoperatively to 72.3% ± 6.1% at final follow-up (p < 0.05). Functional outcomes also improved, with SRS-22 scores rising from 2.9 ± 0.5 to 4.3 ± 0.4. Complications included two transient neurological deficits that resolved completely and three superficial pin-site infections, with no permanent morbidity or mortality. All patients reported improved balance, posture, and pain relief at follow-up. Conclusion: Pre-operative staged SFT followed by spinal osteotomy and PSF is a safe and effective strategy for severe rigid spinal deformities. This protocol achieved substantial coronal and sagittal correction, significant pulmonary improvement, and durable functional gains with low complication rates. The staged approach represents a valuable alternative to high-risk single-stage osteotomies in carefully selected patients.
Keywords: Rigid scoliosis, skull-femoral traction, spinal osteotomy, posterior spinal fusion, pulmonary outcomes

## A153: Geriatric nutritional risk index as a predictor of postoperative outcomes in elderly patients undergoing spinal deformity surgery

Ataollah Shahbandi

1

, Kevin Wojcik

1

, Saman Shabani

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, United States

Introduction: The Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI) is widely applied to evaluate malnutrition in older adults, yet its relevance in the context of spine surgery for deformity correction remains unclear. This study aimed to examine the relationship between nutritional status before surgery, as assessed by GNRI scores, and 30-day postoperative outcomes in geriatric patients undergoing spinal deformity surgery. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the 2008-2023 American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database. Patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent corrective surgery for spinal deformity were retrieved using Current Procedural Terminology codes or International Classification of Diseases, 9th and 10th Revision. Participants were stratified based on GNRI score: normal (> 98), malnourished (92-98), and severely malnourished (< 92). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses and multivariable regression models were used to assess the independent association and predictive value of GNRI compared with the 5-item modified Frailty Index (mFI-5) and chronological age for perioperative outcomes, including length of hospital stay, non-home discharge, and 30-day postoperative complications. Results: A total of 2,186 patients were included: 1,705 (78%) had normal nutrition, 332 (15.2%) were malnourished, and 149 (6.8%) were severely malnourished. Malnourished (40.1%) and severely malnourished (68.5%) groups exhibited significantly higher rates of preoperative anemia (27.2% in the normal group, p < 0.001), lower body mass index (28.7 ± 6.3 and 28 ± 6.5 kg/m2, respectively, versus 29.7 ± 5.9 in normal group, p = 0.001), and lower albumin levels (3.6 ± 0.2 and 3 ± 0.4 g/dL, respectively, vs 4.2 ± 0.3 in normal cohort, p < 0.001) compared with the normal group. After adjusting for potential confounders, malnourished status was independently associated with significantly greater odds of wound disruption (0.6% versus 2.1%, odds ratio [OR] 3.3, p = 0.014), prolonged mechanical ventilation (4.8% vs 1.8%, OR 2.2, p = 0.019), postoperative transfusion (59% vs 46.7%, OR 1.5, p = 0.001), increased transfusion volume (coefficient 0.452, p = 0.044), and non-home discharge (59.9% vs 47.3%, OR 1.6, p < 0.001) compared to normal patients. Severe malnutrition independently correlated with significantly longer hospital stay (9.7 ± 8.4 versus 6.4 ± 4.5 days; coefficient 2.4, p < 0.001), greater likelihood of prolonged hospitalization (32.9% vs 14.9%, OR 2.1, p < 0.001), and higher rates of non-home discharge (60.4% vs 47.3%, OR 1.6, p = 0.017) compared to normal patients. In ROC analyses, GNRI demonstrated superior discriminatory ability compared with mFI-5 (p = 0.394, p = 0.645, p = 0.179, p = 0.113, p = 0.014, and p = 0.233 respectively) and age (p = 0.277, p = 0.074, p = 0.039, and p = 0.167, p < 0.001, and p < 0.001 respectively) for predicting wound disruption, superficial surgical site infection, prolonged mechanical ventilation, unplanned intubation, the need for transfusion, and prolonged hospitalization. Conclusion: Preoperative malnutrition, as defined by GNRI, is correlated with a greater risk of adverse 30-day outcomes following spinal deformity surgery in older adults. This finding highlights the importance of incorporating nutritional assessment into preoperative evaluation for spinal deformity surgery in the geriatric population.

## A154: Complications in cervical minimally invasive spine surgery: a proportional meta-analysis of tubular, uniportal, and biportal approaches

Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi

1

, Sean Inzerillo

1

, Eesha Gurav

1

, Noah Willett

1

, Mousa Hamad

1

, Galal Elsayed

1

, Osama Kashlan

1

, Roger Härtl

1

1

Department of Neurological Surgery, Och Spine at New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: Minimally invasive spine surgery (MISS) for cervical pathologies has demonstrated superior clinical outcomes compared to the open approaches, but differences in complication rates among the tubular, uniportal, and biportal techniques remain unclear. This proportional meta-analysis compares complication rates across these techniques utilizing studies published in the last decade. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024594335). PubMed, Medline, Embase, and Cochrane Library were queried for cervical MISS studies (Jan 2013-Mar 2024) utilizing tubular, uniportal, or biportal approaches. Included studies reported complication rates in adult cohorts. Exclusions were abstracts, reviews, and non-English articles. A random-effects model was applied, and the I2 statistic assessed heterogeneity. All analyses were conducted using R Studio. Results: Twenty-one studies (1299 patients) were included, with average patient ages ranging from 47 to 74.5 years and 64% male. All studies had low bias risk. Follow-up periods ranged from 3 to 33 months. The pooled complication rate for cervical MISS was 5% (95% CI [3%-7%]), with heterogeneity (I2 = 59%). Subgroup analysis showed complication rates of 4% (95% CI [1%-10%], I2 = 70%) for tubular, 6% (95% CI [2% -12%], I2 = 46%) for uniportal, and 5% (95% CI [2%-8%], I2 = 39%) for biportal. No statistically significant differences were found (p = 0.85). Nerve injury rates were higher with the uniportal approach (6%, 95% CI [2%-16%], p = 0.02). Dural tears (1%, 95% CI [0%-2%], I2 = 0%) and postoperative hematomas (0%, 95% CI [0%-3%], I2 = 0%) had low incidence, with no significant differences between approaches (p = 0.61 and p = 0.78, respectively). Conclusions: Cervical MISS demonstrates a low overall complication rate, with tubular approaches showing a numerically lower risk, though differences were not statistically significant. Larger comparative studies are needed to provide more definitive results for better clinical application.
