## A155: Bipotal endoscopic tranforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (BE-TLIF): evaluation clinical and CT- based radiological outcome

Songwut Sirivitmaitree

1

1

Bandung Crown Prince Hospital, Udon, Thailand

Introduction: Biportal endoscopic spine surgery is a type of minimally invasive spine surgery that uses two small incisions to insert an endoscope and surgical instruments. Biportal endoscope provides various procedures, such as decompression, discectomy, and fusion. BE- TLIF is a surgical technique that combines the advantages of minimally invasive and endoscopic spine surgery. It is a type of spinal fusion surgery through a transforaminal approach that aims to stabilize the spine and relieve pain caused by various spinal disorders, such as degenerative disc disease, spondylolisthesis, and recurrent disc herniation. The advantage of BE- TLIF does not require a tubular retractor which may reduce muscle damage ,independent endoscopic and instrument ports were easily to contralateral decompression and reduce postoperative pain. Biportal endoscopic TLIF is a promising alternative to conventional open or minimally invasive TLIF, but it requires a learning curve and more studies to evaluate its long-term outcomes. Material and Methods: Retrospective cohort study. This study included 72 patients with 81 fusion segments who underwent BE-TLIF between January 2020 and March 2022. All of the patients were observed at least a 12-month follow-up. We collected demographic data, total operation time and length of hospital stay. Clinical outcomes measures included visual analogue scale (VAS) scores for lower back pain and leg pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Plain film x-ray 1, 3, 6,12 months postoperatively and then every year thereafter. Computed tomography (CT) of the lumbar spine 6 and12 months postoperatively. The fusion rate was assessed using the Bridwell interbody fusion grading system. Cage subsidence was classified into no subsidence, no more than 2 mm, and more than 2 mm, Postoperative complications were also noted. Results: There were significant improvement in VAS for lower back pain from 6.3 ± 0.8 to 1.2 ± 0.5, VAS for leg pain from 5.8 ± 1.3 to 1.2 ± 0.4, ODI from 58.1 ± 11.9 to 13.4 ± 4.6. The p-values were all < 0.001. The average hospital stay was 4.7±1.1 days. The CT studies available for 52 fusion segments. 6 months after surgery showed successful fusion (Bridwell grade I or grade II) in 33 segments (63.5%). 1 year after surgery showed successful fusion (Bridwell grade I or grade II) in 49 segments (94.2%). Significant cage subsidence of more than 2 mm was only noted in 46 segments (56.1%). Complications included 2 dural tear, 1 pedicle screws malposition, and 3 transient paresthesia, in which 1 patient required reoperations. Conclusions: BETLIF may have favorable clinical outcomes, high fusion rate and lower complication. BETLIF may be a good alternative treatment for lumbar spine disorder (stenosis, instability, and spondylolisthesis). Further studies with large samples and long-term follow-up are needed.

In the transforaminal group, 8/10 required facet resection (70% complete, 60% partial pediculectomy), and mean laminectomy width was 11.1 ± 7.6 mm. Conclusion: Both interlaminar and transforaminal endoscopic approaches were effective over 12 months, with outcomes comparable or superior to those reported for standard laminectomy in the Preliminary findings from this pilot study suggest the transforaminal approach may achieve greater canal expansion, though interpretation is limited by the small, single-center cohort.

## A158: Endoscopic resection of lumbar intradural spinal tumors: a case series on feasibility, safety, and preliminary outcomes

Facundo Van Isseldyk1,2, Vincent Hagel3

1Hospital Privado de Rosario, Rosario, Argentina, 2Endospine Academy, Zurich, Switzerland, 3Asklepios Hospital Lindau, Spine Center, Lindau, Germany

Introduction: Intradural spinal tumors represent 5-10% of spinal neoplasms and are typically managed with open microsurgical resection, which achieves high rates of gross total resection (GTR) but is associated with substantial morbidity due to extensive muscle dissection and bony removal. Endoscopic spine surgery has proven effective for degenerative pathologies by minimizing tissue disruption, yet its application to intradural lesions remains rare. The technical challenges of dural opening, irrigation management, tumor manipulation within a constrained corridor, and dural closure have limited widespread adoption. This study reports the feasibility, safety, and preliminary outcomes of a fully endoscopic approach for lumbar intradural tumor resection. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 10 consecutive adult patients who underwent endoscopic resection of lumbar intradural-extramedullary tumors between 2020 and 2024. Inclusion criteria were lumbar intradural-extramedullary tumors confirmed on MRI; exclusion criteria included intramedullary lesions, multisegmental disease requiring multilevel laminectomy, or non-lumbar tumors. Demographic, radiologic, surgical, and clinical data were analyzed. Surgical technique involved a uniportal interlaminar approach with continuous irrigation, endoscopic dural opening, tumor dissection, and dural closure by either suture or patch. Outcomes included extent of resection on postoperative MRI, neurological status via modified McCormick scale, complications, hospital stay, and follow-up imaging. Results: Ten patients (6 women, 4 men; mean age 58.3 years, range 46-72) were included. Tumor types were schwannoma (n = 7), meningioma (n = 2), and neurofibroma (n = 1), all located between L2-L5 (mean size 24.5 mm, range 10-38). Presenting symptoms included radicular pain (n = 6), neurogenic claudication (n = 2), and motor deficits (n = 2). Mean operative time was 96.5 ± 19.7 minutes, with no intraoperative complications. Dural closure was performed with endoscopic suturing in 3 patients and patch placement in 7. GTR was confirmed in all cases. No new neurological deficits or cerebrospinal fluid-related complications occurred. Modified McCormick grades improved in 6 patients (60%) and remained stable in 4 (40%); none worsened. Both patients with preoperative motor deficits improved postoperatively. Hospital stay averaged 1.5 ± 0.5 days. Statistical analysis confirmed a significant improvement in McCormick grades (p = 0.014). Subgroup analysis revealed that patients with sutured closure achieved grade 1 function at follow-up, though operative times were slightly longer. No recurrences were observed during a mean follow-up of 15 months (range 12-18). Conclusion: Endoscopic resection of lumbar intradural-extramedullary tumors is feasible and safe in selected patients, achieving 100% GTR and favorable neurological outcomes without added morbidity. The minimally invasive nature of this technique likely contributed to the short hospital stays and rapid recovery observed. Key technical considerations include irrigation pressure modulation, controlled dural opening, and tailored closure strategies, both of which were effective in preventing CSF-related complications. These findings suggest that endoscopy can extend beyond degenerative pathology into intradural tumor surgery without compromising oncological or functional goals. However, the approach is technically demanding and best performed by surgeons with extensive endoscopic experience. Larger, prospective studies with long-term follow-up are warranted to validate these results and further define the role of endoscopy in intradural tumor management.

The operative time and LOS in the UBE group were (69.3 ± 7.4) minutes and (4.8 ± 1.3) days, respectively; in the UE group, these were (67.9 ± 9.5) minutes and (5.1 ± 1.5) days, respectively, with no statistically significant difference (t = 1.64, -0.75, p > 0.05). The times of intraoperative fluoroscopy in the UBE group was (7.5 ± 3.1) fewer than in the UE group (16.1 ± 5.3), with a statistically significant difference (t = -9.14, p < 0.01). In the UBE group, no nucleus pulposus residue, and one patient experienced transient radiating pain in the affected lower limb after surgery, which was resolved after oral gabapentin. In the UE group, one patient experienced cerebrospinal fluid leakage, and three patients had nucleus pulposus residue. Compared with preoperatively, the VAS scores of low back and leg pain, ODI in both groups were significantly improved after surgery (p < 0.01). However, there was no significant difference in the VAS scores of low back and leg pain, ODI between the two groups (p > 0.05). According to the modified Macnab classification evaluation criteria: in the UBE and UE groups were 93.9% and 91.6%, respectively, with no statistically significant difference (χ2 = 0.31, p = 0.59). Conclusion: For patients with SUM-LDH, both UE and UBE are effective in relieving pain symptoms. Compared with UE, UBE can removal of the nucleus pulposus under direct vision. Furthermore, it can reduce the probability of residual nucleus pulposus and reduce the times of intraoperative fluoroscopy.

## A162: Outcomes of posterior endoscopic cervical discectomy: a retrospective study of 30 patients

Atif Ali

1

, Muhammad Farrukh Bashir

1

1

Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital Lahore, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: Cervical disc herniation is one of the major causes of cervical radiculopathy and disability. Traditional surgical options such as anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) or open discectomy are effective but may lead to complications including fusion-related morbidity, dysphagia, and adjacent segment disease. Posterior Endoscopic Cervical Discectomy (PECD) has recently emerged as a minimally invasive, motion-preserving alternative that aims to reduce these risks while maintaining clinical efficacy. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 30 patients (18 males, 12 females; mean age 42.3 ± 8.7 years) diagnosed with single-level cervical disc herniation confirmed by MRI. All patients had persistent radicular pain or neurological symptoms for at least six weeks despite conservative treatment, with clinical findings correlating to imaging. Patients with multilevel disc disease, prior cervical surgery, instability, deformity, infection, trauma, tumor, or significant medical comorbidities were excluded. All underwent PECD, and outcomes were assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for pain, Neck Disability Index (NDI), operative details, complications, and overall satisfaction. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS v27. Results: At 6-12 months follow-up, patients showed marked clinical improvement. The mean VAS score improved from 7.8 ± 1.1 preoperatively to 2.1 ± 0.9 postoperatively (p < 0.001), while the mean NDI decreased from 61.5 ± 7.8% to 18.4 ± 5.6% (p < 0.001). The average operative time was 82 ± 15 minutes, with minimal blood loss (<50 ml). No major intraoperative or postoperative complications were observed. Two patients (6.7%) experienced transient postoperative dysesthesia, which resolved with conservative management. Patient satisfaction was high at 93%, and no reoperations were required during the follow-up period. Conclusion: Posterior endoscopic cervical discectomy is a safe, effective, and motion-preserving technique for managing single-level cervical disc herniation. It provides significant pain relief, functional improvement, and high patient satisfaction while avoiding the risks associated with fusion procedures. Given its excellent short-term outcomes and low complication rates, PECD represents a valuable alternative to conventional ACDF in appropriately selected patients. Larger multicenter studies with longer follow-up are recommended to confirm the long-term durability of these results.

## A163: TDR versus fusion - Live systematic review and metanalysis

Igor Barreira

1

, Rafael Moriguchi

1

, Rodrigo Amaral

1

, Luiz Pimenta

1

, Fernando Marcelino

1

, Igor Arthur Costa

1

, Amabile Galeti

1

, Leandro Resende

1

, Jullyene Pokorny

1

, Gabriel Pokorny

1

, Bianca Soares

1

1

Instituto de Patologia da Coluna, São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Degenerative lumbar spine disease is a leading cause of chronic low-back pain and socioeconomic burden. Lumbar fusion is the long-standing surgical standard, but loss of motion and adjacent-segment degeneration have fuelled interest in total disc replacement (TDR). We performed a living systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the efficacy, safety and functional outcomes of TDR versus fusion in adults with degenerative lumbar disease. Material and Methods: Monthly searches of PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP (inception to March 2024) identified comparative studies of TDR and fusion reporting clinical or radiological outcomes. Two reviewers independently screened records extracted data and assessed risk of bias (Cochrane RoB-2 for RCTs; Newcastle -Ottawa Scale for cohorts). Pooled odds ratios (OR) for binary outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes were calculated with random-effects models; heterogeneity was explored with I2 statistics. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO and set up as a “living” review with quarterly updates. Results: From 1,184 records, 18 studies (six RCTs, 12 cohorts) encompassing 58,447 patients (6 274 TDR, 52 173 fusion) met the criteria. TDR significantly reduced overall complications versus fusion (OR 0.46, 95 % CI 0.29 -0.72; I2 = 80 %). Pain relief favoured TDR (VAS-back MD -0.93, 95 % CI -1.52 to -0.35; I2 = 58%). Disability scores (Oswestry Disability Index) did not differ (MD -3.3, 95 % CI -8.83 to 2.11; I2 = 74 %). Sensitivity and leave-one-out analyses confirmed robustness of the complication and pain findings; evidence certainty was graded “very low” to “low” owing to heterogeneity and study design limitations. Conclusion: Current evidence suggests that lumbar TDR offers comparable functional recovery to fusion while providing modestly better pain relief and a lower incidence of peri-operative and device-related complications. Nevertheless, heterogeneity and predominantly observational data temper confidence. High-quality randomised trials and continuous evidence surveillance via this living review are needed to refine patient selection and inform guideline recommendations.

## A164: Cervical disc arthroplasty versus posterior cervical foraminotomy as motion preserving surgeries for cervical radiculopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Jia Yi Loh

1

, Xian Jun Ngoh

1

, Zhihong Chew

2

, Yee Gen Lim

1

, Lei Jiang

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Changi General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Motion preserving surgery for cervical radiculopathy treats lateral and foraminal disc pathology while causing minimal disruption to the stability of the cervical spine and include cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) and minimally invasive posterior cervical foraminotomy (MI-PCF) including endoscopic PCF (PECF). This study aims to compare the functional and surgical outcomes between CDA and MI-PCF. Material and Methods: This study includes a systematic review of present literature and meta-analysis comparing motion preserving surgeries of CDA and MI-PCF for treatment of cervical radiculopathy. Results: A total of 575 abstracts were reviewed and assessed and 7 comparative studies between MI-PCF and CDA were included. The mean operative time for patients undergoing CDA was between 38.7 to 110.1 min, while the mean operative time for patients undergoing MI-PCF was between 35.9 to 108.3 min, with MI-PCF being performed 3.4 min faster than CDA. The overall complications rate was 5.4% for CDA and 3.4% for MI-PCF and the overall reoperation rate was 0.9% for CDA and 3.8% for PCF. A random effects model meta-analysis was carried out which showed no significant differences in complication rate but MI-PCF had significantly higher reoperation rates compared to CDA. Patients who underwent PCF had non-statistically significant improvement in functional outcomes of Neck Disability Index (NDI) and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) neck and arm scores compared to patients who underwent CDA at 6 months postoperatively. Subsequently, patients who underwent MI-PCF had further improvement in NDI and VAS neck and arm scores 1 year post-operatively, with statistically significant improvements in scores compared to patients who underwent CDA. Subgroup analysis of functional outcomes comparing CDA and PECF showed non-statistically significant improvement in VAS scores but poorer NDI scores for patients undergoing PECF at 6 months post operation. Conclusion: MI-PCF has lower complication rates and better short term functional outcomes compared to CDA despite also having higher reoperation rates. Further studies with longer follow up correlating functional outcomes with radiological parameters measuring cervical motion is required to establish its superiority over CDA.

## A165: Cervical disc arthroplasty in congenital cervical spinal stenosis: outcomes compared to non-stenotic patients

Hannah Shelby

1

, Kiran Alluri

1

, Joseph Shelby

1

, Tara Shelby

2

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, Los Angeles, United States

2

Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, United States

Introduction: Cervical spinal stenosis is the narrowing of the spinal canal that can result in cervical nerve root compression and cause significant radicular pain, numbness, and weakness and in more severe cases can progress to cervical spondylitis myelopathy (CSM). Congenital cervical spinal stenosis (CCSS), caused by abnormal development of the pedicle lamina or vertebral column, predisposes patients to symptomatic compression due to the reduced baseline canal diameter. While anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is the most common surgical treatment, it eliminates motion and increases the risk of adjacent-segment degeneration. Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) is a motion-preserving alternative with proven safety and effectiveness, but its outcomes in patients with CCSS remain poorly defined. This study examines whether CDA provides comparable clinical results in patients with and without CCSS. Material and Methods: IRB approval was obtained for this retrospective review of prospectively collected data. Patients with radiculopathy or myelopathy undergoing one- or two-level cervical disc arthroplasty at a single institution (2017-2020) were included and stratified by the Torg-Pavlov Ratio (TPR), a clinical index of CCSS (< 0.82 = CCSS; ≥ 0.82 = non-CCSS). Patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) included the Neck Disability Index (NDI), Visual Analog Scale for neck and arm pain (VAS-Neck, VAS-Arm), Short Form-12 Physical and Mental Component Scores (SF-12 PCS, SF-12 MCS), and PROMIS Physical Function (PROMIS PF), collected preoperatively, < 6 months, and ≥6 months postoperatively. Correlations between radiographic parameters and PROMs were assessed, and between-group and within-group comparisons were performed using standard parametric and non-parametric tests. MCID (Minimal Clinically Important Difference) thresholds were applied, with significance set at p < .05. Results: Sixty-two patients were included where the average age was 43 years, and the sex split was 54.8% male. 59 patients were available for TPR analysis, (12 CCSS, 20.3%; 47 non-CCSS, 79.7%). No significant correlations were found between TPR or sagittal canal diameter and PROMs, except for a moderate correlation between TPR and SF-12 PCS improvement at ≥ 6 months. Significant postoperative improvement across most PROMs was seen in both cohorts. CCSS patients did show less consistent gains, with no significant improvement in Arm VAS, SF-12 PCS at < 6 months, or SF-12 MCS at ≥ 6 months. At ≥ 6 months, non-CCSS patients had greater improvement in Neck VAS (p = 0.04) and SF-12 MCS (p = 0.02). MCID achievement was similar between groups for most PROMs, except SF-12 MCS at ≥ 6 months, wherein 18 patients (58.1%) and only 1 patient (10%) in the non-CCSS and CCSS respectively achieved the MCID (p = 0.011). Conclusion: While CCSS is an important risk factor for cervical pathology, its impact on outcomes after CDA remains poorly understood. This study provides evidence that while CDA is safe and effective in both CCSS and non-CCSS patients, certain PROMs and functional gains may be less robust in CCSS patients, highlighting the need for careful preoperative counseling. Our results contrast with prior ACDF literature, where CCSS has been linked to higher adjacent segment degeneration, suggesting CDA may offer a motion-preserving alternative in this population.

## A166: Long-term outcomes of cervical disc replacement and anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: a review of FDA IDE trials with real-world comparison
Ali Issani
1
, William Karakash
1
, Henry Avetisian
1
, Daniel Rusu
1
, Aidan Lindgren
1
, Zeeshan Ahsan
2
, Dil Patel
1
, David Riopelle
1
, Kevin Kashanchi
1
, Matthew Gallo
1

Marc A. Abdou1, ,Amyn Malik
3
, Raymond Hah
1
, Kiran Alluri
1
, John Liu
4
, Jeffrey C. Wang
1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

2

Department of Emergency Medicine, Aga Khan University, Karachi, Pakistan

3

O'Donnell School of Public Health, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, United States

4

Department of Neurological Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

Introduction: Degenerative cervical spine disease, presenting with neck pain, radiculopathy, and myelopathy, has historically been treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) as the gold standard of treatment. However, concerns about reduced spinal mobility and adjacent segment disease led to the development of cervical disc replacement (CDR), a motion-preserving alternative approved for clinical use in 2007. Nine devices are now FDA-approved, with evidence showing CDR to be non-inferior to ACDF and offering better long-term outcomes in pain relief, function, ASD, and revision rates. These approvals were based on FDA investigational device exemption (IDE) trials, which have faced criticism for limited post-approval oversight. Post-approval studies (PAS) remain underpowered and poorly generalizable. To address these gaps, this study compares long-term outcomes of CDR and ACDF using real-world data from a national database, focusing on subsequent surgery rates relative to FDA IDE trial findings. Materials and Methods: This study used the PearlDiver Mariner Database (2010-2022) to identify ACDF and CDR cases, excluding patients < 18, those with < 1-year follow-up, prior cervical surgery, hybrid constructs, or procedures for trauma, malignancy, or infection. Cohorts were stratified by subsequent cervical surgeries, with complete follow-up required for inclusion at 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 7-, and 10-year intervals. FDA-approved IDE trials were identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane (April 2025), excluding non-FDA devices and follow-up > 10 years. The primary endpoint was subsequent cervical surgery, comparing FDA trial results with real-world PearlDiver outcomes. Event rates were calculated as surgeries per patients at risk, and Kaplan-Meier-style curves were reconstructed from published data using the Guyot algorithm with monotonicity constraints. Survival probabilities were pooled by weighted means, hazard ratios were estimated at discrete intervals, and differences between cohorts were tested using chi-square or Fisher’s exact test (p < 0.05) in R (v3.4.4). Results: A total of 277,146 ACDF and 25,957 CDR patients were identified in PearlDiver, including 174,135 1-level and 103,011 2-level ACDF cases, and 21,995 1-level and 3,962 2-level CDR cases. From literature review, 44 FDA IDE trials and two additional FDA-approved device studies were included from google scholar. Compared with FDA cohorts, PearlDiver patients undergoing 1-level ACDF had significantly higher survival at 2, 5, 7, and 10 years (p < 0.05), while 1-level CDR showed modest but significant advantages at 2, 7, and 10 years. For 2-level ACDF, survival was similar at 2 years but significantly higher in PearlDiver at 5 and 7 years. In contrast, 2-level CDR demonstrated high survival in both cohorts with no significant differences across all time points. Conclusion: In conclusion, this study demonstrates that CDR performs comparably in real-world settings and controlled trials for 1-level procedures, whereas ACDF shows more favorable real-world outcomes with lower subsequent surgery rates than reported in FDA trials. These differences may reflect trial selection bias or stricter adjudication of ACDF outcomes. Our findings validate the safety and efficacy of both procedures, support CDR as a motion-preserving alternative for select patients and underscore the value of real-world data in complementing trial evidence.

## A167: Long-term clinical outcomes beyond ten years following lumbar total disc replacement: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Arnaud Delafontaine

1,2

, Jean-Baptiste Odent

1

, Jean-Charles Aurégan

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopedic, Traumatological and Reconstructive Surgery, Prosthetic Replacement Unit of the Spine, Hip and Knee, Antoine Béclère Hospital, APHP, University Paris Saclay, Clamart, France, CIAMS, University Paris-Saclay, Orsay, France, CIAMS, University of Orléans, Orléans, France, Clamart, France

2

CIAMS, University Paris-Saclay, Orsay, France, Orsay, France

3

B3OA, University Paris Cité, Paris, France

Introduction: Lumbar total disc replacement (TDR) aims to preserve segmental motion and potentially reduce adjacent segment degeneration compared with fusion. While mid-term outcomes are well documented, evidence beyond 10 years remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes the long-term clinical, radiographic, and implant-related outcomes of lumbar TDR, emphasizing differences between early-generation and modern implants. Material and Methods: A systematic review were conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through September 2025. Studies with ≥ 10-year follow-up reporting clinical outcomes after lumbar TDR were included. Outcomes assessed included Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for back pain, patient satisfaction, revision and reoperation rates, implant survivorship, and radiographic parameters (segmental mobility, heterotopic ossification, and spontaneous fusion). Five key cohorts were included: Putzier et al. (2006; Charité I,II and III, 17-year follow-up), Park et al. (2016; ProDisc-II, 10-year follow-up), Lu et al. (2018; Charité III, 15.4-year follow-up), Kitzen et al. (2020; Charité III, 10 -15-year follow-up), and Marnay et al. (2025; 1 -2 level ProDisc L, 7 -21-year follow-up). Random-effects meta-analysis was applied to continuous outcomes, with subgroup analyses comparing early-generation versus modern implants and mono- versus bisegmental replacements. Results: A total of 1847 patients were included. Modern implants, such as ProDisc-II and ProDisc L, demonstrated sustained clinical improvements (mean ODI reduction -22.1 points, 95% CI -24.7 to -19.5), low index-level revision rates (0.7-3% at 10 -12 years), preserved segmental mobility, and high patient satisfaction (> 70%). Early-generation Charité implants achieved significant initial ODI and VAS improvements; however, long-term follow-up revealed high rates of spontaneous fusion or ankylosis (up to 60%), loss of segmental motion, and reoperation rates up to 38%. Radiographic analysis indicated that heterotopic ossification and spontaneous ankylosis were the primary contributors to functional decline in older implants. Functional implants preserved motion and were associated with low incidence of adjacent segment degeneration, whereas ankylosed or fused segments showed degeneration rates comparable to fusion surgery. Subgroup analyses suggested that patient satisfaction correlated more closely with preserved segmental function or spontaneous ankylosis than with radiographic alignment alone. Conclusion: Lumbar TDR can provide durable clinical improvement beyond 10 years. Modern devices such as ProDisc-II and ProDisc L achieve the most favorable long-term outcomes, preserving motion and maintaining low revision rates. Early-generation Charité implants, while initially effective, are associated with higher rates of spontaneous fusion, segmental motion loss, and reoperation, highlighting the critical role of implant design, surgical technique, and patient selection. Radiographic outcomes reinforce that functional preservation, rather than mere anatomical alignment, is key to long-term success. Continued long-term evaluation of newer TDR designs is essential to optimize indications, improve biomechanics, and maximize patient-centered outcomes.

## A168: Less superior adjacent syndrome and lower reoperation rate. Medium- and long-term results of cervical arthroplasty versus anterior cervical arthrodesis: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials

, Anna Taberner

, Juan Diego Montenegro

Clinica Teknon, Barcelona, Spain

Introduction: To compare medium- and long-term postoperative surgical results, especially the adjacent syndrome rate, adverse event rate, and reoperation rate, of patients operated on with cervical arthroplasty or anterior cervical arthrodesis in published randomized clinical trials (RCTs), at one cervical level. Material and Methods: Systematic Review and meta-analysis. At final follow-up, a mean cervical range of motion of 7.91 degrees was preserved, with a high-grade heterotopic ossification rate of 9.67% in patients who underwent cervical arthroplasty. Conclusion: In the medium and long-term follow-up, cervical arthroplasty showed a lower rate of superior adjacent syndrome and a lower rate of reoperation. No statistically significant differences were found in the rate of inferior adjacent syndrome or in the rate of adverse events.

## A170: Comparison of outcomes between single-level cervical disc arthroplasty and anterior cervical discectomy and fusion in nicotine-dependent patients

Ankit Hirpara

1

, Jalen Warren

1

, Nakul Narendran

1

, Christina Cheng

1

, Christopher Furey

1

, Prashant Rajan

1

1

Case Western Reserve University/University Hospitals, Cleveland, United States

Introduction: Nicotine use is frequently associated with increased complications after cervical fusion, including dysphagia, infection, and revision surgery. Moreover, the conventional cage-plate system used in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) may predispose patients to adjacent segment disease, soft tissue injury, and pain. Studies have shown that cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) may offer advantages compared to ACDF in the general population, but it is unclear whether these benefits extend to nicotine users as well, who are known to be suboptimal surgical candidates. As such, the purpose of this study was to compare rates of post-operative medical complications, opioid use, and revision surgery in nicotine users undergoing CDA versus ACDF. Material and Methods: The TriNetX database, commonly used in the orthopedic literature, was queried to identify patients aged 18 to 60 years with nicotine dependence who underwent isolated, primary single-level ACDF or single-level CDA. Patients in the ACDF cohort were excluded if they had relative or hard contraindications for CDA, including but not limited to cervical fracture, instability, deformity, or disorders of bone density or structure. This was done to ensure that both cohorts consisted of patients who would have been theoretically eligible for either intervention. Cohorts underwent propensity score matching in a 1:1 ratio based on 23 covariates, including demographic variables, medical comorbidities, substance use, and indication for surgery. The following post-operative outcomes were collected: 1) complications and healthcare utilization within 3 months, 2) opioid use within 2 years, and 3) revision surgery within 2 years. Results: Following successful propensity score matching, each cohort contained 1,049 patients. Within 3 months, patients in the ACDF cohort had higher rates of healthcare utilization, including readmission (4.5% vs. 1.8%, p < 0.001) and emergency department visits (13.6% vs. 9.7%, p = 0.005), as well as dysphagia (5.2% vs. 3.2%, p = 0.023). There were no significant differences in medical or respiratory complications. More patients in the ACDF cohort were prescribed opioids at all time points within 2 years (all p < 0.001), and they were given more prescriptions at 1 week (1.4 vs. 1.3, p = 0.015) and 1 month after surgery (2.2 vs. 1.9, p = 0.038). Lastly, patients who underwent ACDF had higher rates of revision cervical fusion at 1 year (2.7% vs. 1.0%, p = 0.004) and 2 years (4.3% vs. 1.1%, p < 0.001). Patients who underwent ACDF also had higher rates of revision cervical surgery at 2 years (5.0% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.013). Conclusion: ACDF, compared to CDA, is associated with higher rates of healthcare utilization, dysphagia, opioid use, and revision surgery in patients who are dependent on nicotine. These results may be used to inform and optimize surgical decision making in this high-risk population.

## A171: Complications following cervical and lumbar artificial disc replacement - A retrospective analysis between 2014 and 2022

Karsten Ritter-Lang

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Spine Surgery, Stenum Ortho GmbH, Ganderkesee, Germany

Introduction: Although artificial disc replacement surgery has been an established method for 40 years, it is still viewed critically. This is likely due to the fact that the complications that occur have not been systematically examined to date. A distinction between implant-associated and non-implant-associated complications has rarely been published in the literature. This retrospective analysis distinguishes between early and late complications and differentiates between implant-associated and non-implant-associated complications. It aims to provide information about typical complications associated with different implants and help to avoid potential errors when determining the indication. Material and Methods: The retrospective analysis is based on 2,614 cases following artificial disc replacement surgery between 2014 and 2022 at the Clinic for Orthopaedics Stenum. During the same period, 172 patients underwent revision surgery. Of these, 100 patients were referred from outside the clinic. The evaluation considered the reasons for the necessary revision and then classified them into early and late complications as well as implant-associated and non-implant-associated complications. Implant-associated complications included: subsidence, migration, prosthesis defect, low-grade infection, acquired spondylolisthesis, osteolysis of unclear origin, stick-slip friction, segmental hypermobility, rotational slippage and aseptic loosening. Non-implant-associated complications included: early/postoperative haematoma, early nerve root irritation, early spondylolisthesis, early paresis, early infection, late infection and persistent stenosis. Results: In 158 cases, we observed implant-related causes. In contrast, 14 cases involved complications not related to the implant. Among the implant-related complications, 67 cases involved core defects (Cadisc) alone. These were followed by 31 cases with low-grade infections, 16 cases with acquired spondylolisthesis, 10 cases with unclear osteolysis, 10 cases with stick-slip friction, 8 cases with subsidence, 8 cases with instability/hypermobility, 4 cases with migration, 2 cases with aseptic loosening and 2 cases with rotational slippage. Looking at the total number of treatments and excluding the Cadisc cases, the revision rate is 3.86%. The data also shows that certain specific problems occur more frequently with certain implants and not at all with others. There are 24 cases of early complications and 81 cases of late complications. Conclusion: The available data show that systematic analysis of apparent causes of failure is necessary. It is also clear that the complications that occurred were predominantly not due to the treatment method. At 3.86%, the revision rate is low. This rate can certainly be reduced further through strict indication and appropriate implant selection. In addition, it is evident that late complications clearly predominate, which is why systematic follow-up observation in the first 24 months after surgery is recommended.

## A174: Impact of the duration of antibiotic prophylaxis on surgical site infection rate in patients undergoing complex spinal surgery for spinal metastases

Omer Ahmed

1,2

, Amina Ait Mouhoub

1,2

, Mahreen Tanveer

2,3

, Jesse Shen

1,2

, Fidaa Al-Shakfa

1,2

, Zhi Wang

1,2

1

Université de Montréal, Montreal, Canada

2

Centre Hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal, Montreal, Canada

3

McGill University, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Traditional guidelines are increasingly discouraging the use of postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis. However, there is limited evidence in support of these recommendations in high-risk groups such as cancer patients undergoing complex spinal surgery. Considerable variation exists in post-operative antibiotic prescribing practices, often guided by individual surgeon judgement and preference. Hence, this study aims to evaluate whether varying durations of postoperative antibiotics influence surgical site infection rates in this population. Ultimately, the goal is to establish whether prolonged prophylaxis offers an additional protective effect or whether current guidelines are sufficient for this high-risk population. Material and Methods: This single-center retrospective observational pilot study identified all patients surgically treated for spinal metastasis between 2010 and 2024, with instrumentation or fusion spanning ≥ 6 spinal levels. Medical data was extracted from the institutional electronic medical record system (Oacis). Patients with primary spinal tumors and who had undergone prior radiotherapy at the site of surgery were excluded. Analysis was conducted in two patient groups based on the antibiotic duration (≤ 24h vs. > 24h). The primary outcome was SSI occurrence within a 90-day postoperative window from the date of surgery. Statistical analyses were conducted using the SAS software (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). A two-sided p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: A total of 139 patients who underwent surgery spanning ≥ 6 spinal levels for spinal metastasis were included. A total of 14 surgical site infections were identified, with an overall rate of 10.07%. Statistical techniques such as the Chi-square test and Ficher’s exact test were used to identify the relationship between ATB duration and SSI rate. The Chi-square test showed no significant difference in infection rates among the two groups with antibiotic durations of > 24 h and ≤ 24 h, with Chi-square p = 0.54, showing no significant difference. The Ficher’s exact test also supported this finding with p = 0.770. Further logistic regression analysis showed that the unadjusted odd ratio was 0.687, which suggests that an antibiotic duration of > 24 h reduces infection odds by ∼31%, compared to a duration of ≤ 24 h. Additionally, the multivariable logistic regression model identified several confounding variables such as diabetes, smoking status, and length of surgery. After adjusting for these confounders, the OR dropped to 0.417, suggesting a stronger protective effect of prolonged antibiotics with a reduction in infection odds by ∼58%. None of the confounder variables reached statistical significance, although smoking status showed a trend towards increased infection odds with OR = 6.166 and borderline significance (p = 0.0678). Conclusion: This study observed a protective effect of prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis in surgically treated spinal metastasis patients, although it was not statistically significant. A trend was observed towards reduced infection odds in the group with extended antibiotics (> 24h), suggesting potential clinical significance despite the absence of statistically significant findings. Prolonged prophylaxis may have a protective effect in patients with spinal metastasis undergoing complex spinal surgery. However, larger, multi-center studies are needed to verify this finding and to establish guidelines for prescribing optimal antibiotic prophylaxis in this population.

## A176: The biopsy dilemma in spinal infections: timing of antibiotics and diagnostic yield

Elie Najjar

1

1

Queen's Medical Centre, Nottingham University Hospitals, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: Spinal infections such as spondylodiscitis carry a risk of severe morbidity if diagnosis and treatment are delayed. Microbiological confirmation is critical for guiding therapy, yet culture yields vary depending on biopsy technique and timing of antibiotics. The effect of prior antimicrobial exposure on diagnostic yield remains uncertain, particularly between CT-guided and open biopsy. Materials and Methods: We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, searching MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Scopus through June 2025. Eligible studies included adults and children with suspected spinal infection undergoing CT-, fluoroscopy-, or open biopsy, with or without prior antibiotics. The primary outcome was culture positivity. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I, and pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models depending on heterogeneity. Results: Thirty-eight studies encompassing > 2,000 patients were included. Nine comparative studies (n = 796) demonstrated that prior antibiotics significantly reduced culture yield (59.6% vs 39.2%; RR = 0.74, 95% CI: 0.63-0.86, p = 0.0001; I2 = 0%). The reduction was most marked within 72 hours of antibiotic initiation. Open biopsy achieved the highest yield (76.1%) compared with CT-guided (50.0%) and fluoroscopy-guided biopsy (28.6%). Pooled analysis confirmed superiority of open biopsy over CT-guided approaches (RR = 0.66, 95% CI: 0.57-0.76, p < 0.00001), while CT and fluoroscopy showed no significant difference. Conclusion: Prior antibiotic therapy reduces microbiological yield in spinal infections, with the strongest effect observed in the first 72 hours. Open surgical biopsy consistently outperforms percutaneous techniques, even after antibiotic exposure. Whenever clinically feasible, a biopsy-first approach should be prioritised in stable patients, whereas early surgical biopsy should be considered when antibiotics cannot be delayed. Standardisation of microbiological protocols and prospective studies are needed to optimise diagnostic pathways.

Harvinder Singh Chhabra

1

, Mayukh Mukherjee

1

, Julian Scherer

2

, S. Rajasekaran

3

1

Sri Balaji Action Medical Institute, Delhi, India

2
University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa, 
3
Ganga Medical Centre & Hospitals, Coimbatore, India
Background: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease) accounts for a significant proportion of extrapulmonary TB, leading to vertebral destruction and potential neurological compromise. Multiple scoring systems have been proposed to quantify instability and guide management. Objective: To identify and critically appraise spinal instability scoring systems specific to spinal TB, as well as relevant instruments extrapolated from neoplastic and infectious contexts, summarizing their components, validation outcomes, and potential applicability. Material and Methods: Systematic searches of PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were conducted. Introduction: Surgical site infections (SSIs) remain a significant complication in spinal surgery, particularly in instrumented procedures, contributing to increased morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, and healthcare costs. Intraoperative wound irrigation (IWI) using antiseptic solutions such as povidone-iodine (PI) has been proposed as a preventive strategy. ## A182: Validation of vertebral Hounsfield Unit measurement on CT against DEXA for the diagnosis of osteoporosis: a cross-sectional study

Javier Matta

1

, Maria Suarez

1

, David Florez

1

, Victor Arrieta

1

, Sebastian Forero

1

Hospital Militar Central, Bogota, Colombia

Introduction: Osteoporosis is a highly prevalent condition in aging populations, associated with fragility fractures, disability, and high healthcare costs. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is the current gold standard for diagnosis, but its availability is often limited in acute or emergency settings. Computed tomography (CT) is widely used for other clinical indications, and vertebral Hounsfield Units (HU) have been proposed as a surrogate marker for bone mineral density (BMD). Establishing a validated correlation between HU and DEXA values could support opportunistic osteoporosis screening and earlier treatment. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the clinical utility of Hounsfield Units (HU) from routine CT scans in estimating the trabecular bone structure and mechanical stability of lumbar vertebrae. Material and Methods: In an ex-vivo study, 65 lumbar vertebral bodies (L1-L5) from 53 human donors (mean age 73.0 ± 10.5 years; 22 females) were analyzed; twelve specimens were excluded based on predefined criteria. HU values were measured using routine CT (according to Schreiber et al.), followed by qCT to determine volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD). Cylindrical cores (20 mm × 15 mm) consisting of trabecular bone were extracted and embedded in PMMA. The cores were then subjected to biomechanical testing using axial loading to determine their load to failure (LOF) and linear stiffness (LS). Results: Osteoporosis was defined using qCT (vBMD < 80 mg/cm3); 27 vertebrae (51%) met this criterion. With the used CT scan setting this corresponded to a HU value of 130. Non-osteoporotic vertebrae exhibited higher mean LOF (527 N vs. 319 N; ΔLOF ≈ 208 N; p < 0.001; d > 1.5). HU values correlated significantly with LOF (R2 = 0.513; p < 0.001). Stiffness of the trabecular bone was also significantly reduced in osteoporotic samples (3.06 N/mm vs. 1.86 N/mm; p < 0.001; d = 1.54). HU values showed a strong positive correlation with stiffness in regression analysis (R2 = 0.507; p < 0.001). Split-sample validation showed moderate generalizability of the HU-based model (R2 training: 0.517; test: 0.366), with expected performance decline due to sample size and the simplicity of a single-parameter model. Conclusion: HU values from standard CT scans correlate well with both mechanical strength and stiffness of lumbar vertebral bodies and represent a practical, imaging-based tool for preoperative assessment of bone quality in spine surgery.

## A184: Mechanical properties estimation of lumbar vertebral endplates based on volumetric bone mineral density

Hanming Bian

1

, Qiang Yang

1

, chao chen

1

, Dong Zhao

1

, Gang Liu

1

1

Tianjin University Tianjin Hospital, Tianjin, China

Introduction: Cage subsidence following lumbar interbody fusion is significantly associated with the biomechanical properties of the vertebral endplate. However, there remains a lack of bone mineral density-based methods for quantitatively assessing these mechanical characteristics. To address this gap, this study aims to measure the volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), mechanical strength, and elastic modulus of cadaveric lumbar vertebral endplates, investigate the fitting relationship between vBMD and the elastic modulus, establish a regression model, and ultimately develop an imaging-mechanical characteristic calculation method based on the bone density of the endplate region. A four-point bending test was employed to measure the elastic modulus and yield strength of the endplate samples. Regression equations between BMD, BV/TV, and the elastic modulus of the endplates were established: ① Superior endplate: E = 2.57 × BMD + 403.10 × (BV/TV) - 523.05; ② Inferior endplate: E = 2.04 × BMD + 621.23 × (BV/TV) - 540.55. Conclusion: The elastic modulus of vertebral endplates is highly correlated with their vBMD and BV/TV. Linear fitting relationships between vBMD, BV/TV, and the elastic modulus of the endplates were established.

## A186: Forearm bone mineral density predicts adjacent segment disease following transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion similar to lumbar Hounsfield unit value in patients with lumbar degenerative disease

Qian Chen

1

, Youwei Ai

2

, Hong Ding

2

1
Affiliated Hospital of North Sichuan Medical College, Nanchong, China, 
2
West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China
Introduction: Adjacent segment disease (ASD) develops in ≈9 % of patients after lumbar fusion and is a leading reason for revision; low bone mineral density (BMD) is a recognized risk factor. While dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the lumbar spine can over-estimate BMD in degenerated spines, CT-based Hounsfield units (HU) at the index levels correlate better with ASD, yet lack validated thresholds and require supplementary imaging. Forearm DXA, unaffected by spinal degeneration, accurately reflects axial BMD and predicts osteoporotic complications, but its association with ASD has not been explored. We hypothesize that forearm BMD is an equivalent, radiation-free predictor of ASD after lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 336 patients who underwent TLIF for lumbar degenerative pathologies. Participants were stratified into two cohorts based on evidence of ASD: The ASD group and the non-ASD group. Demographic parameters including gender distribution, mean age, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, diabetes mellitus prevalence, and operated spinal levels were systematically recorded. BMD was assessed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at the distal one-third of the non-dominant forearm radius and ulna. Additionally, BMD was quantified as Hounsfield units (HU) via computed tomography (CT) imaging of the L1-L4 vertebral bodies. Results: At a minimum follow-up of 24 months, the prevalence of adjacent segment disease (ASD) was 11.6%. Compared to the non-ASD group, patients with ASD exhibited significantly lower BMD in the non-dominant forearm (0.325 ± 0.2 vs. 0.536 ± 0.1, p < 0.001) and lower HU value of the L1-L4 vertebral bodies (109.3 ± 29.1 vs. 140.3 ± 20.0, p < 0.001). Following propensity score matching, statistically significant differences were observed in the forearm T score, BMD and CT HU value between the two groups. In multivariate logistic regression analysis, both forearm BMD (OR 0.882; 95% CI 0.829-0.939; p < 0.001) and HU values of L1-L4 (OR 0.936; 95% CI = 0.903-0.971; p < 0.001) were identified as important risk factors for ASD. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for forearm BMD and HU value in predicting ASD was 0.823 and 0.804, respectively. A forearm BMD cutoff value of 0.392 demonstrated optimal diagnostic performance for predicting ASD, with a sensitivity of 74.4% and specificity of 84.6%. Conclusion: The forearm BMD was an important risk factor for ASD. The forearm BMD was a valid predictor of ASD in patients undergoing lumbar fusion, as was the CT HU value.

## A187: The impact of preoperative MRI-defined mild instability on outcomes after posterior open-door laminoplasty: a retrospective cohort study

Haijun Tian

1

, Shichang Zhao

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China

Introduction: The standard treatment for traumatic cervical spinal cord injury (tCSCI) is dichotomous: fusion for unstable spines and laminoplasty for stable ones. This paradigm fails to address a “gray zone” of patients with mild instability, where the optimal surgical strategy is unknown. The novelty of this study lies in proposing and evaluating a specific set of preoperative MRI criteria to define this cohort, questioning whether motion-preserving laminoplasty is a safe and effective alternative to fusion. We hypothesized that for patients selected by these novel criteria, laminoplasty would provide excellent neurological recovery without compromising long-term spinal stability. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 68 patients with tCSCI treated with posterior open-door laminoplasty. The key inclusion criterion was the presence of preoperative MRI-defined mild instability, defined as having one or more of the following without signs of gross instability: 1) Indeterminate posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) injury (high signal on T2/STIR without complete disruption; SLIC DLC score = 1); 2) Minor traumatic disc injury without significant cord compression; or 3) Subtle static malalignment (vertebral translation < 2.0 mm or kyphosis < 7°). Primary outcomes were changes in ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS) grade and ASIA Motor Score (AMS). Secondary outcomes included radiographic stability, assessed by the C2-7 Cobb angle and the development of delayed instability. Mean follow-up was 12.5 months. Results: Significant neurological recovery was observed. At final follow-up, 52 patients (76.5%) improved by at least one AIS grade (p < 0.001), and the mean AMS improved significantly from 64.8 to 85.9 (p < 0.001). Crucially, radiographic stability was maintained across the cohort. There was no significant change in the mean C2-7 Cobb angle (12.8° preoperatively vs. 12.1° postoperatively, p = 0.28). No patient developed progressive kyphosis (> 10°) or delayed spondylolisthesis requiring revision surgery. The overall complication rate was low (5.2%). Conclusion: In a carefully selected cohort defined by specific preoperative MRI criteria for mild instability, posterior open-door laminoplasty is a safe and effective treatment that yields excellent neurological recovery while preserving long-term radiological stability. The use of these nuanced MRI findings to identify suitable candidates is a critical innovation, suggesting that this motion-preserving technique is a viable and advantageous alternative to instrumented fusion for this specific “gray zone” population.

## A188: Impact of screw diameter on the mechanical performance of cement-augmented lumbar spinal fusion constructs

Akar Jani

1

, Nicole DeVries Watson

1

, Douglas Fredericks

1

, Catherine Olinger

1

1

University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics, Iowa City, United States

Introduction: Pedicle screw instrumentation (PSI) is a well-established surgical approach to treat degenerative spinal conditions. However, osteoporosis severely compromises bone quality, reducing screw fixation strength—measured as pullout strength—by up to 80%. Cement augmentation with polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), delivered via fenestrated pedicle screws, reinforces the screw-bone interface and can improve pullout strength up to twofold. Increasing screw diameter enhances fixation strength by increasing surface area of the screw-bone interface, but in osteoporotic vertebrae, the benefit of larger screws with cement augmentation may be limited. Augmentation increases construct rigidity, potentially concentrating stress at the screw-bone interface and reducing the advantage of larger screws. Thus, the benefit of larger screws in cement-augmented fixation remains unclear. This study utilizes anatomically accurate osteoporotic-grade synthetic L3 lumbar vertebrae (Sawbones®, Pacific Research Labs) to evaluate how increased screw diameters in cement-augmented constructs affect performance following cyclic loading. We hypothesize that larger-diameter fenestrated screws will have greater cement distribution within cancellous bone, enhancing construct stability and pullout strength. Materials and Methods: Fifty-millimeter length titanium polyaxial fenestrated pedicle screws of 5.5 mm (n = 8) or 6.5 mm (n = 8) diameter were bilaterally implanted into osteoporotic L3 lumbar Sawbones. 3D-printed drill guides ensured consistent screw trajectories parallel to the vertebral endplates. Each fenestrated screw was augmented with 3 cc of PMMA. Non-fenestrated 6.5 mm screws (n = 8) were used for non-augmented constructs. All constructs were stabilized with 100 mm pre-bent rods and mounted to a Material Testing System (MTS) following modified ASTM F1717-21. Implants underwent 90,000 cycles of compressive loading (100-200 N at 3 Hz) with axial rotation (± 1.5° at 1.8 Hz) to simulate three months of walking at 110 steps/min. Additional cement-augmented fenestrated screws (5.5 mm and 6.5 mm, n = 2 each) not subjected to loading served as passive controls. CT scans before and after loading assessed damage, screw-hole volume changes, and cement distribution. Pullout strength was measured according to modified ASTM F543-23. Results: Initial CT confirmed intact cortical shells after screw implantation. Cement injection caused superior endplate extravasation in one of four vertebrae with 5.5 mm fenestrated screws and three of four vertebrae with 6.5 mm fenestrated screws. All screws withstood cyclic loading. Comparison between left and right screws showed no significant differences in pullout strength for 5.5 mm screws (left: 1726.23 ± 333.12 N, right: 1672.72 ± 285.36 N, p = 0.64) or 6.5 mm screws (left: 1806.20 ± 314.90 N, right: 2033.68 ± 106.70 N, p = 0.12). 6.5 mm screws demonstrated higher mean pullout strength than 5.5 mm screws (1919.94 ± 249.37 N vs 1699.47 ± 288.73 N), but this difference was not significant (p = 0.124). Conclusion: Preliminary findings suggest increasing screw diameter does not significantly improve biomechanical performance in cement-augmented fixation. Larger screws were associated with more frequent extravasation, indicating elevated structural risk without increased fixation strength. This study uses osteoporotic Sawbone, standardized screw placement, and combined compression with axial rotation to better replicate physiological conditions. Compared with prior cadaveric models, this novel approach provides a controlled, clinically relevant evaluation of cement-augmented pedicle screw constructs.

## A189: Predicting cage subsidence after TLIF using HU: a combined model with PROMs and machine learning validation

Elie Najjar

1

, Khalid Salem

1

1

Queen's Medical Centre, Nottingham University Hospitals, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Background: Cage subsidence is a common radiographic finding following transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF), but its clinical significance remains uncertain. While Hounsfield Unit (HU) values from preoperative CT scans have emerged as surrogates for local bone quality, few studies have validated HU-based models for predicting subsidence risk or explored their impact on functional outcomes. We aimed to develop and validate a simple, clinically applicable model for predicting cage subsidence using HU measured at the fused vertebral level, and to assess the relationship between subsidence and patient-reported outcomes. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 76 patients who underwent single-level TLIF between 2019 and 2023 with complete preoperative CT imaging and 12-month clinical follow-up. HU values were measured at the fused vertebral bodies, and cage subsidence was defined as ≥ 2 mm vertical migration or disc height loss on CT at 6-12 months. Logistic regression and ROC analysis were used to derive a threshold-based predictive model. Outcomes included the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), EQ-5D VAS, and patient satisfaction. Results: The overall subsidence rate was 31.6%. HU at the fused level was significantly lower in patients with subsidence (108.3 vs. 135.7, p = 0.048). Logistic regression confirmed HU as an independent predictor (β = −0.0121, p = 0.023); each 10-unit decrease in HU increased the odds of subsidence by 12.1%. A threshold of HU < 130 identified a high-risk group with a 50.0% subsidence rate, compared to 22.0% in the low-risk group (AUC = 0.68). No significant differences in ODI, EQ-5D, or satisfaction were observed between groups at 12 months. Conclusion: HU measured at the fused vertebra is a reliable predictor of cage subsidence following TLIF. A simplified threshold model offers a reproducible tool for preoperative risk stratification. Importantly, radiographic subsidence did not correlate with poorer functional outcomes, reinforcing the need to focus on patient-centered metrics in surgical success.

Introduction: Concurrent cervical and lumbar stenosis, a.k.a tandem spinal stenosis (TSS), is a rare degenerative disease, affecting multiple spinal levels with paucity of literature describing the incidence, natural history, and operative management strategy. , Pouya Alijanipour

2

1

University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, United States

Department of Orthopedics, University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, United States

Introduction: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common and has been linked to increased perioperative cardiopulmonary complications. However, its relationship to postoperative outcomes following elective posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF) remains uncertain. Leveraging a large national database, this study aimed to evaluate whether a preoperative diagnosis of OSA is associated with 30-day postoperative complications after elective PCDF and to assess the extent to which comorbid conditions linked to OSA may mediate this association. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective, propensity-matched cohort analysis using the TriNetX Research Network. Adult patients (18-80 years) who underwent PCDF between January 2010 and September 2025 were included. The exposure group comprised patients with a documented diagnosis of OSA (within two years prior to surgery), while the control group consisted of patients without OSA. Patients with cervical trauma, malignancy, spinal cord tumors, active infection within 30 days, or those undergoing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were excluded. All patients were required to have at least one postoperative follow-up within 30 days. Primary outcomes were acute respiratory failure and prolonged mechanical ventilation within 30 days. Propensity score matching (1:1, greedy nearest-neighbor, caliper = 0.1) was performed in two stages. In the first stage, patients were matched based on demographics and procedural variables (number of additional fusion levels and concurrent laminectomy). In the second stage, matching was repeated with the addition of major comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and COPD). Risk ratios (RRs), risk differences (RDs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, with significance determined using two-sided z-tests and chi-square tests (p < 0.05). Results: A total of 3,586 patients with OSA and 17,268 patients without OSA undergoing PCDF were included. Patients with OSA had significantly higher rates of hypertension (83.4% vs 60.3%), obesity (56.4% vs 21.4%), diabetes (47.5% vs 25.1%), chronic kidney disease (17.4% vs 8.8%), and COPD (20.2% vs 10.8%) compared with those without OSA (p < 0.001 for all). After propensity score matching on demographics and procedural variables, 3,582 patients remained in each group. In this matched cohort, OSA was associated with higher risks of surgical site infection (3.4% vs 2.4%), acute kidney failure (4.7% vs 3.3%), acute respiratory failure (3.8% vs 2.6%), and hospital readmission (14.7% vs 12.8%). However, after additional matching for comorbidities all outcomes were comparable within the two groups. Conclusion: OSA is associated with a substantially higher burden of metabolic and cardiopulmonary comorbidities among patients undergoing PCDF. Apparent associations between OSA and postoperative complications, including infection, renal failure, and respiratory failure, are significantly attenuated after accounting for these comorbidities. These findings highlight the need for OSA to be considered alongside its associated comorbid conditions rather than an isolated risk factor, and its presence alone should not preclude patients from undergoing PCDF.

## A194: Angiotensin receptor blockers are associated with lower pseudarthrosis and revision rates after multilevel posterior cervical fusion: a propensity-matched analysis

Seungjun Lee

1

, Matthew Kim

2

, Graham Goh

2

, Tony Tannoury

2

, Chadi Tannoury

2

1

Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, United States

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston University Medical Center, Boston, United States

Introduction: The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) influences bone remodeling. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) act via distinct pathways that could differentially affect arthrodesis and perioperative outcomes after posterior cervical fusion (PCF). However, their impact on PCF outcomes remains unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to compare perioperative complications, revision rates, and resource utilization in hypertensive adults undergoing multilevel PCF treated with ARBs versus ACEIs. We hypothesized that ARB therapy would be associated with lower pseudarthrosis and infection rates without a concomitant increase in adverse events. Material and Methods: The TriNetX Global Collaborative Network was queried to identify hypertensive adults undergoing multilevel PCF using CPT and ICD-10 codes. Cohorts were defined as ARB users or ACEI users based on prescriptions within 6 months before and after surgery. Propensity score matching (1:1) controlled for age, sex, BMI, smoking, osteoporosis, HbA1c, and Charlson Comorbidity Index comorbidities. Outcomes assessed included medical complications at 90 days, and surgical complications, revision rates, and resource utilization at 90 days, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years. Results: After matching, 4,315 patients were included in both ARB and ACEI cohorts (n = 8,630). ARB use was associated with lower pseudarthrosis rates at 90 days (OR 0.879, p = 0.046), 6 months (OR 0.869, p = 0.023), 1 year (OR 0.843, p = 0.004), and 2 years (OR 0.858, p = 0.008). ARB patients also had lower revision rates at 1 year (OR 0.814, p = 0.049) and 2 years (OR 0.792, p = 0.010). In addition, ARB use was associated with reduced 90-day acute kidney injury (6.0% vs 7.1%; OR 0.837, p = 0.041). No significant differences were observed for other medical or surgical complications, readmissions, or ED utilization. Conclusion: ARB therapy was associated with significantly lower pseudarthrosis rates across all timepoints and fewer revisions at 1-2 years after multilevel PCF. A modest reduction in acute kidney injury was also observed. These findings suggest that RAS inhibitor class influences spinal fusion outcomes and perioperative risk. Prospective studies are warranted to confirm these associations and to guide perioperative optimization in hypertensive spine surgery patients.

## A195: The submandibular retropharyngeal approach: a safe corridor to the upper anterior cervical spine - Anatomical stepwise dissection and clinical case illustration

Alexander F. Küffer

1

, Manuel A. Molina-Vega

2

, Mohammad H. Nour El Dine

3

, Harry Van Loveren

3

, Siviero Agazzi

1,3

1

Department of Neurosurgery,

2

Department of Surgical Oncology, Lakeland Regional Medical Center, Lakeland,United States,

3

Department of Brain and Spine, University of South Florida, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Surgical access to the anterior upper cervical spine and craniovertebral junction is technically demanding due to limited space and the presence of critical neurovascular and visceral structures. Traditional anterior routes, such as the transoral, transnasal or anterolateral approaches, are associated with limitations in exposure and increased morbidity. The submandibular retropharyngeal approach (SRA) has been proposed as an alternative to access the upper anterior cervical spine and the cranio-cervical junction, but detailed anatomical documentation and clinical validation remain limited. Materials and Methods: A cadaveric head specimen was prepared with colored vascular injections to enhance anatomical delineation. Stepwise dissection was performed to document the surgical corridor of the SRA, complemented by high-resolution photography and illustrations. Endoscopic assistance was employed to extend cranial visualization to the anterior arch of C1. The approach was compared with transoral, transnasal, and anterolateral techniques in terms of exposure, safety, and surgical accessibility. A clinical case of a patient undergoing anterior C2 corpectomy for metastatic destruction of the C2 vertebral body was presented to illustrate practical application. Results: The SRA provided a safe, direct, and oblique surgical trajectory to the anterior C2 vertebral body and craniovertebral junction, with reduced need for pharyngeal retraction and preservation of the pharyngeal plexus. Endoscopic assistance further enhanced cranial exposure. The illustrative case demonstrated successful anterior reconstruction with a bone strut graft and plate fixation, achieving spinal stability without significant postoperative dysphagia or speech deficits. Conclusion: The submandibular retropharyngeal approach represents a viable alternative to traditional anterior routes for upper cervical spine surgery, combining effective exposure with reduced risk to critical structures. Its integration into neurosurgical practice may broaden surgical options for complex anterior cervical pathologies.

## A196: Postoperative neurologic and functional outcomes in myasthenia gravis patients undergoing cervical spine surgery for myelopathy

Hanna von Riegen

1

, Erica Greiner

1

, Mario Keko

1

, Aimee Boegle

2

, Jason Pittman

1

, Sapan Gandhi

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School in Boston, MA, Boston, United States

2

Department of Neurology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, United States

Introduction: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder associated with potential postoperative complications, yet data on surgical outcomes in this population remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether MG patients experience worse neurologic and functional outcomes following cervical spine surgery compared to non-MG patients. Material and Methods: Using the TriNetX research platform, we conducted a retrospective, multicenter, cohort study. Adult patients with MG (ICD-10: G70.0) who underwent cervical spine surgery for degenerative myelopathy (ICD: M47.12, M48.02) were matched 1:1 to non-MG controls based on age, sex, race, ethnicity and BMI. Patients with malignant bone diseases were excluded. In exploratory analyses, we further evaluated MG subgroups based on preoperative immunosuppressive therapy and included a lumbar spine surgery cohort to assess systemic versus procedure-specific risks. Results: A total of 290 matched patient pairs were analyzed. The average age of the patients in both groups was 65.9 ± 10.5 years, with the majority being white (76.3%), and male (54.0%). MG patients had a significantly higher risk of postoperative dysphagia within 3 months (21.5% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.001) and 1 year (31.4% vs. 15.7% , p < 0.001). In the immunosuppression subgroup, most outcomes were comparable, though fatigue was significantly more common among immunosuppressed MG patients. In the lumbar surgery comparison group, MG patients also had higher rates of postoperative dysphagia and neurologic complications, suggesting a broader perioperative vulnerability beyond the cervical procedure itself. Conclusion: MG patients undergoing cervical spine surgery for cervical myelopathy are at increased risk for postoperative neurologic and functional complications. These findings suggest a higher rate of residual or ongoing neurologic conditions in MG patients following surgery and highlight the importance of perioperative planning, MG-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care strategies in this high-risk patient group. Exploratory findings indicate that these risks may not be limited to the cervical spine and could reflect systemic effects of MG, underscoring the need for tailored perioperative strategies.

## A197: Dual-rod modification in posterior cervical instrumentation: minimum 5-year follow-up results

Mehmet Aydoğan

1

, Abdülhalim Akar

1

, Muhammed Fatih Serttaş

2

1
Bosphorus Spine Center, İstanbul, Turkey, 
2
Kocaeli City Hospital, Kocaeli, Turkey
Introduction: Posterior cervical instrumentation extending from the upper cervical to the cervicothoracic region often requires excessive rod bending and wide soft tissue dissection, particularly at the C6 level. These technical challenges may complicate the procedure, increase operative time, and necessitate the use of lateral connectors to bridge pedicle and lateral mass screws. To overcome these limitations, we developed a modified double-rod technique for posterior cervical instrumentation and evaluated its clinical and radiological outcomes in patients with multilevel cervical spinal stenosis. Material and Methods: Between 2012 and 2020, 63 patients (mean age: 68.1 years, range: 45-78) with at least three-level cervical spinal stenosis underwent posterior cervical decompression and stabilization using the modified double-rod technique. Of these, 57 patients underwent posterior-only decompression, while 6 patients underwent combined anterior-posterior decompression (3 discectomy, 3 corpectomy). Standard posterior approaches were used to insert pedicle and lateral mass screws, which were then connected by two rods on each side, forming a four-rod construct. Radiological evaluation included measurement of cervical lordosis (C2-C7) on anteroposterior and lateral radiographs, and assessment of fusion by CT and radiographs. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, Neck Disability Index (NDI), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for arm and neck pain. Mean follow-up was 118.7 months (range: 60-156). Results: All patients had multilevel cervical stenosis, with a mean of 3.4 decompressed levels (range: 3-4). Cervical lordosis improved significantly from 12.2° preoperatively to 20.7° at final follow-up (p < 0.001). Mean JOA score increased from 11.1 to 16.3 (p = 0.003), while NDI improved from 35.6 to 10.1 (p < 0.001). VAS scores decreased from 5.8 (arm) and 6.3 (neck) to 1.1 and 1.9, respectively (both p < 0.001). CT scans showed three cases of suspected delayed fusion; however, no loosening or implant failure was detected, and solid fusion was ultimately confirmed in all patients. No pseudoarthrosis was observed. Conclusion: The modified posterior cervical double-rod technique facilitates easier connection between pedicle and lateral mass screws, reduces the need for extensive rod contouring and soft tissue dissection, and avoids the use of lateral connectors. With excellent fusion rates, significant improvements in clinical scores, and a low complication profile, this technique represents a safe and effective option for the surgical management of multilevel cervical spinal stenosis.

## A198: Developmental cervical spinal stenosis in degenerative cervical myelopathy: distinct clinical features, surgical patterns, and recovery ceiling effect

Rui Chen

1

, Xiaoxiong Yang

1

, Feifei Zhou

1

1

Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Developmental cervical spinal stenosis (DCS) is increasingly recognized as an important modifier of degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM). However, whether DCS influences baseline severity, surgical strategies, and postoperative recovery remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to compare clinical characteristics, surgical patterns, and functional outcomes between DCS and non-DCS (nDCS) patients, and to explore the potential “ceiling effect” of recovery in DCS. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort of cervical surgery patients was analyzed. Baseline comorbidities, symptoms/signs, functional scores [modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA), Neck Disability Index (NDI), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), and SF-36], surgical approaches, and follow-up outcomes (3-24 months) were compared between DCS and nDCS groups. Chi-square/Fisher tests and logistic regression were applied, with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated. Results: DCS was significantly associated with ossification-related pathologies [OPLL: OR = 1.65, 95%CI 1.28-2.13; DISH: OR = 3.76, 95%CI 1.14-12.40], and hypertension (OR = 1.44, 95%CI 1.07-1.94). Symptomatically, DCS patients more frequently exhibited limb numbness, lower limb weakness, band-like sensation, and “stepping-on-cotton” gait (all p < 0.05), but less neck pain. Baseline mJOA scores were lower in DCS (12.6 vs. 13.4, p < 0.001), while NDI and VAS showed no difference. DCS patients more often required posterior (44.9% vs. 26.9%) or combined approaches (20.4% vs. 10.5%, both p < 0.001). During follow-up, DCS patients showed greater absolute mJOA improvement, but a smaller proportion achieved ≥ 75% recovery, especially at 12 months (35.8% vs. 46.9%, p = 0.035), reflecting a ceiling effect. Conclusion: DCS represents a distinct clinical entity within DCM, characterized by ossification-related comorbidities, sensory-motor dominant symptomatology, and greater need for extensive surgery. Although DCS patients can achieve marked postoperative improvement, their likelihood of reaching the highest recovery thresholds is limited, likely due to baseline low scores and structural constraints. Recognizing this recovery ceiling may inform surgical decision-making and prognostic counseling, while highlighting DCS as a target for refined imaging and predictive modeling
