## A199: Risk factors for reoperation after minimally invasive tubular transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion: a cohort study of 756 patients

Aaron Lerch

1,2

, Martin Wood

1

, Anthony Chau

1

1
Brisbane Clinical Neuroscience Centre, Brisbane, Australia, 
2
University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia
Introduction: There is a paucity of high-volume series identifying the complication profile and risk factors for reoperation after minimally invasive spinal (MIS) surgery. We analysed our department’s experience with short-term (< 30 days) and long-term (> 30 days) reoperation for lumbar MIS tubular transforaminal lumbar interbody fusions (TLIFs). Material and Methods: All tubular TLIF procedures from 2011 to February 2024 were retrospectively reviewed, with incidence of reoperation determined from patient follow-up until March 2024. Eight neurosurgeons performed operations at our single centre. Two case-controls per complication were manually selected. Each control had undergone the same primary procedure within six months of the index case, at the same levels and, if possible, by the same surgeon. Parameters assessed included age, sex, BMI, frailty (measured by the Modified Charlson Comorbidity and mFI-5), comorbidities (including diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis/osteopenia, depression/anxiety and smoking/drinking status), private/public status, workplace injury, preoperative antithrombotics, preoperative platelet, haemoglobin, cholesterol and fasting glucose levels, the symptomatic indications, prior spinal surgery, preoperative imaging findings, side of approach, operative time, use of postoperative drains/antibiotics, length of stay, time to follow-up, and clinical outcome. All variables were assessed with a series of univariate logistic regressions, with a broad statistical threshold of p < 0.2 for identifying candidates as per convention. Multivariate logistic regressions were then conducted to reveal true associations. Results: From our database of 756 patients who underwent tubular TLIF, there was a 6.6% reoperation rate (n = 50) at a mean follow-up of 1.5 years (SD 1.7 years). Short-term reoperation was predominantly for cage migration and had no statistical risk factors. Long-term reoperation was also mainly for cage migration and was associated with private status, workcover status, osteoporosis/osteopenia, and previous lumbar surgery (at a different level). Combined timeframe reoperations were associated with workcover status, osteoporosis/osteopenia, diabetes, and previous lumbar surgery (at a different level). Patients who had reoperations fared worse than their matched controls. Additionally, a worse patient outcome was associated with diabetes, a higher Modified Charlson Comorbidity Index, and previous lumbar surgery (at the same level). Conclusion: This retrospective case-control series reports our institution’s complication profile and risk factors for reoperation and poor patient outcomes after tubular TLIFs. Our results suggest reoperation is associated with osteoporosis/osteopenia, diabetes, private-funding, being a workcover patient, and previous lumbar surgery at another spinal level.

Introduction: Cervical disc herniation in the posterior cervical discectomy is a well-accepted treatment. ## A203: 3D-navigation-guided endoscopic lumbar medial branch rhizotomy for failed back surgery syndrome

Sheng Jia Huang

1

, Chien-Min Chen

1

1

Changhua Christian hospital, Changhua, Taiwan

Introduction: Failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS), characterized by persistent pain after spinal procedures, remains diagnostically challenging and therapeutically demanding. Facet joint pain is a frequent but often under-recognized etiology. This study retrospectively evaluated the outcomes of full endoscopic lumbar medial branch rhizotomy in FBSS patients with facetogenic pain. Material and Methods: Material: Adults with FBSS derived from facet joint pain treated between 2020-07 and 2025-06 were reviewed. Eligibility required ≥ 6 weeks of unsuccessful conservative management and positive response on medial branch block. Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), prior surgery and intraoperative detail were summarized. The primary endpoint was 12-month pain-free survival (PFS), defined as the interval from surgery to recurrence of significant pain (VAS ≥ 4 for ≥ 7 days), escalation of analgesics, or re-intervention. Patients without such events were censored at last follow-up. Subgroups were classified as Instrumented-MIS, Instrumented-Open, and Non-instrumented. Analgesic use was standardized to morphine milligram equivalents (MME) for opioids and defined daily doses (DDD) for non-opioids. Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank testing compared subgroup PFS, and Cox proportional hazards regression estimated hazard ratios (HR) for instrumented versus non-instrumented patients. Methods: Procedures were performed under local anesthesia in a hybrid operating room with 3D navigation. A 6-mm incision allowed insertion of 30° endoscope toward the target-level base of transverse process. Under irrigation, bipolar cautery achieved hemostasis, and soft tissues were dissected to expose the medial branch. Nerves were transected with endoscopic punches; if obscured by scarring, dissection followed anatomic landmarks such as the mamillo-accessory ligament or pedicle screws. Residual stumps were ablated until pain resolved. For facet pain at a given level, both the targeted branch and the immediately cranial branch were ablated to ensure complete denervation. Results: Twenty patients (mean age 57 years, mean BMI 24.2 kg/m2) were included: Instrumented-MIS (n = 5), Instrumented-Open (n = 8), and Non-instrumented (n = 7). Median PFS follow-up was 5.6 months; median overall follow-up was 12.1 months. Twelve-month PFS rates were 20%, 54%, and 71%, respectively. No significant differences were observed across subgroups (log-rank p = 0.88). Cox analysis indicated a non-significant trend toward inferior PFS in instrumented patients (HR 2.49, 95% CI 0.66-9.43, p = 0.18). Overall, 50% of patients achieved durable 1-year PFS. Conclusion: Half of the patients maintained pain-free survival at 1 year, supporting full endoscopic lumbar medial branch rhizotomy as an effective and advantageous minimally invasive strategy for FBSS with facetogenic pain. Patients with prior instrumentation exhibited a trend toward poorer satisfaction, although not statistically significant. Study limitations include small sample size and short-term follow-up; further multicenter investigations with more large sample size are warranted to validate these findings.

Muhamad Aulia Rahman

## A205: Open fixation with arthrodesis versus percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis in pure ligamentous B2 thoracolumbar fractures: a comparative non-inferiority study

Oscar Bravo

, José Via Dorado

2

, Guillermo Izquierdo

2

, Felipe Novoa Tonda

2

, Manuel Valencia Carrasco

2

1

Hospital Clínico Mutual de Seguridad ChCh, Hospital Clínico de la Fuerza Aérea de Chile, Santiago, Chile

2

Hospital Clínico Mutual de Seguridad ChCh, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Thoracolumbar type B2 fractures with ligamentous disruption are potentially unstable injuries, with open fixation with arthrodesis traditionally regarded as the gold standard. Minimally invasive fixation without arthrodesis has emerged as an alternative in trauma management; however, its role in this specific scenario remains controversial. This study aims to compare clinical and radiological outcomes between open fixation with arthrodesis and percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis in pure ligamentous type B2 thoracolumbar fractures. Material and Methods: This non-inferiority study included the totality of consecutive cases of patients surgically treated for pure ligamentous type B2 thoracolumbar fractures between 2017 and 2025, divided according to surgical technique: open fixation with arthrodesis or percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis. Parametric and non-parametric tests were applied according to data distribution. For angular variables, a clinical non-inferiority margin of 5° was established. For all other variables, a non-inferiority margin of 10% was adopted, defined as a clinically acceptable threshold to support therapeutic equivalence. Non-inferiority was declared when the 95% confidence interval of the difference between techniques remained above the predefined margins. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Results: A total of 39 cases were analysed: 21 treated with open fixation with arthrodesis and 18 with percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis. Demographic characteristics were similar between groups. Percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis demonstrated non-inferiority in angular radiological variables (regional and vertebral kyphosis), with no loss of regional kyphosis correction, in contrast to open fixation with arthrodesis, where loss occurred in 14.3% of cases. Moreover, percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis was associated with reduced intraoperative blood loss (100 cc vs. 200 cc; p < 0.0001) and shorter operative time (90 vs. 120 minutes; p = 0.0037), both statistically significant differences compared with open fixation with arthrodesis. Regarding clinical outcomes, the percutaneous technique demonstrated non-inferiority in total length of hospital stay (mean 14.8 days [95% CI: 9.9-19.7] vs. 14.3 days [95% CI: 7.0-21.6]) and in medical leave duration (mean 3.1 months [95% CI: 2.4-3.7] vs. 3.2 months [95% CI: 2.5-4.0]). A favourable trend was also observed in postoperative hospital stay (median 9 vs. 11 days), although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.18). Conclusion: Although open fixation with arthrodesis has historically been the reference treatment for pure ligamentous type B2 thoracolumbar fractures, our findings indicate that, in appropriately selected patients, percutaneous fixation without arthrodesis represents a valid therapeutic alternative. This technique proved non-inferior in terms of clinical and radiological safety, while offering significant advantages in reduced intraoperative blood loss and shorter operative time compared with open fixation with arthrodesis.

## A206: The “one-and-a-half” minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion: a single-center retrospective case series

Minaam Farooq1, Ahmet Kartal1, Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi1, Mousa Hamad1, Anthony Robayo1, Evan Wang1, Noel Manalil1, Noah Willett1, Andreas Kramer2, Rodolfo Villalobos-Díaz3, Ibrahim Hussain1, Roger Härtl1

1Department of Neurological Surgery, Och Spine at New York Presbyterian Hospital, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, United States, 2Department of Neurosurgery, LMU University Hospital, LMU Munich, Munich, Germany, 3Department of Neurosurgery at National Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery “Manuel Velasco Suárez”, Mexico City, Mexico

Introduction: Symptomatic lumbar spondylolisthesis with multilevel spinal stenosis poses a complex surgical challenge, often managed through multilevel decompression and fusion. We evaluated a hybrid surgical approach termed “One-and-a-Half” TLIF, combining minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (mTLIF) at the unstable segment with a unilateral laminotomy for bilateral decompression (ULBD) at an adjacent stenotic level without fusion. Our objective is to assess the reoperation rate, specifically fusion extension to adjacent decompressed segments, in patients undergoing One-and-a-Half mTLIF. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 36 patients who underwent One-and-a-Half mTLIF between January 2016 and February 2023, evaluating revision surgery rates along with radiographic and clinical outcomes. Results: 33 patients met the inclusion criteria for the One-and-a-Half mTLIF cohort, with a median follow-up of 26 months. Fusion was achieved in 96.2% of cases. The reoperation rate was 9.1% - two patients (6.1%) required subsequent fusion at the previously decompressed (ULBD-treated) level and one patient (3.0%) at the index level. The perioperative complication rate was 12.1%; neurological complications were not observed. Conclusion: The One-and-a-Half mTLIF technique is a promising alternative to traditional multilevel fusion in patients with lumbar spondylolisthesis and concurrent multilevel stenosis. This hybrid approach offers a biomechanically stable alternative to multilevel fusion by selectively fusing the unstable segment while preserving spinal motion through decompression alone at the adjacent stenotic level. Our findings highlight its long-term effectiveness in reducing the necessity for reoperation and fusion extension, suggesting it as a less invasive yet durable solution for managing complex lumbar spine pathology with promising clinical and radiographic outcomes.

## A207: Comparative study between MIS TLIF and OLIF in management of lumber degenerative spondylolisthesis: clinical and radiological outcome

Apurba Gorain

1

, Prashant Baid

1

1

Apollo Multispeciality Hospitals, Kolkata, India

Introduction: Degenerative spondylolisthesis (DS) is a common spinal pathology often managed surgically. Minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MIS TLIF) and oblique lateral interbody fusion (OLIF) are two contemporary fusion techniques gaining popularity due to their purported advantages over open approaches. However, a direct comparative analysis of their efficacy in treating DS remains limited. This study aims to compare the clinical and radiological outcomes of MIS TLIF and OLIF in the management of degenerative spondylolisthesis. Material and Methods: This retrospective comparative study included patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis, age matched and preop ODI matched who underwent MIS TLIF or OLIF at our institution between May 2019 and May 2024. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for back and leg pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at baseline, 6 months, 1 year, and final follow-up. Intra operative time, blood loss, days of hospital admission, Radiological outcomes included segmental lordosis, restoration of total lumber lordosis, and fusion rates and presence of complications such as early post operative leg pain, neurological injury, late in form of cage subsidence, pseudoarthrosis, or adjacent segment disease. Statistical analysis was performed using [appropriate statistical tests, e.g., independent t-tests, chi-square tests, ANOVA] to compare the two groups. Results: A total of 50 patients were included in the study, with 25 in the MIS TLIF group and 25 in the OLIF group. Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in VAS and ODI scores from baseline to final follow-up. Preliminary findings suggest comparable pain relief, better lordosis restoration with OLIF. Complication rates were similar between the two groups. OLIF group had significant less peri operative blood loss, and lesser duration of hospital stay. Conclusion: Both MIS TLIF and OLIF are effective surgical options for the treatment of degenerative spondylolisthesis, leading to favorable clinical and radiological outcomes. While both techniques offer significant benefits, OLIF may provide superior restoration of sagittal alignment, earlier pain relief quicker return to normal activities. Both have similar fusion rates in our study. Further prospective and randomized controlled trials with larger cohorts are warranted to validate these findings and establish definitive guidelines for surgical approach selection in degenerative spondylolisthesis.

## A208: Average 20 year clinical and radiographic follow up of short segment anterior spinal fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

Neel Thakkar

1

, Theodore Choma

1

, Devin Stclair

1

, Don Moore

1

1

University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, United States

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) affects up to 4% of adolescents, with surgical treatment rates increasing by 193% between 1997 and 2012. While posterior segmental fusion is the standard surgical approach, anterior short segment fusion offers a potential advantage by achieving similar curve correction with fewer fused segments, thereby preserving more spinal mobility. This study evaluates long-term clinical and radiographic outcomes - averaging 20 years postoperatively - of a consecutive cohort of AIS patients treated at a single center using an anterior short segment “bone-on-bone” fusion technique. Material and Methods: Patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis who underwent anterior short segment instrumented fusion at the University of Missouri between 1994 and 2012 were identified. PROMIS and SRS-22R surveys were administered, and a subset also completed in-person clinical and radiographic follow-up. Of 101 patients contacted, 62 completed outcome measures and 22 completed full in-person evaluations. Descriptive statistics and two-factor ANOVA were used to analyze outcomes and satisfaction. Results: Over 90% of patients were female, and ∼50% had no family history of scoliosis; half had a mental health diagnosis. Mean age at surgery was 16 years, with an average follow-up of 21 years. Forty of 55 respondents (73%) were satisfied or very satisfied with surgery, and 69% would choose it again. Mean SRS-22R score was 4.01; mean PROMIS physical and mental health scores were 51.61 and 48.07, respectively. On average, 4.5 spinal levels were fused (highest in Lenke I, lowest in Lenke V); 12% underwent revision surgery for adjacent segment disease. Satisfaction and radiographic outcomes did not differ by fusion level or mental health status. Mean initial correction was 28° (56%), with a mean loss of 13° (9%) at long-term follow-up. Conclusion: This is the largest reported 20-year follow-up of anterior bone-on-bone fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, demonstrating favorable long-term subjective and objective outcomes.

Paweł Łajczak

Shifa College of Medicine, Islamabad, Pakistan., Islamabad, Pakistan

Jinnah Medical and Dental College, Karachi, SINDH, Pakistan., Karachi, Pakistan

National University of Cuyo, Argentina., Cuyo, Argentina, 
10
Healthcare Institution of South Iceland, Selfoss, Iceland, Selfoss, Iceland

11

Spine Surgery, Hospital Ortopédico do Estado (Soc. Ben. Israelita Albert Einstein), Salvador, Bahia, Brazil., Salvador, Brazil

12

Department of Neurosurgery, Professor at the Federal University of Espirito Santo. (UFES), Vitória, Brazil

Introduction: TXA is an antifibrinolytic agent widely used in spine surgery. However, the optimal TXA dose remains unclear, especially for younger patients. We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) to evaluate the clinical efficacy and safety of various doses of Tranexamic acid (TXA) for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) instrumentation. Methods: We performed a systematic search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library up to March 2025. We included studies that compared different TXA doses or patients without TXA in AIS surgery. We evaluated five TXA doses: TXA 0 (control without TXA); TXA 1 (10 mg/kg bolus + 1 mg/kg/hr infusion); TXA 2 (15-20 mg/kg bolus + 1-10 mg/kg/hr infusion); TXA 3 (30-50 mg/kg bolus of TXA + 5-10 mg/kg/hr infusion); and TXA 4 (100 mg/kg bolus of TXA + 10 mg/kg/hr infusion). This meta-analysis compared bleeding volume, surgical time, transfusion rates, length of hospital stay, and complications. Random-effects frequentist NMA was employed. Treatments were ranked with P-scores. Results: A total of 1,523 patients, mainly aged 13 to 18 years from 16 studies were included in this analysis (eight retrospective studies). TXA 4 outperformed other doses in reducing intraoperative bleeding, operation time, and cell saver volume. TXA 3 also showed significant benefits but was less effective than TXA 4. There was no difference in complication rates, although these data were not uniformly reported in the studies. No evidence of publication bias was found. Quality concerns were observed. Conclusion: The tranexamic acid dose of 100 mg/kg bolus + 10 mg/kg/hr infusion (TXA 4) was the most effective in bleeding control during AIS instrumentation in teenagers. While these results are promising, more randomized trials are needed to directly compare various TXA doses.
Keywords: Tranexamic acid, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, network meta-analysis, blood loss, spinal fusion.

## A210: A step closer to bringing idiopathic scoliosis monitoring at home: a smartphone app accurately generates digital twins in 624 pediatric patients

Paolo Brigato

1,2

, GianMario Sangiovanni

3

, Sabina Fehric

4

, Kevin Smit

5

, Andrew Tice

5

, Firoz Miyanji

6

, Stefan Parent

7

, Thierry Odent

8

, Neil Saran

9

, Anne Tabard-Fougère

10

, Nathaly Gavira

10

, Romain Dayer

10

, Jean Ouellet

2

1

University Hospital Campus Bio-Medico of Rome, Rome, Italy,

2

McGill University, Montreal, Canada,

3

Sapienza University, Rome, Italy,

4

University of Montréal, Montréal, Canada,

5

Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO), Ottawa, Canada,

6

BC Children's Hospital, Vancouver, Canada,

7

CHU Sainte-Justine, Montréal, Canada,

8

CHRU de Tours, Tours, France,

9

McGill University, Montréal, Canada,

10

HUG - Hôpitaux universitaires de Genève, Geneva, Switzerland

Introduction: Idiopathic scoliosis (IS) accounts for about 80% of pediatric spinal deformities, with Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) affecting 1-4% of individuals aged 10-16 years. Standard radiographic monitoring exposes patients to repeated radiation, despite only ∼10% requiring intervention. Surface topography (ST) offers a non-invasive, radiation-free alternative by correlating torso asymmetry with spinal deformity. This study evaluates the accuracy and reproducibility of Cobb angle measurements using a smartphone-based 3D imaging application, compared with conventional radiography. Material and Methods: This prospective cohort study was conducted between November 2022 and March 2025 across five sites in three countries. Patients aged 5 to 21 years with confirmed or suspected IS were consecutively enrolled. At each clinical visit, participants underwent both standard biplanar radiographs and a smartphone-based 3D surface scan. Exclusion criteria included radiographs obtained in brace, pregnancy, and additional deformities potentially affecting topographic assessment (e.g., limb length discrepancy > 2 cm). Collected demographic and clinical data included age, sex, Body Mass Index (BMI), skin type (Fitzpatrick scale), bracing status, primary curve location, Risser stage, and relevant medical history. Radiographic parameters included manually calculated primary curve Cobb angle, thoracic kyphosis (T1-T12), and lumbar lordosis (T12-L5). Each surface scan was graded on a 0-2 image quality scale. All statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.4.3). Agreement between surface scan-derived and manual Cobb angle measurements was assessed using Spearman’s correlation and Bland-Altman analysis. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) were also calculated to quantify prediction accuracy. Factors influencing discrepancies were explored with Kruskal-Wallis and correlation tests, with statistical significance set at α = 0.05. Results: Among 624 patients with IS (76.7% female; mean age 13.6 ± 2.4 years), a total of 624 paired surface scans and radiographs were analyzed. The mean manually measured primary curve Cobb angle was 32.1° ± 16.1°. Surface scan-derived values showed strong correlation with these measurements (r = 0.775, p < 0.001). Bland-Altman analysis indicated a mean bias of -3.6° with limits of agreement from -16.9° to 24.0°. Prediction errors were significantly associated with bracing, study site, Cobb angle class, skin type, and image quality (p < 0.05), while no significant relationships emerged with age, sex, weight, height, or BMI. Scan quality strongly influenced prediction accuracy: errors were highest with poor-quality images (MAE 11.87°, RMSE 15.95°), intermediate with fair quality (MAE 10.02°, RMSE 13.06°), and lowest with high-quality scans (MAE 6.98°, RMSE 8.89°). Conclusions: The smartphone-based 3D imaging system demonstrated good agreement with manual Cobb angle measurements, with only a modest systematic underestimation. Prediction accuracy was influenced by factors such as image quality, bracing status, skin type, and study site, with higher-quality images yielding the most reliable results. These findings support the potential of this tool as a complementary aid in scoliosis assessment, while also underscoring areas where further refinement and validation could enhance clinical utility.

## A211: Association between correction index and patient reported outcome scores in severe spine deformity

Arthur Sackeyfio

1

, Alexander Upfill-Brown

2

, Sarah Obiri

1

, Kwadwo Yankey

1

, Derrick Owusu

1

, Francis Addai

1

, Irene Wulff

1

, Liudmila Gross

1

, Oheneba Boachie-Adjei

1

1

FOCOS Orthopedic Hospital, Accra, Ghana

2

UCLA Health, Los Angeles, United States

Introduction: A significant component of the success of complex spine deformity surgery is the patient reported outcome measures. These corrective spine surgeries in curves above 100° are considered risky, as they may be complicated by neurologic deficit, cardiopulmonary complications and implant related complications. In the event where these complications do not occur, patient reported outcomes become a significant measure of success of such surgeries. We seek to see if there is an association between correction index and patient reported outcomes in severe spine deformity correction surgery. Material and Methods: Patient with pre-operative coronal or sagittal curves greater than or equal to 100 degrees retrospectively reviewed at a single institution in Ghana between 2015 and 2017. Inclusion criteria included pre-operative sagittal or coronal curve ≥ 100 degrees and follow-up of two-years or greater. Exclusion criteria included revision surgeries or growing rods. Correction index defined as ratio of post-operative cobb measurement over pre-operative measurement. When patient had sagittal and coronal cobb angles ≥ 100, the larger CI was selected. Analysis was also performed separately for sagittal CI and coronal CI. Outcomes included the change in SRS total score and component scores between pre-op and post-op. Results: A total of 41 patient identified. Fifteen patients were diagnosed with adolescent idiopathic kyphoscoliosis, 8 with congenital kyphoscoliosis, 5 with neurofibromatosis and 13 with tuberculosis. Median age was 15 years (IQR 13 to 18). 37 patients were treated with halo traction. Twenty-three patients were treated with VCR, 1 had one-level, 11 had two-level and 6 patients had a three-level VCR. Twenty-two patients had a coronal cobb ≥ 100 degrees, with a median of 138 (range 100-174). Of these, median coronal CI was 0.51 (range 0.15 to 0.80). All 41 patients had a sagittal cobb ≥ 100 degrees, with a median of 141 (range 100-240). Of these, the median sagittal CI was 0.59 (range 0.27 to 0.90). The median overall CI was 0.60 (range 0.27-0.90). The total SRS score improved significantly in all patients (mean pre-op 3.5, mean post-op 4.1, p < 0.0001). Of the sub-scores, SRS Self Image (2.4 to 3.9, p < 0.0001) and Mental Health (4.0 to 4.3, p = 0.039) improved significantly. Change in SRS score significantly associated with correction index (ß = 2.15, p = 0.006, ) and sagittal correction index (ß = 2.22, p = 0.0039), but not coronal correction index (p = 0.24). Change in sub-scores were not independently associated with CI. Analysis of the relationship of CI and change in total SRS score as non-linear resulted in substantial improvement in model fit (Adj R2 0.246 vs 0.159, ). On threshold analysis, a threshold of CI > 0.40 was identified using global CI, resulting in the best model fit (Adj R2 0.267). This was found to be significantly associated with an improvement in total SRS scores of 1.4 for global CI (p = 0.00036) and 1.1 for sagittal CI (p = 0.0027). Conclusion: In patients presenting with large kyphoscoliotic deformities (> 100°), we find that the degree of correction is associated with improvement in SRS scores, with a critical CI of 0.4. We also find that excessive corrections beyond a CI of 0.4 may not be necessary for improved patient reported outcomes, and to mitigate high surgical risk, surgical options which may result in satisfactory alignment within a CI of 0.4 should be opted for. This implies that for a kyphotic curve of 120°, a correction to 70° degrees will result in similar outcomes compared to a correction to 30°. This is similar to work done in less severe deformities, showing a CI of approximately 0.50 resulting in reliable improvement in outcomes.

## A212: Wiltse approach and inter-apophisary fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: analysis of complications at the 2-year follow-up

Georgios Bakaloudis

1

, Lorenzo D'Apice

1

, Alice Baroncini

1

1

Casa di Cura Humanitas San Pio X, Milano, Italy

Introduction: In the past years, posterior instrumentation utilizing a Wiltse approach and inter-apophisary fusion has been introduced to reduce the invasiveness of surgical management for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). However, the safety and efficacy of this approach have not yet been fully investigated. This work aimed to evaluate the radiographic results and complication rate in a single-surgeon case series. Material and Methods: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data. All consecutive AIS patients managed with Wiltse approach and inter-apophisary fusion between Sept 2016 and Jan 2023, who had a minimum follow-up of two years, were included. The amount of correction at the last follow-up and the rate of complications were recorded. Results: The study included 123 patients (88 female), mean age 15.6 ± 2.6 years, follow-up 26-75 months. Most patients had a Lenke 1 or 3 curve, mean Cobb angle 69 ± 7°. The skin incision was a single, median incision in 62 cases, while 61 patients had three separate midline incisions. Screws were placed through a paramedian, multilevel Wiltse approach in all cases; screw placement was guided fluoroscopically in 84 cases, with spinal navigation in 15 cases, and with robotic neuronavigation in 24 cases. 6mm titanium rods were used in almost all cases. On average, 9.8 ± 2.6 levels had been instrumented, with a mean implant density of 58% (range 53-67%). None of the patients required a blood transfusion. The length of hospital stay was 3-5 days, opioid analgesia was suspended within 15 days from surgery, and patients returned to school 2-3 weeks after surgery. At the last available follow-up, a mean correction by 60.8 ± 9.3% (47.3 ± 6.6°) was observed, and the mean Cobb angle measured 23.3 ± 5.4°. In terms of complications, 5 cases of wound dehiscence were observed, all in patients with separate midline incisions. Two cases healed secondarily, and two required implant removal. The latter did not show bacterial growth on the implant, and no loss of correction was observed at the 2-year follow-up. Three distal screw breakages, one implant exchange due to allergy (with revision with different materials), one proximal screw pullout and one rod mobilization were observed, three patients required revision surgery. No rod breakages were observed. Conclusion: The Wiltse approach with inter-apophisary fusion is a safe and effective technique for posterior spinal instrumentation in AIS. The revision rate is in line with that for open posterior fusion. The observation of wound dehiscence with the use of separate incisions suggests that the use of a single midline incision might be a safer approach.

## A213: Beyond bending films: estimating scoliosis flexibility from standing and supine radiographs

Altug Yucekul

1

, Feyzi Kilic

2

, Suha Aktas

3

, Elif Gizem Carus

2

, Tais Zulemyan

2

, Caglar Yilgor

4

, Ahmet Alanay

1

1

Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Comprehensive Spine Center, Acibadem Maslak Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

3

Istanbul Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation Training and Research Hospital Orthopedics and Traumatology Clinic, Istanbul, Turkey

4

Koc University Hospital Spine Center, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Flexibility assessment is a fundamental component in the preoperative evaluation of patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). The degree of curve reducibility is crucial for determining surgical strategy, selecting the levels of instrumentation, and anticipating postoperative alignment. Traditionally, flexibility is measured using special radiographs such as side-bending, fulcrum, and TRUGA (traction radiograph under general anesthesia) radiographs. These radiographs are time-consuming, technician-dependent, and expose the patient to additional radiation. The present study aimed to formulate a simple radiographic predictor of maximum curve flexibility (SUFLEX) using only standard standing and supine Cobb angles, and to test whether SUFLEX can accurately identify curves that bend below 25°. Materials and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on 142 consecutive AIS patients for whom a complete set of flexibility radiographs (standing, supine, side-bending, fulcrum, and TRUGA) were available. Patients with a main curve magnitude ≥40° on standing radiographs were included in the SUFLEX formulation, yielding 102 main thoracic (MT) and 89 thoracolumbar/lumbar (TL/L) curves. Maximum flexibility (%) for each curve was defined as the greatest percentage reduction from standing Cobb angle observed on any of the special flexibility radiographs. Two separate multiple linear regression models were constructed, one for MT and one for TL/L, with standing and supine Cobb angles as predictors. Model performance was assessed using five-fold cross-validation, reporting R2 and mean absolute error (MAE). Logistic regression analyses using the same predictors were performed to estimate the probability that a given curve would bend to less than 25°. Model discrimination was evaluated by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis with out-of-fold probabilities, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated. Classification thresholds were determined using the Youden index. Results: The study cohort consisted of 142 patients, of whom 118 were female and 24 were male. The mean age was 14.5 ± 2.1 years. The mean Risser stage was 2.8 ± 1.3, and the mean Sanders stage was 4.9 ± 1.2. Curve classification according to Lenke type was type 1 (54 patients), type 2 (17 patients), type 3 (24 patients), type 4 (15 patients), type 5 (22 patients), and type 6 (10 patients). Lumbar modifier distribution was A (59 patients), B (52 patients), and C (31 patients). For main thoracic curves (n=102), cross-validated model performance was R2 = 0.50 ± 0.09 with MAE 9.34% ± 1.29. For thoracolumbar/lumbar curves (n=89), performance was R2 = 0.30 ± 0.18 with MAE 10.04% ± 1.42. Using the SUFLEX formula, prediction for minimum Cobb angles for MT curves were within ± 5° in 51.0% of cases, within ± 5-10° in 32.4%, and within ± 10-13° in 9.8% ( ). For TL/L curves, the proportions were 59.6%, 27.0%, and 5.6%, respectively. In logistic regression analyses, the discrimination of SUFLEX for identifying curves that would bend below 25° was strong (AUC of 0.921 (95% CI 0.864-0.966) for MT and 0.853 (95% CI 0.645-0.981) for TL/L. Accuracy was 87.3% for MT and 96.6% for TL/L. Conclusions: A SUFLEX estimator derived from standing and supine Cobb angles provides a practical and validated estimate of maximum curve flexibility, accurately identifying curves likely to bend below 25°. This simple approach can streamline preoperative assessment, minimize the need for additional flexibility films, and reduce radiation exposure. By reliably predicting curves below 25°, SUFLEX may also facilitate Lenke classification without routine bending radiographs, offering a low-cost and efficient adjunct for surgical planning in AIS.

## A214: Selective thoracic fusion with postoperative bracing versus non-selective fusion in Lenke 1C adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a propensity score-matched analysis

Giovanni Viroli

1

, Matteo Traversari

1

, Marco Manzetti

1

, Alberto Ruffilli

1

, Cesare Faldini

1

1

Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: The surgical treatment of Lenke 1C adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) remains controversial. While non-selective fusion (NSF) addresses both thoracic and lumbar curves, selective thoracic fusion (STF) aims to preserve lumbar mobility but may risk coronal imbalance. The use of postoperative corrective bracing has been proposed to enhance lumbar curve control after STF. This study compared radiographic and patient-reported outcomes of STF+brace versus NSF in Lenke 1C AIS using a propensity score-matched cohort. Materials and Methods: A retrospective series of 76 Lenke 1C AIS patients was reviewed: 38 underwent STF with postoperative bracing until skeletal maturity, and 38 underwent NSF. Propensity scores were estimated using age, sex, skeletal maturity (Risser, CVM), curve magnitudes, lumbar flexibility, sagittal parameters, and baseline PROMs (SRS-22, QLPSD). One-to-one optimal matching yielded 30 well-balanced pairs (n = 60). Balance was assessed using standardized mean differences (|SMD < 0.10). Post-matching comparisons were performed using paired t-tests for continuous variables and McNemar’s test for categorical variables. All patients had a minimum of 24 months follow-up (range 24-41 months). Results: At last follow-up, radiographic outcomes showed no significant differences between groups. Thoracic Cobb correction was comparable (STF+brace 67 ± 9% vs. NSF 69 ± 8%, p = 0.42). Lumbar Cobb angles at follow-up were slightly lower in the NSF group (18 ± 6° vs. 21 ± 7° in STF+brace), but this trend was not statistically significant (p = 0.09). PROMs demonstrated no significant differences in overall SRS-22 total (STF+brace 4.3 ± 0.3 vs. NSF 4.4 ± 0.4, p = 0.28) or QLPSD total scores (STF+brace 42 ± 6 vs. NSF 41 ± 5, p = 0.31). However, analysis of subdomains revealed distinct patterns: SRS-22 function was significantly better in the STF+brace group (4.5 ± 0.3 vs. 4.2 ± 0.4, p = 0.02), while SRS-22 satisfaction was slightly but significantly lower (4.1 ± 0.4 vs. 4.3 ± 0.3, p = 0.04). Regarding QLPSD domains, back flexibility was significantly better in STF+brace (2.2 ± 0.8 vs 3.3 ± 0.5, p = 0.01), whereas body image was worse (1.8 ± 0.9 vs. 1.4 ± 0.7, p = 0.04). Conclusion: In Lenke 1C AIS, selective thoracic fusion with postoperative bracing provides equivalent global radiographic and overall quality-of-life outcomes compared with non-selective fusion, while preserving lumbar mobility. Subdomain analyses highlight trade-offs: STF+brace improves function and back flexibility but may modestly reduce patient satisfaction and body image perception. These findings suggest STF+brace as a viable motion-preserving strategy, although longer-term prospective studies are warranted.

## A215: Multicenter retrospective validation study of artificial intelligence-assisted bone age estimation from left-hand radiographs: comparison of idiopathic scoliosis patient groups and healthy controls

Bilge Yilmaz

1

, Soheil Sabet

1

, Yunus Akman

1

, Huseyin Ozturk

1

, Cem Sever

1

, Huseyin Coskun

1

, Mutlu Cobanoglu

1

, Celaleddin Bildik

1

, Gokce Guven

2

, Deniz Karasahin

2

, Sinan Kahraman

1

, Tunay Sanli

1

1

Anatolian Spine Study Group, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Osteoid Health Technologies, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Accurate skeletal maturity assessment is essential for predicting curve progression and optimizing treatment timing in idiopathic scoliosis (IS). While traditional bone age methods (Greulich-Pyle, Tanner-Whitehouse) and scoliosis-specific scales are widely used, deep learning models have recently shown promising accuracy. This study aimed to validate an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted program (Osteoid-BAA 0,1) for bone age estimation in the Turkish population and to compare skeletal maturity patterns between IS subgroups and healthy controls. Material and Methods: A multicenter retrospective review was conducted across 8 centers. The study cohort comprised IS patients aged 8-18 years with scoliosis who underwent left hand-wrist radiography, together with age-matched healthy controls. Subjects were categorized into: Group 1 (IS, Cobb 10-40°), Group 2 (IS, Cobb > 40°, surgical candidates), and Group 3 (Age-matched healthy controls). All bone age was assessed by AI and an experienced radiologist. Accuracy was evaluated using Pearson correlation, mean absolute error (MAE), and bias. Group differences were tested with ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis, including subgroup analyses by sex and age (8-12, 13-15, 16-18 years). Results: A total of 208 individuals (237 left hand-wrist radiographs; mean age 13.6 ± 2.3 years, 157F/51M) were analyzed. All individuals were categorized into three groups: G1 (n = 103, 88 females/15 males, mean age 13.3 years), G2 (n = 63, 53 females/10 males, mean age 13.8 years), and G3 (n = 71, 39 females/32 males, mean age 12.7 years). AI showed strong correlation with chronological age (r = 0.74, MAE = 15.6 months) as well as with the radiologist (r = 0.87, MAE = 11.1 months). The radiologist achieved a correlation of r = 0.89 with chronological age and a MAE of 9.9 months. Between-group comparisons revealed the following biases: AI bias was +3.6 ± 16.6 months in G1, +6.9 ± 19.2 months in G2, and -2.5 ± 19.8 months in G3 (ANOVA p = 0.009; G2 vs. G3 p = 0.0087), whereas radiologist bias was +5.8 ± 11.0 months in G1, +6.1 ± 13.0 months in G2, and +5.4 ± 14.8 months in G3 (p = 0.945). AI predicted more advanced bone age in surgical IS patients (p = 0.0099), suggesting accelerated maturation in severe curves. In sex-specific analyses, AI showed a bias of -7.7 months in females and +13.4 months in males (p < 0.001), while radiologist bias was -6.5 months in females and -3.6 months in males (p = 0.18). In age subgroup analyses, AI bias was -10.2 months in the 8-12 years group, -6.7 months in the 13-15 years group, and +16.6 months in the 16-18 years group (p < 0.001), whereas radiologist bias was -4.6 months, -9.8 months, and +1.3 months across the same age groups, respectively (p < 0.001). Conclusion: AI-assisted bone age estimation demonstrated accuracy comparable to expert evaluation and revealed maturity differences between IS subgroups and controls. AI predicted advanced bone age in the surgical IS group, suggesting accelerated skeletal maturation in patients with severe curves. This approach holds promise as a scalable, objective decision-support tool in IS management. Further external validation and clinical outcome studies are warranted.

## A217: Surgical management of multiple myeloma vertebral column lesions - Results from an international survey distributed to the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Tumor

Vanessa Hubertus

1,2

, Emily von Bronewski

, Lucius Fekonja

1

, Anton Früh

1

, Christian Entenmann

, Hannah Miller

, Charlotte Buhre

1

, Michael Fehlings

3

, Ilya Laufer

4

, Peter Vajkoczy

1

, Julia Onken

1,5

1

Charité University Hospital Berlin, Department for Neurosurgery, Berlin, Germany,

2

Berlin Institute of Health, BIH Charité Clinician Scientist Program, Berlin, Germany,

3

Division of Neurosurgery and Spinal Program, Toronto Western Hospital, Krembil Neuroscience Center, and University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada,

4

Department of Neurosurgery, New York University Langone Health, New York, United States,

5

German Consortium for Translational Cancer Research, German Cancer Research Centre, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Vertebral fractures and epidural infiltration are common complications in Multiple Myeloma (MM), causing vertebral pain and neurological deficits. Non-surgical management is universally preferred, but internationally accepted guidelines are lacking. The aim of this study was to assess the current international treatment standards and clinical conditions guiding surgical decision-making in MM vertebral lesions. Material and Methods: A survey was distributed to the members of the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Tumor, an international, interdisciplinary key opinion leader group specialized on the treatment of oncologic spine disease. The survey, consisted of 25 questions, of which 15 assessed the participant`s background, clinical expertise, and experienced treatment standards regarding MM vertebral lesions, followed by ten case examples with seven possible treatment scenarios. The distribution was supported by AO Spine Network Clinical Research and facilitated via the web-based application REDCap®. Results: 51 international experts, from 14 countries and five continents completed the survey, with 51% being of orthopaedic, and 44% of neurosurgical background, while 6% were radio-oncologists. 87% of the participants were university-associated, and 96% part of interdisciplinary cancer centers. 84% of the participants stated that they “see vertebral lesions in MM in general as a non-surgical disease”. ## A219: Bone graft substitutes and spinal fusion outcomes in spine oncology

Esteban Ramirez-Ferrer

1

, Juan Zuluaga

1

, Romulo Augusto Andrade de Almeida

1

, Francisco Call-Orellana

1

, Gil Kimchi

1

, Christopher Alvarez-Breckenridge

1

, Rob North

1

, Laurence Rhines

1

, Claudio Tatsui

1

1

The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, United States

Introduction: Surgery for spine tumors prioritizes oncologic control spinal cord decompression, and structural stabilization while achieving spinal fusion remains a secondary goal. This study aimed to assess fusion rates across three different bone grafts materials andtheir association with hardware failure. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent tumor resection and spinal instrumentation from January 2018 toJanuary 2024. Patients with overall survival (OS) of less than 6 months or incomplete follow-up data were excluded. Descriptive statistics summarized the cohort characteristics. Group comparison test, Kaplan-Meier curves estimated fusion probabilities over time, and Cox proportional hazard models identified predictors of spinal fusion. Results: A total of 159 patients were included: 93 treated with demineralized bone matrix (DBM), 30 with biphasic calcium phosphate (BCP), and 36 with bioactive glass fiber (BGF). Groups showed no significant differences in age, sex, BMI, KPS, neurological status, Spinal Instabitily Neoplastic Scores (SINS), bone graft volume, radiation therapy, hardware failure, or pseudoarthrosis rates. Mean time to spinal fusion was 54, 14, and 22 months for the DBM, BCP, and BGF, respectively. On multivariate analysis all grafts materials were positively associated with spinal fusion, with BCP showing the strongest effect. Prior radiation therapy was negatively associated with fusion rates, while BMI > 25 kg/m2 was associated with a higher risk of hardware failure. Conclusion: Bone grafts substitutes improve spinal fusion rates in spine oncology, with ceramic-based grafts demonstrating the highest and earliest fusion rates. Conversely, postoperative radiation therapy negatively affects fusion, and further prospective studies are needed to determine the optimal graft selection, volume, and timing with adjuvant radiation therapy to balance oncologic controland mechanical stability.

## A220: Hybrid spine reconstruction using an expandable cage combined with vascularized free fibula autograft after en bloc spondylectomy for primary bone tumors of the mobile spine

Gil Kimchi

1

, Garrett Walsh

1

, Reza Mehran

1

, Alex Mericli

1

, Paul Shay

, Edward Chang

1

, David Adelman

1

, Christopher Nguyen

1

, Francisco Call-Orellana

1

, Juan Zuluaga

1

, Laurence Rhines

1

1

MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, United States

Introduction: En bloc spondylectomy for primary spinal tumors creates extensive bony defects that require durable anterior column reconstruction. Unlike metastatic cases, these patients are often young and potentially curable, necessitating long-term bony fusion. Conventional reconstruction with cages and allograft frequently fails to achieve solid arthrodesis and is associated with high failure rates. The objective of this study was to compare outcomes of a novel hybrid reconstruction using expandable cages combined with vascularized autologous fibula grafts versus traditional cage/allograft-only techniques. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent en bloc spondylectomy for primary spinal bone tumors by a single surgeon (2002-2024). Patients were grouped by reconstruction type: hybrid (expandable cage packed with allograft with adjacent vascularized fibula with microvascular anastomosis) or control (cage with allograft alone). Conclusion: Hybrid reconstruction with an expandable cage and vascularized fibula autograft significantly improves fusion rates and time to fusion compared to conventional methods, without increased morbidity. This approach may offer a more durable long-term solution in patients undergoing curative surgery for primary spinal tumors.

## A221: Local disease control and survival analysis after surgical treatment of spinal metastases: comparison between carbon fiber-reinforced polythertherketone and titanium implants for posterior stabilization

Luigi Falzetti

1

, Cristiana Griffoni

1

, Simona Rosa

2

, Silvia Terzi

1

, Chiara Alcherigi

1

, Mariarita Intagliata

1

, Stefano Bandiera

1

, Giovanni Barbanti Bròdano

1

, riccardo ghermandi

1

, Giuseppe Tedesco

1

, Gisberto Evangelisti

1

, Valerio Pipola

1

, Marco Girolami

1

, Stefano Pasini

1

, Giovanni Tosini

1

, Chiara Cini

1

, Alessandro Gasbarrini

1,2

1

Complex Spinal Surgery Unit, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

2

Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Sciences, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Metastatic involvement of the spine can lead to significant morbidity, including intractable pain, pathological fractures, spinal instability, and neurological deficits due to spinal cord compression. While systemic therapies and radiotherapy remain central in the treatment of metastatic cancer, surgery plays a pivotal role in selected cases, particularly when mechanical instability or neurological compromise is present. Carbon fiber-reinforced PEEK (CRFP) spinal instrumentation has emerged as a promising alternative in the oncological setting: CFRP is radiolucent, producing minimal artifacts on CT and MRI, and it interacts less with radiation therapy, resulting in reduced backscatter and shielding effects, thereby allowing for superior postoperative imaging and radiotherapy planning. Considering the lack of comparative clinical trials, we proposed analyzing differences in terms of survival, local disease control and quality of life in a population of spinal metastatic patients surgically treated with CFRP or titanium implants. Methods: We performed a prospective monocentric cohort clinical study on patients with vertebral metastases who underwent spinal surgery from August 2018 to October 2022. Demographic, clinical and surgical data were collected, as well as adverse events, clinical outcomes and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) during the follow up period. Results: 160 patients were included in this study: 129 patients were treated with titanium instrumentation and 31 patients were treated with CFRP instrumentation. A local disease progression was recorded in 36 patients (22.5%), 27 patients with titanium instrumentation (20.9%) and 9 patients with CFRP instrumentation (29.0%). Kaplan Meier analyses: The median survival time of the entire population was 24.3 months (95% CI 15.0-32.1), no statistically significant difference was observed between the two groups (Log- rank test, p = 0.637). The type of instrumentation had no significant impact on the local progression (Log-rank test, p = 0.577). Local progression during the first year after surgery had no significant impact on the long-term risk of death (Log rank test, p = 0.531) and on the risk of death during the first 12 months (Log- rank test, p = 0.363). After the surgery, 31.9% of patients underwent radiotherapy at the index spinal lesion: 13 cases (41.9%) in the group treated with CFRP and 38 cases (29.5%) in the group treated with titanium. Cox model showed that adjuvant radiotherapy performed within the first year after surgery reduced the risk of local progression by 69% with a statistically significant protective result (p = 0.035). Adjuvant radiotherapy also decreased the risk of death by 46% (p = 0.011). Seven cases of mechanical complications (5.4%) were detected in the group treated with titanium implants, while no cases were registered in the group treated with CFRP, however, the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.347). Concerning PROMs, no statistically significant difference appeared between the two groups of patients (CFRP implants versus titanium implants) during the follow up period. Conclusion: The use of CFRP instrumentation can improve the adjuvant radiotherapy treatment after surgery for spinal metastases, which is demonstrated to have a protective effect on the local progression of the disease and on the risk of death, if carried out in the first year after surgery.

Introduction: The Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score is a widely used and cited referral tool to identify patients with potentially unstable spinal metastases; however, treatment decision (ie. need for stabilization) may also be influenced by various morphological and clinical factors. ## A223: First use of cesium-131 embedded collagen tiles for brachytherapy in the spine: combined surgical resection and brachytherapy for recurrent rectosigmoid adenocarcinoma metastasis to the sacrum with 1-year follow up

Anisse Chaker

1

, Heegook Yeo

1

, Jessie Huang-Vredevoogd

2

, Anthony Doemer

2

, Lisa Scarpace

1

, Alexandra Moceri

3

, Mira Shah

2

, Ian Lee

1

, Steven Kalkanis

1

, Salim Siddiqui

2

, Adam Robin

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery

2

Department of Radiation Oncology, Henry Ford Hospital Detroit, United States

3

Henry Ford Innovations, Henry Ford Health System, Detroit, United States

Introduction: Cesium-131 embedded collagen tiles (Cs131CT) for high-dose rate brachytherapy has thus far primarily been utilized for intracranial applications. Advantages of Cesium-131 include less tissue penetration thus lowering the risk of damage to nearby organs and neural elements. Utilization of brachytherapy allows for a surgically targeted radiation source that takes effect immediately upon intraoperative implantation. We aim to present the first utilization of Cs131CT brachytherapy in the spine with 1-year follow up. Material and Methods: Patient selection was conducted via multidisciplinary discussion amongst our institutional Spine Tumor Board. Inclusion criteria were limited to patients with metastatic cancer resistant to multiple lines of chemotherapy, biologic therapy, and radiation with symptomatic metastasis to the lumbosacral spine. A 55 year-old male was selected who presented with symptomatic lumbosacral compressive polyradiculopathy from locally advanced and recurrent rectosigmoid adenocarcinoma involving the sacrum and lumbosacral nerve roots. After Spine Tumor Board review, determined options included continued observation with expected disease progression and neurological decline, resection via sacrectomy, or off-label compassionate Cs131CT brachytherapy with tumor debulking and partial sacrectomy. Given the associated morbidity with a high sacrectomy, patient declined this option. A shared-decision was made to proceed with a L5-S3 decompression and partial sacrectomy with tumor debulking and placement of Cs131CT brachytherapy. Patient was followed post-operatively with surveillance imaging for 1-year. Results: In order to simulate the operation in a lab setting prior to surgery, a 3D model of the patient’s spine with the tumor included was first created. An important aspect of the operative simulation utilizing the 3D model was to place the Cs131CT in the surgical cavity and estimate the local radiation dose delivered. This would allow for development of an intra-operative Cs131CT placement strategy that avoids radiation damage to the cauda equina. Once a safe Cs131CT placement plan was achieved in the 3D model, surgery was performed on the patient with successful debulking of the tumor and circumferential decompression. This was followed by placement of the Cs131CT with adequate distance from the neural elements. Post-operative dosimetry calculation based on the patient’s imaging was 106.4Gy - within 10% of the predicted Cs131CT dosimetry. Three-, six-, and 1-year post-operative MRIs were completed without apparent evidence of recurrence at the area of intended brachytherapy. Conclusion: Through the utilization of a pre-surgical model for feasibility and radiation safety planning, we present the first ever use of Cs131CT brachytherapy in the spine. Given the lack of radiographic recurrence at 1 year, this promising technique may warrant further investigation in appropriately selected patients. Strategic planning and establishment of a multi-disciplinary team were critical in providing a potential new alternative for patients faced with limited treatment options.

## A224: Neurological recovery after delayed surgery for MESCC: outcomes in patients with paralysis exceeding 48 hours

Pan-pan HU

1

, Yan Li

1

, Feng Wei

1

, Zhongjun Liu

1

, Ben Wang

1

1

Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Metastatic epidural spinal cord compression (MESCC) represents one of the most debilitating sequelae of advanced cancer, often resulting in rapid neurological decline and loss of ambulation. Current guidelines emphasize decompression within 24-48 hours, yet many patients present outside this window due to delayed recognition or the need for systemic oncologic evaluation. The efficacy of surgery in patients with paralysis exceeding 48 hours remains uncertain. This study assessed neurological and functional recovery in MESCC patients who underwent delayed decompressive surgery. Materials and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of consecutive MESCC patients treated surgically between 2012 and 2020 at a single tertiary spine center. Inclusion criteria comprised severe neurological deficit (Frankel A-C), non-ambulatory status for > 48 hours, life expectancy >3 months, and pathologically confirmed spinal metastasis. Clinical variables, operative details, complications, neurological outcomes (Frankel grade), ambulatory status, Karnofsky Performance Score (KPS), and survival were analyzed. The primary endpoint was postoperative neurological recovery. Results: Thirty-seven patients met inclusion criteria, with a median preoperative paralysis duration of 9 days (range, 2-35 days). The cohort included 24 males and 13 females, mean age 55.2 years. Lung, prostate, and kidney cancers were the most frequent primary tumors. All patients underwent circumferential decompression with stabilization, and cement augmentation was applied when appropriate. Postoperatively, 30 patients (81.1%) improved at least one Frankel grade. Ambulation was regained in 22 cases (59.5%), including 28.6% of Frankel A, 57.1% of Frankel B, and 75.0% of Frankel C patients. Significant improvements were observed in pain scores and KPS (p < 0.001). Complications occurred in 13 patients (35.1%), but no neurological deterioration was recorded. Median survival was 19 months, with 1-year and 2-year survival rates of 58.9% and 40.3%, respectively. No single clinical factor significantly predicted neurological recovery. Conclusion: Decompressive surgery for MESCC patients with prolonged paralysis (> 48 hours) can still achieve substantial neurological and functional recovery. Nearly 60% of non-ambulatory patients regained walking ability, demonstrating that meaningful benefit remains possible beyond the conventionally recommended surgical window. These findings highlight the value of surgery even in delayed presentations and support a proactive surgical approach in appropriately selected patients.

## A226: Towards digital outcome measures in spine care: psychometric properties of movemed for degenerative cervical myelopathy

Ali Gharooni

1,2

, Tatiana Houhou

2

, Alvaro Yanez

2

, Benjamin Davies

1

1

University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom

2

MoveMed Ltd, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) suffers from subjective outcome measures with low granularity contributing to imprecise measurements, leading to delayed care in clinics and inflated sample sizes in trials. These limitations have spurred interest in the development of novel assessment tools as a top 10 research priority in DCM. MoveMed app is a smartphone based battery of patient-performed performance outcomes (PerfOMs) targeting dexterity, upper-limb stability, and gait via fast tap, typing, hold, and stand-and-walk tasks administered in natural environments under standardized instructions. It allows high-frequency, remote and objective measurement of DCM. The aim of this abstract is to synthesize validity and reliability evidence and outline a pragmatic roadmap for adoption, cost-effectiveness evaluation, and real-world deployment in spine pathways and research. Material and Methods: Prospective, decentralized observational studies enrolled adults with DCM who completed at least weekly MoveMed in-app battery of tests and periodic ePROMs over a period of 12 weeks. Primary endpoints for MoveMed were fast-tap count (dexterity) and hold stability score (upper-limb stability); typing speed and stand-and-walk cadence were secondary, with COSMIN risk-of-bias appraisal. Construct validity was assessed by testing a priori hypotheses about directionality and magnitude of correlation of MoveMed tests to patient-derived modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association score (P-mJOA) and WHOQOL-Bref. Reliability analyses used a clinically stable subset with repeated measures to compute intraclass correlation (ICC) of agreement and measurement error (standard error of mean(SEM), and smallest detectable change (SDC) for each MoveMed task endpoint, with sufficiency judged at ICC ≥ 0.70 per Criteria from the Consensus-Based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN). Results: Construct validity (n = 27) was rated “very good” overall as per COSMIN criteria: 74% (67/90) of unidimensional correlations (fast tap, hold, typing) and 47% (8/17) of multidimensional correlations (stand-and-walk) met a priori hypotheses, with greatest convergence to neuromuscular P-mJOA domains and expected divergence from WHOQOL-Bref. Reliability (n = 7) was “very good” overall as per COSMIN criteria: ICCs were moderate-to-excellent for unidimensional tests (fast tap, hold, typing), with coefficients generally ≥ 0.70 across MCID subgroups, while the multidimensional gait task trended lower and is undergoing optimization. Measurement error thresholds supported individual-level interpretation: ±3-7 taps (fast tap), ±4-10% stability points (hold), ±0.2 keys/s (typing), and ±27 steps/min (gait), enabling discrimination of real change beyond noise. Standardized, smartphone-based PerfOMs demonstrated feasibility for decentralized, high-frequency assessment, complementing PROMs and improving sensitivity to clinically meaningful change in DCM. Conclusion: MoveMed, a smartphone based digital outcome measure, demonstrates good construct validity and test-retest reliability in adults with DCM, supporting remote monitoring and in spine care pathways and trials. Next steps: 1) hybrid implementation-effectiveness studies for adoption in clinics and peri-operative pathways, with electronic healthcare record integration; 2) health-economic modeling and trial simulations to quantify cost-effectiveness by reduced sample sizes and visit burden when using MoveMed; 3) multicenter real-world evidence cohorts embedding MoveMed into registries and 4) further trials assessing psychometric properties (i.e. responsiveness and MCID). Use cases span in-clinic triage and risk stratification, post-operative recovery tracking, decentralized interventional and observational studies, and registry-based surveillance across spine populations.

## A227: From CT to 3D-printable guide in minutes: automated design of patient-specific pedicle screw templates via point transformer

Qingzhi Xiang

1,2

, Xiao Xia

1,2

, Yan Yu

1,2

, Liming Cheng

1,2

1
Division of Spine, Department of Orthopaedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China, 
2
Key Laboratory of Spine and Spinal Cord Injury Repair and Regeneration (Tongji University), Ministry of Education, Shanghai, China
Introduction: Pedicle screw insertion is a cornerstone of spinal fixation procedures, requiring sub-millimeter positional accuracy and precise angular alignment to avoid neurovascular injury and ensure biomechanical stability. Conventional freehand techniques are highly operator-dependent and associated with variability in accuracy. Manual computer-aided design (CAD) workflows for patient-specific drill guides can improve precision but remain labor-intensive, requiring 1-2 hours of interactive modeling by trained engineers. Surgical robots represent another solution, offering high precision and intraoperative navigation. However, their clinical adoption is constrained by high capital costs, substantial setup time, and the requirement for a specialized operating-room environment. The aim of this research is to develop a fully automated design pipeline that converts spinal CT data into a 3D-printable, patient-specific surgical guide within minutes. Material and Methods: A standardized nnU-Net segmentation pipeline was established to ensure robust vertebral reconstruction across variable image quality and anatomical deformities. Following segmentation, vertebral surface meshes were generated for subsequent processing.A multi-task Point Transformer network was trained to simultaneously (i) localize optimal screw entry points and (ii) segment guide-plate contact regions on the vertebral surface. This architecture leverages both global anatomical context and local geometric features, enabling accurate and reproducible feature extraction without manual annotation.Candidate screw trajectories were computed using a geometric optimization framework with a multi-objective cost function. The function balanced: Safety (cortical breach avoidance, pedicle wall thickness), Biomechanical criteria (trajectory length, maximal bone purchase), Clinical alignment with established surgical guidelines. Patient-specific guides were automatically generated by conforming a base plate to the segmented vertebral surface and embedding guiding channels along optimized screw trajectories. Results: The mean localization error was 2.90 ± 1.16 mm, with 92.5% of entry points falling within 3 mm of expert-defined references. Contact-region segmentation achieved a mean IoU of 0.742 ± 0.050. Optimized screw trajectories avoided cortical breach in 98.2% of vertebrae, and the mean minimal pedicle wall distance was 2.4 ± 0.8 mm. In vitro validation with 3D-printed templates yielded a mean angular deviation of 1.53 ± 0.76° and a translational deviation of 1.82 ± 0.94 mm compared with planned trajectories. These values are comparable to, or in some cases better than, accuracies reported for commercial robotic systems (1.5-2.0° angular deviation, 1.5-2.5 mm translational error). The automated pipeline completed guide generation in under 3 minutes per vertebra, representing a >95% reduction in design time compared with conventional manual CAD workflows (1-2 hours). Conclusion: This study demonstrates a automatic framework for surgical guide design achieved through the integration of deep learning and geometric optimization. The proposed system eliminates labor-intensive manual CAD steps, standardizes guide quality, and offers a cost-effective alternative to surgical robots without sacrificing accuracy. By integrating deep-learning based feature recognition with geometric optimization, our framework provides efficiency, reproducibility, and precision comparable to robotic systems while maintaining the simplicity and low cost of guide-based approaches.

## A228: Cervical spinal cord stimulation can have promising outcomes: early results of a clinical trial

Harvinder Singh Chhabra

1

, Sunpreet Singh Hanspal

1

, Ankush Gera

1

, Ankit Sharma

1

1

Sri Balaji Action Medical Institute, Delhi, India

Introduction: Despite advancements in management, there have been no effective interventions for restoring voluntary motor control in individuals with SCI. Recent breakthroughs in neuromodulation, particularly spinal cord epidural stimulation (SCES), have shown encouraging potential in facilitating motor recovery and enhancing functional independence in individuals with SCI. This study presents early findings from a clinical trial investigating the effects of SCES when combined with task-specific rehabilitation in individuals with cervical SCI. To our knowledge this is the largest such case series so far. Material and Methods: A total of five participants with chronic tetraplegia (C2, C2-C3, C4, C4, C5 vertebral levels) with AIS-A neurology underwent surgical implantation of a 16-electrode array epidural stimulator, strategically positioned over the cervical spinal cord. Following implantation spinal mapping was done and participants were engaged in an intensive rehabilitation program, incorporating motor retraining and neuromodulation-assisted task-specific training. The study’s primary outcome measures included ISNCSCI upper limb motor scores, spinal cord independence measure (SCIM-III), and capabilities of upper extremity questionnaire (CUE-Q). Results: 1. Improvement in UEMS with Stimulation. oMedian improvement in motor score was found to be from 0 (range 0-16) to 16 (range 0- 21). Functional Independence Gains. oMedian improvement in scores of SCIM-III was found to be from 9 (range 0-12) to 12 (range 0-23). Also, median of CUE-Q scores improved from 0 (range 0-11) to 8 (range 0-47). One out of five participants demonstrated improved ability to perform self-care tasks, such as grooming, feeding, and object manipulation when combined with SCES. Another participant could initiate feeding. 3. Neuroplasticity and Retention of Motor Gains. oNotably, one participant retained functional gains even after stimulation was turned off, indicating activity-dependent neuroplasticity and possible synaptic reorganization in spared neural pathways. Conclusion: These early findings highlight SCES as a transformative intervention when combined with neuro-rehabilitation with the potential to enhance motor function and improve independence in individuals with severe cervical SCI. As research advances, a deeper exploration into tailored SCES protocols, optimal SCES parameters, integration with functional training, and long-term neuroplastic adaptation will be crucial in maximizing its clinical impact. Studies with larger number of participants and randomized controlled trials are required to validate and refine SCES-based rehabilitation outcomes.

## A229: Extended reality-enhanced spine consultations positively impact patient experience

Richard Price

1

, Gabriel Urreolla

1

, Giselle Ghabussi

2

, Jose Castillo

1

, Michael Le

1

, Alan Harris

3

, Safdar Khan

1

1

University of California Davis, Sacramento, United States

2

Lincoln Memorial University, Harrogate, United States

3

University of Louisville, Louisville, United States

Introduction: Spinal disorders, including degenerative disc disease and stenosis, are among the leading causes of global disability. Traditional consultation appointments with patients, which rely on verbal explanations and 2D imaging, can fail to meet the educational needs of patients, particularly those with limited health literacy. When surgical intervention is required, these shortcomings may contribute to increased anxiety, misunderstanding of procedures, and suboptimal surgical outcomes. Augmented reality and virtual reality, collectively termed extended reality (XR), merges digital images with the physical world to create immersive, interactive experiences. XR can be employed to develop 3D models of patient imaging that offers an interactive, patient-centered solution that could enhance comprehension and engagement. Material and Methods: This study evaluated the impact of XR-enhanced consultations on patient understanding, satisfaction, anxiety, and conversion to surgery. Adult patients undergoing evaluation for spinal surgery at a tertiary academic center were enrolled. Each consultation incorporated patient-specific, patient specific 3D spinal models presented through the Surgical Theater ConveyXR platform. Interactive 3D models based on MRI and/or CT were professionally developed with the ConveyXR software. Patients viewed and interacted with the models on a monitor or through a VR headset with the attending surgeon describing the pathology and discussing the planned intervention. Post-consultation surveys assessed patient understanding of their pathology and overall experience with MR. Anxiety related to the procedure was measured using the Amsterdam Preoperative Anxiety and Information Scale (APAIS). Descriptive statistics were calculated using R statistical software. Results: Nineteen patients (mean age 68.9 ± 9.8 years) with surgical pathology were identified by the attending surgical based imaging and consented to participate. Patients reported high comprehension of their condition and treatment (injury: 4.05; location: 4.37; plan: 4.74 on a 5-point scale). Moderate understanding was observed for anatomical models and procedures, though comprehension of complications was lower (2.95). Anxiety scores averaged 16.7/30, with low concern about incisions or inadequate information. Eighty four percent of patient (16/19) proceeded with surgical intervention. Overall, XR consultations were well received, with patients expressing moderate interest in future XR use and reduced desire for second opinions. Ultimately this led to a higher conversion of proceeding with surgery. Conclusion: This proof of concept study demonstrates the potential of XR to improve patient education and engagement in spinal surgery consultations. XR tools enhanced understanding of spinal conditions and treatment plans as well as decreasing anxiety regarding proceeding with spinal surgery. These findings support further evaluation and implemntation of XR tools in spine surgery to improve patient-centered care.

## A230: The use of a custom 3D-printed patient-specific native PEEK implant for complex en bloc spinal sarcoma resection and reconstruction

Shalin Patel

1

, Karthik Tappa

1

, Tyler Hodge

2

, Joseph Fullerton

2

, Devarsh Vyas

2

, Elsa Arribas

1

, Paul Shay

1

, Christopher Nguyen

1

, Justin Bird

1

1

The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, United States

2

3D Systems Inc., Rock Hill, United States

Introduction: Primary spinal sarcomas require complex en bloc resection and reconstruction. Anterior column reconstruction is commonly achieved with vertebral body replacement (VBR), either with titanium or more recently, carbon fiber-reinforced polyetheretherketone (PEEK) implants. However, conventional off-the-shelf VBRs do not account for unique patient anatomy or sacral slope, cannot incorporate vascularized structural autograft to biologically augment fusion, may require additional stabilization to prevent subsidence or implant displacement, and often cause CT/MRI imaging artifacts that make radiation treatment planning and oncologic surveillance challenging. Native PEEK is a biomaterial with a modulus of elasticity similar to cortical bone, is radiolucent, and is now amenable to additive manufacturing allowing for custom 3D printing. To our knowledge, we report the first case of a custom 3D-printed patient-specific native PEEK implant used for complex vertebral reconstruction. Materials and Methods: The patient is a 60-year-old male with a localized rhabdomyosarcoma involving the caudal portion of the L4 vertebral body and a majority of the L5 vertebral body. Staging workup demonstrated no evidence of metastatic disease. The patient was evaluated by our institution’s multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board. Consensus recommendation was to proceed with neoadjuvant systemic therapy, en bloc surgical resection, and adjuvant radiation therapy. The planned resection included the L4 vertebral body caudal to the L4 pedicles, the L4-L5 disc, and the L5 vertebral body. Additionally, the decision was made to preserve the anterior and right lateral vertebral body walls and disc annulus to limit the risk of major neurovascular injury during retroperitoneal dissection and to maintain the anterior longitudinal ligamentous anatomy. A custom, patient-specific native PEEK implant was then designed in conjunction with our engineering and surgical colleagues with the following goals in mind: to maximize anterior column biomechanical support, incorporate a free vascularized fibula autograft to augment biologic fusion, accommodate the patient’s sacral slope, provide secure fixation of the implant to the L4 and S1 vertebral bodies, and to facilitate MRI-based 1) treatment planning for adjuvant radiation therapy and 2) oncologic surveillance. Institutional IRB approval, FDA compassionate use approval, and patient consent was obtained for the use of this implant. Results: A two-stage en bloc resection of the lumbar sarcoma was successfully performed with negative margins. The custom 3D-printed patient-specific native PEEK implant was successfully implanted as planned along with the free vascularized fibula autograft. The patient tolerated surgery and postoperative recovery well. He received adjuvant radiation therapy without issue and routine sarcoma surveillance MR imaging demonstrates the patient has no evidence of disease. Conclusions: This case illustrates the feasibility of using a custom, patient-specific 3D-printed native PEEK implant in complex spinal tumor resection and reconstruction. This novel reconstructive approach highlights the potential of additive manufacturing in improving anatomical fit, optimizing biomechanical performance, facilitating integration of vascularized structural autograft, and limiting imaging artifact for postoperative radiation treatment and oncologic surveillance. Further studies are warranted to assess long-term outcomes in more patients, implant durability, and cost-effectiveness.
