## A231: The validity and educational impact of virtual reality in training spine surgeons: a systematic review

Matthew Cecere

1

, Luke Reda

1,2,3

, Jeremie Larouche

1,2,3

1

Temerty Faculty of Medicine, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

2

Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, Toronto, Canada

3

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Virtual reality (VR) simulation is an emerging educational tool in spine surgery, offering a risk-free, immersive environment for surgical skill development. However, its validity and educational impact in spine-specific training remains to be comprehensively evaluated. We aimed to systematically assess the validity evidence and educational outcomes of VR simulation in training spine surgeons. Material and Methods: A systematic review was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, and SCOPUS to identify English-language studies published between 2000 and 2024. Eligible studies evaluated VR simulation for orthopedic spine surgery training. Studies focusing on patient education, rehabilitation, augmented reality, or non-spine procedures were excluded. Of 7,456 articles screened, 58 underwent full-text review, and 13 met final inclusion criteria. Extracted data included simulator features, spine procedures simulated, participant characteristics, and outcomes related to face, content, and construct validity, as well as performance differentiation and correlation with validated assessment tools. Results: Thirteen studies involving over 300 participants were included. Simulated procedures included pedicle screw placement, spinal decompression, balloon kyphoplasty, and minimally invasive fusions. Eleven studies demonstrated face and content validity, often using Likert-based realism scores and procedural fidelity checklists. Construct validity was supported in 10 studies through performance stratification by training level. Several studies reported statistically significant improvements in post-training performance. For example, one study demonstrated increased OSATS and PPDIS scores in 93% of trainees. While validated metrics such as OSATS and GRS were used, their application was inconsistent across studies. VR-based training improved surgical competency in four core domains: anatomical understanding, purposeful motion, complex coordination, and force/vector-based kinematics. Conclusion: VR simulation demonstrates consistent validity evidence and measurable performance benefits in spine surgery training, particularly among early-stage learners. Its integration into competency-based curricula shows promise, though broader adoption will require greater standardization of assessment tools and validation protocols.

## A232: Descriptive study of artificial intelligence-assisted preoperative evaluation in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis

Sebastian Moreno Herrera

1

, Hugo Vilchis Sámano

2

, Luis Herrera Alcaraz

2

1

Consejo Mexicano de Ortopedia y Traumatología, AO Spine Latin America, Ciudad de Mexico, Mexico,

2

Consejo Mexicano de Ortopedia y Traumatologia, Asociacionismo Mexicana de Cirugia de Columna, Ciudad de Mexico, Mexico,

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis is one of the leading causes of low back pain and neurogenic claudication in the adult population, with a high incidence in patients over 60 years of age. This condition is characterized by a progressive narrowing of the spinal canal and/or intervertebral foramina, which causes compression of the nerve roots with significant functional impairment. Preoperative analysis is a fundamental step in therapeutic decision-making, as it allows for the identification of critical radiological parameters such as the lumbar lordotic angle, pelvic incidence, pelvic tilt, and sagittal imbalance, which are associated with a patient's surgical prognosis. However, these measurements are often manual, require time and specialized expertise, and can present interobserver variability. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as an innovative tool in the healthcare field. The use of AI in preoperative analysis could optimize surgical planning, reduce diagnostic variability, and promote greater accuracy in predicting outcomes. Material and Methods: An observational, descriptive, and cross-sectional study was conducted in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis treated at the Spine Service of the Lomas Verdes Traumatology and Orthopedics Hospital between March and September 2025. Clinical records and digital images (X-rays and MRIs) in DICOM format were collected and processed using artificial intelligence software for the automatic detection of radiological parameters (PI, PT, SS, LL, sagittal balance), and surgical treatment was proposed based on the AI analysis. Clinical variables, radiological findings, and AI performance metrics (analysis time, success rate) were recorded. Results: Thirty-five patients were analyzed (mean age 64.8 ± 8.4 years; 48.6% men). The IA quantified PI 53.8°, PT 23.0°, SS 34.6°, LL 45.2°; a PI-LL mismatch > 10° was observed in 45.7%. Roussouly morphology was: Type 3 48.6%, Type 1 22.9%, Type 2 20.0%, Type 4 8.6%. The most affected levels were L5-S1 (60.0%) and L4-L5 (45.7%); multilevel stenosis occurred in 42.9%. The dominant Schizas was B 48.6%, C 28.6%, D 20.0%, and A 2.9%. In the clinical indication, Decompression was proposed in 15/35 (42.9%) and Decompression + Fusion in 20/35 (57.1%). In the fusion subgroup (n = 20): TLIF 65.0%, ALIF 25.0%, LLIF/OLIF 10.0%; MIS 70.0% vs open 30.0%; TLIF 1 level 75.0% and 2 levels 25.0%. In the exploratory analysis, Decompression showed PI 55.8°, LL 43.8° and |PI-LL| > 10° in 53.3%; Fusion had PI 52.2°, LL 46.3° and |PI-LL| > 10° in 40.0%. Conclusion: AI-assisted preoperative evaluation of lumbar spinal stenosis was feasible and efficient, with a high rate of automatic measurement of spinopelvic parameters and short processing times. Systematic characterization of the sagittal profile (PI, PT, SS, LL, PI-LL) and severity/radiology (Schizas, levels) provided useful information to guide the indication (decompression vs. decompression + fusion) and define the most common management strategy in practice. However, AI should complement, not replace, comprehensive clinical judgment. Prospective studies with larger sample sizes and comparisons with manual measurements are needed to validate the accuracy, reproducibility, and impact on clinical outcomes and surgical planning.

Giuseppe Loggia

, Fedan Avrumova

, Michael Kelly

, Franziska Altorfer

, Maksym Polt

, Jiaqi Zhu

, J. Levi Chazen

, Ek Tsoon Tan

, Darren R. Lebl

1

Hospital for Special Surgery, Balgrist Zurich, New York, United States

Introduction: Robotic-assisted systems have enhanced precision in spinal instrumentation, but their use in decompression procedures remains underexplored. Robotic-assisted muscle-preserving (RAMP) decompression is a novel technique designed to achieve controlled laminar bone removal while preserving paraspinal musculature. ## A234: Comparative analysis of machine learning models for osteoporosis prediction using lumbar CT-derived Hounsfield Units

Akihiko Hiyama

1

, Nobuaki Hattori

1

, Daisuke Sakai

1

, Masahiko Watanabe

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Tokai University School of Medicine, Isehara, Kanagawa, Japan

Introduction: Osteoporosis is a major risk factor for implant loosening, nonunion, and postoperative complications following spine surgery. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is widely used as the standard diagnostic tool; however, its availability is often limited, and degenerative spinal changes can lead to overestimation of bone mineral density (BMD). Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of lumbar CT-derived Hounsfield Unit (HU) values as a surrogate marker for BMD, offering the advantage of opportunistic assessment without additional imaging. Machine learning (ML) techniques have further enabled the development of predictive models that can improve diagnostic accuracy. Nevertheless, a comprehensive comparison of different ML algorithms using CT-derived HU values for osteoporosis screening remains limited. The present study aimed to evaluate and compare the diagnostic performance of seven commonly used ML models using mean HU values from L1-L4 vertebrae in patients undergoing spine surgery. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 172 patients (mean age 71.2 ± 9.8 years; 68 males, 104 females) who underwent both lumbar CT and DXA between 2016 and 2025 prior to spine surgery. Osteoporosis was defined as a T-score < -2.5 at either the lumbar spine or femoral neck. The mean HU value across L1-L4 vertebrae was measured on preoperative CT scans and used as the sole feature to train seven ML models: logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine (SVM), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), naïve Bayes, decision tree, and gradient boosting. Fivefold cross-validation was performed to evaluate accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Optimal HU thresholds for osteoporosis classification were determined using Youden’s Index. Class imbalance was addressed using model-based weighting strategies. Learning curves were constructed to assess model generalizability and risk of overfitting. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: Among the 172 patients, 59 were classified into the osteoporosis group, and 113 into the non-osteoporosis group. The osteoporosis group exhibited significantly lower HU values compared with the non-osteoporosis group (105.1 ± 47.5 vs. 140.1 ± 61.3, p < 0.01). KNN demonstrated the most balanced diagnostic performance, achieving an F1 score of 0.466 ± 0.073, accuracy of 0.714 ± 0.048, and AUC of 0.705 ± 0.046. Logistic regression (AUC = 0.785) and SVM (AUC = 0.745) also showed high discriminatory ability, although with lower recall, while tree-based models such as decision tree and gradient boosting tended to overpredict osteoporosis cases, leading to reduced specificity. Conclusion: ML models utilizing lumbar CT-derived HU values offer a practical and cost-effective approach for opportunistic osteoporosis screening in preoperative spinal fusion surgery settings. Among the evaluated algorithms, KNN achieved the best balance between sensitivity and specificity, suggesting its suitability as a screening tool when DXA is unavailable or impractical. Logistic regression and SVM also demonstrated strong classification performance and may be preferable when higher diagnostic precision is required. These findings support the integration of ML-based HU analysis into routine preoperative assessment protocols to optimize surgical planning and reduce osteoporosis-related complications.

## A235: Dynamic MRI in cervical myelopathy: factors associated with new compression findings

Juan Ignacio Perez Abdala

1

, Gonzalo Kido

1

, Ivan Huespe

1

, Marcelo Gruenberg

1

, Matias Petracchi

1

1

Orthopedic Department, Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires, Argentina

Introduction: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy is the compression of the spinal cord secondary to degenerative narrowing of the canal. Dynamic cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can reveal new compressions that are not evident in neutral cervical MRI. However, there is currently no consensus on the indications for dynamic MRI. This study aimed to identify radiographic and MRI factors associated with increased spinal cord compression when comparing neutral and dynamic MRI. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional study from 2017 to 2024, encompassing all patients with symptoms of spondylotic cervical myelopathy who underwent both dynamic and neutral cervical MRI and cervical X-rays. We collected alignment and stability variables from neutral and dynamic lateral cervical X-rays. Static MRI variables included paraspinal muscle quality, assessed using the Goutallier classification. The canal diameter at C7 and the spinal cord-to-canal ratio (CCR) were measured on axial and sagittal MRI, respectively. Additionally, we recorded disc degeneration according to the Pfirrmann classification, intramedullary T2 high-intensity signal (HIS), facet joint degeneration, and the presence of facet effusion. Anterior and posterior spinal cord compression were graded using the Muhle scale. A cervical compression change was defined as an increase of ≥ 2 grades in the Mulhe classification from neutral to dynamic MRI. Therefore, levels graded as Mulhe 2 or 3 on neutral MRI were not considered suitable for further compression changes. We calculated the proportion of cervical compression changes between neutral and dynamic cervical MRI. Subsequently, we analyzed the risk of cervical compression change based on neutral and dynamic X-rays and regional parameters obtained from neutral cervical MRI. Finally, we compared each cervical level by clustering them into groups with and without compression changes. We performed mixed-effects logistic regression analyses with random intercepts for patients to account for multiple cervical levels per subject. Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated, and model fit was evaluated using likelihood ratio tests. Results: 82 patients were included, and 57 (69.5%) had a cervical compression change at some level. The C4-5 level showed the highest number of changes, which were more frequent in extension than in flexion dynamic MRI. No significant associations were observed between demographic, radiological, or MRI factors and the presence of cervical compression changes. When comparing cervical levels, Pfirrmann grades 4 and 5 were significantly associated with compression changes, with ORs of 5.90 (95% CI: 1.08-32.22; p = 0.041) and 6.97 (95% CI: 1.23-39.45; p = 0.028), respectively. The CCR also showed a strong association (OR = 1.08; 95% CI: 1.04-1.13; p < 0.01). However, we did not find an association with HIS and the degree of facet arthropathy. Conclusion: Dynamic cervical MRI detected new levels of spinal cord compression in nearly 70% of cases. Higher Pfirrmann grades and increased CCR were significantly associated with these changes. These findings underscore the value of dynamic MRI in detecting hidden compression and guiding clinical decision-making in cervical myelopathy.

32

Introduction: The diagnosis of degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is often delayed due to its heterogeneous presentation and the lack of standardized diagnostic and screening criteria. Delayed diagnosis of DCM has significant consequences, including the development of more permanent or severe neurological impairment, incomplete or suboptimal postoperative recovery and increased dependence on caregivers. The AO Spine RECODE-DCM (Research Objectives and Common Data Elements for DCM) initiative identified developing diagnostic criteria as one of the top three research priorities. Objective: The objectives of this study were to (i) develop pragmatic, evidence-based screening criteria to help frontline healthcare providers identify patients at risk for DCM and (ii) define key clinical scenarios in which the application of the screening criteria would be most appropriate. Methods: A three-step process was used to develop screening criteria for DCM. First, two systematic reviews were conducted to determine the frequency and diagnostic accuracy of DCM-related symptoms and signs. Second, an international survey was distributed to a multidisciplinary group of clinicians asking them to rank thirty-nine symptoms and thirty-four signs in terms of their importance for diagnosing DCM. Third, an Expert Working Group engaged in a structured consensus process to refine and rank candidate criteria. The group also identified key clinical scenarios for application through discussion. Results: Fifteen symptoms and twelve signs identified as having high diagnostic utility in an international expert survey were presented to an Expert Working Group for consensus discussion. The group comprised 21 specialists, including neurologists (n = 6), spine surgeons (n = 10), rehabilitation specialists or physiotherapists (n = 4), and a primary care physician (n = 1). Following consensus discussions, the top eight features were consolidated into six core criteria: Clumsy or weak hands, Hoffmann or Tromner sign, Ataxia or imbalance, Numb or tingling hands, Gait abnormalities, and Exaggerated reflexes, forming the mnemonic “CHANGE.” The group recommended applying these criteria to any patient with motor or sensory complaints of the extremities or gait dysfunction, with special emphasis on five clinical scenarios: suspected carpal tunnel syndrome, neck pain with or without cervical radiculopathy, lumbar radiculopathy or spinal stenosis, recurrent falls, and incidental cervical cord compression on MRI. Conclusion: By integrating evidence from the literature with multidisciplinary and geographically diverse expert input, we developed a clinically relevant tool to support frontline healthcare providers in the early recognition of DCM. The screening criteria integrate common symptoms and easily elicited signs of DCM into a simple mnemonic “CHANGE” to support early recognition by non-specialists. By prompting targeted neurological assessment, this tool aims to reduce diagnostic delays and expedite surgical referral when indicated. Widespread adoption of CHANGE has the potential to improve detection, prevent progression, and enhance outcomes for patients with DCM.

## A237: Development of a predictive model for the use of dynamic cervical MRI in patients with degenerative cervical myelopathy

Juan Ignacio Perez Abdala

1

, Gonzalo Kido

1

, ivan huespe

1

, Marcelo Gruenberg

1

, Matias Petracchi

1

1

Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires - Orthopedic Department, Buenos Aires, Argentina

Introduction: The use of dynamic cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for the diagnosis and management of degenerative cervical myelopathy remains a subject of debate. Our objective is to develop a predictive model based on radiographs and static MRI to identify patients who would benefit from dynamic cervical MRI. Materials and Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study from 2017 to 2024, including adults (≥ 18 years) with clinical features of cervical myelopathy and available static and dynamic cervical MRI, as well as lateral radiographs in neutral, flexion, and extension positions. Exclusion criteria for patients were trauma, prior cervical surgery, inflammatory disease, congenital anomalies, or poor-quality imaging. We collected alignment and stability variables from neutral and dynamic lateral cervical radiographs. Static MRI variables included paraspinal muscle quality, assessed using the Goutallier classification. The canal diameter at C7 and the spinal cord-to-canal ratio (CCR%) were measured on axial and sagittal MRI, respectively. Additionally, we recorded disc degeneration according to the Pfirrmann classification, intramedullary T2 high-intensity signal (HIS), facet joint degeneration, and the presence of facet effusion. Anterior and posterior spinal cord compression were graded using the Muhle scale. Cervical levels with anterior or posterior compression ≥ grade 2 on static MRI were excluded from the final analysis. The outcome was new dynamic compression, defined as a ≥ 2-point increase in Muhle grade-both anterior and posterior-between static and dynamic cervical MRI. Predictors included variables explained previously. Each cervical level was analyzed, with clustering accounted for within individual patients. Predictor variables were evaluated using a log-odds analysis. We developed a predictive model and assessed its discrimination and calibration. Results: We included 81 patients, of whom 47% were male, with a mean age of 55.7 years. Among 491 cervical levels from 81 patients, 284 levels without baseline compression were included in the analysis. New dynamic compression was identified in 56 levels (19.7%). Disc degeneration grade and the CCR% showed strong and statistically significant associations with the outcome, with p-values of 0.055 and < 0.001, respectively. After testing multiple predictive models, we selected a final model that incorporated these two variables. Model performance was strong, with an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.896 (95% CI: 0.846-0.946) and good calibration (Brier score: 0.117). To assess clinical utility, we applied a sensitivity-focused probability threshold of 0.19. Using this cutoff, the model achieved 100% sensitivity, 59.0% specificity, and an overall accuracy of 80.3%. Conclusion: The predictive model we developed, based on just two variables from static MRI, demonstrated strong accuracy in identifying patients at risk of dynamic spinal cord compression. This approach allows for the safe reduction of dynamic MRI use in low-risk patients, optimizing resource utilization and enhancing clinical efficiency. Additionally, this tool may assist in identifying previously unrecognized sites of compression and support clinical decision-making.

## A238: Recovery patterns from C5 palsy after anterior cervical decompression and fusion, posterior cervical decompression and fusion, and laminoplasty for degenerative cervical myelopathy: systematic review and meta-analysis of 748 C5 palsy cases

Sathish Muthu

1,2

, Vibhu Krishnan Viswanathan

1,3

, Guna Pradeep

1,4

1

Department of Spine Surgery, Orthopaedic Research Group, Coimbatore, India

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Government Medical College, Karur, India

3

Department of Spine Surgery, Devadoss Multispeciality Hospital, Madurai, India

4

Department of Orthopaedics - Spine Division, Meenakshi Mission Hospital, Madurai, India

Introduction: Despite the favorable postoperative prognosis of C5 palsy (C5P), a certain proportion of these patients have less satisfactory outcomes. The current systematic review and meta-analysis thus aimed to comprehensively evaluate existing literature and identify the onset, recovery patterns, and outcomes of C5P following diverse surgical approaches. Materials and Methods: Five different databases (Google Scholar, Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library) were thoroughly searched for relevant literature on October 15, 2024. Studies reporting on incidences of C5P following surgery for degenerative cervical conditions with recovery data published until 2024 were scrutinized. Narrative or systematic reviews, opinions, letters to the editor, and manuscripts published in non-English languages were excluded. Results: A total of 30 articles involving 8,116 patients who underwent undergoing surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy with 748 reported C5P cases were included for analysis. The overall time to palsy reported in the included studies was 3 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.56-3.60). Palsy occurred earliest with anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) at 2 days (95% CI, 0.35-4.54), followed by laminoplasty (LP) at 3.2 days (95% CI, 2.02-4.34) and posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF) at 3.6 days (95% CI, 2.81-4.37). Patients with palsy showed improved recovery with time. At the 1-year follow-up, the reported recovery rates were 100%, 52.9%, and 50% for ACDF, LP, and PCDF, respectively. Conclusions: C5P demonstrated a delayed presentation, with mean onset of 3 days after surgery, which can range from 2 days for ACDF to 3.6 days for PDCF. Recovery improved progressively with time and varied for different surgical procedures, with ACDF showing the best recovery and PDCF for cervical myelopathy showing the poorest recovery.

## A240: Performance on tandem gait does not predict the presence of cervical myelopathy or stenosis

Brody Fitzpatrick

1

, Jakub Ratkowski

1

, Nathaniel Luketich

1

, Kyle Holmberg

1

, Julio Rodriguez Jr.

1

, Felicity Fisk

1

, Jonathan Karnes

1

, Scott Daffner

1

, John France

1

1

West Virginia University, Morgantown, United States

Introduction: The diagnosis of degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is based on the combination of subjective complaints and clinical findings in the setting of radiographically-confirmed cervical stenosis. Patients often report a history of gait disturbance, which is a major component of the Nurick and Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) scales. These scales, however, are limited by the subjectivity of their assessments. Clinically, the tandem gait test is utilized to evaluate gait disturbance; however, there is limited evidence in its ability to predict the presence of myelopathy. The purpose of this study is to determine whether performance on a graded 10-step tandem gait test predicts the presence of myelopathy. Material and Methods: Patients referred to our spine clinic for evaluation of cervical pathology over a six-week period were prospectively enrolled. Inclusion criteria were age ≥ 18 and cervical MRI obtained within two years of the clinic visit date. Exclusion criteria included alternative pathology contributing to gait disturbance, chronic non-ambulators, prior cervical surgery, and inadequate quality of MRI precluding accurate assessment of cervical stenosis. Data collected included patient demographics, medical history, subjective symptoms, and physical examination. Our primary and secondary outcomes were the correlations between performance on tandem gait and: 1) signs and symptoms of myelopathy, 2) Nurick and JOA classifications, and 3) severity of cervical stenosis on MRI. All patients completed a standardized 10-step tandem gait assessment, which was performed twice. To complete the assessment, patients ambulated 10 steps in a heel-to-toe fashion. The number of steps completed before the first misstep was counted. The test with the higher score was collected and graded using a 0-4 scale (see Figure). Severity of cervical stenosis on MRI was graded using the Kang scale. Results: Performance on tandem gait was inversely correlated with age (p < 0.0001), history of falls (p = 0.0059), balance/gait disturbance (p < .0001), and hyperreflexia (p = .0278). Performance on tandem gait otherwise did not correlate with other signs or symptoms of DCM. Performance on tandem gait was correlated with JOA and inversely correlated with Nurick classifications (p < 0.0001 and p = .0009, respectively). However, it was not correlated with severity of cervical stenosis. Conclusion: In this study, a standardized 10-step tandem gait test was correlated with Nurick and JOA, validating its utility as a clinical screening tool. Tandem gait was correlated with history of falls, balance/gait disturbance, and hyperreflexia, but was not correlated with signs or symptoms of DCM or degree of radiographic stenosis. Notably, patient age may be a confounding factor when utilizing tandem gait in the assessment of DCM. The utility of tandem gait in predicting the presence of DCM remains controversial. Although a useful objective screening tool for DCM, definitive diagnosis continues to require a comprehensive assessment of history, physical examination, and imaging studies.

## A241: A retrospective comparative study of unilateral biportal endoscopy versus anterior cervical decompression and fusion for cervical spondylotic radiculopathy: an analysis of 166 cases

Hu Dong

1

1

Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Surgical treatment for cervical spondylotic radiculopathy (CSR) focuses on nerve root decompression. Anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) remains the gold standard, while unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) surgery is an emerging minimally invasive technique whose efficacy requires further evidence. This study retrospectively compares perioperative indicators and early clinical outcomes between UBE and ACDF for CSR to inform clinical decision-making. Material and Methods: Data from patients who underwent surgery for CSR between January 2023 and August 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Complications in the ACDF group included 2 cases of dysphagia and 1 case of symptomatic cage subsidence; the UBE group had 1 minor intraoperative dural tear (resolved with conservative treatment) and no severe neurovascular injuries. Conclusion: Both UBE and ACDF provide excellent pain relief and neurological recovery. UBE demonstrates advantages including less bleeding, shorter hospitalization, and effective preservation of cervical motion. Long-term outcomes and adjacent segment degeneration require further follow-up.

## A242: Safety and effectiveness of anterior corpectomy surgery for cervical myelopathy due to the ossification of posterior longitudinal ligaments

Soobin Im

1

, Je Hoon Jeong

1

, Jeng Hoon Kang

1

1

Soonchuhyang University Bucheon Hospital, Bucheon, South Korea

Purpose: Anterior decompression and reconstruction is one of the standard surgical treatments for cervical OPLL. “Floating the ossified PLL” is the traditional method, which is described in the textbook for the anterior decompression. However, the detailed method was not described and we encounter the postoperative neurologic aggravation despite using the “floating method” with maximum attention during the decompression. This disastrous cord injury happens in especially severe OPLL cases. The “floating” method can not radically eliminate the pressure on the cord during decompression. Another fact is that even if we fully decompress the surrounding structure of the main compressing lesion, the ossified PLL will not easily float because of its thickness. This presentation will describe the typical pattern of ossified PLL and the detailed decompression method of ossified PLL. The presentation also introduces the technical tips for the more safe method of lifting PLL up method for anterior OPLL surgery. Materials and Methods: Between 2003 and 2024, 245 patients with cervical OPLL underwent anterior corpectomy and reconstruction using these technical tips. Drill the posterior part of the vertebrae until the soft part of the ventral cord is exposed. Usually the main compressing lesion forms a cruciate shape at the ventral surface of the dura. The most compressive part is usually located at the level of the bony endplate and disc level. Technical Tip: To prevent postoperative neurological aggravation, the pressure on the ossified PLL should be eliminated during decompression with a drill. After exposure of the ossified PLL by drilling the posterior part of the vertebra, drilling on the ossified PLL of the critical area will put pressure on the cord, which is very prone to being damaged. In order to eliminate the pressure on the cord, drilling of the PLL should be done by lifting it up and separating it from the cord. The bent sonopet tip can be used for undermining the PLL. The sharp tip of the hook will be able to hook up the hard edge of the main compressing lesion and detach from the cord. If we elevate the edge of OPLL, the CSF spreads behind OPLL. This makes safe drilling and can avoid disastrous cord damage. As the operator needs both hands to hold the drill and arachnoid knife, suction or irrigation should be done with assistance. Results: Among the 245 corpectomy patients with OPLL, one patient aggravated neurologically due to the fault of implant installation, not by this lifting ossified PLL up method just after the operation. 24 cases (10%) of overt CSF leakage on the operative field were managed by sealant application or direct suture. If CSF came out through the operative wound through the skin, the lumbar drain was inserted postoperatively. Lumbar drain is maintained for 5∼7 days. If the skin integrity is well maintained, we don’t insert a lumbar drain even if the CSF collection is detected in the subcutaneous tissue. Conclusion: To prevent neurological aggravation in OPLL surgery, we have to understand the detailed structure of ossified PLL. Anterior corpecomy provides a wide and clear visualization. Combining with the lifting PLL method, anterior cervical corpectomy is an effective and safe tool for the myelopathy due to cervical OPLL.

## A243: Adverse impact of frailty on postoperative outcomes of cervical laminoplasty

Ataollah Shahbandi

1

, Pegah Ghamasaee

1

, Abdul Mounnem Yassin Kassab

1

, Saman Shabani

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, United States

Introduction: As the global population ages, frailty is increasingly acknowledged as a crucial factor in predicting health outcomes in the elderly population. Although prior studies have examined the impact of frailty on surgeries for degenerative cervical spine conditions, these studies often involved heterogeneous sample populations regarding surgical approaches. Resultantly, there is a lack of large database studies focusing on cervical laminoplasty. This study aimed to examine the impact of frailty and its severity on 30-day postoperative outcomes after cervical laminoplasty. Material and Methods: This study examined the data from the 2007-2022 American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program. Patients who underwent cervical laminoplasty were queried and grouped according to the modified Frailty Index (mFI-5) into four categories: non-frail, pre-frail, frail, and severely frail. The primary outcome was the occurrence of at least one complication within 30 days, excluding blood transfusions. Secondary outcomes were major and minor complication rates, readmission rates, and the length of hospital stay. Results: A total of 2,250 patients were included, categorized as 829 non-frail, 873 pre-frail, 474 frail, and 74 severely frail patients. Frail patients (7.8%, p = 0.049) and severely frail patients (24.3%, p < 0.001) experienced at least one complication (excluding blood transfusions) significantly more frequently compared to non-frail patients (4.9%). Severely frail patients experienced major complications (18.9% versus 2.6%, p < 0.001) and minor complications (14.9% versus 4.5%, p = 0.001) at significantly higher rates than those observed in non-frail patients. Severely frail patients also showed a significantly increased occurrence of pneumonia (4.1% versus 0.5%, p = 0.014), urinary tract infections (5.4% versus 0.8%, p = 0.009), postoperative renal insufficiency (1.4% versus 0%, p = 0.031), postoperative dialysis (2.7% versus 0%, p = 0.007), vein thrombosis requiring therapy (4.1% versus 0.4%, p = 0.009), and cardiac arrest requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation (2.7% versus 0.2%, p = 0.036) compared to non-frail patients. Furthermore, frail patients (5.8%, p = 0.039) and those who were severely frail (12.3%, p = 0.002) had significantly higher readmission rates compared to non-frail patients (3.1%). The presence of frailty (23.7%, p < 0.001) and severe frailty (46.6%, p < 0.001) were associated with a significantly increased risk of extended hospitalization compared to non-frail patients (11.2%). After controlling for confounders, frailty (odds ratio [OR] 1.661, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.122-2.463; P = 0.011) and severe frailty (OR 4.328, 95% CI 2.271-8.253; p < 0.001) were independently associated with prolonged hospitalization. Additionally, severe frailty was independently correlated with a heightened risk of readmission (OR 3.976, 95% CI 1.392-10.959; p = 0.008), increased overall complication rates (OR 2.831, 95% CI 1.282-6.12; p = 0.009), and a higher likelihood of experiencing at least one major complication (OR 4.879, 95% CI 1.947-12.229; p = 0.001). Conclusion: Frailty and its severity may be associated with a higher rate of unfavorable perioperative outcomes after cervical laminoplasty. As a result, implementing preoperative strategies such as strict serum glucose control and diligent management of other existing comorbidities might help lower surgical risks and associated costs.

## A244: More than a spinal injury: the clinical significance of sternal fractures in thoracic spine trauma - A retrospective analysis of 4th column fractures of the spine

Josina Straub

1

, Melanie Ardelt

2

, Jan Reinhard

3

, Fabian Katzhammer

1

, Addisu Mesfin

4

, Jonas Krueckel

1

, Volker Alt

1

, Daniel Popp

1

, Siegmund Lang

1

1

University Hospital Regensburg, Department for trauma surgery, Regensburg, Germany

2

Division of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, University Hospital Krems, Krems, Austria

3

Clinic of Orthopaedics, University Hospital Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany

4

Strong Memorial Hospital, University of Rochester Orthopaedics, , Rochester, United States

Introduction: The thoracic spine and sternum are pivotal for the thoracic stability. High-energy trauma can compromise both, resulting in complex injury patterns. However, the prevalence and associated factors of concurrent thoracic spinal and sternal fractures remain poorly defined. This study aimed to assess the prevalence, the associated factors and risk factors for increased mortality of combined thoracic spine and sternal fractures. Material and Methods: Patients admitted to our level 1 trauma centre between 2006 and 2022 with thoracic vertebral fractures were retrospectively analysed and stratified into two cohorts based on the presence or absence of a concurrent sternal fracture. Results: Overall, N = 366 patients were included: N = 311 with isolated thoracic vertebral fracture and N = 55 with concomitant sternal fracture (4th column fractures). In the total cohort, 76.2% of patients were male, with a mean age of 48.7 years and a mean Injury Severity Score of 32.6. In the group with combined sternal fracture, 72.7% of spinal fractures were classified as AO Spine Type A, 5.5% as AO Spine Type B and 21.8% as AO Spine Type C. The overall in-hospital mortality was 16.7%, with 18.0% of deaths occurring in patients with sternal fracture (OR = 1.24). Spinal cord injury was more frequently observed in patients with sternal fracture (24% vs. 14.4%). Intubation duration was significantly longer in patients with sternal fracture (10.7 ± 11.7 vs. 7.2 ± 9.9 days; p = 0.018), while hospital length of stay did not differ significantly (22.6±16.3 with sternal fracture vs. 20.9 ± 18.3 without; p = 0.526). Mortality was significantly higher in patients with thoracoabdominal injuries (p = 0.044) and those older than 65 years (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Concomitant sternal fractures in case of thoracic spine trauma are markers of high-energy mechanisms and are significantly associated with luxation fractures and longer intubation times. Frequent coexistence of thoracoabdominal injuries underscores the complexity of these trauma cases, contributing to increased morbidity and mortality, particularly in elderly patients. These findings highlight the need for heightened clinical vigilance and a multidisciplinary approach in managing patients with combined thoracic spine and sternal injuries.

## A245: Spinopelvic dissociation in polytrauma: challenges, complications and the role of triangular fixation

Alicia Collado Gosalvez

1

, Rafael Luque

2

, Eduardo Gómez

1

, Jose Luis Perez Gonzalez

1

, Pedro Lalueza

1

, Ignacio Dominguez

1

1

Hospital Clínico San Carlos, Madrid, Spain

2

Hospital Clinico San Carlos, Madrid, Spain

Introduction: Spinopelvic dissociations (SD) are high-energy injuries with unstable fracture patterns that invariably require surgical fixation. These lesions are associated with severe morbidity and often present with neurological impairment. They represent a major challenge for trauma centers in terms of surgical decision-making and postoperative management. The aim of this study was to analyze our institutional experience in the surgical treatment of SD and to discuss the outcomes of individualized fixation strategies aimed at restoring mechanical stability. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of polytrauma patients with SD admitted to a Level I trauma center between 2020 and 2024, with a minimum follow-up of 12 months. Data collected included demographics, mechanism of injury, associated lesions, neurological status, time to surgery, ICU and hospital stay, and complications. Fractures were classified according to Roy-Camille and AO/OTA systems. Surgical variables included number of vertebrae instrumented, use of iliac or transiliac-transsacral screws (TTS), decompression, and open versus percutaneous approach. Follow-up data included time to weight-bearing, fracture consolidation, neurological sequelae, and hardware removal. Results: Ten patients were included (median age 38.5). The predominant mechanism was fall from height (9/10). Associated injuries included pneumothorax (40%), intra-abdominal hematoma (1), traumatic brain injury (3), lower-limb fractures (70%), upper-limb fractures (3), and spinal fractures (4). Fracture classification revealed Roy-Camille type II (4) and III (3). AO type C3 was seen in 6 patients and type B3 in 4. Neurological deficit was presented in 70%, all involving sacral root compromise. The median number of instrumented vertebrae was 3; patients with associated spinal fractures required longer constructs (6-10 levels). Triangular fixation with TTS was achieved in 4 patients; lumbopelvic fixation with iliac or S2AI screws was used in 90%. A fully percutaneous approach was feasible in 3 cases, while decompression was performed in 4 patients. Mean ICU stay was 10.9 days, with a mean total hospital stay of 76 days. The most frequent postoperative complication was surgical site infection (50%). No correlation was found between infection rate and open surgery. Weight-bearing was initiated at a mean of 52 days, delayed in patients with lower-limb fractures. Radiographic consolidation was achieved in 7 cases. Hardware removal was performed in 2 patients, both at 20 weeks postoperatively. At final follow-up, outcomes were heterogeneous. 4 patients achieved full recovery. Three patients remained unable to return to work due to pain (VAS 3-4) or sphincter dysfunction. Overall, urinary incontinence persisted in 4 patients, and moderate-to-severe disability was observed in 5. Conclusion: The surgical management of SD remains complex due to their heterogeneous fracture patterns and frequent association with pelvic injuries. Early restoration of vertical and horizontal stability is essential, with triangular fixation representing the most standardized approach. However, achieving triangular constructs is not always feasible, as shown in our cohort (4/10), due to anatomical and technical limitations. These patients present high morbidity, consume considerable resources, and experience frequent complications. Early and appropriate fixation may help reduce these burdens. Development of standardized treatment algorithms is warranted to guide surgical decision-making, while maintaining flexibility for individualized strategies.

## A246: Management of AO Classification Type B2 thoracolumbar fractures: results of classic open arthrodesis versus percutaneous posterior fixation

Juan José Zamorano

1

, José Gengler Prieto

1

, Esteban Peña

1

, Nicolas Wolff hoepke

1

, Ignacio Cirillo

1

, Iris Castillo

1

, Marcos Gimbernat

1

, Ignacio Farías

1

, Carlos Tapia

1

1

Hospital del Trabajador, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures represent one of the most common spinal injuries, with the majority located at the thoracolumbar junction (T10-L2). While the therapeutic consensus for patients with neurological deficits is decompression and instrumented fixation, the management of fractures without neurological compromise remains a topic of debate. Among these, flexion-distraction fractures (FDI), classified by AO as type B, account for up to 15% of cases and are considered intrinsically unstable. In particular, B2 injuries, which are predominantly ligamentous, exhibit a poor potential for spontaneous consolidation, historically motivating the recommendation for instrumented arthrodesis. In recent decades, percutaneous fixation has emerged as an attractive alternative to open surgery, offering advantages such as reduced tissue dissection, decreased intraoperative bleeding, less postoperative pain, and lower infection rates. This study presents a change in surgical technique for patients with AO classification type B2 thoracolumbar fractures, showing the results of patients treated with percutaneous posterior fixation compared to those operated on using classic posterior arthrodesis in the same workers' compensation hospital. Material and Methods: A clinical record and imaging analysis were performed on 40 patients with AO classification type B2 thoracolumbar fractures treated in a workers' compensation hospital between 2023 and 2025, with 20 patients treated using classic open posterior arthrodesis and 20 patients treated with percutaneous posterior technique. Results were analyzed for operative time, intraoperative bleeding, return to work, and reoperation rates with a follow-up of 9 months. Results: A total of 40 cases of AO classification type B2 thoracolumbar fractures were recorded, with 20 managed via percutaneous posterior approach (Group A) and 20 cases via open posterior arthrodesis (Group B). The average intraoperative bleeding was 46.75 ml in Group A and 234 ml in Group B. The average operative time was 121 minutes in Group A and 166 minutes in Group B. The number of reoperations in Group A was 4 patients, while in Group B it was 8 patients. Return to work was limited in both groups due to comorbid conditions present at the time of the accident. Conclusion: The treatment via percutaneous posterior approach presents shorter surgical times, less intraoperative bleeding, and lower reoperation rates, yielding favorable results for patients. No significant differences were demonstrated regarding return to work, given the high variability due to concomitant injuries at the time of the accident. The percutaneous posterior approach is an optimal therapeutic option, with favorable outcomes compared to the classic open posterior arthrodesis technique. This study aims to provide information for future research regarding the surgical management of this type of fracture.

## A247: Can we all use the OF score? A validation study in a Chilean cohort

Oscar Bravo

1

, Lucas Rifo

1

, Joaquín Cortés

1

, Dusan Ancic

1

, Vicente Jimenez

2

, Alvaro Silva González

1,2

, Andres Lisoni

1,2

1

Hospital Clínico de la Fuerza Aérea de Chile, Santiago, Chile

2

Clinica Alemana de Santiago, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVF) are a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and reduced quality of life with rising incidence due to population aging. In Chile, this represents a growing clinical and public health challenge. Despite their impact, there are no validated predictive tools for treatment selection in the Chilean population. The Osteoporotic Fracture Score (OFS) has been proposed to guide management, but its external validity remains uncertain. Our objective is to assess the utility of the OFS in predicting therapeutic strategies, particularly its ability to identify patients requiring surgical management. Material and Methods: We performed a single-center, retrospective observational study approved by the institutional ethics board. Patients > 50 years with OVF between 2021-2025 were included. The follow up period was 3 to 60 months, with a mean of 13.9 months. They were classified according to treatment strategy (conservative vs surgical) and OFS. Univariate logistic regression was used to evaluate associations with surgical treatment. The discriminative ability of the OFS and a modified version was tested using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, with calculation of area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. Results: Eighty-four patients were included. Most (86.9%) received conservative management, while 13.1% underwent surgery. Pain relief rates exceeded 90% according to the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) in the conservative treatment group, despite their high OFS. Both OFS and modified OFS were significantly associated with surgical treatment (OR 1.96; 95% CI: 1.39-3.12, and OR 2.05; 95% CI: 1.42-3.43; both p < 0.001). ROC analysis showed good discriminative capacity: for the OFS, AUC was 0.87 with cut-off > 6.5 yielding sensitivity 72.7%, specificity 83.6%, and accuracy 82.1%. For the modified OFS, AUC was 0.88, with cut-off > 5.5 yielding sensitivity 90.9%, specificity 71.2%, and accuracy 73.8%. Conclusion: Findings show a strong institutional preference for conservative treatment, even in patients with high OFS values suggesting surgery. Despite this, pain relief was good to excellent, supporting the effectiveness of conservative approaches in selected patients. While the OFS demonstrated value in stratifying patients, it failed to reflect the complexity of clinical decision-making in our setting. Important variables such as frailty, comorbidities, functional demands, bone quality, and patient preferences likely influence outcomes and should be incorporated into future predictive models. Adjusting cut-off points or integrating clinical modifiers may improve the tool’s applicability across diverse populations. In this Chilean cohort, the OFS algorithm did not demonstrate sufficient reliability as a stand-alone tool for identifying patients requiring surgical management of OVF. Refinement of predictive systems through incorporation of clinical and patient-centered variables is needed to optimize individualized treatment strategies.

## A248: Clinical comparation of two surgical methods in the treatment of re-fracture of the cemented vertebrae: re-percutaneous vertebroplasty or posterior fixation?

Chaoyuan Ge

1

, Wenlong Yang

1

, Zhengwei Xu

1

1

Xi'an Honghui Hospital, Xi'an, China

Introduction: Percutaneous vertebral augmentation has been widely used for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (OVCF) in the elderly. However, re-fracture or re-collapse of the cemented vertebrae after initial surgery are common. Currently, surgical treatment for re-fracture of the cement vertebrae mainly includes re-percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) or posterior open reduction, fixation and fusion using cement augmented screws (CAS), and which surgery is better is still controversial. This study aims to compare the efficacy of the two surgical methods in treatment of cement vertebral re-fracture after percutaneous vertebral augmentation. Material and Methods: The clinical data of patients with cemented vertebral refracture after percutaneous vertebral augmentation treated with re-PVP or CAS in our hospital from January 2020 to January 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. A total of 50 patients with OVCF were included in the study, including 20 males and 30 females, aged 68-82 years [(72.6 ± 5.8) years]. All patients presented with low back pain and varying degrees of local kyphosis. The distribution of cemented vertebrae: T10 in 1 case, T11 in 10 cases, T12 in 18 cases, L1 in 20 cases, and L2 in 1 case. According to the different surgical methods, they were divided into the re-PVP group (n = 28 cases) under local anesthesia and the CAS group (n = 22 cases) under general anesthesia. The clinical efficacy indicators including the visual analogue scale (VAS) and Oswestry disability index (ODI) before surgery, 6 days and 6 months after surgery and at the last follow-up were recorded and compared between the two groups. The imaging indicators including the vertebral body index (VBI), the kyphosis angle (KA) of the injured vertebra and the local kyphosis Cobb angle were also recorded. The intraoperative complications and the occurrence of new vertebral fractures during the follow-up period were recorded between the two groups. Results: There was no statistically significant difference in the preoperative general information between the two groups (p > 0.05). All patients successfully completed the operation. There were 2 cases of asymptomatic bone cement leakage in the re-PVP group and 1 case of asymptomatic bone cement leakage in the CAS group. No serious complications such as nerve or blood vessel injury occurred in both groups. The clinical efficacy indicators and imaging indicators of the two groups after surgery and during the follow-up period were significantly improved compared with those before surgery (p < 0.05). In terms of clinical efficacy indicators, the VAS scores of the patients in the re-PVP group improved better than those in the CAS group 6 days after surgery (p < 0.05), but there was no statistically significant difference at 6 months after surgery and at the last follow-up (p > 0.05); There was no statistically significant difference in ODI after surgery and during the follow-up period; in terms of imaging indicators, both the re-PVP group and the CAS group could significantly improve the height of the injured vertebra and correct local kyphosis. There was no statistically significant difference in VBI, KA and local Cobb of kyphosis between the two groups after surgery and during the follow-up period (p > 0.05). During the follow-up period, no adjacent vertebral body or other vertebral body fractures occurred in both groups. Conclusion: For OVCF patients with bone cemented vertebral refracture after percutaneous vertebral augmentation, re-PVP or posterior open reduction, fixation and fusion using CAS can effectively relieve low back pain, improve quality of life, effectively restore the height of the injured vertebra and correct local kyphosis. Compared with CAS, re-PVP has better analgesic effect in the early stage (1 week after surgery) due to its minimally invasive characteristics, but there is no difference in analgesic effect between the two groups in the later stage.

## A249: Surgical management of osteoporotic vertebral fractures: current techniques, indications, and knowledge gaps

University del Desarrollo, Clinica Alemana de Santiago, Chile, Santiago, Chile

Emergency Hospital, Iasi, Romania, Iasi, Romania,

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology, Inselspital, University Hospital, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland, Bern, Switzerland

Department of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, Assiut University, Assiut, Egypt, Assiut, Egypt

Department of Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine, Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA, Seattle, United States,

Neurosurgery Division, Department of Neurology, State University of Campinas, Campinas-Sao Paulo, Brazil, Sao Paulo, Brazil

Center for Spinal and Scoliosis Surgery, Malteser Waldkrankenhaus St. Marien Erlangen, Erlangen, Germany, Erlangen, Germany

18

Unfallchirurgie und Orthopädie, München Klinik Harlaching, Germany, München, Germany

19

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Rothman Institute, Thomas Jefferson University Hospital, Philadelphia, PA, USA, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVF) represent the most frequent fragility fractures worldwide and pose major clinical and socioeconomic challenges. Their management differs substantially from traumatic fractures in younger patients due to poor bone quality, higher comorbidity burden, and lack of universally accepted treatment guidelines. Recent developments, including the AO Spine-DGOU Osteoporotic Fracture (OF) classification and OF score, have provided a framework for decision-making. This review summarizes current surgical techniques for thoracic and lumbar OVF, highlights their indications and limitations, and outlines key knowledge gaps. Materials and Methods: A narrative review was performed through a non-systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, complemented by manual screening of reference lists. Both prospective and retrospective studies focusing on surgical techniques for OVF were included, while case reports and cadaveric studies were excluded. Selection was guided by critical appraisal and author expertise. Results: Minimally invasive cement augmentation techniques, such as vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty, are recommended for less severe OVF (OF-1 to OF-3), with kyphoplasty showing superior vertebral height restoration and reduced cement leakage. Short segmental fixation (SSF) is suitable for moderately unstable fractures but carries a higher risk of implant failure unless combined with screw or vertebral augmentation. Long segmental fixation (LSF) offers greater stability in severe cases (OF-4), particularly in the mid-thoracic spine, but increases surgical invasiveness and the risk of adjacent segment disease. Pedicle screw augmentation significantly enhances implant stability in osteoporotic bone. Hybrid stabilization, combining posterior instrumentation with vertebral augmentation, provides promising mid-term results, reducing implant failure with less invasiveness than combined anterior-posterior (AP) fusion. AP surgery remains the most robust option for highly unstable or collapsed fractures with neurological deficits or rigid kyphosis but is often limited by surgical morbidity in elderly or frail patients. Recent minimally invasive AP approaches show potential to expand indications. Conclusion: Surgical management of OVF requires tailored decision-making that balances mechanical stability, invasiveness, and patient frailty. Cement augmentation is appropriate for less severe fractures, while SSF and LSF are reserved for unstable patterns depending on severity and location. Screw augmentation improves fixation strength, and hybrid stabilization represents a less invasive alternative to combined AP surgery with comparable outcomes. Combined AP reconstruction remains the gold standard for highly unstable fractures but should be reserved for select patients due to its invasiveness. Despite recent advances, evidence gaps remain regarding optimal management of OF-4 fractures, the role of prophylactic augmentation, and the necessity of sagittal balance restoration in elderly patients. Future research should aim to refine treatment algorithms and align global practice standards.

## A250: A new classification of Kummell disease based on imaging features and clinical manifestations of 168 cases

Chaoyuan Ge

1

, Wenlong Yang

1

, Zhengwei Xu

1

1

Xi'an Honghui Hospital, Xi'an, China

Introduction: The aim of this study is to propose a new system for classifying Kummell disease and evaluates its feasibility for guiding clinical treatment. Material and Methods: A retrospective study of 168 cases of Kummell disease with complete follow-up data was conducted at our institute from January 2019 to December 2022. Patients were divided into types I-V based on a combination of clinical manifestations and different morphological changes detected by imaging. Type I is characterized by bone non-union imaging; percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) is the primary treatment option for this basic imaging morphological change in Kummell disease. Type II is characterized by imaging findings indicating instability; posterior fixation and fusion is the primary treatment option. Type III is characterized by imaging findings indicating spinal stenosis, accompanied by symptoms of neurological damage; the primary treatment option is posterior decompression fixation and fusion. Type IV is characterized by imaging showing kyphosis. These patients exhibit malunion, often with a kyphotic angle ≥ 30°, and no change in kyphotic angle as assessed by dynamic radiography; the primary treatment option is posterior osteotomy, fixation, and fusion. Type V is characterized by a combination of 3 or 4 of the above imaging signs; the treatment provided is related to the specific types responsible. Treatment outcomes were evaluated based on postoperative visual analogue scale (VAS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores. During the follow-up period, we observed whether the damaged vertebra exhibited compression or local secondary kyphosis and whether neurological function improved in patients accompanying with neurological symptoms. Results: All patient received average 38.4 ± 7.8 months of follow-up care. Patients of each type had statistically significant improvements in postoperative VAS and ODI scores compared with preoperative scores. The height of the damaged vertebra in all patients with Kummell disease and the local kyphotic angle of patients with kyphosis improved postoperatively. During the follow-up period, 19 patients (11.3%) exhibited compression of the damaged vertebra or local secondary kyphotic deformity. At the final follow-up of patients with neurological deficits, the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) grades of D in 3 patients and E in 12 patients were seen postoperatively, compared with preoperative ASIA grades of C in 12 patients and D in 3 patients. Conclusion: This study shows that this new classification of Kummell disease into types I-V can effectively guide clinical treatment.

## A251: Compression rate progression of osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture in conservative treatment

Jaewan Soh

1

, Jae Chul Lee

2

1

Hanyang University Guri Hospital, College of Medicine,, Guri, South Korea

2

Soonchunhyang University Seoul Hospital, College of Medicine,, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: When osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures (OVCF) occur, the purpose of treatment is to reduce pain and prevent progression of compression, and many results have been reported. In OVCF, vertebral body compression often progressed. We analyzed whether there were any factors affecting the progression of the compression rate and also investigated the period when the compression rate progressed the most, and analyzed the correlation with clinical outcomes. Material and Methods: One hundred twenty-two patients with OVCF, followed for more than six months, were included. Factors such as age, gender, fracture level, bone mineral density (BMD), body mass index (BMI), osteoporosis medication, initial compression rate, fracture location, and pelvic incidence were assessed. Compression rates were measured initially and at 1, 2, 3, and 6 months. The correlation between these factors and compression rate progression of more than 50% was analyzed using univariate and multivariable Cox regression analysis. Compression rate progression over time was evaluated using a repeated measures general linear model, and clinical outcomes were assessed via paired t-test. Results: Univariate analysis showed that an initial compression rate of less than 50% was significantly associated with progression (p = 0.001). Multivariable Cox regression confirmed this association (p = 0.013, Hazard ratio = 3.018, 95% Confidence Interval 1.265-7.200). The most significant compression rate progression occurred within the first month of follow-up (p = 0.038). At the final follow-up, both VAS for back pain (p = 0.009) and ODI (p = 0.026) were significantly higher in the compression rate progression group. Conclusion: An initial compression rate of less than 30% was associated with a higher correlation of compression rate progression, particularly within the first month after injury. Compression rate progression was correlated with poorer clinical outcomes in terms of pain and quality of life.

## A252: Impact of paravertebral sarcopenia on long-term survival and functional recovery after percutaneous kyphoplasty in older adults with osteoporotic thoracolumbar compression fractures: a prospective dual-center cohort study

Wenjie Wu

1

, Xiaojing Si

1

, Junxiong Cao

1

, Boxing Wang

1

, Chuanqi Zou

1

1

The People's Hospital of Banan District, Chongqing, China

Introduction: Percutaneous kyphoplasty (PKP) is a widely used minimally invasive procedure for osteoporotic thoracolumbar compression fractures (OTLCF). While effective, a subset of elderly patients continues to experience poor functional recovery and elevated mortality. Sarcopenia, particularly of the paravertebral muscles-key stabilizers of the spine-may be a critical yet understudied predictor of long-term outcomes. This study investigates whether pre-operative paravertebral sarcopenia independently predicts 12-month all-cause mortality and functional recovery after PKP. Material and Methods: A prospective, non-randomized, observational cohort study was conducted across two centers in Chongqing, China. We enrolled 200 patients aged ≥ 65 years with acute or subacute single-level OTLCF (T10-L2) scheduled for PKP. Sex-specific thresholds were applied to define sarcopenia. Primary outcome was 12-month all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included pain intensity (VAS) and functional disability (ODI) assessed at pre-op, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-op. Statistical analyses included Kaplan-Meier survival curves, multivariable Cox regression, and linear mixed-effects models. Results: A total of 194 patients completed follow-up (mean age 74.2 ± 6.1 years; 78% female). Preoperative paravertebral sarcopenia was identified in 36.1% (70/194) of patients. The sarcopenia group showed significantly higher 12-month all-cause mortality (8.6% vs. 2.4%, p = 0.018) and a significantly increased risk of death (adjusted HR = 3.84, 95% CI: 1.21-12.18, p = 0.022) after controlling for age, sex, BMI, number of comorbidities, and baseline ODI. Functional recovery was also poorer in the sarcopenia group, with less improvement in ODI scores at 12 months (mean change: -15.3 ± 8.4 vs. -24.6 ± 9.1, p < 0.001) and higher VAS scores (2.8 ± 1.5 vs. 1.9 ± 1.2, p = 0.003). The incidence of adjacent vertebral fractures was also higher in the sarcopenia group (11.4% vs. 4.8%, p = 0.049). Conclusion: Preoperative paravertebral sarcopenia is an independent predictor of increased 12-month mortality and inferior functional recovery following PKP in older adults with OTLCF. Routine MRI-based assessment of paravertebral muscles should be integrated into preoperative risk stratification to identify high-risk patients who may benefit from targeted prehabilitation and intensified postoperative support.
Keywords: Percutaneous Kyphoplasty, Osteoporotic Fracture, Paravertebral Muscles, Sarcopenia, Mortality, Functional Outcomes, Elderly, Prospective Cohort

## A253: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) prophylaxis is safe in patients undergoing staged thoracolumbar fusion

Harsh Wadhwa

1

, Austin Stoner

1

, Jayme Koltsov

1

, James Mok

1

, John Kleimeyer

1

, Atman Desai

1

, Corinna Zygourakis

1

, Jon Park

1

, Kirkham Wood

1

, Anand Veeravagu

1

, John Ratliff

1

, Todd Alamin

1

, Serena Hu

1

1

Stanford University, Stanford, United States

Introduction: Longer thoracolumbar fusions sometimes include anterior approaches, which, due to retraction of the great vessels, can carry higher risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) prophylaxis may ameliorate these risks. Materials and Methods: Retrospective review of adults undergoing combined thoracolumbar fusion of ≥ 5 levels (single institution 2014-2024). Anticoagulation was driven by surgeon choice. Patients receiving LMWH versus no VTE prophylaxis were compared. Patient demographics, comorbidities, perioperative data (EBL, transfusions, etc.), and postoperative data (90-day complications, readmissions, reoperations) were collected. Analyses were performed separately for staged and unstaged patients, with differences with LMWH assessed via chi-squared and Fisher’s exact tests (α = 0.05). Results: Overall, 191 staged [131 (68.6%) female, 66.7 ± 9.2 years] and 216 unstaged [146 (67.6%) female, 67.7 ± 9.8 years] patients were included. LMWH was given in 133 (70%) of staged surgeries and 107 (50%) of unstaged surgeries. Patients receiving LMWH had higher BMI (29.1 [28.2, 30.1] vs. 27.0 [25.7, 28.2], p = 0.011). Among staged patients, rates of PE were 3.1% [95%CI 1.2, 7.8] with LMWH vs. 9.1% [4.0, 19.6] without LMWH (p = 0.132), and rates of DVT were 4.7% [2.2, 9.9] with LMWH vs. 5.5% [1.9, 14.9] without LMWH (p > 0.999). Among unstaged patients, rates of PE were 3.9% [1.5, 9.6] with LMWH vs. 3.1% [1.1, 8.8] without LMWH (p = 0.185) and rates of DVT were 2.9% [1.0, 8.2] with LMWH vs. 4.2% [1.6, 10.2] without LMWH (p = 0.338). In both staged and unstaged cohorts, transfusion rates (and amounts) were comparable with vs. without LMWH (Staged: 96.4% [87.7, 99.0] vs. 92.1% [86.1, 95.7], (p = 0.352); Unstaged: 73.8% [64.6, 81.3] vs. 76.0% [66.6, 83.5], p = 0.387). Complications, readmission, and 6 month reoperation were also comparable with vs. without LMWH. In the staged cohort, wound complication (9.4% [5.5, 15.8] vs. 3.6% [1.0, 12.3], (p = 0.234)) and deep or superficial infection rates (6.3% [3.2, 11.9] vs. 3.6% [1.0, 12.3], (p = 0.726)) were comparable with vs. without LMWH. In the unstaged cohort, wound complications (8.3% [4.3, 15.6] vs. 1.9% [0.5, 6.8], (p = 0.052)) were comparable, but deep or superficial infections (8.3% [4.3, 15.6] vs. 1.9% [0.5, 6.8], (p = 0.042)) were more common in the LMWH group. Conclusion: In the largest study to date directly comparing combined thoracolumbar fusion with vs. without LMWH prophylaxis, LMWH did not increase bleeding or transfusions. LMWH may provide benefits, particularly in PE reduction; however, infection rates were greater in unstaged surgeries, and wound complications may trend higher. Large population-based study is needed for confirmation.

## A254: Is surgery for AIS always successful? A Delphi consensus study including patient participation to define poor outcomes and subsequent identification of incidence in a large multicenter database

Raf Mens

1,2

, Pepijn Bisseling

1

, Marinus De Kleuver

2

, Peter Newton

3

, Michael Kelly

3

, Michelle Marks

4

, Miranda van Hoff

2

1

Sint Maartenskliniek, Nijmegen, The Netherlands

2

Radboudumc, Nijmegen, The Netherlands

3

Rady Children’s Hospital, San Diego, United States

4

Setting Scoliosis Straight Foundation, El Cajon, United States

Introduction: Surgery for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is considered successful for the majority of patients. To identify those patients who currently least benefit from surgery, a definition of treatment failure is needed. The aim of this study was to draft a definition of treatment failure for AIS-surgery, and identify its incidence in a large multicenter database. Material and Methods: A three-round modified Delhi-procedure with experts (physicians (n = 14) and physical therapists (n = 8)), preceded by a patient survey (n = 33). Consensus threshold was 70%. Incidence of failure according to the resulting definition was analyzed in the multicenter Harms study group database (HSGdb, N = 4974, mean follow-up: 3.6 yrs [0-23]). Results: Failure of AIS-surgery was defined as: 1) Clinical deterioration: - clinically relevant decrease in condition-specific quality-of-life compared to preoperative scores, - Permanent disability due to neurologic symptoms, - Mortality related to index surgery, and/or. 2) Revision surgery for following indications: - Deterioration of instrumented curve, - Deterioration of non-instrumented motion segments, - Overcorrection, - Pseudoarthrosis, and/or. 3) Radiologic deterioration: - Progression of instrumented curve > 50, Incidence in HSGdb: - Clinical: i. Relevant decrease on SRS-22r*: 8.7% [428/4894], ii. Neurologic: 2/4974, iii. Mortality: 0, - Revision surgery: 1.3% [64/4974], - Radiologic deterioration: 17.2% [817/4751], * Minimal detectable measurement difference was taken as threshold for clinical relevancy. Conclusion: This is the first attempt to define ‘treatment failure’ of AIS-surgery. Utilizing patient-participation, expert consensus was reached that failure can be considered: Clinical deterioration and/or revision surgery and/or radiologic deterioration. With the presented Delphi-consensus definition a clinical- or revision failure-rate of 1.3%-8.7% was identified in a large multicenter database. A radiologic failure-rate of 17% does not seem in line with clinical experience. Clinical relevancy of this criterium needs further investigation. ## A255: False postoperative PI-LL mismatch due to altered hip coverage: implications onthe surgical outcome of adult spinal deformity

Li Jie Li Jie

1

, Zhen Liu

1

1

Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Nanjing, China

Introduction: Exploring the correlation between changes in hip joint coverage and postoperative PI in adult spinal deformity (ASD) patients after fixation with S2 alar iliac screws (S2AI), and whether there is a link between PI-LL mismatch and mechanical complications immediately after surgery and during follow-up, in order to provide reference for clinical treatment evaluation. Material and Methods: Retrospective analysis of clinical and imaging data of 91 ASD patients who underwent posterior S2AI screw fixation surgery in the Orthopedics Department of Nanjing Gulou Hospital from January 2019 to January 2021. According to the change in hip joint coverage (HJC) immediately after surgery, patients were divided into two groups: HJC-C group (with immediate postoperative Δ HJC at the upper half level, > Q2) and HJC-NC group (with immediate postoperative Δ HJC at the lower half level, < Q2). In the HJC-C group, further divided into the HJC-R group (follow-up period Δ HJC > Q2) and the HCJ-NR group (follow-up period Δ HJC < Q2) based on whether the hip joint coverage rate rebounded during the 2-year follow-up. During preoperative and postoperative first standing, as well as 2-year follow-up, the patient underwent standing position X-ray imaging of the entire spine. The following spinal parameters were measured and recorded: Cobb angle, proximal lumbar lordosis (PLL), distal lumbar lordosis (DLL), lumbar lordosis (LL), Lordosis distribution index (LDI), sagittal vertical axis (SVA), coronal balance distance (CBD), thoracic kyphosis (TK), and T1 pelvic angle (T1). Pelvic angle (T1PA), pelvic incidence angle (PI), pelvic tilt angle (PT), sacral slope (SS), PI-LL, and proximal junction angle (PJA); Related parameters of hip joint coverage include HJC, Lateral Center Edge angle (LCE angle), Acetabular index (AI), Sharp angle, and hip protrusion index (EI). Analyze and compare the differences in preoperative, postoperative, and final follow-up imaging indicators between two groups of patients. Results: In the overall cohort, ASD patients showed an increasing trend in HJC immediately after S2AI fixation surgery (2.2 ± 3.9%), accompanied by a rebound during follow-up (-2.1 ± 3.8%), and a positive correlation was observed between the changes in Δ PI and Δ HJC immediately after surgery and during follow-up (r = 0.587, p = 0.008). Although the immediate postoperative PI-LL of patients in the HJC-C group (n = 46) was significantly lower than that of patients in the HJC-NC group (n = 45) (-22.4 ± 10.8 vs. -10.3 ± 9.3, p = 0.023). However, at the last follow-up, the HJC-C group showed more rebound in PI, and there was no significant statistical difference in PI-LL between the two groups of patients at the last follow-up (-14.6 ± 11.2 vs. -9.7 ± 8.5, P = 0.135).And there was a significant difference in the incidence of PJK between the HJC-C group and the HJC-NC group at the last follow-up [26.1% (6/23) vs. 23.8% (5/21), p = 0.298]. Although there was no significant difference in immediate postoperative PI-LL between the HJC-R group and the HCJ-NR group (-21.1 ± 11.2 vs. 22.6 ± 10.1, p = 0.675). But at 2-year follow-up, the PI-LL of patients in the HJC-R group was significantly higher than that of patients in the HCJ-NR group (-8.3 ± 6.9 vs. -15.9 ± 13.2, p = 0.038). The incidence of PJK in the HJC-R group (n = 12) was significantly lower than that in the HCJ-NR group (n = 11) at the last follow-up [8.7% (2/23) vs. 43.5% (10/23), p = 0.008]. Conclusion: The changes in PI after S2AI surgery in ASD patients are closely related to changes in hip joint coverage. An increase in hip joint coverage after surgery can lead to immediate PI-LL mismatch, but during follow-up, hip joint coverage and PI rebound gradually match the hip pelvic spinal balance. However, for patients with poor hip joint coverage during follow-up, the persistent presence of PI-LL mismatch during follow-up can affect the maintenance of sagittal balance and lead to complications such as PJK.

## A256: Best in class prediction of PJK with a novel T1-T9 pelvic angle mismatch

Nuri Demirci

1

, Yasemin Yavuz

2

, Munish Gupta

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Washington University in St. Louis, Saint Louis, United States

2

Department of Biostatistics, Faculty of Medicine, Ankara University, Ankara, Turkey

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is a frequent complication after adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery. Traditional sagittal alignment parameters such as thoracic kyphosis (TK), PI-LL mismatch, and C7 sagittal vertical axis (SVA) have been widely studied, while more recent targets including the GAP score and T4L1 pelvic angle (T4L1PA) have also been proposed. However, their ability to independently predict PJK remains uncertain. We defined the T1-T9 pelvic angle (T1T9PA) mismatch as a novel sagittal alignment parameter to quantify proximal thoracic alignment and investigated whether it independently predicts PJK. Materials and Methods: A prospective cohort of 207 ASD patients who underwent thoracic-to-pelvis fusion with ≥ 7 instrumented levels and pelvic fixation, all with ≥ 2 years of follow-up was analyzed. PJK was defined as a ≥20° increase in proximal junctional angle from baseline or revision for a PJK. Predictors included demographic factors, surgical approach, UIV level, and radiographic parameters (PI-LL, lumbar lordosis (LL), TK, C7-SVA, GAP, T4L1PA, and T1T9PA). TK and LL were continuous; all others categorical: PI-LL (± 10°), SVA (< 5 vs ≥ 5 cm), GAP (proportioned vs disproportionate), T4L1PA (within vs outside -1° to +3°), T1T9PA (ROC-defined cutoff), UIV (upper ≤ T6 vs lower ≥ T7), and approach (posterior-only vs combined). Univariate logistic regression identified predictors; those with p < 0.25 entered a forward stepwise multivariate model. Results: Mean age was 62.1 ± 11.1 years, BMI 29.7 ± 5.7, and 77.8% were female; 72.9% had upper thoracic UIVs, 27.1% lower thoracic UIVs, PSO was performed in 20.8% and VCR in 6.3%. Over a mean 46-month follow-up, 32 patients (15.5%) developed PJK. ROC analysis identified 10° as the optimal cutoff for T1T9PA. On univariate analysis, TK was significant as a continuous variable (p = 0.011), T1T9PA ≥ 10° was strongly predictive (p < 0.001), and T4L1PA outside its literature-defined safe zone was predictive (p = 0.034) for PJK. Surgical approach (p = 0.057), UIV level (p = 0.060), and GAP score (p = 0.22) met the candidate threshold (p < 0.25). Other demographic and radiographic factors were not predictive. Although age, sex, and BMI were not below the p < 0.25 threshold, they were included in the multivariate model due to clinical relevance. The multivariate model included T1T9PA, T4L1PA, TK, surgical approach, UIV level, GAP, age, sex, and BMI. In forward stepwise regression, only T1T9PA ≥ 10° remained independently significant (OR 4.64, 95% CI 2.0-10.0, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Only T1T9PA was an independent risk factor in predicting PJK. No traditional TK, PI-LL mismatch, C7-SVA or recent GAP, T4L1PA parameters independently predicted PJK. A 10° threshold was established, with patients above this cutoff having a 4.6-fold increased risk of PJK (OR 4.64, 95% CI 2.0-10.0) and reduced PJK-free survival. These findings support T1T9PA as a novel thoracic alignment target to mitigate proximal junctional failure.
