## A257: Efficacy of halo pelvic traction versus halo gravity traction in treating severe rigid spinal deformity - A matched retrospective study

Jianqiang Wang

1

, Yong Hai

1

1

Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Severe rigid spinal deformity (SRSD)-defined by > 100° Cobb angle and < 30% flexibility-causes restrictive pulmonary dysfunction, cardiopulmonary compromise, and reduced quality of life. Advanced techniques like vertebral column resection enable significant correction albeit with substantial neurologic risks. Preoperative halo traction serves as a crucial adjunct to reduce osteotomy dependency. Halo gravity traction (HGT) and halo pelvic traction (HPT) both allow gradual correction with functional improvements, yet comparative efficacy data remain scarce. This matched retrospective study evaluates HGT versus HPT in optimizing deformity correction, pulmonary/nutritional status, and surgical safety to inform evidence-based preoperative planning for SRSD. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 104 severe rigid spinal deformity patients treated with preoperative Halo traction and posterior correction surgery (2016.1-2022.12). Patients were matched 1:1 by main curve Cobb angle and age into HGT and HPT groups (33 participants in each group). Radiographic parameters (main curve, kyphosis, coronal/sagittal balance, apical vertebral translation) were assessed before and after traction, preoperatively, and at final follow-up. Surgical planning for osteotomy and fusion segments used pre-traction imaging, compared with actual outcomes. Traction duration, surgical parameters, and complications were recorded. Results: HGT patients had 4.5 ± 1.5 months of traction, improving main curve Cobb angle from 138.4° to 94.9° (23.5%) and kyphosis from 87.9° to 73.1° (22.6%), with postoperative values of 51.1° and 39.7°. HPT patients had 5.1 ± 1.1 months of traction, improving main curve from 143.2° to 69.6° (51.3%) and kyphosis from 117.7° to 56.8° (49.1%), with postoperative values of 56.1° and 34.5°. HPT showed significantly better improvement rates (p < 0.05). HPT achieved 50% deformity improvement after 3 months, vs. 5 months for HGT. By 7 months, > 60% of HPT vs. < 10% of HGT patients reached this threshold. Planned three-column osteotomy use dropped from 90.9% to 51.5% (actual 36.4%) in HGT and 84.8% to 21.2% (actual 9.1%) in HPT. HPT reduced osteotomy grade (p < 0.05) and fusion segments (p = 0.02) more effectively. Complication rates were similar. Conclusion: Halo gravity traction (HGT) and halo pelvic traction (HPT) effectively correct severe rigid spinal deformity and imbalance. Both reduce high-grade osteotomy needs compared to initial plans. HPT outperforms HGT in deformity correction, osteotomy grade reduction, and fusion segment minimization.

## A258: Risk stratification and clinical classification for postoperative neurological complications in post-tuberculosis kyphosis: a retrospective cohort study

Jianqiang Wang

1

, Yong Hai

1

1

Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Spinal tuberculosis, affecting over a billion people in developing countries, is a leading cause of severe kyphotic deformity. Untreated cases progress to rigid angular kyphosis, with significant risk of spinal cord compression, neurological deficits (occurring in 23%-76% of cases), and paraplegia (15%-42.5%). This results in chronic pain, spinal imbalance, and reduced quality of life. Conservative management often fails, necessitating surgery for neurological compromise or spinal instability. Modern techniques like pedicle screw instrumentation and posterior osteotomy improve deformity correction and fusion outcomes. However, surgical challenges include rigid deformities, structural abnormalities, and prolonged cord compression, increasing neurological complication risks (reported up to 30%). Overcorrection may cause cord stretching or ischemia-reperfusion injury, while abrupt decompression can induce neuronal apoptosis, potentially leading to paralysis. Current strategies lack robust preoperative risk identification. This study analyzes risk factors for postoperative neurological complications in tuberculous kyphosis patients and proposes a clinical classification system to identify high-risk individuals, guiding preoperative interventions to minimize surgical risks. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 51 patients with post-tuberculosis kyphosis who underwent single-stage posterior osteotomy and correction at our institution. Radiographic parameters, including the kyphotic angle, cross-sectional area ratio of the spinal cord (CSAR), and spinal cord angle (SCA), alongside surgical factors such as intraoperative blood loss and osteotomy grade, were evaluated. Postoperative neurological complications were recorded. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were employed to identify potential influencing factors. Based on the interaction between these factors, a clinical classification system for post-tuberculosis kyphosis was established to stratify the risk of postoperative neurological complications. Results: A minimum 2-year follow-up was conducted for the 51 patients with post-tuberculosis kyphosis. Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that the Baltalimani sign, spinal cord MRI type, Rajasekaran classification, three-column osteotomy, C-reactive protein (CRP), and SCA were significant risk factors for postoperative neurological complications. Two risk prediction models were developed accordingly. Synergistic interactions were identified between spinal cord MRI type and Rajasekaran classification, as well as between CRP and SCA. These findings informed the development of two clinical classification systems: the Mechanical Classification (AUC = 0.751) and the Imaging-Biomarker Classification (AUC = 0.883). The area under the curve (AUC) for both classifications demonstrated good predictive performance, with the DeLong test indicating superior efficacy for the Imaging-Biomarker Classification (p = 0.039). Conclusion: Spinal structural instability, spinal cord compression, osteotomy grade, and elevated CRP levels may all contribute to an increased risk of postoperative neurological complications in patients with post-tuberculosis kyphosis. The clinical classification systems established herein facilitate precise risk stratification, enabling targeted preoperative interventions to mitigate surgical risks and enhance surgical outcomes.

## A259: Impact of pelvic fusion on walking performance following scoliosis correction surgery

Sara McMahan

1

, Bethany Wilson

1

, Kyle Robinson

1

, Isador Lieberman

2

1

Texas Back Institute, Plano, TX, United States

2

Texas Back Institute, Frisco, TX, United States

Introduction: Scoliosis correction surgery is increasingly involving fusion to the pelvis in order to stabilize the construct, providing improved outcomes for appropriately selected patients with spinal deformity (ASD). For patients undergoing these procedures, it is important to consider how the patient’s day-to-day function will be impacted. Maintaining walking ability is vital for independent function. It is presently not thoroughly investigated how pelvic fusion in a corrective fusion construct affects patient walking performance. The purpose was to investigate how fusion to the pelvis affects function in patients with ASD. Material and Methods: This was a post-hoc analysis of a prospective study with 45 ASD patients receiving corrective alignment surgery without fusion to the pelvis (N) (35F/10M, 56.9 ± 19.1y, 27.3 ± 4.4 kg/m2, SVA: 28.7 ± 54.2 cm, PI-LL: 10.6 ± 20.1o, Cobb: 36 ± 16.5o) and 35 receiving fusion to the pelvis (Y) (28F/7M, 65.9 ± 7.1y, 28.6 ± 6.5 kg/m2, SVA: 48.5 ± 47.8 cm, PI-LL: 24.3 ± 20.8o, Cobb: 40.4 ± 16.5o) and 35 asymptomatic adult controls (C) (20F/15M, 39 ± 13.3y, 24.7 ± 3.6 kg/m2). Patient reported outcome measures included Visual Analog scale for midback (VASmb) low back (VASlb), and leg (VASleg) pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Walking measures included Cadence, Single support time, double support time, step length, width, height, and time, and gait deviation index. ASD subjects were divided into two cohorts based on whether their pelvis was fused during their procedure (PF), or not (NPF). Evaluations were conducted preoperatively (P0), 3 months post-surgery (P3), and 1-year post-surgery (P12). At each visit patients were assessed with VAS and ODI and performed three over ground walking tests to assess spatiotemporal parameters of the gait cycle. Results: PF were significantly older with significantly larger PI-LL than NPF but were comparable in all other demographics. PF also reported significantly higher preoperative ODI than NPF. C were significantly younger and had lower BMI’s than both PF and NPF. All reported pain and disability improved significantly following surgery at all follow ups. At P3, all walking measures were comparable between PF and NPF and remained significantly different to C with the exception of single support time and step width which were comparable between PF, NPF and C at all follow ups. At P12, significant differences were observed in cadence (PF:95.4 ± 15.6step/min; NPF:103.5 ± 8.4step/min), step time (PF:0.6 ± 0.1s; NPF:0.6 ± 0.1s), and double support time (PF:0.4 ± 0.2s; NPF: 0.3 ± 0.1s) for treatment groups. Cadence in NPF normalized to C and step height normalized to C in PF while all other measures continued in the same pattern (all p < 0.05). Conclusion: Patients who were not fused to the pelvis exhibited delineation from patients who were fused to the pelvis by improving gait measures at one year postop. Interestingly, NPF showed cadence normalized to controls at one year postop despite significant age, height, and BMI differences, while PF showed similar normalization to C in step height despite the same demographic differences. These findings suggest that pelvic fusion may have a differential impact on specific aspects of gait dynamics over time. Further research is needed to explore the long-term functional outcomes and compensatory mechanisms that may develop in patients with pelvic fusion to optimize recovery strategies and improve quality of life.

## A260: Dystrophinopathy in the paravertebral muscle of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a prospective case-control study in China

Junyu Li

1

, Xiang Zhang

1

, Zekun Li

2

, Hanwen Zhang

1

, Y Zhang

3

, Miao Yu

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing Key Laboratory of Spinal Disease Research, Engineering Research Center of Bone and Joint Precision Medicine, Beijing, China

2

Peking University Health Science Center, Beijing, China

3

Department of Neurology, Peking University Third Hospital, Peking University, Beijing, China

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) features vertebral rotation with lateral curvature, affecting 2%-4% of children under 16, with 0.04%-0.3% progressing to > 40°. Its cause is unclear despite genetic, epigenetic, endocrine, and developmental clues. Accumulating evidence points to the paraspinal muscles: fiber-type imbalance, multifidus ultrastructural changes, core-myopathy-like findings in some AIS cases, and parallels with neuromuscular disorders. Protein dysregulation, including altered vitamin D-binding protein, may also influence spinal morphology. Conclusion: Dystrophin protein deficiency in the paraspinal muscles plays a crucial role in AIS formation and progression. The severity of scoliosis in patients with AIS is correlated with the extent of dystrophin loss in the paravertebral muscles. Therefore, dystrophin dysfunction may be relevant to AIS occurrence and development.

## A261: PI-LL should be replaced by PI-L4S1 to determine optimal lordosis in lumbar fusions

Fatemeh Alavi

1

, Christopher J. Nielsen

1

, Michael Kelly

2

, Jeffrey Hills

3

, Stephen Lewis

1

1

University of Toronto, University Health Network (UHN), Toronto, Canada

2

Rady Children’s Hospital, University of California San Diego, San Diego, United States

3

UT Health San Antonio, San Antonio, United States

Introduction: Understanding the correlations within the normal spine is essential to properly plan alignment targets that minimize the risk of mechanical complications following spinal deformity surgery. The PI-LL relationship has been used as a prominent measure in the past, however its inability to account for distribution of segmental lordosis has led to its inaccuracies in achieving ideal outcomes. Among sagittal parameters, the L1–pelvic angle (L1PA) has been shown to be a more reliable clinical measure that integrates pelvic morphology with lumbar curvature. However, its correlation with segmental sagittal parameters is unclear. The aim of this study is to investigate the relationship between L1PA and segmental parameters of spinal alignment in a normal population. Material and Methods: A cross-sectional radiographic analysis was conducted on international volunteers with full body standing radiographs. Study subjects with ODI >20, and radiographic disc degeneration or scoliosis were excluded. Spinopelvic parameters such as PI, L4-S1 lordosis (L4S1), and L1PA were measured. Linear regression analysis was used to quantify the relationship between sagittal parameters. Results: 320 healthy individuals with mean PI of 52° 10 (60% female) were available for analysis. The mean value of L1-S1 lordosis was 58° 10 and L4S1 was 37° 7. There were no correlations between PI-LL and PI, as well as L4S1 and PI. However, a strong correlation was found between PI-L4S1 and PI, using the following formula: PI-L4S1=0.9 PI-30±7.4 (r2=0.62). The mean value of L1PA was 4.3° 6.5. A highly significant association was observed between PI-L4S1 and L1PA: L1PA=0.56 (PI-L4S1)-4 (r2=0.95). Combining the proposed relation and the suggested L1PA=0.5 PI-20 results in ideal value for L4S1: L4S1=0.12 PI+30. Conclusion: PI–L4S1 is a novel sagittal alignment parameter, revealing several important correlations within the sagittal alignment of the spine. A significantly strong association between L1PA and PI–L4S1 demonstrated that upper lumbar alignment is closely linked to the orientation of the lower lumbar segments. Incorporating PI–L4S1 rather than relying solely on L1PA provides a more accurate and physiologically relevant reference for spinal alignment, particularly when planning surgical realignment or fusion procedures involving L4 to S1. This approach improves the generalizability of L1PA-based alignment targets to lower lumbar fusion constructs and may help optimize postoperative sagittal balance and mechanical loading, potentially reducing the risk of mechanical complications.

## A262: Patients with chronic low back pain without advanced disk degeneration exhibit gut microbiome dysbiosis: evidence from an age, sex and BMI matched study

Stone Sima

1

, Thomas Jeffries

2

, Alisha Sial

1,3,4

, Suhani Sharma

1

, Neha Chopra

1,3

, Fan Zhang

5

, Georgina Hold

5

, Victor Chen

1

, Lauren Barber

6

, Ashish Diwan

1,3,4

1

Spine Labs, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, St George and Sutherland Clinical Campuses, School of Clinical Medicine, UNSW, Sydney, Sydney, Australia

2

School of Science, Western Sydney University Hawkesbury Campus, Richmond, New South Wales, Sydney, Australia

3

Spine Service, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, St George Hospital, School of Clinical Medicine, UNSW, Sydney, Australia

4

Spinal Unit, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Royal Adelaide Hospital, University of Adelaide, Adelaide, Australia

5

Microbiome Research Centre, St George and Sutherland Clinical Campuses, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW, Sydney, Australia

6

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, United States

Introduction: Chronic low back pain (LBP) is the leading cause of disability worldwide, yet its underlying pathophysiology remains poorly understood. Current diagnostic techniques rely heavily on imaging, which is insufficient for identifying inflammatory or systemic contributors. Emerging evidence suggests a role for gut microbiome dysbiosis in inflammatory pain pathways, yet its specific contribution to chronic LBP remains unclear. The aim of this study is to investigate gut microbiome alterations in chronic LBP patients compared to healthy controls. Materials and Methods: Twenty-eight patients with chronic LBP (> 3 months) without advanced disk degeneration (Pfirrmann grade <4) and 28 age-, sex-, and BMI-matched healthy controls were recruited. Stool samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA V4 gut microbiome analysis. Alpha diversity and beta diversity were assessed to determine microbial diversity differences. Taxonomic composition was compared at the phylum and genus levels. Results: There were no significant differences in age, sex, BMI, and race between the two groups. Patients with chronic LBP exhibited significantly reduced alpha diversity compared to controls (U = 517, p = 0.003, r = 0.395). Future research should explore causal relationships and strain-specific microbial effects to refine microbiome-based interventions for chronic LBP.

## A263: Bilateral transforaminal microdiscectomy (TFMD) combined with ponte osteotomy in thoracic disc surgery

Buse Sarigul

1

, Mesut Yilmaz

2

, Sedat Dalbayrak

3

1

Umraniye Research and Training Hospital, Department of Neurosurgery, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Medicana Atasehir Hospital, Norospinal Akademi, Istanbul, Turkey

3

Medicana Atasehir Hospital, Department of Neurosurgery, Norospinal Akademi, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Surgical management of thoracic disc herniations, particularly those with calcified or hard disc morphology, remains challenging. Posterior approaches are associated with neural complications, whereas anterior approaches carry considerable morbidity and mortality. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the clinical and radiological outcomes of a combined technique of Ponte osteotomy and bilateral transforaminal microdiscectomy (PO+TFMD) in patients with thoracic disc herniation. Material and Methods: Medical records of 18 patients in whom thoracic disc herniation was detected and underwent PO+TFMD were evaluated retrospectively. The surgery was performed in a prone position with a median skin incision. Cranial and caudal pedicles and ascending neural roots were exposed using a Ponte osteotomy. The operating table was adjusted to extension to reduce spinal cord tension. The herniated disc was approached bilaterally via the foramina using microsurgical techniques. Disc material, including calcified central fragments, was excised with a high-speed drill and osteotome. A transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) cage, filled with local autograft from facets, was inserted, and compressive segmental instrumentation was applied in extension. All patients underwent thoracic MRI, CT and AP/lateral scoliosis X-rays preoperatively and postoperatively. Duration of surgery, intraoperative blood loss, complications, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores, segmental and thoracic kyphosis (T2-T12) were recorded preoperatively, on postoperative day 1, and at 6-month follow-up. Results: Of the 18 patients, 7 were female (38.9%) and 11 were male (61.1%), with a mean age of 41.37 ± 9.26 years. All patients presented with back pain, and 12 patients (66.7%) exhibited paraparesis preoperatively. The mean operative time was 111.8 ± 17.6 minutes, with an average intraoperative blood loss of 457.4 ± 142.3 mL. The mean preoperative VAS score was 7.42 ± 1.13, which decreased to 4.18 ± 0.87 on postoperative day 7 (p < 0.001) and further to 0.76 ± 0.71 at 6 months (p < 0.001). The mean preoperative ODI was 47.6 ± 10.4%, which improved significantly to 9.3 ± 6.4% at 6 months (p < 0.001). Thoracic kyphosis (T2-T12) improved from 47.83 ± 7.62° preoperatively to 39.27 ± 6.84° on postoperative day 1 (p < 0.001) and was maintained at 40.14 ± 6.91° at 6 months (p < 0.001). Segmental kyphosis corrected from 18.36 ± 4.73° preoperatively to 9.58 ± 3.82° postoperatively (p < 0.001) and stabilized at 10.21 ± 3.87° at 6 months (p < 0.001). No intraoperative complications were observed. Two patients (11.1%) developed transient postoperative paresthesia, which resolved spontaneously within 2 weeks. At the 6-month follow-up, all patients were pain-free, ODI ≤ 20%, and neurologically intact. Conclusion: The combination of Ponte osteotomy and bilateral transforaminal microdiscectomy provides a safe and effective posterior-only approach for thoracic disc herniation, with low complication rates, significant pain relief, and favorable kyphotic correction at mid-term follow-up. This technique may represent a viable alternative to conventional anterior or posterior strategies, particularly in cases involving calcified discs.

## A264: Clinical and economic outcomes of open, microscopic, and endoscopic techniques for thoracic discectomy: a single institution study

Garrison Bentz

1

, Dillon Stone

1

, John Ogunlade

2

, Salim Yakdan

2

, Karan Joseph

2

, Mark Lambrechts

1

1

Washington University in St. Louis Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, St. Louis, United States

2

Washington University in St. Louis Department of Neurosurgery, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Symptomatic thoracic disc herniations are a rare and difficult to treat pathology. Historically, open thoracic discectomy and fusion (TDF) was considered the primary treatment, however the introduction of minimally invasive options such as the anterolateral retropleural thoracic microdiscectomy (TAD) and posterolateral transforaminal endoscopic thoracic discectomy (TETD) with less soft tissue disruption and neural complications led to a decline in TDF use. Few studies have directly compared TDF, TAD, and TETD within a single institution. Materials and Methods: 37 patients over 10 years from a single institution were reviewed. Surgical outcomes, complications, cost, and other operative variables were compared between TDF, TAD, and TETD procedures used to treat single-level, symptomatic thoracic disc herniations. A minimum follow-up of 1 year was required. Cases with indications of trauma, malignancy, or infection were excluded. The Kruskal-Wallis test and the Chi-square test were used to analyze continuous and categorical variables, respectively. Significance was p < 0.05. Results: 37 patients were included (TDF: 15, TAD: 10, TETD: 12). TETD had a mean estimated blood loss (EBL) of 9 ml, lower than both TAD and TDF (p < 0.001). TETD has displayed a shorter length of stay at 1.75 days than both TAD (3.3 days) and TDF (4.67 days) (p = 0.008). TETD and TAD had a similar index cost of surgery at $13,122.33 and $14,816.78, however both were lower than the TDF procedures at $34,518.51 (p < 0.001). TDF also required intervention on a greater number of levels to achieve posterior fusion, whereas TETD and TAD only involved the single level (p < 0.001). There was no difference between the three cohorts in operative duration, rate of dural tears, post-operative complications, or emergency department visits. Conclusion: Minimally invasive techniques such as TETD and TAD have multiple advantages over traditional TDF in the treatment of thoracic disc herniations including EBL, length of stay, and cost. TETD was shown to have lower mean estimated blood loss and length of stay with a similar index cost when compared to TAD procedures. While both TAD and TETD have the benefits of a minimally invasive approach, TETD can provide similar outcomes with a similar cost, less blood loss, and a shorter hospital stay at the expense of a significant learning curve. Ultimately, the type and location of the disc herniation will play a large role in the optimal treatment approach, however TETD provides a valuable option for the non-centrally calcified symptomatic thoracic disc herniation.

## A265: Stem cell therapy for degenerative disc disease: a systematic review of preclinical evidence, clinical translation, and future directions: systematic review

Vinicius Ricieri Ferraz

1

, Carlos Goulart

2

, Maria Ricieri Ferraz Franco de Souza

3

, Philippe A. Mercier

4

, Tobias Mattei

4

, Marcelo Ochoa Coelho de Souza Furlan

5

1

Dr. José de Carvalho Florence Hospital, The Regional Hospital of São José dos Campos - Dr. Rubens Savastano, São José dos Campos, São Paulo, Brazil

2

Division of Neurological Surgery, Essentia Health, Duluth, Minessota, United States

3

Division of Neurology, Irmandade da Santa Casa de Misericordia de Santos, Santos, São Paulo, Brazil

4

Division of Neurological Surgery, Saint Louis University School of Medicine,, Saint Louis, Missouri, United States

5

Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, Curitiba, Brazil

Introduction: Degenerative disc disease (DDD) represents a predominant cause of chronic low back pain and associated disabilities on a global scale. Traditional treatment modalities, such as analgesics, physical therapy, and spinal fusion procedures, are primarily palliative and do not facilitate the restoration of disc structure or physiological function. The field of regenerative medicine has gained prominence as a promising alternative, with stem cell-based therapies demonstrating potential to reestablish disc functionality and to prevent or delay mechanical complications. This systematic review endeavors to synthesize the evidence derived from preclinical and clinical investigations concerning the efficacy, safety, and translational challenges associated with stem cell-based interventions for DDD. Material and Methods: A systematic review of the literature was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from January 2000 to July 2025, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies encompassed both preclinical and clinical trials assessing intradiscal injection or implantation of stem cells (including mesenchymal stem cells, adipose-derived stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and stem cell-derived products) in degenerative disc disease (DDD). The outcomes evaluated comprised disc regeneration (via histology, imaging, and disc height measurements), patient-reported measures (such as Visual Analog Scale [VAS] and Oswestry Disability Index [ODI]), and adverse events. Data extraction and synthesis were performed independently by two reviewers. Results: Thirty-one studies met the inclusion criteria: 18 preclinical (animal models) and 13 clinical (1,299 patients, including five randomized controlled trials). Preclinical studies, all conducted in animal models, demonstrated consistent disc regeneration evidenced by increased proteoglycan content, enhanced disc hydration, and restoration of disc height. In human subjects, stem cell therapies yielded modest yet statistically significant improvements in pain (measured by VAS) and disability (assessed by ODI), although radiographic evidence of genuine disc regeneration remained inconsistent. The largest randomized controlled trial (Beall et al., 2025; n = 404) did not achieve its primary endpoint; however, subgroup analyses suggested potential benefits in specific populations. The safety profiles were favorable, predominantly indicating mild, transient adverse events; serious complications such as discitis were infrequent. No reports of tumorigenesis or severe immune reactions were documented. Conclusion: Stem cell-based therapies for DDD demonstrate encouraging regenerative effects in preclinical animal studies and provide modest clinical benefits in early human studies with an acceptable safety profile. However, consistent structural regeneration in humans remains unproven. Translational barriers include the hostile disc microenvironment, limited durability of transplanted cells, and heterogeneous patient selection. Future directions emphasize multimodal strategies-combining stem cells with biomaterials, exosomes, or genetic modifications-and the need for large, multicenter randomized trials to establish efficacy and optimize patient-specific applications.

## A266: Benchmarking surgical approaches to thoracic disc herniation: a retrospective database study

Manish Kasliwal

1

1

University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, Case Western reserve University School of Medicine, Cleveland, United States

Introduction: Thoracic disc herniations are a relatively uncommon form of degenerative disc disease, comprising an estimated 0.1-3 % of all spinal disc herniations. Surgical treatment may utilize an anterior, lateral, or posterior/posterolateral approach, and approach selection is based on a number of factors. This study investigated national trends in surgical approach utilization as well as patient characteristics predictive of receiving a specific surgical approach. Material and Methods: This was a retrospective study querying the TriNetX national database. Patients were identified through specific ICD-9 coding for degenerative thoracic disc herniation and CPT coding for thoracic spinal procedures. Results: Of 3009 total patients meeting inclusion criteria, 2703 patients (89.8%) underwent decompression through a posterior or posterolateral approach, 222 (7.4%) via anterior approach, and 84 (2.8%) via lateral extracavitary approach. Although the annual number of surgeries performed for thoracic disc herniation patients increased after 2017, there was a decreased utilization of anterior approaches. ## A267: Progression of disc degeneration over 23 years from adolesence to adulthood

Teija Lund

1

, Anni Aavikko

2

, Leena Ristolainen

3

, Hannu Kautiainen

4

, Martina Lohman

5

, Dietrich Schlenzka

3

1

Helsinki University, Helsinki University Hospital, Helsinki, Finland

2

Päijät-Häme Central Hospital, Lahti, Finland

3

Research Institute Orton, Helsinki, Finland

4

Folkhälsan Research Center, Helsinki, Finland

5

Helsinki University Hospital, Helsinki University, Helsinki, Finland

Introduction: Disc degeneration (DD) is commonly observed in both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals and tends to increase with age. In adults, the most rapid progression occurs before the age of 50, with a strong genetic influence at younger age. This study aimed to investigate the longitudinal progression of DD and its relationship to lifetime low back pain (LBP) in healthy volunteers from adolescence into adulthood. Material and Methods: This longitudinal observational study included healthy volunteers examined at ages 11, 19 and 34 years. Each assessment comprised a structured interview, clinical examination, and lumbar spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The interview addressed lifetime occurrence of LBP without specific trauma. Mid-sagittal T2-weighted MRI images were independently analyzed by a musculoskeletal radiologist and two spine surgeons. Intervertebral discs from L1/L2 to L5/S1 were graded using the 5-point Pfirrmann classification, with grade 3 or higher indicating degeneration (DD). A Pfirrmann Summary Score (PSS, range 5-25) was calculated by summing the scores across discs. Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) model was applied to establish the rate of discs with Pfirrmann grade 3 or higher and the annual change in PSS. Results: Forty subjects had complete data sets at all three time points. The proportion of participants with DD was 12% at age 11, 48% at age 19, and 72% at age 34. At ages 19 and 34, no significant demographic or clinical differences were observed between participants with and without DD. PSS increased significantly in both groups over time, with significant between-group differences at ages 19 and 34. Across the cohort, the annual PSS increase was significantly greater from age 11 to age 19 (0.55, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.63) than from age 19 to age 34 (0.08, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.11). During adolescence, individual PSS increase varied considerably (range 1-7 grades), with no significant relationship to sex, sex-adjusted Body Surface Area (BSA) growth, or physical activity at age 19. After adjustment for sex, BMI, smoking and physical activity, participants with DD in at least one lumbar disc at age 19 or 34 reported significantly more lifetime LBP than those without DD. Conclusion: Progression of DD is strongly age dependent, with adolescence emerging as the critical phase marked by high inter-individual variability. The occurrence of DD increased steeply from early adolescence to adulthood. The presence of DD at ages 19 and 34 was associated with a higher lifetime report of LBP compared with those without DD.

## A268: Recurrent lumbar disc herniation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of risk factors, surgical timing, and outcomes of revision discectomy versus fusion

Sydney Rucker

1

, Aidan Gillespie

1

, Robert Ferdon

2

, Warren Roth

1

, Jason Silvestre

1

, Charles Reitman

1

, James Lawrence

1

, Robert Ravinsky

1

1

Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, United States

2

University of South Carolina - School of Medicine, Columbia, United States

Introduction: Recurrent lumbar disc herniation (RLDH) occurs in up to 15% of patients following primary discectomy and poses significant challenges in surgical decision-making. Two common reoperative strategies include revision discectomy (RD) and spinal fusion (SF), yet the optimal treatment approach remains a subject of debate. Additionally, the ideal timing for reoperation is poorly defined, with limited data available. This study aimed to systematically review the risk factors associated with RLDH, evaluate the impact of surgical timing, and compare outcomes between RD and SF. Materials and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were performed in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered with PROSPERO. Literature searches were conducted through December 2024 using PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL databases. Studies were included if they reported on patients undergoing revision surgery for RLDH and provided data on surgical techniques, timing, and clinical outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the ROB-2 tool for randomized controlled trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. A random-effects meta-analysis was used to evaluate 12-month improvements in back pain (VAS back), leg pain (VAS leg), and disability (ODI) scores. Secondary outcomes included perioperative parameters, complication rates, recurrence rates, and patient satisfaction. Results: Ten studies comprising a total of 939 patients met inclusion criteria. Commonly reported risk factors for RLDH included male sex, obesity, smoking, diabetes, and large annular defects. Surgical timing was inconsistently reported across studies, preventing meaningful pooled analysis on this variable. When comparing surgical approaches, spinal fusion was associated with significantly greater intraoperative blood loss (p = 0.039), while no significant differences were observed in operative time or hospitalization duration. Recurrence rates were not significantly different between RD and SF (p = 0.262), although open fusion showed a trend toward reduced recurrence. No significant differences were found in 12-month VAS or ODI scores between the two groups (p > 0.3). Minimally invasive techniques such as MIS-TLIF and PELD were associated with fewer complications and higher patient satisfaction. Conclusion: Both RD and SF are viable surgical options for the treatment of RLDH, each presenting unique risk-benefit considerations. While fusion may reduce recurrence in some cases, it is associated with greater blood loss. Importantly, the inconsistent reporting of surgical timing emerged as a major limitation across studies. To better inform surgical decision-making, future research should focus on high-quality studies with standardized definitions of recurrence and consistent reporting of reoperation timeframes, supported by long-term follow-up data.

## A270: Outcomes of endoscopic vs. traditional lumbar microdiscectomy: a comparitive cohort analysis

Hanna von Riegen

1

, Erica Greiner

1

, Jason Pittman

1

, Sapan Gandhi

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School in Boston, MA, Boston, United States

Introduction: Endoscopic lumbar discectomy is increasingly adopted as a minimally invasive alternative to traditional (i.e.open or tubular) lumbar microdiscectomy. While single-center studies suggest reduced perioperative complications with endoscopic approaches, real-world evidence across broader healthcare systems remains limited. We compared short- and long-term outcomes between endoscopic and traditional lumbar microdiscectomy in a large international database. Material and Methods: We queried the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (> 150 healthcare organizations, ∼20 countries) for adults (≥ 18 years) undergoing traditional lumbar microdiscectomy (CPT 63030; excluding CPT 63035) or endoscopic lumbar discectomy (CPT 62380) between 2005-2025. To ensure sufficient follow-up, only patients with index procedures up to August 2023 were included in 2-year analyses. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed across all available demographic, comorbidity, and laboratory variables. Risk differences, ratios, and odds ratios were calculated; patients were censored at their last recorded fact. Sensitivity analyses including later index dates and excluding patients with pre-existing outcomes yielded similar results. Conclusion: In this large real-world cohort, endoscopic discectomy was associated with fewer short-term complications and readmissions compared with traditional microdiscectomy, but also with higher rates of persistent pain and repeat endoscopic procedures at long-term follow-up. ## A271: Prevalence of radiculitis after TLIF with expandable cage: our experience and comparison with the literature

Diego Prado

1

, Andres Chahín

1

, Cristian Ricardo Correa Valencia

1

, Álvaro Soteres

1

, Javiera Babarovich

1

, Sofia Chahin

1

, Andrés Leiva Rivera

2

1

Clinica Las Condes, Instituto de Neurocirugía Doctor Asenjo, Santiago, Chile

2

Clinica Meds, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) with expandable cages has gained widespread acceptance for the treatment of degenerative lumbar spine pathology. This technique enables restoration of disc height and foraminal space with less manipulation of neural structures compared with traditional static cages. These advantages may reduce the risk of postoperative radiculitis, a complication characterized by new or worsened radicular pain after surgery. However, international literature reports highly variable prevalence rates with static cages, ranging from 2.8% to 57%, reflecting heterogeneity in definitions, implant designs, and patient populations. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective descriptive review of consecutive patients who underwent TLIF with expandable cages between January 2023 and March 2025. Inclusion criteria were patients with degenerative lumbar spine pathology treated with TLIF using an expandable interbody device. Exclusion criteria included infection, trauma, tumor, or incomplete clinical records. Clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, comorbidities), surgical characteristics (operative level, duration, estimated blood loss), and hospital course were collected. The primary outcome was the presence of postoperative radiculitis, defined as new or persistent radicular pain within the first postoperative month not attributable to residual stenosis, hematoma, or implant malposition. Secondary variables included severity of symptoms, duration of hospital stay, and need for surgical reintervention. Results: A total of 102 patients met inclusion criteria. The observed prevalence in this cohort lies within the range reported in contemporary literature. Conclusion: In our two-center experience, the prevalence of postoperative radiculitis following TLIF with expandable cages was 17.6%, consistent with previously published rates. Although expandable cages provide technical and radiographic benefits, such as restoration of disc height and foraminal enlargement, they do not appear to significantly reduce the incidence of postoperative radiculitis compared with traditional static devices. These findings suggest that factors beyond implant design-such as surgical technique, patient-specific anatomy, and biological responses-may play a more decisive role in the development of this complication. Further prospective studies with standardized definitions and larger sample sizes are warranted to better clarify risk factors and potential preventive strategies.

Introduction: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is considered a multifactorial condition in which structural and functional changes of the paraspinal musculature are increasingly considered important contributors as they play a crucial role in stabilization of the spine. The mean Age was 40.75 (13.06) and 42.37 (11.58), respectively. However, no significant association with multifidus fCSA existed. For or the erector spinae, fCSA - but not FI - showed a significant association with mobility (Eta2 = 0.017, p = 0.004). No significant associations of muscle and lumbar sagittal mobility were found in the asymptomatic group or for coronal lumbar mobility in either group. Conclusion: This study provides clinical evidence that paraspinal muscle degeneration is independently associated with reduced spinal mobility, particularly in individuals with chronic low back pain, demonstrating a larger independent effect than age, disc degeneration or pain intensity. In contrast to previous studies that primarily examined associations with strength or pain, our analysis focused on unloaded spinal mobility, capturing a distinct functional domain relevant to everyday activities. Notably, associations differed between cLBP and controls and also differed by muscle, evaluated morphological characteristics and direction of movement, highlighting the need for comprehensive measurements in future research.

## A273: Forearm bone mineral density predicts screw loosening after lumbar fusion similar to lumbar Hounsfield unit value in patients with lumbar spondylolisthesis

## A274: ALIF standalone vs ALIF + posterior instrumentation: precise indications and long-term outcomes. A systematic review

Oscar Molina-Romero

1

, Santiago Vallejo-Puerta

2

, Julio Fonnegra-Pardo

3

, Andres Segura-Hernandez

3

, Andrés Fonnegra-Caballero

3

, Juan Carlos Diez-Palma

3

, Jorge Aristizabal-Maya

2

1

Neurosurgery program, Universidad el bosque, Bogotá, Colombia, Colombia

2

Fundación Cardioinfantil, Bogotá, Colombia

3

Clinica Shaio, Bogotá, Colombia

Introduction: The optimal surgical approach for lumbar degenerative pathology remains controversial. While ALIF with posterior instrumentation (ALIF+PI) provides maximum stability, standalone ALIF (sa-ALIF) offers reduced morbidity with preservation of posterior elements. The present review aims to compare long-term clinical and radiographic outcomes between sa-ALIF and ALIF+PI, establishing precise indications for each technique. Material and Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidelines. Comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases (2000-2024) for comparative studies evaluating sa-ALIF versus ALIF+PI. Inclusion criteria: adult patients with lumbar degenerative pathology, minimum 2-year follow-up, data on clinical and radiographic outcomes. Data extraction included fusion rates, clinical improvement (ODI, VAS), complications, and reoperation rates. Results: Comparative analysis revealed similar fusion rates: sa-ALIF 89.3% vs ALIF+PI 92.1% (p = 0.18). Clinical outcomes showed comparable improvements: ODI reduction sa-ALIF -21.6 points vs ALIF+PI -16.0 points (p = 0.12), with sa-ALIF demonstrating superior SF-36 physical component improvement (+12.6 vs +8.8 points, p < 0.03). ## A275: Risk of nerve injury in LLIF: a propensity-matched assessment of retractor time and postoperative neurologic outcomes

Kyle Dann

1

, Michael McDermott

2

, Alfred-John Bayaton

2

, Ashish Patel

1

1

The Spine Center at Duly Health and Care, Naperville IL, United States

2

Kettering Health Grandview Hospital Orthopedic Surgery Residency Program, Dayton OH, United States

Introduction: For many lateral surgeons, a psoas retraction time under 20 minutes has been considered a surrogate marker for minimizing nerve injury risk since Bendersky first suggested it in 2015. However, this threshold was merely an observation of that study, not the product of multivariate analysis. This has led to an emphasis on minimizing retractor time in conventional teaching, often adhering to a “20-minute rule.” Our recent multi-center analysis examined the retractor time theory with a study of 658 patients, finding no relationship between retractor time and injury, highlighting that emphasizing speed over technical precision may not be what is best for our patients. This study aims to re-examine the relationship between retraction time and nerve injury in Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion (LLIF) using a rigorously propensity-matched cohort to provide a more robust evaluation of the “20-minute rule.” Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study of 658 patients undergoing LLIF was propensity matched based on gender, age, surgical positioning, and number of operative levels, with a matching tolerance of 0.05. After matching, the cohort was split into groups based on retractor time above and below the 20-minute threshold, yielding two comparable groups: 172 patients with retractor times < 20 minutes and 170 patients with retractor times > 20 minutes. Following a statistical comparison of the groups, a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the predictive value of using retractor time as a threshold for injury. Results: The overall injury rate in the propensity-matched cohort was 2.9% (10/342). The average retractor time for injured patients was 19.8 ± 12.4 minutes compared to 21.2 ± 9.2 minutes for non-injured patients (p = 0.634). There was no statistical difference in the injury rates between patients above or below the 20-minute threshold (3.5% vs 2.3%, p = 0.541). The ROC curve analysis yielded an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.498, indicating that using a retractor time as a surrogate marker for injury had no predictive power, performing equivalently to a random guess. Conclusion: This propensity-matched analysis strongly indicates that postoperative quadriceps motor palsy after LLIF is not primarily caused by prolonged retractor time alone, and the “20-minute rule” is a poor predictor of injury. There is a need for a more sophisticated understanding of the injuries in LLIF and a modality that can identify injuries in real time. Until then, surgeons should prioritize meticulous technique over adherence to a strict time limit.

## A276: Discharge hemoglobin impacts functional recovery after lumbar fusion

Mitsuhiro Nishizawa

1

, Steven Glassman

, Mladen Djurasovic

, Charles Crawford, III

, Jeffrey Gum

1

, John Dimar

, Kirk Owens

, Justin Mathew

1

, Leah Carreon

1

1

Norton Leatherman Spine Center, Louisville, Kentucky, United States

Introduction: Acute blood loss anemia is common following lumbar spine surgery. Current protocols emphasize limiting transfusions resulting in more patients discharged with lower hemoglobin. The purpose of this study is to identify the impact of anemia at discharge on surgical outcomes and functional recovery following lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: Records of a consecutive series of patients who underwent one- or two-level transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) from 2013 to 2022 were reviewed. Standard demographics, surgical parameters, and complications within a year after discharge were recorded. ## A278: Preoperative opioid prescribing prior to lumbar decompression surgery markedly increases the risk of chronic opioid use at 6- and 12-month postoperatively

Nam Hunyh

1

, Darcy Fay

1

, Aaron Buckland

1

1

Spine and Scoliosis Research Associates Australia, Windsor, Australia

Introduction: Lumbar decompression surgeries are common procedures for lumbar canal stenosis and disc herniation. Opioids are commonly prescribed for lumbar back pain pre- and postoperatively. However they carry the risk ongoing usage and associated morbidity. This study aims to analyse the effects of preoperative opioid prescribing on chronic opioid use following 1-2 level lumbar decompression. Material and Methods: Consecutively, prospectively enrolled 1-2 level lumbar decompression patients were analysed. Patient demographics, complications and patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) were compared amongst opioid-sensitised and opioid-naïve patients. Opioid dosage was measured in morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Results: Of 254 patients, 77 were opioid-sensitised and 177 opioid-naïve. Demographics and complication rates were similar. Six-month postoperative MME was 3x higher amongst opioid-sensitised patients (1931 vs. 641 mg, p < 0.001) and correlated with MME prescribed 1-month (r = 0.428, p < 0.001) and 3-months preoperatively (r = 0.594, p < 0.001). More opioid-sensitised patients continued opioids at 6-weeks (36.4% vs. 11.3%, p < 0.001), 6-months (31.5% vs. 8.5%, p < 0.001) and 12-months (33.8% vs. 13.6%, p < 0.001) postoperatively. Six-week, 6-months and 12-months postoperative ODI, VAS-back, VAS-leg and EQ-5D-3L were similar. At 12-months postoperatively, opioid-sensitive patients scored worse for anxiety/depression (EQ-5D-3L) (1.44 vs. 1.21, p = 0.033) and social life (ODI) (1.33 vs. 0.68, p = 0.017). Conclusion: Preoperative opioid prescribing predisposes lumbar decompression patients to increased perioperative opioid requirements and higher rates of continued use postoperatively, particularly when prescribed for > 1 month preoperatively, with no differences in postoperative PROMs. Minimising preoperative opioid use and/or timely surgical referral can help minimise long-term opioid use.

## A279: Lateral interbody fusion at l4-5: safety and outcomes from a series of over 100 cases

Puya Alikhani

1

, Diego Soto Rubio

1

, Nikhil Dholaria

2

, Katherine Baker

1

, Sawyer Bauer

1

, Joshua Vignolles-Jeung

1

, Dana Saleh

1

, Mohamed Emara

1

, Mohsen Rostami

1

, Patrick Kim

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Brain and Spine, University of South Florida, Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States

2

University of Arizona College of Medicine - Phoenix, Phoenix, United States

Introduction: The lateral retroperitoneal approach has been widely adopted as a minimally invasive option for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis and adult spinal deformities, offering high fusion rates while preserving the posterior tension band. A major concern during lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF/XLIF) is the proximity of the femoral nerve, which varies by disc level and may increase the risk of postoperative motor and sensory deficits. Because knee extension is directly dependent on femoral nerve function, it serves as a reliable marker of nerve injury. Notably, as the femoral nerve descends caudally, it lies closer to the lumbar spine, and the safe working corridor narrows at L3-L4 and L4-L5, raising concern for higher complication rates at these levels. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent single-level LLIF at our tertiary center between 2014 and 2022. Demographic, operative, and complication data were collected, including intra- and postoperative outcomes. Descriptive statistics were generated using SPSS. Only patients with a minimum six-month follow-up were included. Results: A total of 133 patients underwent LLIF: L1-L2 (n = 8), L2-L3 (n = 18), L3-L4 (n = 32), and L4-L5 (n = 75). Patients treated at higher levels were older (71.6 ± 5.0 years at L1-L2 vs. 59.3 ± 9.4 years at L4-L5, p < .001). Sex, BMI, and hospital length of stay did not differ significantly. Percutaneous screw use was highest at L4-L5 (52%) and absent at L1-L2 (p < .001). Standalone procedures were most common at L2-L3 (83.3%) and least common at L4-L5 (41.3%, p = .007). Transient weakness occurred in 16.7% at L2-L3, 15.6% at L3-L4, and 9.3% at L4-L5 (p = .489). Pain- or effort-limited weakness was observed in 32% at L4-L5 and 46.9% at L3-L4 (p = .251). Acute thigh paresthesia was most frequent at L3-L4 (21.9%) but not statistically significant (p = .182). Transient paresthesia occurred in 15.6% at L3-L4 and 6.7% at L4-L5 (p = .157). Conclusion: LLIF is an effective, minimally invasive fusion technique with an acceptable safety profile. Although anatomical considerations suggest greater risk at L4-L5, due to the more anterior location of the lumbar plexus, we found no significant increase in neurological complications at L4-L5. Transient motor and sensory alterations were similarly distributed across levels. These findings indicate that femoral nerve-related complications are not uniquely elevated at L4-L5, though minimal traction time remains essential.

Borriwat Santipas

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Faculty Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand

Introduction: Cervical radiculopathy, a common consequence of cervical foraminal stenosis, often necessitates surgical intervention after conservative treatments fail. Among the available surgical options, posterior cervical foraminotomy (PCF) is a less invasive alternative to anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, aiming to relieve nerve root compression effectively. The evolution of minimally invasive techniques, including uniportal and biportal endoscopic approaches, has further refined this procedure, potentially offering reduced muscle dissection, less postoperative pain, and faster recovery. However, despite the advancements, a critical gap remains in the current understanding-specifically, the comparative effectiveness of the contralateral versus ipsilateral approaches during uniportal and biportal endoscopic PCF. Preliminary findings suggest that approach angles and the extent of facet resection might significantly impact clinical outcomes such as pain relief, functional recovery, and complication rates. The contralateral approach, potentially allowing a more favorable angle for decompression with minimal facet resection, might reduce the risk of postoperative instability and preserve the structural integrity of the cervical spine. Therefore, this study aims to conduct a systematic comparison of the clinical and radiographic outcomes of the contralateral and ipsilateral approaches in uniportal and biportal endoscopic PCF. By examining variables such as foraminal expansion rates, facet joint preservation, and postoperative clinical scores, this research could illuminate optimal surgical techniques and influence practice guidelines, thereby improving patient outcomes in the treatment of cervical radiculopathy due to foraminal stenosis. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 147 patients with cervical foraminal stenosis who underwent endoscopic spine surgery from single private specialized hospital. Clinical outcomes were assessed using operative time, complications, Macnab grading, and VAS scores for neck and arm pain. Radiographic outcomes included midforaminal diameter (MFD), distal foraminal diameter (DFD), midforaminal height (MFH), facet joint resection rate, and sagittal alignment change. The mean reduction in VAS scores for neck pain was 4.04 ± 1.46 in the uniportal group, 3.30 ± 1.69 in the contralateral biportal group, and 3.84 ± 1.52 in the ipsilateral biportal group (p = 0.107). Most radiographic parameters, including foraminal expansion ratios for MFD, DFD, and MFH, were similar among the groups. However, the contralateral biportal group had a significantly narrower facet joint width postoperatively (p = 0.014) and a higher, though not statistically significant, facet joint resection rate (p = 0.054). Conclusion: All three endoscopic surgical approaches provided similar clinical outcomes and radiographic improvements for cervical foraminal stenosis. The contralateral biportal approach resulted in a significantly narrower facet joint width postoperatively and a higher facet joint resection rate compared to the uniportal and ipsilateral biportal approaches. Long-term outcomes should be followed to further assess the benefits and potential risks of these surgical techniques.

## A281: Endoscopic discectomy reduces subsequent fusion: a multinational, real-world comparative study

Sung Huang Laurent Tsai

1

1

Taipei Medical University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: The choice between percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy (PELD) and open lumbar discectomy (OLD) for managing lumbar disc herniation (LDH) remains debated. While both techniques achieve comparable short-term outcomes, their long-term effects, particularly regarding the progression to spinal fusion, are underexplored. This study evaluates the risk of subsequent spinal fusion associated with PELD versus OLD and examines how patient demographics and comorbidities influence these outcomes. This study evaluates the long-term risk of spinal fusion following PELD versus OLD, with a focus on subgroup-specific differences, including age, race, BMI, and comorbidities. Material and Methods: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we analyzed data from 123,405 patients diagnosed with LDH between 2000 and 2023, including 93,853 PELD and 29,552 OLD cases. Mechanistically, PELD's preservation of paraspinal tissues and reduction of inflammation may explain its long-term advantages in minimizing adjacent segment degeneration and instability. Conclusion: PELD offers substantial long-term benefits in reducing the need for spinal fusion, particularly for younger, obese, and racially diverse patients. These findings support PELD as a personalized surgical approach that minimizes invasive burden while optimizing outcomes. Further research should investigate mechanisms underlying subgroup-specific differences and evaluate additional long-term endpoints, including functional recovery and quality of life.

Results: Among the 100 patients who met the inclusion criteria, UBE-LIF was performed in 76 and conventional open TLIF in 24. Clinical scores did not differ significantly between the groups at any time point (p > 0.05). Postoperative blood transfusion was required in 3 patients (11.5%) in the conventional group, whereas none was needed in the UBE-LIF group (p = 0.003). Length of hospital stay was also significantly shorter in the UBE-LIF group (45.4 vs. 98.6 hours, p < 0.001). The difference in 12-month postoperative fusion rates between UBE-LIF (100%) and conventional open TLIF (92.3%) was not significant (p = 0.07). Postoperative progression of Goutallier grade (paraspinal muscle degeneration) was not observed in the UBE-LIF group, whereas it occurred in 21 patients (80.8%) in the conventional open TLIF group (p < 0.001).1
Conclusion: Clinical outcomes improved similarly with both techniques. However, postoperative muscle degeneration, intraoperative blood loss, and length of hospital stay were more favorable in the UBE-LIF group. UBE-LIF appears to be a strong alternative to conventional open TLIF.
Keywords: Degenerative lumbar instability, degenerative lumbar spine disease, unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE), lumbar interbody fusion (LIF), UBE-LIF, conventional open surgery, conventional open TLIF

5

Introduction: Endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion has become a popular minimally invasive approach for treating degenerative lumbar spine disease. Among available techniques, unilateral biportal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion (UBE-LIF) and full-endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion (FE-LIF) are commonly performed. ## A285: Comparative analysis of full endoscopic unilateral laminotomy with bilateral decompression using 3D versus 2D spine endoscopy for the treatment of spinal stenosis: a retrospective study

Yuhsuan Chung

1

1

Show Chwan Memorial Hospital, Taiwan, Changhua, Taiwan

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is a common degenerative disease characterized by the narrowing of the spinal canal, leading to nerve compression and neurogenic claudication. This study aimed to compare the efficiency, safety, and surgical outcomes of unilateral laminotomy with bilateral decompression (ULBD) using a novel three-dimensional (3D) endoscopic technology versus the conventional two-dimensional (2D) endoscopic system. Material and Methods: This study included 62 consecutive patients who underwent full endoscopic ULBD for lumbar spinal stenosis at a tertiary medical center between January 2023 and December 2024. Patients were retrospectively assigned to either the 3D Endoscopy Group or the 2D Endoscopy Group. Data collected included demographic information, comorbidities, Charlson comorbidity index (CCI), operative details (surgery time, time to drill, time to yellow ligament, blood loss), and functional outcomes (Visual Analog Scale for pain, Oswestry Disability Index, patient satisfaction scores) evaluated at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results: In terms of surgical efficiency, the 3D group had significantly shorter times from skin incision to drill positioning (p = 0.047) and from skin incision to yellow ligament exposure (p < 0.001), demonstrating superior procedural navigation and speed. While intraoperative blood loss was lower in the 3D group, this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.079). The 3D endoscopic system also demonstrated significant advantages over the traditional 2D system in clinical outcome measures. The 3D group showed significantly lower back pain VAS scores at 6 months postoperatively compared to the 2D group (1.935 vs. 2.355, p = 0.050). Additionally, at 12 months postoperatively, the 3D group exhibited significantly lower ODI percentages (0.194 vs. 0.232, p = 0.050), reflecting better long-term pain relief and functional recovery. Although leg VAS scores in the 3D group were slightly higher than in the 2D group at 1, 3, and 12 months postoperatively, these differences did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05). Conclusion: The novel 3D endoscopic system significantly improves surgical efficiency by reducing the time from skin incision to drill positioning and yellow ligament exposure, demonstrating enhanced navigational accuracy during ULBD procedures. This optimization of surgical exposure and procedural workflow leads to better long-term pain relief and functional outcomes compared to conventional 2D endoscopy. By expediting the critical early stages of surgery and improving decompression processes, the 3D endoscopic system not only enhances surgical efficiency and safety but also effectively promotes postoperative pain relief and functional recovery, demonstrating its potential for widespread application in endoscopic spine surgery.

## A286: Clinical comparative study of video-assiste thoracoscopic surgery and uniportal endoscopic spine surgery in the treatment of thoracic disc herniation

Kunfeng Song

1

, Daniel Rosenthal

2

, Honggang Zhou

1

, Hejun Yang

1

, Mingkui Shen

1

1

Third People's Hospital of Henan Province, Zhengzhou, China

2

Hochtaunus-Kliniken, Bad Homburg, Germany

Introduction: Minimally invasive treatment techniques for thoracic disc herniation are constantly evolving. Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) has become a mature option, while Uniportal Endoscopic Spine Surgery (UESS), as a new minimally invasive technique, lacks sufficient comparative studies on its clinical efficacy with VATS. This study aimed to systematically compare the surgical efficacy, safety, and economic benefits of VATS and UESS in the treatment of thoracic disc herniation, clarify the clinical advantages and application scenarios of the two techniques, explore the potential direction of technical integration, and verify the application value of the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) concept in minimally invasive thoracic spine surgery. Material and Methods: A multicenter, prospective randomized controlled study was conducted. From January 2019 to December 2023, 520 patients with thoracic disc herniation from 5 tertiary hospitals nationwide were enrolled and randomly divided into the VATS group (260 cases) and UESS group (260 cases) at a 1:1 ratio. A stratified randomization method was used, with lesion segments (upper thoracic T1-T4, middle thoracic T5-T8, lower thoracic T9-T12), herniation types (soft herniation, calcified herniation), patient age (< 45 years, 45-60 years, > 60 years), and comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes) as stratification factors to ensure balanced baseline data between groups. The evaluation indicators included: ① Surgery-related indicators (operation time, intraoperative blood loss, incision length); ② Clinical efficacy (VAS pain score, mJOA neurological function score at 1 week, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively); ③ Long-term prognosis (1-year postoperative recurrence rate, complication rate); ④ Economic indicators (hospitalization cost, postoperative rehabilitation cost); ⑤ Patient-reported outcomes (SF-36 quality of life score). Innovatively, three-dimensional kinematic analysis was introduced to evaluate spinal stability, advanced intraoperative neuromonitoring system (transcranial motor evoked potentials + somatosensory evoked potentials) was used to reduce the risk of nerve injury, and diffusion tensor imaging was applied to assess spinal cord microstructure changes. Meanwhile, both groups systematically implemented the ERAS protocol (including preoperative nutritional support, intraoperative temperature protection, postoperative multimodal analgesia, and early ambulation guidance). Results: All patients in both groups completed follow-up (follow-up rate 100%) with no loss to follow-up. ① Surgery-related indicators: The average operation time in the UESS group (92.3 ± 15.7 min) was significantly shorter than that in the VATS group (108.6 ± 18.2 min) (t = 8.72, p < 0.001); the average intraoperative blood loss in the UESS group (35.6 ± 12.8 mL) was significantly less than that in the VATS group (89.2 ± 21.5 mL) (t = 26.35, p < 0.001); the incision length in the UESS group (1.2 ± 0.3 cm) was significantly smaller than that in the VATS group (3.5 ± 0.8 cm) (t = 38.16, p < 0.001). ② ERAS application effect: After implementing the ERAS protocol, the average length of hospital stay was reduced from 7.2 days (in the preoperative pilot study) to 4.3 days in the UESS group, and from 8.1 days to 5.1 days in the VATS group, with significant reductions in both groups (all p < 0.001); the ERAS protocol had a more significant effect on elderly patients (> 60 years old), with the postoperative complication rate in this subgroup decreasing from 12.5% (16/128) to 7.2% (9/125) (χ2 = 4.23, p < 0.05), and the incidence of major complications (pulmonary infection, pleural effusion) all decreased. ③ Learning curve and long-term efficacy: After completing 30 surgical operations, the operation time in the UESS group shortened from the initial (115.4 ± 18.6) min to a stable level (88.2 ± 10.5) min, with a flatter learning curve than that in the VATS group; at 1 year postoperatively, the mJOA scores of both groups significantly improved (UESS group: 7.8 ± 1.6 points preoperatively → 11.2 ± 1.3 points postoperatively; VATS group: 7.6 ± 1.5 points preoperatively → 10.8 ± 1.4 points postoperatively), with no significant difference between groups (p > 0.05). However, the scores of “bodily pain” and “physical function” dimensions in the SF-36 score of the UESS group were significantly higher than those of the VATS group (all p < 0.05); there was no significant difference in the recurrence rate between the two groups (UESS group: 1.5% (4/260), VATS group: 1.9% (5/260), p > 0.05). Conclusion: The UESS technique breaks the traditional perception that “higher minimally invasive degree leads to longer operation time”. It is significantly superior to VATS in terms of operation time, intraoperative blood loss, and incision trauma, with a flat learning curve that is easier to promote. The systematic application of the ERAS concept can further shorten the length of hospital stay for patients in both groups, especially reducing the risk of postoperative complications in elderly patients and significantly improving prognosis. The two techniques have comparable effects in long-term neurological function recovery and recurrence rate, but UESS has more advantages in improving patients' subjective quality of life. In the future, the technical integration model of “UESS precise decompression + VATS spinal stability reconstruction” can be explored to provide a more optimized plan for the minimally invasive treatment of thoracic disc herniation.

## A287: Intraoperative local methylprednisolone in single-position lateral decubitus oblique lumbar interbody fusion (OLIF) for postoperative anterior thigh pain prevention: a randomized controlled trial

Kantadon Prateepswangwong

1

, Worawat Limthongkul

1

, Vit Kotheeranurak

1

, Weerasak Singhatanadgige

1

, Wicharn Yingsakmongkol

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, Faculty of Medicine, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand

Introduction: Oblique lumbar interbody fusion (OLIF) is a minimally invasive lumbar fusion surgery in which interbody cage is inserted through an oblique lateral approach, positioned anterior to psoas major muscle (PMM). Although this approach reduces the risk of complications from direct injury to PMM or lumbar plexus, anterior thigh pain (ATP) remains one of the most common postoperative problems. Hypothesis of this study is that locally administered steroid, methylprednisolone, may reduce the inflammation of PMM and consequently prevent ATP. Material and Methods: This study was a prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial in single institute. Patients with degenerative spine disease who underwent single level OLIF using single lateral position with percutaneous pedicle screw fixation were randomized into two groups. A 3x3 cm sterile, absorbable gelatin sponge soaked with 2 cc of 80mg methylprednisolone (intervention; I group) or 2 cc of saline (control; C group), was placed anterior to PMM (OLIF cage corridor). The primary outcome was postoperative ATP, measured using the visual analog scale (VAS) at nine time points: 0, 1, and 2 days; 1 and 2 weeks; 1, 3, and 6 months; and 1 year postoperatively. Secondary outcomes consist of muscle damage cytokines: creatinine (Cr), creatinine phosphokinase (CK), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH); inflammatory cytokines: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α); cross-sectional area of psoas major muscle (PMM-CSA) from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); and morphine consumption during admission. Results: Forty patients were included, with 20 in each group. The most common surgical level was L4/5 (95% in I group and 85% in C group). There were no statistically significant differences in demographic data, operative time, or psoas retraction time. Both groups showed significant clinical improvement, with no significant difference between them. No statistically significant differences were found in any biomarkers or morphine consumption. PMM-CSA was slightly lower in I group (955.8 mm2) compared to C group (1046.7 mm2), albeit not statistically significant. However, when comparing participants with and without ATP, PMM retraction time was identified as the only significant factor (37.5 min in the ATP group vs. 29.1 min in the no-ATP group; p = 0.023). Conclusion: Local methylprednisolone in the OLIF corridor was not effective as an intervention to prevent ATP. Additionally, serum muscle damage markers and inflammatory cytokines could not be used as indicators to predict ATP. Based on our study, the factor that related to ATP is PMM retraction time of more than 30 minutes.

## A288: Minimally invasive lateral lumbar interbody fusion showed a lower incidence of radiologic adjacent segment pathology than conventional posterior lumbar interbody fusion

Jaewan Soh

1

, Jae Chul Lee

2

1

Hanyang University Guri Hospital, College of Medicine, Guri, South Korea

2

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Soonchunhyang University Seoul Hospital, College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Radiologic adjacent segment pathology (R-ASP) is a significant consequence following lumbar spinal fusion, potentially resulting from compromised integrity of posterior structures. Few studies have directly compared the incidence of R-ASP between minimally invasive lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) and conventional posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF). To analyze risk factors for R-ASP and compare clinical outcomes between minimally invasive LLIF supplemented with percutaneous pedicle screw fixation and open conventional PLIF. Material and Methods: This study included 107 patients who underwent one- or two-segment spinal fusion for degenerative lumbar disease. Fifty-one patients underwent minimally invasive LLIF, while 56 received conventional PLIF. Factors related to the occurrence of R-ASP were investigated by analyzing demographic profiles, radiological results, and clinical outcomes. The correlation between clinical results was analyzed based on fusion methods and the presence of R-ASP. We analyzed patient-related factors, preoperative spinal diagnosis, number of fused segments, and radiologic evaluations. Clinical outcomes were also assessed. Cox regression survival analysis was performed to determine risk factors for R-ASP. The annual incidence and cumulative survival rate of R-ASP were calculated using the life-table method and Kaplan-Meier survival curve. Results: Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified three significant risk factors for R-ASP: PLIF over LLIF (p = 0.028, Hazard Ratio (HR) = 2.321, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) = 1.096-4.913), postoperative PI-LL mismatch ≥ 10° (p = 0.022, HR = 2.280, 95% CI = 1.126-4.617), and preoperative facet arthropathy grade ≥ 2 (p = 0.016, HR = 3.491, 95% CI = 1.266-9.629). Clinical outcomes showed that the final VAS for lower back pain was significantly lower in patients who underwent the LLIF and in the patients who did not develop R-ASP. Conclusion: Minimally invasive fusion techniques that preserve posterior structures may slow the progression of degenerative changes in adjacent segments. To reduce R-ASP, preoperative assessment of facet degeneration and adequate restoration of sagittal balance during surgery are crucial considerations.

## A290: Comparing the prognostic value of standard, modified, calibrated, and T2-weighted vertebral bone quality scores for cage subsidence following single-level anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: a retrospective observational study

Omar Lubbad

1

, Laila Lubbad

2

, Suzanne Murphy

3

, Nektarios K Mazarakis

4

1

Brighton and Sussex Medical School, Brighton, United Kingdom

2

Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland Medical School, Manama, Bahrain

3

Department of Surgery, Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, Brighton, Ireland

4

Department of neurosurgery, Royal Sussex County Hospital, Brighton, United Kingdom

Introduction: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived vertebral bone quality (VBQ) scores have emerged as potential predictors of cage subsidence after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). Several modifications of the VBQ method have been proposed, but their relative predictive performance remains uncertain. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 114 patients undergoing single-level ACDF (71 without subsidence, 43 with subsidence). Demographic, clinical, surgical, and imaging variables were recorded. Bone quality was assessed using VBQ, calibrated VBQ (cVBQ), modified VBQ (MVBQ), posterior VBQ variants, and T2-weighted signal-based measures (T2CSF, T2FAT). Logistic regression was used to assess associations with subsidence. Predictive performance was evaluated with ROC analysis, DeLong’s test, calibration slopes and intercepts, McNemar’s test, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and Bland-Altman agreement. Results: Baseline demographic and comorbidity profiles were comparable between groups, although subsidence occurred more frequently at C3/4 (p = 0.014). On univariate regression, higher VBQ-derived scores and T2CSF were all significantly associated with subsidence (odds ratios 1.7-5.1, all p < 0.05), with VBQ showing the strongest effect (OR 5.14, 95% CI 2.42-10.94, p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis adjusting for age, sex, cage material, and plate use did not identify independent demographic or surgical predictors. ROC analysis showed that cVBQ achieved the highest discrimination (AUC 0.824, 95% CI 0.744-0.903), followed by cPVBQ and cMVBQ (AUCs 0.806-0.814), while T2CSF and T2FAT performed poorly (AUC 0.672-0.663). Pairwise DeLong testing confirmed that VBQ-based scores significantly outperformed T2CSF (p ≤ 0.04), but not each other. McNemar’s test demonstrated significant classification differences between VBQ, cVBQ, and MVBQ (all p < 0.05). NRI showed modest improvement for cVBQ over VBQ (+0.26), whereas T2CSF consistently reduced classification performance. Calibration analysis indicated acceptable slopes for VBQ-derived metrics (1.20-1.64) but poor calibration for T2CSF (slope 4.76). Bland-Altman analysis confirmed close agreement between VBQ, cVBQ, and MVBQ, with wide bias and poor concordance for T2CSF. Conclusion: MRI-derived bone quality scores, particularly cVBQ, demonstrate strong predictive performance for cage subsidence after ACDF, independent of patient or surgical factors. In contrast, T2-based measures show poor discrimination and calibration. These findings support cVBQ as the most robust MRI-derived predictor of bone quality-related implant failure.
