## A291: Preoperative malnutrition is associated with increased postoperative complications following lumbar fusion: a propensity-matched analysis

Ali Mehaidli

1

, Muaaz Wajahath

2

, Jad Lawand

3

, Omar Abdalla

4

, Haytham Alqasmi

4

, Ahmad Almaat

4

, Alqasim Elnaggar

4

, Lorenzo Deveza

5

, Noah Hodson

1

, Kevin Taliaferro

1

, Ryan Berger

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Henry Ford Hospital, Detroit, United States

2

Michigan State University College of Human Medicine, East Lansing, United States

3

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, John Peter Smith Health Network, Fort Worth, United States

4

Wayne State University School of Medicine, Detroit, United States

5

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, United States

Introduction: Lumbar fusion (LF) is a common surgical intervention used to manage a variety of spinal conditions, including degenerative disc disease, spondylolisthesis, and spinal instability. While effective for improving pain and function in select patients, LF is also associated with significant short- and long-term risks, including surgical site infection, pseudoarthrosis, readmission, and the need for revision procedures. One increasingly recognized yet under-addressed modifiable risk factor is preoperative malnutrition, which has been previously associated with impaired wound healing and increased susceptibility to infection. This study aimed to evaluate the association between preoperative malnutrition and postoperative outcomes after LF using a large, multicenter dataset with long-term follow-up. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort analysis was performed using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, including adults undergoing LF between 2003 and 2023. Malnutrition was defined as serum albumin < 3.5 g/dL or leukocyte count < 1,500/mm3 within one year before surgery. Patients were matched 1:1 by propensity scoring for demographics, comorbidities, body mass index, and surgical approach, yielding two cohorts of 20,693 each. Outcomes were assessed at 90 days and 5 years postoperatively. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models. Results: Malnourished patients experienced significantly higher 90-day rates of transfusion (8.4% vs 4.5%; HR 1.87, 95% CI 1.73-2.02), wound complications (2.6% vs 1.5%; HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.48-1.95), infection (3.2% vs 2.3%; HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.22-1.54), and hospital readmission (17.3% vs 13.8%; HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.20-1.32). All-cause mortality was lower in the malnourished cohort (4.3% vs 5.8%; HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.69-0.82), likely reflecting selection bias. Conclusion: Preoperative malnutrition is independently associated with significantly higher short- and long-term complication rates after LF, including infection, transfusion, readmission, pseudoarthrosis, and revision surgery. These findings underscore the importance of routine nutritional screening and optimization as part of preoperative planning in spine surgery. Incorporating nutritional assessment into perioperative risk stratification may reduce morbidity, improve surgical success, and decrease healthcare utilization.

## A292: Presentations, management strategies, and outcomes of intracardiac cement embolism following spinal vertebral augmentation: a systematic review of case reports

Omar Lubbad

1

, Laila Lubbad

2

, Guiseppe Morassi

3

, Nektarios K Mazarakis

3

1

Brighton and Sussex Medical School, Brighton, United Kingdom

2

Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland Medical School, Manama, Bahrain

3

Department of neurosurgery, Royal Sussex County Hospital, Brighton, United Kingdom

Introduction: Intracardiac cement embolism (ICE) is a rare, but potentially life-threatening complication of percutaneous vertebroplasty (PV), percutaneous kyphoplasty (PK), and cement augmented pedicle screw (CAPS) fixation. This systematic review aims to summarise and compare patient presentations, management approaches, and clinical outcomes of ICE. Material and Methods: PRISMA guidelines were followed. Standard medical databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, Pubmed, and Cochrane Library were searched to find case reports or series on patients with ICE following PV, PK, or CAPS. Data on patient demographics, embolus location, diagnostic modalities, management strategies, and outcomes were recorded. Results: 67 case reports and 2 case series were included with 71 patients in total. 67 patients presented symptomatically with the most common complaints being chest pain and dyspnoea, the other 4 cases were incidentally discovered. Emboli were predominantly found in the right heart and were primarily discovered via echocardiography or computed tomography. Open-heart surgery was the most adopted management strategy (46 cases, 100% retrieval success), especially in complicated symptomatic cases. Endovascular (11 cases, 72% retrieval success) or conservative approaches (14 cases, 2 mortalities) were reserved for asymptomatic cases with smaller emboli or patients not deemed fit for surgery. Reported mortality was low across all patients, but delayed diagnosis was associated with more severe cardiopulmonary complications. Notably, 28 patients presented within the first day postoperatively, indicating an early peak in presentation. Conclusion: Open-heart surgery seems to be the preferred, most effective intervention for ICE, while endovascular and conservative management were viable in select cases. However, due to the potential for delayed complications, conservative management should be avoided. Earlier diagnosis is imperative for improving patient outcomes and preventing severe complications.

## A293: Complications after anterior lumbar interbody fusion in patients with prior abdominal surgery

Hannah Shelby

1

, Sarah Bergren

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) is a widely utilized surgical technique for the treatment of numerous spinal pathologies. The ALIF approach necessitates mobilizing the intra-abdominal viscera and vasculature, understandably, there is a unique morbidity profile associated with this approach. Adhesions, scarring, and altered anatomy following procedures such as laparotomy, cesarean section, colectomy, or other major abdominal operations may increase operative difficulty and elevate the risk of complications. Existing literature often cites significant prior abdominal surgery with adhesions as a relative contraindication to ALIF. There is a paucity of data regarding the rates of ALIF post-op complications following specific abdominal surgeries and the nature of these complications. Of the 1,123,841 ALIF patients from 2010-2024, patients were stratified according to history of prior cesarean section (CSEC; n = 5,085), prior non-obstetric abdominal surgery (ABD; n = 49,734), any prior abdominal surgery (ANYABD; n = 54,819), and no prior abdominal surgery (NOABD; n = 1,069,022). Outcomes included complications within 30 days, 90 days, and one year. Complication subtypes included vascular injury, gastrointestinal complications (e.g., ileus, fistula), venous thromboembolism, infection, reoperation, and mechanical complications. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression were performed with predictor variables of age, sex, and Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI). Results: Among 1,123,841 ALIF patients (57% male), total complications occurred in 28,698 (2.6%) at 30 days, 39,858 (3.5%) at 90 days, and 60,824 (5.4%) at 1 year. Univariate analyses demonstrated that prior abdominal surgery significantly increased the odds of complications in nearly all sub-groups. Patients with prior non-obstetric abdominal surgery (ABD) or any abdominal surgery (ANYABD) had more than double the odds of complications compared to those without abdominal surgery (NOABD) at all time points (1-year OR 2.3, 95% CI 2.2-2.4; p < 0.0001). On the other hand, patients with a history of cesarean section (CSEC) showed no significant increase in risk compared to NOABD (1-year OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.99-1.35; p = 0.07). However, after adjusting for age, sex, and comorbidity burden (ECI) the differences between groups were no longer significant (ABD vs NOABD at 1 year: OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.97-1.04; p = 0.82). The ECI in the adjusted model was the strongest predictor of complications (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.07-1.09, p < 0.0001). Conclusion: This study investigates the importance of surgical history in predicting ALIF complications and specific post-operative outcomes. Patients with prior abdominal surgery represent a vulnerable subgroup and would benefit from comorbidity optimization rather than solely surgical history guiding perioperative risk assessment and surgical planning.

## A294: Prevention of revision surgery through wound drainage in elderly patients undergoing posterior spinal fusion surgery - A prospective randomized multicenter study

Klaus Schnake

1

, Denis Rappert

1

, Olga Cheremina

1

, Matthias Pumberger

2

, Thilo Khakzad

2

, Lars Klapproth

3

, Jorg Franke

3

, Torsten Kluba

4

, Alexander Hammer

1

1

Center for Spinal and Scoliosis Surgery, Malteser Waldkrankenhaus St. Marien, Erlangen, Germany

2

Center for Musculoskeletal Surgery, Charité - University Medicine Berlin, Berlin, Germany

3

Department of Orthopedics, Klinikum Magdeburg, Magdeburg, Germany

4

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Städt. Klinikum Dresden, Dresden, Germany

Introduction: The purpose of this study was to examine whether wound drainage prevents the need for revision surgery in elderly patients undergoing posterior thoracolumbar spinal fusion surgery involving up to four segments. Material and Methods: Multicenter, prospective, randomized study including patients (age > 65 years) with degenerative diseases, deformities, or fractures. The drainage group (DG) received two drains, which were removed after at least two and no more than four days. The exclusion criteria were: dural tears, infections (e.g. spondylodiscitis), inflammatory diseases, tumours, multiple injuries, polytrauma, unstable fractures and known coagulation disorders. Categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square test and Mann-Whitney U-test. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with revision surgery after three months. Linear regression analysis was performed to detect factors modifying LOS. Results: The evaluation included 123 patients, with an average age of 74.55 years (range 66-89 years). Revision rate was significantly higher in the non-drainage group (NDG) (19 of 64 patients; 29.7%), compared to DG (7 of 59 patients; 11.9%) (p = 0.016; odds ratio (OR) 3.14; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.21 - 8.14). There were no revisions due to hematoma in the DG compared with NDG (7 of 64; 10.9%) (p = 0.0087). Multivariate analysis revealed that the use of drainage (p = 0.015; OR 0.25; 95% CI 0.08-0.77), low body mass index (BMI) (p = 0.012; OR 1.15; 95% CI 1.03-1.28), and a greater number of operated segments (p = 0.024; OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.22-0.90) were significant predictors of avoiding revision surgery in this group. The application of a wound drainage had no significant impact on length of stay (LOS) (LOS no drain: 13.13 days ± 7.79 days; LOS with drain: 12.59 days ± 7.58 days; p = 0.67). In multivariate analysis LOS was not significantly predicted by the use of a drainage system (p = 0.25). Conclusion: Using wound drainage significantly decreases the early revision rate in elderly patients undergoing posterior thoracolumbar spinal fusion surgery. This is especially true for revisions caused by hematoma.

## A295: Extended oral antibiotic prophylaxis after anterior cervical spinal fusion is associated with increased infection and sepsis rates

Michael Kim

1

, Melissa Romoff

1

, Emily Tse

1

, Courtney Spitzer

1

, Andy Ton

1

, Vivian Chen

1

, Ryan Le

1

, Abhinav Sharma

1

, Justin Chan

1

, Emily Mills

1

, Hao-Hua Wu

1

, Don Park

1

, Yu-po Lee

1

, Nitin Bhatia

1

, Sohaib Hashmi

1

1

Univeristy of California, Irvine, Orange, United States

Introduction: Extended oral antibiotic prophylaxis, commonly employed in hip and knee arthroplasty beyond the standard 24-hour perioperative period1, has gained popularity as a preventive measure2. However, recent large-scale matched cohort studies have reported no reduction in prosthetic joint infection rates and, in some cases, an increase in complications. Despite limited evidence, the practice remains widespread, particularly among high-risk patients3,4. In spine surgery, the efficacy of extended oral antibiotics in reducing postoperative infection, sepsis, or revision rates has not been evaluated in large, multi-institutional studies. Given the rising concerns over antibiotic resistance and microbiome disruption, this study investigates the clinical utility of extended prophylaxis following anterior cervical spinal surgery. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was performed using data from the TriNetX United States Collaborative Network. Adult patients (≥ 18 years) who underwent anterior cervical spinal surgery were identified via CPT codes. All patients were assumed to have received standard intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis within 24 hours postoperatively. Cohorts were defined by the presence or absence of extended oral antibiotic prescriptions administered between 24 hours and 7 days following surgery. Propensity score matching (1:1) was used to control for age, sex, BMI, smoking status, and relevant comorbidities (e.g., renal failure, diabetes mellitus). The primary outcome was 90-day postoperative spinal surgical site infection. Secondary outcomes included reoperation and sepsis. Outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier survival estimates, hazard ratios, and cumulative incidence statistics. Results: A total of 4,964 patients who received extended oral antibiotics following anterior cervical spinal fusion were propensity score matched 1:1 to 4,964 patients who did not. The 90-day incidence of surgical site infection was not statistically significant between cohorts (16.277% vs. 15.008%; RR: 1.10, p = 0.0818). Reoperation rates were also similar, with 3.71% in the extended antibiotic group and 3.10% in controls (p = 0.0969). However, incidence of sepsis was significantly higher in the extended antibiotic group (2.56% vs. 1.23%; RR: 2.11, p < 0.0001). Wound infections were also more common in the extended antibiotic group (4.029% vs. 2.115%; RR 1.943, p < 0.0001). Conclusion: Extended oral antibiotic prophylaxis following cervical spinal fusion was not associated with a significant reduction of surgical site infection or reoperation. However, patients who received extended antibiotics experienced significantly higher rates of sepsis and wound infection compared to matched controls. These findings, while accounting for potential selection bias, challenge the presumed protective benefit of extended antibiotic use in this context. In light of the increased complication rates and the broader implications for antimicrobial resistance and microbiome disruption, the routine use of extended prophylaxis warrants critical reevaluation in anterior cervical spinal surgery.

## A296: Should venous thromboembolism chemoprophylaxis be utilized following spinal fusions? A clinical decision analysis

Sofia Perez

1

, Owen Dean

1

, Jackson Pophal

1

, Emmanuel Fatodu

1

, Jack Eichman

1

, Ilyas Aleem

1,2

1

University of Michigan Medical School, Ann Arbor, United States

2

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Michigan Medicine, Ann Arbor, United States

Introduction: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), which includes deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is a life-threatening complication that can occur after major surgery. Despite increasing rates of spinal fusions nationally, the efficacy of VTE chemoprophylaxis remain unknown, and chemoprophylaxis comes with the risk of bleeding, epidural hematoma, and possible reoperation. The current literature is limited by heterogeneous patient populations, surgical techniques, and inconsistent timing and dose of chemoprophylaxis. As direct comparisons of each intervention may not reflect health utility values for the different outcomes and associated probabilities, we sought to synthesize the available evidence and construct a clinical decision tree model to better guide clinicians in the use of VTE prophylaxis following spinal fusion. Material and Methods: We constructed a decision analytic model representing potential outcomes after spinal fusions with and without VTE prophylaxis. Probabilities of outcomes (epidural hematoma, VTE event) were derived from a systematic review of randomized trials and observational studies. Five reviewers independently screened abstracts and full texts, with data extracted to derive probabilities and health utility values. A clinical decision tree was constructed using the weighted averages of each outcome probability and utility values among the studies collected. Weighted probabilities and utility values were combined to conduct a rollback analysis and subsequent sensitivity analysis to determine the strength of utilities. Results: A total of 8 studies with 2,177 patients were included in the final analysis. The base-case analysis demonstrated that VTE Chemoprophylaxis (n = 1113) yielded an expected utility of 0.79 compared to 0.89 for No VTE Chemoprophylaxis (n= 1064). Results from one-way sensitivity analyses indicated that the model conclusions were robust to plausible variations in key parameters, including utility values and probabilities associated with VTE and epidural hematomas. Across tested ranges, the expected utility values varied minimally (range: 0.85 to .94 for No VTE Chemoprophylaxis versus 0.75 to 0.84 for VTE Chemoprophylaxis), and No VTE Chemoprophylaxis remained the preferred option at all threshold changes for both utility values and probabilities. Conclusion: When outcomes and their health utilities are evaluated in a systematic manner, VTE chemoprophylaxis does not show any added benefit after spinal fusions, even over a wide range of outcome probabilities and health utility values.

## A297: The use of the psoas-to-lumbar vertebrae index and modified frailty index in predicting postoperative complications in degenerative spine surgery: can sarcopenia or frailty be underestimated?

Marco Manzetti

1,2

, Alberto Ruffilli

1,2

, Giovanni Viroli

1,2

, Matteo Traversari

1

, Marco Ialuna

1

, Cesare Faldini

1

1

Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Clinica Ortopedica e Traumatologica I, Bologna, Italy

2

Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Science - DIBINEM, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Degenerative spine disease (DSD) is increasingly prevalent due to aging populations, leading to higher surgical interventions and associated complications. This necessitates a comprehensive preoperative assessment, evaluating frailty through tools such as the modified Frailty Index 5 and modified Frailty Index 11 (mFI-5 and mFI-11). Despite the utility of mFI-5 and mFI-11 in predicting postoperative complications, these indices do not account for sarcopenia, a syndrome related to but distinct from frailty, which is associated with higher complication rates. This paper aims to retrospectively evaluate the influence of sarcopenia and frailty on postoperative adverse events in a cohort of patients who underwent posterior spine fusion for degenerative disease of the lumbar spine. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 286 patients aged 50-85 years who underwent posterior lumbar fusion of up to three levels for DSD between 2010 and 2023. Exclusion criteria included trauma, tumor, revision surgery, scoliosis, rheumatologic disease, and malabsorptive disorders. Frailty was assessed with mFI-5 and mFI-11, while sarcopenia was measured on preoperative MRI using the psoas-to-lumbar vertebral index (PLVI). Primary outcomes were adverse events within 30 days, including surgical site infection, reoperation, cardiopulmonary, neurological, and systemic complications. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to identify independent predictors. Results: Higher frailty scores were significantly associated with increased postoperative complications (p < 0.05). Both mFI-5 and mFI-11 were predictive, with strong correlation between the two (r = 0.916). mFI-11 provided slightly higher discrimination, but receiver operating characteristic curves demonstrated comparable accuracy, supporting mFI-5 as a practical alternative. Complication rates rose progressively with higher frailty categories, including infections, reoperations, and systemic events. Sarcopenia, as measured by PLVI, was not associated with overall complication rates. A significant association emerged only with pulmonary complications (p = 0.031), while no correlations were observed for other outcomes. Multivariate logistic regression confirmed frailty as a strong independent predictor of postoperative complications, whereas sarcopenia did not retain significance. Odds ratios for frailty remained robust across different complication subgroups, but PLVI showed limited prognostic contribution and was excluded as an independent factor. Conclusion: Frailty, as measured by mFI-5 or mFI-11, is a reliable and independent predictor of early postoperative complications following lumbar fusion for DSD. In contrast, sarcopenia assessed by PLVI has limited predictive power, with relevance only to pulmonary outcomes. These findings highlight the superiority of frailty indices for preoperative risk stratification, offering a comprehensive reflection of biological reserve and vulnerability beyond muscle mass alone. Incorporating frailty screening into routine surgical planning may improve patient counseling, perioperative management, and outcome prediction. Further research should refine sarcopenia assessment methods and explore integrated models combining frailty, muscle quality, and systemic biomarkers.

## A298: Dynamic assessment of sagittal balance in patients with degenerative spinal deformity: a controlled biomechanical study

Armand Dominik Škapin

1 2

, Janez Vodičar

3

, Matej Supej

3

, Miha Vodičar

1 2

1

University Medical Centre Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia

2

Faculty of Medicine, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia

3

Faculty of Sport, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia

Introduction: Spinal degeneration is becoming increasingly common within the aging population and often leads to progressive deformity and worsening of sagittal balance. The resulting persistent pain and disability may necessitate surgical intervention. Surgical planning to restore optimal spinal alignment typically relies on preoperative standing full spine radiographs. However, this approach has limitations as it captures the spine only during a brief period of forced upright stance and does not always reflect the dynamic sagittal profile of the patient. This occurs because compensatory mechanisms may maintain normal sagittal balance during radiographic imaging but can sometimes fail during gait as the postural muscles become fatigued. To further explore this discrepancy, a controlled clinical biomechanical study was conducted to analyze sagittal balance dynamics during walking and compare it with sagittal balance during upright stance in patients with adult spinal deformity. Material and Methods: A total of 33 patients with pathological sagittal balance parameters on standing radiographs and clinical complaints of pain and disability, together with 31 matched controls, were enrolled. Standing full spine x-rays were obtained before and immediately after six minutes of walking. All participants underwent three-dimensional motion capture analysis during a six-minute walking assessment. Additionally, we analyzed body composition, muscle strength, and patient-reported outcome measures (VAS, ODI, EQ-5D-5L). Results: Radiological measurements after walking revealed statistically significant deterioration in all sagittal balance parameters, such as SVA (68.4 ± 52.1 mm to 80.4 ± 60.9 mm), as well as lumbar lordosis and thoracic kyphosis in the study group, while no such changes were observed in the control group. Measurements during three-dimensional motion capture showed substantial deterioration of sagittal balance during the transition from standing to walking, with significantly larger changes observed in the study group (for example, an increase in C7-L5-sagittal trunk shift from 69.1 ± 50.6 mm to 138.7 ± 51.9 mm) compared with the control group (20.9 ± 18.8 mm to 69.2 ± 19.7 mm). No additional deterioration occurred on average during the walk itself, although notable worsening was observed in three individual patients in the study group. Predictive factors for sagittal balance deterioration during walking included higher VAS scores, a subjective feeling of forward trunk tilt while walking, an increased extracellular to total body water ratio, and specific radiological parameters (PI, SS, LL, PI-LL, SVA, CAM-HA, OD-HA, GT). Conclusion: Sagittal balance compensatory mechanisms are significantly more effective in a standing position than during walking. The most significant deterioration occurs during the transition from standing to walking and mostly returns to baseline levels after walking. While sagittal balance remains stable in most patients during the walking phase, noticeable deterioration occurred in several individuals. The severity of spinal deformity appears to be the main factor influencing sagittal balance deterioration during walking.

## A299: Intervertebral disc degeneration: age-related mechanical changes and possible influence on adjacent vertebrae

Margherita Pasini

1

, Gaia Youssef

1

, Davide Alberti

1

, Luca Cristofolini

1

, Marco Palanca

1

1

Department of Industrial Engineering, Alma Mater Studiorum - University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration is a common age-related process and a leading cause of low back pain. Despite the crucial role of IVDs in maintaining spinal stability and flexibility, IVD degeneration is currently only partially considered by clinicians when assessing spine-related complications, such as osteoporotic (T-score, FRAX) or metastatic (SINS) fractures. Indeed, the IVD condition is typically assessed by providing morphological information through the Pfirrmann scale [1], which does not capture the associated mechanical changes. A comprehensive characterization of the IVDs biomechanical behaviour is essential to advance the current clinical knowledge. This study aimed to characterise mechanical changes in human IVDs across different ages and degeneration conditions to better understand their interaction with adjacent vertebrae. Material and Methods: Ten T12-L1 IVD specimens were harvested and prepared from human donors: 5 young (33 ± 2) and 5 elderly (63 ± 1) (Prot. 113043). Specimens were imaged using 3T-Magnetic Resonance (sagittal and axial T2-weighted sequences) and Computed Tomography to assess the degeneration of the IVDs (using the Pfirrmann scale [1]) and exclude pathological bone conditions. The specimens were mechanically tested using a spine simulator (MIB4.0-MAS2-S) under axial compression (up to 0.5% of the body weight), clockwise/counterclockwise torsion (up to 4Nm) and flexion/extension (up to 4Nm) loading in the elastic regime. A four-camera 3D-Digital Image Correlation system (Aramis Adjustable, Zeiss) was used to measure the full-field displacements and strains on the surface of the IVDs. The stiffness was calculated as the slope of the load-displacement curve between 20% and 80% of the maximum load. Deformations were measured and compared between the two age groups. Results: The young specimens showed no/mild IVD degeneration (Pfirrmann 1/2 [1]), while the elderly ones had moderate degeneration (Pfirrmann 3 [1]). Elderly IVDs were stiffer in axial compression (+111%), in flexion (+102%) and extension (+94%), while no differences were observed in torsion. Elderly IVDs showed larger deformations compared to young IVDs. Elderly IVDs also exhibited higher variability (+53%). The direction of the deformations was consistently oriented in young IVDs and scattered in elderly IVDs. Conclusion: The higher stiffness of degenerated/elderly IVDs represents a contributing factor to low back pain. It also increases the physical effort required to achieve certain spinal positions and restore the neutral posture, making these movements more difficult to perform. The deformation maps on the surface of the IVDs revealed localised zones of high strain in the elderly IVDs, reflecting their reduced ability to withstand high loads. Moreover, such deformation concentrations may be transmitted to adjacent vertebrae [2, 3], suggesting that degenerated IVDs may further compromise vertebral mechanical behaviour, potentially increasing the risk of fracture in case of vertebrae affected by pathologies. This study provides essential data to advance clinical and scientific understanding of the effects of IVD degeneration and ageing on spine biomechanics. Such insight could help identify predictive markers to support clinical decision-making and improve the quality of life for patients suffering from vertebral pathologies.
References
1. Pfirrmann. Spine 2001
2. Pasini. JMBBM 2025
3. Cavazzoni. Acta 2025
Acknowledgements: HEU-Funded METASTRA project (grant 101080135) and Fondazione del Monte (MULTIDISC project).

## A300: Early adjacent segment degenration and disc biochemical markers

Theodore Choma

1

, Jacob Kramer

1

, Aaron Stoker

1

, Dan Hogan

1

, Quayd Robertson

1

, Don Moore

1

, Nikhil Jain

1

, Abdul Buyuk

1

1

University of Missouri, Columbia, United States

Introduction: Adjacent segment degeneration (ASD) is a known complication following spinal fusion. Biomechanical mechanisms have been implicated but it remains unclear whether these patients share common underlying biochemical mechanisms. This study aims to investigate the biochemical differences in intervertebral disc cells in patients who experienced subsequent early ASD by analyzing tissue markers and cellular behavior in the discs that were surgically explanted, using these cells as a proxy for those involved in the ASD segment. Material and Methods: Intervertebral disc samples were routinely collected from 211 patients undergoing one- or two-level cervical and lumbar fusion surgeries between 2018 and 2022. Patients were followed for a minimum of one year (mean follow-up: 27 months) and stratified based on the presence of radiographic ASD. Tissue samples were analyzed for biochemical markers. Results: Disc cells from patients with early ASD exhibited significantly lower levels of sclerostin (p = .029) compared to unaffected segments. Perhaps the most striking is the substantially lower levels of TIMP (-1, -2, and -4) expression in the early ASD patients. It is unclear if these differences are based in genetic variations or epigenetics. These findings contribute to a basic understanding of ASD and may inform future strategies to mitigate its development in spine surgery.

## A301: Spino-pelvic sagittal changes during growth: result from a longitudinal retrospective study on 134 patients

Matteo Traversari

1

, Alberto Ruffilli

1

, Giovanni Viroli

1

, Marco Manzetti

1

, Chiara Ricci Petitoni

2

, Cesare Faldini

1

1

IRCCS - Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Dipartimento di Scienze Biomediche e Neuromotorie - DIBINEM, Bologna, Italy

2

IRCCS - Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Spinopelvic sagittal alignment evolves during growth, influenced by both morphological and biomechanical maturation. While few cross-sectional studies have described age-related changes in pelvic and spinal parameters, the lack of longitudinal data following the same individuals throughout skeletal development remains a major gap in the literature. A better understanding of these changes is essential to improve the characterization and management of adolescent patients with spinal deformities, both in conservative and surgical settings. The aim of the present retrospective longitudinal study was to characterize the evolution of spinopelvic morphological parameters during growth in a cohort of subjects treated conservatively for spinal deformities involving the cervical and/or thoracic spine, based on serial radiographic evaluations performed throughout skeletal maturation. Material and Methods: This was a retrospective longitudinal study based on full-spine standing bi-planar x-rays of 134 children or adolescent patients (mean age at baseline: 11.6 ± 1.8 years; mean follow-up: 2.6 ± 1.6 years), each undergoing between 2 and 8 spinal radiographic evaluations (mean: 2.88 x-rays, IQR: 1 x-ray) throughout skeletal maturation. A total of 386 radiographs were analyzed. All subjects were treated conservatively for spinal deformities involving the cervical and/or thoracic spine. Exclusion criteria included prior spinal surgery, neuromuscular or syndromic etiology, and any pathology affecting the lumbopelvic region. For each radiograph, spinopelvic morphologic parameters such as pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic thickness (distance between the center of the femoral heads and the midpoint of the S1 endplate), anteroposterior length of the S1 superior endplate, and relative pelvic thickness (pelvic thickness divided by S1 plateau width) were measured using Surgimap by two independent observers blinded to age and skeletal maturity stage. Skeletal maturity was assessed by a separate expert in pediatric orthopaedics using CVM stage, Risser sign, triradiate cartilage status, and Pesenti maturity classification (a five-stage system based on a combination of chronological age, triradiate cartilage closure, and Risser grade: stage 1 = prepuberty; stage 2 = early pubertal growth spurt; stage 3 = late pubertal growth spurt; stage 4 = deceleration; stage 5 = skeletal maturity). Patients were then stratified into subgroups representing distinct stages of skeletal development. Based on published data on the intra-observer measurement error of pelvic incidence, which typically ranges from 2° to 6° depending on imaging modality and observer experience, we considered as “true variation” only those changes greater than 3.5° between two timepoints. This threshold was chosen as a conservative approximation of the minimal detectable change. Changes in spinopelvic morphologic parameters were annotated in both absolute and relative terms across different skeletal maturity stages. The probability of observing a subsequent significant change in PI was calculated for each Pesenti maturity stage. Results: During growth, patients showed an average individual increase in PI, across multiple timepoints, resulting in a transition from 40.3° at Pesenti maturity stage 1 to a peak of 47.8° at stage 4-5. Patients who began longitudinal radiographic follow-up during Pesenti maturity stages 1 and 2 commonly experienced a significant absolute increase in PI over time. In contrast, such increases became progressively less frequent starting from stage 3, with the probability of observing further significant increases in PI dropped significantly after stage 2 (the first part of the pubertal growth spurt), suggesting a reduced potential for morphological spinopelvic changes once mid-pubertal development is reached. The probability of a true absolute increase in PI between two timepoints was 64.7% for transitions starting from Pesenti stage 1 (95% CI: 47.9%-78.5%), 60.0% from stage 2 (95% CI: 45.5%-73.0%), 14.3% from stage 3 (95% CI: 7.4%-25.7%), and 17.2% from stage 4 (95% CI: 7.6%-34.5%). Similar proportions were observed when considering relative PI changes, confirming that most spinopelvic morphological changes occur during the early stages of skeletal maturation, and that further modifications become unlikely once the triradiate cartilages are closed. Conclusion: Our results show that PI undergoes significant increase during skeletal maturation, with the most pronounced changes occurring between Pesenti maturity stages 1 and 3. In conclusion, only limited modifications in PI were seen once the triradiate cartilage was closed.

## A302: Greater cage angle ≠ greater alignment: rethinking TLIF planning

Schahin Salmanian

1

, Kiana Yeganeh

1

, Ryan Screven

1

, Diego Soto Rubio

1

, Mohammad Hassan A. Noureldine

1

, Jay I. Kumar

1

, Mohsen Rostami

1

, Mark S. Greenberg

1

, Puya Alikhani

1

1

University of South Florida, Department of Neurosurgery, Brain, and Spine, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) aims to arrest motion, restore spinal stability, and improve sagittal alignment. A common assumption in surgical planning is that interbody cages with greater lordosis will create larger changes in lumbar lordosis. However, the extent to which cage angle directly influences sagittal alignment remains poorly defined. This study assessed the relationship between the cage angle and the degree of segmental and global lordosis correction achieved following TLIF. Material and Methods: A retrospective review was performed on 106 adult patients who underwent TLIF between 2021 and 2024. Pre- and postoperative lateral radiographs were analyzed to measure segmental and global lumbar lordosis. Cage angle (in degrees) was recorded for each level. Correlation and linear regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between cage angle and achieved lordosis. Results: There was no statistically significant correlation between greater cage angles and lordosis correction at any spinal level. A slight inverse trend was observed overall (r = -0.173, p = 0.2058). L2-L3 showed the strongest negative correlation (r = -0.566, p = 0.434), while L3-L4 had a weak positive trend (r = 0.183, p = 0.550). L4-L5 and L5-S1 both demonstrated non-significant inverse correlations (r = -0.187, p = 0.340and r = -0.344, p = 0.331, respectively). Linear regression further supported these results, showing no significant association between cage angle and either segmental (R2 = 0.012, p = 0.21) or global (R2 = 0.008, p = 0.234) lordosis correction. Conclusion: This study challenges the assumption that larger cage angles lead to greater lordosis correction. No significant correlation was found across spinal levels, and higher cage angles may even be counterproductive. By avoiding hyperlordotic cages, surgeons may reduce the risk of subsidence while focusing on factors like technique, placement, and patient anatomy that more reliably impact alignment.

## A303: Biomechanical comparison of realignment strategies in patients with lumbar fusion to the pelvis

Christopher J. Nielsen

1

, Fatemeh Alavi

1

, Stephen Lewis

1

1

University of Toronto, University Health Network (UHN), Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Inadequate restoration of spinopelvic parameters following surgery has been associated with elevated mechanical loads, junctional failure, and worse clinical outcomes. While several realignment strategies have been proposed to optimize postoperative balance, the biomechanical implications of each strategy remain incompletely understood. The objective of this study is to compare different realignment strategies and clarify how specific alignment targets influence spinal forces at the proximal junction in patients undergoing lumbar fusion to the pelvis. Material and Methods: 41 patients (46 % female) with mean age of 68.9 7.2 with lumbar fusion to the pelvis were retrospectively reviewed. UIV in 90% was L2 and 10% was L1. The mean PI was 52.9o 11.9. Five realignment strategies including Age-adjusted, GAP, Segmental, Roussouly, T4-L1-axis were simulated. Sex-matched generic musculoskeletal (MSK) models were individualized for each suggested alignment. In total, 205 models were evaluated in standing posture, with spinal shear and compressive forces computed. Alignment strategies resulting in the lowest spinal forces were identified as optimal. Results: Across all patients, spinal forces varied significantly between simulated alignments. The optimal strategy with the lowest proximal junction compression was T4–L1-axis in 53.5% of cases, followed by Segmental, Roussouly, and GAP. In contrast, Age-adjusted, Roussouly, Segmental alignments most often minimized shear. On average, inter-alignment compression differences reached 149.8 N, with optimal strategies reducing forces by 15.6% compared with the next-best alternative. In several subgroups, reductions exceeded 20%, underscoring the clinical relevance of alignment selection. Stratified analysis showed that higher PI and older age were associated with greater inter-alignment variability. Conclusion: Realignment strategies have a substantial impact on proximal junction biomechanics after lumbar fusion to the pelvis. No single strategy was universally optimal, as the best alignment depended on individual pelvic incidence and age. However, the T4–L1-axis most consistently minimized compression, while Age-adjusted often reduced shear. These findings highlight the need for individualized alignment targets to optimize biomechanical efficiency, reduce junctional loading, and consequently mechanical complications.

## A305: Comparison of posterior atlantoaxial spondylodesis procedures: a biomechanical cadaver study

Adrian Cavalcanti Kußmaul

1

, Titus Kuehlein

1

1

Musculoskeletal University Center Munich (MUM), Munich, Germany

Introduction: Fractures of the atlas and axis remain the primary indication for C1-C2 fusion, largely due to demographic shifts increasing fracture incidence and the decline of rheumatic disease-related instability. While anterior screw osteosynthesis is often feasible in younger patients with minor instability, dorsal stabilisation remains the gold standard in complex fractures and severe dislocation. Among dorsal procedures, rigid screw fixation according to Harms is widely applied, consisting of a combination of atlas massa lateralis screws and axis isthmus srews. Recently, Harati et al. proposed a modified approach combining transarticular C1-C2 screws with atlas massa lateralis screws in a screw-rod system, generating three-point fixation. Biomechanical studies suggest this provides superior stability, but cadaveric validation has been lacking. This study aimed to compare the primary stability of the Harati and Harms techniques in human C1/C2 cadaver specimens. Material and Methods: Sixteen human cadaver cervical spines were collected, of which thirteen met inclusion criteria after radiological and structural assessment. Each specimen was tested in native, injured (Type II dens fracture), Harms, and Harati states. Testing followed established biomechanical protocols using flexion/extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation at 1 Nm with a axial preload of 50 N. Specimens were mounted in custom-designed pots with physiological alignment, and motion was recorded using a 3D optical measurement system. Statistical analysis employed Friedman tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons. Results: Both the Harms and Harati methods significantly reduced motion compared to native and injured states. Mean ROM values (°) were: flexion/extension, Harms 0.67 ± 0.25, Harati 0.59 ± 0.23; lateral flexion, Harms 0.95 ± 0.48, Harati 0.67 ± 0.47; and rotation, Harms 0.92 ± 0.24, Harati 0.55 ± 0.19. Direct comparison showed no significant differences between Harms and Harati in flexion/extension (p = 0.649). However, in rotation, the Harati technique achieved significantly greater stability (p = 0.048) and also in lateral flexion (p = 0.004). Conclusion: Both the Harms and Harati techniques demonstrated effective stabilization of C1/C2 instability. The Harati method provided superior stability regarding rotation and lateral flexion compared with the Harms procedure, while sagittal stability was comparable. These findings suggest that the Harati three-point fixation may offer biomechanical advantages in clinical scenarios requiring enhanced primary stability.

Diego Soto Rubio

1

, Chloe Chose

1

, Albert Brotgandel

, Dana Saleh

1

, Mohsen Rostami

1

, Daniel Colome

3

, Patrick Kim

1

, Puya Alikhani

1

, Jay I. Kumar

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Brain and Spine, University of South Florida, Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States

2

USF Health Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States

3

Florida Atlantic University Charles E. Schmidt College of Medicine, Boca Raton, FL, USA, Boca Raton, United States

Introduction: Prone positioning alone has been shown to increase lumbar lordosis before any surgical intervention. However, the ability to predict the degree of correction achieved from positioning has not been well established. This study evaluates whether preoperative imaging can reliably predict intraoperative positional correction in adult spinal deformity patients. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed adult patients with degenerative thoracolumbar deformity undergoing fusion from L2 or above to the pelvis. 1İstinye University, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Private Practice, Istanbul, Turkey

## A308: Distribution characteristics of vertebral CT Hounsfield unit values in patients with degenerative lumbar scoliosis

Fei Xu

1

, Weishi Li

1

1

Orthopaedic Department, Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: This study aims to identify how CT HU values vary in degenerative lumbar scoliosis (DLS) patients with different scoliotic apexes and in those with different degree of scoliosis. Material and Methods: We included 222 DLS patients and 140 lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) patients, dividing the DLS patients into two groups based on scoliotic apex location. Junyu Li

1

, Junjie Ma

2

, Hanwen Zhang

, Zhuo Ran Sun

1

, Yongqiang Wang

1

, Miao Yu

1

, Weishi Li

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing Key Laboratory of Spinal Disease Research, Engineering Research Center of Bone and Joint Precision Medicine, Beijing, China

2

Peking University Health Science Center, Beijing, China

Introduction: Degenerative lumbar scoliosis (DLS) is a prevalent spinal condition in the elderly, with an incidence of approximately 2%-68%. Numerous studies have verified the significant effect of SI on appearance and satisfaction of patients, and have regarded SI as one of the main determinants of evaluating the outcome of orthopedic surgery. Currently, there is only few systematic studies on the radiographic characteristics of DLS patients with SI. For DLS patients with SI, whether postoperative SB is important and how to achieve postoperative SB is unclear. By radiological observation, we identified two subtypes of SI in DLS patients, each with distinct clinical traits requiring tailored surgical approaches. Direct comparison between the two shoulder imbalance types showed that type II was associated with higher postoperative Cobb (p = 0.032) and AVT (p = 0.035), higher last-follow-up T1 tilt (p = 0.044), CRIA (p = 0.015), and Cobb angle (p = 0.012), and greater Cobb angle progression (p < 0.001). Conclusion: The Obeid classification stratifies prognosis: shoulder imbalance type II in Obeid I patients predicts poor coronal shift correction, while type I in Obeid II patients indicates residual apical translation. Preoperative identification is crucial for surgical planning.

## A310: AI-assisted prediction of RLDH using preoperative MRI and radiographic parameters

Sebastiano Mazzotta

1

, Francesco Certo

1

, Giulio Bonomo

1

, Giuseppe Barbagallo

1

1

A.O.U. Policlinico G. Rodolico - San Marco, Catania, Italy

Introduction: Recurrent lumbar disc herniation (rLDH) is a major complication after surgical discectomy, with an incidence ranging from 5% to 15% in published series. rLDH can worsen symptoms and necessitate reoperation, with substantial impact on patients’ quality of life. Numerous studies have explored the role of radiological parameters in predicting biomechanical changes of the spine and the risk of recurrence, but definitive conclusions remain lacking. Therefore, the aim is to analyze the association between preoperative radiological parameters and rLDH in order to identify potential predictors of recurrence and, based on these, optimize the surgical strategy. ## A311: Paraspinal fat index for assessment of sarcopenia in spine research

Murat Ekşi

1

, Emre Unal

2

, Mehmetzeki Yıldız

2

, Akın Akakın

2

, Türker Kılıç

1

, Deniz Konya

2

, Emel Özcan-Ekşi

3

1

İstinye University, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Bahçeşehir University, Istanbul, Turkey

3

Private Practice, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: The global population is aging at an unprecedented rate, increasing the importance of geriatric care. Age-related spinal deformities are expected to become more prevalent, and frailty represents a critical concern in elderly patients undergoing spine surgery. Previous studies have demonstrated a strong correlation between fat-infiltrated or atrophied paraspinal muscles and frailty. The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) has long been used to predict clinical outcomes in spine-related disorders and surgeries, preceding frailty assessments. However, no prior studies have evaluated the relationship between CCI and de novo spinal or paraspinal muscle degeneration. This study aimed to examine whether CCI is associated with spinal degeneration and fatty infiltration of the paraspinal muscles. Furthermore, if such an association existed, we aimed to develop a paraspinal fatty infiltration index to predict patients with higher CCI scores. Material and Methods: A previously established CCI cut-off value of 2.5 was used to stratify patients into two groups: CCI ≥ 2.5 and CCI < 2.5. The groups were compared in terms of intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), Modic changes, intradiscal vacuum phenomenon (IVP), intrafacet vacuum phenomenon (IfVP), and fatty infiltration of the paraspinal muscles across all lumbar levels. Results: A total of 208 participants were included, of whom 72.6% (n = 151) were women. The mean CCI score was 2.77 ± 2.08 (range: 0-11). Overall, 110 patients (52.9%) had a CCI score ≥ 2.5. The association was consistent for the multifidus across all lumbar levels whereas it was limited to L1-L2, L2-L3, and L4-L5 for the erector spinae. A combined fatty infiltration score of 2.25 for the multifidus and erector spinae at L2-L3 yielded a sensitivity of 59.3% and a specificity of 62.7% for predicting patients with CCI ≥ 2.5. Conclusion: A combined fatty infiltration score of 2.25 for the multifidus and erector spinae at L2-L3 represents the most appropriate index (PFI) for identifying patients with CCI > 2.5. PFI may serve as a practical tool for detecting comorbid patients prior to spinal interventions. Clinicians should consider increased comorbidity risk in patients with fatty paraspinal muscles. Further validation of PFI is warranted in clinical practice and spine research.

## A312: Comparison of diagnostic accuracy of CT and SPECT in pseudarthrosis diagnosis: a systematic review

Miguel Cartagena

1

, Elyette Lugo

2

, Nicholas Schiller

1

, Diego Lopes de Lima

1

, Brett Schlifka

1

, Milad Alam

1

1

HCA Florida JFK, Atlantis, United States

2

Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, United States

Introduction: Pseudoarthrosis is a significant complication of fusion surgery, often causing pain, instability, and the need for revision surgery. CT scanning (CT) remains the gold standard for detecting bony nonunion due to its high resolution, but it can still fail to accurately confirm the presence of solid fusion regardless of metallic artifact. SPECT-CT has emerged as an alternative, offering better material differentiation and reduced artifact interference, yet its diagnostic accuracy remains unclear. This study compares SPECT-CT and CT in detecting pseudoarthrosis using surgical exploration as the gold standard. Material and Methods: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Studies were included if they evaluated CT or SPECT-CT as a diagnostic tool for pseudoarthrosis using surgical exploration as the reference standard. A comprehensive literature search was performed across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library using the following keywords: imaging modalities, pseudoarthrosis, CT scan, single photon emission CT, thoracolumbar fusion. Pooled estimates for sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV were calculated using a random-effects model, with subgroup analysis performed for each imaging modality. Between-study and between-group heterogeneity were assessed using Cochran’s Q test and the I2 statistic. Results: A total of 674 patients from 13 studies were included in this analysis. The pooled analysis showed that CT had higher sensitivity (0.89, 95% CI: -22.67 to 24.45) compared to SPECT-CT (0.68, 95% CI: -32.83 to 34.19), but SPECT-CT demonstrated superior specificity (0.83, 95% CI: -35.03 to 36.60) vs. CT (0.57, 95% CI: -22.99 to 24.13). Regarding predictive values, SPECT-CT had a slightly higher PPV (0.74, 95% CI: -32.77 to 34.25) vs. CT (0.57, 95% CI: -22.99 to 24.13), however, CT had a superior NPV (0.88, 95% CI: -22.68 to 24.44) compared to SPECT-CT (0.69, 95% CI: -32.82 to 34.20). Cochran’s Q test confirmed no significant heterogeneity between modalities (p > 0.99). Conclusion: Our results suggest that CT remains the preferred imaging modality for pseudoarthrosis detection, though SPECT-CT may offer advantages in specific clinical scenarios where specificity is prioritized.

## A313: Assessment of bone mineral density in patients with degenerative spinal disease by MRI-based vertebral bone quality score at different lumbar vertebral levels: an observational prospective study

, Hong Ding

, Qian Chen

, Limin Liu

, Yueming Song

Introduction: Osteoporosis is highly prevalent in the elderly population and often remains asymptomatic until complications occur, leading to increased intraoperative risks and poor prognosis. Current bone mineral density (BMD) assessment methods such as DEXA and QCT have inherent limitations and suboptimal compliance in screening. ## A314: Pediatric developmental spondylolisthesis may be the first presenting symptom of hereditary connective tissue disorders

Kexin Xu

1,2,3

, Xiangjie Yin

1,2,3

, Jialuo Han

1,2,3

, Sen Zhao

1,2,3

, Jianguo Zhang

1,2,3

, Nan Wu

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Peking Union Medical College and Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, People’s Republic of China, Bejing, China

2

Beijing Key Laboratory of Big Data Innovation and Application for Skeletal Health Medical Care, People’s Republic of China, Bejing, China

3

Key Laboratory of Big Data for Skeletal Deformities, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, People’s Republic of China, Beijing, China

Introduction: Spondylolisthesis affects 4%-6% of children. It may be associated with genetic syndromes or occur as “clinically isolated” developmental spondylolisthesis of unclear etiology. The genetic landscape of developmental spondylolisthesis has never been characterized. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included patients who: (1) were diagnosed with developmental spondylolisthesis before the age 18; (2) had an indication for surgical intervention; (3) were not suspected or diagnosed with a genetic syndrome on preoperative assessment; and (4) underwent genome or exome sequencing (GS or ES). Medical records were reviewed, and genetic data were interpreted according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines. Patients with diagnostic results were categorized into Syndromic Group, while others were categorized into Isolated Group. Results: A total of 19 patients were included. None were suspected or diagnosed with a genetic syndrome during preoperative assessment. After genetic testing, eight patients were diagnosed with genetic syndromes, reaching a diagnostic rate of 42%. Notably, six of them had hereditary connective tissue disorders (HCTDs), including Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS, n = 4) and Marfan syndrome (n = 2), indicating that 32% of patients with “clinically isolated” developmental spondylolisthesis actually had HCTDs. Additionally, one patient was diagnosed with Kabuki syndrome, a disorder also associated with connective tissue defects. To investigate whether clinical features could distinguish syndromic cases from isolated cases, we next compared spinal and extra-spinal features between the groups. Age at preoperative assessment and sex distribution were comparable: 12 ± 4 years and 12% male in the Syndromic Group, while 11 ± 2 years and 10% male in the Isolated Group. Body mass index was slightly lower in the Syndromic Group (18 kg/m2 vs. 20 kg/m2). Patients with genetic syndromes had a lower prevalence of spondylolysis (50% vs. 64%) but were more likely to present with extra-spinal skeletal features (63% vs. 18%) and extra-skeletal features (50% vs. 27%). However, all extra-spinal features in both groups were mild and non-specific, such as pediatric generalized joint hypermobility and highly arched eyebrows. Without genetic testing, it was not possible to determine whether these features represented manifestations of genetic syndromes, normal phenotypic variation, or environmental influences. Notably, one patient underwent surgical reduction for “clinically isolated” developmental spondylolisthesis at the age of 5. She experienced a cascade of major complications, including multiple implant- and alignment-related complications requiring five revision surgeries, two episodes of intraoperative anaphylactic shock, and one postoperative cerebral infarction. Prior GS performed at an outside institution was negative. Mild features suggestive of HCTDs were not apparent until the age of 19, and reanalysis of the GS data led to a definitive diagnosis of LDS. The previous false-negative result may have been due to incomplete phenotypic presentation at a young age and the underrecognized association between spondylolisthesis and HCTDs. Conclusion: Approximately 40% of pediatric developmental spondylolisthesis cases have an underlying genetic etiology. Pediatric developmental spondylolisthesis may represent the initial presenting feature of HCTDs. Spine surgeons are the first specialists these patients visit, and preoperative genetic testing is essential for achieving a timely and accurate diagnosis.

## A315: Survival prediction based on machine-learning in severe traumatic cervical spinal cord injury patients: a multicenter study

Quanchang Tan

1

, Tao Jiang

1

, Zixiang Wu

1

1

Xijing Hospital, Xi'an, China

Introduction: Traumatic cervical spinal cord injury (TCSCI) is recognized as one of the most severe traumatic conditions with a high mortality rate. However, clinical tool for assessing mortality risk in TCSCI patients is still lacking. This study aimed to design and validate a tool to evaluate death risk in patients with motor complete TCSCI by using an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm and aimed to developer an online application for predicting patient mortality risk to offer valuable insights for treatment. Various machine-learning survival models were used, including random survival forest (RSF), gradient boosting machine (GBM), extra survival tree (eST) and Cox proportional hazards (CPH) models. Results: The mortality rate in the development cohort was 38.04%. The final model included fifteen predictors (sex, age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, injury severity score, time of injury, energy of damage, spinal cord injury severity classification, neurological level of impairment, important organs damage, transfusion, cervical fracture level, surgical timing, ventilator support, nutritional approach, complications). The GBM model showed the best integrated area under the curve (iAUC) in internal validation (0.901, 95%CI: 0.879-0.923), and external validation showed RSF model with the best iAUC (0.84, 95%CI: 0.813-0.867). The comprehensive performance from internal and external validation indicates that the RSF model achieved the highest score (49), followed closely by the GBM model (45). Therefore, the RSF model was identified as the optimal model and online visualization was implemented as an AI tool. Conclusion: This study developed and validated an AI application to evaluate death risk in patients with motor complete TCSCI. This application can offer healthcare professionals more valuable insight to help clinical decision-making. This advancement holds significant potential for improving outcomes in patients with motor complete TCSCI.

## A316: Outcomes of intradural extramedullary tumor resection in the elderly: a 10-year multicenter analysis

John Zhang

1

, A Aravin Kumar

1

, Zheting Zhang

1

, Shane Zaw

1

, David Mak

1

, Damian Lee

1

, Choo Heng Tan

1

, Nishal Primalani

1

, Krishan Kumar Sharma

1

, Robin Pillay

1

, Dinesh Shree Kumar

2

, Ji Min Ling

1

, Lester Lee

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, National Neuroscience Institute, Singapore, Singapore

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Changi General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Intradural extramedullary (IDEM) tumors account for two-thirds of all primary intraspinal tumors, and their incidence increases with age. As most of these tumors are benign, surgery is offered primarily for control of symptoms or neurological deficits. Outcomes of IDEM tumor resection in the elderly are not well studied, and the risk-benefit ratio is challenging to assess in older patients with perceived higher surgical risks. We aimed to evaluate the outcomes of IDEM tumor resection in our institutions to determine the safety of such operations in the elderly population. Material and Methods: Patients who underwent IDEM tumor resection at three tertiary neurosurgical centers from January 2015 to December 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Data collected included preoperative (demographics, comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index [CCI], symptoms), intraoperative (pathology, details of surgery, duration of surgery) and postoperative variables. Primary outcome measures included postoperative morbidity or mortality either within 30 days or within the same admission, whichever was longer. Complications were classified using the Clavien-Dindo (CD) classification, where grades I and II comprise medically-managed complications, grade III comprises complications requiring procedural or surgical intervention, grade IV comprises complications involving single or multi-organ failure, and grade V refers to patient death. Secondary outcome measures included length of stay and discharge location. Results: 211 patients comprising 79 males and 132 females were included. Median age was 61 years (interquartile range [IQR] 50-70, range 18-94). There were 53 (25.1%) and 13 (6.2%) patients above the ages of 70 and 80 years, respectively. Overall, complications occurred in 36 patients (17.1%). These included 28 (13.3%) CD I or II, 4 (1.9%) CD III, 2 (0.9%) CD IV and 2 (0.9%) CD V complications. Age and CCI were not found to be significant risk factors of postoperative complications (p = 0.454 and p = 0.209, respectively). Patients above the age of 80 years old had similar complication rates both in general and across various CD grades compared to those below 80 (p = 0.554 for all complications, p = 0.817 for CD I or II, p = 0.994 for CD III, p = 0.053 for CD IV, and p = 0.996 for CD V complications). Likewise, complication rates were similar between patients above 70 years old and those below 70 (p = 0.391 for all complications, p = 0.345 for CD I or II, p = 0.994 for CD III, p = 0.437 for CD IV, and p = 0.437 for CD V complications). Age was not significantly correlated with length of hospital stay (p = 0.239). However, patients with older age were more likely to discharge to rehabilitation facilities or nursing homes (p < 0.001). Conclusion: While advanced age predicted the need for eventual discharge to rehabilitation facilities or nursing homes, age was not a significant predictor of postoperative complications both in general and across various CD grades. The decision for IDEM tumor resection in elderly patients should encompass considerations on eventual care needs and discharge destination. Age alone should not be a contraindication to IDEM tumor resection surgery in elderly patients.

## A317: Pre-operative embolization does not reduce blood loss in surgery for hypervascular spinal tumors

Mohammad Daher

1

, Ethan Cottrill

1

, Amer Sebaaly

2

, Peter Passias

1

, Alan Daniels

3

, William Eward

1

1

Duke University, Durham, United States

2

Hotel Dieu de France, Beirut, Lebanon

3

Brown University, Providence, United States

Introduction: Hypervascular tumors present a surgical challenge, due to their substantial intraoperative blood loss. Although preoperative embolization is often employed to mitigate intraoperative bleeding, its consistent advantage has not been conclusively demonstrated across existing studies. The purpose of this meta-analysis is to appraise the evidence comparing surgical outcomes with and without preoperative embolization. Material and Methods: Following the PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Cochrane, and Google Scholar (pages 1-20) were accessed and explored until May 2025. Articles were included if they reported comparative studies evaluating perioperative outcomes of preoperative embolization (E) versus no embolization (NE) in the surgical treatment of hypervascular spinal tumors. A sub-analysis was performed based on whether studies controlled for operative characteristics between the two groups. Results: Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria, including 225 patients in group NE and 340 in group E. When all studies were analyzed collectively, no significant differences were observed between NE and E for any of the outcomes. However, in the subgroup of studies that did not control for specific surgical variables, the NE group showed greater blood loss (mean difference = 270.60 ml; 95% CI: 21.52- 519.67, p = 0.03) and longer operative time (mean difference = 48.00 minutes; 95% CI: 16.67- 79.33, p = 0.003). In contrast, studies that controlled for these variables showed no significant differences in blood loss (p = 0.75) or operative time (p = 0.41) between the NE and E groups. Conclusion: Pre-operative embolization was not associated with consistent benefits in surgical outcomes for hypervascular spinal tumors. While some studies reported reduced blood loss and operative time with embolization, these findings were limited to analyses lacking control for specific surgical characteristics. This suggests that the perceived advantages may reflect confounding factors rather than the true effect of embolization. However, surgical equipoise remains and the decision to embolize should be individualized based on surgical and patient-related factors.

## A318: Intralesional surgery with adjuvant charged-particle therapy in the treatment of intact and recurrent primary spinal tumors

Valerio Pipola

1

, Emanuela Cosentino

1

, Cristiana Griffoni

1

, Monica Cosentino

2

, Laura Maria Beatrice Belotti

2

, Riccardo Ghermandi

1

, Marco Girolami

1,3

, Stefano Bandiera

1

, Giovanni Barbanti Brodano

1

, Silvia Terzi

1

, Giuseppe Tedesco

, Gisberto Evangelisti

1

, Stefano Pasini

1

, Luigi Falzetti

1

, Giovanni Tosini

1

, Chiara Cini

1

, Maria Rosaria Fiore

4

, Marco Cianchetti

5

, Alessandro Gasbarrini

1,6

1

Complex Spinal Surgery Unit, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy,

2

Scientific Direction, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy,

3

Spine Unit, Hospital Universitario Fundacion Jimenez Diaz, Madrid, Spain,

4

Radiation Oncology Unit, Clinical Department, CNAO Centro Nazionale di Adroterapia Oncologica, Pavia, Italy,

5

Proton Therapy Unit, Azienda Provinciale per i Servizi Sanitari, Trento, Italy,

6

Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Sciences, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: The management of primary tumors of the mobile spine has long been a challenge in oncological spinal surgery. Historically, en bloc resection with wide or marginal margins has been considered the gold standard for achieving local control and reducing recurrence rates, particularly for aggressive benign and malignant tumors. Recent advancements in adjuvant radiotherapy, particularly charged-particle therapies such as proton therapy and carbon ion radiotherapy, have begun to shift this paradigm. Complementing these advancements in radiotherapy, the development of carbon fiber implants has further enhanced the feasibility and safety of intralesional surgery. Unlike traditional metallic implants, carbon fiber-reinforced polyether ether ketone (CFR-PEEK) implants are radiolucent, minimizing artifacts on postoperative imaging and allowing for more accurate radiation planning and delivery. Methods: The study is a retrospective analysis of data prospectively collected. It includes patients affected by primary tumors of the mobile spine who were treated by intralesional surgery at a tertiary center specialized for spinal diseases between March 2015 and February 2024. Demographic and clinical information, surgical data, complications, and local recurrences were collected. After the intralesional surgery, all patients underwent charged- particle radiotherapy, Carbon ion radiation therapy (CIRT) or Proton Beam Therapy (PBT), at specialized external centers. Patients were followed up longitudinally through clinical visits and imaging studies. Local recurrences (LR) after surgery were monitored and recorded. Results: A total of 36 patients were included in the study: 24 males and 12 females, with a mean age of 57.5 years at the time of surgery (range 11-83 years). The most frequent tumor type was chordoma (26 cases, 72.2%), and the most frequent localization was lumbar (44.4%). Most patients (27/36, 75%) had already undergone prior surgeries for the same lesion: 20 patients (58.3%) were re-operated because of one or more local recurrences before the index surgery; 7 patients were re-operated because of a previous Enneking-inappropriate (EI) treatment without LR. Nine patients (25%) had virgin tumors at the time of index surgery. Patients underwent intralesional excision (19, 52.8%) or intralesional vertebrectomy (6, 16.7%) with CFR-PEEK posterior instrumentation for most patients (27, 75%). All patients underwent charged-particle therapy after the intralesional surgery: 27 patients (75%) were treated by PBT and 9 patients (25%) were treated by CIRT. The survival probability at 3 years of follow-up was 87.7% (95% CI: 77.1-99.8), decreasing to 57.6% (95% CI: 40.7-81.4) at 5 years. Potential risk factors for 5-year mortality were also evaluated, and only the occurrence of LR at any point during follow-up emerged as a significant predictor (HR = 10.6 [95% CI 2.26,49.3]). Fifteen patients (41.7%) had one or more post-operative local recurrences after the index surgery and 12 of them were re-operated. Thirteen out of 15 patients (86.7%) with post-operative LR had also local recurrence before the index surgery. Univariate regression analysis did not identify pre-operative LR as a significant predictor of LR occurring during the follow up period. Conclusion: Intralesional surgery followed by charged-particle radiotherapy provides good results in terms of local control and survival rates, even in cases of recurrent tumors.

## A319: Symptom-to-surgeon interval in metastatic spinal cord compression: a single-center retrospective analysis

Tiago Ribeiro da Costa

1,2

, António Pinto

1

, Filipe Vaz da Silva

1

, Gonçalo Figueiredo

1

, Eduardo Cunha

1

, Luís Rocha

1

, Joaquim Reis

1,2

, Alfredo Calheiros

1,2

1

Unidade Local de Saúde de Santo António, Porto, Portugal

2

Instituto de Ciências Biomédicas Abel Salazar, University of Porto, Porto, Portugal

Introduction: Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) is a frequent neurosurgical emergency with potentially catastrophic neurological outcomes if not managed promptly. Although early surgical evaluation and decompression-within 24 to 48 hours of symptom onset-are generally considered critical to optimize functional outcomes, the actual timeframes achieved in clinical practice are not well characterized. Clinical perception suggests that significant delays in referral and assessment may occur. This study aimed to objectively evaluate the interval between the onset of neurological symptoms and the first contact with a spine surgeon, in patients undergoing urgent decompression for metastatic epidural spinal cord compression. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed all patients in whom surgical decompression for MSCC was considered at our institution between January 2018 and September 2025. Demographic data, tumor type, neurological status at presentation, and referral pathway were collected. The main outcome was the time from symptom onset (defined as first neurological deficit compatible with acute myelopathy) to first contact with a spine surgeon (neurosurgeon or orthopedic spine surgeon). Patients presenting with complete paraplegia (ASIA A) and with symptom-to-contact intervals exceeding 48 hours were not included, as surgery was not considered in this subgroup. Results: A total of 60 patients were identified, of whom 2 had insufficient data to determine symptom-to-surgeon interval. Among the remaining 58 patients, 42 (72.4%) presented with an interval longer than 72 hours, while 16 (27.6%) were assessed within 72 hours of symptom onset. In this subgroup, the mean interval was 26.7 hours (range 0-60h). Nine patients (15.5%) were seen within 24 hours, and twelve (20.7%) within 48 hours. Conclusion: This study provides an objective characterization of referral times in MSCC. Fewer than one-third of patients considered for surgery were assessed by a spine surgeon within 72 hours, and only one in five within 48 hours. The exclusion of patients with complete paraplegia after delayed referral represents a methodological limitation, likely leading to an underestimation of the true burden of delayed pathways. Future prospective and multicentric registries should aim to capture all patients with MSCC, and to analyze referral determinants such as triage processes and first-point recognition, to optimize timely referral and preserve neurological outcomes.

Combined Neurosurgical and Orthopedic Spine Program, Vancouver, Canada

IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

12

Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford, United Kingdom

Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, United States

14

Johns Hopkins Hosital, Baltimore, United States

15

University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

16

University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada

Brown University, Providence, United States

National Center for Spinal Disorders, Budapest, Hungary

19

New York University Grossman School of Medicine, New York, United States

20

University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Surgery for spinal metastases encompasses a broad spectrum of procedures, from percutaneous fixation to en bloc resection in select cases. However, no standardized framework exists to describe surgical invasiveness in this population. Existing indices were not designed for metastatic spine disease and do not incorporate modern minimally invasive, lateral, or hybrid approaches. Prior attempts at invasiveness scores remain unvalidated and not widely adopted. This review sought to map how invasiveness has been defined and measured in the current literature on metastatic spinal tumor surgery (MSTS). Material and Methods: A literature search was performed by searching the PubMed/Medline database for papers published up to February 29, 2023. The search algorithm included terms related to operative variables, technique, and factors and their association with complications and/or adverse events in MSTS. We evaluated which operative variables were studied, which outcomes they were linked to, and how these associations were reported. An exploratory data analysis and narrative synthesis were conducted. Results: A total of 78 articles representing 86,353 patients met our final inclusion criteria. Eleven different groups of covariates were found, with the most common being surgical technique, number of levels, approach, and operative time. The most common examined outcomes included complications, length of stay, and operative time. Two-thirds of studies (68%; 53 of 78) found a positive association between operative variables and the studied outcome(s).
