## A321: Statistical description of relevant mechanical parameters of metastatic vertebrae

Silvia Casadei

1

, Giulia Cavazzoni

1

, Margherita Pasini

1

, Luca Cristofolini

1

, Saulo Martelli

2

, Marco Palanca

1

1

Department of Industrial Engineering-University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

2

Faculty of Engineering, School of Mechanical, Medical & Process Engineering-Queensland University, Brisbane, Australia

Introduction: Bone metastases compromise the stability of the spine, increasing the risk of fracture [1]. Currently, the mechanisms of failure in metastatic vertebrae and the influence of metastasis type or location are still unclear. The Spine Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) is the most widely used clinical tool for fracture risk assessment in metastatic spine disease, but it presents several limitations [2]. This study had two aims: (1) to identify the principal sources of variation in shape and material properties in vertebrae with lytic metastases, by using statistical methods, and (2) to evaluate if and how these components may explain the mechanical behaviour under compressive loading conditions. Material and Methods: Twenty-eight human cadaveric vertebrae with lytic metastases were mechanically tested under axial compression in the elastic regime, and full-field surface displacements and strains were measured with a four-camera 3D Digital Image Correlation system (Aramis Adjustable, Zeiss). The same specimens were CT-scanned (in-plane resolution = 0.39 mm, slice thickness = 0.625 mm). The vertebral body and the metastatic regions were segmented to generate surface meshes. Volumetric meshes were mapped to the original CT images to extract local density values from the Hounsfield Units, which were subsequently converted into elastic modulus values [3]. The lytic regions were also mapped onto the volumetric meshes. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to capture the main source of variation in vertebral shape and material properties. PCA is a statistical technique that reduces the complexity of the data by maximizing the variance explained and making possible to highlight the “main associations” of variability of bone shape and quality. These main associations were then used in a linear regression model to predict the minimum compressive strain and the percentage strain difference respect to control vertebrae under compressive loading. Model generalization was assessed using leave-one-out cross-validation, and performance was quantified by the root mean square error (RMSE) and the coefficient of determination (R2). Results: Principal component analysis identified 25 parameters that accounted for 95% of the variation in shape and density. Among the 25 principal components, only 15 were found to accurately predict the mechanical behaviour under compressive loading conditions, by minimizing the RMSE. The linear regression model predicting minimum compressive strain showed a median RMSE below 100 µε (strain range -1000 -9400 µε, median percentage error of 5%) and a R2 was 0.95. The percentage compressive strain difference median RMSE error was 34% (percentage range -39 -1135 % and a median percentage error of 14%) and R2 was 0.93. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that statistical models of vertebral shape and material properties can extract principal components to capture the main sources of variation, while accurately predicting compressive strain in vertebrae with lytic metastases. Since strain is one indicator of fracture risk [1], these results highlight that a larger set of specific factors, both morphological and material, provide stronger predictive power than the limited parameters considered in currently clinical assessments.
References
1. Palanca. Bone (2023)
2. Palanca. Bone (2021)
3. Garavelli. PLoS One (2022)
Acknowledgements: HEU-Funded METASTRA project (grant 101080135).

## A323: Vertebral artery trapping in metastatic cervical spine tumors: propensity-matched analysis of surgical outcomes

Wei-Lin Pan

1

, Yen-Heng Lin

1

, Fon-Yih Tsuang

1

1

National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: Vertebral artery (VA) trapping during metastatic cervical spine tumor surgery is technically demanding, and its safety profile remains debated. While it facilitates more extensive tumor resection, evidence regarding perioperative outcomes compared with non-VA trapping procedures is limited. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 73 patients who underwent surgery for metastatic cervical spinal tumors at our institution, including 12 with VA trapping and 61 without. Surgical methods, intraoperative parameters, and perioperative outcomes were compared. To minimize selection bias, 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using Tomita, SINS, Tokuhashi, and ESCCnew scores to balance preoperative tumor burden and spinal stability. Results: Debulking surgery was significantly more frequent in the VA trapping group than in the non-VA trapping group. A trend toward greater use of combined surgical approaches was also observed in the VA trapping group, though not statistically significant. Conclusion: VA trapping allows surgeons to pursue more aggressive resection strategies in metastatic cervical spine tumor surgery without compromising perioperative safety. These findings suggest that VA trapping can be safely considered in selected patients when radical tumor control is indicated.

## A324: Predictive factors for spinal deformity following resection of intramedullary spinal cord tumors: a 15-year retrospective cohort study

Vitor Viana Bonan de Aguiar

1

, Caio Perret

1

, Ricardo de Amoreira Gepp

1

1

Sarah Network of Rehabilitation Hospitals, Brasilia, Brazil

Introduction: Spinal deformity is a significant long-term complication that can occur after the resection of intramedullary spinal cord tumors (IMSCT), especially in younger patients and in cases where surgical instrumentation is not used. Although there are various reports identifying potential risk factors, the specific roles of these factors in the development of deformities-such as kyphosis or scoliosis-in both the sagittal and coronal planes remain underexplored. The objective of this study is to clearly identify the clinical, anatomical, and surgical predictors of spinal deformity following IMSCT resection in patients who do not undergo routine fusion. Posterior decompression was carried out through either laminectomy or laminoplasty, without prophylactic fusion. We analyzed demographic, clinical, surgical, and radiographic variables. Both univariate and multivariable penalized logistic regression analyses were employed to identify independent predictors. Results: A total of sixty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria for the study. These factors include younger age, preoperative sagittal deformity, and the location of thoracic tumors. The findings underscore the importance of conducting preoperative risk assessments and ensuring long-term radiographic monitoring, particularly for skeletally immature patients and those with high-risk anatomical characteristics.

## A325: Clinical outcomes of dual-pin reference frame placement in MI-TLIF: a retrospective review of 266 pins using a three-zone grading system

Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi

1

, Noah Willett

1

, Mousa Hamad

1

, Andreas Kramer

1

, Rachel Bratescu

1

, Natasha Kharas

1

, Galal Elsayed

1

, Ibrahim Hussain

1

, Osama Kashlan

1

, Roger Härtl

1

1

Department of Neurological Surgery, Och Spine at New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: Percutaneous dual-pin reference frames enable image-guided minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MI-TLIF) but carry risks of pin-related morbidity, notably sacroiliac (SI) joint dysfunction. While single-pin systems have been studied, clinical data on dual-pin systems remain limited. We report our experience identifying complications related to dual-pin placement and evaluating their distribution using a three-zone anatomical grading system that defines optimal and suboptimal pin trajectories. Two independent, blinded spine surgeons graded 266 total pins into one of three anatomical zones: Green zone: medial PSIS/ilium; Yellow zone: abutting or breaching the SI joint or with inadequate bony purchase; Red zone: sacrum, neural foramen, or pelvic cavity. One patient (0.8%) reported persistent pin-site pain. No hematomas, infections, fractures, or visceral injuries were observed. All complications occurred exclusively in the yellow or red zones. Among the 266 reference frame pins evaluated, 192 (72%) were in the green zone, 64 (24%) in the yellow zone, and 10 (4%) in the red zone. Interrater reliability for zone assignment was excellent (quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ = 0.89, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Dual-pin RF placement in MI-TLIF demonstrated a low complication rate, with SI joint dysfunction nearly exclusively associated with suboptimal (yellow or red zone) placement. The green-zone placement was complication-free. Strict adherence to green-zone anatomical guidelines may reduce morbidity and improve the safety of navigated minimally invasive spine surgery.

## A327: Trends in navigation-guided spinal instrumentation surgeries in the United States

Maxwell Sahhar

1

, Ahmed Sulieman

2

, Ishandeep Singh

3

, Sang Hun Lee

2

1

Brown University Warren Alpert Medical School, Providence, United States

2

Johns Hopkins University Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Baltimore, United States

3

University of East Anglia Norwich Medical School, Norfolk, United Kingdom

Introduction: Navigation-guided instrumentation has been increasingly applied in spine surgery globally as well as in the United States. This study evaluates national adoption trends and reports descriptive, population-level outcomes across pathology types and spine regions. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed using the MarketScan Claims Database on 158,168 spine fusion surgeries between 2011 and 2020, including 15,382 navigated and 142,786 non-navigated cases. Demographics were summarized, and adoption trends were compared before and after 2016. Outcomes were assessed using unadjusted 2-year reoperation rates and mean hospital length of stay, stratified by pathology and spinal region indicated by ICD-10 Codes. Results: The mean age was 49.6 years with 46.5% being female in navigated cases and 48.9 years with 44.7% being female in controls. Navigation adoption increased significantly after 2016 across all pathologies (p < 0.001). Deformity cases rose from 6.2% pre-2016 to 14.6% post-2016, degenerative from 6.2% to 15.9%, trauma from 6.5% to 17.2%, and neoplastic from 9.2% to 25.1%. By spinal region, adoption increased from 4.3% to 12.0% in cervical, 7.0% to 20.0% in thoracic, and 6.3% to 16.4% in lumbar procedures. Crude outcome comparisons showed no significant differences in 2-year reoperation rates between navigated and non-navigated cohorts. In deformity surgery, reoperation occurred in 3.86% of navigated cases versus 4.32% of controls (p = 0.41), with mean length of stay of 4.0 versus 4.2 days (p = 0.32). Degenerative surgery showed reoperation in 3.62% versus 3.87% (p = 0.47), with mean stay of 3.5 days in both groups (p = 0.88). Trauma cases had reoperation in 2.23% versus 2.43% (p = 0.56) and mean stay of 5.8 versus 6.5 days (p = 0.04). Neoplastic procedures showed reoperation in 2.53% versus 2.92% (p = 0.38), with mean stay of 5.8 versus 6.8 days (p = 0.02). Kyphosis cases had reoperation in 5.19% versus 5.68% (p = 0.44) and scoliosis 4.23% versus 4.47% (p = 0.51), with mean stays of 4.9 versus 5.0 (p = 0.62) and 4.2 versus 4.5 days (p = 0.21), respectively. Conclusion: Between 2011 and 2020, computer navigation in spine surgery increased significantly across all pathology groups and spinal regions, with the largest growth observed in neoplastic, thoracic, and lumbar cases. At the population level, crude reoperation rates were not significantly different between navigated and non-navigated cohorts. Length of stay was shorter for navigated trauma and neoplastic cases, while differences in other groups were not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate the growing role of navigation in spine surgery, especially in surgeries that require precise localization in highly unpredictable anatomy such as neoplastic or trauma cases.

## A328: Trajectory mismatch between navigation-guided and anatomically ideal C3-6 cervical pedicle screws: clinical implications

Yoshitaka Nagashima

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine., Nagoya, Japan

Introduction: Navigation systems have facilitated safer placement of C3-6 cervical pedicle screws. However, the ideal anatomical trajectory remains poorly defined, and the extent to which actual screw paths deviate from this ideal has not been systematically evaluated. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients who underwent C3-6 pedicle screw placement with either preoperative CT-based navigation or intraoperative O-arm navigation between 2019 and 2024 at three institutions. Cases with alternative skin entry were excluded. Pre- and postoperative CT scans were fused on a workstation to reconstruct the actual screw trajectory and the anatomically ideal trajectory. Entry point distance from the lateral border of the lateral mass, medial placement ratio, and screw angle were compared between trajectories. Screw perforation was graded according to the Neo classification, and parameters were compared between screws with and without perforation. Results: A total of 127 screws were placed in 33 patients (66 with CT-based navigation and 61 with O-arm navigation). Screw distribution was C3: 29, C4: 31, C5: 35, and C6: 32. Perforation grading was Grade 0: 79.5%, Grade 1: 15.7%, Grade 2: 4.7%, and Grade 3: 0%. Compared with the ideal trajectory, actual screws demonstrated significantly more medial entry (median 6.4 mm vs. 2.3 mm), higher medial ratio (0.480 vs. 0.183), and smaller insertion angle (28.0° vs. 44.3°) (all p < 0.001). Screws with perforation (Grades 1-2) had greater medial entry distance (8.0 mm vs. 6.1 mm) and medial ratio (0.582 vs. 0.452) than those without perforation (both p < 0.001), while insertion angle did not differ significantly (p = 0.20). Conclusion: Navigation-guided C3-6 cervical pedicle screws were consistently placed more medially and at shallower angles than the anatomically ideal trajectory. Excessively medial entry points, especially those medial to the midpoint of the lateral mass, increased the risk of perforation. These findings underscore a specific pitfall of navigation-guided screw placement that must be considered to enhance accuracy and safety.

## A329: New innovation for spine navigation

Ufuk Aydinli

, Zlatko Kolic

4

CDI, Houston, United States

Introduction: Image-guided navigation in spinal interventions and related procedures commonly relies on fluoroscopy or CT imaging, which are costly, expose patients and clinicians to radiation, and are often limited by complex intraoperative registration challenges. Material and Methods: We present a novel computer navigation system designed to overcome these limitations through real-time, radiation-free, and contactless surgical guidance. This new system integrates proprietary computer vision algorithms with streamlined hardware to enable accurate anatomical landmark identification, patient registration, and trajectory correction. The system supports hybrid electromagnetic (EM) and computer vision (CV) navigation and includes optional real-time ultrasound verification. Conclusion: This new system represents a transformative, low-cost, and portable solution that enhances safety, accuracy, and efficiency in minimally invasive spine and pain management procedures. ## A331: Navigation-guided spinal instrumentation: an exact-matched analysis of outcomes

Maxwell Sahhar

1

, Ahmed Sulieman

, Sang Hun Lee

Brown University Warren Alpert Medical School, Providence, United States, 
2
Johns Hopkins University Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Baltimore, United States
Introduction: Previous research has reported modest benefits of navigation in spine surgery reoperation rates but has not adequately addressed confounding factors or examined whether outcomes have improved over time. This study evaluates the association of navigation with postoperative outcomes using a cohort matched exactly on primary procedure, pathology, and spinal region. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed using the MarketScan Claims Database on patients undergoing spine fusion between 2011 and 2020. Navigated surgeries were identified using the navigation CPT code and matched exactly to non-navigated surgeries by primary procedure, spine region, and pathology type (deformity, degenerative, trauma, and neoplastic, non-mutually exclusive) using ICD-10 and CPT codes. Outcomes included 2-year reoperation, 90-day reoperation, and hospital length of stay (LOS). Logistic and linear regression models controlling for age and sex were also performed to evaluate whether the odds of 2-year reoperation and LOS varied over time. Results: Propensity matching produced 10,847 navigated and 10,847 non-navigated cases. Mean age was 50.0 ± 13.8 years in navigated cases and 49.8 ± 14.0 years in controls, with 45.4% and 44.2% female, respectively. A total of 4,535 navigated cases were excluded for having insufficient data or lacking an exact match. In deformity cases (n = 6,214), 2-year reoperation was 3.57% versus 4.18% (p = 0.21), 90-day reoperation 0.55% versus 0.84% (p = 0.17), and LOS 3.92 versus 4.05 days (p = 0.14). Neoplastic cases (n = 292) showed 2-year reoperation 2.74% versus 3.42% (p = 0.73), 90-day reoperation 2.05% versus 1.37% (p = 0.65), and LOS 5.75 versus 7.32 days (p = 0.008). By region, cervical (n = 1,738) had 2-year reoperation 5.75% versus 4.49% (p = 0.23), 90-day reoperation 0.69% versus 0.92% (p = 0.59), and LOS 3.79 versus 3.60 days (p = 0.23). Thoracic (n = 944) showed 2-year reoperation 6.14% versus 6.36% (p = 0.89), 90-day reoperation 1.91% versus 1.27% (p = 0.43), and LOS 5.67 versus 5.99 days (p = 0.45). Lumbar (n = 17,436) demonstrated 2-year reoperation 3.57% versus 4.45% (p = 0.12), 90-day reoperation 0.34% versus 0.56% (p = 0.03), and LOS 3.39 versus 3.26 days (p = 0.001). Logistic regression relating time of surgery to odds of reoperation showed no significant association in either navigated (p = 0.436) or non-navigated (p = 0.457) models. Conclusion: In an exact-matched national cohort of 21,694 spine surgeries, navigation was associated with lower reoperation rates in trauma surgery, and with markedly shorter hospital stays in neoplastic cases. Although these benefits were not consistent across all groups, the findings suggest that navigation may confer advantages in specific clinical contexts and demonstrates the need for further investigation into scenarios where navigation technology provides the greatest benefit.

Giuseppe Loggia

1

, Aron Alakmeh

Hospital for Special Surgery, Balgrist Zurich, New York, United States

Balgrist, Zurich, Switzerland

Introduction: Accurate pedicle screw placement is crucial in spinal fusion surgery to ensure optimal fixation and avoid complications. Augmented Reality (AR) navigation is currently emerging as a novel radiation-sparing alternative to conventional freehand (FH) techniques in pedicle screw placement, with potential benefits including improved accuracy, workflow efficiency, and surgical ergonomics. This study aims to compare the accuracy of AR-guided versus conventional FH techniques in lumbosacral pedicle screw placement. Material and Methods: All patients who underwent pedicle screws placement from L1 to S1 using either Xvision® AR navigation or conventional FH technique, with available postoperative CT imaging for screw accuracy assessment, were analyzed. Demographic and surgical characteristics were compared between both cohorts. Generalized linear mixed models were used to examine the association between screw placement technique (AR vs. FH) and breach outcomes, accounting for clustering of screws within patients. Results: A total of 202 patients were analyzed, comprising 1,109 pedicle screws placed (AR: n = 548; FH: n = 561). Yu Zhang

1

1

The Fifth Clinical Medical College of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou city, China

Introduction: Unilateral Biportal Endoscopy (UBE) surgery, when applied in the treatment of severe lumbar spinal stenosis, relies on the surgeon's experience for operation. It is associated with issues such as insufficient decompression accuracy, limited decompression range, and high radiation exposure. This study compared the efficacy of traditional UBE and robot-assisted navigated UBE to provide evidence for clinical practice. Material and Methods: A total of 72 patients diagnosed with severe lumbar spinal stenosis in the Department of Spinal Orthopedics of our hospital from March 2022 to April 2024 were enrolled and divided into two groups: the UBE group (33 cases) and the robot-assisted navigated UBE group (39 cases). The traditional group underwent conventional UBE decompression; the navigated group received preoperative CT-based planning and intraoperative robot-assisted positioning for decompression. Observation indicators included: perioperative indicators (operation time, intraoperative blood loss, intraoperative effective radiation dose); clinical function scores Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA). lumbar score before surgery and at 3 and 12 months after surgery; imaging indicators (sagittal diameter of the spinal canal and nerve root canal volume at the lesioned segment at 6 months after surgery). Results: In the navigated group: The operation time for two-level segments was (109.2 ± 15.2) minutes, which was shorter than that of the traditional group (124.5 ± 17.8) minutes; The intraoperative blood loss was (43.9 ± 11.5) mL, lower than that of the traditional group (67.5 ± 16.3) mL;The effective radiation dose was (3.6 ± 1.2) mSv, lower than that of the traditional group (7.9 ± 2.2) mSv (all p < 0.05). Conclusion: Robot-assisted navigated UBE is superior to traditional UBE in the treatment of severe lumbar spinal stenosis, as it shortens the operation time, reduces blood loss and radiation exposure, and enhances therapeutic efficacy and decompression effect. ## A334: Retrospective review on the trend of lumbar spinal decompression surgery in Singapore

Kai Lin Lee

1

, Yilun Huang

2

, John Thng

1

, Dhivakaran Gengatharan

2

, Athanasios Sivridis

3

1

national university of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore

2

Sengkang General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

3

Sofia University St. Kliment Ohridski, Sofia, Bulgaria

Introduction: Spinal stenosis and degenerative spinal disorders are becoming increasingly common and have a substantial impact on patients’ quality of life. Surgical decompression, performed through either open microscopic or endoscopic approaches, remains a cornerstone in the management of these conditions. While microdecompression has consistently demonstrated favorable outcomes, endoscopic techniques are gaining traction due to their minimally invasive nature. This study aims to investigate the evolving trends in single-level lumbar spinal decompression procedures at a tertiary academic hospital in Singapore. Material and Methods: A retrospective observational study involving 588 patients (unilateral biportal endoscopic: n=364; microdecompression: n = 224) undergoing single-level spinal decompression surgery between 2021 and 2024 was conducted. Primary outcome measures included changes in SF-36 and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores at 3 months, 6 months, and 2 years postoperatively. Secondary outcomes were length of hospital stay, reoperation rates, and operative time. Collected data encompassed patient demographics, level and anatomical distribution of pathology, surgical techniques employed, and postoperative outcomes. Difference-in-differences (DID) analysis compared outcomes between both groups. Results: Both groups showed significant improvements in SF-36 and VAS scores postoperatively. At 1 month, endoscopic surgery resulted in greater early improvement in physical functioning (SFPF mean difference (MD): +11.2, p < 0.001 vs +7.0, p < 0.005) and VAS leg pain (MD: -3.64, p < 0.001 vs -3.50, p < 0.001). Overall, no DID comparisons across domains reached statistical significance. Operative time for endoscopic cases decreased over the years (2022: mean 249 min vs 2024: mean 145 min), reflecting a learning curve. Surgeons with higher endoscopic caseloads demonstrated greater improvements in functional outcomes. Conclusion: Both endoscopic and open microscopic decompression achieve comparable short- and long-term outcomes. Endoscopy surgery offers comparable outcomes with faster recovery and shorter hospital stays. However, the presence of a subset of patients who do not achieve full symptom relief or require revision surgery suggests the need for further investigation into factors influencing surgical success. Future research with long-term follow-up is needed to further assess the durability and comparative efficacy of different surgical methods.

## A335: Reactive sagittal realignment drives low back pain improvement following fusionless decompression for degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis: a prospective analysis

Mahmoud A.F Amin

1

, Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad

1,2

, Ahmed M. Sayed

1

, Mahmoud saleh

1

, Mohamed El-Meshwawy

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Assiut University Hospitals, Assiut, Egypt

2

Department of Spinal Deformities, Helios Hospitals Erfurt, Erfurt, Germany

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is one of the most common causes of pain and disability in the aging population, frequently presenting with neurogenic claudication, radicular symptoms, and low back pain (LBP), and usually associated with sagittal spinal imbalance. Surgical decompression reliably alleviates neurogenic claudication and radicular pain. Traditionally, fusion surgery is considered necessary for associated sagittal imbalance correction and LBP relief. Emerging evidence suggests that fusionless decompression may induce reactive sagittal realignment, allowing restoration of more physiological global and spinopelvic harmony once neural compression, compensatory stooping and longstanding muscle strain resolve. However, prospective studies evaluating alignment changes following lumbar spinal canal decompression without fusion and their clinical correlates are scarce. This study aimed to examine the short term impact of fusionless decompression surgery on sagittal spinal alignment, explore its association with LBP improvement, and identify predictors of residual postoperative pain in patients with degenerative LSS. Material and Methods: In this prospective cohort, 55 consecutive patients with symptomatic degenerative LSS refractory to ≥ 3 months of conservative therapy underwent decompression without fusion. Patients with high-grade spondylolisthesis, instability, or deformity were excluded. Clinical outcomes included Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for LBP and leg pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and EuroQol-5D-5L. Radiographic evaluation comprised pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), sacral slope (SS), lumbar lordosis (LL), thoracic kyphosis (TK), sagittal vertical axis (SVA). Patient’s sagittal profiles were evaluated and classified preoperatively and at the final follow-up using Roussouly’s system. Patients were stratified into satisfactory pain relief (Group S) and residual pain (Group R) based on achieving the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for VAS-LBP and achieving end VAS-LBP score of ≤ 3. Follow-up averaged 6 months. Results: The whole cohort’s PROMs significantly improved following decompression surgery [LBP VAS (3.01 vs 6.06), LLP VAS (2.36 vs 6.4), ODI (19.26 vs 48.05), and EQ 5D 5L (0.788 vs 0.212 all p < 0.001]. Radiographically, PI-LL mismatch significantly decreased postoperatively (9.25° ± 11.4° vs 14.15° ± 15.7°, p = 0.007), and SVA significantly decreased (15.59 mm ± 42 vs 37.15 mm ± 61, p = 0.029), reflecting significant sagittal realignment. Roussouly type changed in 32.7% of patients, most commonly from hypolordotic type 2 to more physiological type 3, although this trend did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.141). No significant association was found between preoperative Roussouly type and pain relief (p = 0.255). On subgroup analysis,70.9% of patients achieved satisfactory LBP relief (Group S) vs 29.1% with residual pain (Group R). Group S demonstrated greater sagittal alignment improvement than Group R, as evidenced by reduction of SVA, PT, and PI-LL and increase of SS. Residual pain correlated with older age (57.1 vs 51.1 years) and multilevel surgery (2.07 vs 1.38 levels, p < 0.01). Conclusion: Fusionless lumbar spinal decompression surgery not only relieves symptoms of LSS but also promotes reactive sagittal realignment, marked by restoration of lumbar lordosis and reduction of sagittal imbalance. Patients achieving greater realignment experienced superior improvement in low back pain and quality of life. Younger age and fewer operated levels are associated with better outcomes.

## A336: Physiologic decompression of lumbar spinal stenosis through anatomic restoration using trans-kambin oblique lateral posterior lumbar interbody fusion (OLLIF): a retrospective analysis

Amir Sharif

1,2

, Hamid Reza Abbasi

1

1

Inspired Spine, Burnsville, United States

2

Sana Regio Klinikum Pinneberg, Pinneberg, Germany

Introduction: Introduction Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is one of the most common indications for spinal surgery. Traditionally, decompression is achieved by removing bony and ligamentous structures through open surgery. However, recent studies have shown that symptomatic relief can be accomplished in many patients by increasing intervertebral and interpedicular height using fusion alone. In this study, we evaluate whether trans-Kambin oblique lateral lumbar interbody fusion (OLLIF) can effectively and safely relieve symptoms of LSS when an indication for fusion is present. Material and Methods: This is a retrospective single surgeon cohort study of 187 patients with LSS who underwent 189 OLLIF procedures between 2012 and August 2, 2019. Inclusion criteria for this study were age > 18 years with symptoms of LSS, including pain, sensory, and motor deficits, and an additional indication for fusion, which included spondylolisthesis, degenerative disk disease, disk herniation, or scoliosis. Exclusion criteria were the bony obstruction of the approach, osteogenic spinal canal stenosis, large facet hypertrophy, and listhesis grade II or greater. The primary outcome was a change in the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) one year after surgery. Secondary outcomes were the resolution of radiculopathy at the first follow-up visit and one year after surgery, complication rates, surgery time, blood loss, and hospital stay. Results: Results ODI improved from 52% pre-op to 37% at the one-year follow-up. At the first follow-up, radiculopathy had resolved in 39% of patients, and 72% of patients experienced improvement of 50% or greater. One year after surgery, radiculopathy had resolved in 52% of patients and 74% experienced improvement of 50% or greater. Single-level surgeries required 56.4 ± 21.5 minutes, with a mean hospital stay of 1.6- ± 2.4 days. Nerve irritation occurred in 12% of patients at the first postoperative follow-up and persisted in 6.8% of patients one year after surgery. There was one case each of persistent weakness at one year, infection, and cage subsidence. Conclusion: Trans-Kambin OLLIF delivers anatomic restoration of intradiscal and interpedicular distance, which results in physiologic decompression of lumbar spinal stenosis in patients undergoing lumbar fusion for degenerative or herniated disk disease, spondylolisthesis, or scoliosis. Amongst patients with LSS, OLLIF results in significant improvement of radiculopathy and patient-reported disability in the majority of patients with low rates of long-term complications. Unlike other minimally invasive surgery (MIS) fusions, OLLIF can be safely used from T12-S1.

## A337: Risk of asymmetric cage overhang in standalone LLIF: a patient-specific finite element analysis

Samuel Wakelin

1

, Armani Manov

1

, Ben Carnovale

1

, Andrew Legarreta

1

, Joseph Hudson

1

, Kojo Hamilton

1,2,3

, Nitin Agarwal

1,2,3

1

Medical Center, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, United States

2

University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, United States

3

Veterans Affairs Pittsburgh Healthcare System, Pittsburgh, United States

Introduction: Standalone LLIF is a minimally invasive option to indirectly decompress the neural elements. Postoperative subsidence is a risk following standalone procedures, and cage characteristics and placement profiles are associated with subsidence risk. Though previous finite element (FEA) studies have examined subsidence following standalone LLIF, most prior FEA models are not patient-specific and do not consider the effect of asymmetric graft overhang. Objective: To develop a patient-specific FEA model incorporating Hounsfield Unit (HU) based bone density calculation to analyze the effect of asymmetric cage overhang on subsidence risk. Methods: A non-pathologic CT abdomen and pelvis was obtained from a publicly available database. A Python pipeline was developed using previously developed deep learning segmentation tools. This pipeline was used for segmentation, surface meshing, and HU to Elastic modulus conversion for patient-specific bone material generation. The vertebrae surface meshes were imported to FEBio studio version 2.10 (University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT), for volumetric meshing and FEA. LLIF cages were created in fusion based on publicly available specifications for PEEK and titanium cages. A 500 N compressive force was applied to L2, with lateral bending and flexion/extension ROM elicited by 7.5 N·m moment. Von-Mises stress was extracted from the L3 inferior and L4 superior endplates, using the 99.9th percentile value to limit the effect of single-element outliers. Results: For PEEK cages, the symmetrically and asymmetrically overhung cages caused the greatest von-Mises stress in all degrees of freedom at the L3 endplate. The symmetrically placed 55 mm cage caused the highest von-Mises stress in pure compression (8.49 MPa), left lateral bending (8.10 MPa), flexion (7.59 MPa), and extension (7.87 MPa). The asymmetrically placed 55 mm cage caused the highest stress in right lateral bending (13.70 MPa). At the L4 endplate, the asymmetrically placed 55 mm cage produced the highest von-Mises stress in all ROM with 7.22 MPa in pure compression, 16.68 MPa in right lateral bending, 11.33 MPa in left lateral bending, 5.79 MPa in flexion, and 10.68 MPa in extension. For titanium cages, at the L3 endplate, the 40 mm cage produced the highest von-Mises stress in pure compression (4.23 MPa), right lateral bending (7.87 MPa), left lateral bending (4.20 MPa), and flexion (4.07 MPa), while the asymmetrically placed 55 mm cage produced the highest stress in extension (5.01 MPa). Stresses were relatively stable with lower von-Mises stress values across all ROM at the L3 inferior endplate. At the L4 superior endplate, the 55 mm cages caused the highest von-Mises stress in all ROM. The symmetric cage caused the highest stress in pure compression (3.99 MPa) and flexion (3.83 MPa), while the asymmetric cage caused the highest stress in right lateral bending (13.88 MPa), left lateral bending (5.26 MPa), and extension (6.02 MPa). Conclusions: In this patient-specific LLIF model, symmetric and asymmetric cage overhang consistently increased endplate stress in PEEK cages. The results were more varied in the titanium model, suggesting a possible impact of overall cage geometry on subsidence risk.

## A338: Machine learning-driven clinical and imaging clustering of degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis: implications for stratified surgical care

Karlo Pedro

1

, Aazad Abbas

2

, Chris Bailey

3

, Jennifer Urquhart

3

, Greg McIntosh

4

, Andrew Glennie

5

, Charles Fisher

6

, Philippe Phan

7

, Raja Rampersaud

2,8

, CSORN Investigators

1

Division of Neurosurgery and Spine Surgery, Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, Canada

2

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

3

Combined Orthopaedic and Neurosurgical Spine Program, London Health Sciences Centre, London, Canada

4

Canadian Spine Outcomes and Research Network, Toronto, Canada

5

Department of Surgery, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada, Halifax, Canada

Combined Neurosurgical and Orthopedic Spine Program, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, Vancouver, Canada

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, The Ottawa Hospital, Ottawa, Canada

8

Schroeder Arthritis Institute, Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Recent randomized trails for the surgical management of degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (DLS) report non-inferiority of decompression alone. Yet decompression and fusion remains the most common procedure for DLS patients. Previous work from the Canadian Spine Outcomes and Research Network (CSORN) including a modified Delphi process, suggest that the significant clinical and radiographic heterogeneity demonstrated by DLS patient creates substantial variability in surgeon reported decision-making. In this study, we applied unsupervised clustering techniques to identify distinct DLS groups, aiming to inform clinical decision-making in selecting the right patients for decompression or decompression and fusion. Material and Methods: We performed a sub-analysis of an ongoing prospective observational CSORN DLS study from 2015 to 2022 at eight Canadian sites. The CSORN-DLS study aims to ultimately develop a consensus-based surgeon decision aid to guide surgical management of DLS in a stratified manner to optimize outcome and resource utilization (i.e. value). Consensus cluster analysis was used based on demographic, clinical, and radiological characteristics of patients enrolled in phase one (baseline current surgeon practice). We selected clinically relevant variables to guide feature selection and evaluated the optimal number of clusters. Euclidean distance metric was used to determine the cluster number and structure, with up to seven clusters considered and 50 sampling iterations. Key characteristics of each cluster were identified, and post-surgical outcomes were compared using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) with pairwise statistical tests. Results: Consensus cluster analysis of 486 DLS patient (mean standard deviation [SD] age, 55.4 [9.2] years, 180 men (37%)) identified four distinct clusters. Cluster 3 (n = 91) mainly consisted of male (97%) patients with moderate disability, low comorbidity, low depression symptoms, and imbalanced (mean SVA = 57mm, PI-LL mismatch = 18 degrees, PT = 24 degrees) spine; while Cluster 4 (n = 135) included elderly patients with severe disability, high comorbidity, high depression, and balanced spine. Clusters 1 and 3 showed the most favorable final ODI outcomes at 1- and 2-years follow-up (Figure 1). Cluster 2 had the highest rate of fusion surgery (84%) and the greatest ODI change at 1 year (ΔODI mean [SD] 27.97 (19.32)). Decompression alone provided sustained benefit in Cluster 1 and 3, while improvement significantly regressed in Cluster 2 and to a lesser degree cluster 4 at two years. Conclusion: Unsupervised machine learning identified four clinically distinct clusters of DLS patients with varying outcome and responses to surgical interventions, highlighting the importance of stratified care strategies to optimize patient outcomes. Furthermore, our results confirm the clinical and radiographic heterogeneity of the surgical DLS population and inform the need for stratified recruitment strategies in future trial design for the evaluation of surgical management of DLS.

## A340: To determine the optimal extent of fusion in anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) for degenerative disc disease. A retrospective analysis based on the university of Michigan Hospital experience

Jawad Saad

1,2

, Peyton Goethe

2

, Noojan Kazemi

2

1

Central Michigan University, Saginaw, United States

2

University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, United States

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) provides durable pain relief and functional improvement for degenerative disc disease but carries increasing approach related and perioperative risks with additional fused levels. Prior studies suggest higher estimated blood loss (EBL), operative time, complication rates, and reoperation risk with multi-level ALIF. This study comprehensively evaluates preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative risks of one-, two-, and three-level ALIFs, using estimated blood loss and operative time to quantify the incremental surgical burden of each additional level fused. Methods: A single-institute retrospective analysis of 141 patients undergoing ALIF (112 single-level, 22 two-level, 7 three-level) was performed. Intraoperative metrics (EBL and operative time), postoperative outcomes (length of stay, reoperations, readmissions, and complications), and patient demographics were analyzed. Statistical analyses used Kruskal–Wallis tests for continuous variables and Fisher–Freeman–Halton exact tests for categorical variables. Significant omnibus tests were followed by post-hoc Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction or Fisher’s exact tests with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05, with a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of p < 0.0167. Results: Baseline characteristics were comparable across all groups. Operative time increased significantly with fusion levels (single: 232.6 min; two-level: 311.6 min; three-level: 350.0 min; p< 0.0001), with significant differences between single and two-level procedures (p=0.0001). EBL differed across groups (p=0.0325) on omnibus analysis, though no individual pairwise comparisons were significant after correction. Mean EBL was 92.8 cc (single-level), 213.9 cc (two-level), and 146.4 cc (three-level). LOS showed a non-significant increasing trend (single: 2.98±1.85 days; two-level: 3.18±1.07 days; three-level: 4.57±2.82 days; p=0.110). Postoperative complications occurred in all groups, with the highest absolute number observed in the single-level cohort, including radicular pain and weakness. Although not significant, reoperations during any readmission occurred exclusively in single-level patients. Conclusion: Multi-level ALIF procedures demonstrated expected increases in intraoperative demands, with operative time differing significantly across fusion levels, increasing from 232.6 min in single-level to 311.6 min in two-level to 350.0 min for three-level procedures (p < 0.0001). EBL shows an increasing trend with each additional fused level, though it lacked statistical significance following correction for multiple comparisons. Contrary to existing literature, our study found complications predominantly in the single-level cohort, with no reoperations or readmissions in the two- or three-level groups. While multi-level procedures require greater surgical effort as measured by operative time, the absence of statistically significant postoperative complications in our multi-level cohorts suggests that higher intraoperative demands may not necessarily translate to worse clinical outcomes. However, our study's findings warrant further investigation to optimize surgical selection while mitigating the risks and benefits of a multilevel ALIF.

## A341: Impact of preoperative sagittal malalignment on patient-reported outcomes following decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis

Shota Tamagawa

1

, Hidetoshi Nojiri

1

, Hiromitsu Takano

1

, Arihisa Shimura

1

, Juri Teramoto

1

, Yuta Sugawara

1

, Muneaki Ishijima

1

1

Juntendo University Faculty of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan

Introduction: Although the relevance of sagittal alignment in adult spinal deformity is well-established, its role in lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) remains controversial. T1 pelvic angle (TPA) and composite indices, such as the Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) score and Sagittal Age-Adjusted Score (SAAS), may better characterize global balance and compensatory mechanisms than sagittal vertical axis (SVA) alone. The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of preoperative sagittal malalignment (MA) on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) following decompression with or without short-segment fusion for LSS. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included LSS patients with predominant neurogenic claudication who underwent decompression ± interbody fusion at ≤ 3 levels between March 2021 and July 2024 and completed 1-year follow-up. Patients were divided into MA (TPA ≥ 20°) and non-MA (TPA < 20°) groups. Whole-body EOS radiographs were obtained preoperatively and 1-year postoperatively to measure spinopelvic parameters and calculate GAP and SAAS. PROMs included Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for low back pain (LBP), leg pain, and leg numbness; Japanese Orthopaedic Association Back Pain Evaluation Questionnaire (JOABPEQ); and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Group comparisons were performed using chi-square or Mann-Whitney U tests. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of achieving the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) in ODI, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, American Society of Anesthesiologists classification, spondylolisthesis, fusion, number of surgical levels, baseline ODI, and TPA ≥ 20°. Results: Of the 176 patients included in this study (mean age 70.1 ± 10.7 years, 57.4% male), 97 patients (55.1%) were classified as MA. The MA group demonstrated significantly worse baseline VAS LBP (6.5 ± 2.6 vs. 5.4 ± 2.9, p = 0.009), JOABPEQ walking ability (23.1 ± 23.1 vs. 32.7 ± 28.7, p = 0.032), and ODI (46.4 ± 14.9 vs. 40.8 ± 17.9, p = 0.012). Radiographically, the MA group had greater pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch, pelvic tilt, SVA, and TPA (all p < 0.001). At 1 year, both groups improved significantly, and ODI MCID achievement rates were comparable (52.1% vs 53.8%, p = 0.817). Multivariable analysis identified younger age (OR 0.95; 95% CI 0.92-0.98; p = 0.002) and higher baseline ODI (OR 1.04; 95% CI 1.02-1.07; p < 0.001) as independent predictors of MCID achievement; TPA ≥ 20° was not significant (OR 1.18; 95% CI 0.60-2.31; p = 0.638). GAP and SAAS stratification showed non-significant trends toward poorer outcomes in severely disproportioned and over-corrected groups. Conclusion: Preoperative sagittal MA was associated with worse baseline LBP and function but did not adversely affect 1-year PROMs. Decompression ± short fusion yields satisfactory outcomes even in patients with sagittal imbalance, suggesting deformity-based thresholds may not directly apply to LSS with neurogenic symptoms.

## A342: Enhanced recovery after spine fixation surgery: an international survey on current practice

Hein Jonkman

1,2

, Floris van Tol

2

, Tim Govers

1,3

, Silje Debets

1

, Tom Wainwright

4

, Bertrand Debono

5

, Michael Yang

6

, Hans De Boer

7

, Maroeska Rovers

1

, Jorrit-Jan Verlaan

2,8

1

Department of Medical Imaging, Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, The Netherlands

2

SentryX, Utrecht, The Netherlands

3

Medip Analytics, Nijmegen, The Netherlands

4

Orthopaedic Research Institute, Bournemouth University, Bournemouth, United Kingdom

5
Centre Francilien Du Dos, Clinique des Franciscaines, Versailles, France,

6

Department of Clinical Neurosciences, Division of Neurosurgery, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada

7

Department of Anesthesiology, Pain Medicine and Procedural Sedation and Analgesia, Martini General Hospital Groningen, The Netherlands, Groningen

8

Department of Radiotherapy, University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands

Introduction: The demand for spine fixation surgery is rising globally, mostly due to an ageing population and corresponding increase in degenerative spinal conditions. Meanwhile, perioperative care delivery faces growing pressure in terms of cost and capacity. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) aims to standardize and improve perioperative care to enhance patient outcomes, reduce complications, and shorten hospital stays. Although well-established in other surgical fields, its application in spine fixation surgery is relatively new, and it remains unclear to what extent recommendations have been adopted in clinical practice. The ERAS-DSF (Degenerative Spine Fixation) study is the first international survey to assess spine surgeons’ perspectives on the importance, implementation, and barriers related to ERAS in spine surgery. Material and Methods: A cross-sectional, web-based survey was distributed in May 2024 to members of AOSpine, the global academic network of spine professionals. The survey focused on instrumented procedures for degenerative spine disease and was structured around eight ERAS components adapted from the published 2021 consensus statement for perioperative care in lumbar spinal fusion. The current work reports one section of the survey, in which respondents were asked to identify which ERAS components had the biggest impact on patient recovery, which ones could be improved the most, what barriers to implementation exist in their hospital, and what support is needed to facilitate adoption. Responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results: The survey was accessed by 400 individuals, filled in by 322 (80.5% response rate), and completed by 247 (76.7% completion rate). Respondents were spine surgeons from a range of clinical settings, including academic (50.6%), private (28.9%), and local/community hospitals (20.5%) from all over the world. The ERAS components most often perceived as having the biggest impact on patient recovery were multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia (73.3%), early mobilization (63.8%), and preoperative education & counselling (58.6%). These same three components were also most frequently selected as leaving the greatest room for improvement, albeit in a different order: preoperative education & counselling (62.6%), early mobilization (41.4%) and multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia (39.4%). Key barriers to ERAS implementation were the absence of clear protocols and guidelines (56.2%), staff shortages (53.8%), and difficulties in coordinating implementation and adherence (43.0%). In terms of support, respondents expressed the need for clear (inter)national recommendations (75.3%), tools for compliance monitoring (60.3%), online training and education (56.3%), and more evidence on the cost-effectiveness (44.5%). Conclusion: Spine surgeons worldwide recognized the ERAS components of multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, early mobilization, and preoperative education & counselling as having the biggest impact on patient recovery. Meanwhile, these same three areas could also be improved the most, suggesting a gap between scientific evidence and clinical practice. To close this gap, clinicians require more practical guidance, training resources, and institutional support. Future research should focus on developing clear and actionable treatment protocols, defining reliable indicators of patient recovery, providing more robust evidence on the cost-effectiveness of ERAS in spine fixation surgery, and establishing best practices for implementation and multidisciplinary collaboration.

## A343: The role of pelvic compensation in sagittal balance and imbalance: the impact of pelvic compensation on spinal alignment and clinical outcomes following adult spinal deformity surgery

Introduction: The Scoliosis Research Society (SRS)-Schwab system does not include a pelvic compensation (PC) subtype, potentially contributing to gaps in clinical characteristics and treatment strategy for deformity correction. ## A344: Long-term impact of total hip arthroplasty on subsequent lumbar spine surgery in patients with hip-spine disease: a nationwide analysis of risk factors and outcomes

Ali Issani

1

, William Karakash

1

, Henry Avetisian

1

, Aidan Lindgren

1

, Daniel Rusu

1

, Mirbahador Athari

1

, Dil Patel

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, Kiran Alluri

1

, John Liu

2

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

2

Department of Neurological Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

Introduction: Degenerative hip and spine pathologies often coexist, with total hip arthroplasty (THA) and lumbar fusion addressing localized disease but showing complex biomechanical interplay. Although THA was once thought to relieve low back pain, recent studies suggest limited benefit, raising questions about its effect on lumbar procedures in patients with HOA and LDD. Prior evidence is conflicting and often lacks adjustment for comorbidities or unilateral versus bilateral THA. This study aims to evaluate whether THA alters the risk of subsequent lumbar decompression or fusion and to identify patient-specific risk factors. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study used the PearlDiver Mariner Database to identify adults with LDD and HOA who underwent THA between 2010 and 2023, with exclusions for prior lumbar surgery, trauma, malignancy, or infection; 1,000,000 matched patients without THA served as controls. The primary outcome was subsequent lumbar decompression or fusion, with secondary analyses assessing comorbidities, lumbar pathologies, and unilateral versus bilateral THA within the THA cohort. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, gender, comorbidities, and scoliosis, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Among 1,194,269 patients with LDD and HOA, 194,269 (16.3%) underwent THA. Compared to controls, the THA cohort was older, had higher comorbidity burden, and showed significantly lower rates of subsequent lumbar decompression (1.4% vs. 4.2%) and fusion (0.7% vs. 2.4%), with multivariable regression confirming reduced odds for both (OR 0.42, p < 0.001). In the THA cohort, decompression risk was increased with male sex (OR 1.7, p < 0.001), obesity (OR 1.3, p < 0.001), opioid use (OR 1.4, p < 0.001), fibromyalgia (OR 1.3, p < 0.001), diabetes (OR 1.2, p < 0.001), depression (OR 1.2, p < 0.001), scoliosis (OR 2.97, p < 0.001), spondylolisthesis (OR 1.96, p < 0.001), myelopathy (OR 2.65, p < 0.001), radiculopathy (OR 1.98, p < 0.001), and spinal stenosis (OR 2.1, p < 0.001); Within the THA cohort, bilateral THA was protective (decompression OR 0.9, 95% CI 0.77 -0.99, p = 0.05; fusion OR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7 -0.96, p = 0.02), compared to unilateral THA (decompression OR 1.1, 95% CI 1.0 -1.29, p = 0.05; fusion OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.03 -1.5, p = 0.02). Predictors for fusion were similar, with strongest associations for scoliosis (OR 4.5, p < 0.001) and spondylolisthesis (OR 2.95, p < 0.001), while osteoporosis (OR 0.75, p < 0.001) and bilateral THA (OR 0.8, p = 0.02) were associated with reduced subsequent surgery. Patients aged 60 -69 had the highest odds of decompression (OR 1.4, p < 0.01) and fusion (OR 1.3, p < 0.001), whereas age > 69 was protective for both (OR 0.8 and 0.6, p < 0.001). Time to subsequent surgery was longer in THA patients (6.5 years) compared to controls (∼3 years). Conclusion: THA in patients with LDD and HOA was associated with reduced risk of lumbar decompression (OR 0.42, p < 0.001) and fusion (OR 0.42, p < 0.001), with bilateral THA protective and unilateral THA increasing risk. Scoliosis, spondylolisthesis, myelopathy, radiculopathy, and spinal stenosis were the strongest predictors of surgery, while comorbidities including opioid use, fibromyalgia, depression, diabetes, and obesity further elevated risk. THA also delayed time to lumbar surgery, suggesting timely hip intervention may influence spinopelvic biomechanics. These findings highlight the need for multidisciplinary management of hip -spine syndrome with careful consideration of patient-specific risk factors.

Introduction: The prevalence of patients requiring lumbar spinal fusion (LSF) with prior total joint arthroplasty (TJA) (total knee and hip arthroplasty (TKA, THA)) is increasing. ## A347: Sagittal alignment as a major prognostic determinant in degenerative spine surgery: from 3D biomechanical planning to spinal instrumentation optimization through robotic assistance and intraoperative navigation

Grouz Khalil

1

, Amine Selmene

1

, Elyes Zoghlami

2

1

Centre de Traumatologie et Des Grands Brulées de Ben Arous, Tunis, Tunisia

2

Hopital Militaire, Tunis, Tunisia

Introduction: Degenerative spine surgery has evolved toward a comprehensive reconstructive approach emphasizing sagittal balance restoration. This study aims to demonstrate that sagittal alignment represents the primary prognostic determinant of therapeutic success and to quantify the contribution of computer-assisted surgical technologies in optimizing biomechanical and clinical outcomes. Materials and Methods: Prospective single-center study including 85 consecutive patients undergoing lumbosacral arthrodesis for symptomatic degenerative pathologies (degenerative spondylolisthesis, adult scoliosis, spinal stenosis with instability). ## A348: Normal spino-pelvic alignment in healthy adolescents: defining the PI-SS relationship and laying the foundations for pre-operative sagittal planning

Matteo Traversari

1

, Alberto Ruffilli

2

, Giovanni Viroli

2

, Marco Manzetti

2

, Alessandro Cargeli

1

, Cesare Faldini

1

1

IRCCS - Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

2

IRCCS - Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Dipartimento di Scienze Biomediche e Neuromotorie - DIBINEM, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Surgical treatment of adolescent spinal deformities requires preoperative planning. Few studies confirmed that sagittal alignment restoration is crucial to reduce the risk of early degeneration, yet sagittal alignment targets are lacking in adolescents. No predictive formula for ideal SS has been developed specifically for surgical planning in adolescents. The aim of the present study was to investigate the relationship between pelvic incidence (PI) and sacral slope (SS) in healthy adolescents aged 11-18 years to identify the most accurate model for SS prediction. Material and Methods: Full-spine standing biplanar X-rays were analyzed. PI, SS and pelvic tilt (PT) were measured. Three regression models (linear, polynomial, and logarithmic) were generated to describe the PI-SS relationship. The adult-derived model by Yilgor et al. was also applied to the study cohort. Accuracy and precision of all models were assessed globally and within PI-based subgroups. External validation was performed using a previously published dataset. Results: A total of 122 patients (mean age 14 years) were included. Logarithmic and polynomial models achieved the best fit within the study cohort (R2 = 0.63 and 0.63). The Yilgor et al. model showed substantially lower fit (R2 = 0.39). Residual and absolute error pairwise analyses confirmed significantly lower errors for the polynomial and logarithmic models compared to the Yilgor model (p < 0.01), which exhibited systematic underestimation of SS in intermediate and high PI subgroups. Conclusion: Our results suggest that the formula SSideal = 0.61 x PI + 11.5 can be reliably employed in the pre-operative planning of adolescent spinal deformities. However, logarithmic model of PI-SS relationship showed high performances in study cohort, particularly in patients with low PI.

## A349: The association between spinopelvic parameters and thoracolumbar spinal forces

Fatemeh Alavi

1

, Christopher J. Nielsen

1

, Michael Kelly

2

, Jeffrey Hills

3

, Stephen Lewis

1

1

University of Toronto, University Health Network (UHN), Toronto, Canada

2

Rady Children’s Hospital, University of California San Diego, San Diego, United States

3

UT Health San Antonio, San Antonio, United States

Introduction: Sagittal malalignment is a well-established risk factor for mechanical complications following adult spinal deformity correction surgery. Excessive spinal force has been proposed as one of the key mechanisms linking malalignment to these complications. However, little is known about how spinopelvic parameters influence spinal forces in individuals without deformity. The present study aims to investigate the association between spinopelvic alignment and spinal forces at the thoracolumbar junction in a normal population. Methods: Full-body low dose stereoradiographic evaluation was performed in an international multi-ethnic cohort of 319 asymptomatic adult volunteers. Demographic data and spinopelvic parameters such as pelvic incidence (PI), T1-pelvic angle (TPA), L1-S1 lordosis (LL), L4-S1 lordosis (L4S1), L1 pelvic angle (L1PA), and L4 pelvic angle (L4PA) were measured. Individualized musculoskeletal (MSK) models based on sex, weight, height, and spine curvature were created and spinal forces (shear and compression) were calculated using MSK analysis. The associations between demographic data, spinopelvic alignment parameters, and spinal forces were evaluated using multivariate regression analyses. Results: 192 out of 319 individuals (60%) were female. The mean weight was 62 13kg, height was 1.6 0.8m. The mean PI was 52° 10°, pelvic tilt (PT) was 12° 6°, and LL was 58° 10°. The spinal forces were calculated using MSK analysis. The mean compressive forces at L2 and L1 were 346 100N and 369 106N, while mean shear forces were 55 27N and 70 36N. The shear forces at L1 and L2 levels were associated with PI, PT, L1PA, weight, L4-S1 horizontal distance, and the Cobb angle between these levels and S1 (r2=0.86). The compressive forces at these levels were associated with PI, PT, L1PA, weight, L4S1, and L1-sacrum horizontal distance (r2=0.78). Conclusion: Understanding the association between spinopelvic parameters and spinal forces in asymptomatic individuals provides essential baseline data that may help distinguish compensatory mechanisms from pathological loading patterns. These insights could ultimately contribute to improved pre-planning, risk stratification and preventative strategies for mechanical complications in spinal deformity surgery.

## A350: Impact of lumbar disc arthroplasty on spinopelvic parameters and sagittal balance

Anthony Nguyen

1

, Daniele Morelli

1

, Henri-Benjamin Pouleau

1

, Nicolas Massager

1

, Alexander Jodaitis

1

1

University Hospital of Tivoli, La Louvière, Belgium

Introduction: Lumbar disc arthroplasty has emerged as an alternative to fusion in the treatment of refractory discogenic low back pain, aiming to preserve motion and reduce adjacent segment degeneration. However, its effect on sagittal balance parameters remains insufficiently documented. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective monocentric study including 81 patients (mean age 43.8 ± 6.6 years; 68% female) who underwent lumbar arthroplasty between 2017 and 2024. Patients with less than 6 months of follow-up or lacking postoperative full-spine radiographs were excluded. Radiographic parameters analyzed pre- and postoperatively included pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), sacral slope (SS), lumbar lordosis (LL), segmental lordosis, and segmental range of motion (ROM). Sagittal balance was defined according to Schwab’s formula (LL = PI ± 9°). Results: Arthroplasty significantly increased LL (52.0° ± 11.1° to 58.2° ± 8.9°, p < 0.001), segmental lordosis (5.9° ± 4.0° to 11.7° ± 4.1°, p < 0.001), and ROM (5.2° ± 4.2° to 13.6° ± 4.9°, p < 0.001). Adverse events included adjacent disc degeneration in 6.1% and facet syndrome in 9.9%. Conclusion: Lumbar arthroplasty significantly restores lumbar lordosis and disc mobility, thereby improving sagittal alignment in most patients. These results support its role as a motion-preserving alternative to fusion, with promising radiological and clinical outcomes.

## A351: Validation of pelvic inclination angle as a novel sagittal parameter in adult spinal deformity surgery: association with postoperative radiographic and clinical results

Se-Jun Park

1

, Jin-Sung Park

1

, Dong-ho Kang

1

1

Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Pelvic tilt (PT) is a widely used parameter to assess pelvic compensation in adult spinal deformity (ASD), but its normal values are influenced by pelvic incidence (PI), limiting its universal applicability. The pelvic inclination angle (PIA) is a novel sagittal parameter reportedly independent of PI, with a normal value near 0°, but its clinical relevance in surgically treated patients has not been established. This study aims to validate the clinical utility of PIA in patients with sagittal spinal malalignment (SSM) undergoing corrective surgery, and to compare its correlation with clinical outcomes to established sagittal parameters. Material and Methods: Retrospective cross-sectional study was performed. A total of 211 consecutive patients (mean age, 69.6 years; 88.2% female) who underwent ≥ 6-level fusion including the sacrum or pelvis for symptomatic SSM between 2015 and 2022 and completed 2-year follow-up. Radiographic parameters including PIA, PI-LL (lumbar lordosis), PT, T1 pelvic angle (T1PA), and sagittal vertical axis (SVA) and clinical outcome including Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Scoliosis Research Society-22r (SRS-22r) questionnaire were evaluated. Correlations between PIA and other sagittal parameters, as well as with ODI and ODI change (ΔODI), were assessed. In addition to PROM scores, the proportion of patients achieving minim clinically important difference (MCID) was evaluated. PIA thresholds corresponding to mild and severe disability were calculated. Linear regression analysis was performed to identify factors affecting the postoperative PIA values. Results: Postoperative PIA showed stronger correlation with ODI (cc = 0.43) than PI-LL (cc = 0.22), PT (cc = 0.23), T1PA (cc = 0.30), or SVA (cc = 0.27). ΔPIA correlated more strongly with ΔODI (cc = 0.24) than changes in other parameters (cc ranging from 0.02 to 0.12). PIA thresholds for mild and severe disability were calculated as 8.0° and 12.0°, respectively. Low PIA (< 8.0°) group demonstrated the most favorable postoperative ODI, SRS-22r scores, and highest MCID achievement. Multivariate linear regression analysis revealed that postoperative PIA was significantly affected by postoperative LL and PT, but not affected by PI. Conclusion: PIA demonstrated significant correlations with established sagittal parameters and a stronger association with disability than conventional measures. Postoperative PIA was unaffected by PI, supporting its universal applicability. A threshold of 8.0° was linked to optimal outcomes, while values > 12.0° were associated with greater disability. PIA may serve as a reliable, PI-independent metric for assessing pelvic compensation and guiding surgical targets.

## A352: A decade of lumbar tubular minimally invasive spine surgery: analyzing complication trends through a systematic review and meta-analysis

Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi

1

, Sean Inzerillo

1

, Eesha Gurav

1

, Noah Willett

1

, Mousa Hamad

1

, Galal Elsayed

1

, Osama Kashlan

1

, Roger Härtl

1

1

Department of Neurological Surgery, Och Spine at New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: Tubular Minimally Invasive Spine Surgery (MISS) is an effective approach for treating lumbar spine disorders. This study aimed to comprehensively quantify the incidence of overall and specific complications associated with tubular lumbar MISS through a systematic review and proportional meta-analysis of studies published over the last decade. Material and Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library (January 2013 to March 2024) was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Studies were included if they involved ten adult patients undergoing tubular lumbar MISS and provided extractable complication data. A random-effects model was used to pool complication rates, and study quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. All analyses were done using R studio. Results: Seventy-five studies involving approximately 12,600 patients were included in the analysis. The complication rate was 10% (95% CI: 8%-14%, I2 = 93%). Specific complication rates were: dural tears 4% (95% CI: 3%-5%, I2 = 69%) in 56 studies (6,651 patients); nerve injuries 1% (95% CI: 1%-3%, I2 = 70%) in 41 studies (5,278 patients); postoperative hematoma 1% (95% CI: 1%-2%, I2 = 31%) in 19 studies (2,454 patients); surgical site infections 1% (95% CI: 0%-1%, I2 = 27%) in 46 studies (10,439 patients); revision surgeries 2% (95% CI: 2%-3%, I2 = 77%) in 43 studies (8,948 patients); and disc re-herniation 3% (95% CI: 1%-7%, I2 = 84%) in 14 studies (1,928 patients). Conclusion: This meta-analysis provides a comprehensive overview of complication rates in tubular lumbar MISS, revealing generally low rates but significant heterogeneity across studies. These findings offer valuable insights for patient counseling and surgical planning, though individual patient factors and surgeon experience should be considered. Standardized complication reporting and research into outcome variability are needed to improve future studies.

## A353: Oblique lumbar interbody fusion with anterolateral screw-rod fixation versus posterior pedicle screws for adjacent segment degeneration: a two-year comparative study

Khanathip Jitpakdee

1

, Weerasak Singhatanadgige

2

, Vit Kotheeranurak

2

, Worawat Limthongkul

2

, Wicharn Yingsakmongkol

2

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Queen Savang Vadhana Memorial Hospital, Chonburi, Thailand

2

Department of Orthopaedics, King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand

Introduction: Surgical management of adjacent segment disease (ASD) often involves extending the previous fusion to include the degenerated adjacent segments. Oblique lumbar interbody fusion (OLIF) is a minimally invasive option for treating ASD following primary lumbar fusion. Traditionally, following retroperitoneal approach for OLIF, a separate extended posterior approach needs to be performed to revise posterior construct and extend fusion with posterior pedicle screws (OLIF-PPS). However, OLIF with anterolateral screw-rod fixation (OLIF-ASR) allows single-position fixation through the same retroperitoneal approach with less invasiveness, however, its comparative outcomes remain unclear. This study compares the two-year clinical and radiographic outcomes of OLIF-ASR versus OLIF-PPS for ASD. Material and Methods: Fifty-five patients undergoing single-level OLIF for symptomatic ASD at L2-3 or L3-4 between January 2018 and September 2023 were reviewed. Twenty patients received OLIF-ASR, and 35 received OLIF-PPS. Clinical outcomes included Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and visual analog scale scores for back (VAS-B) and leg pain (VAS-L) at 1 month, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years postoperatively. Radiographic outcomes included disc height, foraminal height, segmental and lumbar lordosis. Fusion status and cage subsidence were assessed on CT scan. Operative time, blood loss, hospitalization, and complications were also analyzed. Results: Both groups showed significant improvement in ODI, VAS-L, and VAS-B at all follow-up intervals compared with baseline (p < 0.01). VAS-L improvement was comparable between groups. However, VAS-B reduction was significantly greater in the OLIF-ASR group at all time points, with a mean 2-year score of 1.9 ± 0.6 versus 2.6 ± 0.7 in OLIF-PPS (p < 0.05). ODI improvements did not differ significantly at final follow-up. Both groups demonstrated significant postoperative improvement in disc height, foraminal height, and sagittal alignment, but no significant differences between groups were observed. Fusion was achieved in 88% of OLIF-ASR and 93% of OLIF-PPS cases (p = 0.53). Subsidence rates were similar (13% vs 8.6%, p > 0.05). Perioperatively, OLIF-ASR was associated with significantly shorter operative time (95 ± 22 min vs. 143 ± 29 min, p < 0.01), less blood loss (50 ± 24 mL vs. 97 ± 46 mL, p < 0.01), and shorter hospitalization (3.0 ± 0.9 vs. 4.3 ± 1.1 days, p < 0.01). The overall complication rate was not significantly different between groups; no major vascular complications or major neurological injury were observed. There was one patient with cage migration following OLIF-ASR which subsequently needed revision surgery. Conclusion: Both OLIF-ASR and OLIF-PPS provide favorable clinical and radiographic outcomes for ASD at two years. OLIF-ASR offers comparable fusion and safety profiles while offering the advantages of reduced operative time, blood loss, hospital stay, and superior back pain improvement. These findings support OLIF-ASR as a less invasive alternative to posterior fixation in selected patients requiring revision surgery for ASD.

## A354: Learning curve and CUSUM analysis of the interlaminar approach in full-endoscopic spine surgery: a phase-specific evaluation

Takeshi Kaneko

1

1

Inanami Spine and Joint Hospital, Tokyo, Japan

Introduction: Full-endoscopic spine surgery (FESS) via the interlaminar approach has been increasingly adopted as a minimally invasive and effective technique. However, its mastery requires stepwise skill acquisition. This study aimed to analyze the learning curve of FESS by dividing the procedure into operative phases and applying Cumulative Summation (CUSUM) analysis to determine phase-specific proficiency thresholds. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 123 consecutive single-level lumbar FESS cases performed by three novice surgeons (Surgeon A: 52 cases, Surgeon B: 41 cases, and Surgeon C: 30 cases) between June 2023 and August 2025. Each procedure was segmented into three phases: • Phase 1: Skin incision to ligamentum flavum exposure • Phase 2: Flavum exposure to flavum removal and nerve root visualization, • Phase 3: Nerve root visualization to herniated disc removal and wound closure, Operative time was recorded for each phase. Learning curves were assessed using CUSUM analysis to evaluate stabilization and proficiency thresholds. Results: CUSUM analysis revealed distinct patterns of proficiency across the three surgeons. In Phase 1, proficiency was achieved relatively early, with Surgeon A reaching the decision limit at the 12th case, Surgeon B at the 13th case, and Surgeon C at the 8th case. Phase 2 showed greater variability: Surgeon A achieved proficiency at the 3rd case and Surgeon C at the 4th case, while Surgeon B required more experience, reaching proficiency only at the 23rd case. Phase 3 demonstrated the steepest learning curve, with proficiency achieved at the 21st case for Surgeon A, the 32nd case for Surgeon B, and the 8th case for Surgeon C. Overall, Phases 1 and 2 tended to stabilize earlier, whereas Phase 3 consistently demanded more cases, highlighting its technical complexity and the need for accumulated surgical experience in herniated disc removal. Conclusion: The learning curve of interlaminar FESS is phase-dependent. Phase 1 and Phase 2 can be mastered within a relatively small number of cases, although variability exists among surgeons. In contrast, Phase 3, which involves herniated disc removal, consistently required more operative experience before proficiency was achieved, underscoring its technical complexity. These findings suggest that accumulated surgical experience plays a decisive role in mastering advanced steps of FESS. While cadaveric training may be sufficient for Phase 1 and Phase 2, complementary strategies such as structured video-based learning and observation of expert-performed surgeries may be necessary to accelerate proficiency in Phase 3 and ensure safe and effective adoption of endoscopic spine surgery.

Xilin Liu

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital, School of Medicine,University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China

Introduction: Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis is a leading cause of axial back pain and radiculopathy in adults and frequently necessitates instrumented interbody fusion to restore segmental alignment and achieve neural decompression. Oblique lumbar interbody fusion (OLIF) has emerged as a minimally invasive technique that enables indirect decompression and reliable disc-height restoration while minimizing exposure-related morbidity. The optimal choice of supplemental fixation after OLIF remains contentious: posterior percutaneous pedicle screw constructs afford strong posterior support and slip reduction, whereas lateral vertebral or plate fixation avoids a posterior approach but raises concerns about cage subsidence and long-term maintenance of disc height. Robot-assisted single-position OLIF may combine OLIF’s advantages with enhanced implant accuracy and procedural efficiency. This retrospective study compares clinical, radiographic, and perioperative outcomes among RA-OLIF, OLIF+VF, and OLIF+PPS to guide evidence-based surgical selection. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed the clinical data of 85 patients with single-level lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis who underwent RA-OLIF (n = 35), OLIF+PPS (n = 28), or OLIF+VF (n = 22) between March 2017 and January 2024 in the Department of Orthopedics, Sichuan Provincial People’s Hospital,Chengdu,China. Clinical outcomes and complications were assessed, along with radiographic parameters at 6 and 12 months postoperatively, including disc height (DH), slip ratio, cage subsidence, lumbar lordosis (LL), fused segmental angle (FSA), and fusion rate. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0, with one-way ANOVA and LSD-t tests applied for group comparisons. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. No major complications such as vascular or visceral injury were observed.
