Intraoperative blood loss was minimal across groups, with the OLIF+VF group showing the least blood loss due to the absence of a posterior incision (p < 0.05). Operative duration was shortest in the OLIF+VF group, followed by RA-OLIF, and longest in OLIF+PPS (all pairwise p < 0.05). At 6- and 12-month follow-ups, RA-OLIF and OLIF+PPS demonstrated comparable improvements in DH restoration and slip correction (p > 0.05), both superior to OLIF+VF (p < 0.05). Cage subsidence was significantly higher in the OLIF+VF group than in the other two groups (p < 0.05), while RA-OLIF and OLIF+PPS showed no difference (p > 0.05). Improvements in LL, FSA, and fusion rate were similar across all groups (p > 0.05). Conclusion: RA-OLIF, OLIF+VF, and OLIF+PPS are all effective surgical options for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis. RA-OLIF and OLIF+VF offer notable advantages in surgical efficiency. Compared with OLIF+VF, RA-OLIF provides superior maintenance of postoperative disc height, better slip reduction, and reduced risk of cage subsidence. Further validation with multicenter, large-sample, and long-term studies is warranted.

The traditional TESSYS technique performs foraminaloplasty under X-ray fluoroscopy guidance, which has a relatively steep learning curve and poses risks of nerve and dural sac injury during the stepwise foraminaloplasty. In recent years, the visualized foraminaloplasty technique proposed by Chinese scholars integrates the advantages of open and minimally invasive surgeries, enabling targeted articular process resection/plasty with clear visualization of anatomical structures. This study aims to compare the clinical efficacy and perioperative indicators of visualized reamer foraminaloplasty versus fluoroscopy-guided foraminaloplasty in TELD, and to explore the clinical value of the fully visualized technique in reducing intraoperative fluoroscopy times and optimizing surgical workflow. Material and Methods: A retrospective study was conducted on 54 patients who underwent TELD from January to December 2023. Patients were divided into the visualized reamer group (27 cases, 18 males and 9 females) and the TESSYS group (27 cases, 16 males and 11 females) according to the foraminaloplasty method. There were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between the two groups. All patients were followed up for at least 12 months postoperatively. Clinical efficacy was evaluated using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for low back and leg pain at preoperative and follow-up visits. Functional outcomes were assessed by the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and McNab criteria. Perioperative indicators (including intraoperative fluoroscopy times, surgical duration, and intraoperative blood loss) were recorded for both groups. Results: Both groups showed significant improvement in VAS scores for low back and leg pain at postoperative and all follow-up time points compared with preoperative baseline (all p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed between the two groups in VAS, ODI, or McNab criteria at follow-up. Compared with the TESSYS group, the visualized reamer group had fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times [(6.19 ± 0.74) times vs. (12.22 ± 0.97) times, p < 0.05], shorter surgical duration [(71.26 ± 10.74) min vs. (82.95 ± 14.51) min, p < 0.05], and less intraoperative blood loss [(6.44 ± 2.68) ml vs. (9.07 ± 4.17) ml, p < 0.05]. Conclusion: Visualized reamer foraminaloplasty and fluoroscopy-guided foraminaloplasty yield comparable postoperative clinical outcome in TELD. However, the fully visualized technique significantly reduces intraoperative fluoroscopy times, shortens surgical duration, and reduces intraoperative blood loss. For beginners in minimally invasive spine surgery, with the assistance of visualized reamer spinal endoscopic technology, it is easier to identify anatomical structures in the foraminal region, accurately determine the location and extent of articular process plasty, and gradually establish a standardized and highly reproducible surgical workflow.

## A359: Expanding endoscopic application to neuromodulation: novel biportal endoscopic insertion technique for surgical paddle lead

Young San Ko

, Yong Jin Park

Kyungpook National University, School of Medicine, Kyungpook National University Hospital, Daegu, South Korea

Suncheon Hana Hospital, Suncheon, South Korea

Introduction: Surgical paddle-lead insertion for spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is a cornerstone therapy for chronic refractory pain, offering lower impedance and reduced battery usage compared with percutaneous leads. ## A360: Mid-term clinical outcomes of unilateral biportal endoscopic discectomy via the contralateral sublaminar approach for very high-grade lumbar disc migration

Yong Jin Park

, Sang Kyu Son

, Young San Ko

Good Moonhwa Hospital, Busan, South Korea

3

Kyungpook National University Hospital, Daegu, South Korea

Introduction: Lumbar disc herniation (LDH) with very high-grade migration presents a significant surgical challenge due to the difficulty in accessing migrated fragments without excessive bone resection or neural manipulation. The unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) contralateral sublaminar approach offers a minimally invasive alternative, enabling decompression through an existing sublaminar corridor, thereby minimizing bone removal and preserving spinal stability. This study aimed to evaluate the mid-term clinical and radiological outcomes of this technique in a larger patient cohort. Material and Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included 30 patients who underwent UBE discectomy via the contralateral sublaminar approach for LDH with very high-grade upward or downward migration between June 2022 and July 2024. ## A361: Evidence-based AI decision support system for spine surgery: a novel approach using dynamic PubMed integration

Begüm Aslantaş Kaplan

1

, Ali Kaplan

1

, İlker Solmaz

2

1
Tokat Erbaa State Hospital, Tokat, Turkey, 
2
Private Practice, Ankara, Turkey
Introduction: Decision-making in spine surgery is a complex process defined by evolving evidence and nuanced patient factors. While evidence-based medicine is the standard of care, the rapid expansion of literature makes it challenging for clinicians to remain constantly updated. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential for information synthesis, but their clinical use is limited by risks of hallucination and generic responses. This study introduces a novel evidence-based AI decision support system that dynamically integrates real-time PubMed database queries to provide contemporary, literature-supported clinical recommendations. Material and Methods: We developed an AI system using Model Context Protocol (MCP) methodology, enabling ChatGPT-5 to access PubMed API in real-time. Unlike fine-tuning, which freezes knowledge at a point in time, or static RAG systems that query a fixed local database, our approach establishes a direct, real-time query-response loop with the PubMed API for every clinical prompt. This eliminates the need for manual model updates and guarantees the system remains perpetually up-to-date with the latest medical publications. A senior spine surgeon curated twelve challenging clinical scenarios from anonymized past cases, covering trauma, infection, tumor, and degenerative pathologies, each with confounding variables to challenge the decision-making process. The AI system generated comprehensive reports for each scenario. These AI recommendations were then independently evaluated by three spine surgeons, blinded to the MCP methodology: (1) diagnostic accuracy (1-10 scale), (2) treatment approach appropriateness (conservative vs. surgical), (3) surgical technique selection rationale, (4) evidence quality and citation accuracy, (5) absence of hallucinations or fabricated references, (6) clinical reasoning coherence, and (7) risk-benefit analysis completeness. Results: The evidence-based AI system demonstrated high performance across all evaluation domains. Mean diagnostic accuracy scores ranged from 9.2-9.8 across the three evaluators (ICC = 0.82). Treatment approach appropriateness achieved consistently high ratings (mean 8.5, range 7.9-9.1), with 91.7% agreement between AI recommendations and expert consensus. Surgical technique selection showed moderate agreement (mean 7.8), reflecting inherent variability in surgical approaches among experts. Critically, no hallucinated references were identified, with 100% of cited literature verified as authentic and accurately represented. Evidence quality scores averaged 8.4, indicating robust literature synthesis. Clinical reasoning coherence and risk-benefit analysis completeness both exceeded 8.0 mean scores across all evaluators. The system successfully avoided generic recommendations, with all outputs directly traceable to specific PubMed articles. Conclusion: This novel evidence-based AI decision support system represents a significant methodological advancement from traditional AI applications by ensuring real-time literature integration through MCP, which is distinct from static RAG systems and fine-tuning approaches that require manual updates and become progressively outdated. The high expert validation scores demonstrate the system's potential for reliable clinical decision support in complex spine surgery cases. The MCP-enabled dynamic querying provides transparent, traceable evidence sources while maintaining perpetually current knowledge without manual intervention, achieving clinical accuracy comparable to expert recommendations. This methodology offers a promising framework for developing trustworthy, automatically up-to-date AI tools in surgical specialties, addressing key limitations of conventional AI systems through evidence-based, real-time knowledge synthesis.

## A362: Distance-aware augmented reality rendering platform with enhanced accuracy through user-specific eye calibration

Sepehr Madani

1,4

, Carlo Santaguida

2

, Robert Turcotte

1,3,4

, Amir Hooshiar

4

, Ahmed Aoude

1,3,4

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, McGill University

2

Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery, McGill University

3

Department of Surgical Oncology, Gerald Bronfman Department of Oncology, McGill University

4

McGill SuPER Center for Robotic Surgery

*At the time of submission of this abstract for GSC2026 the complete version of this work where we have discussed all the mathematical models and technical implementations has been submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics and is under review.
Introduction: Augmented reality(AR) in minimally invasive spine surgery(MISS) offers real-time enhanced visualization of target anatomy and critical structures such as boundaries of a bone tumor or vertebrae submerged under the skin. However, clinically significant parallax-induced projection errors (particularly during close AR goggle–anatomy distances) drastically deteriorate its projection accuracy. These optical distortions are amplified by individual user eye variations. Objective: To develop and validate a device-agnostic, indifferent to inter-user optical variabilities, active parallax-effect compensated (APC) framework that minimizes projection error across variable surgeon-to-target distances without reliance on fiducial markers. Methods: Major AR projection system components are as follows: Optical See-through Head-Mounted Display(OSTHMD) and Target Anatomy Tracked by Infrared Surgical Navigation System(NAV). We devised a fiducial-free OSTHMD–NAV non-linear optimization-based spatial registration framework. Afterwards, two canonical working distances were sampled: “near”(≈350 mm) and “far”(≈800 mm). Using an ASTM-F2554-22 reference block, the operator first probes 4 physical landmarks with an IR-tracked stylus, then acquires the corresponding virtual points rendered by the OSTHMD in the workspace. The system automatically calibrates itself using our newly devised APC algorithm. Five clinicians participated in a prospective validation. Our user-specific calibration protocol was performed prior to real-anatomy visualization, followed by AR projection accuracy assessments on a 3D-printed lumbar spine model. Six anatomical landmarks were used: L4 spinous process base(p1), L3 right transverse process(p2), L3 spinous process(p3), L2 left transverse process(p4), L2 spinous process(p5), and L1 mid-right transverse process(p6). The devised real-time algorithm dynamically adjusted rendering based on goggle-to-anatomy distance using interpolated transformation matrices derived from six individual hyperbolic tangent functions in tune-space. Projection accuracy was quantified in APC ON vs. OFF conditions at near and far viewing distances using stratified sphere indicators on both ASTM block and spine model anatomic landmarks. Results: Without APC, projection errors averaged 8.50 ± 2.98 mm(near) and 6.26 ± 2.54 mm(far). Enabling APC reduced these to 2.10 ± 1.35 mm and 1.72 ± 1.27 mm, respectively. Our method successfully represents a 75.2%(near) and 72.5%(far) spatial projection accuracy enhancement. Our projection accuracy is unprecedented in literature. Two one-sided t-tests(TOST) confirmed statistical equivalence of near and far projection errors(p < 0.05) within submillimeter equivalency margins. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that user-calibrated APC enables millimeter-scale AR accuracy for both near and far operating distances, addressing a critical barrier to clinical precision AR-assisted MISS deployment. Our fiducial-free, distance-aware system supports precise visualization in spine and orthopedic-oncology surgery and may advance AR integration into our robotic workflows.

## A363: New treatment approaches for early-onset scoliosis: early results of the combined use of magnetically controlled growing rod and active apex control technique

Mehmet Balioğlu

1

, Muhammet Işık

1

, Kadir Abul

1

1

Basaksehir Cam and Sakura City Training and Research Hospital, Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, University of Health Sciences, Hamidiye Faculty of Medicine, Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, İstanbul, Turkey

Introduction: While various growth methods have been described for the surgical treatment of early-onset scoliosis (EOS), studies on hybrid techniques are limited. Active apical control (APC) hybrid surgical technique is one of the newer methods that allows growth while correcting the deformity. This study evaluated changes in radiological parameters associated with deformity and spinal lengthening over time using APC. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of magnetically controlled growing rods (MCGR) on the concave side of the curve and APC on the convex side in the treatment of EOS. This study aimed to maintain convex apical growth, unlike previously described convex apical fusion and compression. Material and Methods: The study included patients with a Cobb angle > 50°, a bone age of < 10 years, a minimum follow-up of 12 months, and no previous surgery for scoliosis. Twenty patients (14 female) who met these criteria were retrospectively evaluated. The system was designed to allow distraction with the MCGR on the concave side and growth with the APC on the convex side. For APC, growth was allowed between the convex apical screws, compression and fusion were not applied. Major Cobb angle (MCA), apicall vertebral translation (AVT), T1-S1 and T1-T12 heights, kyphosis and lordosis were measured preoperatively, early postoperatively, and at final follow-up. There was no significant change in kyphosis or lordosis angles. The mean operative time was 366 minutes, and the mean bleeding volume was 451 ml. Blood transfusion were required in 10 cases. Complications and unplanned surgery were required in 5 patients, 7 required additional surgery. Conclusion: The hybrid technique was concluded to be a promising method for both deformity control and preservation of growth potential, making it a useful early-stage treatment for EOS. Multicenter studies with longer follow-up periods and larger series are needed to better evaluate the hybrid technique compared to other methods

Luke Jouppi

1,2

, Clifford Pierre

, Jeremiah Laichena

, Oliver Mrowczynski

, Mohsen Karami

1,2

, Arnav Gambir

1,2

, Tara Heffernan

, Rod Oskouian

, Jens Chapman

1,2

2

Seattle Science Foundation, Seattle, United States

3

Mount Kenya University, Nairobi, Kenya

Introduction: The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to spine surgery has experienced a dramatic rise in interest in recent years. A critical gap persists between existing proof-of-concept models and our understanding of the real-world needs of practicing surgeons. This study aims to identify global spine surgeons’ priorities, perceived benefits, and barriers for AI deployment. Secondarily, we aim to support the ethical deployment of AI across diverse practice settings by elucidating whether any regional differences exist. Material and Methods: On August 23, 2025, the authors distributed a 9-question Qualtrics survey through the Seattle Science Foundation’s electronic mailing list. The questionnaire began with demographics and information about respondents’ practice settings before inquiring whether respondents had used AI in their practice. Next, Likert scales assessed physicians’ interest in several applications for AI, ranging from 0 to 5: 0 was presented as “not useful at all” and 5 was equivalent to “essential for my practice.” Respondents were then asked to select their top three barriers to implementing AI in their practice. Results: As of September 11, 2025, we received 134 responses. Regarding experience, 45 respondents (34%) identified as spine surgeons in training, 15 respondents (11%) identified as having practiced for under 5 years, 18 (15%) identified as having practiced between 5-10 years, 18 respondents (13%) reported between 10-20 years, and 41 respondents (31%) reported over 20 years in practice. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed significant differences in physicians’ priorities for AI (p < 0.0001). Administrative and practice optimization technologies and patient education assistance presented the greatest interest. Subsequent analysis via Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference revealed administrative AI received significantly greater interest than radiology AI models (p<0.01) and decision-making support models (p < 0.001). Models supporting patient education also received significantly greater interest than radiological AI (p = 0.01) and AI for decision-making support (p < 0.001). Respondents identified technological maturity, ethical and legal concerns, and familiarity with these technologies as the most impactful to their adoption with 56%, 50%, and 48% of respondents reporting these concerns as the most impactful barriers to adopting AI, respectively. Conclusion: Many physicians and a majority of respondents have already begun integrating AI into their practice. Ensuring AI best supports physicians’ and patients’ needs may prove essential as this technology continues to mature. Spine surgeons expressed the strongest interest in AI to decrease the administrative burdens of clinical practice and to support patient education. Our study also underscored the need for further validation of these technologies, updated regulations on their implementation, and educational materials to familiarize physician-colleagues with AI.

## A365: Objective measurement of surgical forces and jerks for a more analytical future in spinal surgical training and practice - A study with novel sensorised force-gloves and interpretable machine learning

Chan Hee Koh

1,2,3

, James Booker

1,2

, Carmen Salvadores Fernandez

4

, Yang Xue

4

, David Choi

1,2

, Parag Sayal

2

, Danail Stoyanov

5

, George Prezerakos

1,2,3

, Manish Tiwari

4

, Hani Marcus

1,2

1

Department of Translational Neuroscience and Stroke, Queen Square Institute of Neurology, University College London, London, United Kingdom

2

Department of Neurosurgery, National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London, United Kingdom

3

Neurosciences Institute, Cleveland Clinic London, London, United Kingdom

4

Nanoengineered Systems Laboratory, Department of Mechanical Engineering, University College London, London, United Kingdom

5

Department of Computer Science, Hawkes Institute, University College London, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: The ability to apply appropriate surgical forces is crucial for mastery in spinal surgery. However, these have traditionally been difficult for an external assessor to measure and objectively assess, more often relying on subjective visual assessments and feedback. We have developed universal sensorized force gloves that were able to reliably measure force applied at the hand-tool interface. This also allows the measurement of “jerk”, which is the instantaneous change in force over time. This study leveraged interpretable machine learning and distributional analysis of surgical forces and jerks in spinal surgical simulations to assess surgical proficiency, with a view to advancing a more objective and analytical approach to surgical training and practice. Material and Methods: 373 force segments were collected from 28 novice and expert surgeons. High-fidelity simulated lumbar decompressions were performed while wearing sensorized surgical gloves. The jerk was calculated by taking the derivative of force with respect to time. These segments were used to train 510 interpretable machine learning algorithms to predict proficiency in lumbar decompressions. The distributional properties of forces and jerks were used as input features for machine learning. These were: (1) the first raw moment of the distribution (the mean); (2) the second unstandardized central moment (the variance i.e. variability in force applied); (3) the third standardized central moment (the skewness i.e. asymmetry in distribution of forces applied); (4) the fourth standardized central moment (the kurtosis i.e. propensity to outliers). Nested crossvalidation schemes were used to tune and train interpretable machine learning algorithms, and then to evaluate the performance on unseen data. The outputs of the best performing algorithm was inspected to investigate how the application of forces and jerks impact on surgical proficiency. Results: Objective and quantitative thresholds of surgical expertise, as it pertains to surgical forces and jerks, were derived from the machine learning algorithms. These thresholds were able to classify surgical proficiency with an excellent balanced accuracy of 95.9% (CI: 74.0% to 100.0%). The excellent overall discriminative utility of the model was demonstrated by AUC-ROC of 96.4% (CI: 84.0% to 100.0%). The outputs of machine learning algorithms showed that strongest predictors of surgical proficiency were: (1) greater mean force applied (log-odds - weak hand: 1.4 /N; strong hand: 0.4 /N); (2) smaller variance of force (log-odds - weak hand: -0.5 /N; strong hand: 0.2 /N); (3) smaller kurtosis of force (log-odds - weak hand: -0.02 /unit; strong hand: -0.01 /unit); and (4) smaller variance of jerk (log-odds - strong hand: -3.0 /N ms-1; weak hand: 0.3 /N ms-1). Conclusion: The attainment of surgical proficiency requires the ability to (1) apply greater force but (2) within tighter margins of variability and control, and (3) avoiding outliers in force application, while (4) also reducing sudden changes in force (jerks). These properties can be objectively measured using sensorised surgical gloves, and interpretable machine learning algorithms can be used to set objective and quantitative thresholds of surgical proficiency. These technologies may enable more objective and analytical spinal surgical training, assessments, and practice in the future.

## A366: Spatial spinal fixation: a new image-guided robotic technique for enhanced implant fixation in compromised vertebral bone

Yash Kulkarni

1

, Daniyal Maroufi

1

, Mobina Tavangarifard

1

, Maryam Tilton

1

, Justin Bird

2

, Shalin Patel

2

, Laurence Rhines

2

, Zachary Lawson

2

, Jeffrey Siewerdsen

2

, Farshid Alambeigi

1

1

University of Texas, Austin, United States

2

MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, United States

Introduction: Traditional spinal fixation techniques rely on rigid drills and straight screws to stabilize the spine. However, the complex anatomy of the spine often limits the surgeon’s ability to place implants along optimal trajectories. This challenge is especially critical in osteoporotic patients and patients with metastatic cancer of the spine, where low bone mineral density and/or lytic lesions increase the risk of screw loosening, pullout, and implant failure. To address these limitations, there is a growing need for steerable drilling systems and more adaptable implant designs that enable safer and more effective fixation in compromised bone. Material and Methods: To overcome the limitations of rigid instruments and linear drilling, we developed an image-guided minimally invasive Steerable Drilling Robotic system capable of creating straight and curvilinear trajectories, both in-plane and out-of-plane, within the vertebral body. We refer to this technique as Spatial Spinal Fixation, as it enables secure placement of flexible implants along patient-specific, non-linear paths that would not be feasible with conventional tools. These results confirm the accuracy and robustness of Spatial Spinal Fixation for complex spinal trajectories. Conclusion: The Spatial Spinal Fixation approach shows strong potential to improve spinal fixation, especially in bone disease states such as osteoporosis, multiple myeloma, and metastatic cancer of the spine. By enabling screw placement along curved and off-axis trajectories, Spatial Spinal Fixation overcomes key limitations of rigid, linear fixation systems, enabling the surgeon to provide patient specific stabilization solutions, targeting higher bone density regions within the vertebrae.

## A367: The performance and clinical translation of artificial intelligence in preoperative spine surgical planning: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Vinicius Ricieri Ferraz

1

, Guilherme Santos Piedade

2

, Carlos Goulart

3

, Maria Ricieri Ferraz Franco de Souza

4

, Marcelo Ochoa Coelho de Souza Furlan

5

, Philippe A. Mercier

6

, Tobias Mattei

6

1

Dr. José de Carvalho Florence Hospital, The Regional Hospital of São José dos Campos - Dr. Rubens Savastano, São José dos Campos, São Paulo, Brazil

2

Department of Neurosurgery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

3
Division of Neurological Surgery, Essentia Health, Duluth, Minessota, United States,

4

Division of Neurology, Irmandade da Santa Casa de Misericordia de Santos, Santos, São Paulo, Brazil

5

Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, Curitiba, Brazil

6

Division of Neurological Surgery, Saint Louis University School of Medicine,, Saint Louis, Missouri, United States

Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) has seen growing application in preoperative planning for spine surgery, enhancing image analysis, optimizing pedicle screw placement, simulating sagittal alignment, and predicting potential adverse events. Despite significant progress in academic research, the integration of AI into clinical practice remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluate the effectiveness of AI systems in preoperative spine surgical planning and identify barriers to their clinical implementation. Material and Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, the Cochrane Library, and arXiv from 2010 through July 2025. We included studies that developed or validated artificial intelligence tools for preoperative spine surgical planning, such as CT/MRI segmentation and 3D reconstruction, pedicle screw trajectory planning, alignment simulation, risk stratification for mechanical complications, and outcome prediction. The quality and potential bias of studies were evaluated using QUADAS-2, PROBAST-AI, and ROBINS-I. When applicable, meta-analyses were performed; otherwise, results were synthesized narratively and aligned with implementation frameworks. Results: Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria. The majority were retrospective, single-center investigations, while a minority were prospective studies. Two randomized controlled trials were identified among the included research. Additionally, several proof-of-concept preclinical studies using animal models were incorporated. In technical tasks, artificial intelligence (AI) demonstrated high performance, particularly in image segmentation, reconstruction, and pedicle screw planning, often achieving strong accuracy metrics. Comparative clinical studies indicated that AI- or navigation-assisted workflows could improve screw placement accuracy and reduce fluoroscopy time or radiation exposure, although sometimes at the cost of longer operative durations. Conversely, models designed to predict complex outcomes such as proximal junctional kyphosis, implant failure, or reoperations showed only modest to moderate discrimination capabilities. Furthermore, the generalizability of these models outside their original datasets remains limited. The heterogeneity in datasets, reporting practices, and endpoints prevented meta-analysis in several areas. Conclusion: AI in preoperative spine surgical planning demonstrates strong technical performance and early clinical benefits in specific tasks such as pedicle screw placement accuracy and radiation dose reduction. However, evidence for reliably predicting complex postoperative outcomes remains limited, and its adoption is hindered by problems such as dataset bias, lack of external validation, workflow integration challenges, and medico-legal considerations. Human-in-the-loop deployments, standardized reporting protocols, and multicenter prospective trials are needed to validate efficacy and define patient populations most likely to benefit.

Introduction: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) is a well-established procedure for treating degenerative lumbar spine conditions. With technological advance, Augmented Reality (AR) has emerged as a tool to improve precision, workflow, and reduce complications. Traditional TLIF relies heavily on fluoroscopy or neuronavigation to guide surgeons during critical phases such as pedicle screw placement. However, recent studies suggest that AR may improve outcomes by offering surgeons a more intuitive visual overlay that facilitates real-time guidance throughout the procedure. This study aims to evaluate the role of AR in minimally invasive (mini-open) TLIF compared to fluoroscopy-only and neuronavigation-assisted techniques. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 59 patients (17 male, 42 female; mean age 64.4 years, range 35-87) who underwent mini-open TLIF between January 2024 and June 2025. Patients were divided into three groups: fluoroscopy-only (17), neuronavigation (30), and AR-supported (12). Data collected included patient demographics, surgery duration, radiation exposure, pedicle screw placement accuracy, postoperative complication rates, and hospital stay. Postoperative imaging was segmented using the Elements Smartbrush software by BrainLab (BrainLab, Munich, Germany) to evaluate surgical accuracy, alignment, and osteotomy volume. Statistical analysis was performed to compare operative times, radiation exposure, and clinical outcomes among the groups. Results: Radiation exposure differed significantly across groups: 195.8 Cy·cm2 in the fluoroscopy group, 12.1 Cy·cm2 with navigation, and 3.4 Cy·cm2 with AR (p < 0.0001). Clinical outcomes improved significantly within each group. Mean NRS decreased from baseline to follow-up in all groups (all p < 0.005 vs baseline): 8.6 versus 5.9 (Fluoro), 8.5 versus 4.9 (Nav), and 7.3 versus 4.3 (AR). Intergroup comparison showed no significant differences (p = 0.685), although AR patients demonstrated a greater numerical reduction. Similarly, ODI improved significantly in all groups (all p < 0.01 vs baseline): 62.5 versus 41.2 (Fluoro), 59.3 versus 38.5 (Nav), and 58.2 versus 35.7 (AR), with no significant intergroup differences (p = 0.504). Spinopelvic parameters remained stable across groups. At follow-up, PI was comparable (≈57-60°, p = 0.843), PT values were within normal compensation ranges (14-20°, p = 0.257), and SS tended to be higher in Fluoro and lower in Nav, with AR intermediate (p = 0.140). No significant differences were found, confirming alignment preservation across techniques. No group differences emerged in screw accuracy or complication rates, although AR showed a trend toward fewer revisions. Mean hospital stay was 6.1 days, with differences between groups (p = 0.0378). Surgeons reported that AR improved anatomical orientation and intraoperative confidence, particularly in complex or revision cases. Conclusion: Augmented reality in mini-open TLIF significantly reduces radiation exposure compared with fluoroscopy and neuronavigation. All groups experienced significant clinical improvement in pain and disability, with AR showing the greatest numerical reduction, although intergroup differences were not statistically significant. Spinopelvic parameters were preserved in all groups, confirming the safety of the approach. AR therefore represents a promising adjunct to conventional guidance systems, with potential to refine surgical precision and improve outcomes. Larger prospective studies are warranted to confirm long-term benefits and clarify its role in complex and revision cases.

## A369: The diagnostic efficacy of MRI-based vertebral bone quality score in assessing bone mineral density in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a retrospective cohort study

Shahzaib Riaz Baloch

1

, Mohammad Sohail Rafi

1

, Raghad Barri

2

1

Dr. Ziauddin Hospital, Clifton Campus, Ziauddin University, Karachi, Pakistan

2

Dr. Soliman Fakeeh Hospital Riyadh, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is frequently associated with low bone mineral density (BMD), which is crucial to assess pre-surgically. Current diagnostic methods like QCT involve ionizing radiation, highlighting the need for alternative screening tools. This study evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of a radiation-free, MRI-based Vertebral Bone Quality (VBQ) score for assessing BMD in patients with AIS. The objective is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the MRI-based vertebral bone quality (VBQ) score in assessing bone mineral density (BMD) in patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), and to compare its performance against existing modalities. Material and Methods: In this retrospective investigation, the hospital database (EMR) was searched for resources of tertiary care institution to identify AIS patients who received lumbar MRI scans between January 2020 and December 2024. Following approval of the ethical review committee, 200 patients with simultaneous MRI and quantitative computed tomography (QCT) data were enrolled. VBQ scores were derived from T1-weighted MRIs. Patients were divided into normal BMD (QCT Z-score > -2.0) or low BMD (QCT Z-score ≤ -2.0) groups. The univariate analysis was used to compare the variables between the groups. Pearson's test was used to evaluate the relationship between VBQ score and QCT Z-score as well. Independent factors for low BMD were determined by a multivariate logistic regression model. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic value of the VBQ score. Results: Out of the 200 patients with AIS (average age 14.9± 2.2 years) there were 68 patients with low BMD. Within the low BMD cohort there was a statistically significant difference between the VBQ scores of the low and normal BMD cohorts (3.59 ± 0.81 vs 2.58 ± 0.59, p < 0.001). A weak negative correlation was noted between the VBQ score and the QCT Z-score (r = -0.492, p < 0.001). After adjusting for other variables, VBQ score low BMD became an independent associated factor of low BMD (OR: 5.221, 95% CI 2.845-9.583, p < 0.001). According to ROC analysis the VBQ score was able to predict low BMD with an AUC score of 0.86. The optimal VBQ score of 3.24 had a sensitivity of 80.9% and a specificity of 84.8%. Conclusion: The VBQ score, derived from standard MRI, is a highly accurate and non-invasive tool for identifying low BMD in AIS patients. Its diagnostic performance is robust, making it a powerful opportunistic screening tool for pre-surgical evaluation and a valuable complementary measure to QCT.

## A370: Accuracy and feasibility of S2AI screw placement using fluoroscopic guidance: a prospective clinical study

Nilesh Barwar

1

1

ALL India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bathinda, India

Introduction: S2 alar-iliac (S2AI) screw placement provides robust sacropelvic anchorage, especially in cases requiring lumbopelvic fixation. Traditional S1 pedicle and alar screws engage primarily cancellous bone, making them prone to failure, particularly in osteoporotic patients, and contributing to complications such as L5-S1 pseudoarthrosis. Given the junctional biomechanics and compromised bone quality in such cases, S2AI screws offer enhanced fixation strength. This study evaluates the feasibility, accuracy, and outcomes of fluoroscopy-guided S2AI screw placement in a clinical setting. Materials and Methods: A prospective analysis was conducted on 16 patients (total of 32 S2AI screws) who underwent fluoroscopy-assisted S2AI screw placement between 2020 and 2025. A non-radiolucent operating table was used, with intraoperative C-arm imaging utilizing both lateral and pelvic outlet-obturator views. To improve visualization, patients were manually shifted away from the table’s side bar, enhancing access to the hemipelvis targeted for screw insertion. Postoperative CT scans were performed to assess screw trajectory accuracy and potential breach. Results: The cohort had a mean age of 46 years (range: 23-57 years). The most common indication was adult degenerative scoliosis and lumbar spondylosis with endplate degeneration (7/16, 44%) followed by tuberculous spondylodiscitis at the lumbar/lumbosacral junction (4/16, 25%). Mean screw insertion time was 22 minutes (range: 15-30 minutes), with an overall mean operative duration of 4 hours (range: 3-6 hours). One intraoperative dural tear occurred (1/16, 6.2%). Postoperative CT revealed a mean transverse plane angulation of 35° anteriorly (range: 25°-38°), and a mean caudal angulation of 28° in the coronal plane (range: 20°-34°). The average distance from the screw to the anterior sacral cortex was 3 mm (range: 1-4 mm). No cortical breaches or neurovascular complications were observed. No wound-related complications were reported at 3-month follow-up. Conclusion: S2AI screw placement using standard fluoroscopic guidance is a reliable and accurate technique for lumbopelvic fixation, even in osteoporotic bone. The use of lateral and pelvic outlet-obturator views provides sufficient intraoperative visualization. Adjusting patient positioning to optimize imaging on non-radiolucent tables significantly enhances screw placement accuracy. This method offers a practical solution for centers without advanced navigation systems.

## A371: Comparison of muscle fat infiltration index of lumbar paraspinal muscles in people with chronic low back pain and healthy individuals

Dipak Shrestha

1

, Jagadish Thapa

1

, Bikash Parajuli

1

1

Dhulikhel Hospital, Kathmandu University Hospital, Dhulikhel, Nepal

Introduction: Low back pain is one of the common cause of significant morbidity. Among the various causes of low back pain, fatty infiltrations of para spinal muscles have also been attributed for the cause of back pain. However, consensus is lacking for clear correlation between fatty infiltration of lumbar para spinal muscle and chronic low back pain. The present study compares lumbar paraspinal muscle fat infiltration in MRI in patients with chronic low back pain with healthy volunteers. Material and Methods: Standardized MRI examination of patients with persistent low back pain for at least for three months and healthy volunteers were evaluated for fatty infiltration of Multifidus and Erector spinae muscle at the level of L3/L4, L4/L5 and L5/S1 using and Image J software to calculate muscle fat infiltration index (MFI) which was defined as a ratio of relative cross-sectional area (rCSA) pixel intensity of the muscle and extra muscular fat pixel intensity. Relative muscle cross-sectional area (rmCSA) was calculated in T1-weighted MRI image by using formula rmCSA = (1 - MFI) *rCSA. Right and left side values were averaged for each of the independent measurements for the analysis. Correlation of MFI was also calculated for numeric pain scale measured by Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Oswestry disability index (ODI) and body mass index (BMI). Results: Of the 190 participants, 97 (Male: 53; mean age 41.09 ± 10 yrs, Female: 44; mean age 39 ± 11.47 yrs) cases were included in the chronic low back pain group and 93 (Male: 65; mean age 40.42 ± 8.46 yrs, Female: 28; mean age 31.61 ± 8.86 yrs) individuals were in the healthy volunteers group. MFI of multifidus (0.14 ± 0.07 vs 0.12 ± 0.05) and erector spinae (0.13 ± 0.66 vs 0.11 ± 0.04) at the level of L3/L4 were significantly different (p = 0.01, 0.03 respectively) between two groups but not significant at L4/L5 and L5/S1 level. There was no correlation between VAS pain score and muscle fatty infiltration index and cross-section area of the paraspinal muscles at all three levels except MFI of multifidus at the L3 and L4 levels (p = 0.005, 0.007). At the L3 level, both MFI and rmCSA of multifidus and erector spinae were correlating with ODI. At the L4 level, MFI and rmCSA of ES only had correlation with ODI. Whereas at the L5 level there was no correlation between the muscle parameters and ODI. With an increase in BMI, there was an increase in the muscle fatty infiltration index of the multifidus at L3 level and the erector spinae at L3, L4 and L5 levels. Conclusion: Muscle fat infiltration index of multifidus and erector spinae at the L3 and L4 levels, but solely of multifidus at the L5 level, was substantially different between patients with chronic low back pain and healthy volunteers. The cross-section area and the muscle fat infiltration index of the erector spinae at both L3 and L4 and the cross-section area of the multifidus at only the L3 level strongly predicted disability from chronic back pain.

## A372: Redefining the learning curve in UBE-XTLIF: why endplate preparation matters most

Young San Ko

1

, Dae-Chul Cho

1

, Yong Jin Park

2

, Subin Kweon

3

1

Kyungpook National University, School of Medicine, Kyungpook National University Hospital, Daegu, South Korea

2

Suncheon Hana Hospital, Suncheon, South Korea

3

Armed Forces Daegu Hospital, Daegu, South Korea

Introduction: Although numerous studies have investigated the learning curve of unilateral biportal endoscopic transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (UBE-TLIF), the operative phase that most strongly determines proficiency remains uncertain. For UBE-assisted TLIF utilizing a large XLIF-type cage (UBE-XTLIF), no phase-specific learning curve analysis has been reported. This study aimed to identify the procedural step that drives the learning curve for UBE-XTLIF and to establish a pragmatic threshold for surgical proficiency. Materials and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 62 consecutive UBE-XTLIF procedures performed via a posterolateral approach by a single surgeon. Operative times were prospectively recorded for two key steps: (1) decompression and (2) endplate preparation with cage insertion. Complications and patient-reported outcomes (VAS and ODI) were collected. The learning curve was assessed using cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis of endoscopic time, with the elbow point demarcating Early (cases 1-30) and Late (cases 31-62) phases. Between-phase comparisons were conducted using standard statistical tests. A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA evaluated the Step × Phase interaction, and Pearson correlation coefficients examined associations between step times and total operative time. Results: The CUSUM curve demonstrated an inflection point near 30 cases, after which operative times stabilized, and adverse events declined. Efficiency gains were not uniform across steps: the endplate preparation with cage insertion phase demonstrated the greatest reduction in time and a significant Step × Phase interaction, indicating that proficiency was primarily achieved during this stage (p < 0.001). This step also showed a stronger correlation with total operative time compared with decompression (r = 0.95, p < 0.001). The overall complication rate was 11.3% (7/62). Most complications clustered in the Early phase and were primarily implant-related, including cage rotation failure, vertebral endplate violation, and nerve root injury during cage insertion.VAS and ODI improved from baseline with similar trajectories across phases. Conclusion: The learning curve for UBE-XTLIF exhibits a distinct inflection point at approximately 30 cases. Endplate preparation with cage insertion is the primary driver of operative efficiency and represents a practical surrogate marker of procedural proficiency. Focused cadaveric training emphasizing standardized contralateral endplate preparation, preservation of the subchondral plate, and controlled cage manipulation may shorten the learning curve and reduce implant-related complications.

, AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative

Fondazione Policlinico Campus Bio-Medico, Rome, Italy

BG Klinikum Bergmannstrost Halle, Halle, Germany

University Hospital Centre Sestre Milosrdnice, Zagreb, Croatia

7

NYU Grossman School of Medicine, New York, United States

8

AO Spine, Davos, Switzerland

Introduction: Lumbar disc herniation (LDH) is among the most prevalent spinal disorders encountered in clinical practice, frequently resulting in significant morbidity and imposing substantial socioeconomic burdens worldwide. Despite considerable advancements in diagnostic imaging and surgical interventions over recent decades, no universal consensus remains on the optimal management strategy for LDH. This ongoing debate is reflective of the diverse array of clinical presentations and disability leading to different treatment modalities offered to patients, from conservative approaches, such as physical therapy and pharmacological management, to more invasive options, including various surgical techniques. The heterogeneity in treatment approaches can be attributed to multiple factors, including differences in surgeon training, regional medical practices, and, primarily, the variable natural history of the disease This study aimed to characterize global practice patterns in the surgical management of primary LDH among AO Spine surgeons. Gabriel Gonzalez

, Zvipo Chisango

, Michael Farias

1

, Joseph Nassar

, Bryce Basques

Brown University, Providence, United States

Introduction: Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis is a common spinal pathology, especially in the caudal levels, that can contribute to severe pain and functional limitations. Surgical interventions are frequently pursued to decompression the foramen, stabilize the vertebral bodies, and restore sagittal alignment. However, a comparison of the available interbody techniques to manage L5-S1 degenerative spondylolisthesis is lacking. Material and Methods: Adults who underwent one-level interbody fusion for L5-S1 degenerative spondylolisthesis were included in this retrospective cohort study. Results: Among 123 included patients, mean age was 55.1 years, 57.7% were female, mean BMI was 30.3kg/m2, and mean CCI was 1.9. Conclusion: In this investigation, ALIF+PLF was shown to be the most effective at correcting spondylolisthesis slip magnitude and segmental alignment. Standalone ALIF and TLIF, on the other hand, demonstrated comparable correction, with standalone ALIF patients experiencing higher rates of pseudoarthrosis/subsidence and reoperations. Combined anterior-posterior support appears beneficial to achieve optimal radiographic and clinical outcomes in patients with L5-S1 degenerative spondylolisthesis.

## A375: Does adding direct decompression impact indirect decompression in one to two level lumbar fusion?

Rowen Lin

1

, Kevin Mo

2

, Justin Chung

1

, William Fang

2

, Shanthan Challa

2

, Daniel Lee

2

, Hugh Bassewitz

2

1

Touro University Nevada, College of Medicine, Henderson, United States

2

Valley Hospital Medical Center, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Las Vegas, United States

Introduction: In one to two-level lumbar fusion, indirect decompression increases the height of intervertebral discs and can relieve neural compression. While direct decompression can further enlarge canal dimensions, it can also increase operative time and increase blood loss. The aim of this study was to determine whether adding direct decompression alongside an initial indirect decompression would impact outcomes following lumbar spinal fusion. Material and Methods: Adult patients undergoing one to two-level indirect decompression were identified from a single surgeon database from 2018-2022. Patients were then sub-stratified into two groups: 1) Patients who received only indirect decompression, 2) patients who received both a direct and indirect decompression. All patients received an indirect decompression through interbody realignment. Pre-operative, intraoperative, perioperative, 6 weeks, and 6 months post-operative data were gathered. Bivariate and multivariable analysis was conducted using STATA 17.0 College Station, TX. Penalized logistic regression was utilized when variables had perfect fit with direct decompression. Results: 125 adult patients were identified who underwent a one to two-level robotic-assisted lumbar fusion. 14 patients received a direct plus indirect decompression. The average age of all patients was 54 (SD 13), 60 were female (478.0%), 42 were smokers (33.6%), and 73 were opiate users (58.4%). Bivariate analysis only showed statistical significance with increased operative time (246.972 ± 65.4 mL vs 292.5 ± 73.5 mL; p = 0.017). However, there was no significance between both cohorts in respect to hospital length of stay (3.12 ± 1.42 days vs 3.42 ± 1.74 days; p = 0.47), post-operative day 1 mobility (168.1 ± 200.5 m vs 87.1 ± 125.2 m; p = 0.14), or VAS scores at 6 weeks (5.7 ± 3.2 vs 6.43 ± 3.8; p = 0.45). On multivariable analysis, when controlling for age, laminectomy, workers' compensation status, preoperative smoking status, robotic assisted, and intercept, direct decompression was not a statistically significant predictor of 6 month satisfaction (OR: 2.44 [-0.48-5.36; p = 0.1021]. Conclusion: While direct decompression added to indirect decompression prolonged operative time, it did not have a statistically significant association with intra-operative blood loss, length of stay, early ambulation, or patient-reported pain at 6 weeks and 6 months. Multivariable regression also showed direct decompression had no statistical impact on patient satisfaction at 6 months. These findings suggest that a direct decompression may be unnecessary when performing indirect decompression to achieve similar outcomes. Further multi-institutional and prospective studies should be performed to confirm these findings.

## A376: Preoperative geriatric nutritional risk index is useful factor for predicting postoperative delirium among elderly patients with degenerative lumbar diseases

Qian Chen

1

, Youwei Ai

2

, Hong Ding

2

, Limin Liu

2

1

Affiliated Hospital of North Sichuan Medical College, Nanchong, China

2

West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China

Introduction: Post-operative delirium (POD) complicates up to one-third of lumbar fusions in older adults, prolonging stay, increasing morbidity and mortality. Malnutrition is an emerging, modifiable risk factor, and the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI)-a simple score derived from serum albumin, weight and height-predicts adverse outcomes in elderly surgical patients. While GNRI correlates inversely with POD after cardiac surgery, its utility after lumbar fusion remains untested; we therefore evaluated whether pre-operative GNRI reliably forecasts POD in geriatric patients undergoing lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: A retrospective study was conducted to assess the outcomes of TLIF surgery in elderly patients with lumbar degenerative disease between the years 2016 and 2022. Delirium was diagnosed by reviewing postoperative medical records during hospitalization, utilizing the Confusion Assessment Method. The geriatric nutritional risk index was calculated using the baseline serum albumin level and body weight. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was employed to identify the association between preoperative GNRI and postoperative delirium (POD). Additionally, a receiver operating characteristic curve was utilized to determine the optimal GNRI cutoff for predicting POD. Results: POD was observed in 50 of the 324 patients. The GNRI was visibly reduced in the delirium group. The mean GNRI was 93.0 ± 9.1 in non-delirium group and 101.2 ± 8.2 in delirium group. On multivariate logistic regression, Risk of POD increases significantly with low GNRI and was an independent factor in predicting POD following TLIF (OR 0.714; 95% CI 0.540-0.944; p = 0.018). On receiver operating characteristic curve, the area under curve (AUC) for GNRI was 0.738 (95% CI 0.660-0.817). The cutoff value for GNRI according to the Youden index was 96.370 (sensitivity: 66.0%, specificity: 70.4%). Conclusion: Our study indicated that lower GNRI correlated significantly with POD after TLIF. Performing GNRI evaluation prior to TLIF may be an effective approach of predicting the risk for POD among elderly patients with degenerative lumbar diseases.

## A377: Static vs. expandable cages in posterior lumbar interbody fusion: effects on spinopelvic alignment and adverse events

Enrico Giordan

1

, Nicola Bresolin

1

, Alessandro Trento

1

, Jacopo Del Verme

1

, Roberto Zanata

1

1

AULSS 2 Marca Trevigiana, Treviso, Italy

Introduction: Posterior lumbar interbody fusion techniques (PLIF and TLIF) have a known limitation in their relatively modest ability to restore and maintain physiological lumbar lordosis compared with anterolateral approaches (ALIF). In recent years, expandable cages have been increasingly adopted as an alternative. However, evidence regarding their effects on spinopelvic parameters, sagittal balance, and particularly lumbar lordosis restoration remains limited. The present study aims to compare changes in spinopelvic parameters in patients undergoing transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF / PLIF) using oblique static lordotic cages versus expandable cages. Specifically, we investigate whether expandable cages promote greater overall and single-level improvements in lumbar lordosis and spinal alignment, and whether their safety profile and incidence of adverse events are comparable to those of static cages. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective study on adult patients who underwent posterior lumbar interbody fusion at one or more lumbar or lumbosacral levels between 2015 and 2024, comparing outcomes between expandable cages and oblique static lordotic cages. Patient data collected included age, sex, bone quality, degree of disc degeneration (Pfirrmann classification), and disc height before and after the procedure. In both cohorts, several radiological parameters were analyzed, including spinopelvic alignment before and after surgery, as well as the occurrence of mechanical adverse events or revisions in the postoperative period (such as cage migration or subsidence, adjacent segment disease, pseudoarthrosis). Patients who met the inclusion criteria were divided into two groups: those who underwent posterolateral fusion with static cages (S group) and those who underwent fusion with expandable cages (E group). The mean differences in spinopelvic parameters (i.e., lumbar lordosis, pelvic tilt, pelvic incidence, and pelvic mismatch) were compared between different groups and within groups by categorizing the analysis by surgical approach and fusion level. Analyses were adjusted for age, and sex. Results: Of 257 reviewed patients, 177 met the inclusion criteria (129 static vs. 48 expandable cages). Median age was 56 years (IQR 48-66), with a female predominance (54.8%). The most common fusion levels were L4-L5 (46.0%) and L5-S1 (36.7%); 36 patients underwent multilevel fusion. At last follow-up, revision was required in 5.2% of cases (p = 0.704). Subsidence occurred in one expandable cage (0.48% overall, p = 0.585), with no loosening recorded. Adjacent segment disease occurred in 1.9% (p = 0.918). There were no significant differences between groups. Overall, the mean difference in PT values was 1.6° ± 0.9 between static and expandable cages (p-value: 0.0621), PI 0.8° ± 1.21° (p-value: 0.694), SS 1.7° ± 0.8° (p-value: 0.036), LL 0.37 ± 0.92 (p-value: 0.689) and PI-LL 0.9° ± 0.8°. After stratifying each group by level of fusion we found that the mean difference in PT values in L4-L5 was 2.7° ± 1.1 between static and expandable cages (p-value: 0.187), PI 3.7° ± 1.6° (p-value: 0.023), SS 2.2° ± 1.21° (p-value: 0.072), LL 1.34 ± 1.58 (p-value: 0.339) and PI-LL 0.5° ± 0.81° (p-value: 0.541). In the L5-S1 subgroup we found the mean difference in PT values for was 1.7° ± 1.4 between static and expandable cages (p-value: 0.222), PI 0.1° ± 2.14° (p-value: 0.964), SS 1.7° ± 1.3° (p-value: 0.183), LL 0.76 ± 1.38 (p-value: 0.577) and PI-LL 1.70° ± 1.7° (p-value: 0.313). We observed a significant difference in the distribution of disc degeneration grades, with the expandable cage group showing a significantly lower Pfirrman grade (p-value: 0.001) and a notably higher ability to restore disc height (p-value: 0.001). Conclusion: Our analysis indicates that well-positioned static and expandable cages show no significant differences in their ability to restore lordosis or influence spinopelvic parameters. However, expandable cages offer advantages in surgical access and demonstrate superior restoration of disc height, and can cope with a higher degree of degeneration. These features make them particularly effective for managing more advanced discopathies through a posterior approach.

## A378: Multidimensional burden of low back pain: a prospective cross sectional study of patient-reported outcomes and sociodemographic factors at a tertiary neurosurgical center

Pavlina Lenga

Department of Neurosurgery, Heidelberg University Hospital, Heidelberg, Germany

Institute of Medical Informatics, Heidelberg, Germany

Introduction: Low back pain (LBP) significantly impacts patients’ physical function, mental health, sexual wellbeing, and occupational status. However, comprehensive prospective assessments of these interrelated dimensions in specialized neurosurgical outpatient settings remain sparse. This study aimed to prospectively evaluate functional disability, depression, erectile dysfunction (ED), occupational impairment, and their associations with demographic and lifestyle factors among patients presenting to a neurosurgical outpatient clinic. Material and Methods: Between February and June 2025, we prospectively enrolled 247 consecutive patients (mean age 60.4 ± 16.0 years, 53.8% male) presenting to the neurosurgical outpatient clinic at Heidelberg University Hospital with degenerative lumbar spine disorders, of whom 110 (44.5%) subsequently underwent decompression surgery. Patients completed validated patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), including pain intensity (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS]), functional disability (Oswestry Disability Index [ODI]), depression (PHQ-9), and erectile dysfunction (IIEF-5). Correlation analyses and regression models assessed associations among these outcomes and relevant demographic and lifestyle variables. Results: Patients reported high pain intensity (NRS 7.0 ± 2.2), severe functional disability (ODI 57.4 ± 16.5; 82.2% severely disabled or worse), frequent moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms (42.2%), and prevalent erectile dysfunction among males (55%). Multivariate analyses identified depression severity (PHQ-9; B = 1.30, p < 0.001), older age (B = 0.20, p = 0.045), and surgery (B = 6.13, p = 0.049) as significant predictors of greater disability. Erectile dysfunction severity in males was independently associated with higher disability (B = -0.18, p = 0.002) and older age (B = -0.32, p < 0.001). Undergoing surgery was significantly predicted by higher baseline disability (ODI; OR = 1.04, p = 0.032) and private insurance (OR = 22.39, p < 0.001). Among working-age patients (≤ 65 years, n = 142), occupational disability was notably high, with 39.4% currently work-disabled and an additional 15.5% having experienced disability within the past year. Conclusion: This prospective study highlights the significant multidimensional burden of low back pain among neurosurgical outpatients, characterized by substantial functional disability, high prevalence of depression, frequent erectile dysfunction, and marked occupational impairment. Our results underscore the critical need for routine psychological screening, proactive sexual health assessment, and targeted occupational rehabilitation within specialized neurosurgical care pathways. Implementing these comprehensive approaches may improve patient outcomes, support return to work, and mitigate potential socioeconomic impacts associated with degenerative lumbar spine disorders.

## A379: Patient counselling with educational videos may reduce postoperative pain scores in AIS patients
Yağız Akcan1, Ahmet Özaslan2, Asim Ahmadov2, Aliekber Yapar3, Alim Baymurat2, Alpaslan Senkoylu2

1

Çorum Erol Olçok Training and Research Hospital, Çorum, Turkey

2

Gazi University, Ankara, Turkey

3

Antalya Training and Research Hospital, Antalya, Turkey

Introduction: Due to the increasing use of smartphones and social media today, adolescents experience a rapid loss of attention while reading or listening while they tend to focus on audiovisual resources more efficiently. Aim of the study is to evaluate the impact of educational videos, educational brochures, and routine verbal counseling on preoperative anxiety and postoperative outcome. Material and Methods: Participants were randomly assigned into three groups: educational video (n = 14), educational brochure (n = 14), and verbal counseling (n = 14). Patients were given the SRS-22 questionnaire, the Spinal Appearance Questionnaire (SAQ), the State-Trait Anxiety Index, the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, and the Pain Catastrophizing Scale three days before the surgery. Patients were informed about the surgical process according to their assigned group. At the same day before the surgery, the STAI was administered to assess the patients' situational anxiety levels. During postoperative follow-up, the same scales and questionnaires were administered at 3-month follow-up. Results: Among the cohort (n = 42), those who received educational videos or brochures during preoperative counseling had significantly less reduction in their SRS-22 pain scores at the third postoperative month compared to the verbally informed group (p = 0.03). These findings suggest that video education may increase anxiety by raising morning STAI scores. Conclusion: Preoperative anxiety is a common response experienced by AIS patients undergoing surgical intervention, with one of its primary causes being fear of the unknown. It has been demonstrated that sharing these unknown elements with patients through videos may increase anxiety; however, it has also been shown to have a positive effect on pain management and the recovery process in the postoperative period.

Introduction: Pelvic incidence (PI) is a key morphological parameter governing sagittal spinal alignment and serves as the foundation for the theoretical Roussouly classification in adults. ## A383: Radiation exposure in posterior fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a comparison between low-dose, 2D fluoroscopy, navigation on preoperative CT scan and navigation on intraoperative CT scan

Georgios Bakaloudis

1

, Lorenzo D'Apice

1

, Alice Baroncini

1

1

Casa di Cura Humanitas San Pio X, Milano, Italy

Introduction: The limitation of radiation exposure for the surgical team and the patients is one of the key advantages of enabling technologies. However, currently available data that compares the radiation exposure with different enabling technologies is limited. The aim of this work was thus to evaluate the radiation exposure with three different technologies in the setting of posterior fusion for adolescent idiopathic deformity (AID). Material and Methods: Retrospective study on all consecutive cases operated by a single surgeon. The instrumentation was performed with one or more midline skin incisions and a paramedian Wiltse approach. Screw placement was guided with either low-dose 2D fluoroscopy - 2DF, robotic neuronavigation on preoperative CT scan - preCT, or navigation based on intraoperative CT scan - intraCT. The surgical time (skin-to-skin), the time required for screw placement and the radiation exposure were compared among the three techniques. Results: Between Sept 2016 and Dec 2024, 146 consecutive AID patients (101 female) underwent posterior fusion and were included in the study. The mean age was 15.6 ± 2.6 years. 2DF was used for 104 cases, preCT for 24 and intraCT for 18. There was no significant difference between the groups in term of number of instrumented levels, screw density or number of placed screws. The average time for screw placement was significantly lower in the 2DF group compared to preCT and intraCT (60 min vs 180 vs 140, respectively; r = 0.34 and 0.56, p < 0.0001). The surgical time was also lower in the 2DF group compared to preCT and intraCT (140 ± 20 min vs. 250 ± 25 vs. 210 ± 10, p = 0.0003). In the 2DF group, the radiation exposure was 132 ± 8 mGy with a mean radiation time of 5min; in the preCT group, the radiation exposure was 400 mGy for the preoperative scan plus 20-30 intraoperative X-ray shots for image matching; in the intraCT the mean dose was 80 ± 5Gy. None of the patients experienced major complications, no screw misplacement was recorded. Conclusion: Navigation based on an intraoperative CT scan is the enabling technology that can most effectively reduce radiation exposure in posterior fusion for ASD. However, at present, these technologies still require a longer surgical time and longer time for screw placement.

## A384: Preoperative planning with gap score and virtual simulation improves sagittal alignment in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis surgery

Giovanni Viroli

1

, Matteo Traversari

1

, Marco Manzetti

1

, Alberto Ruffilli

1

, Cesare Faldini

1

1

Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) surgery, despite continuous evolution, still faces challenges in restoring the sagittal profile. Extensive corrections in the coronal and axial planes do not always result in optimal sagittal balance, potentially impacting quality of life and complication rates. This study aimed to evaluate whether the integration of the Gap Score into preoperative planning, together with sagittal correction simulation using dedicated surgical planning software, improves radiographic outcomes in AIS patients. We hypothesized that precise planning based on objective parameters and virtual simulation may optimize surgical results in terms of sagittal alignment. Materials and Methods: A retrospective case-matched study was conducted on AIS patients undergoing corrective surgery. Fifty patients operated between 2018 and 2020 (Group 1) were compared with 50 patients treated between 2020 and 2022 (Group 2). Groups were matched according to curve pattern (Lenke classification), magnitude of the main curve, curve flexibility as measured on side-bending radiographs, and preoperative sagittal alignment parameters including thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, and pelvic parameters. This strict matching procedure ensured comparability between the two cohorts and minimized potential confounding variables. All patients underwent the same surgical technique consisting of high-density pedicle screw constructs, concave translation, and direct vertebral derotation maneuvers, performed by the same surgical team. In addition, Group 2 received a dedicated preoperative planning protocol: the surgical target was determined using the Gap Score, and the planned correction was virtually simulated with specialized software to predict postoperative sagittal alignment and optimize implant positioning. Patients were between 10 and 18 years of age at the time of surgery and had a minimum follow-up of two years. Results: The main Cobb angle decreased from 64° to 18° in Group 1 and from 63° to 20° in Group 2. Thoracic kyphosis increased from 9° to 16° in Group 1 and from 10° to 26° in Group 2 (p < 0.05). Cervical alignment changed from 11° kyphosis to 3° kyphosis in Group 1, and from 10° kyphosis to -14° lordosis in Group 2 (p < 0.05). Sacral slope remained stable in Group 1 (44° to 43°), but significantly decreased in Group 2 (43° to 36°, p < 0.05). Three junctional complications (PJK, DJK, adding-on) were recorded in Group 1, while none occurred in Group 2 (p > 0.05). Conclusion: Preoperative planning strategies based on target values derived from the Gap Score, combined with surgical simulation using dedicated software, allow for improved restoration of physiological sagittal alignment in AIS patients. Significant improvements in thoracic kyphosis and reversal of compensatory mechanisms (cervical kyphosis, pelvic anteversion) were observed. This approach may also contribute to a reduction in junctional complications, although this did not reach statistical significance.

## A385: Outcomes of posterior spinal fusion in AIS: a minimally invasive vs. open technique analysis

Mario Ropelato

1

, Jacopo Vitale

1

, Anne Mannion

1

, Jani Puhakka

1

, Markus Loibl

1

, Tamas Fekete

1

1

Schulthess Clinic, Zurich, Switzerland

Introduction: The most popular surgical treatment method for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is posterior spinal fusion. Recent innovations in implant designs have facilitated the development of minimally invasive (MISS) approaches in spinal surgery. However, these techniques have not yet achieved widespread adoption in the treatment of spinal deformities due to various challenges. Although MISS techniques are associated with reduced tissue damage, they present greater intraoperative challenges due to limited visualization. Few previous studies have analysed surgical/patient outcomes in patients with AIS undergoing MISS; even fewer have compared MISS with the open approach. This study aimed to compare the results of AIS patients treated with MISS with those of a historical cohort treated using traditional open methods. Material and Methods: This was a single-center retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively within the EUROSPINE Spine Tango Registry framework. Inclusion criteria were as follows: idiopathic scoliosis; posterior spinal fusion as surgical treatment; major coronal Cobb < 80°; and patient age 10-30 years. A total of 71 patients operated on using an conventional approach (OPEN) between 2005 and 2015 were compared with 39 patients treated with a minimally invasive posterior transmuscular approach (MINI-OPEN) between 2016 and 2021. For both groups a free-hand pedicle screw insertion technique was utilized. Complications, blood loss, operation time, and length of stay were documented on Tango surgery forms. Preoperative and postoperative standing whole-spine X-rays were analyzed. Patients completed the Core Outcome Measures Index (COMI) preoperatively and at 3, 12, and 24 months postoperatively. Results: The preoperative main curve was 55.8 ± 8.5° in the MINI-OPEN group and 58.1 ± 8.8° in the OPEN group (p = 0.21). Blood loss was significantly lower in the MINI-OPEN group than in the OPEN group (439.1 ± 272.6mL vs 1184.5 ± 704.8mL, respectively; p < 0.0001). Conversely, operating time was significantly longer in the MINI-OPEN group (452 ± 104 minutes vs 328 ± 84 minutes in the OPEN group; p < 0.0001). Length of stay from surgery to discharge was almost half as long in the MINI-OPEN group as in the OPEN group (5.1 ± 1.3 days vs 9.3 vs 9.2 ± 2.2 days, respectively; p < 0.0001). The percentage of coronal correction of the main curve did not differ significantly between groups (75.7 ± 14.3% for MINI-OPEN vs 74.5 ± 10.5% for OPEN; p = 0.37). There was no significant difference in COMI score reduction between groups, and improvements were maintained for up to 2 years postoperatively. Conclusion: Compared with the conventional open approach, the minimally invasive approach using a freehand pedicle screw insertion technique was associated with a significantly lower blood loss and shorter hospital stay and similar patient rated outcomes. Refinements in surgical technique and reductions in surgical invasiveness can help minimize patient suffering immediately after surgery while maintaining similar midterm outcomes to conventional methods.

## A386: Balancing motion and correction: mid-term outcomes of hybrid fixation in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

Feyzi Kilic1, Altug Yucekul2, Gokhan Ergene3, Sahin Senay4, Elif Gizem Carus1, Tais Zulemyan1, Caglar Yilgor5, Ahmet Alanay2

1Comprehensive Spine Center, Acibadem Maslak Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, istanbul, Turkey, 3Department of Operating Room Services, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University Vocational School of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey, 4Department of Cardiovascular Surgery, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey, 5Koc University Hospital Spine Center, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Vertebral body tethering (VBT) provides growth-modulated correction for scoliosis while preserving segmental motion. In patients with double major curves or thoracic deformities accompanied by thoracolumbar/lumbar curves, selective thoracic fusion alone may not provide sufficient control. UT, MT, and TLL Cobb angles were 36.0 ± 11.1°, 61.8 ± 17.3°, and 50.9 ± 13.9° preoperatively; improved to 8.1 ± 5.0°, 7.8 ± 5.0°, and 12.8 ± 6.6° at first erect; and measured 8.8 ± 6.3°, 11.0 ± 8.7°, and 12.3 ± 8.3° at latest follow-up. SRS-22 self-image improved significantly (? +0.84, MCID achievement 67%, p. < 0.001), while Function (Δ -0.16), Pain (Δ -0.16), and Mental Health (Δ +0.02) remained unchanged (all p > 0.05). PFT percent-predicted changes were -4.25 for FVC% and +0.21 for FEV1% (p > 0.05). Two mechanical complication occurred (tether break in 8%); no readmissions or reoperations were recorded Conclusion: In this consecutive hybrid fixation cohort with median follow-up exceeding two years, UT, MT, and TLL Cobb angles improved substantially and were maintained. Patient self-image improved with preservation of pulmonary function. The mid-term implant profile was favorable, with low mechanical complication rates and survival without tether break >95% at one year and >80% at two years. These results highlight hybrid fixation as a promising motion-preserving alternative, warranting confirmation in larger cohorts with longer follow-up.

Anastasios Charalampidis

1

, Kasim Abul-Kasim

Clinical and Molecular Osteoporosis Unit, Department of Clinical Sciences, Malmö, Lund University, Lund, Sweden, Malmö, Sweden

Introduction: Changes in curve patterns over time in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) may reflect different progression types. ## ID: AGS26/1166

## A388: Cartilaginous endplate and disc resorption failure: evidence from histological and immunohistochemical analysis

Samina Ashraf

1

, Huma Qamar

1

, Muhammad Saad Ilyas

2

, Amer Aziz

2

, Uruj Zehra

1

1

University of Health Sciences, Lahore, Pakistan

2

Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: Herniated discs are a common cause of low back and leg pain; spontaneous resorption often facilitate recovery under conservative management. This process is mediated by inflammatory responses and neovascularization driven by cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes such as TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, MMPs, and ADAMTS. Resorption is favored in hydrated, less-degenerated nucleus pulposus, whereas cartilaginous endplate tissue may slow the resorption process. This study explores key inflammatory markers to better understand and predict disc resorption in the presence of CEP. Material and Methods: Lumbar intervertebral disc samples were collected from adult patients undergoing disc excision surgery for herniated discs. The relevant demographic and clinical data were also obtained in detail including age, sex, and duration of low back pain, body mass index (BMI) and history of smoking. Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores were recorded by using professional numerical rating scales for evaluating back pain pre surgery. Paraffin embedded five-micron thick sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin, Alcian blue periodic acid-Schiff stain; examined for histological degeneration scores (HDS; 0-15), inflammation (0 [absence]-3 [severe]), and presence of cartilage endplate (CEP). Three-micron thick sections were immunostained with anti TNFα antibody and IL-1β expression. Disc samples with and without CEP were compared for the expression of these immunostains. Results: Total of 109 patients (69M/40F) with average age & BMI of 39.4 ± 9.9 years & 25.3 ± 5.1kg/m2 were included in the study after informed consent and ethical approval of the institution. Spinal levels ranged from L2 to L5 and most (52%) of the patients had L4 disc herniation. Histological degeneration scores ranged from 4-13, with a mean ± SD of 9.0 ± 2.0. Age, gender, spinal level and VAS did not show any relation with histological degeneration scores. Presence of inflammatory infiltrates was found in almost 73.5 % of the samples while proteoglycan loss was found in 95% of samples. CEP was detected in 69.7% samples, age, sex, BMI, spinal level and VAS score did not show any significant relation with the presence and absence of cartilage endplate. Samples with cartilage endplate showed increased mucous degeneration (p = 0.001), granular changes (p = 0.02) and total histological degeneration scores (p = 0.01) as compared to the samples without cartilage endplate. However, factors such as inflammation and proteoglycan loss did not display any significant association with the presence of cartilage endplate in herniated disc samples. Interestingly, the samples with the presence of CEP had significantly decreased expression of IL-1β (p = 0.03) and TNF-α (p = 0.01). Conclusion: Our findings suggest that while CEP contributes to structural degeneration of the disc, its suppressive effect on inflammatory mediators such as TNF-α and IL-1β may impair the natural resorption process. This paradox highlights that degeneration alone does not guarantee resorption; rather, a robust inflammatory and angiogenic response is required for spontaneous regression of herniated disc material.
