CIAMS, University Paris-Saclay, Orsay, France

4

Haute École ICHEC-ECAM-ISFSC, ECAM Brussels Engineering School, Bruxelles, Belgium

Introduction: Accurate pedicle screw placement is essential in spine surgery, as malposition can result in neurological, vascular, or visceral injury and compromise construct stability. Traditional qualitative classifications, such as Gertzbein-Robbins or Heary, remain observer-dependent and poorly reproducible, limiting cross-study comparisons and objective assessment. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a dual quantitative framework: (1) coaxiality, an engineering-derived metric summarizing the geometrical accuracy of screw insertion, and (2) pedicle wall distance (dpw), a novel parameter providing surgeons with direct, millimetric, clinically actionable feedback. This approach bridges the gap between engineering precision and operative applicability, offering both rigorous assessment and immediate clinical relevance. Material and Methods: Eight operators (four orthopedic senior surgeons, four residents) performed a total of 240 pedicle screw insertions on synthetic lumbar spine models, using three techniques: freehand, cone-beam CT (CBCT)-assisted, and navigation-assisted. Preoperative trajectories were defined in 3D, and actual screw positions were digitized with sub-millimetric precision using a coordinate measuring system. Insertion errors (entry point, target point, orientation angle), coaxiality, and dpw were computed. Correlations assessed whether coaxiality captured overall insertion accuracy. dpw was validated against intraoperative CBCT grading according to Gertzbein and Heary classifications. Agreement coefficients (Kappa, Gwet), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated. Results: Of 236 analyzable screws, coaxiality correlated strongly with entry point (ρ = 0.41), target point (ρ = 0.85), and orientation angle errors (ρ = 0.48), confirming its robustness as a standardized engineering metric. However, as a composite measure, coaxiality is difficult to interpret directly during surgery. In contrast, dpw quantified screw proximity to the pedicle wall in millimeters, providing immediate, actionable feedback. Compared with CBCT grading, dpw demonstrated almost perfect agreement (Kappa = 0.86, Gwet = 0.96), with sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.97, PPV 0.79, and NPV 0.99. dpw additionally detected breaches not captured by qualitative classifications, including superior pedicle violations, highlighting its complementary clinical value. Conclusion: This study presents a dual-metric, ISO-based framework for pedicle screw evaluation in spine surgery. Coaxiality offers a rigorous, standardized measure of geometrical accuracy suitable for research, multicenter comparisons, and reproducibility. Pedicle wall distance, in contrast, delivers direct, millimetric, and clinically interpretable feedback, enabling surgeons to identify and correct potential breaches in real-time. Together, these complementary parameters bridge the traditional gap between engineering precision and intraoperative utility, establishing a new standard for quantitative, reproducible, and clinically actionable assessment of pedicle screw placement. Implementation in clinical practice and multi-institutional studies could enhance surgical safety, reduce complication rates, improve educational outcomes, and ultimately optimize patient care. This dual approach represents a transformative step in combining engineering rigor with tangible surgical relevance.

## A390: Pre-transfusion testing in cervical spine surgery: are we over-prepared?

Jorge Nuñez

1,2

, Anna Taberner

1

, Juan Diego Montenegro

1

, Victoria San Gil

1

, Berta Escudero

1

1

Hospital Universitari MútuaTerrassa, COT & CARE Institute SL, Terrassa, Spain

2

Clinica Teknon, Barcelona, Spain

Introduction: Previous studies have shown that routine pre-transfusion testing is unnecessary for most patients undergoing cervical spine surgery, except for those with preoperative hemoglobin (Hb) levels below 12 g/dL. However, the applicability of this recommendation in patients undergoing anterior cervical arthrodesis (ACA) remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the necessity of pre-transfusion testing in this specific patient subgroup. Material and Methods: A prospective study was conducted including patients undergoing ACA for degenerative conditions between 2014 and 2023 at our center. Out of 672 patients, 318 fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Demographic, clinical, and radiological data were analyzed. The variables collected included: age at the time of surgery, sex, ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) classification, need for transfusion, number of fused levels, and preoperative and postoperative laboratory values, particularly hemoglobin (Hb) and hematocrit (Hct). Bivariate analyses were performed to identify predictive factors for transfusion based on preoperative Hb (< or ≥ 12 g/dL). The crossmatch-to-transfusion ratio (C/T), likelihood of transfusion (%T), and transfusion index (TI) were also assessed. Results: The overall transfusion rate was 0.6% (2/318 patients). No cases of emergency transfusion or same-day transfusions at the time of surgery were recorded. Regarding laboratory values, mean preoperative Hb and Hct were 14.2 ± 1.5 g/dL and 42.3% ± 4.6%, respectively, while mean postoperative values were 12.8 ± 1.6 g/dL for Hb and 35.1% ± 4.4% for Hct. A mean decrease of 1.4 g/dL (standard deviation [SD] 1.1) in Hb and 7.2% (SD 4.1) in Hct was observed between the preoperative and postoperative measurements. The difference in hemoglobin decrease between patients who required transfusion and those who did not was 0.6 g/dL. Thirteen patients underwent surgery with preoperative Hb < 12 g/dL. Bivariate analysis showed that patients with preoperative Hb < 12 g/dL had an odds ratio (OR) of 25.33 (95% CI: 1.49-429.8; p = 0.02) for requiring transfusion compared with those with Hb ≥ 12 g/dL. Moreover, statistically significant differences were identified between the groups according to preoperative Hb levels, specifically in age (p = 0.002), ASA classification (p < 0.001), and transfusion rate (p = 0.001), the latter being 7.7% in the Hb < 12 g/dL group versus 0.3% in the Hb ≥ 12 g/dL group. In the group of patients with Hb < 12 g/dL, suboptimal values were found in transfusion efficiency indicators: a C/T ratio of 13.0, a %T of 7.69%, and a TI of 0.08. The TI was notably different between groups (0.08 in patients with Hb < 12 g/dL versus 1 in those with Hb ≥ 12 g/dL), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.14). Conclusion: Routine blood reservation and pre-transfusion testing are unnecessary in patients undergoing ACA, regardless of their preoperative hemoglobin level. These findings support the optimization of preoperative protocols by eliminating routine pre-transfusion testing in this surgical subgroup.

## A391: Expression of LBX1 and TGFβ1 in paraspinal muscles: correlation with curve severity and muscle remodeling in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

Kinza Fatima

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a complex three-dimensional spinal deformity, with genetic and molecular factors thought to play central roles in its pathogenesis. Genome-wide association studies have consistently implicated LBX1 and TGFβ1 in AIS susceptibility, yet their functional role in paraspinal muscle pathology remains poorly understood. Since the concave and convex sides of scoliotic curves exhibit distinct structural and histological changes, exploring the differential expression of LBX1 and TGFβ1 in these muscles may provide valuable insights into mechanisms driving curve severity, muscle remodeling, and disease progression. However, the impact of kyphoplasty on adjacent disc degeneration (ADD) remains controversial. While some studies have reported increased rates of ADD following cement augmentation, others have suggested that age-related degeneration may play a more dominant role. Proposed mechanisms include thermal and chemical effects of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), altered biomechanical load distribution, and endplate injury. Recent literature highlights intradiscal cement leakage and preexisting advanced disc degeneration as major predictors of ADD. Nevertheless, data on additional risk factors remain limited. Conclusion: Approximately one-third of patients developed adjacent disc degeneration within one year after kyphoplasty. While classical predictors such as osteoporosis severity and cement leakage were not significant, two notable associations were identified: higher vitamin D levels were linked with degeneration at the superior adjacent disc, and AO type A3 fractures predisposed to degeneration at the inferior second adjacent level. These findings suggest that factors beyond traditional biomechanical explanations may contribute to ADD following kyphoplasty. Recognition of such unexpected risk profiles could refine patient counseling and postoperative monitoring. Introduction: Minimally invasive spine surgery (MIS), particularly full endoscopic lumbar discectomy, has transformed the management of lumbar disc herniation by enabling shorter hospitalization, faster recovery, and reduced tissue trauma compared to traditional open surgery. ## A398: Two portals, two paths, one goal: who reaches proficiency first?

Yanting Liu

1

, Yi-Hao Liang

2

, Kun Wu

3

, Jin-Sung Kim

4

1

Department of Neurosurgery, CHA Bundang Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea

2

Orthopaedic Hospital of Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou, China

3

Department of Orthopedics, The Second Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China

4

Department of Neurosurgery, Seoul St. Mary's Hospital, College of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: The principal barrier to widespread dissemination of ESS lies not in equipment availability, but in the steepness of its learning curve. How quickly surgeons reach proficiency, and what helps them get there, remains inconsistently defined across uniportal and biportal approaches. This study compares learning-curve dynamics head-to-head and distills a competency-based, stage-matched training roadmap. Material and Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane (inception-Aug 2025) identified original studies reporting learning-curve metrics for uniportal or biportal ESS. Eligible designs included RCTs and observational cohorts/series (≥ 10 cases) with outcomes such as operative time, complications, conversions, radiation exposure, and CUSUM/risk-adjusted CUSUM (RA-CUSUM) thresholds. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB-2 (RCTs) and NOS (non-randomized). Where feasible, random-effects meta-analysis was performed; predefined subgroups examined prior surgical experience, case complexity, and enabling technologies (navigation/simulation/AR). Results: From 1,532 unique records screened, 59 full texts were assessed; 42 studies were synthesized qualitatively and 32 contributed to meta-analysis. Evidence from decompression cohorts shows that interlaminar endoscopic approaches, whether uniportal or biportal, generally stabilize after a modest number of cases, with biportal surgery reaching stable performance earlier and uniportal procedures requiring somewhat longer exposure. These trajectories are well represented by a four-stage model: surgeons begin as novices, practicing basic docking under supervision while susceptible to trajectory deviations and inadvertent neural irritation; progress as beginners to independent handling of simple herniations, where incomplete decompression and durotomy remain risks; advance to competence with reliable management of stenosis and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, challenged by bleeding control and facet preservation; and finally achieve proficiency when capable of consistently treating multilevel or revision cases with reproducible outcomes and low complication rates. In contrast, the transforaminal uniportal pathway demonstrates greater variability and technical demand. To capture this trajectory, a six-stage model is warranted. Novices achieve safe access in protrusion-type herniations but remain vulnerable to nerve irritation and excessive fluoroscopic exposure. Beginners consolidate basic foraminoplasty and cannula docking. Competence, typically reached in standard cases, allows stable outcomes but complications persist in migrated or extruded fragments, leading to a consolidator stage that requires repeated exposure to adhesions, engorged vessels, and recurrent disease. Surgeons who progress to proficiency demonstrate reliable outcomes in multilevel and revision pathology, while expert performance is defined not by case numbers alone but by the consistent reproducibility of results in anatomically demanding scenarios and the ability to innovate and mentor others. Conclusion: Overall, biportal surgery offers a shallower learning curve slope during the novice and beginner phases, facilitating safer early adoption, whereas uniportal techniques, particularly transforaminal, require prolonged consolidation but ultimately reward mastery with durable efficiency, reduced tissue disruption, and sustained clinical benefits. A competency-based, stage-specific curriculum that aligns case selection with anticipated complication risks, supported by mentorship, simulation, and enabling technologies, provides the most pragmatic and safe pathway to shorten the ESS learning curve and optimize surgical outcomes.

Introduction: Whether full-endoscopic decompression (FED) achieves patient-reported outcomes comparable to the long-established microsurgical decompression (MSD) for lumbar disc herniation remains debated. Material and Methods: We conducted a single-centre, prospective comprehensive cohort study with two parallel arms: a randomized arm (1:1 FED:MSD) for patients accepting allocation and a contemporaneous preference arm for decliners, all treated under one protocol and follow-up schedule. Adults with single-level symptomatic herniation were eligible; conversions from FED to MSD were permitted and counted as FED complications under intention-to-treat in the randomized arm. The primary endpoint was the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at 1 year. Secondary outcomes comprised VAS back/leg, SF-36 domains, operative time, length of stay, complications (including readmission/revision), and perioperative laboratory indices. Patient-reported measures were analyzed as change scores (Δ) across prespecified timepoints-preoperative baseline, immediate postoperative, 3 weeks, and 1 year-using the contrasts post-pre, 3-weeks-pre, 1-year-pre, 3-weeks-post, and 1-year-3-weeks. Laboratory markers were evaluated as Δs at preoperative baseline, immediate postoperative, and 48 h (contrasts: post-pre, 48 h-pre, and 48 h-post). Analyses were prespecified for the pooled cohort and, separately, the randomized and non-randomized subsets. Continuous data were summarized as median (IQR); Welch’s t-test was used if both groups were approximately normal by Shapiro-Wilk, otherwise Mann-Whitney U; categorical data used χ2/Fisher’s exact tests; p < 0.05 two-sided. All analyses were performed in Python. Results: We enrolled 127 patients (FED 87, MSD 40); 37 accepted randomization (FED 23, MSD 14) and 90 entered the preference arm (FED 64, MSD 26). Operative time, length of stay, complications, and readmission/revision did not differ between techniques across analytic sets. PROMs improved substantially in both groups. At 1 year, ODI, VAS, and SF-36 outcomes were comparable between FED and MSD in pooled, randomized-only, and non-randomized-only analyses. Several early differences around 3 weeks favored MSD-e.g., greater additional ODI reduction from post-op to 3 weeks (pooled p < 0.001; randomized p = 0.003; non-randomized p = 0.005), higher SF-36 physical functioning at 3w-post (pooled p = 0.017; randomized p = 0.040), and lower VAS back at 3w-post in pooled and non-randomized cohorts (both p = 0.002)-but these did not persist at 1 year. Laboratory kinetics indicated a stronger 48-h inflammatory response after MSD (CRP and IL-6, p < 0.001 in pooled analyses), while other hematologic and metabolic changes were largely similar. Conclusion: FED and MSD yielded equivalent, clinically meaningful 1-year improvements in disability, pain, and health-related quality of life, with transient early advantages for MSD that resolved by 1 year and biomarker evidence of less systemic inflammation after FED. Both procedures are safe, effective options; longer-term multicentre data will clarify durability and refine patient selection.

## A401: Minimally invasive versus open transforaminal or posterior lumbar interbody fusion for degenerative lumbar disease and the long-term risk of adjacent segment pathology: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Farzin Farahbakhsh

1,2

, Faramarz Roohollahi

1,2

, Mohammad Mohammadi

3

, Shervin Molavi

1,2

1

Neuroscience Institute, Sports Medicine Research Center, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran

2

Spine Center of Excellence, Yas Hospital, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran

3

School of Medicine, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran

Introduction: Minimally invasive surgery (MISS) for lumbar fusion offers well-established short-term benefits over traditional open approaches, including reduced blood loss and shorter hospital stays. However, its long-term effect on adjacent segment pathology (ASP) remains a subject of debate. It is hypothesized that by preserving the posterior tension band, MISS techniques may reduce biomechanical stress on adjacent levels. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to compare the long-term incidence of ASP-specifically radiographic adjacent segment degeneration (ASDeg), adjacent segment disease (ASDis), and operative ASP (OASP)-between MISS and open transforaminal/posterior lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF/PLIF). Material and Methods: A comprehensive search was performed on August 6, 2025, across four electronic databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL to identify relevant randomized controlled trials and cohort studies. Data from eligible studies were synthesized by calculating pooled odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a common-effects model. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies and the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool for RCTs. All analyses were performed using R version 4.2.3. We performed subgroup analyses based on follow-up duration: < 2 years, 2 to < 5 years, 5 to < 10 years, and ≥ 1 0 years. Results: Twenty-five studies (2 RCTs, 23 cohorts) comprising 3,227 patients (1,408 MIS, 1,819 open) met the inclusion criteria. The pooled meta-analysis demonstrated that the MISS approach was associated with a significantly lower incidence of all forms of adjacent segment pathology compared to the open approach. • ASDeg: OR 0.39 (95% CI 0.27-0.56; p < 0.001). A subgroup analysis showed a consistent benefit for MIS with an OR of 0.36 (95% CI 0.18-0.71) for a 2-5 year follow-up and an OR of 0.41 (95% CI 0.27-0.62) for a 5-10 year follow-up. • ASDis: OR 0.54 (95% CI 0.34-0.85; p = 0.008). This protective effect was also seen in subgroup analyses for follow-ups of 2 to 5 years (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.15-0.90) and 5 to 10 years (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.23-0.82). • OASP: OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39-0.79; p = 0.001). For follow-ups between 2 and 10 years, the results were consistently in favor of MISS. Low statistical heterogeneity was observed across all analyses (I^2 < 25%). The two RCTs had “some concerns” for the overall risk of bias. Studies with follow-up beyond 10 years for OASP showed no statistical significance, likely due to small sample sizes. Conclusion: This meta-analysis provides strong evidence that MISS TLIF/PLIF is associated with a significantly lower long-term risk of adjacent segment pathology compared to the open approach. These findings suggest that the muscle- and ligament-preserving nature of MISS techniques may confer a durable protective effect on adjacent spinal levels. The significant reduction in OASP, a hard clinical endpoint, is particularly impactful.

## A402: Patient-reported outcome measures following endoscopic decompression for cauda equina syndrome: an 18-month prospective cohort study

Joel Stoy

1

, Santhosh G. Thavarajasingam

, Samira Akmal

, Darren Lui

4

, Jin-Sung Kim

5

, Salvatore Russo

1

Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Munich, Germany

3

Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, London, United Kingdom

4

St. George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom

5

The Catholic University of Korea, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: While open laminectomy has traditionally been the standard surgical approach for cauda equina syndrome (CES), endoscopic lumbar decompression is increasingly utilized. This endoscopic approach minimizes collateral tissue damage, which we hypothesize will reduce long-term morbidity while achieving immediate postoperative clinical outcomes equivalent to open laminectomy. To date, no prospective studies have evaluated long-term patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) following endoscopic decompression for CES; this study assesses these outcomes over an 18-month period. Material and Methods: This prospective, longitudinal cohort study was conducted at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust between November 2023 and September 2025. EQ-5D-5L increased from 0.59 ± 0.24 at 3 M to 0.72 ± 0.22 at 6 M, with values of 0.66 ± 0.19 at 12 M and 0.76 ± 0.17 at 18 M. EQ-VAS rose from 41.0 ± 17.3 at 3 M to 66.3 ± 11.7 at 6 M, with later values of 57.5 ± 25.5 at 12 M and 59.3 ± 29.8 at 18 M. Conclusion: Endoscopic decompression for CES provided sustained leg pain relief over 18 months. Early improvements in PROMs, such as ODI and EQ-5D-5L, showed variable trajectories beyond 12 months, reflecting small cohort limitations. At 18 months, outcomes were comparable to, and in some cases slightly better than, those reported in the literature for open laminectomy.

## A403: Impact of lateral plate and screw fixation on long term radiographic subsidence in lateral lumbar interbody fusion

Joseph Hudson

1

, David McCarthy

1

, Andrew Legarreta

1

, Thomas Buell

1

, Nitin Agarwal

1

, David Hamilton

1

, David Okonkwo

1

, Vincent Miele

1

1

University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, United States

Introduction: Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion (LLIF) can be performed in a stand-alone manner, with lateral plate and screw fixation, or with supplemental posterior instrumented fusion. In vitro biomechanical data suggests lateral plate fixation limits segmental motion. This study aims to evaluate the impact of lateral screw and plate fixation on the rate and grade of long-term radiographic implant subsidence after LLIF. Material and Methods: A review of patients who underwent LLIF between 2014 and 2022 at two quaternary referral centers was conducted. All patients had CT scans at a minimum of one year after surgery. Patients with posterior instrumented fusion were excluded. Age, sex, BMI, smoking status, cage material, and operative level bone density (Hounsfield units) were collected. Post-operative implant subsidence at long-term follow-up was graded according to Marchi criteria by two separate spine surgeons. A stepwise multivariate logistic regression was performed. Results: 146 patients (219 surgical levels) met inclusion criteria. LLIF with lateral plate and screw fixation was performed in 65 patients (45%) and 81 patients (55%) underwent standalone LLIF. No intraoperative subsidence was observed. On univariate analysis, age, sex, smoking status, operative level bone density, and BMI were not significantly associated with radiographic subsidence on a per level basis (p > 0.05). Multivariable logistic regression revealed 3D printed porous titanium cages was moderately associated with reduced subsidence (OR 0.401, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.069, p = 0.07). Lateral plate fixation was significantly associated with (OR 0.484, 95% CI 0.099 to 0.652, p = .006) reduced subsidence. All 4 cases (3.5%) of grade two (severe) subsidence occurred in stand-alone LLIF patients. One delayed vertebral body fracture occurred in a lateral plate patient. All patients with lateral plates received 18 mm wide interbody grafts, while all but two stand-alone patients received 22mm wide implants. Conclusion: LLIF with lateral plate and screw fixation is significantly associated with a lower rate of radiographic subsidence at long term follow up when compared with stand-alone LLIF. There was no significant difference in reoperation rate. Our results trend towards the superiority of 3D printed porous titanium cages over PEEK cages. No cases of reoperation were identified in patients receiving 3D printed porous titanium stand-alone implants. The results of this study may be interpreted to suggest that lateral plate and screw fixation has potential to protect against severe (grade two or worse) radiographic subsidence.

Introduction: Thoracoscopic spine surgery is a technically demanding procedure with a steep learning curve, often limiting its widespread adoption.This study analyzes the learning curve and complication rates over a 10-year period to assess how surgical experience impacts outcomes in thoracoscopic treatment of thoracic disc herniation. Material and Methods: A total of 182 thoracoscopic procedures were divided chronologically into three stages (early: cases 1-60, mid: 61-120, late: 121-182). Gonzalo Moros-Daza

, Feras Rawagah

Introduction: Cervical pedicle screws offer superior biomechanics compared to lateral mass screws resulting in stronger and more durable constructs. Here, we present the case series of fully percutaneous cervical und upper thoracic pedicle screw instrumentation assisted by navigation. Material and Methods: A Prospective observational study between October 2024 and September 2025 was performed. The primary outcomes assessed were the accuracy of pedicle screw placement-radiologically evaluated using the Gertzbein and Robbins classification- and clinically defined by the lack of need for screw revision. Additional data collected included intraoperative blood loss, operative time, length of hospital stay, and the incidence of intraoperative and postoperative complications. Conclusion: Percutaneous navigated cervical pedicle screw instrumentation is a safe and effective technique for patients with various spinal pathologies.

## A407: Independent risk factors for retrograde ejaculation after anterior versus posterior lumbar fusion in male patients: a cox proportional hazards retrospective analysis

Anthony Baumann

1

, Robjert Trager

2

, Omkar Anaspure

3

, Ethan Cottrill

4

, Peter Passias

4

, Jacob Hoffmann

1

1

Cleveland Clinic Akron General, Akron, United States

2

Department of Rehabilitation Services, University Hospitals, Cleveland, United States

3

Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, United States

4

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Duke University, Durham, United States

Introduction: RE is a feared yet uncommon complication after ALF in males that can lead to infertility. However, knowledge of the incidence and risk factors for RE is sparse due to limitations of the current literature. Our purpose is to examine the incidence and independent risk factors for retrograde ejaculation (RE) after anterior lumbar fusion (ALF) versus posterior lumbar fusion (PLF) in males to enhance decision-making. Material and Methods: This pre-registered retrospective database study (TriNetX) included adult males (≥ 18 years) without prior RE who underwent primary ALF (ALF cohort) or PLF (PLF cohort). The outcome was the two-year incidence of RE after ALF or PLF, estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis, with hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model (p < 0.05). Results: There were 68 cases (< 0.1%) of RE among 106,005 males who underwent fusion with 26 cases (0.1%) in the ALF cohort (n = 18,437) and 42 cases (< 0.1%) in the PLF cohort (n = 87,568). ALF was an independent risk factor for RE as compared to PLF, although the clinical relevance of this risk likely varies on a case-by-case basis. Other independent risk factors for RE identified in this study included the intraoperative use of rhBMP-2 and a history of thyroid disorders, while increasing patient age was protective. Importantly, diabetes, alpha-adrenergic antagonists, and antipsychotics were not independent risk factors for RE after fusion. Spine surgeons should consider both the incidence and risk factors for RE in their decision-making process with male patients. More clinical research is needed regarding the resolution of RE after ALF to further enhance shared decision-making.

## A411: Pre-operative intake of antipsychotic medications is associated with higher rates of healthcare utilization, medical comorbidity, and opioid use following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion

Ankit Hirpara

1

, Nakul Narendran

1

, Jalen Warren

1

, Christina Cheng

1

, Christopher Furey

1

, Prashant Rajan

1

1

Case Western Reserve University/University Hospitals, Cleveland, United States

Introduction: Several studies have examined the impact of psychiatric disorders on outcomes following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). However, literature on the impact of psychotropics, such as antipsychotic medications (APMs), is limited. This is an important gap considering 40.4% of patients with mental health disorders receive pharmacologic treatments, many of which are also used for off-label or non-psychiatric purposes. Moreover, APMs are associated with metabolic, cardiovascular, and hormonal side effects that may compromise surgical outcomes. As such, the purpose of this study was to evaluate the impact of pre-operative use of APMs on rates of healthcare utilization, post-operative complications, revision surgery, and opioid use following ACDF. Cohorts were also matched based on underlying psychiatric diagnoses and concomitant psychotropic use, like antidepressants, in order to attribute observed associations to the pharmacologic profile of APMs. Lastly, patients were matched on suicidal ideation and prior healthcare utilization, which has been previously used as a proxy for the severity of underlying mental illness. The following outcomes were collected: 1) medical complications and healthcare utilization within 3 months, 2) opioid use within 2 years, and 3) surgical complications and revision surgery within 2 years. Results: Following propensity score matching, both cohorts were appropriately matched with respect to all covariates. Within 3 months, patients taking APMs (n = 6,138), compared to those who were not (n = 6,138), had significantly higher rates of healthcare utilization, including readmission (12.5% vs. 9.0%, p < 0.001), outpatient services (44.7% vs. 41.9%, p = 0.002), physical or occupational therapy evaluation (43.5% vs. 41.0%, p = 0.004), and emergency department visits (17.2% vs. 13.6%, p < 0.001). Patients taking APMs also had higher rates of acute kidney injury (2.8% vs. 1.5%, p < 0.001), venous thromboembolism (2.1% vs. 1.6%, p = 0.022), pneumonia (2.9% vs. 1.8%, p < 0.001), surgical site infection (1.1% vs. 0.5%, p < 0.001), sepsis (1.9% vs. 1.0%, p < 0.001), cerebrovascular accident (1.9% vs. 1.2%, p = 0.003), pulmonary embolism (1.2% vs. 0.8%, p = 0.032), and dysphagia (10.4% vs. 8.2%, p < 0.001). In terms of opioid use, patients taking APMs received more prescriptions at all time points up to two years (all p < 0.001). In addition, more patients taking APMs were prescribed opioids than control patients at every time point after 1 month (all p < 0.005). There were no differences in rates of surgical complications and revision surgery at 2 years. Conclusion: Pre-operative use of APMs is not associated with higher rates of surgical complications or revision surgery following ACDF. However, APMs are associated with greater healthcare utilization, medical morbidity, and opioid use. These findings may be related to the antagonistic effects of APMs on histamine, muscarinic, dopamine, and alpha-adrenergic receptors. Potential risks may be mitigated through opioid stewardship, multi-disciplinary peri-operative care, and patient counseling.

## ID: AGS26/3117

## A412: Incidence of proximal junctional kyphosis and failure in long spinal fusions with and without sublaminar bands

Marcos Parreira

1,2

, Marcelo Wajchenberg

1,2

, Delio E. Martins

1,2

, Felipe Monteiro

1,2

, Matheus Castanheira

1,2

, Nelson Astur

1,2

1

Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein, São Paulo, Brazil

2

Instituto Cohen, São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and proximal junctional failure (PJF) are major complications after long spinal fusions, with incidence ranging from 5% to 46%. PJF is the most severe form, often requiring revision surgery with high morbidity and cost. Risk factors include patient characteristics, surgical strategy, and biomechanical stress at the transition between fused and mobile segments. Recently, the soft landing concept has been proposed, aiming to create a transition zone that reduces proximal stress. Placement of a sublaminar band at UIV+ represents a practical approach to achieve this goal. This study evaluated the incidence of PJK and PJF in patients undergoing long spinal fusions with and without sublaminar bands, focusing on reoperation rates as the most clinically relevant outcome. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single tertiary institution, including patients over 18 years who underwent posterior spinal fusion of at least three levels with a minimum follow-up of 12 months. Radiographs were assessed preoperatively, postoperatively, and at last follow-up. PJK was defined as a proximal junctional Cobb angle ≥10° and ≥10° greater than baseline. PJF was defined as PJK associated with structural failure leading to reoperation. Patients were divided into two groups: with sublaminar bands at UIV+ (n = 14) and without bands (n = 10). Fusion constructs were stratified as ending at T10 or below versus extending into the upper thoracic spine. Primary outcomes were incidence of PJK, PJF, and reoperation. Results: Twenty-four patients were included, mean age 62 years (39-80), with 60% female. In the group without bands (n = 10), most had degenerative etiologies (80%), with fusions of 3-8 levels usually ending at T10. Three patients (30%) developed PJK progressing to PJF, all requiring revision, resulting in a 30% reoperation rate. In the band group (n = 14), etiologies were more heterogeneous (10 degenerative, 2 deformity, 1 trauma, 1 tumor). Patients were older (mean 64.6 years) and had longer constructs (3-15 levels), many extending to the upper thoracic spine. Despite these higher-risk features, only two patients (14.3%) developed PJK, and none progressed to PJF or required reoperation. Overall, the incidence of PJK/PJF was halved in the band group compared with the non-band group (14.3% vs. 30%). Importantly, while three patients in the non-band group required revision due to junctional failure, no patient in the band group underwent reoperation for PJF. Conclusion: The use of sublaminar bands at UIV+ was associated with lower incidence of PJK/PJF and complete absence of reoperations for PJF, even in older patients with more extensive constructs. These findings support sublaminar bands as a potential soft landing strategy to reduce proximal stress and prevent catastrophic failure. Although limited by small sample size, the clear contrast in outcomes highlights the protective potential of this technique. Larger prospective studies are warranted to confirm these results and define the role of sublaminar bands in long spinal fusions surgery.

## A413: Perioperative visual loss in spine surgery: risk factors, pathophysiology, and management strategies

Sebastiano Mazzotta

1

, Giulio Bonomo

1

, Francesco Certo

1

, Giuseppe Barbagallo

1

1

A.O.U. Policlinico G.Rodolico - San Marco, Catania, Italy

Introduction: Perioperative visual loss (POVL) is a rare but serious complication associated with spine surgery under general anesthesia, often linked to ischemic optic neuropathy (ION), central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), and cortical blindness (CB). This study aims to explore the pathophysiology, risk factors, and management strategies of POVL, with a focus on a clinical case. Material and Methods: We reviewed 38 studies on POVL, including case reports, case series, and cohort studies. A clinical case of a 59-year-old male with lumbar stenosis undergoing posterior hemilaminectomy is presented. Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative data were collected, including imaging, ophthalmologic assessments, and surgical parameters. A literature review was conducted using PubMed and Scopus to identify additional studies on POVL. Results: The literature review included 38 studies with a total of 72 patients (35 males and 37 females, mean age 49.9 years). Surgical sites were predominantly lumbar (54.1%), followed by cervical (12.7%), thoracic (8.5%), and thoracolumbar (11.4%), with the most common pathologies being degenerative diseases (23/72) and scoliosis (8/72). The majority of patients (87.1%) underwent surgery in the prone position, with a median operative time of 300 minutes and an estimated blood loss of 1400 mL. The identified POVL subtypes were 25 cases of PION (36.8%), 20 CRAO (30.9%), 13 ION (19.1%), 6 CB (8.8%), and 3 AION (4.4%), with early onset in 67.3% of cases. Visual loss was unilateral in 76.3% and bilateral in 23.7%. Visual recovery was absent in 64.1% of cases, partial in 9, and complete in 6. Statistical analysis showed significant associations between POVL and longer operative duration, prolonged prone positioning, higher blood loss, postoperative anemia, and elevated BMI. In particular, PION cases had the longest operative and prone times, while postoperative anemia was present in 92.3% of patients. Bilateral visual loss was associated with longer surgical times and higher BMI. Periorbital edema, observed in 65.1% of cases, correlated with extended operative time, prone positioning, and increased BMI. Conclusion: POVL is a rare but serious complication in spinal surgery, most commonly presenting as PION, and is strongly associated with prolonged operative time, prone positioning, blood loss, anemia, higher BMI, and peri-orbital edema. Visual recovery is often limited, yet our illustrative cases hawed reversible and progressive improvement, suggesting that not all cases follow classical ischemic mechanisms. Early recognition and careful intraoperative management are essential, while further studies are needed to refine risk stratification and preventive strategies.

## A414: Propensity matched analysis of anticoagulation after spine surgery: more complications and longer stay without thromboembolic gain

Reme Arhewoh

1

, Elias Schwartz

1

, Aayush Unadkat

1

, Jack Eichman

1

, Abdel Diab

1

, Joshua Piche

1

, Rakesh Patel

1

, Ilyas Aleem

1

1

University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, United States

Introduction: The routine use of anticoagulation (AC) in elective spine surgery remains debated given the competing risks of venous thromboembolism (VTE)/pulmonary embolism (PE) and epidural hematoma. Prior retrospective studies are limited by unclear anticoagulation criteria and inherent biases. Our institution's contrasting anticoagulation protocols between Orthopedic and Neurosurgery services created a unique opportunity to evaluate outcomes using prospectively collected data. Material and Methods: A prospectively collected multicenter database was queried for all patients treated at an academic tertiary care center from 2013–2023. After excluding patients with prior blood clots, hypercoagulability, or unclear anticoagulation status, 5,014 patients were identified. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed based on age, gender, BMI, ASA grade, and diabetes history. Composite outcomes for overall and neurologic complications were created. T-tests and Chi-square tests were used for continuous and categorical variables, respectively. Binary logistic regression was employed with Firth correction for rare events. Results: The final cohort included 2,420 patients equally divided between treatment (n = 1,210) and control (n = 1,210) groups with balanced demographics. Cohorts were approximately 56% male, 78% white, with a mean age of 60. Anticoagulated patients demonstrated higher rates of deep vein thrombosis (1.2% vs. 0.3%, p = 0.011) and wound dehiscence (2.3% vs. 1.0%, p = 0.011). New neurological deficits were more prevalent in the AC group, including weakness (12.9% vs. 8.5%, p < 0.001) and myelopathy (0.5% vs. 0%, p = 0.031). The AC group also experienced higher rates of neurogenic bowel/bladder dysfunction (p < 0.001) and urinary retention (5.6% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.002). Overall complications were more frequent in AC patients (36.9% vs. 32.4%, p = 0.021), and length of stay was prolonged (3.9 vs. 2.0 days, p < 0.001), though 90-day readmission, reoperation, and mortality were comparable. Logistic regression identified key predictors of postoperative complications. For any complication, longer time to discharge (OR 1.222, p < 0.001), coronary artery disease (OR 1.465, p = 0.018), and increasing age (OR 0.982, p < 0.001) were significant, while lumbar decompression was protective (OR 0.724, p = 0.023). For neurologic complications, time to discharge remained a strong predictor (OR 1.203, p < 0.001), with lumbar fusion (OR 0.422, p < 0.001) and lumbar decompression (OR 0.338, p < 0.001) both protective. Anticoagulant use was associated with increased DVT risk (OR 4.16, p = 0.028) but not PE (p = 0.779). Conclusion: Utilizing dichotomous anticoagulation prescribing practices and prospectively collected outcomes, this study demonstrates that routine early anticoagulation is associated with increased complications, largely neurological. Importantly, routine anticoagulation did not reduce DVT or PE incidence, underscoring the need for individualized risk assessment in elective spine surgery. Prolonged hospital stay emerged as a key predictor of adverse events, highlighting the importance of timely and safe discharge.

## A415: Lumbar microdiscectomy and post-operative activity restrictions: a single blinded randomised controlled trial

Jack Roadley

1,2

, Myron Rogers

3

, Andrew Danks

4

, Jeremy Kam

4

, Idrees Sher

4

, Mendel Castlebaum-Kirschnow

4

, Scott Ayton

5

, Kylie Fryer

4

, Phillipa Risbey

3

, Tony Goldschlager

3,4

1

University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia

2

Princess Alexandria Hospital, Brisbane, Australia

3

Cabrini Hospital, Melbourne, Australia

4

Monash Medical Centre, Melbourne, Australia

5

The Florey Institute, Melbourne, Australia

Introduction: Lumbar microdiscectomy is the most common spinal procedure in the United States. While effective in relieving radicular pain in 75-80% of cases, there is significant variability in post-operative activity restrictions prescribed by surgeons. Many surgeons impose restrictions on sitting, bending, and lifting to prevent recurrent disc herniation. However, limited evidence exists to guide these recommendations. This study aims to provide objective data on whether post-operative activity restrictions impact recovery outcomes following lumbar microdiscectomy. Material and Methods: This single-blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted across three centers in Melbourne, Australia. Patients aged 18-75 years undergoing unilateral microdiscectomy for lumbar radiculopathy with concordant MRI findings were enrolled. Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either a restricted group (n = 101) or unrestricted group (n = 99). The restricted group received specific instructions limiting sitting to 15-30 minutes per two-hour period, avoiding lifting over 5kg, refraining from heavy household tasks, and avoiding strenuous sexual activity for two weeks. The unrestricted group was encouraged to resume normal activities as tolerated. All patients wore an electronic activity monitor (Activ8) for the first post-operative month. Patients were assessed pre-operatively and at day 1, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-surgery using visual analogue scales (VAS) for leg and back pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and quality of life questionnaires (SF-12, EQ-5D). The primary endpoint was a composite of reduced pain scores, functional improvement, and absence of further interventions at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included reherniation rates, individual functional measures, and time to return to work. Results: At one year, the primary composite endpoint showed no significant difference between restricted and unrestricted groups (45.6% vs 47.1%, p > 0.99). Individual components of the primary endpoint, including VAS back improvement (69.1% vs 63.2%, p = 0.587), VAS leg pain improvement (72.1% vs 73.5%, p > 0.99), ODI improvement (66.2% vs 80.9%, p = 0.08), and need for reoperation (2.9% vs 5.5%, p = 0.68) showed no significant differences. Secondary outcomes were also similar between groups. Reherniation occurred in 10.1% of restricted patients versus 14.1% in the unrestricted group (p = 0.61). Both groups showed significant improvements in all functional measures from baseline to 12 months. Electronic activity monitoring revealed poor adherence to restrictions, with only 10% of patients in the restricted group adhering to sitting limitations. Notably, sitting duration did not differ significantly between groups (4,102 vs 4,140 minutes/week, p = 0.89), nor did time spent in other activities (lying, standing, walking, or running). Conclusion: This randomized trial provides robust evidence that liberalizing post-operative restrictions following lumbar microdiscectomy does not negatively impact outcomes. No significant differences were found in pain reduction, functional recovery, or complication rates between either arm. The study challenges conventional concerns about activities like sitting, as objective monitoring showed similar activity patterns regardless of assigned group, with poor adherence to restrictions in the restricted group. The findings support a patient-driven approach to recovery guided by comfort and pain levels rather than rigid restrictions. This evidence may help standardize post-operative care guidelines, potentially reducing unnecessary limitations, facilitating faster return to normal activities, and improving patient satisfaction without compromising safety or outcomes.

Puya Alikhani

Introduction: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) is often taken into consideration for patients with deformity and degenerative conditions, yet the relationship between the number of fused levels and outcomes after surgery is still lacking complete understanding. ## A417: Delayed initiation of physical therapy following lumbar fusion can be associated with increased risk of mechanical complications, nonunion, and surgical revision: a 5-year matched cohort analysis

1

, Allen Wang

1

, Pouya Alijanipour

1

1

University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, United States

Introduction: Current guidelines suggest initiating postoperative physical therapy (PT) within 6 to 12 weeks after lumbar fusion. However, the long-term effects of not initiating PT within this window remain underexplored. We aimed to study the impact of delayed or absent PT on mechanical complications, nonunion, hardware failure, opioid use disorder, and need for surgical revision after lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: A retrospective matched cohort study was conducted using a large, multi-institutional electronic health record database. Adult patients who underwent lumbar spinal fusion were stratified based on whether they received PT within the first 3 months postoperatively. No significant difference in opioid use disorder was observed at this time point. Conclusion: Failure to initiate physical therapy within 3 months following lumbar fusion was associated with significantly increased risks of nonunion, hardware failure, mechanical complications, and surgical reintervention in this cohort over a 5-year period. These findings may underscore the critical role of timely rehabilitation and support current guidelines recommending early PT to optimize fusion outcomes and reduce complications.

Island Interventional Pain Management, Commack, NY, United States

Midwestern University Chicago - College of Osteopathic Medicine, Chicago, United States

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis is common in older adults and presents with neurogenic claudication and back and leg pain. Percutaneous minimally invasive lumbar decompression targets the hypertrophied ligamentum flavum using a percutaneous approach under fluoroscopy. ## A419: The Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome Score (SuCESS): development and validation of a clinical triage tool

Elie Najjar

1

, Michael Grevitt

1

1

Queen’s Medical Centre, Nottingham University Hospitals, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Background: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a rare but critical spinal emergency. However, over 80% of urgent MRIs for suspected CES show no cauda equina compression. This diagnostic uncertainty places strain on imaging services and delays care. We aimed to develop and validate a clinical triage tool-SuCESS (Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome Score)-to safely rule out CES and improve triage accuracy. Methods: We retrospectively developed the SuCESS score using 259 patients referred to a UK tertiary spinal unit between 2016 and 2018. Six clinical variables-saddle anaesthesia, reduced perianal sensation, motor weakness, bilateral sciatica, bladder post-void residual volume (PVR), and urethral catheterisation-were identified via multivariable logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost, and combined into an eight-point scoring system. Penalised regression was applied to minimise overfitting. External validation was performed using two temporally independent cohorts from 2020 and 2023 (n = 444). Primary outcomes were sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) for surgically confirmed CES. Model performance was assessed using area under the curve (AUC), Brier scores, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. Results: At a threshold of ≥ 3.0, SuCESS achieved 100% sensitivity and 100% NPV across all cohorts, correctly identifying all 64 cases of confirmed CES. Specificity increased from 37% in the development cohort to 54% in validation. AUC improved from 0.70 to 0.85, and Brier scores improved from 0.26 to 0.13. Use of the score might have safely deferred 38.7% of urgent MRIs, based solely on bedside clinical data. Conclusion: SuCESS is the first validated triage tool for CES to demonstrate perfect sensitivity. It offers a pragmatic and safe framework for reducing unnecessary MRI requests and improving diagnostic accuracy in urgent spinal referrals.

## A420: Comparison of predictive value for cage subsidence between MRI-based endplate bone quality and vertebral bone quality scores following transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion: a retrospective propensity-matched study

, Hong Ding

1

, Qian Chen

2

, Limin Liu

, Yueming Song

Introduction: Cage subsidence after TLIF is closely related to low vertebral bone mineral density (BMD). Recently, MRI-based vertebral bone quality (VBQ) and endplate bone quality (EBQ) scores have been proposed as radiation-free measures of bone quality, both associated with cage subsidence. EBQ demonstrated superior predictive performance, particularly due to its higher specificity, and may serve as a more reliable tool for preoperative risk assessment.

## A421: Discoplasty and decompression as a novel approach for advanced lumbar degeneration and spinal stenosis: a case series

Introduction: The aim of this study is to describe a novel, minimally invasive technique-percutaneous discoplasty combined with decompression-for the management of low back pain and lower limb symptoms in elderly patients with advanced degenerative disease. University of California Irvine, Orange, United States

Introduction: In the past two decades, the frequency of lumbar spine fusion surgeries has risen markedly. This increase has coincided with a rise in postoperative complications, notably pseudoarthrosis-a failure in spinal fusion manifesting as recurring pain and mechanical instability. The association between glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist use and complications following lumbar fusion has yet to be explored. The goal of this study is to examine the association between GLP-1 agonist usage and the incidence of pseudoarthrosis, adjacent segment disease, revision surgery, and other perioperative complications following lumbar fusion surgery. Material and Methods: TriNetX, a global health research network, was queried from 2004-2024 for patients undergoing open lumbar fusion using a posterior/transforaminal (CPT 22633, 22630, 22612), anterior (CPT 22558), or lateral approach (CPT 22533), and who had documented GLP-1 agonist usage within 1-year post-operation. Analysis included chi-squared tests with a control cohort propensity score matched for age, sex, race, smoking, diabetes, BMI, and uremia who did not have post-operative GLP-1 agonist usage. Outcomes of interest were DVT, emergency department (ED) visits, inpatient hospitalization, opioid abuse, PE, sepsis, surgical site infection, and wound complications within 90 days, and adjacent segment disease, implant failure, pseudoarthrosis, and revision within 2 years. Subgroup analysis based on surgical approach was conducted. Results: A total of 2,972 patients who received GLP-1 were compared to propensity matched controls. After matching, patients were 61.5 ± 11 years old, 39% male, 70% white, 81% diabetic, and 69% obese. In the posterior approach subcohort, GLP-1 agonist use was significantly associated with reduced odds of DVT (OR 0.58, CI 0.42-0.80), ED visits (OR 0.64, CI 0.55-0.75), inpatient hospitalization (OR 0.22, CI 0.19-0.25), sepsis (OR 0.31, CI 0.20-0.47), post-operative SSI (OR 0.46, CI 0.34-0.62), wound complications (OR 0.56, CI 0.42-0.76) within 90 days post-operation, implant failure (OR 0.58, CI 0.36-0.94) and pseudoarthrosis (OR 0.51, CI 0.44-0.58) within 2 years post-operation. In the anterior approach subcohort, GLP-1 agonist use was significantly associated with reduced odds of DVT (OR 0.43, CI 0.20-0.90), ED visits (OR 0.57, CI 0.40-0.81), inpatient hospitalization (OR 0.21, CI 0.16-0.28), post-operative SSI (OR 0.29, CI 0.14-0.60), wound complications (OR 0.45, CI 0.22-0.92) within 90 days, pseudoarthrosis (OR 0.65, CI 0.47-0.88) and revision surgery (OR 0.33, CI 0.22-0.51) within 2 years post-operation. The study population was insufficient to assess lateral approaches independently. Conclusion: Lumbar fusion patients prescribed GLP-1 agonists in the post-operative period experienced lower rates of pseudoarthrosis, revision surgery, postoperative infections, and overall hospitalizations compared to those who did not receive GLP-1 agonists. GLP-1 agonists may offer a therapeutic benefit in improving spinal fusion outcomes, and further prospective research is needed to validate these findings and investigate the underlying mechanisms.

## A424: Timing of thromboprophylaxis in acute spinal cord injury patients: a TQIP study

Aazad Abbas

1

, Jay Toor

2

, Albert Yee

3

, Cari Whyne

4

, Stephen Lewis

5

, Michael Fehlings

5

, Jetan Badhiwala

3

1

University of Toronto, Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, Department of Surgery, Toronto, Canada

2

University of Manitoba, Division of Spine Surgery, Winnipeg, Canada

3

Division of Spine Surgery, Sunnybrook Hospital, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

4

Sunnybrook Research Institute, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

5

Division of Spine Surgery, Toronto Western Hospital, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Optimal timing of venous thromboembolism prophylaxis (VTEp) after acute spinal cord injury (SCI) remains is debated, with most guidelines recommending VTEp be given within 72 hours. However, these recommendations are largely consensus-based and are lacking in primary large scale clinical data. As such, the goal of this study was to evaluate an ideal timeframe for delivery of thromboprophylaxis in the setting of acute SCI. Material and Methods: The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Trauma Quality Improvement Program (TQIP) was used to identify adults with acute SCI due to blunt trauma undergoing operative treatment within 24 hours from 2017-2022. Inclusion criteria were patients receiving LMWH or UFH within five days postoperatively. Exclusion criteria were age < 16, non-blunt trauma, low-volume centers (< 10 cases/year), missing data, non-LMWH/UFH prophylaxis, VTEp before surgery or >5 days postop, early care withdrawal, and death within five days. Restricted cubic splines modeled risk-adjusted outcome probabilities versus hours from surgery to VTEp to identify an inflection point, which defined early versus late VTEp for propensity score-matched comparisons. Covariates for propensity matching included patient, injury, treatment, and hospital characteristics. Primary outcome was in-hospital VTE; secondary outcomes were return to operating room, in-hospital mortality, and hospital length of stay (LOS). Effect size was calculated odds ratio (OR) with associated 95% confidence interval (CI). Significance level was set at p = 0.05. Results: A total of 15,960 patients across 511 trauma centres met inclusion criteria (mean age 48.6 years, 23.9% female). Spline analysis indicated increasing risk after approximately 24-48 hours, motivating two cutoffs for early versus delayed thromboprophylaxis: 1) 24-hours (postoperative day 0) and 2) 48-hours (postoperative day 1). In propensity-matched cohorts for the postoperative day 0 cutoff (i.e. early < 24 hours; late ≥ 24 hours) (N = 2,807 per group), there was no difference in rates of VTE, return to operating room, and in-hospital mortality. However, there was a borderline significant difference in length of stay (15.1 vs 16.2 days; p = 0.011; OR 3.16 [95% CI: 1.31, 7.66]). In propensity-matched cohorts for the postoperative day 1 cutoff (i.e. early < 48 hours; late ≥ 48 hours) (N = 6,867 per group), early VTEp was associated with lower VTE (4.7% vs 5.9%; p = 0.002; OR 1.26 [95% CI: 1.09, 1.46]), fewer returns to operating room (2.2% vs 2.9%; p = 0.004; OR 1.38 [95% CI 1.11, 1.71]), lower mortality (4.0% vs 4.9%; p = 0.003; OR 1.28 [95% CI: 1.09, 1.51]), and shorter length of stay (15.8 vs 16.9 days; p < 0.001; OR 2.89 [95% CI: 1.6; 5.2]). Conclusion: In acute SCI patients undergoing early surgery, initiating postoperative VTE prophylaxis within 48 hours was associated with reduced VTE, return to OR, mortality, and hospital LOS, supporting a < 48-hour target i.e. postoperative day 1 as a clinically meaningful threshold for early prophylaxis. These data from a large, multicenter cohort provide outcome-based timing guidance beyond consensus opinion and suggest that delaying VTEp beyond postop day 1 may worsen postoperative outcomes.

## A425: Minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and long-term prospective validation of the AO Spine PROST (Patient Reported Outcome Spine Trauma)

Said Sadiqi

1,2

, Charlotte Dandurand

3

, Richard Bransford

4

, Andrei Joaquim

5

, Ulrich Spiegl

6

, Alex Vaccaro

7

, F. Cumhur Oner

2

1

St. Antonius Hospital, Utrecht, The Netherlands

2

University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands

3

University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada

4

University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, United States

5

State University of Campinas, Campinas-Sao Paulo, Brazil

6

University of Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany

7

Rothman Institute, Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: The AO Spine PROST was developed as the first comprehensive, patient-centered instrument specifically designed for spine trauma. Although prior validation has confirmed its reliability and cross-cultural utility, Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) of this outcome instrument has not yet been established. The goal of this study was to determine the MCID of PROST as well as conducting a long-term prospective validation. Materials and Methods: This study utilized the data from a prospective observational international multicenter cohort study. Adults aged 18-65 acute thoracolumbar (TL) burst fractures without neurologic deficits were enrolled across multiple global regions, with follow-up extending to two years post-injury. Next to PROST, patients completed the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D), and Pain NRS. Characteristics were analyzed using descriptive statistics. MCID for PROST was assessed with distribution-based approach using the standard deviation (SD) of change in scores. Floor and ceiling effects were also assessed. Internal consistency was evaluated by Cronbach’s alpha, item-total correlation coefficient (ITCC) and pairwise Spearman correlation. Construct validity was determined through Pearson correlations (rs) with the ODI, EQ-5D, and Pain NRS. Responsiveness was assessed by calculating effect sizes (ES) and standardized response mean (SRM). Results: A total of 93 patients were included. The MCID for a moderate change (0.5*SD) in the PROST score was 10.6. No floor or ceiling effects were identified. Internal consistency was good with Cronbach’s α ranging from 0.9-1.0 and acceptable ITCC. No consistent pattern was found in correlations with the Pain NRS. Responsiveness was very good, with ES = 3.2 and SRM = 3.1 (p < .001). Conclusion: The AO Spine PROST identified an MCID of 10.6 as indicative of a moderate clinically meaningful change using a distribution-based approach. The instrument also showed strong internal consistency, construct validity, and excellent responsiveness in long-term follow-up, supporting its utility in evaluating outcomes in spine trauma patients.

## A427: Is time really spine? A systematic review and meta-analysis of early versus delayed intervention in spinal cord injury

Wilhelm Hansen

1

, Reaz Moolla

2

, Duval Jugganath

3

, Matthew Velcich

4

, Kylen Govender

4

, Kofi Nyarko

4

, Olusegun Ogunbanjo

5

, Badar Munir

6

1

Independent Researcher, Düsseldorf, Germany

2

Independent Researcher, Johannesburg, South Africa

3

Frere Hospital, East London, South Africa

4

Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital, Johannesburg, South Africa

5

Thelle Mogoerane Regional Hospital, Vosloorus, South Africa

6

Helen Joseph Hospital, Johannesburg, South Africa

Introduction: Spinal cord injury (SCI) results in significant disability, and the optimal timing of surgical decompression remains debated. Early intervention may mitigate secondary injury mechanisms such as ischaemia and inflammation; however, definitions of “early” vary, and implementation is often limited, particularly in low-resource settings like South Africa. Landmark studies, including Surgical Timing in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study (STASCIS), indicate improved outcomes with decompression within 24 hours, whereas others, such as Prospective, Observational European Multicenter study on the efficacy of acute surgical decompression after traumatic Spinal Cord Injury (SCI-POEM), question the universality of this benefit. This review systematically evaluates global evidence comparing early and delayed decompression, with emphasis on feasibility in resource-constrained health systems. Material and Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD420251000074). MEDLINE, Google Scholar, Scopus, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched to February 2025. A total of 4081 records were identified and screened on Rayyan by three reviewers. After deduplication, 330 full texts were evaluated. All authors participated in the full-text screening, resulting in 91 studies included and 202 excluded; 37 could not be retrieved. An additional 7 studies were identified through reference searches. Data were extracted using a standardised form and analysed with standard Cochrane meta-analytic methods: RoB 2 for assessing bias, random-effects pooling where applicable, and heterogeneity evaluated by I2 and Cochran’s Q. Results: Ninety-eight full texts, primarily observational cervical SCI cohorts, were included. Early decompression (≤ 24 hours) was consistently associated with improved neurological recovery at 6-12 months, with the greatest benefits in incomplete injuries, particularly AIS (ASIA Impairment Scale) C and central cord syndrome (CCS). In contrast, benefits in complete injuries (AIS A) were modest and more variable. Ultra-early decompression (≤ 6-8 hours) was associated with additional gains in select cohorts. In cervical facet dislocation, reduction within ∼6 hours was associated with better outcomes than later intervention. Motor recovery, especially upper-extremity function in CCS, and functional outcomes (Spinal Cord Independence Measure and Functional Independence Measure) also favoured earlier surgery. Early intervention did not consistently increase complications or mortality. Instead, decompression within 72 h was associated with shorter ventilation, reduced Intensive Care Unit (ICU) stay, and decreased hospital stay. Variability reflected differences in baseline severity, injury phenotype, co-interventions such as mean arterial pressure augmentation and corticosteroid use, and centre-level logistics. Certainty remains limited by the predominance of observational data and residual confounding; however, higher-quality cohorts using multivariable adjustment support these findings. Conclusion: This systematic review and meta-analysis reaffirm the principle that “Time is Spine.” Early decompression, particularly within 24 hours, is associated with better neurological recovery and a shorter hospital stay without an added safety risk. The strongest benefits are seen in incomplete injuries and CCS. Ultra-early intervention may offer additional benefits, although supporting evidence remains limited. Effects in complete injuries are less clear, and applying these findings to resource-limited health systems is challenging. Pragmatic clinical trials and targeted system strategies are necessary to facilitate timely surgery in settings where access and capacity are limited.

## A430: The Paris method: a new decision-making algorithm for the management of sacral fractures

Danilo Casasola

1

, Christophe Travert

1

, Laura Marie-Hardy

1

, Pascal-Moussellard Hugues

1

1

Pitié-Salpêtrière University Hospital, Sorbonne University, Paris, France

Introduction: Sacral fractures are rare but complex injuries that compromise both pelvic ring and spinopelvic stability, often with neurological involvement. Existing classifications (Tile, Roy-Camille, Denis) address different aspects of these injuries but lack a unified framework to guide surgical decision-making. This study proposes and validates a stepwise algorithm integrating these three systems for comprehensive management of high-energy sacral fractures. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective monocentric study including all patients ≥16 years admitted to a Level I trauma center between January 2021 and October 2023 with CT-confirmed sacral fractures. Fractures were classified through a three-step algorithm evaluating (1) pelvic ring stability (Tile), (2) spinopelvic stability (modified Roy-Camille), and (3) neurological prognosis (Denis). Two independent orthopedic surgeons performed double readings to assess intra- and interobserver reproducibility. Agreement was measured using Cohen’s kappa (κ). Results: Seventy-eight patients were included (mean age 39; 60% female). Falls from height represented the leading cause (67%), including 45% suicide attempts. Neurological deficits occurred in 18% of cases, all in Denis type II-III fractures. Surgical stabilization was performed in 36% of patients. Observer agreement was substantial across all steps: Tile classification κ = 0.67 (interobserver), Roy-Camille κ = 0.64, Denis κ = 0.76. Intraobserver reproducibility was also substantial (κ range 0.69-0.75). Notably, all Tile C fractures correlated with Roy-Camille type 3, and all Denis III fractures were associated with neurological impairment. Conclusion: The proposed “Paris Method” integrates Tile, Roy-Camille, and Denis systems into a reproducible three-step algorithm for sacral fracture management. It provides a systematic assessment of pelvic ring and spinopelvic stability while anticipating neurological risk, with substantial inter- and intraobserver agreement. This unified tool may improve decision-making and surgical strategy in complex sacral fractures. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted.

## A431: Hyperextension injuries in patients with ankylosing spine disorder: impact of pre-injury mobility status on mortality

Collin Lamba

1

, John Bartoletta

1

, Emily Hunt

1

, Karina Katchko

1

, Haitao Zhou

1

, Carlo Bellabarba

1

, Richard Bransford

1

1

University of Washington/Harborview Medical Center, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) and ankylosing spondylitis (AS) are the primary ankylosing spinal disorders (ASDs). ASDs share key clinical features, including functional spinal ankylosis, poor bone quality, advanced age, and multiple associated medical comorbidities which contribute to an increased risk of fractures, as the rigid, ankylosed spinal column amplifies the effect of even minor trauma. These fractures lead to significantly higher rates of neurologic compromise, morbidity, and mortality as compared to hyperextension injuries in the absence of ASD. This study evaluates the impact of pre-injury ambulation status on mortality rates for hyperextension injuries in patients with ASD. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed ASD patients who underwent surgery for hyperextension injuries at a single, Level 1 trauma center between 2005 and 2020. Patients were stratified by pre-injury ambulatory status: independent ambulation, cane/walker use, or wheelchair dependence. Collected variables included demographics, comorbidities, ASD type, pre-operative American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA PS), American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (IS), fracture location, injury type (single versus multilevel versus combined spine/pelvic), mechanism, and Surgical Invasiveness Index (SII). The primary outcome was mortality; secondary outcomes included post-operative ambulation and reoperations within 90 days. Statistical analyses included Mann-Whitney U test, Student T-test, and Chi-Squared test as appropriate; survival was estimated with Kaplan-Meier. A Cox proportional hazards model assessed predictors of mortality with age and ASA PS as covariates and pre-injury ambulation and 90-day reoperation as factors. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Of 467 identified patients, 387 met inclusion criteria; 72.5% were independent ambulators, 21.2% used a cane/walker, and 6.3% used a wheelchair pre-injury. Assistive device use was associated with older age, higher ASA class, and hypertension, but not with BMI, sex, ASD type, neurologic status, injury characteristics, or surgical factors. Mortality differed significantly by ambulatory status: 90-day mortality was 1.4% for independent ambulators, 39.3% for cane/walker users, and 84.0% for wheelchair users; 1-year mortality was 1.7%, 47.6%, and 96.0%, respectively (p < 0.001). Age (HR 1.05 per year, p < 0.001) and ASA class (HR 1.65 per class, p = 0.018) independently predicted mortality, while hypertension was not associated. At last follow-up, 42.0% of previously ambulatory patients required an assistive device. Reoperation occurred in 14.6% of patients, most commonly for infection, and was not associated with mortality. Conclusion: Pre-injury assistive device use, older age, and higher comorbidity burden were associated with markedly increased mortality after hyperextension injury in patients with ASD. One-year mortality exceeded 95% in wheelchair users compared with <2% in independent ambulators. Pre-injury ambulatory status is a simple yet powerful predictor of mortality and functional decline after hyperextension injuries in ASD, surpassing traditional injury-specific metrics. These data offer valuable prognostic insights, helping to facilitate improved guidance for patients and their families who are navigating treatment and recovery for these injuries.

## A432: Percutaneous stabilization of AO b3 fractures in patients with ankylosing spinal disorders (ASD) is associated with lower complication rates compared to open stabilization

Eli Bunzel

, Emily Hunt

1

, Jonathan Lawson

1

, Haitao Zhou

, Richard Bransford

University of Washington/Harborview Medical Center, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Ankylosing Spine Disorders (ASD), either in the form of ankylosing spondylitis (AS) or diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH), characteristically result in autofusion of the spine with abnormal rigidity and a long level arm. Patients with ASD have a fourfold increased risk of fracture compared with the general population. Patients were divided into open versus percutaneous fixation groups. Demographic, comorbidity, operative, hospital, and 90-day postoperative data were collected. Independent-samples t-tests and Fisher’s exact tests were used for continuous and categorical variables, respectively. Results: Two hundred cases (64 AS, 136 DISH) were identified from 2005 to 2020. 174 patients underwent open instrumentation, and 26 patients underwent percutaneous instrumentation. Overall, surgical site infection (SSI) rate was 11% (22/200). SSI infection rate was 12% (21/174) in the open group, versus 4% (1/26) in the percutaneous group. 90-day reoperation rate was 14% (24/174) in the open group versus 4% (1/26) in the percutaneous group. Mean estimated blood loss (EBL) was 575.0 ± 39.6 mL in the open group versus 184.0 ± 67.7mL in the percutaneous group. In-hospital mortality was 10% (17/174) in the open group versus 4% (1/26) in the percutaneous group. These were all significant with a p value <0.05. Length of ICU stay and discharge environment did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion: Compared with open instrumentation, percutaneous posterior instrumentation of AO B3 fractures in patients with ASD was associated with significantly reduced blood loss, lower SSI, lower 90-day reoperation, and decreased in-hospital mortality. Percutaneous posterior instrumentation should be strongly considered for stabilization of AO B3 fractures to decrease morbidity in this high-risk population.

## A433: Patients receiving GLP-1 agonists have reduced odds of pseudoarthrosis and revision following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion surgery

Manaav Mehta

1

, Abhinav Sharma

2

, Ryan Beyer

2

, Vivian Chen

, Michael Kim

, Paramveer Birring

2

, Hao-Hua Wu

, Sohaib Hashmi

2

, Yu-po Lee

2

, Nitin Bhatia

2

, Don Park

2

1

University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, United States

2

University of California Irvine, Orange, United States

Introduction: In accordance with the aging population, a significant increase in the volume of anterior cervical fusion procedures is expected over the next two decades. This increase has coincided with a rise in postoperative complications, notably pseudoarthrosis-a failure in spinal fusion manifesting as recurring pain and mechanical instability. The association between glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist use and complications following anterior cervical fusion surgery has yet to be explored. The goal of this study is to examine the association between GLP-1 agonist usage and the incidence of pseudoarthrosis, adjacent segment disease, revision surgery, and perioperative complications in patients undergoing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) surgery. Material and Methods: TriNetX, a global health research network, was queried from 2004-2024 for patients undergoing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (CPT 22551) and who had documented GLP-1 agonist usage within 1-year post-operation.
