## A434: Ligament reconstruction of the cervical spine: the anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) And its biomechanical role in anterior surgical approaches

Jana Felicitas Schader

1,2,3

, Mauro Suter

4

, Marie-Rosa Fasser

4

, Warnecke Daniela

5

, Anna Schuler

1,4

, José Spirig

2

, Jess Snedeker

1,3

, Mazda Farshad

1,2

, Jonas Widmer

4

1

Department of Orthopedics, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, University Spine Center Zürich, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, Institute of Biomechanics, Balgrist Campus, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

2

University Spine Center Zurich, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

3

Institute of Biomechanics, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

4

Spine Biomechanics, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

5

Research Department, Arthrex GmbH, Munich, Germany

Introduction: Typically, degenerative conditions of the cervical spine are managed via an anterior surgical approach. Nevertheless, this approach may lead to complications such as adjacent segment degeneration or instability due to biomechanical changes following the removal of the anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) during surgery. This study leverages orthopedic strategies focused on ligament reinforcement to stabilize joints. It examines the effects of reconstructing the ALL to provide targeted stabilization at the anterior spine, while avoiding complete immobilization of the segment. The study’s purpose was to evaluate the biomechanical impacts of removing the ALL and to assess if its reconstruction could maintain stability and range of motion akin to the cervical segment's intact state. Material and Methods: Biomechanical testing of ten spinal segments from four cadaveric human cervical spines (C2/3: 2, C3/4: 2, C4/5: 2, C5/6: 2, C6/7: 2) was performed. Spinal segments were fixed using 3D-printed clamps. ALL reconstruction was executed using surgical tape and human gracilis tendon allografts, attached with bone anchors. Testing was performed on each specimen in three phases: pre-resection (native state), post-ALL resection, and post-ALL reconstruction. ROM was evaluated in flexion-extension (FE), lateral shear (LS), lateral bending (LB), anteroposterior shear (AS), and axial rotation (AR). Results: After the ALL was removed, median ROM in FE increased to 131% [25th-75th percentile: 122%-163%] (p < 0.01) and reduced to 103% [93%-115%] (p > 0.05) after ALL reconstruction compared to the intact state (100%). Similar trends were observed in LS, LB, AS, and AR, with the least change seen in AR after ALL resection (111% [108%-125%], p < 0.05) and in LS after ALL reconstruction (116% [103%-119%], p < 0.05). Absolute ROM in FE increased progressively from intact to reconstructed to resected state (8.5° [6.2°-11.7°], 10.0° [5.7°-12.9°], 12.1° [8.3°-14.3°], respectively). Conclusion: The ALL is crucial for maintaining the stability of the cervical spine in all motion directions, particularly in flexion-extension and to a lesser extent in axial rotation. Reconstructing the ALL nearly restores the spine's ROM to its original state in most loading directions, which may help decrease the likelihood of complications from ligament resection during anterior cervical surgeries.

## A435: Ultra-early postoperative pain reduction predicts long-term outcomes following ACDF: preliminary results from a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial

Jon Håvard Sommernes

1,2

, Jarle Sundseth

2

, Mirad Taso

1,2

, Siri Bjorland

2

, Are Hugo Pripp

1,2

, Frode Kolstad

2

, Jens Ivar Brox

1

, John-Anker Zwart

1,2

1

University of Oslo, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway

2

Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway

Introduction: Cervical radiculopathy is a common condition caused by cervical disc herniation or spondylosis, often leading to disabling arm pain and functional impairment. When conservative treatment fails, anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) is widely performed. Although most patients improve, recovery trajectories vary considerably, and clinicians lack tools to identify early who will achieve lasting benefit. Identifying reliable predictors of long-term outcomes shortly after surgery could improve counseling, guide of follow-up allocation, and support individualized care. Previous studies in lumbar surgery suggest a prognostic role for early postoperative pain reduction, but evidence in cervical radiculopathy and especially in the ultra-early period is sparse. We investigated whether pain relief on postoperative day 1 (POD1) predicts 12-month pain and disability outcomes following ACDF. Material and Methods: We conducted a secondary cohort analysis of 83 patients from the surgical arm of a randomized controlled trial comparing ACDF with nonsurgical management for cervical radiculopathy [1]. Eligible patients were 20-65 years with ≥ 3 months of radicular arm pain and imaging-confirmed disc herniation or spondylosis at C5/C6 and/or C6/C7. Exclusion criteria included cervical myelopathy and prior cervical surgery. Pain was assessed with the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) for arm, neck, and headache at baseline, POD1, and 12 months. Disability was measured with the NDI. Early improvement was defined as a ≥ 2-point NRS reduction on POD1. Multivariable linear and logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, smoking, ASA class, diagnosis, surgical levels, operative time, baseline intensity. Results: On POD1, 94% of patients experienced a ≥ 2-point arm pain reduction. These responders had higher odds of maintaining meaningful arm pain relief at 12 months compared with non-responders (90.9% vs. 40.0%, p = 0.0077). Similar associations were observed for neck pain (87.0% vs. 53.8%, p = 0.0028) and headache (73.9% vs. 20.0%, p < 0.001). In adjusted analyses, greater POD1 arm pain reduction predicted larger improvements in arm pain (β = 0.64, p < 0.001) and NDI (β = 0.93, p < 0.001). Absolute arm pain on POD1 independently predicted 12-month arm pain (β = 0.28, p = 0.040). By contrast, associations for neck and headache pain were less consistent, and were not robust predictors of NDI. Patients with early arm pain relief were also less likely to use analgesics at one year. Conclusion: Ultra-early reduction in arm pain after ACDF is a clinically relevant predictor of long-term recovery. A simple NRS assessment on POD1 represents a feasible tool to stratify patients’ expected trajectories. Those with marked early relief may require less intensive follow-up, whereas patients without improvement could be prioritized for closer monitoring and supportive interventions. The predictive value was most evident for arm pain and disability, underscoring the role of radicular symptoms in cervical radiculopathy. External validation in larger multicenter cohorts is warranted, and future studies should explore whether combining ultra-early PROMs with psychosocial and multidomain recovery measures can further refine prognostic accuracy.
References
1. Taso M, Sommernes JH, Sundseth J, et al. Surgical versus Nonsurgical Treatment for Cervical Radiculopathy. NEJM Evid. 2025; 4(4):EVIDoa2400404.

## A436: Complications of staged versus same-day circumferential cervical spine fusion for degenerative disease

Mirbahador Athari

1

, Henry Avetisian

1

, William Karakash

1

, Aidan Lindgren

1

, Daniel Rusu

1

, Jordan Gasho

1

, Matthew Gallo

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, Kiran Alluri

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

Introduction: Cervical degenerative disc disease may be managed with anterior, posterior, or circumferential fusion. Circumferential procedures can be performed during a single anesthetic episode or staged across separate operations. While both strategies are used clinically, evidence comparing complication rates between same-day and staged procedures is limited. This study compared perioperative complications between same-day and staged circumferential cervical fusions using a large national database. Materials and Methods: We queried the PearlDiver Mariner database (2010-Q3 2022) to identify adults undergoing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) combined with posterior cervical fusion. Patients with trauma, infection, malignancy, deformity, rheumatoid arthritis, or age < 18 were excluded. Patients were grouped into Same-Day Surgery (circumferential fusion during one anesthetic) and Staged Surgery (procedures within 1-14 days). Demographics, comorbidities, and perioperative complications were assessed. Outcomes included 30-day medical and surgical complications, readmissions, and revision rates. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated; p < 0.05 was considered significant. Results: A total of 8,578 patients were identified: 6,496 underwent same-day surgery and 2,082 underwent staged surgery. Staged patients were slightly older (60.7 vs 60.0 years, p < 0.01) with higher comorbidity indices (5.21 vs 4.75, p < 0.001). Diabetes was more common in the staged group (p < 0.001), while sex, obesity, and tobacco use were comparable. Staged procedures were associated with significantly higher 30-day complication rates, including infection (8.5% vs 5.6%, OR 1.57, p < 0.001), radiculopathy (34.8% vs 16.0%, OR 2.58, p < 0.001), anemia (18.0% vs 12.2%, OR 1.42, p < 0.001), pneumonia (0.9% vs 0.4%, OR 2.29, p = 0.03), urinary tract infection (7.6% vs 5.7%, OR 1.40, p < 0.001), ileus (1.1% vs 0.7%, OR 1.99, p = 0.04), stroke (3.8% vs 2.2%, OR 1.55, p = 0.02), neurologic complications (32.3% vs 17.9%, OR 1.89, p < 0.001), mechanical complications (5.7% vs 2.1%, OR 2.82, p < 0.001), and transfusion (1.5% vs 0.7%, OR 2.00, p = 0.02). Same-day surgery had lower overall complication rates despite comparable demographics aside from comorbidity burden. Conclusion: Staged circumferential cervical fusions were associated with significantly higher complication rates compared with same-day procedures, including infection, anemia, respiratory, thromboembolic, neurologic, and mechanical complications. These findings suggest that same-day circumferential fusion may provide a safer perioperative profile in appropriately selected patients, while staged procedures may carry higher risks due to prolonged hospitalization and recovery. Optimizing patient selection and perioperative management is essential to reduce morbidity in this population.

## A437: Cervical sagittal alignment after multilevel ACDF: correction goes along with loss of compensation

Marco Manzetti

1,2,3

, Fabio Galbusera

4

, Andrea Cina

4

, Dezsö Jeszenszky

1

, Francois Porchet

1

, Jani Puhakka

1

, Raluca Reitmeir

1

, Mario Ropelato

1

, Maja Gocević

1

, Daniel Haschtmann

1

, Frank Kleinstuck

1

, Alberto Ruffilli

2,3

, Cesare Faldini

2,3

, Tamas Fekete

1

, Markus Loibl

1

1

Schulthess Klinik, Spine Center, Zürich, Switzerland

2

Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Clinica Ortopedica e Traumatologica I, Bologna, Italy

3

Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Science - DIBINEM, Bologna, Italy

4

Schulthess Klinik, Department of Teaching, Research and Development, Zürich, Switzerland

Introduction: Cervical spondylosis can lead to loss of lordosis or even kyphosis, altering sagittal alignment and triggering compensatory mechanisms to maintain horizontal gaze. Although multilevel anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is commonly used, its impact on sagittal alignment and compensatory changes remains unclear. This study investigates changes in cervical sagittal alignment before and after multilevel ACDF and the associated compensatory mechanisms. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of 298 patients undergoing 2- or 3-level ACDF for cervical spondylosis. Preoperative and postoperative sagittal parameters including C0-C2 lordosis, C2-C7 lordosis, surgical (fused-level) lordosis, unfused-level lordosis, T1 slope (T1S), T1S minus cervical lordosis (T1S-CL), and cervical sagittal vertical axis (c-SVA) were measured using a previously described deep learning model. Demographic data were collected at the same time points. Changes from baseline to follow-up were calculated. Correlations between changes in surgical lordosis and sagittal parameters were assessed via linear regression, Pearson’s correlation, and multiple logistic regression analysis. Results: The mean preoperative C2-C7 lordosis was 11.3° ± 13.6°, increasing significantly to 20.7° ± 15.6° after surgery (p < 0.0001). Segmental correction at fused levels averaged 6.5° in two-level and 8.6° in three-level ACDF cases. C0-C2 lordosis decreased from 20.5° ± 13.0° to 12.6° ± 12.6° (p < 0.0001), while T1S-CL also decreased from 20.9° ± 11.5° to 13.1° ± 14.7° (p < 0.0001). Changes in surgical lordosis correlated negatively with changes in unfused-level lordosis (R = -0.26, p < 0.01) and with C0-C2 lordosis (R = -0.11, p = 0.061). A strong inverse correlation was also observed between changes in C2-C7 and C0-C2 lordosis (R = -0.60, p < 0.01). Notably, the strongest correlation overall was found between changes in T1S-CL and C0-C2 lordosis (R = 0.63, p < 0.0001), suggesting that greater sagittal mismatch is associated with increased cranio-cervical extension. A moderate positive correlation was also found between surgical lordosis and changes in T1 slope (R = 0.29, p < 0.01). Conclusion: Multilevel ACDF can increase surgical lordosis and reduce compensatory mechanisms in the upper cervical and subaxial spine, via restoration of C2-C7 lordosis and correction of cervical mismatch. Notably, the observed relationship between T1S-CL and C0-C2 lordosis highlights the biomechanical role of cranio-cervical hyperextension as a compensatory response to sagittal mismatch. These findings support a shift toward viewing cervical alignment as a dynamic, multi-segmental system in which segmental correction can influence adjacent segment behavior, as described by the unfused lordosis. While long-term outcomes remain multifactorial, reducing compensation may lessen mechanical stress on unfused levels and help prevent future deterioration. Routine preoperative assessment of sagittal alignment-including mismatch and upper cervical compensation-should be integrated into surgical planning to guide alignment goals and improve long-term stability.

## A438: Impact of preexisting heart failure on postoperative adverse events after cervical spine fusion: a matched cohort analysis

Muaz Wahid

1

, Elias Nasser

1

, Zuhair Zaidi

1

, Salah Aoun

1

, Andrew Simpson

1

1

UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, United States

Introduction: Heart failure (HF) is a major perioperative risk factor, yet its impact after cervical spine fusion is under-characterized. As cervical fusions increase in an aging population, surgeons increasingly encounter patients with preexisting HF. We quantified 90-day and 1-year adverse events among adults undergoing cervical fusion, comparing those with versus without HF in a large, multicenter electronic health-record network to inform risk stratification and perioperative pathways. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective matched-cohort study in the TriNetX US Research Network (2010-2023). Adults (≥ 18 years) undergoing anterior or posterior cervical fusion below C2 were eligible. Patients with a documented HF diagnosis before index surgery were matched 1:1 to non-HF comparators using propensity scores from 38 covariates (demographics, comorbidities, medication use, baseline laboratories). Nearest-neighbor matching used a 0.1 SD caliper; balance was verified via standardized mean differences. Seventeen outcomes were assessed from postoperative day 1 through 90 days and 1 year, including mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, pulmonary embolism (PE), deep-vein thrombosis (DVT), pneumonia, sepsis, acute renal failure, emergency department (ED) visits, wound disruption, superficial infection, and selected neuropsychiatric/substance-use endpoints. Effects were estimated as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and p-values. Final matched cohorts included 3,716 HF and 3,716 non-HF patients. Results: At 90 days, HF was associated with substantially higher odds of mortality (OR 5.01, p < 0.0001), MI (9.43, p < 0.0001), PE (3.41, p < 0.0001), DVT (2.60, p < 0.0001), stroke (2.13, p < 0.0001), pneumonia (5.51, p < 0.0001), sepsis (4.20, p < 0.0001), acute renal failure (2.41, p < 0.0001), and ED visits (1.18, p = 0.0118); superficial infection (0.77, p = 0.14), wound disruption (0.76, p = 0.079), and opioid use disorder (1.00, p = 1.00) were not significantly different. Somatic symptoms were more frequent in HF, including chest pain (3.57, p < 0.0001), dizziness (1.67, p = 0.0002), and shortness of breath (4.47, p < 0.0001); alcohol use disorder was also higher (1.72, p = 0.0002). At 1 year, elevated risks persisted or intensified: mortality (3.78, p < 0.0001), MI (6.96, p < 0.0001), PE (3.08, p < 0.0001), DVT (3.30, p < 0.0001), stroke (1.84, p = 0.0002), pneumonia (3.79, p < 0.0001), sepsis (3.49, p < 0.0001), acute renal failure (2.35, p < 0.0001), and ED visits (1.45, p < 0.0001). Absolute rate differences illustrated clinical magnitude-for example, 90-day mortality was 6.76% in HF vs 1.43% in non-HF, and 1-year mortality was 11.62% vs 3.36%. Wound disruption and superficial infection remained nonsignificant at both horizons; opioid use disorder remained nonsignificant at 1 year (1.18, p = 0.27). Dementia (1.40, p = 0.027) and alcohol use disorder (1.49, p = 0.0011) were higher at 1 year in HF. Conclusion: Preexisting HF confers a broad, durable increase in postoperative risk after cervical fusion, spanning cardiopulmonary complications (MI, pneumonia), thromboembolism (DVT/PE), sepsis, acute renal failure, health-care utilization (ED visits), and mortality at 90 days and 1 year, without corresponding increases in superficial wound complications. These findings support incorporating HF status into preoperative counseling and risk models, optimizing guideline-directed medical therapy, and deploying enhanced perioperative bundles (e.g., pulmonary hygiene, VTE prophylaxis stratified for HF, vigilant hemodynamic/renal management, and early infection surveillance). Future work should stratify by HF subtype and severity (ejection fraction, NYHA class) to personalize mitigation strategies for this high-risk cervical fusion population.

## A440: Substance-specific outcomes after cervical fusion: multicenter, propensity-matched analysis of tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, and cannabis

Abdel Diab

1

, Reme Arhewoh

1

, Omar Diab

1

, Elinor Stern

1

, Ilyas Aleem

1

, Rakesh Patel

1

, Joshua Piche

1

1

University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, United States

Introduction: The negative impact of tobacco use on surgical outcomes, including cervical fusion procedures, is well-established, with evidence linking it to impaired healing, increased infections, and higher rates of complications. However, the effects of non-tobacco nicotine products (e.g., e-cigarettes) and cannabis use remain poorly defined, despite their growing prevalence. As these substances become more commonly used, understanding their specific associations with postoperative outcomes is crucial for risk stratification and perioperative management. This study evaluates the distinct effects of tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine dependence (NTND), and cannabis use on both short-term and long-term outcomes in cervical fusion procedures addressing a critical gap in perioperative risk stratification. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX database, encompassing 104 healthcare organizations, and included only patients undergoing cervical fusion. Propensity matching was performed using age, sex, BMI, race, and comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, and CKD. Primary outcomes included 90-day complications (hospital readmission, sepsis, infection, myocardial infarction, mortality, and renal failure). Secondary outcomes included 2-year mechanical complications (pseudoarthrosis, proximal junctional kyphosis [PJK], reoperations, wound disruption, and spinal infections). Statistical analyses included risk differences (RD), odds ratios (OR), and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis for reoperations. Results: The study included three distinct substance-use cohorts: NTND (n = 414), cannabis (n = 659), and tobacco (n = 8,273), and respectively matched controls. After matching, baseline characteristics were well-balanced across groups. • NTND Cohort: NTND users exhibited significantly higher 90-day hospital readmissions compared to controls (11.1% vs. 5.6%, p = 0.004; OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.26-3.58). At 2 years, pseudoarthrosis rates were significantly lower in NTND users compared to controls (7.4% vs. 13.7%, p = 0.004; OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.31-0.81). Other mechanical complications could not be assessed due to limited sample sizes. • Cannabis Cohort: Cannabis users demonstrated increased 90-day hospital readmission rates compared to controls (11.8% vs. 7.0%; RD = 4.9%, p = 0.003; OR 1.789, 95% CI 1.221-2.620). No significant differences were observed in 2-year pseudoarthrosis or other mechanical complications. • Tobacco Cohort: Tobacco users experienced significantly higher rates of 90-day complications, including sepsis (1.2% vs. 0.6%, p < 0.001), infection (1.3% vs. 0.7%, p = 0.001), myocardial infarction (0.7% vs. 0.3%, p < 0.001), mortality (0.7% vs. 0.4%, p = 0.011), and hospital readmissions (11.1% vs. 7.0%, p < 0.001). At two years, tobacco use remained associated with increased risks of reoperation (p = 0.02), wound disruption (p = 0.017), spinal infection (p < 0.001), and proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) (p = 0.004). Paradoxically, tobacco users demonstrated lower rates of pseudoarthrosis compared to controls (10.2% vs. 17.1%, p < 0.001; OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.50-0.60). Conclusion: NTND and cannabis use primarily contribute to increased hospital readmissions within 90 days. Tobacco use, serving as a positive control, is strongly associated with increased short-term complications, including infection, sepsis, and readmissions, as well as higher long-term risks of reoperation and wound-related complications following cervical fusion. Paradoxically, both tobacco and NTND users exhibited unexpectedly lower rates of pseudoarthrosis. These may reflect data artifacts, survivorship bias, difference in follow up patterns etc. Overall, these findings emphasize the comparatively reduced harm of other substances in comparison with tobacco but underscore the need for targeted preoperative counseling and tailored perioperative care for patients with substance use, with further research required to clarify underlying mechanisms and refine management strategies tailored to substance use patterns.

## A441: Discordance between minimal clinically important difference and patient satisfaction after surgery for cervical spondylotic myelopathy: a 5-year analysis from the quality outcomes database

Abraham Dada

## A442: Does duration of symptoms in metastatic spine disease affect recovery and outcomes? A systematic review and meta-analysis

Harsh Jain

1

, Nick De Oliviera

2

, Advith Sarikonda

1

, Ilya Laufer

3

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1

1

Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, United States

2

Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, Nashville, United States

3

NYU Langone Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: Despite widespread recognition that earlier intervention may improve outcomes in metastatic epidural spinal cord compression (MESCC), the specific impact of symptom duration on post-treatment recovery remains understudied. We sought to evaluate the association between the duration of pre-treatment symptoms, specifically motor function, and clinical outcomes, specifically motor recovery and survival, in patients undergoing radiotherapy (RT) or surgery for MESCC, through a systematic review and meta-analysis. This project was initiated by AO Spine Knowledge Forum Tumor. Material and Methods: A systematic literature review was performed in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines using PubMed/Embase databases (01/01/1990-05/03/2025). Study inclusion criteria were: adults with MESCC with pre-treatment symptom duration and its association with outcomes after RT or surgery. Primary exposure was duration of pre-treatment symptoms, which was most often motor deficits. Covariates included age, sex, visceral metastases, and extent of vertebral involvement. Interventions included RT or surgery. Primary outcomes were motor recovery and ambulation; secondary outcomes included survival and local control. Pooled risks were estimated using random-effects models, stratified by intervention and outcome. Due to limited sample size, meta-analysis was performed for the following interventions/outcomes: RT with motor recovery and survival; surgery with survival. Results: Of 4639 articles reviewed, 37 met the inclusion criteria (26 RT cohorts, 11 surgical cohorts). RT: Symptom duration in all RT studies (26/26,100%) was defined as the time from the onset of motor weakness to RT initiation. Longer duration or slower development of motor symptoms was associated with improved motor recovery (Pooled-Risk = 2.08, 95%CI: 1.68-2.58, p < 0.001) and decreased risk of mortality (improved survival) (Pooled-Risk = 0.72, 95%CI: 0.69-0.76, p < 0.001). Although the literature consistently reported that longer symptom duration was associated with better ambulatory function and a reduced risk of local recurrence, the small number of studies precluded a meta-analysis and pooled-risk. Surgery: Symptom duration was defined as the time from onset of neurological deficit to surgery in 7/11 studies (64%); three studies (27%) used ambulatory status, and one study (9%) used both definitions. In the surgical cohort, longer duration of symptoms was associated with increased risk of death (worse survival) (Pooled-Risk = 1.28, 95%CI: 0.54-3.03, p = 0.575), although it was not statistically significant. Though a meta-analysis and pooled risk could not be conducted for motor recovery due to small numbers, most studies demonstrated that longer duration of symptoms was associated with worse motor recovery, although findings regarding ambulatory function were inconsistent. Covariate analysis revealed visceral metastases were associated with lower rates of positive outcomes in both surgical and RT cohorts. Conclusion: Symptom duration significantly influenced outcomes in MESCC, with opposing effects by treatment modality. Longer duration was associated with improved survival and motor recovery in the RT cohort, whereas it was associated with decreased survival in the surgical cohort, though this was not statistically significant. Most surgical studies demonstrated an inverse association between symptom duration and motor recovery. Visceral metastases consistently predicted lower rates of favorable outcomes across both treatment groups. These findings highlight the importance of tailoring intervention strategies not only to symptom trajectory but also to underlying disease burden, supporting an individualized, modality-specific approach to the management of MESCC.

## A443: Utility of intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (iMRI) in spinal intramedullary tumor surgery

Wei-Ting Lee

1

, Yen-Heng Lin

2

, Yu Cheng Huang

2

, Keng-Chian Lin

2

, Dar-Ming Lai

1

, Fon-Yih Tsuang

1,3

1

Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Surgery, National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

2

Division of Neuroradiology, Department of Medical Imaging, National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

3

Spine Tumor Center, National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: Spinal intramedullary tumors are uncommon and present significant surgical challenges due to their delicate anatomical location within the spinal cord and their frequently ill-defined margins. Preservation of neurological function while achieving maximal tumor resection remains the primary surgical goal. Intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (iMRI), which has proven beneficial in brain tumor surgery, offers real-time imaging that may assist in assessing the extent of resection and guiding further surgical decisions. This study evaluates the clinical utility and feasibility of iMRI during spinal intramedullary tumor resection, with an emphasis on the extent of resection, tumor localization, and intraoperative guidance. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective case series at a single tertiary referral center, enrolling 22 patients who underwent spinal intramedullary tumor resection with iMRI guidance between April 2022 and August 2025. Preoperative assessments included conventional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) in selected cases for tumor characterization and surgical planning. Intraoperatively, iMRI was performed after initial resection to evaluate residual tumor and to guide further resection where feasible. Postoperative MRI was conducted during follow-up to assess resection extent and early outcomes. Results: Among the 22 cases, tumors were located in the cervical (36.4%), thoracic (50.0%), and lumbar (13.6%) spine. Histopathological diagnoses included ependymomas, hemangioblastomas, astrocytomas, and other tumor types. iMRI detected residual tumors in 8 cases (36.3%) that were aiming for gross total resection, leading to additional resection in 5 cases. The mean operative time was 342.2 minutes (229-535 minutes), with an average iMRI examination duration of 53.5 minutes (30-70 minutes). The mean postoperative MRI follow-up period was 82.7 days. Among the patients who underwent postoperative MRI, no residual tumor was detected during follow-up, except for one case where recurrence occurred at a different spinal level. Case demonstrations are included to illustrate the clinical application of iMRI in guiding both additional resection and localization of subtle lesions. Notable imaging artifacts included air bubbles, hematomas, and contrast leakage. Conclusion: iMRI is a valuable tool in the resection of spinal intramedullary tumors, providing real-time intraoperative information that enhances surgical precision and may improves the gross total resection rate. Although not all residual tumors can be safely resected, the integration of iMRI into the surgical workflow can increase resection confidence and potentially improve surgical outcomes. Future research should focus on refining iMRI-integrated surgical protocols and evaluating their long-term impact on patient outcomes.

## A444: Incidence and predictors of local recurrence following surgical management of spinal metastases

Zainah Moukahhel

1,2

, Olivia Zhou

1,2

, Leonardo Olijnyk

1,2

, Jesse Shen

1,2

, Fidaa Al-Shakfa

1,2

, Zhi Wang

1,2

1

Université de Montréal, Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal, Montréal, Canada

2

Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal, Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Spinal metastases represent a common complication of advanced malignancies and remain a significant source of morbidity. Although recent advances in surgical technique and adjuvant therapies have improved the prognosis, local recurrence after operative management continues to pose a major clinical challenge. A better understanding of this population is essential to guide treatment strategies and offer better quality of life. In this context, we evaluated the incidence, associated risk factors, and outcomes of spinal metastases in patients treated surgically at the Centre Hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal (CHUM). Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed all patients who underwent surgery for histologically confirmed spinal metastases at CHUM and had the first operation between January 2015 and October 2024. In patients with surgeries at distinct, non-adjacent levels, each operated level was analyzed independently for recurrence at that site. Collected data included demographics, primary tumor type, spinal level, surgical modality, time to recurrence, and survival time. Recurrence was defined as symptomatic and radiological tumor regrowth at the same operated level. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS v.25. Results: A total of 377 patients were included in the analysis. Mean overall survival of 541 days (95% CI 482-600). The average age at the time of surgery was 63.2 years. Among all patients, 70, 178 and 113 were smokers, non-smokers and former smokers respectively (18.6%, 47.3% and 30%). Symptomatic local recurrence occurred in 8.5% of patients (n = 32), including 5.1% (n = 19) within the first 6 months, 1.1% (n = 4) between 6-12 months, and 2.7% (n = 9) beyond 1 year postoperatively. Recurrence rates varied significantly by spinal level (p = 0.011), with similar rates observed in the cervical (8%, 15/175) and thoracic (7%, 12/155), but higher in the lumbar spine (30%, 3/7). Recurrence ranged from 0% to 50% according to cancer types. Although there was a tendency of association with primary tumor, it did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.054). The highest rates were seen in esophageal (50%, 2/4), pancreatobiliary (33%, 2/6), neuroendocrine (14%, 1/7), and prostate tumors (13%, 8/60). Lung cancer was the most common operated primary tumor (28%, n = 104), yet recurrences occurred in 7.7% of patients (8/104). Breast cancer was the second most frequent (19%, n = 72), with 4.2% of patients experiencing recurrence (3/72). Renal cancer represented 11% of cases (n = 40) and showed a recurrence of 10% (4/40). No demographic, operative (including surgical approach and type), or radiotherapy-related factors (pre-operative or post-operative) were associated with recurrence. Conclusion: Symptomatic local recurrence after surgery for spinal metastases was uncommon (<10%), but significantly higher in the lumbar spine. Primary tumor type showed a possible, though non-significant, association. Importantly, these findings derive from the largest single-center series to date, with a substantial cohort of 377 patients, enhancing the robustness and generalizability of the results. This study underscores that both compression severity and tumor location should be carefully considered in postoperative risk stratification and surveillance planning.

## A445: Evaluating the real-world predictive utility of Karnofsky and ECOG performance status for 90-day survival after oncologic surgery for metastatic spinal tumors

Rafael De la Garza Ramos

1

, Ali Haider Bangash

2

, Sertac Kirnaz

2

, Rose Fluss

2

, Victoria Cao

2

, Alexander Alexandrov

2

, Liza Belman

2

, Saikiran Murthy

2

, Yaroslav Gelfand

2

, Reza Yassari

2

1

Montefiore Medical Center, New York, United States

2

Montefiore Einstein, New York, United States

Introduction: Performance status is frequently cited in the literature as an independent predictor of survival following surgery in patients with metastatic spine disease. However, there is limited evidence regarding its standalone predictive performance for short-term postoperative outcomes. In this study, we aimed to directly evaluate how well Karnofsky (KPS) and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status scores (ECOG-PS) predict 90-day survival-a commonly used threshold for surgical candidacy-in patients undergoing surgery for metastatic spinal tumors. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 175 adult patients who underwent surgery for metastatic spine disease at a single institution between 2012 and 2025. All patients had documented preoperative KPS and ECOG-PS scores and at least 90 days of follow-up or death. Univariable logistic regression was used to assess the association between performance status and 90-day survival. Predictive performance was assessed across three domains: discrimination (AUC), calibration (Brier score and calibration plots), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis [DCA]). Results: The crude 90-day survival rate was 73%. Both KPS (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.01-1.05; p = 0.001) and ECOG-PS (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.36-0.73; p < 0.001) were statistically associated with survival on univariable analysis. However, discrimination was modest (AUC 0.65 for KPS, 0.68 for ECOG-PS), and calibration was fair (Brier scores 0.185 and 0.182, respectively). DCA revealed minimal net benefit for either score across most threshold probabilities, with ECOG-PS showing slightly better performance at intermediate thresholds (30-60%)-the zone of greatest clinical uncertainty. Conclusion: Despite being widely cited as an independent predictor of postoperative survival in patients with metastatic spinal tumors, performance status assessed via the KPS and ECOG-PS demonstrated only modest discriminatory ability, calibration, and clinical utility when used alone to predict 90-day survival. These findings highlight the important difference between statistical association and real-world clinical utility of a single metric to predict outcome in this patient population.

## A446: European retrospective multicenter study in patients with vertebral metastases (Train-METASTRA)

Giovanni Barbanti Bròdano

1

, Áron Lazáry

2

, Jorrit-Jan Verlaan

3

, Peter Vajkoczy

4

, Mariarita Intagliata

1

, Cristiana Griffoni

, Julia Szita

2

, Netanja Harlianto

3

, Hannah Miller

4

, Serena Moscato

5

, Ariele Santello

5

, Sabato Mellone

5

, Luca Cristofolini

6

1

Complex Spinal Surgery Unit, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

2

National Center for Spinal Disorders, Buda Health Center, Budapest, Hungary

3

Department of Orthopedics, University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht, Netherlands

4

Department of Neurosurgery, Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Berlin, Germany

5

Department of Electrical, Electronic, and Information Engineering, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

6

Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Train-METASTRA is a retrospective multicentre study conducted within the framework of the European project METASTRA: “Computer-aided effective fracture risk stratification of patients with vertebral metastases for personalized treatment through robust computational models validated in clinical settings.” Currently, fracture risk assessment in vertebral metastases is imprecise. Clinicians rely on the Spine Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS), which evaluates five radiographic criteria and mechanical pain to classify the spine as stable, potentially unstable, or unstable, with cases requiring referral to spine surgeons. However, SINS alone has low reliability, with sensitivity and specificity < 50%, due to limited parameters, dependence on expert opinion, and small validation cohorts. METASTRA aims to improve the prevention of pathological fractures in patients with vertebral metastases and to provide patient-tailored treatment by developing computational and biomechanical models that reliably stratify patients according to their fracture risk and can be incorporated into a decision support system (DSS). To develop these computational models, a large dataset of clinical and radiographic data from patients with vertebral metastases was collected through the retrospective multicentre study “Train-METASTRA”, carried out in four European clinical centres. Material and Methods: Patients included in the study were ≥ 18 years old, with vertebral metastases in the thoracic or lumbar spine not surgically treated, had a CT scan available at the time of lesion diagnosis and at least one follow-up visit at ≥ 3 months after the first evaluation. Clinical data were collected in pseudo-anonymized form using an electronic case report form (eCRF) based on RedCap, and imaging data were uploaded to a dedicated platform, in compliance with privacy regulations. Data quality was ensured by centralized monitoring across participating centres. SINS scores were collected for the metastatic lesions. For approximately 90% of lesions, SINS was calculated using a standardized RedCap form based on the established parameters: radiographic spinal alignment, vertebral body collapse, posterolateral element involvement, lesion location, bone lesion type, and mechanical/postural pain. For the remaining lesions, SINS values were retrieved from the clinical records, representing scores previously assigned by treating clinicians. Results: The total number of patients enrolled across the participating centres was 2,041, of whom 53.5% were male. The mean age was 65 years. The most common primary tumours metastasizing to the spine were breast cancer (35.05%) and prostate cancer (25.35%). A total of 3,467 lesions were analysed (1,838 thoracic, 1,629 lumbar), predominantly lytic (47.44%). Approximately 77.31% of the lesions were treated with surgery, systemic therapy, and/or radiotherapy: 86.53% remained stable, while 362 lesions (9.39%) progressed to pathological fracture, with 10.40% of these associated with grade 2 epidural spinal cord compression (Bilsky classification). SINS scores were available for 2,490 lesions, with a mean value of 5.18. Among the lesions that progressed to fracture, the mean SINS score was 8.81. Conclusions: Preliminary analysis suggests that while SINS score provides a general indication of instability, it does not fully predict fracture progression, highlighting the need for complementary computational models to improve risk stratification and enable more personalized, targeted interventions. Acknowledgement: METASTRA project funded by the European Union HEU topic HLTH-2022-12-01 grant 101080135.

## A447: Effect of treatment center volume on clinical outcomes for primary malignant intramedullary spinal tumors

Ataollah Shahbandi

1

, Peter Palmer

1

, Kevin Wojcik

1

, Pegah Ghamasaee

1

, Saman Shabani

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, United States

Introduction: The impact of facility volume on patient outcomes for primary malignant intramedullary tumors remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate survival differences based on facility volume, analyze variations in treatment approaches, and assess the independent association between facility caseload and survival as well as perioperative outcomes. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study utilized data from the National Cancer Database from 2004 to 2022. Patients diagnosed with primary malignant spinal intramedullary tumors were included in the present study. To determine the optimal caseload cutoff for survival prediction, maximally selected rank statistics were employed, revealing a threshold of 32 patients spanning the period from 2004 to 2022. Patients were categorized based on facility volume: high-volume facilities (> 32 cases over the study period) and low-volume facilities (≤32 cases). The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), while secondary outcomes included treatment utilization and perioperative outcomes in surgically treated patients. Results: A total of 3,667 patients were included, with 502 treated at high-volume facilities and 3,165 at low-volume facilities. Patients treated at high-volume facilities were significantly younger (46.8 ± 15.2 years versus 49.5 ± 15.8 years; p < 0.001) and had a significantly higher proportion of males (56.2% versus 50.4%; p = 0.018) compared to those at low-volume facilities. Patients treated at high-volume facilities were significantly more likely to have private insurance or managed care (73.6% versus 59.7%), whereas those at low-volume facilities had significantly higher rates of government-sponsored insurance (36.7% versus 25.6%) or were uninsured (3.6% versus 0.8%; p < 0.001). Additionally, a significantly greater proportion of patients at high-volume facilities resided in ZIP codes with a median household income of ≥ $63,000 (44.1% versus 34.4%; p < 0.001) and in metropolitan areas (78% versus 74.4%; p = 0.017). Treatment at high-volume facilities was associated with significantly improved OS (p < 0.001), with a 10-year survival rate of 81.4% compared to 69.8% at low-volume facilities. While surgical procedures, radiation therapy, and systemic therapy utilization remained stable at high-volume facilities, low-volume facilities exhibited a significant increase in surgical procedures (rate ratio [RR] 1.021, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.011-1.032; p < 0.001) and a significant decline in radiation therapy use (RR 0.971, 95%CI 0.955-0.987; p < 0.001). After adjusting for confounding variables, treatment at high-volume facilities remained independently associated with lower mortality risk (hazard ratio 0.737, 95%CI 0.578-0.94; p = 0.014), a reduced likelihood of receiving radiation therapy (odds ratio [OR] 0.539, 95%CI 0.413-0.697; p < 0.001), and significantly lower 30-day readmission rates following surgical resection (2.1% versus 6.9%; OR 0.313, 95%CI 0.147-0.586; p = 0.001). Conclusion: Despite the rarity of primary malignant intramedullary tumors, treatment at high-volume facilities was associated with significantly improved survival and lower 30-day readmission rates following surgical resection, even after adjusting for potential confounders. These findings underscore the importance of specialized centers in optimizing patient outcomes and can inform referral patterns and treatment strategies for these complex tumors.

## A448: Proposal of a novel approach to minimally invasive stabilization and short-course neoadjuvant denosumab treatment before en bloc resection in enneking stage 3 giant cell tumors of the mobile spine

Introduction: En bloc resection of giant cell tumor (GCT) is technically more demanding as this tumor is typically soft and friable. A few studies investigated the technical limits of en bloc resection and the role of Denosumab in less accessible GCTs of spine. The aim of our study is to compare a cohort of consecutive cases of GCTs of the mobile spine treated with a minimally invasive stabilization (MIS) followed by neoadjuvant Denosumab treatment (NDT) before en-bloc resection and patients treated with NDT followed by en-bloc resection. Dosage was always 120 mg subcutaneous each month with loading doses in the first month on days 1, 8, 15, 22. The operative time was lower in Group 1 (495 ± 138 vs 575 ± 220 min). No evidence of mechanical complication was observed in Group 1 at the final follow-up (78 ± 2.3 months). A rod fracture occurred in one patient of Group 2 who underwent revision surgery at 11 months of follow-up. 2 (22.2%) patients of Group 2 experienced distal junctional failure and required revision surgery. No evidence of LR was found in our population. Conclusion: MIS associated with Denosumab as a planned neoadjuvant treatment offers advantages in preoperative surgical planning and downstage the surgical procedure preventing segmental kyphosis allowing a better reconstruction to reduce the risk of mechanical complication.

## A449: Emergent vs. delayed decompression in cauda equina syndrome secondary to tumors: what does the evidence say?

Humaid Al Farii

1

1

Sultan Qaboos University, Muscat, Oman

Background: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a severe neurological condition resulting from compression of the cauda equina nerve roots. Its prevalence secondary to tumors is relatively low but presents significant diagnostic and treatment challenges. CES can lead to serious complications, including permanent neurological deficits, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and chronic pain. In the case of disc herniation, there is a well-established body of literature showing that delayed surgery worsens neurological recovery due to irreversible damage to these compressed nerves. Understanding the impact of surgical timing on patient outcomes in tumor-related CES is crucial, as it can guide clinical decision-making and optimize surgical planning. If evidence supports that delayed intervention does not compromise neurological outcomes, this allows the opportunity to conduct thorough preoperative evaluations, obtain tissue biopsies to guide treatment, and plan for complete tumor resection with appropriate instrumentation. Thus, the aim of this study is to examine the relationship between surgical timing and patient outcomes in tumor-related CES. Materials and Methods: PubMed and Embase databases were used to conduct searches for relevant articles evaluating the effect of surgical timing on patient outcomes in tumor-related CES. Included studies were those of CES with neoplastic involvement, wherein the outcomes were evaluated and timing (emergent vs. delayed) of the operations were mentioned. Excluded articles were non-surgical studies and those with no outcome data. A total of 36 patients were included in the study of whom satisfied the inclusion criteria. Results: There was a male predominance (21/36, 58.3%), and the patients’ mean (standard deviation [SD]) age was 46.75 (15.8) years. The most common tumor type were paragangliomas (14/36, 38.9%), and the most common presenting symptoms included pain (35/56, 97.2%), weakness (25/36, 69.4%), and incontinence (16/36, 44.4%). Of these patients, 29 of them underwent an emergent operation (80.5%), while 7 of them underwent an elective operation (19.4%). All elective procedures yielded persistent symptoms, while of the emergent operations, 3/29 (10.3%) passed away due to disseminated disease, 6/29 (20.7%) fully recovered, and 20/29 (69%) had residual symptoms. Mean (SD) follow-up time was 21.2 (33.4) months. Conclusions: Our review found that emergent operations reduce the risk of symptom persistence in tumor-related CES. However, it is worth noting that there is an underwhelming body of literature assessing the time interval between hospital admission and initiation of surgery in CES caused by tumors. Most studies included here only referenced whether the admission was emergent or elective, rather than precise quantitative measures of time. Thus, we advocate for more specific research evaluating how surgical timing specifically affects outcomes in tumor-related CES.

## A450: Knowledge, attitudes and practices of intraoperative autologous blood cell salvage in tumour-related spine surgery: a survey of singapore spine society members

Hui Zhen Grace Chua

1

, Derek Chao Kuan Twan

, Yeong Huei Ng

, Naresh Kumar

, Jiong Hao Tan

, Youheng Ou Yang

1
Singapore General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore, 
2
National University Hospital, Singapore, Singapore
Background: Intraoperative autologous blood cell salvage (IOCS) allows blood lost intraoperatively to be processed and re-transfused, reducing allogenic blood transfusion requirements. IOCS used in tumour-related spine surgery is limited due to concerns of tumour-cell reinfusion. Recent studies suggest that the risk of reintroduction of viable tumour cells is low and meta-analyses have not found increased tumour recurrence. This study aims to investigate the knowledge, attitudes and practices of members of the Singapore Spine Society (SSS) regarding usage of IOCS in metastatic spine tumour surgery (MSTS) and primary spinal tumour surgery (PSTS). Material and Methods: An online questionnaire was sent by electronic-mail to all 108 members of SSS in July 2025. The questionnaire included surgeon’s demographics, practice settings, case volumes, availability of IOCS and their support and usage of IOCS in both metastatic and primary spinal tumour surgeries respectively. Participants rated their support for IOCS on a five-point Likert scale, and listed their perceived benefits and concerns with usage of IOCS. Results: A total of 36 valid responses were received. Majority were Orthopaedic surgeons (83.3% vs 16.7% Neurosurgeons) working in public hospitals (69.4%), with more than 10 years of working experience as a spinal surgeon (55.6%). Most (91.7%) work in institutions that are able to provide IOCS, of which 72.7% had IOCS available for more than five years. The main perceived benefits of IOCS across both MSTS and PSTS are reduction in allogenic transfusion (86.1% MSTS vs 75.0% PSTS), decreased morbidity/complications (44.4% vs 50.0%), cost savings (38.9% vs 33.3%), and decreased mortality (27.8% vs 22.2%). Concerns regarding its use include potential systemic tumour seeding (63.9% MSTS vs 69.4% PSTS), coagulopathy (52.8% vs 38.9%), infection (36.1% vs 25.0%), and high costs (27.8% vs 27.8%). In MSTS, 77.8% of surgeons supported using IOCS but only 50.0% reported clinical usage. Mean support ratings were significantly higher in public-hospital surgeons (4.24 vs 2.55 private-hospital, p-value < 0.0001), surgeons performing more than ten MSTS cases a year (4.16 vs 3.24, p-value = 0.003), and those who use it in clinical practice (4.50 vs 2.94, p-value < 0.0001). This is compared to PSTS, where 58.3% of surgeons support its use, but only 22.2% use it. Seventeen surgeons had not performed surgery for PSTS before. Mean support ratings in PSTS were significantly higher in surgeons who use it (4.38 vs 2.61, p-value < 0.0001), but not significant based on practice settings (3.20 public vs 2.55 private, p-value=0.068). Overall mean support ratings were higher for MSTS (3.72) than PSTS (3.00, p-value = 0.034). Conclusion: The surveyed members of the SSS expressed support for IOCS use in both MSTS and PSTS, with MSTS receiving significantly higher support. Higher surgical volume and personal experience with IOCS significantly increased support for IOCS in both MSTS and PSTS. The greatest perceived benefit was a reduction in allogenic transfusion, while potential systemic tumour seeding was the most common concern. Research focused on defining the actual risk of potential systemic tumour seeding, and promoting education of the existing evidence base which suggests that this risk is low, may help spur IOCS adoption in clinical practice.
